I.

我。

DISCOVER YOUR CALLING:
发现你的使命：
THE LIFE’S TASK
人生的使命

You possess an inner force that seeks to guide you toward your Life’s Task—what you are meant to accomplish in the time that you have to live. The first move toward mastery is always inward—learning who you really are and reconnecting with that innate force. Knowing it with clarity, you will find your way to the proper career path and everything else will fall into place. It is never too late to start this process.

你拥有一股内在的力量，它会引导你走向你的人生目标——你注定要在有限的生命中完成的目标。通往精通的第一步永远是向内——了解真正的自我，并与那股内在的力量重新连接。清晰地认识它，你就能找到通往正确职业道路的道路，其他一切都会水到渠成。开始这个过程永远不会太晚。

II.

二.

SUBMIT TO REALITY:
接受现实：
THE IDEAL APPRENTICESHIP
理想的学徒制

After your formal education, you enter the most critical phase in your life—a second, practical education known as The Apprenticeship. Before it is too late you must learn the lessons and follow the path established by the greatest Masters, past and present—a kind of Ideal Apprenticeship that transcends all fields. In the process you will master the necessary skills, discipline your mind, and transform yourself into an independent thinker, prepared for the creative challenges on the way to mastery.

完成正规教育后，你将进入人生中最关键的阶段——第二个实践性教育阶段，即学徒期。趁为时未晚，你必须汲取教训，追随古今最伟大的大师们所制定的道路——这是一种超越所有领域的理想学徒期。在这个过程中，你将掌握必要的技能，训练你的思维，并将自己转变为一个独立的思考者，为通往大师之路上的创造性挑战做好准备。

III.

三

ABSORB THE MASTER’S POWER:
THE MENTOR DYNAMIC

汲取大师的力量：导师动力

Life is short, and your time for learning and creativity is limited. Without any guidance, you can waste valuable years trying to gain knowledge and practice from various sources. Instead, you must follow the example set by Masters throughout the ages and find the proper mentor. Choose the mentor who best fits your needs and connects to your Life’s Task. Once you have internalized their knowledge, you must move on and never remain in their shadow. Your goal is always to surpass your mentors in mastery and brilliance.

人生苦短，你学习和创造的时间有限。如果没有指导，你可能会浪费宝贵的岁月，试图从各种渠道获取知识和实践。相反，你必须效仿历代大师的榜样，找到合适的导师。选择最符合你的需求、并与你的人生目标相契合的导师。一旦你内化了他们的知识，你就必须继续前进，永远不要活在他们的阴影下。你的目标永远是超越你的导师，在精通和才华上超越他们。

知识的炼金术

IV.

四

SEE PEOPLE AS THEY ARE:
看清人的本质：
SOCIAL INTELLIGENCE
社交智能

Often the greatest obstacle to our pursuit of mastery comes from the emotional drain we experience in dealing with the resistance and manipulations of the people around us. We misread their intentions and react in ways that cause confusion or conflict. Social intelligence is the ability to see people in the most realistic light possible. Navigating smoothly through the social environment, we have more time and energy to focus on learning and acquiring skills. Success attained without this intelligence is not true mastery, and will not last.

我们追求精通的最大障碍往往来自于应对周围人的阻力和操纵时所经历的情感耗竭。我们误读了他们的意图，并做出引起困惑或冲突的反应。社交智力是一种以最现实的眼光看待他人的能力。在社交环境中游刃有余，我们就能有更多时间和精力专注于学习和掌握技能。缺乏这种智力而获得的成功并非真正的精通，也不会持久。

AWAKEN THE DIMENSIONAL MIND:
唤醒维度思维：
THE CREATIVE-ACTIVE
创造性活跃

As you accumulate more skills and internalize the rules that govern your field, your mind will want to become more active, seeking to use this knowledge in ways that are more suited to your inclinations. Instead of feeling complacent about what you know, you must expand your knowledge to related fields, giving your mind fuel to make new associations between different ideas. In the end, you will turn against the very rules you have internalized, shaping and reforming them to suit your spirit. Such originality will bring you to the heights of power.

随着你积累更多技能，并将你所在领域的规则内化，你的思维会变得更加活跃，寻求以更符合你兴趣的方式运用这些知识。你不应满足于现有的知识，而应将知识扩展到相关领域，为你的思维注入新的活力，在不同的想法之间建立新的联系。最终，你会反抗你内化的规则，并根据你的精神去塑造和改造它们。这种独创性将引领你走向权力的巅峰。

FUSE THE INTUITIVE WITH
THE RATIONAL: MASTERY

将直觉与理性融合：精通

All of us have access to a higher form of intelligence, one that can allow us to see more of the world, to anticipate trends, to respond with speed and accuracy to any circumstance. This intelligence is cultivated by deeply immersing ourselves in a field of study and staying true to our inclinations, no matter how unconventional our approach might seem to others. This power is what our brains were designed to attain, and we will be naturally led to this type of intelligence if we follow our inclinations to their ultimate ends.

我们每个人都拥有一种更高级的智慧，它能让我们看清世界，预测趋势，并快速准确地应对任何情况。这种智慧的培养需要我们深入钻研某个领域，并忠于自己的兴趣，无论我们的方法在别人看来多么标新立异。这种力量正是我们大脑的本能，如果我们始终追随自己的兴趣，最终达到目的，我们自然就会获得这种智慧。

INTRODUCTION

介绍

THE ULTIMATE POWER

终极力量

Everyone holds his fortune in his own hands, like a sculptor the raw material he will fashion into a figure. But it’s the same with that type of artistic activity as with all others: We are merely born with the capability to do it. The skill to mold the material into what we want must be learned and attentively cultivated.

每个人都掌握着自己的命运，就像雕塑家掌握着他要塑造的人物一样。但这种艺术活动与其他所有艺术活动一样：我们生来就拥有这种能力。将材料塑造成我们想要的样子的技能必须经过学习和精心培养。

—J OHANN W OLFGANG VON G OETHE

-约翰·沃尔夫冈·冯·歌德

There exists a form of power and intelligence that represents the high point of human potential. It is the source of the greatest achievements and discoveries in history. It is an intelligence that is not taught in our schools nor analyzed by professors, but almost all of us, at some point, have had glimpses of it in our own experience. It often comes to us in a period of tension—facing a deadline, the urgent need to solve a problem, a crisis of sorts. Or it can come as the result of constant work on a project. In any event, pressed by circumstances, we feel unusually energized and focused. Our minds become completely absorbed in the task before us. This intense concentration sparks all kinds of ideas—they come to us as we fall asleep, out of nowhere, as if springing from our unconscious. At these times, other people seem less resistant to our influence; perhaps we are more attentive to them, or we appear to have a special power that inspires their respect. We might normally experience life in a passive mode, constantly reacting to this or that incident, but for these days or weeks we feel like we can determine events and make things happen.

有一种力量和智慧，代表着人类潜能的巅峰。它是历史上最伟大成就和发现的源泉。这种智慧并非学校教授，教授们也未对其进行分析，但几乎我们所有人都曾在自身经历中，或多或少地体验过它的魅力。它常常在我们面临压力时出现——例如面临最后期限、亟待解决问题、身陷危机等等。它也可能源于持续不断的项目工作。无论如何，在环境的压力下，我们都会感到异常的活力和专注。我们的思绪会完全沉浸在眼前的任务中。这种高度集中的思维会激发各种各样的灵感——它们在我们入睡时，仿佛凭空而来，仿佛从潜意识中迸发而出。在这些时候，其他人似乎更难抗拒我们的影响；或许我们会更加关注他们，又或许我们似乎拥有一种让他们敬佩的特殊力量。我们通常可能会以被动的方式体验生活，不断对这样或那样的事件做出反应，但在这些日子或几周里，我们感觉我们可以决定事件并让事情发生。

We could express this power in the following way: Most of the time we live in an interior world of dreams, desires, and obsessive thoughts. But in this period of exceptional creativity, we are impelled by the need to get something done that has a practical effect. We force ourselves to step outside our inner chamber of habitual thoughts and connect to the world, to other people, to reality. Instead of flitting here and there in a state of perpetual distraction, our minds focus and penetrate to the core of something real. At these moments, it is as if our minds—turned outward—are now flooded with light from the world around us, and suddenly exposed to new details and ideas, we become more inspired and creative.

我们可以用以下方式来表达这种力量：大多数时候，我们活在一个充满梦想、欲望和强迫性思维的内心世界。但在这个创造力非凡的时期，我们被某种需要驱使，去完成一些具有实际意义的事情。我们强迫自己走出习惯性思维的内心世界，与世界、与他人、与现实建立联系。我们的思绪不再在永恒的分心状态中四处游荡，而是集中精力，深入到某种真实事物的核心。在这些时刻，我们的思绪仿佛转向外部，被周围世界的光芒所淹没，突然接触到新的细节和想法，我们变得更有灵感，也更富有创造力。

Once the deadline has passed or the crisis is over, this feeling of power and heightened creativity generally fades away. We return to our distracted state and the sense of control is gone. If only we could manufacture this feeling, or somehow keep it alive longer…but it seems so mysterious and elusive.

一旦截止日期过去或危机结束，这种力量感和创造力的提升感通常会逐渐消退。我们又回到了心不在焉的状态，掌控感也消失了。如果我们能制造这种感觉，或者以某种方式让它持续更久就好了……但它似乎如此神秘莫测，难以捉摸。

The problem we face is that this form of power and intelligence is either ignored as a subject of study or is surrounded by all kinds of myths and misconceptions, all of which only add to the mystery. We imagine that creativity and brilliance just appear out of nowhere, the fruit of natural talent, or perhaps of a good mood, or an alignment of the stars. It would be an immense help to clear up the mystery—to name this feeling of power, to examine its roots, to define the kind of intelligence that leads to it, and to understand how it can be manufactured and maintained.

我们面临的问题是，这种力量和智慧要么被忽视，要么被各种神话和误解所包围，所有这些都只会增加它的神秘感。我们想象创造力和才华凭空而来，是天赋的结晶，也许是好心情的产物，又或是星辰的安排。解开这个谜团——命名这种力量感，探究它的根源，定义导致这种力量的智慧类型，并理解如何创造和维持这种力量——将会大有裨益。

Let us call this sensation master y—the feeling that we have a greater command of reality, other people, and ourselves. Although it might be something we experience for only a short while, for others—Masters of their field—it becomes their way of life, their way of seeing the world. (Such Masters include Leonardo da Vinci, Napoleon Bonaparte, Charles Darwin, Thomas Edison, and Martha Graham, among many others.) And at the root of this power is a simple process that leads to mastery—one that is accessible to all of us.

我们不妨将这种感觉称之为“掌控感”——一种能够更好地掌控现实、他人以及自身的感觉。虽然我们自身的体验可能只是短暂的，但对于其他人——他们各自领域的大师——来说，它已经成为他们的生活方式，他们看待世界的方式。（这些大师包括列奥纳多·达·芬奇、拿破仑·波拿巴、查尔斯·达尔文、托马斯·爱迪生和玛莎·格雷厄姆等等。）而这种力量的根源在于一个简单的过程，它通向掌控——一个我们每个人都可以做到的过程。

The process can be illustrated in the following manner: Let us say we are learning the piano, or entering a new job where we must acquire certain skills. In the beginning, we are outsiders. Our initial impressions of the piano or the work environment are based on prejudgments, and often contain an element of fear. When we first study the piano, the keyboard looks rather intimidating—we don’t understand the relationships between the keys, the chords, the pedals, and everything else that goes into creating music. In a new job situation, we are ignorant of the power relationships between people, the psychology of our boss, the rules and procedures that are considered critical for success. We are confused—the knowledge we need in both cases is over our heads.

这个过程可以用以下方式来说明：假设我们正在学习钢琴，或者进入一份必须掌握某些技能的新工作。一开始，我们是局外人。我们对钢琴或工作环境的最初印象基于先入为主的判断，并且常常包含一丝恐惧。当我们第一次学习钢琴时，键盘看起来相当令人生畏——我们不理解琴键、和弦、踏板以及创作音乐所需的所有其他元素之间的关系。在新的工作环境中，我们不了解人与人之间的权力关系、老板的心理以及被认为对成功至关重要的规则和程序。我们感到困惑——在这两种情况下我们都需要的知识都超出了我们的理解范围。

Although we might enter these situations with excitement about what we can learn or do with our new skills, we quickly realize how much hard work there is ahead of us. The great danger is that we give in to feelings of boredom, impatience, fear, and confusion. We stop observing and learning. The process comes to a halt.

尽管我们可能对能学到的东西或运用新技能所做的事情感到兴奋，但我们很快就会意识到，前方还有多少艰辛的工作等着我们。最大的危险在于，我们屈服于无聊、不耐烦、恐惧和困惑的情绪。我们停止了观察和学习，整个过程就此停滞。

If, on the other hand, we manage these emotions and allow time to take its course, something remarkable begins to take shape. As we continue to observe and follow the lead of others, we gain clarity, learning the rules and seeing how things work and fit together. If we keep practicing, we gain fluency; basic skills are mastered, allowing us to take on newer and more exciting challenges. We begin to see connections that were invisible to us before. We slowly gain confidence in our ability to solve problems or overcome weaknesses through sheer persistence.

另一方面，如果我们控制这些情绪，让时间自然流逝，一些非凡的事情就会开始成形。随着我们不断观察和效仿他人，我们会获得清晰的思路，学习其中的规则，了解事物如何运作和相互关联。如果我们不断练习，我们就会变得熟练；掌握了基本技能，就能应对更新、更刺激的挑战。我们开始发现以前看不见的联系。我们逐渐对自己解决问题或克服弱点的能力充满信心，这源于我们坚持不懈的精神。

At a certain point, we move from student to practitioner. We try out our own ideas, gaining valuable feedback in the process. We use our expanding knowledge in ways that are increasingly creative. Instead of just learning how others do things, we bring our own style and individuality into play.

在某个时刻，我们从学生变成了实践者。我们尝试自己的想法，并在过程中获得宝贵的反馈。我们运用不断增长的知识，不断提升创造力。我们不再只是学习别人的做法，而是融入自己的风格和个性。

As years go by and we remain faithful to this process, yet another leap takes place—to mastery. The keyboard is no longer something outside of us; it is internalized and becomes part of our nervous system, our fingertips. In our career, we now have a feel for the group dynamic, the current state of business. We can apply this feel to social situations, seeing deeper into other people and anticipating their reactions. We can make decisions that are rapid and highly creative. Ideas come to us. We have learned the rules so well that we can now be the ones to break or rewrite them.

随着岁月流逝，我们始终坚持这一理念，又一次飞跃——精通。键盘不再是我们身外之物；它被内化，成为我们神经系统、指尖的一部分。在职业生涯中，我们如今对团队动态和当前的商业状态有了敏锐的感知。我们可以将这种感知运用到社交场合，更深入地了解他人，并预测他们的反应。我们可以做出快速且极具创意的决策。灵感源源不断。我们已经熟知规则，如今我们可以成为打破或改写规则的人。

In the process leading to this ultimate form of power, we can identify three distinct phases or levels. The first is the Apprenticeship; the second is the Creative-Active; the third, Mastery . In the first phase, we stand on the outside of our field, learning as much as we can of the basic elements and rules. We have only a partial picture of the field and so our powers are limited. In the second phase, through much practice and immersion, we see into the inside of the machinery, how things connect with one another, and thus gain a more comprehensive understanding of the subject. With this comes a new power—the ability to experiment and creatively play with the elements involved. In the third phase, our degree of knowledge, experience, and focus is so deep that we can now see the whole picture with complete clarity. We have access to the heart of life—to human nature and natural phenomena. That is why the artwork of Masters touches us to the core; the artist has captured something of the essence of reality. That is why the brilliant scientist can uncover a new law of physics, and the inventor or entrepreneur can hit upon something no one else has imagined.

在通往这种终极力量的过程中，我们可以划分出三个不同的阶段或层次。第一阶段是学徒期；第二阶段是创造-主动期；第三阶段是精通期。在第一阶段，我们站在自身领域的边缘，尽可能多地学习基本要素和规则。我们对该领域仅有片面的了解，因此我们的力量有限。在第二阶段，通过大量的实践和沉浸，我们能够洞察机制的内部，了解事物之间的联系，从而对这一领域获得更全面的理解。随之而来的是一股新的力量——能够对所涉及的要素进行实验和创造性地运用。在第三阶段，我们的知识、经验和专注力达到了如此深厚的程度，以至于我们现在能够清晰地洞察全局。我们能够触及生命的本质——人性和自然现象。正因如此，大师的作品才能触动我们内心深处；艺术家捕捉到了现实的某些本质。这就是为什么杰出的科学家可以发现新的物理定律，而发明家或企业家可以发现别人无法想象的东西。

We can call this power intuition, but intuition is nothing more than a sudden and immediate seizing of what is real, without the need for words or formulas. The words and formulas may come later, but this flash of intuition is what ultimately brings us closer to reality, as our minds suddenly become illuminated by some particle of truth previously hidden to us and to others.

我们可以将这种力量称为直觉，但直觉无非是对真实之物的突然而直接的把握，无需借助任何文字或公式。文字和公式或许会稍后出现，但这种直觉的闪现最终会让我们更接近现实，因为我们的心灵会突然被一些此前隐藏于我们和他人之间的真理之光所照亮。

An animal has the capacity to learn, but it largely relies on its instincts to connect to its surroundings and save itself from danger. Through instinct, it can act quickly and effectively. The human relies instead on thinking and rationality to understand its environment. But such thinking can be slow, and in its slowness can become ineffective. So much of our obsessive, internal thought process tends to disconnect us from the world. Intuitive powers at the mastery level are a mix of the instinctive and the rational, the conscious and the unconscious, the human and the animal. It is our way of making sudden and powerful connections to the environment, to feeling or thinking inside things. As children we had some of this intuitive power and spontaneity, but it is generally drummed out of us by all of the information that overloads our minds over time. Masters return to this childlike state, their works displaying degrees of spontaneity and access to the unconscious, but at a much higher level than the child.

动物具有学习能力，但它们很大程度上依赖于本能来与周围环境建立联系，并自救于危难。凭借本能，它们能够迅速有效地采取行动。而人类则依赖于思考和理性来理解周围环境。但这种思考可能很慢，而这种慢也可能变得无效。我们许多强迫性的内在思维过程往往会使我们与世界脱节。精通层次的直觉力是本能与理性、意识与潜意识、人性与动物性的混合体。这是我们与环境、与事物内在感受或思考建立突然而强大的联系的方式。孩童时期，我们也拥有一些这种直觉力和自发性，但随着时间的推移，我们大脑中超负荷的信息通常会将其驱散。大师们回归到这种童真状态，他们的作品展现出不同程度的自发性和对潜意识的理解，但其水平远高于孩童时期。

If we move through the process to this endpoint, we activate the intuitive power latent in every human brain, one that we may have briefly experienced when we worked so deeply on a single problem or project. In fact, often in life we have glimpses of this power—for instance, when we have an inkling of what will come next in a particular situation, or when the perfect answer to a problem comes to us out of nowhere. But these moments are ephemeral and not based on enough experience to make them repeatable. When we reach mastery, this intuition is a power at our command, the fruit of working through the lengthier process. And because the world prizes creativity and this ability to uncover new aspects of reality, it brings us tremendous practical power as well.

如果我们完成这个过程并到达终点，我们就会激活每个人大脑中潜藏的直觉力量，这种力量或许在我们深入研究某个问题或项目时短暂地体验过。事实上，在生活中，我们常常能瞥见这种力量——例如，当我们预感到特定情况下接下来会发生什么，或者当一个问题的完美答案突然出现在我们面前时。但这些时刻转瞬即逝，并且缺乏足够的经验来使其可重复。当我们达到精通时，这种直觉就成为一种我们可以掌控的力量，是经过更长时间努力的成果。而且，由于世界重视创造力以及这种发现现实新面向的能力，它也为我们带来了巨大的实践力量。

Think of mastery in this way: Throughout history, men and women have felt trapped by the limitations of their consciousness, by their lack of contact with reality and the power to affect the world around them. They have sought all kinds of shortcuts to this expanded consciousness and sense of control, in the form of magic rituals, trances, incantations, and drugs. They have devoted their lives to alchemy, in search of the philosopher’s stone—the elusive substance that transformed all matter into gold.

不妨这样思考一下精通：纵观历史，人们总是感到自己被意识的局限所困，被缺乏与现实的接触以及影响周遭世界的力量所困。他们寻求各种捷径，以提升意识和掌控感，例如魔法仪式、催眠、咒语和药物。他们毕生致力于炼金术，探寻点金石——一种能够将所有物质转化为黄金的神秘物质。

This hunger for the magical shortcut has survived to our day in the form of simple formulas for success, ancient secrets finally revealed in which a mere change of attitude will attract the right energy. There is a grain of truth and practicality in all of these efforts—for instance, the emphasis in magic on deep focus. But in the end all of this searching is centered on something that doesn’t exist—the effortless path to practical power, the quick and easy solution, the El Dorado of the mind.

这种对神奇捷径的渴望，以简单的成功秘诀的形式流传至今，古老的秘密最终得以揭示，只需改变态度就能吸引正确的能量。所有这些努力都有一定的道理和实用性——例如，魔法强调深度专注。但最终，所有这些探索都集中在一个并不存在的东西上——通往实际力量的毫不费力的途径，快速简便的解决方案，心灵的黄金国。

At the same time that so many people lose themselves in these endless fantasies, they ignore the one real power that they actually possess. And unlike magic or simplistic formulas, we can see the material effects of this power in history—the great discoveries and inventions, the magnificent buildings and works of art, the technological prowess we possess, all works of the masterful mind. This power brings to those who possess it the kind of connection to reality and the ability to alter the world that the mystics and magicians of the past could only dream of.

许多人沉溺于这些无尽的幻想之中，却忽视了他们真正拥有的那股力量。与魔法或简单的公式不同，我们可以在历史中看到这种力量的物质影响——伟大的发现和发明，宏伟的建筑和艺术作品，我们拥有的科技实力，所有这些成就都出自大师的智慧。这种力量赋予拥有它的人与现实的联系，以及改变世界的能力，而这在以往的神秘主义者和魔法师看来只能是梦想。

Over the centuries, people have placed a wall around such mastery. They have called it genius and have thought of it as inaccessible. They have seen it as the product of privilege, inborn talent, or just the right alignment of the stars. They have made it seem as if it were as elusive as magic. But that wall is imaginary. This is the real secret: the brain that we possess is the work of six million years of development, and more than anything else, this evolution of the brain was designed to lead us to mastery, the latent power within us all.

几个世纪以来，人们在这种精湛技艺周围筑起了一道高墙。他们称之为天才，认为它遥不可及。他们把它看作特权、天赋，或者仅仅是星辰的精准排列的产物。他们把它描绘得像魔法一样难以捉摸。但这道墙只是虚构的。真正的秘密在于：我们拥有的大脑是六百万年进化的成果，而最重要的是，大脑的进化旨在引领我们走向精湛技艺，走向我们每个人内在的潜在力量。

THE EVOLUTION OF MASTERY

精通的演变

For three million years we were hunter-gatherers, and it was through the evolutionary pressures of that way of life that a brain so adaptable and creative eventually emerged. Today we stand with the brains of hunter-gatherers in our heads.

三百万年来，我们一直过着狩猎采集的生活。正是在这种生活方式的进化压力下，我们最终诞生了如此适应性强、富有创造力的大脑。如今，我们依然拥有狩猎采集者的大脑。

—R ICHARD L EAKEY

—理查德·利基

It is hard for us to imagine now, but our earliest human ancestors who ventured out onto the grasslands of East Africa some six million years ago were remarkably weak and vulnerable creatures. They stood less than five feet tall. They walked upright and could run on their two legs, but nowhere near as fast as the swift predators on four legs that pursued them. They were skinny—their arms could not provide much defense. They had no claws or fangs or poison to resort to if under attack. To gather fruits, nuts, and insects, or to scavenge dead meat, they had to move out into the open savanna where they became easy prey to leopards or packs of hyenas. So weak and small in number, they might have easily become extinct.

我们现在很难想象，但大约六百万年前，冒险踏上东非草原的人类祖先，是极其孱弱脆弱的生物。他们身高不足五英尺（约1.5米）。他们直立行走，也能用两条腿奔跑，但速度远不及那些追赶他们的四足迅捷捕食者。他们骨瘦如柴——手臂无法提供多少防御。受到攻击时，他们没有爪子、尖牙或毒液可用。为了采集水果、坚果和昆虫，或者吃死肉，他们不得不迁徙到开阔的大草原，在那里他们很容易成为豹子或鬣狗群的猎物。由于体型如此孱弱，数量如此之少，他们可能很容易就灭绝了。

And yet within the space of a few million years (remarkably short on the time scale of evolution), these rather physically unimpressive ancestors of ours transformed themselves into the most formidable hunters on the planet. What could possibly account for such a miraculous turnaround? Some have speculated that it was their standing on two legs, which freed up the hands to make tools with their opposable thumbs and precision grip. But such physical explanations miss the point. Our dominance, our mastery does not stem from our hands but from our brains, from our fashioning the mind into the most powerful instrument known in nature—far more powerful than any claw. And at the root of this mental transformation are two simple biological traits—the visual and the social —that primitive humans leveraged into power.

然而，在短短几百万年的时间里（在进化的时间尺度上，这真是太短了），我们这些体格上并不起眼的祖先，却一跃成为地球上最强大的猎手。如此神奇的转变究竟是如何发生的呢？有人推测，是因为他们能够直立行走，解放双手，用对生拇指精准抓握，制作工具。但这种生理上的解释错失了要点。我们的统治地位和掌控力并非源于双手，而是源于我们的大脑，源于我们将心智塑造成自然界中最强大的工具——远胜于任何爪子。而这种心智转变的根源，是两个简单的生物学特征——视觉和社会性——原始人类正是利用它们来获取力量。

Our earliest ancestors were descended from primates who thrived for millions of years in a treetop environment, and who in the process had evolved one of the most remarkable visual systems in nature. To move quickly and efficiently in such a world, they developed extremely sophisticated eye and muscle coordination. Their eyes slowly evolved into a full-frontal position on the face, giving them binocular, stereoscopic vision. This system provides the brain a highly accurate three-dimensional and detailed perspective, but is rather narrow. Animals that possess such vision—as opposed to eyes on the side or half side—are generally efficient predators like owls or cats. They use this powerful sight to home in on prey in the distance. Tree-living primates evolved this vision for a different purpose—to navigate branches, and to spot fruits, berries, and insects with greater effectiveness. They also evolved elaborate color vision.

我们最早的祖先起源于在树梢环境中繁衍生息了数百万年的灵长类动物，这些灵长类动物在此过程中进化出了自然界中最卓越的视觉系统之一。为了在这样的环境中快速高效地移动，它们进化出了极其复杂的眼部和肌肉协调能力。它们的眼睛逐渐进化到位于面部正面的位置，赋予了它们双眼立体视觉。这套系统为大脑提供了高度精确的三维立体视角，但视野范围相当狭窄。拥有这种视觉（而非侧眼或半侧眼）的动物通常是高效的捕食者，例如猫头鹰或猫。它们利用这种强大的视觉来追踪远处的猎物。树栖灵长类动物进化出这种视觉是为了不同的目的——导航树枝，以及更有效地识别水果、浆果和昆虫。它们还进化出了精细的色觉。

When our earliest human ancestors left the trees and moved to the open grasslands of the savanna, they adopted an upright stance. Possessing already this powerful visual system, they could see far into the distance (giraffes and elephants might stand taller, but their eyes are on the sides, giving them instead panoramic vision). This allowed them to spot dangerous predators far away on the horizon and detect their movements even in twilight. Given a few seconds or minutes, they could plot a safe retreat. At the same time, if they focused on what was nearest at hand, they could identify all kinds of important details in their environment—footprints and signs of passing predators, or the colors and shapes of rocks that they could pick up and perhaps use as tools.

当我们最早的人类祖先离开树木，迁徙到开阔的热带草原时，他们采取了直立的姿势。凭借着这套强大的视觉系统，他们能够看清远方（长颈鹿和大象虽然身高更高，但它们的眼睛长在两侧，因此视野开阔）。这使得它们能够发现远处地平线上的危险捕食者，即使在暮色中也能察觉到它们的动静。只要有几秒钟或几分钟的时间，它们就能规划出安全的撤退路线。同时，如果它们专注于眼前的事物，就能识别出周围环境中各种重要的细节——足迹和掠食者的踪迹，或者它们可以捡起并用作工具的岩石的颜色和形状。

In the treetops, this powerful vision was built for speed—seeing and reacting quickly. On the open grassland, it was the opposite. Safety and finding food relied upon slow, patient observation of the environment, on the ability to pick out details and focus on what they might mean. Our ancestors’ survival depended on the intensity of their attention. The longer and harder they looked, the more they could distinguish between an opportunity and a danger. If they simply scanned the horizon quickly they could see a lot more, but this would overload the mind with information—too many details for such sharp vision. The human visual system is not built for scanning, as a cow’s is, but for depth of focus.

在树梢上，这种强大的视觉是为了速度而生——快速观察和反应。在开阔的草原上，情况则相反。安全和寻找食物依赖于缓慢而耐心地观察环境，依赖于识别细节并专注于其含义的能力。我们祖先的生存依赖于他们注意力的强度。他们观察的时间越长、越用心，就越能区分机遇和危险。如果他们只是快速扫视地平线，他们可以看到更多，但这会使大脑信息超载——对于如此敏锐的视觉来说，细节太多了。人类的视觉系统并非像牛那样为扫描而生，而是为了获得景深。

Animals are locked in a perpetual present. They can learn from recent events, but they are easily distracted by what is in front of their eyes. Slowly, over a great period of time, our ancestors overcame this basic animal weakness. By looking long enough at any object and refusing to be distracted—even for a few seconds—they could momentarily detach themselves from their immediate surroundings. In this way they could notice patterns, make generalizations, and think ahead. They had the mental distance to think and reflect, even on the smallest scale.

动物被永恒的当下所束缚。它们能够从近期事件中学习，但很容易被眼前的事物分散注意力。经过漫长的时间，我们的祖先逐渐克服了动物的这一基本弱点。通过长时间注视任何物体，并拒绝分心——哪怕只有几秒钟——它们能够暂时将自己从周围环境中抽离出来。通过这种方式，它们能够发现规律，进行概括，并进行前瞻性思考。它们拥有足够的精神距离去思考和反思，即使是在最细微的尺度上。

These early humans evolved the ability to detach and think as their primary advantage in the struggle to avoid predators and find food. It connected them to a reality other animals could not access. Thinking on this level was the single greatest turning point in all of evolution—the emergence of the conscious, reasoning mind.

这些早期人类进化出了超然思考的能力，这是他们在躲避捕食者和寻找食物的斗争中的主要优势。这种能力将他们与其他动物无法触及的现实联系起来。这种层面的思考是整个进化史上最重要的转折点——意识和推理能力的出现。

The second biological advantage is subtler, but equally powerful in its implications. All primates are essentially social creatures, but because of their intense vulnerability in open areas, our earliest ancestors had a much greater need for group cohesion. They depended on the group for vigilant observation of predators and the gathering of food. In general, these early hominids had many more social interactions than other primates. Over the course of hundreds of thousands of years, this social intelligence became increasingly sophisticated, allowing these ancestors to cooperate with one another on a high level. And as with our understanding of the natural environment, this intelligence depended on deep attention and focus. Misreading the social signs in a tight-knit group could prove highly dangerous.

第二个生物学优势更为微妙，但其影响同样巨大。所有灵长类动物本质上都是社会性生物，但由于它们在开阔地带极度脆弱，我们最早的祖先对群体凝聚力的需求更为强烈。他们依靠群体来警惕地观察捕食者并采集食物。总体而言，这些早期类人科动物比其他灵长类动物拥有更多的社会互动。在数十万年的时间里，这种社会智力日益复杂，使这些祖先能够在更高水平上相互合作。与我们对自然环境的理解一样，这种智力依赖于高度的关注和专注。误读紧密群体中的社会信号可能会非常危险。

Through the elaboration of these two traits—the visual and the social —our primitive ancestors were able to invent and develop the complex skill of hunting some two to three million years ago. Slowly, they became more creative, refining this complex skill into an art. They became seasonal hunters and spread throughout the Euro-Asian landmass, managing to adapt themselves to all kinds of climates. And in the process of this rapid evolution, their brains grew to virtually modern human size, some 200,000 years ago.

通过对视觉和社会性这两大特征的精心演绎，我们的原始祖先得以在大约两三百万年前发明并发展出复杂的狩猎技能。慢慢地，他们变得更加富有创造力，将这项复杂的技能精炼成一门艺术。他们成为季节性狩猎者，遍布欧亚大陆，设法适应各种气候条件。在快速进化的过程中，他们的大脑在大约20万年前发展到几乎与现代人类相当的大小。

In the 1990s a group of Italian neuroscientists discovered something that could help explain this increasing hunting prowess of our primitive ancestors, and in turn something about mastery as it exists today. In studying the brains of monkeys, they found that particular motor-command neurons will not only fire when they execute a very specific action—such as pulling a lever to get a peanut or taking hold of a banana—but that these neurons will also fire when monkeys observe another performing the same actions. These were soon dubbed mirror neurons . This neuronal firing meant that these primates would experience a similar sensation in both doing and observing the same deed, allowing them to put themselves in the place of another and perceive its movements as if they were doing them. It would account for the ability of many primates to imitate others, and for the pronounced abilities of chimpanzees to anticipate the plans and actions of a rival. Such neurons, it is speculated, evolved because of the social nature of primate life.

20世纪90年代，一群意大利神经科学家发现了一些新发现，或许可以解释我们原始祖先日益精进的狩猎能力，进而解释当今的掌控力。在研究猴子的大脑时，他们发现，特定的运动指令神经元不仅会在猴子执行特定动作时（例如拉动杠杆取花生或抓起香蕉）激活，而且当猴子观察其他猴子执行相同动作时，这些神经元也会激活。这些神经元很快被称为镜像神经元。这种神经元激活意味着这些灵长类动物在执行和观察同一件事时都会产生类似的感觉，使它们能够设身处地地为他人着想，感知对方的动作，就像自己也在做这些事一样。这或许可以解释许多灵长类动物具有模仿其他动物的能力，以及黑猩猩能够预测对手计划和行动的显著能力。据推测，这类神经元的进化源于灵长类动物的社会性。

Recent experiments have demonstrated the existence of such neurons in humans, but on a much higher level of sophistication. A monkey or primate can see an action from the point of view of the performer and imagine its intentions, but we can take this further. Without any visual cues or any action on the part of others, we can place ourselves inside their minds and imagine what they might be thinking.

最近的实验已经证明，人类也存在类似的神经元，但其复杂程度要高得多。猴子或灵长类动物可以从表演者的视角观察动作，并想象其意图，而我们还可以更进一步。无需任何视觉提示或他人的任何动作，我们就能设身处地地理解他们的内心，想象他们可能在想什么。

For our ancestors, the elaboration of mirror neurons would allow them to read each other’s desires from the subtlest of signs and thus elevate their social skills. It would also serve as a critical component in toolmaking—one could learn to fashion a tool by imitating the actions of an expert. But perhaps most important of all, it would give them the ability to think inside everything around them. After years of studying particular animals, they could identify with and think like them, anticipating behavioral patterns and heightening their ability to track and kill prey. This thinking inside could be applied to the inorganic as well. In fashioning a stone tool, expert toolmakers would feel as one with their instruments. The stone or wood they cut with became an extension of their hand. They could feel it as if it were their own flesh, permitting much greater control of the tools themselves, both in making and in using them.

对于我们的祖先来说，镜像神经元的精细演绎使他们能够从最细微的信号中解读彼此的欲望，从而提升社交技能。它也是工具制造的关键要素——人们可以通过模仿专家的动作来学习制作工具。但或许最重要的是，它赋予他们内在思考周围一切的能力。经过多年研究特定动物，他们能够与它们产生共鸣，像它们一样思考，预测它们的行为模式，并提升追踪和捕杀猎物的能力。这种内在思考也可以应用于无机物。在制作石器时，专业的工具制造者会感觉与他们的器具融为一体。他们用来切割的石头或木头成为了他们手的延伸。他们能够感受到它们如同自己的血肉，从而能够更好地控制工具本身，无论是在制造还是使用过程中。

This power of the mind could be unleashed only after years of experience. Having mastered a particular skill—tracking prey, fashioning a tool—it was now automatic, and so while practicing the skill the mind no longer had to focus on the specific actions involved but instead could concentrate on something higher—what the prey might be thinking, how the tool could be felt as part of the hand. This thinking inside would be a preverbal version of third-level intelligence—the primitive equivalent of Leonardo da Vinci’s intuitive feel for anatomy and landscape or Michael Faraday’s for electromagnetism. Mastery at this level meant our ancestors could make decisions rapidly and effectively, having gained a complete understanding of their environment and their prey. If this power had not evolved, the minds of our ancestors would have become easily overwhelmed by the mass of information they had to process for a successful hunt. They had developed this intuitive power hundreds of thousands of years before the invention of language, and that is why when we experience this intelligence it seems like something preverbal, a power that transcends our ability to put it into words.

这种心灵力量只有经过多年的经验积累才能释放。掌握了一项特定技能——追踪猎物、制作工具——之后，它就变成了自动化技能。因此，在练习这项技能时，心灵不再需要专注于具体的行动，而是可以专注于更高层次的事情——猎物可能在想什么，工具作为手的一部分是如何被感知的。这种内在的思考能力是第三级智力的前语言版本——相当于列奥纳多·达·芬奇对解剖学和景观的直觉，或者迈克尔·法拉第对电磁学的直觉。掌握这一层次的技能意味着我们的祖先能够快速有效地做出决策，因为他们对周围环境和猎物有了全面的了解。如果没有进化出这种能力，我们祖先的大脑很容易被为了成功狩猎而必须处理的海量信息所淹没。早在语言发明之前数十万年，他们就已经发展出了这种直觉能力，这就是为什么当我们体验到这种智慧时，它看起来就像是某种前语言的东西，一种超越我们用语言表达的能力的力量。

Understand: This long stretch of time played a critical, elemental role in our mental development. It fundamentally altered our relationship to time. For animals, time is their great enemy. If they are potential prey, wandering too long in a space can spell instant death. If they are predators, waiting too long will only mean the escape of their prey. Time for them also represents physical decay. To a remarkable extent, our hunting ancestors reversed this process. The longer they spent observing something, the deeper their understanding and connection to reality. With experience, their hunting skills would progress. With continued practice, their ability to make effective tools would improve. The body could decay but the mind would continue to learn and adapt. Using time for such effect is the essential ingredient of mastery.

理解：这段漫长的时间在我们的心智发展中扮演着至关重要的基本角色。它从根本上改变了我们与时间的关系。对动物而言，时间是它们最大的敌人。如果它们是潜在的猎物，在空间中游荡太久就可能立即死亡。如果它们是捕食者，等待太久只意味着猎物逃脱。对它们来说，时间也代表着身体的衰退。我们的狩猎祖先在很大程度上逆转了这一过程。他们观察事物的时间越长，他们对事物的理解和与现实的联系就越深刻。随着经验的积累，他们的狩猎技能会不断进步。随着不断练习，他们制造有效工具的能力也会不断提高。身体可能会衰退，但心智会继续学习和适应。利用时间达到这种效果是精通的必要因素。

In fact, we can say that this revolutionary relationship to time fundamentally altered the human mind itself and gave it a particular quality or grain . When we take our time and focus in depth, when we trust that going through a process of months or years will bring us mastery, we work with the grain of this marvelous instrument that developed over so many millions of years. We infallibly move to higher and higher levels of intelligence. We see more deeply and realistically. We practice and make things with skill. We learn to think for ourselves. We become capable of handling complex situations without being overwhelmed. In following this path we become Homo magister , man or woman the Master.

事实上，我们可以说，这种与时间的革命性关系从根本上改变了人类思维本身，并赋予其独特的品质或脉络。当我们花时间深入专注，当我们相信经历数月或数年的过程就能精通时，我们便与这台历经数百万年发展而来的神奇工具的脉络相契合。我们必然会迈向越来越高的智慧水平。我们会看得更深刻、更现实。我们会运用技巧进行实践和创造。我们学会独立思考。我们变得能够应对复杂的局面而不会不知所措。沿着这条道路前行，我们便成为了“大师”（Homo magister），无论男女，皆为大师。

To the extent that we believe we can skip steps, avoid the process, magically gain power through political connections or easy formulas, or depend on our natural talents, we move against this grain and reverse our natural powers. We become slaves to time—as it passes, we grow weaker, less capable, trapped in some dead-end career. We become captive to the opinions and fears of others. Rather than the mind connecting us to reality, we become disconnected and locked in a narrow chamber of thought. The human that depended on focused attention for its survival now becomes the distracted scanning animal, unable to think in depth, yet unable to depend on instincts.

如果我们相信自己可以跳过步骤、避开过程，通过政治关系或简单的公式神奇地获得权力，或者依靠天赋，那么我们就会逆势而行，逆转我们与生俱来的力量。我们成了时间的奴隶——随着时间的流逝，我们变得越来越虚弱，能力越来越弱，最终被困在某个没有前途的职业中。我们被他人的观点和恐惧所俘虏。我们不再依靠连接现实的思维，而是变得与现实脱节，被困在狭隘的思维空间里。曾经依赖专注力生存的人类，如今变成了心不在焉、四处扫视的动物，无法深入思考，也无法依靠本能。

It is the height of stupidity to believe that in the course of your short life, your few decades of consciousness, you can somehow rewire the configurations of your brain through technology and wishful thinking, overcoming the effect of six million years of development. To go against the grain might bring temporary distraction, but time will mercilessly expose your weakness and impatience.

相信在短暂的人生中，在短短几十年的意识历程中，你能够通过科技和一厢情愿的想法重塑大脑结构，从而克服六百万年发展的影响，这简直是极其愚蠢。逆势而行或许能带来暂时的专注，但时间会无情地暴露你的弱点和急躁。

The great salvation for all of us is that we have inherited an instrument that is remarkably plastic. Our hunter-gatherer ancestors, over the course of time, managed to craft the brain into its present shape by creating a culture that could learn, change, and adapt to circumstances, that wasn’t a prisoner to the incredibly slow march of natural evolution. As modern individuals, our brains have the same power, the same plasticity. At any moment we can choose to shift our relationship to time and work with the grain, knowing of its existence and power. With the element of time working for us, we can reverse the bad habits and passivity, and move up the ladder of intelligence.

对我们所有人来说，最大的救赎在于我们继承了一种极具可塑性的工具。我们狩猎采集的祖先，随着时间的推移，通过创造一种能够学习、改变和适应环境的文化，成功地将大脑塑造成如今的形态，而这种文化并非受制于极其缓慢的自然进化进程。作为现代人，我们的大脑拥有同样的力量和可塑性。在任何时候，我们都可以选择转变我们与时间的关系，顺应自然，了解时间的存在和力量。借助时间的力量，我们可以扭转不良习惯和被动性，提升智力。

Think of this shift as a return to your radical, deep past as a human, connecting to and maintaining a magnificent continuity with your hunter-gatherer ancestors in a modern form. The environment we operate in may be different, but the brain is essentially the same, and its power to learn, adapt, and master time is universal.

不妨将这种转变视为回归人类激进而深邃的过去，以现代形式与狩猎采集祖先保持着伟大的延续性。我们生存的环境或许不同，但大脑的本质是相同的，它学习、适应和掌控时间的能力是共通的。

KEYS TO MASTERY

掌握诀窍

A man should learn to detect and watch that gleam of light which flashes across his mind from within, more than the luster of the firmament of bards and sages. Yet he dismisses without notice his thought, because it is his. In every work of genius we recognize our own rejected thoughts; they come back to us with a certain alienated majesty.

一个人应该学会去发现和观察那从内心闪过心灵的光芒，而不是吟游诗人和圣贤的苍穹之光。然而，他却不经意地抛弃了自己的想法，因为那是他自己的。在每一部天才的作品中，我们都能看到自己曾经抛弃的想法；它们带着某种疏离的庄严回到我们身边。

—R ALPH W ALDO E MERSON

—拉尔夫·沃尔多·爱默生

If all of us are born with an essentially similar brain, with more or less the same configuration and potential for mastery, why is it then that in history only a limited number of people seem to truly excel and realize this potential power? Certainly, in a practical sense, this is the most important question for us to answer.

如果我们每个人生来都拥有本质上相似的大脑，拥有或多或少相同的结构和掌握的潜力，那么为什么历史上似乎只有少数人真正出类拔萃，发挥出这种潜在的力量呢？当然，从实际意义上讲，这是我们需要回答的最重要的问题。

The common explanations for a Mozart or a Leonardo da Vinci revolve around natural talent and brilliance. How else to account for their uncanny achievements except in terms of something they were born with? But thousands upon thousands of children display exceptional skill and talent in some field, yet relatively few of them ever amount to anything, whereas those who are less brilliant in their youth can often attain much more. Natural talent or a high IQ cannot explain future achievement.

莫扎特或达芬奇的成名之作，通常都与天赋和才华有关。除了与生俱来的东西，还有什么其他解释能解释他们非凡的成就呢？然而，成千上万的孩子在某个领域展现出非凡的技能和天赋，但最终成就斐然的却寥寥无几，而那些年轻时才华平平的人往往能取得更大的成就。天赋或高智商无法解释他们未来的成就。

As a classic example, compare the lives of Sir Francis Galton and his older cousin, Charles Darwin. By all accounts, Galton was a super-genius with an exceptionally high IQ, quite a bit higher than Darwin’s (these are estimates done by experts years after the invention of the measurement). Galton was a boy wonder who went on to have an illustrious scientific career, but he never quite mastered any of the fields he went into. He was notoriously restless, as is often the case with child prodigies.

举个经典的例子，比较一下弗朗西斯·高尔顿爵士和他的表兄查尔斯·达尔文的生活。据说，高尔顿是一位超级天才，拥有极高的智商，比达尔文高出不少（这些是智商测量发明多年后专家们的估算）。高尔顿是一位神童，后来成就了辉煌的科学生涯，但他从未真正精通他所涉足的任何领域。他以好动而著称，神童们通常都是如此。

Darwin, by contrast, is rightly celebrated as the superior scientist, one of the few who has forever changed our view of life. As Darwin himself admitted, he was “a very ordinary boy, rather below the common standard in intellect…. I have no great quickness of apprehension…. My power to follow a long and purely abstract train of thought is very limited.” Darwin, however, must have possessed something that Galton lacked.

相比之下，达尔文被誉为杰出的科学家，是少数彻底改变我们生命观的科学家之一，实至名归。正如达尔文自己承认的那样，他“是一个非常普通的孩子，智力远低于常人……我的理解力并不敏锐……我理解长篇大论、纯粹抽象的思路的能力非常有限。” 然而，达尔文一定拥有高尔顿所缺乏的某种特质。

In many ways, a look at the early life of Darwin himself can supply an answer to this mystery. As a child Darwin had one overriding passion—collecting biological specimens. His father, a doctor, wanted him to follow in his footsteps and study medicine, enrolling him at the University of Edinburgh. Darwin did not take to this subject and was a mediocre student. His father, despairing that his son would ever amount to anything, chose for him a career in the church. As Darwin was preparing for this, a former professor of his told him that the HMS Beagle was to leave port soon to sail around the world, and that it needed a ship’s biologist to accompany the crew in order to collect specimens that could be sent back to England. Despite his father’s protests, Darwin took the job. Something in him was drawn to the voyage.

从很多方面来看，回顾达尔文本人早年的生活都能解答这个谜团。孩提时代，达尔文最大的爱好就是收集生物标本。他的父亲是一名医生，希望他能追随自己的脚步学习医学，于是就送他去了爱丁堡大学。达尔文对医学不感兴趣，成绩平平。他的父亲担心儿子将来会一事无成，便为他选择了教会职业。就在达尔文为此做准备的时候，他的一位前教授告诉他，贝格尔号即将启航环游世界，需要一位船上的生物学家陪同船员收集标本，然后送回英国。尽管父亲反对，达尔文还是接受了这份工作。他内心深处对这次航行有着强烈的吸引力。

Suddenly, his passion for collecting found its perfect outlet. In South America he could collect the most astounding array of specimens, as well as fossils and bones. He could connect his interest in the variety of life on the planet with something larger—major questions about the origins of species. He poured all of his energy into this enterprise, accumulating so many specimens that a theory began to take shape in his mind. After five years at sea, he returned to England and devoted the rest of his life to the single task of elaborating his theory of evolution. In the process he had to deal with a tremendous amount of drudgery—for instance, eight years exclusively studying barnacles to establish his credentials as a biologist. He had to develop highly refined political and social skills to handle all the prejudice against such a theory in Victorian England. And what sustained him throughout this lengthy process was his intense love of and connection to the subject.

突然间，他对收藏的热情找到了完美的出口。在南美洲，他收集到了数量惊人的标本，以及化石和骨骼。他可以将自己对地球生命多样性的兴趣与更宏大的目标——物种起源的重大问题——联系起来。他将全部精力投入到这项事业中，收集了如此之多的标本，以至于一个理论开始在他脑海中成形。在海上航行五年后，他回到英国，将余生奉献给了阐述进化论这一单一任务。在此过程中，他不得不应对大量的苦差事——例如，他花了八年时间专注于研究藤壶，以确立自己作为生物学家的声誉。为了应对维多利亚时代英国对这一理论的所有偏见，他必须培养高度精湛的政治和社会技能。而支撑他度过这一漫长过程的，正是他对这一主题的热爱和执着。

The basic elements of this story are repeated in the lives of all of the great Masters in history: a youthful passion or predilection, a chance encounter that allows them to discover how to apply it, an apprenticeship in which they come alive with energy and focus. They excel by their ability to practice harder and move faster through the process, all of this stemming from the intensity of their desire to learn and from the deep connection they feel to their field of study. And at the core of this intensity of effort is in fact a quality that is genetic and inborn—not talent or brilliance, which is something that must be developed, but rather a deep and powerful inclination toward a particular subject.

这个故事的基本元素在历史上所有伟大大师的人生中反复出现：青春的热情或偏爱，一次让他们发现如何将其付诸实践的偶然相遇，以及一段让他们充满活力和专注的学徒期。他们之所以出类拔萃，是因为他们能够更加刻苦地练习，并在过程中进步更快，所有这些都源于他们强烈的学习欲望以及他们对所学领域的深厚情感。而这种刻苦努力的核心，实际上是一种与生俱来的基因特质——并非天赋或才华，这些都需要后天培养，而是对某一特定学科深厚而强烈的热爱。

This inclination is a reflection of a person’s uniqueness. This uniqueness is not something merely poetic or philosophical—it is a scientific fact that genetically, every one of us is unique; our exact genetic makeup has never happened before and will never be repeated. This uniqueness is revealed to us through the preferences we innately feel for particular activities or subjects of study. Such inclinations can be toward music or mathematics, certain sports or games, solving puzzle-like problems, tinkering and building, or playing with words.

这种倾向反映了一个人的独特性。这种独特性并非仅仅是诗意或哲学层面的事物——它是一个科学事实，即从基因角度来看，我们每个人都是独一无二的；我们确切的基因构成从未发生过，也永远不会被复制。这种独特性通过我们天生对特定活动或学习科目的偏好展现出来。这些偏好可以是音乐或数学、某些运动或游戏、解决类似谜题的问题、修修补补和建造，或者玩文字游戏。

With those who stand out by their later mastery, they experience this inclination more deeply and clearly than others. They experience it as an inner calling. It tends to dominate their thoughts and dreams. They find their way, by accident or sheer effort, to a career path in which this inclination can flourish. This intense connection and desire allows them to withstand the pain of the process—the self-doubts, the tedious hours of practice and study, the inevitable setbacks, the endless barbs from the envious. They develop a resiliency and confidence that others lack.

那些在后天精进中脱颖而出的人，比其他人更深刻、更清晰地体会到这种倾向。他们将其视为一种内在的召唤，并倾向于主宰他们的思想和梦想。他们或偶然或纯粹的努力，找到了一条能够充分发挥这种倾向的职业道路。这种强烈的联系和渴望使他们能够承受过程中的痛苦——自我怀疑、冗长的练习和学习时间、不可避免的挫折，以及嫉妒者无休止的嘲讽。他们培养出了一种其他人所缺乏的韧性和自信。

In our culture we tend to equate thinking and intellectual powers with success and achievement. In many ways, however, it is an emotional quality that separates those who master a field from the many who simply work at a job. Our levels of desire, patience, persistence, and confidence end up playing a much larger role in success than sheer reasoning powers. Feeling motivated and energized, we can overcome almost anything. Feeling bored and restless, our minds shut off and we become increasingly passive.

在我们的文化中，我们倾向于将思维和智力与成功和成就联系起来。然而，在很多方面，真正的情感特质才是区分精通某一领域之人与仅仅从事一份工作之人的根本。我们的渴望、耐心、毅力和自信最终在成功中发挥着比纯粹的推理能力更大的作用。当我们感到动力十足、充满活力时，我们几乎可以克服一切。而当我们感到无聊和焦躁不安时，我们的思维就会封闭，变得越来越被动。

In the past, only elites or those with an almost superhuman amount of energy and drive could pursue a career of their choice and master it. A man was born into the military, or groomed for the government, chosen among those of the right class. If he happened to display a talent and desire for such work it was mostly a coincidence. Millions of people who were not part of the right social class, gender, and ethnic group were rigidly excluded from the possibility of pursuing their calling. Even if people wanted to follow their inclinations, access to the information and knowledge pertaining to that particular field was controlled by elites. That is why there are relatively few Masters in the past and why they stand out so much.

在过去，只有精英或拥有近乎超人般精力和动力的人才能追求并精通自己选择的职业。一个人出生在军人家庭，或被培养为政府官员，从合适的阶层中选拔而出。如果他恰好展现出对这类工作的天赋和渴望，那大多是巧合。数百万不属于合适社会阶层、性别和种族的人被严格排除在追求自己职业的可能性之外。即使人们想追随自己的意愿，获取特定领域相关信息和知识的渠道也掌握在精英阶层手中。这就是为什么过去的大师相对较少，而他们却如此杰出。

These social and political barriers, however, have mostly disappeared. Today we have the kind of access to information and knowledge that past Masters could only dream about. Now more than ever, we have the capacity and freedom to move toward the inclination that all of us possess as part of our genetic uniqueness. It is time that the word “genius” becomes demystified and de-rarefied. We are all closer than we think to such intelligence. (The word “genius” comes from the Latin, and originally referred to a guardian spirit that watched over the birth of each person; it later came to refer to the innate qualities that make each person uniquely gifted.)

然而，这些社会和政治障碍大多已消失。如今，我们拥有了获取信息和知识的渠道，这在以往的大师们看来简直是梦寐以求的。如今，我们比以往任何时候都更有能力和自由地去追求我们所有人与生俱来的独特基因。“天才”一词是时候褪去神秘色彩，不再稀有。我们比想象中更接近这种智慧。（“天才”一词源于拉丁语，最初指守护每个人诞生的守护神；后来，它被用来指代赋予每个人独特天赋的先天特质。）

Although we may find ourselves at a historical moment rich in possibilities for mastery, in which more and more people can move toward their inclinations, we in fact face one last obstacle in attaining such power, one that is cultural and insidiously dangerous: The very concept of mastery has become denigrated, associated with something old-fashioned and even unpleasant. It is generally not seen as something to aspire to. This shift in value is rather recent, and can be traced to circumstances peculiar to our times.

尽管我们正处于一个充满掌控可能性的历史时刻，越来越多的人可以顺应自身意愿，但事实上，我们在获得这种权力的过程中面临着最后一个障碍，这个障碍是文化上的，而且潜藏着危险：掌控的概念本身已被贬低，与某种过时甚至令人不快的东西联系在一起。它通常不被视为值得追求的东西。这种价值观的转变是最近才出现的，可以追溯到我们这个时代特有的情况。

We live in a world that seems increasingly beyond our control. Our livelihoods are at the whim of globalized forces. The problems that we face—economic, environmental, and so on—cannot be solved by our individual actions. Our politicians are distant and unresponsive to our desires. A natural response when people feel overwhelmed is to retreat into various forms of passivity. If we don’t try too much in life, if we limit our circle of action, we can give ourselves the illusion of control. The less we attempt, the less chances of failure. If we can make it look like we are not really responsible for our fate, for what happens to us in life, then our apparent powerlessness is more palatable. For this reason we become attracted to certain narratives: it is genetics that determines much of what we do; we are just products of our times; the individual is just a myth; human behavior can be reduced to statistical trends.

我们生活在一个似乎越来越失控的世界。我们的生计受制于全球化力量。我们面临的问题——经济、环境等等——无法靠我们个人行动解决。我们的政客们对我们的愿望漠不关心，毫无回应。当人们感到不堪重负时，自然的反应就是退缩到各种被动状态中。如果我们在生活中不付出太多努力，如果我们限制自己的行动范围，我们就会给自己一种掌控一切的幻觉。我们尝试得越少，失败的可能性就越小。如果我们能让自己看起来对命运、对生活中发生的事情毫不负责，那么我们表面上的无力感就更容易被接受。正因如此，我们才会被某些叙事所吸引：基因决定了我们的行为；我们只是时代的产物；个体只是一个神话；人类行为可以归结为统计趋势。

Many take this change in value a step further, giving their passivity a positive veneer. They romanticize the self-destructive artist who loses control of him-or herself. Anything that smacks of discipline or effort seems fussy and passé: what matters is the feeling behind the artwork, and any hint of craftsmanship or work violates this principle. They come to accept things that are made cheaply and quickly. The idea that they might have to expend much effort to get what they want has been eroded by the proliferation of devices that do so much of the work for them, fostering the idea that they deserve all of this—that it is their inherent right to have and to consume what they want. “Why bother working for years to attain mastery when we can have so much power with very little effort? Technology will solve everything.” This passivity has even assumed a moral stance: “mastery and power are evil; they are the domain of patriarchal elites who oppress us; power is inherently bad; better to opt out of the system altogether,” or at least make it look that way.

许多人将这种价值观的转变更进一步，为自己的被动性披上一层积极的外衣。他们把那些自我毁灭、失去控制的艺术家理想化。任何带有纪律或努力意味的东西都显得繁琐和过时：重要的是艺术品背后的情感，任何工艺或工作的暗示都违背了这一原则。他们开始接受廉价快速制作的东西。他们原本认为需要付出巨大努力才能得到想要的东西，如今却被各种设备的普及所侵蚀，这些设备为他们完成了大量的工作，反而滋生了这样一种观念：他们理应拥有这一切——拥有和消费自己想要的东西是他们与生俱来的权利。“既然我们只需付出很少的努力就能拥有如此强大的力量，为什么还要费尽心思多年去精通呢？科技将解决一切问题。”这种被动甚至已经呈现出一种道德立场：“统治和权力是邪恶的；它们是压迫我们的父权制精英的领域；权力本质上是坏的；最好完全退出这个体系”，或者至少看起来是这样。

If you are not careful, you will find this attitude infecting you in subtle ways. You will unconsciously lower your sights as to what you can accomplish in life. This can diminish your levels of effort and discipline below the point of effectiveness. Conforming to social norms, you will listen more to others than to your own voice. You may choose a career path based on what peers and parents tell you, or on what seems lucrative. If you lose contact with this inner calling, you can have some success in life, but eventually your lack of true desire catches up with you. Your work becomes mechanical. You come to live for leisure and immediate pleasures. In this way you become increasingly passive, and never move past the first phase. You may grow frustrated and depressed, never realizing that the source of it is your alienation from your own creative potential.

稍不留神，这种态度就会潜移默化地感染你。你会无意识地降低对人生成就的期望。这会降低你的努力程度和自律性，使其达不到预期的效率。为了迎合社会规范，你会更多地听从他人而非自己的声音。你可能会根据同龄人和父母的建议，或者根据看似有利可图的职业来选择职业道路。如果你失去了与内心召唤的联系，你可能会在生活中取得一些成功，但最终你会因为缺乏真正的渴望而自食其果。你的工作变得机械化。你开始追逐休闲和即时的享乐。就这样，你变得越来越被动，永远无法摆脱最初的阶段。你可能会感到沮丧和抑郁，却从未意识到，这一切的根源在于你疏远了自身的创造潜力。

Before it is too late you must find your way to your inclination, exploiting the incredible opportunities of the age that you have been born into. Knowing the critical importance of desire and of your emotional connection to your work, which are the keys to mastery, you can in fact make the passivity of these times work in your favor and serve as a motivating device in two important ways.

趁还没太迟，你必须找到自己的兴趣所在，充分利用你所处的时代赋予你的各种机遇。了解渴望以及你与工作之间的情感联系至关重要——它们是成就卓越的关键——你就能将这些时代的被动性转化为优势，并在两个重要方面成为一种激励手段。

First, you must see your attempt at attaining mastery as something extremely necessary and positive. The world is teeming with problems, many of them of our own creation. To solve them will require a tremendous amount of effort and creativity. Relying on genetics, technology, magic, or being nice and natural will not save us. We require the energy not only to address practical matters, but also to forge new institutions and orders that fit our changed circumstances. We must create our own world or we will die from inaction. We need to find our way back to the concept of mastery that defined us as a species so many millions of years ago. This is not mastery for the purpose of dominating nature or other people, but for determining our fate. The passive ironic attitude is not cool or romantic, but pathetic and destructive. You are setting an example of what can be achieved as a Master in the modern world. You are contributing to the most important cause of all—the survival and prosperity of the human race, in a time of stagnation.

首先，你必须将追求掌控的尝试视为极其必要且积极的事情。这个世界充满了问题，其中许多是我们自身造成的。解决这些问题需要付出巨大的努力和创造力。依赖基因、科技、魔法，或者保持友善和自然都无法拯救我们。我们不仅需要精力来处理实际问题，还需要建立适应我们变化的环境的新制度和秩序。我们必须创造自己的世界，否则我们将因无所作为而灭亡。我们需要回归数百万年前定义我们物种的掌控理念。这种掌控并非为了主宰自然或他人，而是为了决定自身的命运。消极的反讽态度并不酷炫或浪漫，而是可悲且具有破坏性。你正在树立一个榜样，展现在现代世界中，作为一名掌控者所能取得的成就。你正在为最重要的事业——在停滞不前的时代，人类的生存与繁荣——做出贡献。

Second, you must convince yourself of the following: people get the mind and quality of brain that they deserve through their actions in life. Despite the popularity of genetic explanations for our behavior, recent discoveries in neuroscience are overturning long-held beliefs that the brain is genetically hardwired. Scientists are demonstrating the degree to which the brain is actually quite plastic—how our thoughts determine our mental landscape. They are exploring the relationship of willpower to physiology, how profoundly the mind can affect our health and functionality. It is possible that more and more will be discovered about how deeply we create the various patterns of our lives through certain mental operations—how we are truly responsible for so much of what happens to us.

其次，你必须确信以下几点：人们通过其生活中的行为获得了他们应得的思维和大脑品质。尽管基因学对我们行为的解释颇为流行，但神经科学领域的最新发现正在颠覆长期以来认为大脑是基因决定的观念。科学家们正在证明大脑实际上具有很强的可塑性——我们的思维如何决定我们的精神世界。他们正在探索意志力与生理机能的关系，以及思维如何深刻地影响我们的健康和功能。我们或许会越来越多地发现，我们如何通过某些心理活动深刻地创造着我们生活的各种模式——我们如何真正地对发生在我们身上的如此多的事情负责。

People who are passive create a mental landscape that is rather barren. Because of their limited experiences and action, all kinds of connections in the brain die off from lack of use. Pushing against the passive trend of these times, you must work to see how far you can extend control of your circumstances and create the kind of mind you desire—not through drugs but through action. Unleashing the masterful mind within, you will be at the vanguard of those who are exploring the extended limits of human willpower.

消极被动的人，其精神世界往往空洞无物。由于经验和行动有限，大脑中各种连接因缺乏运用而逐渐消亡。为了对抗当今时代的消极趋势，你必须努力探索自己能将掌控自身境况的程度提升到何种程度，并创造你渴望的那种精神状态——不是通过药物，而是通过行动。释放内在的掌控力，你将成为探索人类意志力极限的先锋。

In many ways, the movement from one level of intelligence to another can be considered as a kind of ritual of transformation. As you progress, old ideas and perspectives die off; as new powers are unleashed, you are initiated into higher levels of seeing the world. Consider Mastery as an invaluable tool in guiding you through this transformative process. The book is designed to lead you from the lowest levels to the highest. It will help to initiate you into the first step—discovering your Life’s Task , or vocation, and how to carve out a path that will lead you to its fulfillment on various levels. It will advise you how to exploit to the fullest your apprenticeship—the various strategies of observation and learning that will serve you best in this phase; how to find the perfect mentors; how to decipher the unwritten codes on political behavior; how to cultivate social intelligence; and finally, how to recognize when it is time to leave the apprenticeship nest and strike out for yourself, entering the active, creative phase.

从许多方面来看，从一个智力层次到另一个智力层次的转变可以被视为一种转变的仪式。随着你的进步，旧的想法和观点逐渐消亡；随着新力量的释放，你将开启更高层次的世界观。将“精通”视为引导你完成这一转变过程的宝贵工具。本书旨在引领你从最低层次走向最高层次。它将帮助你迈出第一步——发现你的人生任务或使命，以及如何开辟一条通往各个层面实现它的道路。它将指导你如何充分利用你的学徒期——在这个阶段最适合你的各种观察和学习策略；如何找到完美的导师；如何解读政治行为的不成文准则；如何培养社交智力；以及最后，如何识别何时离开学徒期，独立自主，进入积极主动、富有创造力的阶段。

It will show you how to continue the learning process on a higher level. It will reveal timeless strategies for creative problem solving, for keeping your mind fluid and adaptable. It will show you how to access more unconscious and primitive layers of intelligence, and how to endure the inevitable barbs of envy that will come your way. It will spell out the powers that will come to you through mastery, pointing you in the direction of that intuitive, inside feel for your field. Finally, it will initiate you into a philosophy, a way of thinking that will make it easier to follow this path.

它会告诉你如何在更高的层次上继续学习。它会揭示创造性解决问题的永恒策略，让你的思维保持流畅和适应性。它会告诉你如何触及更深层次的潜意识和原始智慧，以及如何忍受不可避免的嫉妒。它会阐明你通过精通所能获得的力量，指引你找到对你所在领域的直觉和内在感受。最终，它会引导你进入一种哲学，一种思维方式，让你更容易地走上这条道路。

The ideas in the book are based on extensive research in the fields of neuro-and cognitive science, studies on creativity, as well as the biographies of the greatest Masters in history. These include Leonardo da Vinci, the Zen Master Hakuin, Benjamin Franklin, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, the poet John Keats, the scientist Michael Faraday, Charles Darwin, Thomas Edison, Albert Einstein, Henry Ford, the writer Marcel Proust, the dancer Martha Graham, the inventor Buckminster Fuller, the jazz artist John Coltrane, and the pianist Glenn Gould.

本书的理念基于神经科学和认知科学、创造力研究以及历史上最伟大大师的传记。这些大师包括列奥纳多·达·芬奇、白隐禅师、本杰明·富兰克林、沃尔夫冈·阿马德乌斯·莫扎特、约翰·沃尔夫冈·冯·歌德、诗人约翰·济慈、科学家迈克尔·法拉第、查尔斯·达尔文、托马斯·爱迪生、阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦、亨利·福特、作家马塞尔·普鲁斯特、舞蹈家玛莎·格雷厄姆、发明家巴克敏斯特·富勒、爵士乐艺术家约翰·科尔特兰和钢琴家格伦·古尔德。

To make it clear how this form of intelligence can be applied to the modern world, nine contemporary Masters have been interviewed at length as well. They are neuroscientist V. S. Ramachandran; anthropologist-linguist Daniel Everett; computer engineer, writer, and tech-startup mastermind Paul Graham; architect-engineer Santiago Calatrava; former boxer and now trainer Freddie Roach; robotics engineer and green technology designer Yoky Matsuoka; visual artist Teresita Fernández; professor of animal husbandry and industrial designer Temple Grandin; and U.S. Air Force fighter pilot ace Cesar Rodriguez.

为了阐明这种智慧如何应用于现代世界，我们还对九位当代大师进行了深入采访。他们分别是神经科学家V. S. Ramachandran；人类学家兼语言学家Daniel Everett；计算机工程师、作家兼科技创业公司创始人Paul Graham；建筑工程师Santiago Calatrava；前拳击手、现任教练Freddie Roach；机器人工程师兼绿色科技设计师Yoky Matsuoka；视觉艺术家Teresita Fernández；畜牧学教授兼工业设计师Temple Grandin；以及美国空军战斗机王牌飞行员Cesar Rodriguez。

The life stories of these various contemporary figures dispel the notion that mastery is somehow passé or elitist. They come from all different backgrounds, social classes, and ethnicities. The power they have achieved is clearly the result of effort and process, not genetics or privilege. Their stories also reveal how such mastery can be adapted to our times, and the tremendous power it can bring us.

这些当代人物的人生故事驳斥了“精通”已过时或只限于精英阶层的观念。他们来自不同的背景、社会阶层和种族。他们所取得的成就显然源于努力和过程，而非基因或特权。他们的故事也揭示了这种精通如何适应我们的时代，以及它能赋予我们的巨大力量。

The structure of Mastery is simple. There are six chapters, moving sequentially through the process. Chapter 1 is the starting point—discovering your calling, your Life’s Task. Chapters 2 , 3 , and 4 discuss different elements of the Apprenticeship Phase (learning skills, working with mentors, acquiring social intelligence). Chapter 5 is devoted to the Creative-Active Phase, and chapter 6 to the ultimate goal—Mastery. Each chapter begins with the story of an iconic historical figure who exemplifies the chapter’s overall concept. The section that follows, Keys to Mastery, gives you a detailed analysis of the phase involved, concrete ideas on how to apply this knowledge to your circumstances, and the mind-set that is necessary to fully exploit these ideas. Following the Keys is a section detailing the strategies of Masters—contemporary and historical—who have used various methods to advance them through the process. These strategies are designed to give you an even greater sense of the practical application of the ideas in the book, and to inspire you to follow in the footsteps of these Masters, showing how their power is eminently attainable.

《精通》的结构很简单。本书共六章，按顺序贯穿整个过程。第一章是起点——发现你的使命，你的人生任务。第二、三、四章分别探讨学徒阶段的不同要素（学习技能、与导师合作、获得社交智慧）。第五章探讨创造-主动阶段，第六章则探讨最终目标——精通。每一章都以一位标志性历史人物的故事开篇，这些人物体现了本章的整体概念。接下来的部分“精通的关键”将对所涉及的阶段进行详细分析，提供如何将这些知识应用于自身情况的具体思路，以及充分利用这些思路所需的思维方式。“追寻关键”部分详细介绍了当代和历史上的大师们运用各种方法推进精通的策略。这些策略旨在让您更加深刻地理解书中思想的实际应用，并激励您追随这些大师的脚步，展示他们的力量是如何实现的。

For all of the contemporary Masters and some of the historical ones, their stories will continue over several chapters. In such cases there may be a slight repetition of biographical information in order to recap what happened in the previous phase of their lives. Hyperlinks in parentheses will refer back to these earlier narrations.

所有当代大师以及部分历史大师的故事将跨越多个章节。在这种情况下，传记信息可能会略有重复，以回顾他们人生前期所发生的事情。括号中的超链接将指向这些早期的叙述。

Finally, you must not see this process of moving through levels of intelligence as merely linear, heading toward some kind of ultimate destination known as mastery. Your whole life is a kind of apprenticeship to which you apply your learning skills. Everything that happens to you is a form of instruction if you pay attention. The creativity that you gain in learning a skill so deeply must be constantly refreshed, as you keep forcing your mind back to a state of openness. Even knowledge of your vocation must be revisited throughout the course of your life as changes in circumstance force you to adapt its direction.

最后，你绝不能将这种智力水平的提升过程仅仅视为线性的，朝着某种被称为“精通”的终极目标前进。你的整个人生就像一段学徒期，你需要将学习到的技能运用到其中。如果你用心观察，你身上发生的一切都是一种指导。你在深入学习一项技能的过程中所获得的创造力必须不断更新，因为你必须不断强迫自己的思维回归开放的状态。即使是你对职业的认知，也必须在你的人生历程中不断重温，因为环境的变化会迫使你调整它的方向。

In moving toward mastery, you are bringing your mind closer to reality and to life itself. Anything that is alive is in a continual state of change and movement. The moment that you rest, thinking that you have attained the level you desire, a part of your mind enters a phase of decay. You lose your hard-earned creativity and others begin to sense it. This is a power and intelligence that must be continually renewed or it will die.

在迈向精通的过程中，你的心智正逐渐接近现实，接近生命本身。任何鲜活的事物都处于持续变化和运动的状态。当你停下来，自以为已经达到了渴望的境界时，你心智的一部分便会进入衰退期。你失去了辛苦积累的创造力，而其他人也开始察觉到这一点。这是一种必须不断更新的力量和智慧，否则它就会消亡。

Do not talk about giftedness, inborn talents! One can name great men of all kinds who were very little gifted. They acquired greatness, became “geniuses” (as we put it), through qualities the lack of which no one who knew what they were would boast of: they all possessed that seriousness of the efficient workman which first learns to construct the parts properly before it ventures to fashion a great whole; they allowed themselves time for it, because they took more pleasure in making the little, secondary things well than in the effect of a dazzling whole.

别再谈天赋异禀，天生的才能了！各种各样看似平凡的伟人都能被列举出来。他们凭借着一些品质，最终获得了伟大，成为了我们所说的“天才”，而这些品质是任何了解他们的人都不会自夸的：他们都拥有高效工匠的那种认真，这种认真首先要学会正确地构建各个部分，然后再着手打造一个伟大的整体；他们为此留出了时间，因为他们更乐于把细小、次要的部分做好，而不是享受一个令人眼花缭乱的整体效果。

—F RIEDRICH N IETZSCHE

—弗里德里希·尼采

I

我

DISCOVER YOUR
发现你的
CALLING: THE
使命：
LIFE’S TASK
人生的使命

You possess a kind of inner force that seeks to guide you toward your Life’s Task—what you are meant to accomplish in the time that you have to live. In childhood this force was clear to you. It directed you toward activities and subjects that fit your natural inclinations, that sparked a curiosity that was deep and primal. In the intervening years, the force tends to fade in and out as you listen more to parents and peers, to the daily anxieties that wear away at you. This can be the source of your unhappiness—your lack of connection to who you are and what makes you unique. The first move toward mastery is always inward—learning who you really are and reconnecting with that innate force. Knowing it with clarity, you will find your way to the proper career path and everything else will fall into place. It is never too late to start this process.

你拥有一种内在的力量，它会引导你走向人生目标——你注定要在有限的生命中完成的目标。童年时期，你对这种力量的感知非常清晰。它引导你选择符合你天性的活动和课题，激发你深沉而原始的好奇心。然而，随着你更多地听从父母和同龄人的意见，以及被日常的焦虑所折磨，这种力量会逐渐消退。这或许是你不快乐的根源——你无法与自我以及自身的独特之处建立联系。通往精通的第一步始终是向内——了解真正的自我，并重新连接那股与生俱来的力量。清晰地认识它，你就能找到适合自己的职业道路，其他一切都会水到渠成。开始这个过程永远不会太晚。

# ↩

THE HIDDEN FORCE

隐藏的力量

Toward the end of April 1519, after months of illness, the artist Leonardo da Vinci felt certain that his death was only a few days away. For the past two years Leonardo had been living in the château of Cloux in France, the personal guest of the French king, François I. The king had showered him with money and honors, considering him the living embodiment of the Italian Renaissance, which he had wanted to import to France. Leonardo had been most useful to the king, advising him on all kinds of important matters. But now, at the age of sixty-seven, his life was about to end and his thoughts turned toward other things. He made out his will, received the holy sacrament in church, and then returned to his bed, waiting for the end to come.

1519年4月底，在数月的病痛折磨之后，艺术家列奥纳多·达·芬奇确信自己离世已近在咫尺。过去两年，列奥纳多一直居住在法国克卢城堡，是法国国王弗朗索瓦一世的私人宾客。国王给予他丰厚的金钱和尊荣，视他为意大利文艺复兴的活生生的化身，并希望将这种精神引入法国。列奥纳多对国王非常有帮助，在各种重要事务上为他出谋划策。但如今，他已年届六十七，生命即将走到尽头，他的思绪也随之转向别处。他立下遗嘱，在教堂领受圣礼，然后回到床上，等待着死亡的到来。

As he lay there, several of his friends—including the king—visited him. They noticed that Leonardo was in a particularly reflective mood. He was not someone who usually liked to talk about himself, but now he shared memories from his childhood and youth, dwelling on the strange and improbable course of his life.

当他躺在那里时，他的几位朋友——包括国王——来看望他。他们注意到达芬奇心情格外沉思。他通常不喜欢谈论自己，但现在他分享了童年和青年时期的回忆，细细回味着他奇特而不可思议的人生历程。

Leonardo had always had a strong sense of fate, and for years he had been haunted by one particular question: is there some kind of force from within that makes all living things grow and transform themselves? If such a force in nature existed, he wanted to discover it, and he looked for signs of it in every thing he examined. It was an obsession. Now, in his final hours, after his friends had left him alone, Leonardo would have almost certainly applied this question in some form or another to the riddle of his own life, searching for signs of a force or a fate that had brought about his own development and guided him to the present.

列奥纳多一直对命运有着强烈的感知，多年来，一个特定的问题一直萦绕在他的心头：是否存在某种内在的力量，驱使着所有生物生长、蜕变？如果自然界中真的存在这样的力量，他便渴望发现它，并在他所考察的每件事物中寻找它的踪迹。这几乎成了他的执念。如今，在他生命的最后时刻，在朋友们离他而去之后，列奥纳多几乎肯定会以某种方式将这个问题运用到他自身的人生之谜中，寻找某种力量或命运的迹象，促成他的成长，并引领他走到今天。

Leonardo would have begun such a search by first thinking back to his childhood in the village of Vinci, some twenty miles outside Florence. His father, Ser Piero da Vinci, was a notary and staunch member of the powerful bourgeoisie, but since Leonardo had been born out of wedlock, he was barred from attending the university or practicing any of the noble professions. His schooling therefore was minimal, and so as a child Leonardo was left mostly to himself. He liked most of all to wander through the olive groves around Vinci or to follow a particular path that led to a much different part of the landscape—dense forests full of wild boar, waterfalls cascading over fast-moving streams, swans gliding through pools, strange wildflowers growing out of the sides of cliffs. The intense variety of life in these forests enthralled him.

列奥纳多在开始这样的探索之前，会首先回想起自己在佛罗伦萨郊外二十英里的芬奇村度过的童年时光。他的父亲塞尔·皮耶罗·达·芬奇是一位公证人，也是当时强大的资产阶级的坚定成员。但由于列奥纳多是私生子，他被禁止上大学，也无法从事任何贵族职业。因此，他所受的教育很少，童年时期的列奥纳多大部分时间都独自生活。他最喜欢漫步在芬奇村周围的橄榄树林中，或者沿着一条通往截然不同景色的小径——茂密的森林里野猪成群，瀑布飞流直下，水流湍急，天鹅在水潭中滑翔，悬崖峭壁上生长着奇异的野花。森林里丰富多彩的生命让他着迷。

One day, sneaking into his father’s office, he grabbed some sheets of paper—a rather rare commodity in those days, but as a notary his father had a large supply. He took the sheets on his walk into the forest, and sitting upon a rock he began to sketch the various sights around him. He kept returning day after day to do more of the same; even when the weather was bad, he would sit under some kind of shelter and sketch. He had no teachers, no paintings to look at; he did everything by eye, with nature as the model. He noticed that in drawing things he had to observe them much more closely and catch the details that made them come to life.

一天，他偷偷溜进父亲的办公室，拿了几张纸——在当时，纸张是相当稀缺的物品，但作为公证人，他父亲的存货却非常充足。他带着这些纸走进森林，坐在一块岩石上，开始勾勒周围的各种景象。他日复一日地回到这里，继续画画；即使天气不好，他也会坐在某种遮蔽处写生。他没有老师，也没有画作可供欣赏；他一切都凭眼睛，以自然为范本。他注意到，在绘画时，他必须更加仔细地观察，捕捉那些让它们栩栩如生的细节。

Once he sketched a white iris, and in observing it so closely he was struck by its peculiar shape. The iris begins as a seed, and then it proceeds through various stages, all of which he had drawn over the past few years. What makes this plant develop through its stages and culminate in this magnificent flower, so unlike any other? Perhaps it possesses a force that pushes it through these various transformations. He would wonder about the metamorphosis of flowers for years to come.

有一次，他画了一株白色鸢尾花，仔细观察后，被它奇特的形状深深吸引。鸢尾花最初是一颗种子，然后经历不同的生长阶段，所有这些阶段他都在过去几年里画下来了。是什么让这种植物经历各个阶段，最终绽放出这朵与众不同、美轮美奂的花朵？或许是某种力量在推动着它经历这些变化。在接下来的几年里，他一直在思考花朵的蜕变。

Alone on his deathbed, Leonardo would have thought back to his earliest years as an apprentice in the studio of the Florentine artist Andrea del Verrocchio. He had been admitted there at the age of fourteen because of the remarkable quality of his drawings. Verrocchio instructed his apprentices in all of the sciences that were necessary to produce the work of his studio—engineering, mechanics, chemistry, and metallurgy. Leonardo was eager to learn all of these skills, but soon he discovered in himself something else: he could not simply do an assignment; he needed to make it something of his own, to invent rather than imitate the Master.

临终之际，列奥纳多独自一人，回想起早年在佛罗伦萨艺术家安德烈亚·德尔·韦罗基奥工作室当学徒的时光。他十四岁时就因其非凡的绘画品质而被录取。韦罗基奥教授他的学徒们所有创作工作室作品所需的科学知识——工程学、力学、化学和冶金学。列奥纳多渴望学习所有这些技能，但很快他发现自己身上又出现了新的问题：他不能简单地完成一项任务；他需要将其变成自己的作品，去创造而不是模仿大师。

One time, as part of his studio work, he was asked to paint an angel in a larger biblical scene designed by Verrocchio. He had decided that he would make his portion of the scene come to life in his own way. In the foreground in front of the angel he painted a flowerbed, but instead of the usual generalized renderings of plants, Leonardo depicted the flower specimens that he had studied in such detail as a child, with a kind of scientific rigor no one had seen before. For the angel’s face, he experimented with his paints and mixed a new blend that gave it a kind of soft radiance that expressed the angel’s sublime mood. (To help capture this mood, Leonardo had spent time in the local church observing those in fervent prayer, the expression of one young man serving as the model for the angel.) And finally, he determined that he would be the first artist to create realistic angelic wings.

有一次，作为工作室作业的一部分，达芬奇被要求在韦罗基奥设计的一幅更大的圣经场景中描绘一位天使。他决定以自己的方式赋予这幅场景中他所描绘的那部分生命。在天使前方的前景中，他画了一片花坛，但达芬奇没有像往常那样对植物进行概括性的描绘，而是以一种前所未有的科学严谨性描绘了他儿时曾仔细研究过的花卉样本。在天使的面部，他尝试了各种颜料，并混合了一种新的颜料配方，赋予其一种柔和的光泽，以表达天使崇高的情绪。（为了捕捉这种情绪，达芬奇曾在当地教堂观察那些虔诚祈祷的人，其中一位年轻人的表情就是天使的原型。）最终，他决心成为第一位创作出逼真的天使翅膀的艺术家。

For this purpose, he went to the marketplace and purchased several birds. He spent hours sketching their wings, how exactly they merged into their bodies. He wanted to create the sensation that these wings had organically grown from the angel’s shoulders and would bring it natural flight. As usual, Leonardo could not stop there. After his work was completed he became obsessed with birds, and the idea brewed in his mind that perhaps a human could really fly, if Leonardo could figure out the science behind avian flight. Now, several hours every week, he read and studied everything he could about birds. This was how his mind naturally worked—one idea flowed into another.

为此，他去市场买了几只鸟。他花了几个小时描绘它们的翅膀，描绘它们如何与身体完美融合。他想营造出一种感觉，仿佛这些翅膀是从天使的肩膀自然生长而来，赋予它自然飞翔的能力。像往常一样，达芬奇并没有止步于此。作品完成后，他开始对鸟类着迷，一个想法在他脑海中浮现：如果达芬奇能弄清楚鸟类飞行背后的科学原理，或许人类真的可以飞翔。现在，他每周都会花几个小时阅读和研究所有能找到的关于鸟类的资料。他的思维就是这样自然运转的——一个想法接踵而至。

Leonardo would certainly have recalled the lowest point in his life—the year 1481. The Pope asked Lorenzo de’ Medici to recommend to him the finest artists in Florence to decorate a chapel he just had built, the Sistine Chapel. Lorenzo complied and sent to Rome all of the best Florentine artists, excluding Leonardo. They had never really gotten along. Lorenzo was a literary type, steeped in the classics. Leonardo could not read Latin and had little knowledge of the ancients. He had a more scientific bent to his nature. But at the root of Leonardo’s bitterness at this snub was something else—he had come to hate the dependence forced upon artists to gain royal favor, to live from commission to commission. He had grown tired of Florence and the court politics that reigned there.

列奥纳多肯定还记得他人生中的最低谷——1481年。教皇请洛伦佐·德·美第奇推荐佛罗伦萨最优秀的艺术家来装饰他刚刚建成的西斯廷教堂。洛伦佐答应了，把佛罗伦萨所有最优秀的艺术家都派到了罗马，唯独列奥纳多没有。他们一直相处得并不融洽。洛伦佐是一位文学家，深谙古典文学。列奥纳多不懂拉丁文，对古代文学也知之甚少。他生性更偏向科学。但列奥纳多对这次冷遇感到痛苦的根源另有原因——他开始痛恨艺术家被迫依赖皇室的恩宠，靠一个又一个的委托过活。他已经厌倦了佛罗伦萨以及那里盛行的宫廷政治。

He made a decision that would change everything in his life: He would establish himself in Milan, and he would devise a new strategy for his livelihood. He would be more than an artist. He would pursue all of the crafts and sciences that interested him—architecture, military engineering, hydraulics, anatomy, sculpture. For any prince or patron that wanted him, he could serve as an overall adviser and artist, for a nice stipend. His mind, he decided, worked best when he had several different projects at hand, allowing him to build all kinds of connections between them.

他做了一个改变人生的决定：他要在米兰安顿下来，并制定新的谋生策略。他不仅仅是一名艺术家。他将追求所有他感兴趣的工艺和科学——建筑、军事工程、水力学、解剖学、雕塑。任何一位想要他的王子或赞助人，他都可以担任总顾问兼艺术家，并收取丰厚的报酬。他认为，当他手头有几个不同的项目时，他的思维才能发挥到最佳状态，因为他可以在这些项目之间建立各种联系。

Continuing his self-examination, Leonardo would have thought back to the one great commission that he accepted during this new phase of his life—an enormous bronze equestrian statue in memory of Francesco Sforza, the father of the current duke of Milan. The challenge for him was too irresistible. It would be of a scale no one had seen since the days of ancient Rome, and to cast something so large in bronze would require an engineering feat that had baffled all of the artists of his time. Leonardo worked on the design for months, and to test it out he built a clay replica of the statue and displayed it in the most expansive square in Milan. It was gigantic, the size of a large building. The crowds that gathered to look at it were awestruck—its size, the impetuous stance of the horse that the artist had captured, its terrifying aspect. Word spread throughout Italy of this marvel and people anxiously awaited its realization in bronze. For this purpose, Leonardo invented a totally new way of casting. Instead of breaking up the mold for the horse into sections, Leonardo would construct the mold as one seamless piece (using an unusual mix of materials he had concocted) and cast it as a whole, which would give the horse a much more organic, natural appearance.

达芬奇继续自我反省，不禁回想起人生新阶段接受的一项重要委托——为纪念现任米兰公爵的父亲弗朗切斯科·斯福扎，创作一尊巨大的青铜骑马雕像。对他来说，这挑战实在难以抗拒。这座雕像的规模之大，自古罗马时代以来前所未见，而用青铜铸造如此巨大的雕塑，需要一项工程壮举，这项工程壮举曾让当时所有艺术家都感到困惑。达芬奇耗时数月构思，为了测试效果，他用粘土制作了雕像的复制品，并将其陈列在米兰最宽敞的广场上。这座雕像体量巨大，堪比一座大楼。聚集一堂的人群无不惊叹——它的规模、艺术家捕捉到的骏马奔腾的姿态以及它那令人敬畏的面容。这一奇迹迅速传遍意大利，人们焦急地等待着它以青铜铸造的最终成品。为此，达芬奇发明了一种全新的铸造方法。达芬奇并没有将马的模具分成几部分，而是将模具构建成一个无缝的整体（使用他调制的一种不寻常的混合材料），并将其作为一个整体铸造，这会让马看起来更加有机、自然。

A few months later, however, war broke out and the duke needed every bit of bronze he could lay his hands on for artillery. Eventually, the clay statue was taken down and the horse was never built. Other artists had scoffed at Leonardo’s folly—he had taken so long to find the perfect solution that naturally, events had conspired against him. One time even Michelangelo himself taunted Leonardo: “You who made a model of a horse you could never cast in bronze and which you gave up, to your shame. And the stupid people of Milan had faith in you?” He had become used to such insults about his slowness at work, but in fact he regretted nothing from this experience. He had been able to test out his ideas on how to engineer large-scale projects; he would apply this knowledge elsewhere. Anyway, he didn’t care so much about the finished product; it was the search and process in creating something that had always excited him.

然而几个月后，战争爆发，公爵急需每一点青铜来制造火炮。最终，泥塑被拆除，马也未能完成。其他艺术家嘲笑达芬奇的愚蠢——他花了太长时间才找到完美的解决方案，以至于自然而然地，事态发展对他不利。甚至米开朗基罗本人也曾嘲讽达芬奇：“你造了一匹永远无法用青铜铸造的马，却羞愧地放弃了它。愚蠢的米兰人竟然还相信你？” 他已经习惯了这种关于他工作迟缓的侮辱，但事实上，他并不后悔这段经历。他得以检验自己关于如何设计大型项目的想法；他会将这些知识运用到其他地方。总之，他并不太在意最终成品；真正让他兴奋的是创作过程中的探索和过程。

Reflecting on his life in this way, he would have clearly detected the workings of some kind of hidden force within him. As a child this force had drawn him to the wildest part of the landscape, where he could observe the most intense and dramatic variety of life. This same force compelled him to steal paper from his father and devote his time to sketching. It pushed him to experiment while working for Verrocchio. It guided him away from the courts of Florence and the insecure egos that flourished among artists. It compelled him to an extreme of boldness—the gigantic sculptures, the attempt to fly, the dissection of hundreds of corpses for his anatomical studies—all to discover the essence of life itself.

如此反思人生，他或许能清晰地察觉到自身内心深处某种潜藏力量的运作。孩童时期，这股力量将他引向最荒凉的境界，在那里，他得以观察到生命最强烈、最富戏剧性的多样性。同样的力量驱使他从父亲那里偷纸，全身心投入素描。这股力量促使他在为韦罗基奥工作期间不断进行实验。这股力量引导他远离佛罗伦萨的宫廷，远离艺术家中盛行的不安全感。这股力量驱使他展现出极致的勇气——创作巨型雕塑，尝试飞翔，为解剖学研究解剖数百具尸体——所有这一切都是为了探索生命本身的本质。

Seen from this vantage point, everything in his life made sense. It was in fact a blessing to have been born illegitimate—it allowed him to develop in his own way. Even the paper in his house seemed to indicate some kind of destiny. What if he had rebelled against this force? What if, after the Sistine Chapel rejection, he had insisted on going to Rome with the others and forced his way into the Pope’s good graces instead of seeking his own path? He was capable of that. What if he had devoted himself to mostly painting in order to make a good living? What if he had been more like the others, finishing his works as fast as possible? He would have done well, but he would not have been Leonardo da Vinci. His life would have lacked the purpose that it had, and inevitably things would have gone wrong.

从这个角度看，他生命中的一切都合情合理。事实上，生来非婚生子也是一种福气——这让他得以按照自己的方式发展。就连他家里的那张纸，似乎也预示着某种命运。如果他反抗这股力量会怎样？如果他在西斯廷教堂被拒后，坚持跟随其他人前往罗马，强行获得教皇的青睐，而不是去追寻自己的道路，会怎样？他有能力做到这一点。如果他为了谋生而主要致力于绘画，会怎样？如果他更像其他人，尽快完成作品，会怎样？他会做得很好，但他不会成为列奥纳多·达·芬奇。他的人生将失去它应有的目标，事情不可避免地会出错。

This hidden force within him, like that within the iris he had sketched so many years before, had led to the full flowering of his capacities. He had faithfully followed its guidance to the very end and, having completed his course, now it was time to die. Perhaps his own words, written years before in his notebook, would have come back to him in such a moment: “Just as a well-filled day brings blessed sleep, so a well-employed life brings a blessed death.”

他内心深处隐藏的力量，如同多年前他勾勒的虹膜般，引领他的能力得以充分绽放。他忠实地遵循着这股力量的指引，直至生命的终点，完成了人生的旅程，如今也到了死亡的时刻。或许，多年前他自己在笔记本上写下的那些话，会在这样的时刻浮现在他的脑海里：“正如充实的一天带来幸福的睡眠，充实的一生带来幸福的死亡。”

KEYS TO MASTERY

掌握诀窍
