Among his various possible beings each man always finds one which is his genuine and authentic being. The voice which calls him to that authentic being is what we call “vocation.” But the majority of men devote themselves to silencing that voice of the vocation and refusing to hear it. They manage to make a noise within themselves…to distract their own attention in order not to hear it; and they defraud themselves by substituting for their genuine selves a false course of life.

每个人在他众多可能的存在中，总能找到一个真正属于他自己的存在。那个召唤他走向那个真实存在的声音，就是我们所说的“使命”。然而，大多数人却致力于压制那使命的声音，拒绝倾听。他们设法在内心制造噪音……转移自己的注意力，以便不去倾听；他们用虚假的人生轨迹取代真实的自我，从而欺骗自己。

—J OSÉ O RTEGA Y G ASSET

—何塞·奥尔特加·加塞特

Many of the greatest Masters in history have confessed to experiencing some kind of force or voice or sense of destiny that has guided them forward. For Napoleon Bonaparte it was his “star” that he always felt in ascendance when he made the right move. For Socrates, it was his daemon, a voice that he heard, perhaps from the gods, which inevitably spoke to him in the negative—telling him what to avoid. For Goethe, he also called it a daemon—a kind of spirit that dwelled within him and compelled him to fulfill his destiny. In more modern times, Albert Einstein talked of a kind of inner voice that shaped the direction of his speculations. All of these are variations on what Leonardo da Vinci experienced with his own sense of fate.

历史上许多伟大的大师都承认，他们感受到某种力量、声音或命运感，指引着他们前进。对拿破仑·波拿巴来说，每当他做出正确的举动时，他总能感到自己仿佛“星辰”在升腾。对苏格拉底来说，那是他的守护神，一个他听到的声音，或许来自神灵，这声音总是以负面的方式对他说——告诉他应该避免什么。歌德也称之为守护神——一种栖息在他体内，驱使他去完成命运的精灵。在更现代的时代，阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦也谈到一种内在的声音，它塑造了他思考的方向。所有这些都是列奥纳多·达·芬奇自身命运感体验的变体。

Such feelings can be seen as purely mystical, beyond explanation, or as hallucinations and delusions. But there is another way to see them—as eminently real, practical, and explicable. It can be explained in the following way:

这种感觉或许被视为纯粹神秘、难以解释，或被视为幻觉和妄想。但还有另一种解读方式——它们极其真实、切实可行且易于解释。具体解释如下：

All of us are born unique. This uniqueness is marked genetically in our DNA. We are a one-time phenomenon in the universe—our exact genetic makeup has never occurred before nor will it ever be repeated. For all of us, this uniqueness first expresses itself in childhood through certain primal inclinations. For Leonardo it was exploring the natural world around his village and bringing it to life on paper in his own way. For others, it can be an early attraction to visual patterns—often an indication of a future interest in mathematics. Or it can be an attraction to particular physical movements or spatial arrangements. How can we explain such inclinations? They are forces within us that come from a deeper place than conscious words can express. They draw us to certain experiences and away from others. As these forces move us here or there, they influence the development of our minds in very particular ways.

我们每个人生来都是独一无二的。这种独特性深深地刻在我们的 DNA 中。我们是宇宙中一次性的现象——我们确切的基因构成从未出现过，也不会被重复。对我们所有人来说，这种独特性首先在童年时期通过某些原始倾向表现出来。对达芬奇来说，这种独特性是探索村庄周围的自然世界，并用自己的方式将其生动地呈现在纸上。对其他人来说，这可能是早期对视觉图案的吸引——通常预示着未来对数学的兴趣。也可能是对特定的身体运动或空间布局的吸引。我们如何解释这些倾向？它们是我们内在的力量，来自更深的地方，而不是有意识的语言所能表达的。它们吸引我们去体验某些体验，远离其他体验。当这些力量将我们带到这里或那里时，它们以非常特殊的方式影响着我们心智的发展。

This primal uniqueness naturally wants to assert and express itself, but some experience it more strongly than others. With Masters it is so strong that it feels like something that has its own external reality—a force, a voice, destiny. In moments when we engage in an activity that corresponds to our deepest inclinations, we might experience a touch of this: We feel as if the words we write or the physical movements we perform come so quickly and easily that they are coming from outside us. We are literally “inspired,” the Latin word meaning something from the outside breathing within us.

这种原始的独特性自然地渴望彰显和表达，但有些人的体验比其他人更强烈。大师们的体验如此强烈，以至于感觉它仿佛拥有自身外在的现实——一种力量、一种声音、一种命运。当我们从事一项符合我们内心深处倾向的活动时，我们或许会体验到这种感觉：我们感觉自己写下的文字或做出的肢体动作来得如此迅速和轻松，仿佛它们来自我们之外。我们实际上是受到了“启发”，这个拉丁词的意思是来自外部的某种东西在我们体内呼吸。

Let us state it in the following way: At your birth a seed is planted. That seed is your uniqueness. It wants to grow, transform itself, and flower to its full potential. It has a natural, assertive energy to it. Your Life’s Task is to bring that seed to flower, to express your uniqueness through your work. You have a destiny to fulfill. The stronger you feel and maintain it—as a force, a voice, or in whatever form—the greater your chance for fulfilling this Life’s Task and achieving mastery.

让我们这样表述：你出生时，一颗种子就被种下。那颗种子就是你的独特之处。它渴望成长、蜕变，并绽放出它的全部潜能。它拥有与生俱来的自信能量。你的人生任务就是让这颗种子开花结果，并通过你的努力展现你的独特之处。你肩负着使命。你越能感受到并保持这份使命——无论是力量、声音，还是其他任何形式——你就越有可能完成这项人生任务，并最终成就卓越。

What weakens this force, what makes you not feel it or even doubt its existence, is the degree to which you have succumbed to another force in life—social pressures to conform. This counterforce can be very powerful. You want to fit into a group. Unconsciously, you might feel that what makes you different is embarrassing or painful. Your parents often act as a counter-force as well. They may seek to direct you to a career path that is lucrative and comfortable. If these counterforces become strong enough, you can lose complete contact with your uniqueness, with who you really are. Your inclinations and desires become modeled on those of others.

削弱这股力量，让你感觉不到它，甚至怀疑它的存在，是因为你屈服于生活中的另一种力量——社会压力——的程度。这种反作用力可能非常强大。你想融入一个群体。潜意识里，你可能会觉得你的与众不同之处令人尴尬或痛苦。你的父母也常常扮演着反作用力的角色。他们可能会引导你走上一条收入丰厚、生活舒适的职业道路。如果这些反作用力变得足够强大，你可能会完全失去与自己独特之处的联系，失去与真正的自我的联系。你的倾向和欲望会变得效仿他人。

This can set you off on a very dangerous path. You end up choosing a career that does not really suit you. Your desire and interest slowly wane and your work suffers for it. You come to see pleasure and fulfillment as something that comes from outside your work. Because you are increasingly less engaged in your career, you fail to pay attention to changes going on in the field—you fall behind the times and pay a price for this. At moments when you must make important decisions, you flounder or follow what others are doing because you have no sense of inner direction or radar to guide you. You have broken contact with your destiny as formed at birth.

这可能会让你走上一条非常危险的道路。你最终会选择一份并不真正适合自己的职业。你的渴望和兴趣逐渐消退，你的工作也因此受到影响。你开始将快乐和成就感视为工作之外的某种东西。由于你对职业的投入越来越少，你无法关注该领域正在发生的变化——你落后于时代，并为此付出了代价。在你必须做出重要决定的时刻，你会不知所措，或者盲目跟风，因为你缺乏内在的方向感或雷达来指引你。你已经与你与生俱来的命运断绝了联系。

At all cost you must avoid such a fate. The process of following your Life’s Task all the way to mastery can essentially begin at any point in life. The hidden force within you is always there and ready to be engaged.

你必须不惜一切代价避免这样的命运。追随你的人生目标，直至精通，这个过程实际上可以在人生的任何阶段开始。你内在隐藏的力量始终存在，随时准备被你激发。

The process of realizing your Life’s Task comes in three stages: First, you must connect or reconnect with your inclinations, that sense of uniqueness. The first step then is always inward. You search the past for signs of that inner voice or force. You clear away the other voices that might confuse you—parents and peers. You look for an underlying pattern, a core to your character that you must understand as deeply as possible.

实现人生使命的过程分为三个阶段：首先，你必须连接或重新连接你的倾向，即那种独特的感觉。第一步始终是向内探索。你回顾过去，寻找那种内在声音或力量的痕迹。你清除其他可能让你困惑的声音——父母和同龄人的声音。你寻找一种潜在的模式，一种你必须尽可能深入理解的性格核心。

Second, with this connection established, you must look at the career path you are already on or are about to begin. The choice of this path—or redirection of it—is critical. To help in this stage you will need to enlarge your concept of work itself. Too often we make a separation in our lives—there is work and there is life outside work, where we find real pleasure and fulfillment. Work is often seen as a means for making money so we can enjoy that second life that we lead. Even if we derive some satisfaction from our careers we still tend to compartmentalize our lives in this way. This is a depressing attitude, because in the end we spend a substantial part of our waking life at work. If we experience this time as something to get through on the way to real pleasure, then our hours at work represent a tragic waste of the short time we have to live.

其次，在建立了这种联系之后，你必须审视自己已经踏上或即将踏上的职业道路。选择这条道路——或者说重新定位它——至关重要。为了在这个阶段有所帮助，你需要拓展你对工作本身的概念。我们常常将生活分割开来——有工作，也有工作之外的生活，在工作之外，我们才能找到真正的快乐和成就感。工作常常被视为赚钱的手段，这样我们才能享受我们所拥有的第二人生。即使我们从职业中获得了一定的满足感，我们仍然倾向于以这种方式划分生活。这是一种令人沮丧的态度，因为最终我们将清醒生活中的相当一部分时间都花在了工作上。如果我们把这段时间视为通往真正快乐的必经之路，那么我们在工作上度过的时间就是对我们短暂生命的一种悲剧性浪费。

Instead you want to see your work as something more inspiring, as part of your vocation. The word “vocation” comes from the Latin meaning to call or to be called. Its use in relation to work began in early Christianity—certain people were called to a life in the church; that was their vocation. They could recognize this literally by hearing a voice from God, who had chosen them for this profession. Over time, the word became secularized, referring to any work or study that a person felt was suited to his or her interests, particularly a manual craft. It is time, however, that we return to the original meaning of the word, for it comes much closer to the idea of a Life’s Task and mastery.

相反，你应该把你的工作看作更鼓舞人心的东西，看作你职业的一部分。“vocation”一词源于拉丁语，意为召唤或被召唤。它与工作相关的用法始于早期基督教——某些人被召唤到教堂生活；那是他们的职业。他们可以通过听到上帝的声音来确认这一点，是上帝选择了他们从事这一职业。随着时间的推移，这个词变得世俗化，指的是任何一个人认为适合自己兴趣的工作或学习，尤其是手工艺。然而，现在是我们回归这个词的本义的时候了，因为它更接近于人生的任务和精通。

The voice in this case that is calling you is not necessarily coming from God, but from deep within. It emanates from your individuality. It tells you which activities suit your character. And at a certain point, it calls you to a particular form of work or career. Your work then is something connected deeply to who you are, not a separate compartment in your life. You develop then a sense of your vocation.

在这种情况下，呼唤你的声音不一定来自上帝，而是来自内心深处。它源于你的个性。它告诉你哪些活动适合你的性格。在某个时刻，它召唤你从事某种特定的工作或职业。你的工作与你自身息息相关，而非你生活中一个独立的部分。然后，你便会发展出一种对自身使命的认知。

Finally, you must see your career or vocational path more as a journey with twists and turns rather than a straight line. You begin by choosing a field or position that roughly corresponds to your inclinations. This initial position offers you room to maneuver and important skills to learn. You don’t want to start with something too lofty, too ambitious—you need to make a living and establish some confidence. Once on this path you discover certain side routes that attract you, while other aspects of this field leave you cold. You adjust and perhaps move to a related field, continuing to learn more about yourself, but always expanding off your skill base. Like Leonardo, you take what you do for others and make it your own.

最后，你必须将自己的职业道路视为一段充满曲折而非直线的旅程。首先，选择一个与你的兴趣大致相符的领域或职位。这个初始位置为你提供了回旋的空间和重要的技能去学习。你不应该一开始就选择太高远、太雄心勃勃的目标——你需要谋生并建立自信。一旦踏上这条道路，你会发现一些吸引你的岔路，而这个领域的其他方面则让你感到冷漠。你会进行调整，或许会转向相关领域，继续深入了解自己，但同时也会不断拓展你的技能基础。就像达芬奇一样，你把你为他人所做的一切转化为自己的。

Eventually, you will hit upon a particular field, niche, or opportunity that suits you perfectly. You will recognize it when you find it because it will spark that childlike sense of wonder and excitement; it will feel right. Once found, everything will fall into place. You will learn more quickly and more deeply. Your skill level will reach a point where you will be able to claim your independence from within the group you work for and move out on your own. In a world in which there is so much we cannot control, this will bring you the ultimate form of power. You will determine your circumstances. As your own Master, you will no longer be subject to the whims of tyrannical bosses or scheming peers.

最终，你会偶然发现一个完美契合你的领域、利基市场或机遇。当你找到它时，你会一眼认出它，因为它会激发你那颗童真的好奇心和兴奋之情；你会觉得它恰到好处。一旦找到，一切都会水到渠成。你会学得更快、更深入。你的技能水平将达到一个临界点，让你能够从你所在的团队中独立出来，独立自主。在这个我们无法掌控太多事情的世界里，这将赋予你终极的力量。你将掌控自己的处境。作为你自己的主人，你将不再受制于专横的老板或诡计多端的同事。

This emphasis on your uniqueness and a Life’s Task might seem a poetic conceit without any bearing on practical realities, but in fact it is extremely relevant to the times that we live in. We are entering a world in which we can rely less and less upon the state, the corporation, or family or friends to help and protect us. It is a globalized, harshly competitive environment. We must learn to develop ourselves. At the same time, it is a world teeming with critical problems and opportunities, best solved and seized by entrepreneurs—individuals or small groups who think independently, adapt quickly, and possess unique perspectives. Your individualized, creative skills will be at a premium.

强调你的独特之处和人生使命，或许看似诗意空想，与现实生活毫无关联，但实际上，它与我们身处的时代息息相关。我们正在步入一个越来越少依赖国家、企业、家人或朋友来帮助和保护我们的世界。这是一个全球化、竞争激烈的环境。我们必须学会自我发展。与此同时，这个世界也充满了关键的问题和机遇，而解决和把握这些问题的最佳途径是企业家——那些独立思考、快速适应并拥有独特视角的个人或小团体。你的个性化、创造性技能将备受青睐。

Think of it this way: What we lack most in the modern world is a sense of a larger purpose to our lives. In the past, it was organized religion that often supplied this. But most of us now live in a secularized world. We human animals are unique—we must build our own world. We do not simply react to events out of biological scripting. But without a sense of direction provided to us, we tend to flounder. We don’t how to fill up and structure our time. There seems to be no defining purpose to our lives. We are perhaps not conscious of this emptiness, but it infects us in all kinds of ways.

不妨这样想：在现代社会，我们最缺乏的是对人生更宏大目标的理解。过去，宗教组织常常提供这种理解。但如今，我们大多数人生活在一个世俗化的世界。我们人类是独一无二的——我们必须构建自己的世界。我们不会简单地按照生物脚本对事件做出反应。但如果缺乏方向感，我们往往会陷入困境。我们不知道该如何充实和安排自己的时间。我们的生活似乎没有明确的目标。我们或许没有意识到这种空虚，但它却以各种方式感染着我们。

Feeling that we are called to accomplish something is the most positive way for us to supply this sense of purpose and direction. It is a religious-like quest for each of us. This quest should not be seen as selfish or antisocial. It is in fact connected to something much larger than our individual lives. Our evolution as a species has depended on the creation of a tremendous diversity of skills and ways of thinking. We thrive by the collective activity of people supplying their individual talents. Without such diversity, a culture dies.

感受到自己被召唤去完成某件事，是我们获得这种目标感和方向感的最积极方式。对我们每个人来说，这都是一种宗教般的追求。这种追求不应被视为自私或反社会。事实上，它与某种远超我们个人生命的东西息息相关。我们作为一个物种的进化依赖于极其多样化的技能和思维方式的创造。我们依靠人们贡献个人才能的集体活动而蓬勃发展。没有这种多样性，文化就会消亡。

Your uniqueness at birth is a marker of this necessary diversity. To the degree you cultivate and express it you are fulfilling a vital role. Our times might emphasize equality, which we then mistake for the need for everyone to be the same, but what we really mean by this is the equal chance for people to express their differences, to let a thousand flowers bloom. Your vocation is more than the work that you do. It is intimately connected to the deepest part of your being and is a manifestation of the intense diversity in nature and within human culture. In this sense, you must see your vocation as eminently poetic and inspiring.

你与生俱来的独特性，正是这种必要多样性的标志。你对这种多样性的培养和表达程度，决定了你正在履行着至关重要的角色。我们的时代或许强调平等，我们却误以为人人平等，但我们真正想要表达的是，人们拥有平等的机会表达彼此的差异，让百花齐放。你的职业远不止你所做的工作。它与你内心最深处息息相关，是自然界和人类文化中强烈多样性的体现。从这个意义上讲，你必须将你的职业视为充满诗意和启发性的。

Some 2,600 years ago the ancient Greek poet Pindar wrote, “Become who you are by learning who you are.” What he meant is the following: You are born with a particular makeup and tendencies that mark you as a piece of fate. It is who you are to the core. Some people never become who they are; they stop trusting in themselves; they conform to the tastes of others, and they end up wearing a mask that hides their true nature. If you allow yourself to learn who you really are by paying attention to that voice and force within you, then you can become what you were fated to become—an individual, a Master.

大约2600年前，古希腊诗人品达写道：“通过了解自己，成为真正的自己。” 他的意思如下：你生来就带有特定的气质和倾向，这些特质和倾向标志着你命运的一部分。它们构成了你内心的本质。有些人永远无法成为真正的自己；他们不再相信自己；他们迎合他人的喜好，最终戴上面具，掩盖自己的真面目。如果你允许自己通过关注内心的声音和力量来了解真正的自己，那么你就能成为命中注定要成为的人——一个独立的个体，一个大师。

STRATEGIES FOR FINDING YOUR LIFE’S TASK

寻找人生目标的策略

The misery that oppresses you lies not in your profession but in yourself! What man in the world would not find his situation intolerable if he chooses a craft, an art, indeed any form of life, without experiencing an inner calling? Whoever is born with a talent, or to a talent, must surely find in that the most pleasing of occupations! Everything on this earth has its difficult sides! Only some inner drive—pleasure, love—can help us overcome obstacles, prepare a path, and lift us out of the narrow circle in which others tread out their anguished, miserable existences!

压迫你的痛苦不在于你的职业，而在于你自己！如果一个人选择了一种手艺、一种艺术，甚至任何一种生活方式，却没有感受到内心的召唤，世界上哪个人不会感到难以忍受呢？任何天生有天赋或拥有天赋的人，都一定会在其中找到最令人愉悦的职业！世间万物都有其艰难的一面！只有某种内在的驱动力——快乐、爱——才能帮助我们克服障碍，开辟一条道路，将我们从其他人痛苦悲惨的生活中解救出来！

—J OHANN W OLFGANG VON G OETHE

-约翰·沃尔夫冈·冯·歌德

It might seem that connecting to something as personal as your inclinations and Life’s Task would be relatively simple and natural, once you recognize their importance. But in fact it is the opposite. It requires a good deal of planning and strategizing to do it properly, since so many obstacles will present themselves. The following five strategies, illustrated by stories of Masters, are designed to deal with the main obstacles in your path over time—the voices of others infecting you, fighting over limited resources, choosing false paths, getting stuck in the past, and losing your way. Pay attention to all of them because you will almost inevitably encounter each one in some form.

一旦你认识到它们的重要性，将你的个人爱好和人生使命联系起来似乎会相对简单自然。但事实并非如此。由于会遇到诸多障碍，要做好这件事需要大量的规划和策略。以下五种策略，以大师的故事为例，旨在帮助你应对人生道路上的主要障碍——他人声音的影响、争夺有限的资源、选择错误的道路、沉湎于过去以及迷失方向。关注所有这些障碍，因为你几乎不可避免地会以某种形式遇到它们。

# ↩

1. Return to your origins—The primal inclination strategy

1. 回归本源——原始倾向策略

For Masters, their inclination often presents itself to them with remarkable clarity in childhood. Sometimes it comes in the form of a simple object that triggers a deep response. When Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was five, his father gave him a compass as a present. Instantly, the boy was transfixed by the needle, which changed direction as he moved the compass about. The idea that there was some kind of magnetic force that operated on this needle, invisible to the eyes, touched him to the core. What if there were other forces in the world equally invisible yet equally powerful—ones that were undiscovered or not understood? For the rest of his life all of his interests and ideas would revolve around this simple question of hidden forces and fields, and he would often think back to the compass that had sparked the initial fascination.

对于马斯特斯来说，他们的这种倾向往往在童年时期就清晰地展现出来。有时，它以一个简单的物体的形式出现，却能引发深刻的共鸣。阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦（1879-1955）五岁时，父亲送给他一个指南针作为礼物。小男孩立刻被那根随着指南针转动而改变方向的指针所吸引。这根指针上存在着某种肉眼看不见的磁力，这个想法深深地触动了他。如果世界上还存在其他同样看不见却同样强大的力量——那些未被发现或未被理解的力量呢？在他的余生中，他所有的兴趣和想法都围绕着这个关于隐藏的力量和场的简单问题，他经常回想起最初激发他迷恋的指南针。

When Marie Curie (1867–1934), the future discoverer of radium, was four years old she wandered into her father’s study and stood transfixed before a glass case that contained all kinds of laboratory instruments for chemistry and physics experiments. She would return to that room again and again to stare at the instruments, imagining all sorts of experiments she could conduct with these tubes and measuring devices. Years later, when she entered a real laboratory for the first time and did some experiments herself, she reconnected immediately with her childhood obsession; she knew she had found her vocation.

未来的镭发现者玛丽·居里（1867-1934）四岁时，她会走进父亲的书房，站在一个玻璃柜前，那里摆放着各种用于化学和物理实验的仪器，她对此目不转睛。她会一次又一次地回到那个房间，凝视着这些仪器，想象着用这些管子和测量仪器可以进行的各种实验。多年后，当她第一次走进真正的实验室，亲自做了一些实验时，她立刻又想起了童年时的那份痴迷；她知道自己找到了自己的职业方向。

When the future film director Ingmar Bergman (1918–2007) was nine years old his parents gave his brother for Christmas a cinematograph—a moving picture machine with strips of film that projected simple scenes. He had to have it for himself. He traded his own toys to get it and once it was in his possession, he hurried into a large closet and watched the flickering images it projected on the wall. It seemed like something had magically come to life each time he turned it on. To produce such magic would become his lifelong obsession.

未来的电影导演英格玛·伯格曼（1918-2007）九岁时，父母送给他弟弟一台电影放映机作为圣诞礼物——一台带有胶片的移动电影机器，可以放映简单的场景。他非得拥有它不可。他用自己的玩具换来了它。拿到它后，他便匆匆跑进一个大衣柜，凝视着它投射在墙上闪烁的图像。每次打开它，仿佛有什么东西神奇地活了过来。创造这样的奇迹，成为了他毕生的执念。

Sometimes this inclination becomes clear through a particular activity that brings with it a feeling of heightened power. As a child, Martha Graham (1894–1991) felt intensely frustrated by her inability to make others understand her in a deep way; words seemed inadequate. Then one day, she saw her first dance performance. The lead dancer had a way of expressing certain emotions through movement; it was visceral, not verbal. She started dance lessons soon thereafter and immediately understood her vocation. Only when dancing could she feel alive and expressive. Years later she would go on to invent a whole new form of dance and revolutionize the genre.

有时，这种倾向会通过某种特定的活动清晰地展现出来，这种活动会让她感受到一种增强的力量感。玛莎·格雷厄姆（1894-1991）童年时，曾因无法让别人深刻理解她而感到极度沮丧；语言似乎不足以表达她的感受。后来有一天，她第一次观看了舞蹈表演。领舞者擅长通过动作表达某些情感；这种表达方式发自内心，而非言语。不久之后，她开始学习舞蹈，并立即明白了自己从事舞蹈的使命。只有在跳舞时，她才能感受到活力和表达能力。多年后，她继续创作，创造了一种全新的舞蹈形式，并彻底改变了舞蹈流派。

Sometimes it is not an object or activity but rather something in culture that sparks a deep connection. The contemporary anthropologist-linguist Daniel Everett (b. 1951) grew up on the California-Mexico border, in a cowboy town. From a very early age, he found himself drawn to the Mexican culture around him. Everything about it fascinated him—the sound of the words spoken by the migrant workers, the food, the manners that were so different from the Anglo world. He immersed himself as much as he could in their language and culture. This would transform into a lifelong interest in the Other—the diversity of cultures on the planet and what that means about our evolution.

有时，激发深层联系的并非某个物品或活动，而是文化中的某种特质。当代人类学家兼语言学家丹尼尔·埃弗里特（生于1951年）在加州和墨西哥边境的一个牛仔小镇长大。他从小就被周围的墨西哥文化所吸引。那里的一切都令他着迷——移民工人说话的声音、食物，以及与盎格鲁世界截然不同的风俗习惯。他尽可能地沉浸在墨西哥的语言和文化中。这最终转化为他对“他者”的终生兴趣——地球上文化的多样性以及这些多样性对我们人类进化的意义。

And sometimes one’s true inclinations can be revealed through an encounter with an actual Master. As a young boy growing up in North Carolina, John Coltrane (1926–67) felt different and strange. He was much more serious than his schoolmates; he experienced emotional and spiritual longings he did not know how to verbalize. He drifted into music more as a hobby, taking up the saxophone and playing in his high school band. Then a few years later he saw the great jazz saxophonist Charlie “Bird” Parker perform live, and the sounds Parker produced touched Coltrane to the core. Something primal and personal came through Parker’s saxophone, a voice from deep within. Coltrane suddenly saw the means for expressing his uniqueness and giving a voice to his own spiritual longings. He began to practice the instrument with such intensity that within a decade he transformed himself into perhaps the greatest jazz artist of his era.

有时，一个人的真正倾向可以通过与一位真正的大师的相遇而显露出来。约翰·柯川（1926-1967）在北卡罗来纳州长大，童年时感觉自己与众不同，与众不同。他比同学们严肃得多；他体验到情感和精神上的渴望，却不知如何言表。他开始接触音乐，更多的是出于爱好，开始学习萨克斯管，并在高中乐队演奏。几年后，他观看了伟大的爵士萨克斯管演奏家查理·“伯德”·帕克的现场表演，帕克演奏的音色深深地触动了柯川。帕克的萨克斯管中流露出一种原始而私密的情感，一种来自内心深处的声音。柯川突然找到了表达自身独特之处、表达自身精神渴望的方法。他开始如此投入地练习萨克斯管，以至于在十年之内，他便成为了或许是他那个时代最伟大的爵士乐艺术家。

You must understand the following: In order to master a field, you must love the subject and feel a profound connection to it. Your interest must transcend the field itself and border on the religious. For Einstein, it was not physics but a fascination with invisible forces that governed the universe; for Bergman, it was not film but the sensation of creating and animating life; for Coltrane, it was not music but giving voice to powerful emotions. These childhood attractions are hard to put into words and are more like sensations—that of deep wonder, sensual pleasure, power, and heightened awareness. The importance of recognizing these preverbal inclinations is that they are clear indications of an attraction that is not infected by the desires of other people. They are not something embedded in you by your parents, which come with a more superficial connection, something more verbal and conscious. Coming instead from somewhere deeper, they can only be your own, reflections of your unique chemistry.

你必须明白：要想精通一个领域，你必须热爱它，并与之产生深刻的联系。你的兴趣必须超越领域本身，甚至接近宗教。对爱因斯坦来说，你感兴趣的并非物理，而是对掌控宇宙的无形力量的迷恋；对伯格曼来说，你感兴趣的并非电影，而是创造和赋予生命活力的感觉；对科尔特兰来说，你感兴趣的并非音乐，而是对强烈情感的表达。这些童年的吸引力难以言表，更像是一种感觉——深深的惊奇、感官的愉悦、力量和高度的觉知。认识到这些前语言倾向的重要性在于，它们清晰地表明了一种不受他人欲望影响的吸引力。它们并非由你的父母植入你体内，后者与你有着更肤浅的联系，更语言化、更意识化。相反，它们源自更深层次的事物，它们只能是你自身的，是你独特化学反应的体现。

As you become more sophisticated, you often lose touch with these signals from your primal core. They can be buried beneath all of the other subjects you have studied. Your power and future can depend on reconnecting with this core and returning to your origins. You must dig for signs of such inclinations in your earliest years. Look for its traces in visceral reactions to something simple; a desire to repeat an activity that you never tired of; a subject that stimulated an unusual degree of curiosity; feelings of power attached to particular actions. It is already there within you. You have nothing to create; you merely need to dig and refind what has been buried inside of you all along. If you reconnect with this core at any age, some element of that primitive attraction will spark back to life, indicating a path that can ultimately become your Life’s Task.

随着你日渐成熟，你常常会失去与原始核心的联系。它们可能被你学习过的其他科目所掩盖。你的力量和未来可能取决于能否重新连接这个核心，回归本源。你必须在早年挖掘这种倾向的迹象。在对简单事物本能的反应中寻找它的踪迹；渴望重复一项你乐此不疲的活动；激发你异常好奇心的科目；以及特定行为所带来的力量感。它早已存在于你的内心。你无需创造任何东西；你只需要挖掘并重新发现一直以来深埋在你内心深处的东西。无论你在任何年龄重新连接这个核心，那种原始吸引力的某些元素都会重新焕发活力，指引你走向一条最终可能成为你人生使命的道路。

# ↩

2. Occupy the perfect niche—The Darwinian strategy

2. 占据完美的利基市场——达尔文策略

A. As a child growing up in Madras, India, in the late 1950s, V. S. Ramachandran knew he was different. He was not interested in sports or the other usual pursuits of boys his age; he loved to read about science. In his loneliness he would often wander along the beach, and soon he became fascinated by the incredible variety of seashells that washed up on shore. He began to collect them and study the subject in detail. It gave him a feeling of power—here was a field he had all to himself; nobody in school could ever know as much as he did about shells. Soon he was drawn to the strangest varieties of seashells, such as the Xenophora, an organism that collects discarded shells and uses them for camouflage. In a way, he was like the Xenophora—an anomaly. In nature, these anomalies often serve a larger evolutionary purpose—they can lead to the occupation of new ecological niches, offering a greater chance of survival. Could Ramachandran say the same about his own strangeness?

答：V. S. 拉马钱德兰（V. S. Ramachandran）在20世纪50年代末的印度马德拉斯长大，他知道自己与众不同。他对运动或其他同龄男孩的常见爱好不感兴趣；他喜欢阅读科学书籍。孤独的时候，他常常沿着海滩漫步，很快便被冲上岸的各式各样的贝壳迷住了。他开始收集贝壳，并进行细致的研究。这让他感到无比强大——这是一个他独享的领域；学校里没有人比他更了解贝壳。很快，他就被各种奇特的贝壳所吸引，比如异生藻（Xenophora），一种收集废弃贝壳并用于伪装的生物。在某种程度上，他就像异生藻一样——一个异类。在自然界中，这些异类往往服务于更大的进化目的——它们可以引领生物占据新的生态位，从而提供更大的生存机会。拉马钱德兰对于自己的奇怪之处能做出同样的评价吗？

Over the years, he transferred this boyhood interest into other subjects—human anatomical abnormalities, peculiar phenomena in chemistry, and so on. His father, fearing that the young man would end up in some esoteric field of research, convinced him to enroll in medical school. There he would be exposed to all sides of science and he would come out of it with a practical skill. Ramachandran complied.

多年来，他将童年的兴趣转移到了其他学科——人体解剖异常、化学中的奇异现象等等。他的父亲担心这个年轻人最终会进入某个深奥难懂的研究领域，于是说服他去医学院学习。在那里，他将接触到科学的方方面面，并最终掌握一门实用技能。拉马钱德兰答应了。

Although the studies in medical school interested him, after a while he grew restless. He disliked all of the rote learning. He wanted to experiment and discover, not memorize. He began to read all kinds of science journals and books that were not on the reading list. One such book was Eye and Brain , by the visual neuroscientist Richard Gregory. What particularly intrigued him were experiments on optical illusions and blind spots—anomalies in the visual system that could explain something about how the brain itself functioned.

虽然医学院的学习让他很感兴趣，但过了一段时间，他变得焦躁不安。他讨厌死记硬背的学习方式。他想要尝试和探索，而不是死记硬背。他开始阅读各种不在阅读清单上的科学期刊和书籍。其中一本就是视觉神经学家理查德·格雷戈里所著的《眼睛与大脑》。尤其让他感兴趣的是关于视错觉和盲点的实验——视觉系统中的异常现象，可以解释大脑本身的运作方式。

Stimulated by this book, he conducted his own experiments, the results of which he managed to get published in a prestigious journal, which in turn led to an invitation to study visual neuroscience in the graduate department at Cambridge University. Excited by this chance to pursue something more suited to his interests, Ramachandran accepted the invitation. After a few months at Cambridge, however, he realized that he did not fit in this environment. In his boyhood dreams, science was a great romantic adventure, an almost religious-like quest for the truth. But at Cambridge, for the students and faculty, it seemed to be more like a job; you put in your hours, you contributed some small piece to a statistical analysis, and that was that.

受这本书的启发，他进行了自己的实验，并将结果发表在一份著名期刊上，这让他收到剑桥大学研究生院视觉神经科学专业的邀请。拉马钱德兰对这个可以追求更符合自己兴趣的机会感到兴奋，于是接受了邀请。然而，在剑桥待了几个月后，他意识到自己并不适合这里的环境。在他儿时的梦想中，科学是一场伟大的浪漫冒险，一场近乎宗教般的对真理的追求。但在剑桥，对学生和老师来说，科学更像是一份工作；你投入时间，为统计分析贡献一点点力量，仅此而已。

He soldiered on, finding his own interests within the department, and completed his degree. A few years later he was hired as an assistant professor in visual psychology at the University of California at San Diego. As had happened so many times before, after a few years his mind began to drift to yet another subject—this time to the study of the brain itself. He became intrigued by the phenomenon of phantom limbs—people who have had an arm or leg amputated and yet still feel a paralyzing pain in the missing limb. He proceeded to conduct experiments on phantom limb subjects. These experiments led to some exciting discoveries about the brain itself, as well as a novel way to relieve such patients of their pain.

他坚持不懈，在系里找到了自己的兴趣，并完成了学业。几年后，他被聘为加州大学圣地亚哥分校视觉心理学助理教授。如同之前多次发生过的那样，几年后，他的思绪又开始转向另一个课题——这次是大脑本身的研究。他对幻肢现象产生了浓厚的兴趣——幻肢是指手臂或腿被截肢的人，但缺失的肢体仍然感到麻痹的疼痛。他开始对幻肢患者进行实验。这些实验带来了一些关于大脑本身的激动人心的发现，以及一种缓解此类患者疼痛的新方法。

Suddenly the feeling of not fitting in, of restlessness, was gone. Studying anomalous neurological disorders would be the subject to which he could devote the rest of his life. It opened up questions that fascinated him about the evolution of consciousness, the origin of language, and so on. It was as if he had come full circle to the days of collecting the rarest forms of seashells. This was a niche he had all to himself, one he could command for years to come, that corresponded to his deepest inclinations and would serve best the cause of scientific advancement.

突然间，那种格格不入、焦躁不安的感觉消失了。研究异常神经系统疾病将成为他毕生致力于的课题。这开启了他关于意识进化、语言起源等等令他着迷的问题。他仿佛回到了收集珍稀贝壳的时代。这是一个完全属于他自己的领域，一个他可以在未来数年里掌控的领域，它符合他内心深处的爱好，也最能服务于科学进步的事业。

B. For Yoky Matsuoka, childhood was a period of confusion and blur. Growing up in Japan in the 1970s, everything seemed laid out for her in advance. The school system would funnel her into a field that was appropriate for girls, and the possibilities were rather narrow. Her parents, believing in the importance of sports in her development, pushed her into competitive swimming at a very early age. They also had her take up the piano. For other children in Japan it may have been comforting to have their lives directed in such a fashion, but for Yoky it was painful. She was interested in all kinds of subjects—particularly math and science. She liked sports but not swimming. She had no idea what she wanted to become or how she could possibly fit into such a regimented world.

B. 对于松冈洋基（Yoky Matsuoka）来说，童年是一段迷茫和模糊的时期。她成长于20世纪70年代的日本，一切似乎都已为她安排好了。学校系统会把她引导到适合女孩的领域，而她的机会却相当有限。她的父母相信体育运动对她成长的重要性，很早就鼓励她参加竞技游泳。他们还让她学习钢琴。对于日本的其他孩子来说，以这种方式安排自己的人生或许是一种安慰，但对于洋基来说，这却是痛苦的。她对各种科目都感兴趣——尤其是数学和科学。她喜欢运动，但不喜欢游泳。她不知道自己想成为什么样的人，也不知道自己该如何融入这个被严格管制的世界。

At the age of eleven she finally asserted herself. She had had enough of swimming and wanted to take up tennis. Her parents agreed to her wishes. Being intensely competitive, she had great dreams for herself as a tennis player, but she was starting out in the sport rather late in life. To make up for lost time she would have to undergo an almost impossibly rigorous practice schedule. She traveled outside Tokyo for training and so would do her homework on the ride back at night. Often having to stand up in the crowded car, she would crack open her math and physics books and work out the equations. She loved solving puzzles, and in doing this homework her mind would become so completely absorbed in the problems that she was barely aware of the time passing. In a strange way, it was similar to the sensation she felt on the tennis court—a deep focus where nothing could distract her.

十一岁时，她终于展现了自己的实力。她游泳玩够了，想学打网球。父母同意了她的愿望。她好胜心极强，梦想成为一名网球运动员，但她开始这项运动的时间却比较晚。为了弥补失去的时间，她必须进行几乎难以忍受的高强度训练。她经常到东京以外的地方训练，所以晚上回家的路上她会做作业。在拥挤的车里，她经常站起来，打开数学和物理书，解方程式。她喜欢解谜，做作业时，她的思绪会完全沉浸在题目中，几乎感觉不到时间的流逝。奇怪的是，这种感觉和她在网球场上的感觉很相似——一种高度集中的专注力，任何事物都无法分散她的注意力。

In the few free moments on the train Yoky would think about her future. Science and sports were the two great interests in her life. In them she could express all of the different sides of her character—her love of competing, working with her hands, moving gracefully, analyzing and solving problems. In Japan you had to choose a career that was generally quite specialized. Whatever she chose would require sacrificing her other interests, which depressed her to no end. One day she daydreamed about inventing a robot that could play tennis with her. Inventing and playing against such a robot would satisfy all of the different sides of her character, but it was only a dream.

在火车上为数不多的空闲时间里，Yoky会思考自己的未来。科学和体育是她生命中的两大兴趣。在这两方面，她可以展现自己性格中方方面面——热爱竞争、动手能力强、优雅的舞姿、分析和解决问题。在日本，你通常必须选择一份相当专业的职业。无论她选择什么，都需要牺牲其他兴趣，这让她无比沮丧。有一天，她梦想着发明一个可以和她一起打网球的机器人。发明这样一个机器人并与她比赛，可以满足她性格中方方面面的需求，但这只是一个梦想。

Although she had risen through the ranks to become one of the top tennis prospects in Japan, she quickly realized that this was not to be her future. In practice, no one could beat her, but in competition she would often freeze up, overthink the situation, and lose to inferior players. She also suffered some debilitating injuries. She would have to focus on academics and not on sports. After attending a tennis academy in Florida, she convinced her parents to let her stay in the States and apply to the University of California at Berkeley.

尽管她一路高升，成为日本顶尖的网球新星之一，但她很快意识到，这并非她的未来。训练中无人能敌，但在比赛中，她却常常僵住，过度思虑，最终输给实力较弱的选手。她还遭受了一些严重的伤病。她不得不专注于学业，而不是运动。在佛罗里达州的一所网球学院学习后，她说服父母让她留在美国，并申请了加州大学伯克利分校。

At Berkeley she could not decide on a major—nothing seemed to quite fit her wide-ranging interests. For lack of anything better, she settled on electrical engineering. One day she confided to a professor in her department about her youthful dream to build a robot to play tennis with her. Much to her surprise the professor did not laugh, but instead invited her to join his graduate lab for robotics. Her work there showed so much promise that she was later admitted to graduate school at MIT, where she joined the artificial-intelligence lab of robotics pioneer Rodney Brooks. They were developing a robot with artificial intelligence, and Matsuoka volunteered to design the hand and arms.

在伯克利，她无法决定专业——似乎没有哪个专业能完全符合她广泛的兴趣。由于没有更好的选择，她选择了电气工程。有一天，她向系里的一位教授吐露了自己年轻时的梦想：制造一个机器人陪她打网球。令她惊讶的是，教授并没有嘲笑她，反而邀请她加入他的机器人研究生实验室。她在那里的工作展现出巨大的潜力，后来她被麻省理工学院的研究生院录取，并加入了机器人先驱罗德尼·布鲁克斯的人工智能实验室。他们当时正在开发一款人工智能机器人，松冈自愿设计机器人的手和手臂。

Ever since she was a child she had pondered her own hands while she was playing tennis or the piano or while scribbling out math equations. The human hand was a miracle of design. Although this was not exactly sports, she would be working with her hands to construct the hand. Finding at last something that suited a larger range of her interests, she worked night and day on building a new kind of robotic limb, one that possessed as much as possible the delicate grasping power of the human hand. Her design dazzled Brooks—it was years ahead of anything anyone had ever developed.

从孩提时代起，她就常常在打网球、弹钢琴，或是草草计算数学公式时，琢磨着自己的双手。人类的手真是个设计奇迹。虽然这算不上什么运动，但她会用双手来构造这只手。最终，她找到了更符合自己兴趣的发明，于是夜以继日地致力于打造一种新型的机械肢体，一种能够尽可能地拥有人类手掌般灵巧抓握力的机械肢体。她的设计让布鲁克斯眼花缭乱——它比以往任何发明都要领先数年。

Feeling that there was a critical lack in her knowledge, she decided to gain an additional degree in neuroscience. If she could better understand the connection between the hand and the brain, she could design a prosthetic limb that would feel and respond like a human hand. She continued this process, adding new fields of science to her résumé, culminating in the creation of a completely new field, one that she would dub neurobotic s—the design of robots that possessed simulated versions of human neurology, bringing them closer to life itself. Forging this field would bring her great success in science and put her in the ultimate position of power—the ability to freely combine all of her interests.

她觉得自己的知识严重匮乏，于是决定再攻读一个神经科学学位。如果她能更好地理解手和大脑之间的联系，就能设计出一种拥有类似人手触感和反应的假肢。她继续学习，不断拓展新的科学领域，最终开创了一个全新的领域，她称之为“神经机器人学”——设计拥有模拟人类神经系统的机器人，使其更接近生命本身。开拓这个领域将为她在科学领域带来巨大的成功，并赋予她最终的权力——能够自由地结合她所有的兴趣爱好。

The career world is like an ecological system: People occupy particular fields within which they must compete for resources and survival. The more people there are crowded into a space, the harder it becomes to thrive there. Working in such a field will tend to wear you out as you struggle to get attention, to play the political games, to win scarce resources for yourself. You spend so much time at these games that you have little time left over for true mastery. You are seduced into such fields because you see others there making a living, treading the familiar path. You are not aware of how difficult such a life can be.

职场世界就像一个生态系统：人们占据着特定的领域，必须在其中竞争资源和生存。一个领域里挤的人越多，想要在其中发展壮大就越难。在这样的领域工作，你往往会精疲力竭，因为你要努力博取关注，玩弄政治游戏，为自己争取稀缺的资源。你在这些游戏中花费了太多时间，以至于几乎没有时间去真正精通。你被引诱进入这样的领域，是因为你看到其他人在那里谋生，走着熟悉的道路。你没有意识到这样的生活有多么艰难。

The game you want to play is different: to instead find a niche in the ecology that you can dominate. It is never a simple process to find such a niche. It requires patience and a particular strategy. In the beginning you choose a field that roughly corresponds to your interests (medicine, electrical engineering). From there you can go in one of two directions. The first is the Ramachandran path. From within your chosen field, you look for side paths that particularly attract you (in his case the science of perception and optics). When it is possible, you make a move to this narrower field. You continue this process until you eventually hit upon a totally unoccupied niche, the narrower the better. In some ways, this niche corresponds to your uniqueness, much as Ramachandran’s particular form of neurology corresponds to his own primal sense of feeling like an exception.

你想玩的游戏是不同的：而是在生态系统中找到一个你可以主宰的利基市场。找到这样一个利基市场从来都不是一个简单的过程。它需要耐心和特定的策略。一开始，你要选择一个大致与你的兴趣相符的领域（医学、电子工程）。从那里你可以朝两个方向发展。第一个是拉马钱德兰之路。在你选择的领域内，你寻找特别吸引你的岔路（在他的情况下是感知和光学科学）。如果可能的话，你就转向这个更狭窄的领域。你继续这个过程，直到你最终找到一个完全未被占据的利基市场，越窄越好。在某些方面，这个利基市场对应于你的独特性，就像拉马钱德兰的特殊神经学形式对应于他自己作为例外的原始感觉一样。

The second is the Matsuoka path. Once you have mastered your first field (robotics), you look for other subjects or skills that you can conquer (neuroscience), on your own time if necessary. You can now combine this added field of knowledge to the original one, perhaps creating a new field, or at least making novel connections between them. You continue this process as long as you wish—in Matsuoka’s case, she never stops expanding. Ultimately you create a field that is uniquely your own. This second version fits in well with a culture where information is so widely available, and in which connecting ideas is a form of power.

第二种是松冈路径。一旦你掌握了你的第一个领域（机器人技术），你就会去寻找其他你可以攻克的学科或技能（神经科学），必要时可以充分利用自己的时间。现在，你可以将这个新增的知识领域与原有的知识领域结合起来，或许可以创建一个新的领域，或者至少在它们之间建立新的联系。你可以一直延续这个过程，直到你愿意为止——就松冈而言，她从未停止拓展。最终，你会创造出一个独一无二的领域。第二种路径非常适合信息如此广泛获取、连接思想是一种力量的文化。

In either direction, you have found a niche that is not crowded with competitors. You have freedom to roam, to pursue particular questions that interest you. You set your own agenda and command the resources available to this niche. Unburdened by overwhelming competition and politicking, you have time and space to bring to flower your Life’s Task.

无论选择哪个方向，你都找到了一个没有竞争对手的利基市场。你可以自由探索，去追寻你感兴趣的特定问题。你可以设定自己的议程，并掌控这个利基市场可用的资源。摆脱了铺天盖地的竞争和政治斗争的束缚，你拥有时间和空间去实现你的人生目标。

# ↩

3. Avoid the false path—The rebellion strategy

3. 避开错误的道路——反叛策略

In 1760, at the age of four, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart took up the piano under his father’s instruction. It was Wolfgang who asked to start lessons at this precocious age; his sister, age seven, had already started on the instrument. Perhaps it was partly out of sibling rivalry that he had taken such initiative, seeing the attention and love that his sister received for her playing and wanting it for himself.

1760年，四岁的沃尔夫冈·阿马德乌斯·莫扎特在父亲的指导下开始学习钢琴。正是沃尔夫冈主动要求在这个早熟的年纪开始学习钢琴；他七岁的妹妹已经开始学习钢琴了。或许部分是出于兄弟姐妹之间的竞争，他才主动采取了这样的做法，因为他看到妹妹因弹奏钢琴而受到的关注和喜爱，也想拥有这样的钢琴。

After the first few months of practice, his father, Leopold—a talented player, composer, and teacher himself—could see that Wolfgang was exceptional. Most strange for his age, the boy loved to practice; at night his parents had to drag him away from the piano. He began to compose his own pieces at the age of five. Soon, Leopold took this prodigy and his sister on the road to perform in all the capitals of Europe. Wolfgang dazzled the royal audiences for whom he performed. He played with assurance and could improvise all kinds of clever melodies. He was like a precious toy. The father was now earning a nice income for the family, as more and more courts wanted to see the child genius in action.

经过最初几个月的练习，沃尔夫冈的父亲利奥波德——一位才华横溢的演奏家、作曲家和教师——就看出了沃尔夫冈的非凡之处。与同龄人不同，这个男孩热爱练习；晚上，父母不得不把他从钢琴旁拉出来。他五岁就开始创作自己的作品。不久，利奥波德带着这位神童和他的妹妹踏上了旅程，足迹遍布欧洲各国首都。沃尔夫冈的表演令皇室观众赞叹不已。他演奏得非常自信，能够即兴创作各种巧妙的旋律。他就像一个珍贵的玩具。随着越来越多的宫廷希望看到这个天才儿童的表演，父亲现在为家里带来了一笔可观的收入。

As the patriarch of the family, Leopold demanded total obedience from his children, even though it was now young Wolfgang who was essentially supporting them all. Wolfgang willingly submitted—he owed everything to his father. But as he entered adolescence something else stirred within him. Was it playing the piano that he enjoyed, or simply attracting all of this attention? He felt confused. After so many years composing music he was finally developing his own style, and yet his father insisted that he focus on writing the more conventional pieces that pleased the royal audiences and brought the family money. The city of Salzburg, where they lived, was provincial and bourgeois. In general, he yearned for something else, to be on his own. With each passing year, Wolfgang felt increasingly stifled.

作为家族的族长，利奥波德要求孩子们绝对服从，即便如今年幼的沃尔夫冈才是他们真正的支柱。沃尔夫冈心甘情愿地顺从——他的一切都归功于父亲。但随着青春期的到来，他内心深处却涌动着某种别样的情感。他真正喜欢的是弹钢琴，还是仅仅为了吸引所有人的关注？他感到困惑。经过多年的音乐创作，他终于形成了自己的风格，然而父亲却坚持让他专注于创作更传统的作品，取悦皇室观众，并为家族带来财富。他们居住的萨尔茨堡是一个偏僻而资产阶级的城市。总的来说，他渴望的是别的东西，渴望独立自主。随着时间的流逝，沃尔夫冈感到越来越压抑。

Finally, in 1777, the father allowed Wolfgang—now twenty-one—to leave for Paris, accompanied by his mother. There he must try to gain a prominent position as conductor, so that he could continue supporting his family. But Wolfgang did not find Paris to his liking. The jobs he was offered seemed beneath his talents. And then his mother fell ill while there and died on the way back home. The trip was a disaster in all possible ways. Wolfgang returned to Salzburg, chastened and prepared to submit to his father’s will. He accepted a rather uninteresting position as the court organist, but he could not completely suppress his unease. He despaired of spending his life in this mediocre position, writing music to please these petty provincials. At one point, he wrote his father: “I am a composer…. I neither can nor ought to bury the talent for composition with which God in his goodness has so richly endowed me.”

最终，在1777年，父亲允许当时已21岁的沃尔夫冈在母亲的陪同下前往巴黎。在那里，他必须努力争取一个显赫的指挥职位，以便继续养家糊口。但沃尔夫冈并不喜欢巴黎。他得到的工作似乎与他的才能不相称。之后，他的母亲在巴黎病倒了，并在回家的路上去世。这次旅行从各方面来说都成了一场灾难。沃尔夫冈回到萨尔茨堡，受到了惩罚，并准备遵从父亲的意愿。他接受了一份颇为乏味的宫廷管风琴师职位，但他无法完全抑制自己的不安。他不想一辈子都待在这个平庸的职位上，为取悦这些小气的乡巴佬而作曲。有一次，他写信给父亲：“我是一位作曲家……我无法也不应该埋没上帝仁慈地赋予我的作曲天赋。”

Leopold reacted to these increasingly frequent complaints of his son with anger, reminding him of the debt he owed him for all of the training he had received and the expenses the father had incurred in their endless travels. Finally, in a flash, it came to Wolfgang: it was never really the piano that was his love, nor even music per se. He did not enjoy performing before others like a puppet. It was composing that he was destined for; but more than that, he had an intense love for the theater. He wanted to compose operas—that was his true voice. He would never realize this if he remained in Salzburg. It was his father who represented more than an obstacle; he was in fact ruining his life, his health, his confidence. It was not just about money; his father was actually jealous of his son’s talents, and whether consciously or not, he was trying to stifle his progress. Wolfgang had to take a step, however painful, before it was too late.

利奥波德对儿子日益频繁的抱怨怒不可遏，提醒他欠儿子的，是他所受的训练，以及父亲在无休止的旅行中所花费的金钱。最终，沃尔夫冈突然明白了：他真正热爱的从来都不是钢琴，甚至音乐本身也并非如此。他不喜欢像木偶一样在众人面前表演。作曲才是他命中注定的事业；但更重要的是，他对戏剧有着强烈的热爱。他想创作歌剧——那是他真正的声音。如果他继续留在萨尔茨堡，他永远都无法实现这一点。他的父亲不仅仅是一个障碍；事实上，他正在摧毁他的生活、健康和自信。这不仅仅是金钱的问题；他的父亲实际上嫉妒儿子的天赋，无论有意还是无意，他都在试图扼杀他的进步。沃尔夫冈必须迈出这一步，无论多么痛苦，以免为时已晚。

On a trip to Vienna in 1781, Wolfgang made the fateful decision to stay. He would never return to Salzburg. As if Wolfgang had broken some great taboo, his father could never forgive him for this; his son had abandoned the family. The rift between them would never be repaired. Feeling that he had lost so much time under his father’s thumb, Wolfgang composed at a furious pace, his most famous operas and compositions pouring out of him as if he were possessed.

1781年，沃尔夫冈在维也纳的一次旅行中做出了一个决定命运的决定：留下来。他再也不会回到萨尔茨堡了。沃尔夫冈仿佛触犯了什么天大的禁忌，他的父亲永远无法原谅他；他的儿子抛弃了家庭。他们之间的裂痕永远无法弥合。沃尔夫冈深感自己在父亲的掌控下浪费了太多时间，于是他以迅雷不及掩耳之势创作，他最著名的歌剧和作品如同着了魔般从他身上倾泻而出。

A false path in life is generally something we are attracted to for the wrong reasons—money, fame, attention, and so on. If it is attention we need, we often experience a kind of emptiness inside that we are hoping to fill with the false love of public approval. Because the field we choose does not correspond with our deepest inclinations, we rarely find the fulfillment that we crave. Our work suffers for this, and the attention we may have gotten in the beginning starts to fade—a painful process. If it is money and comfort that dominate our decision, we are most often acting out of anxiety and the need to please our parents. They may steer us toward something lucrative out of care and concern, but lurking underneath this can be something else—perhaps a bit of envy that we have more freedom than they had when they were young.

人生的误区通常是我们因为错误的原因而被吸引——金钱、名望、关注等等。如果我们需要的是关注，我们常常会感到内心空虚，希望用公众认可带来的虚假的爱来填补。由于我们选择的领域与我们内心深处的倾向不符，我们很少能获得渴望的成就感。我们的工作因此受到影响，我们最初可能获得的关注开始消退——这是一个痛苦的过程。如果金钱和舒适主导着我们的决定，我们通常是出于焦虑和取悦父母的需要。他们或许出于关心和关怀引导我们走向有利可图的职业，但潜伏在这背后的原因可能是别的——或许是嫉妒我们比他们年轻时拥有更多的自由。

Your strategy must be twofold: first, to realize as early as possible that you have chosen your career for the wrong reasons, before your confidence takes a hit. And second, to actively rebel against those forces that have pushed you away from your true path. Scoff at the need for attention and approval—they will lead you astray. Feel some anger and resentment at the parental forces that want to foist upon you an alien vocation. It is a healthy part of your development to follow a path independent of your parents and to establish your own identity. Let your sense of rebellion fill you with energy and purpose. If it is the father figure, the Leopold Mozart, that is blocking your path, you must slay him and clear the way.

你的策略必须双重：首先，在你的自信心受到打击之前，尽早意识到你选择职业的理由是错误的。其次，积极反抗那些将你推离真正道路的力量。嘲笑对关注和认可的渴求——它们会将你引入歧途。对那些试图将陌生职业强加于你的父母，感到些许愤怒和怨恨。独立于父母，走一条属于自己的道路，建立自己的身份认同，这对你的成长健康至关重要。让你的反抗精神充满能量和目标。如果阻碍你前行的是父亲般的形象，利奥波德·莫扎特，你必须击败他，扫清道路。

# ↩

4. Let go of the past—The adaptation strategy

4. 放下过去——适应策略

From the time he was born in 1960, Freddie Roach was groomed to be a boxing champion. His father had been a professional fighter himself, and his mother a boxing judge. Freddie’s older brother began learning the sport at an early age, and when Freddie was six he was promptly taken to the local gym in south Boston to begin a rigorous apprenticeship in the sport. He trained with a coach several hours a day, six days a week.

弗雷迪·罗奇自1960年出生起，就被培养成为拳击冠军。他的父亲曾是职业拳击手，母亲则是一名拳击裁判。弗雷迪的哥哥很早就开始学习拳击，六岁时，他被立即带到波士顿南部的一家拳击馆，开始了严格的拳击学徒训练。他每周六天，每天跟随教练训练几个小时。

By the age of fifteen he felt like he was burned out. He made more and more excuses to avoid going to the gym. One day his mother sensed this and said to him, “Why do you fight anyway? You just get hit all the time. You can’t fight.” He was used to the constant criticism from his father and brothers, but to hear such a frank assessment from his mother had a bracing effect. Clearly, she saw his older brother as the one destined for greatness. Now Freddie determined that he would somehow prove her wrong. He returned to his training regimen with a vengeance. He discovered within himself a passion for practice and discipline. He enjoyed the sensation of getting better, the trophies that began to pile up, and, more than anything, the fact that he could now actually beat his brother. His love for the sport was rekindled.

到了十五岁，他感觉自己筋疲力尽。他找了越来越多的借口逃避去健身房。有一天，他的母亲察觉到了这一点，对他说：“你为什么还要打架？你总是被打。你根本打不了架。” 他已经习惯了父亲和兄弟们不断的批评，但听到母亲如此坦率的评价，他感到振奋。显然，她认为他的哥哥注定会成为伟人。现在，弗雷迪决心要证明她错了。他带着复仇的决心回归训练。他发现自己内心深处对训练和自律的热情。他享受着不断进步的感觉，享受着奖杯的不断积累，更重要的是，他现在真的可以打败哥哥了。他对这项运动的热爱重新燃起。

As Freddie now showed the most promise of the brothers, his father took him to Las Vegas to help further his career. There, at the age of eighteen, he met the legendary coach Eddie Futch and began to train under him. It all looked very promising—he was chosen for the United States boxing team and began to climb up the ranks. Before long, however, he hit another wall. He would learn the most effective maneuvers from Futch and practice them to perfection, but in an actual bout it was another story. As soon as he got hit in the ring, he would revert to fighting instinctually; his emotions would get the better of him. His fights would turn into brawls over many rounds, and he would often lose.

由于弗雷迪在兄弟中展现出最大的潜力，他的父亲带他去了拉斯维加斯，以帮助他进一步发展事业。在那里，十八岁的弗雷迪遇到了传奇教练埃迪·富奇，并开始在他的指导下训练。一切看起来都充满希望——他被选入美国拳击队，并开始步步高升。然而，不久之后，他又遇到了另一个障碍。他从富奇那里学到了最有效的招式，并练习得炉火纯青，但在真正的比赛中，情况就完全不同了。一旦在拳击台上被击中，他就会本能地重新投入战斗；他的情绪会占据上风。他的比赛会演变成多回合的斗殴，而且他经常输球。

After a few years, Futch told Roach it was time to retire. But boxing had been his whole life; retire and do what? He continued to fight and to lose, until finally he could see the writing on the wall and retired. He took a job in telemarketing and began to drink heavily. Now he hated the sport—he had given it so much and had nothing to show for his efforts. Almost in spite of himself, one day he returned to Futch’s gym to watch his friend Virgil Hill spar with a boxer about to fight for a title. Both fighters trained under Futch, but there was nobody in Hill’s corner helping him, so Freddie brought him water and gave him advice. He showed up the following day to help Hill again, and soon became a regular at Futch’s gym. He was not being paid, so he kept his telemarketing job, but something in him smelled opportunity—and he was desperate. He showed up on time and stayed later than anyone else. Knowing Futch’s techniques so well, he could teach them to all of the fighters. His responsibilities began to grow.

几年后，富奇告诉罗奇，他该退役了。但拳击就是他的全部生命，退役又能怎样？他继续战斗，不断失败，直到最终看清了命运的真相，决定退役。他找了一份电话营销的工作，开始酗酒。现在，他痛恨这项运动——他为之付出了如此多的努力，却得不到任何回报。有一天，他几乎不由自主地回到富奇的拳馆，观看朋友维吉尔·希尔与一位即将争夺冠军的拳击手的对打。两位拳手都曾师从富奇，但希尔那边却没有人帮他，于是弗雷迪给他送来水，并给他一些建议。第二天，他又来帮希尔，很快便成了富奇拳馆的常客。由于没有工资，他继续做着电话营销的工作，但他内心深处嗅到了机会——他渴望机会。他准时到达，而且比任何人都待得晚。他对富奇的技巧了如指掌，可以教给所有拳手。他的责任开始变得越来越大。

In the back of his mind he could not shake his resentment of boxing, and he questioned how long he could keep this up. It was a dog-eat-dog career and trainers rarely lasted very long in the business. Would this turn into yet another routine in which he would endlessly repeat the same exercises he had learned from Futch? A part of him yearned to return to fighting—at least fighting was not so predictable.

他内心深处始终无法摆脱对拳击的怨恨，并质疑自己还能坚持多久。拳击是一份残酷的职业，教练很少能在这个行业里待很久。这会不会又变成他无休止地重复从富奇那里学到的那些动作的例行公事？他内心深处渴望重返拳击场——至少拳击比赛没那么容易预测。

One day Virgil Hill showed him a technique he had picked up from some Cuban fighters: Instead of working with a punching bag, they mostly trained with the coach, who wore large padded mitts. Standing in the ring, the fighters half-sparred with the coach and practiced their punches. Roach tried it with Hill and his eyes lit up. It brought him back into the ring, but there was something else. Boxing, he felt, had become stale, as had its training methods. In his mind, he saw a way to adapt the mitt work for more than just punching practice. It could be a way for a trainer to devise an entire strategy in the ring and demonstrate it to his fighter in real time. It could revolutionize and revitalize the sport itself. Roach began to develop this with the stable of fighters that he now trained. He instructed them in maneuvers that were much more fluid and strategic.

有一天，维吉尔·希尔向罗奇展示了一种从古巴拳击手那里学到的技巧：他们不再使用沙袋，而是主要跟着戴着大号护垫拳套的教练训练。拳击手们站在拳击台上，与教练进行半实战练习，练习出拳。罗奇和希尔一起尝试了这种方法，他的眼睛一下子亮了起来。这让他重返拳击台，但除此之外，还有别的感受。他觉得拳击已经变得陈旧，它的训练方法也一样。在他看来，他找到了一种让拳套训练不仅仅用于练习出拳的方法。这可以让教练在拳击台上制定出一套完整的策略，并实时向拳击手演示。它可以彻底改变这项运动，并使其焕发活力。罗奇开始在他训练的拳击手们身上发展这种技巧。他指导他们进行更加流畅、更具策略性的出拳动作。

Soon he left Futch to work on his own. He quickly established a reputation for preparing his boxers better than anyone else, and within a few years he rose to become the most successful trainer of his generation.

不久之后，他离开了富奇，独自创业。他很快就因训练拳击手比任何人都出色而声名鹊起，并在几年内成为同辈中最成功的教练。

In dealing with your career and its inevitable changes, you must think in the following way: You are not tied to a particular position; your loyalty is not to a career or a company. You are committed to your Life’s Task, to giving it full expression. It is up to you to find it and guide it correctly. It is not up to others to protect or help you. You are on your own . Change is inevitable, particularly in such a revolutionary moment as ours. Since you are on your own, it is up to you to foresee the changes going on right now in your profession. You must adapt your Life’s Task to these circumstances. You do not hold on to past ways of doing things, because that will ensure you will fall behind and suffer for it. You are flexible and always looking to adapt.

在应对你的职业生涯及其不可避免的变化时，你必须这样思考：你不被束缚于某个特定的职位；你的忠诚不在于某个职业或某个公司。你致力于你的人生使命，并赋予它充分的表达。找到它并正确地引导它，取决于你自己。别人没有义务保护或帮助你。你只能靠自己。变化是不可避免的，尤其是在我们这样一个变革的时刻。既然你是独立的，你就必须预见到你职业中正在发生的变化。你必须根据这些情况调整你的人生使命。你不会固守过去的做事方式，因为那只会让你落后并因此受苦。你是灵活的，并且总是寻求适应。

If change is forced upon you, as it was for Freddie Roach, you must resist the temptation to overreact or feel sorry for yourself. Roach instinctively found his way back to the ring because he understood that what he loved was not boxing per se, but competitive sports and strategizing. Thinking in this way, he could adapt his inclinations to a new direction within boxing. Like Roach, you don’t want to abandon the skills and experience you have gained, but to find a new way to apply them. Your eye is on the future, not the past. Often such creative readjustments lead to a superior path for us—we are shaken out of our complacency and forced to reassess where we are headed. Remember: your Life’s Task is a living, breathing organism. The moment you rigidly follow a plan set in your youth, you lock yourself into a position, and the times will ruthlessly pass you by.

如果你被迫改变，就像弗雷迪·罗奇那样，你必须抵制过度反应或自怨自艾的诱惑。罗奇本能地回到了拳击场，因为他明白自己热爱的并非拳击本身，而是竞技体育和战略制定。如此思考，他就能将自己的爱好调整到拳击界的新方向。像罗奇一样，你不会放弃已经获得的技能和经验，而是想找到一种新的方式来运用它们。你的目光着眼于未来，而不是过去。通常，这种创造性的调整会引导我们走向一条更优越的道路——我们会从自满中惊醒，被迫重新评估自己的方向。记住：你的人生任务是一个活生生的有机体。一旦你墨守成规地遵循年轻时制定的计划，你就把自己禁锢在一个位置上，时代就会无情地将你抛在身后。

# ↩

5. Find your way back—The life-or-death strategy

5. 找到回归之路——生死攸关的策略

As a very young child Buckminster Fuller (1895–1983) knew that he experienced the world differently than others. He was born with extreme nearsightedness. Everything around him was a blur, and so his other senses developed to compensate for this—particularly touch and smell. Even after he was prescribed glasses at the age of five, he continued to perceive the world around him with more than just his eyes. He had a tactile form of intelligence.

巴克敏斯特·富勒（1895-1983）从小就知道自己对世界的体验与他人不同。他天生高度近视，周围的一切都模糊不清，因此他的其他感官得以发展以弥补这一缺陷——尤其是触觉和嗅觉。即使在五岁时戴上眼镜后，他仍然能够用眼睛以外的方式感知周围的世界。他拥有触觉智慧。

Fuller was an extremely resourceful child. He once invented a new kind of oar to help propel him across the lakes in Maine where he spent his summers delivering mail. Its design was modeled after the motion of jellyfish, which he had observed and studied. He could envision the dynamics of their movement with more than his eyes—he felt the movement. He reproduced this motion in his newfangled oar and it functioned beautifully. During such summers he would dream of other interesting inventions—these would be his life’s work, his destiny.

富勒小时候非常机智。他曾经发明了一种新型桨，用来帮助他穿越缅因州的湖泊，他在那里度过了夏天，送邮件。这种桨的设计模仿了他观察和研究过的水母的运动。他不仅能用眼睛想象水母运动的动态，还能用心感受它们。他将这种运动复制到这只新奇的桨上，效果非常好。在这样的夏天，他会梦想着其他有趣的发明——这些发明将成为他毕生的事业，他的命运。

Being different, however, had its painful side. He had no patience for the usual forms of education. Although he was very bright and had been admitted to Harvard University, he could not adapt to its strict style of learning. He skipped classes, began to drink, and led a rather bohemian lifestyle. The officials at Harvard expelled him twice—the second time for good.

然而，与众不同也有痛苦的一面。他对传统的教育毫无耐心。尽管他非常聪明，并被哈佛大学录取，但他却无法适应学校严格的学习方式。他逃课、酗酒，生活放荡不羁。哈佛大学的官员两次开除他，第二次更是永久开除。

After that he bounced from job to job. He worked at a meatpacking plant and then, during World War I, he secured a good position in the navy. He had an incredible feel for machines and how their parts worked in concert. But he was restless, and could not stay too long in one place. After the war he had a wife and child to support, and despairing of ever being able to care for them properly, he decided to take a high-paying position as a sales manager. He worked hard, did a decent job, but after three months the company folded. He had found the work extremely unsatisfying, but it seemed that such jobs were all he could expect from life.

此后，他辗转多地。他先是在一家肉类加工厂工作，后来在第一次世界大战期间，在海军谋得了一份不错的职位。他对机器及其部件的协同工作有着不可思议的洞察力。但他性格焦躁不安，无法在一个地方待太久。战后，他需要养家糊口，却又无力照顾好他们，于是他决定接受一份高薪的销售经理职位。他努力工作，工作得体，但三个月后，公司倒闭了。他觉得这份工作极其不尽如人意，但似乎人生也就只能如此了。

Finally, a few months later, a chance appeared out of nowhere. His father-in-law had invented a way of producing materials for houses that would end up making them more durable and better insulated, and at a much lower cost. But the father could not find investors or anyone willing to help him set up a business. Fuller thought his idea brilliant. He had always been interested in housing and architecture, and so he offered to take charge of implementing this new technology. He put everything he could into the effort and was even able to improve on the materials to be used. Fuller’s father-in-law supported his work, and together they formed the Stockade Building System. Money from investors, mostly family members, allowed them to open factories. The company struggled—the technology was too new and radical, and Fuller was too much of a purist to compromise his desire to revolutionize the construction industry. After five years the company was sold and Fuller was fired as president.

几个月后，一个机会终于出现了。他的岳父发明了一种生产房屋材料的方法，这种材料最终会使房屋更耐用、隔热效果更好，而且成本更低。但他找不到投资者，也找不到任何愿意帮助他创业的人。富勒觉得他的想法很棒。他一直对住房和建筑很感兴趣，于是主动提出负责这项新技术的实施。他倾尽所有，甚至对所使用的材料进行了改进。富勒的岳父支持他的工作，他们共同创立了Stockade建筑系统公司。投资者（大多是富勒的家人）的资金让他们得以开设工厂。公司举步维艰——这项技术太过新颖激进，而富勒是一位极其追求纯粹主义的人，不愿放弃彻底革新建筑行业的梦想。五年后，公司被出售，富勒也辞去了总裁一职。

Now the situation looked bleaker than ever. The family had been living well in Chicago on his salary, beyond its means. In those five years he had not managed to save anything. Winter was approaching and his prospects for work seemed very slim—his reputation was in tatters. One evening he walked along Lake Michigan and thought of his life up until then. He had disappointed his wife, and he had lost money for his father-in-law and his friends who had invested in the enterprise. He was useless at business and a burden to everyone. Finally he decided upon suicide as the best option. He would drown himself in the lake. He had a good insurance policy, and his wife’s family would take better care of her than he had been able to. As he walked toward the water, he mentally prepared himself for death.

如今，情况比以往任何时候都更加糟糕。一家人靠着他的薪水在芝加哥过着优渥的生活，完全超出了他们的承受能力。五年来，他一分钱都没攒下来。冬天将至，他的工作前景黯淡——他的名声也一落千丈。一天傍晚，他漫步在密歇根湖畔，回想着此前的生活。他辜负了妻子，也让岳父和投资这家企业的朋友们损失了钱。他生意不顺，成了所有人的负担。最终，他决定自杀，这是最好的选择。他要投湖自尽。他有一份不错的保险，妻子的家人会比他更好地照顾她。他走向湖边，做好了迎接死亡的心理准备。

Suddenly something stopped him in his tracks—what he would describe later as a voice, coming from nearby or perhaps from within him. It said, “From now on you need never await temporal attestation to your thought. You think the truth. You do not have the right to eliminate yourself. You do not belong to you. You belong to Universe. Your significance will remain forever obscure to you, but you may assume that you are fulfilling your role if you apply yourself to converting your experiences to the highest advantage of others.” Never having heard voices before, Fuller could only imagine it as something real. Stunned by these words, he turned away from the water and headed home.

突然，有什么东西让他停下了脚步——后来他形容那是一个声音，来自附近，或许是来自他的内心。那声音说道：“从现在开始，你无需等待时间的检验，你思考的是真理。你没有权利自我毁灭。你不属于你自己，你属于宇宙。你的意义对你来说将永远模糊不清，但如果你致力于将你的经历转化为对他人的益处，你就可以认为，你正在履行你的使命。” 富勒从未听过任何声音，他只能想象那是真实存在的东西。这句话让他震惊不已，他转身离开水边，朝家走去。

On the way there he began to ponder the words and to reassess his life, now in a different light. Perhaps what he had perceived moments earlier as his mistakes were not mistakes at all. He had tried to fit into a world (business) in which he did not belong. The world was telling him this if he only listened. The Stockade experience was not all a waste—he had learned some invaluable lessons about human nature. He should have no regrets. The truth was that he was different. In his mind he imagined all kinds of inventions—new kinds of cars, houses, building structures—that reflected his unusual perceptual skills. It struck him, as he looked around at row after row of apartment housing on his way back, that people suffered more from sameness, from the inability to think of doing things differently, than from nonconformity.

在路上，他开始琢磨这些话，重新审视自己的人生，眼光也随之改变。或许，片刻之前他自认为的错误，其实根本不是错误。他试图融入一个并不属于他的世界（商业）。只要他倾听，这个世界就会告诉他这一点。在Stockade的经历并非全是浪费——他学到了一些关于人性的宝贵教训。他不应该后悔。事实上，他与众不同。在他的脑海中，他想象着各种各样的发明——新型汽车、房屋、建筑结构——都体现了他非凡的感知能力。回来的路上，他环顾着一排排的公寓楼，突然意识到，人们更痛苦的是千篇一律，无法思考如何以不同的方式做事，而不是不墨守成规。

He swore that from that moment on he would listen to nothing except his own experience, his own voice. He would create an alternative way of making things that would open people’s eyes to new possibilities. The money would eventually come. Whenever he thought of money first, disaster followed. He would take care of his family, but they would have to live frugally for the moment.

他发誓，从那一刻起，他只听从自己的经验和自己的声音。他要创造一种另类的制造方式，让人们看到新的可能性。钱终究会来的。每当他一心想着钱，灾难就会随之而来。他会照顾好家人，但目前他们不得不节衣缩食。

Over the years, Fuller kept to this promise. The pursuit of his peculiar ideas led to the design of inexpensive and energy-efficient forms of transportation and shelter (the Dymaxion car and Dymaxion house), and to the invention of the geodesic dome—a whole new form of architectural structure. Fame and money soon followed.

多年来，富勒始终信守着这一承诺。他对奇思妙想的追求，促成了廉价节能的交通和居住方式的设计（Dymaxion汽车和Dymaxion房屋），以及测地线穹顶——一种全新的建筑结构形式的发明。名利双收很快随之而来。

No good can ever come from deviating from the path that you were destined to follow. You will be assailed by varieties of hidden pain. Most often you deviate because of the lure of money, of more immediate prospects of prosperity. Because this does not comply with something deep within you, your interest will lag and eventually the money will not come so easily. You will search for other easy sources of money, moving further and further away from your path. Not seeing clearly ahead of you, you will end up in a dead-end career. Even if your material needs are met, you will feel an emptiness inside that you will need to fill with any kind of belief system, drugs, or diversions. There is no compromise here, no way of escaping the dynamic. You will recognize how far you have deviated by the depth of your pain and frustration. You must listen to the message of this frustration, this pain, and let it guide you as clearly as Fuller’s voice guided him. It is a matter of life and death.

偏离你注定要走的道路，绝不会有任何好处。你会被各种隐秘的痛苦所困扰。你偏离这条道路，往往是因为金钱的诱惑，以及更直接的繁荣前景。因为这与你内心深处的某种东西格格不入，你的兴趣会逐渐消退，最终金钱来之不易。你会寻找其他轻松的赚钱方式，离你的道路越来越远。看不清前方的路，你最终会陷入一条死胡同。即使你的物质需求得到了满足，你内心也会感到空虚，你需要用任何信仰体系、毒品或消遣来填补。这里没有妥协，也没有办法逃脱这种动态。你会从痛苦和挫折的深度中认识到你已经偏离了多远。你必须倾听这挫折、这痛苦的讯息，并让它像富勒的声音指引他一样清晰地指引你。这是生死攸关的问题。

The way back requires a sacrifice. You cannot have everything in the present. The road to mastery requires patience. You will have to keep your focus on five or ten years down the road, when you will reap the rewards of your efforts. The process of getting there, however, is full of challenges and pleasures. Make your return to the path a resolution you set for yourself, and then tell others about it. It becomes a matter of shame and embarrassment to deviate from this path. In the end, the money and success that truly last come not to those who focus on such things as goals, but rather to those who focus on mastery and fulfilling their Life’s Task.

回归之路需要牺牲。你无法拥有当下的一切。通往精通的道路需要耐心。你必须专注于五年或十年后，那时你将收获努力的回报。然而，通往那里的过程充满挑战和乐趣。把回归之路作为你为自己设定的决心，然后告诉别人。偏离这条道路会成为一件令人羞耻和尴尬的事情。最终，真正持久的金钱和成功并非属于那些专注于目标之类的人，而是属于那些专注于精通并完成人生使命的人。

REVERSAL

逆转

Some people do not become aware of inclinations or future career paths in their childhood, but instead are made painfully aware of their limitations. They are not good at what others seem to find easy or manageable. The idea of a calling in life is alien to them. In some cases they internalize the judgments and criticisms of others, and come to see themselves as essentially deficient. If they are not careful, this can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

有些人在童年时期并没有意识到自己的倾向或未来的职业道路，而是痛苦地意识到自己的局限性。他们不擅长别人觉得容易或可控的事情。人生使命的概念对他们来说很陌生。在某些情况下，他们会将他人的评判和批评内化，并逐渐认为自己本质上存在缺陷。如果他们不小心，这可能会成为一个自我实现的预言。

Nobody faced this fate more powerfully than Temple Grandin. In 1950, at the age of three, she was diagnosed with autism. She had yet to make any progress in learning language, and it was thought that this would remain her condition—and that she would need to be institutionalized her entire life. But her mother wanted to try one last option before giving up: she sent Temple to a speech therapist, who miraculously, slowly managed to teach her language, which allowed her to attend school and begin to learn what other children were learning.

没有人比坦普·格兰丁更能承受这样的命运。1950年，三岁的她被诊断出患有自闭症。她在语言学习方面一直没有任何进步，人们认为这种情况会一直持续下去，她需要终生接受机构治疗。但她的母亲在放弃之前想尝试最后一个选择：她把坦普尔送到了一位语言治疗师那里。这位治疗师奇迹般地慢慢地教会了她语言，让她得以上学，并开始学习其他孩子正在学习的东西。

Despite this improvement, Temple’s future appeared limited at best. Her mind functioned in a different way—she thought in terms of images, not words. In order to learn a word she had to be able to picture it in her mind. This made it hard to understand abstract words or learn mathematics. She was also not good at socializing with other children, who often made fun of her for her differences. With such learning disabilities, what could she hope to do in life beyond some kind of menial job? To make matters worse, she had an extremely active mind, and without something to concentrate on, she would give in to feelings of intense anxiety.

尽管有所改善，但坦普尔的未来似乎依然充满挑战。她的思维方式与以往不同——她思考的是图像，而不是文字。为了学习一个单词，她必须在脑海中描绘它。这使得她很难理解抽象词汇或学习数学。她也不擅长与其他孩子交往，孩子们常常因为她的与众不同而取笑她。在这样的学习障碍下，除了做一些低级的工作，她还能指望做什么呢？更糟糕的是，她的思维非常活跃，如果没有可以集中注意力的事情，她就会陷入强烈的焦虑之中。

Whenever she felt troubled, Temple instinctively retreated to two activities that were comfortable to her: interacting with animals and building things with her hands. With animals, particularly horses, she had an uncanny ability to sense their feelings and thoughts. She became an expert horseback rider. Because she tended to think first in images, when it came to making things with her hands (like sewing or woodwork), she could envision the finished product in her mind and then easily put it together.

每当感到困扰时，坦普尔就会本能地选择两项让她感到舒适的活动：与动物互动和用双手创造事物。她对动物，尤其是马，有一种不可思议的能力，能够感知它们的感受和想法。她成为了一名专业的骑马者。由于她倾向于先用图像思考，所以当她用手制作东西（比如缝纫或木工）时，她可以在脑海中想象成品，然后轻松地将其组装起来。

At the age of eleven, Temple went to visit an aunt who had a ranch in Arizona. There she realized that she had an even greater sense of empathy for cattle than she did for horses. One day she watched with particular interest as some of the cattle were placed in a squeeze chute that pressed them on their sides to relax them before their vaccination shots. Throughout her childhood Temple had had the desire to be held tightly, but could not stand being held by an adult—she felt like she had no control in such a situation, and would panic. She pleaded with her aunt to allow her to be put into the squeeze device herself. The aunt agreed, and for thirty minutes Temple gave in to the feeling of pressure she had always dreamed of. Once it was over, she felt an enormous sense of calmness. After that experience she became obsessed with the machine, and several years later managed to build her own primitive version of it that she could use at home.

十一岁时，坦普尔去亚利桑那州看望一位拥有牧场的阿姨。在那里，她发现自己对牛的同理心甚至超过了对马的同理心。有一天，她饶有兴致地看着一些牛被放进一个挤压槽，挤压槽会将它们侧卧，以便在接种疫苗前放松。坦普尔的童年时期一直渴望被紧紧抱住，但她无法忍受被大人抱住——她觉得自己在这种情况下无法控制自己，会感到恐慌。她恳求阿姨允许她自己被放进这个挤压装置里。阿姨同意了，于是坦普尔在三十分钟里完全沉浸在她一直梦寐以求的压力之中。挤压结束后，她感到无比平静。那次经历之后，她对这台机器产生了浓厚的兴趣，几年后，她自己也制作了一个简易版的机器，可以在家里使用。

Now she was obsessed with the subject of cattle, squeeze chutes, and the effect of touch and pressure on autistic children. In order to satisfy her curiosity, she had to develop reading and researching skills. Once she did, she found she had unusually high powers of concentration—she could read for hours on one subject without getting the slightest bit bored. Her research slowly expanded into books on psychology, biology, and science in general. Because of the intellectual skills she had developed, she was admitted into a university. Her horizons were slowly expanding.

现在，她痴迷于牛、挤压槽以及触觉和压力对自闭症儿童的影响。为了满足好奇心，她必须培养阅读和研究技能。一旦做到了，她发现自己拥有了异常强大的专注力——她可以连续阅读几个小时的同一主题而丝毫不会感到无聊。她的研究逐渐扩展到心理学、生物学以及更广泛的科学书籍。凭借她所培养的智力技能，她被一所大学录取。她的视野正在逐渐开阔。

Several years later, she found herself pursuing a master’s degree in Animal Sciences at Arizona State University. There, her obsession with cattle resurfaced—she wanted to do a detailed analysis of feedlots and cattle chutes in particular, to help understand the behavioral responses of the animals. Her professors there could not understand such an interest, and told her it was not possible. Never being one to take no for an answer, she found professors in another department who would sponsor her. She did her study, and in the process finally caught a glimpse of her Life’s Task.

几年后，她进入亚利桑那州立大学攻读动物科学硕士学位。在那里，她对牛的痴迷再次浮现——她想对饲养场和牛槽进行详细的分析，以了解动物的行为反应。那里的教授们无法理解这种兴趣，并告诉她这是不可能的。她是个不接受拒绝的人，于是在另一个系里找到了愿意资助她的教授。她完成了研究，并最终在这个过程中瞥见了自己人生的使命。

She was not destined for a life in the university. She was a practical person who liked to build things and yet needed constant mental stimulation. She decided she would carve out her own peculiar career path. Starting off freelance, she offered her services to various ranches and feedlots, designing cattle chutes that were much more suited to the animals and more efficient. Slowly, with her visual sense of design and engineering, she taught herself the rudiments of the business. She expanded her services to designing more humane slaughterhouses and systems for managing farm animals.

她并非注定要上大学。她是一个务实的人，喜欢创造，但需要持续的精神激励。她决定开辟一条属于自己独特的职业道路。她从自由职业起步，为各种牧场和饲养场提供服务，设计更适合牲畜、更高效的牛槽。慢慢地，凭借她对设计和工程的视觉感知，她自学了这门生意的基础知识。她将服务范围扩展到设计更人性化的屠宰场和农场动物管理系统。

With this career solidly in place, she proceeded to go further: she became a writer; she returned to the university as a professor; she transformed herself into a gifted lecturer on animals and autism. Somehow she had managed to overcome all of the seemingly insurmountable obstructions in her path and find her way to the Life’s Task that suited her to perfection.

事业稳固之后，她继续前行：她成为了一名作家；她回到大学担任教授；她又转型成为一名才华横溢的动物与自闭症讲师。不知何故，她克服了人生道路上所有看似难以逾越的障碍，找到了最适合自己的人生目标。

When you are faced with deficiencies instead of strengths and inclinations, this is the strategy you must assume: ignore your weaknesses and resist the temptation to be more like others. Instead, like Temple Grandin, direct yourself toward the small things you are good at. Do not dream or make grand plans for the future, but instead concentrate on becoming proficient at these simple and immediate skills. This will bring you confidence and become a base from which you can expand to other pursuits. Proceeding in this way, step by step, you will hit upon your Life’s Task.

当你面对的是不足而非优势和倾向时，你必须采取以下策略：忽略你的弱点，抵制效仿他人的诱惑。相反，像坦普·格兰丁一样，专注于你擅长的小事。不要梦想或为未来制定宏伟计划，而是专注于精通这些简单而直接的技能。这会给你带来自信，并成为你拓展其他追求的基础。循序渐进地这样做，你终将找到你的人生使命。

Understand: Your Life’s Task does not always appear to you through some grand or promising inclination. It can appear in the guise of your deficiencies, making you focus on the one or two things that you are inevitably good at. Working at these skills, you learn the value of discipline and see the rewards you get from your efforts. Like a lotus flower, your skills will expand outward from a center of strength and confidence. Do not envy those who seem to be naturally gifted; it is often a curse, as such types rarely learn the value of diligence and focus, and they pay for this later in life. This strategy applies as well to any setbacks and difficulties we may experience. In such moments, it is generally wise to stick to the few things we know and do well, and to reestablish our confidence.

要明白：你的人生使命并非总是通过某种宏大或充满希望的倾向出现在你面前。它可能以你的不足之处为幌子出现，让你专注于你必然擅长的一两件事。努力掌握这些技能，你会体会到自律的价值，并看到努力带来的回报。就像莲花一样，你的技能会从力量和自信的中心向外扩展。不要羡慕那些天赋异禀的人；这往往是一种诅咒，因为这类人很少懂得勤奋和专注的价值，而他们会在以后的生活中为此付出代价。这一策略也适用于我们可能遇到的任何挫折和困难。在这样的时刻，通常明智的做法是坚持做我们熟悉且擅长的少数事情，并重建自信。

If someone like Temple Grandin, with so much against her at birth, can find her way to her Life’s Task and to mastery, it means it must be a power accessible to us all.

如果像坦普·格兰丁这样的人，在出生时面临着如此多的阻力，却能够找到实现人生目标并取得成就的方法，那就意味着这种力量是我们所有人都能够获得的力量。

Sooner or later something seems to call us onto a particular path. You may remember this “something” as a signal calling in childhood when an urge out of nowhere, a fascination, a peculiar turn of events struck like an annunciation: This is what I must do, this is what I’ve got to have. This is who I am…If not this vivid and sure, the call may have been more like gentle pushings in the stream in which you drifted unknowingly to a particular spot on the bank. Looking back, you sense that fate had a hand in it…. A calling may be postponed, avoided, intermittently missed. It may also possess you completely. Whatever; eventually it will out. It makes its claim…. Extraordinary people display calling most evidently. Perhaps that’s why they fascinate. Perhaps, too, they are extraordinary because their calling comes through so clearly and they are so loyal to it…. Extraordinary people bear the better witness because they show what ordinary mortals simply can’t. We seem to have less motivation and more distraction. Yet our destiny is driven by the same universal engine. Extraordinary people are not a different category; the workings of this engine in them are simply more transparent….

迟早，总有什么东西会召唤我们走上某条特定的道路。你或许还记得，童年时，某种“东西”就像一个信号，召唤着我们：一种突如其来的冲动，一种迷恋，一种奇特的际遇，像天使报喜一样降临：这就是我必须做的事，这就是我必须拥有的。这就是我……如果不是如此清晰明确，那份召唤或许更像是溪流中轻轻的推力，让你不知不觉地漂流到岸边的某个特定位置。回首往事，你会感到命运的安排……一种召唤可能会被推迟，被回避，被断断续续地错过。它也可能完全占据了你。无论如何，最终它会释放出来，宣示它的主权……非凡之人最能彰显召唤。或许这正是他们魅力非凡的原因。或许，他们也正因为他们的召唤如此清晰地传达，并且如此忠诚于它，所以才非凡……非凡之人更能作证，因为他们展现了凡人无法展现的东西。我们似乎缺乏动力，分心的事情也更多了。然而，我们的命运是由同一个通用引擎驱动的。非凡之人并非不同类别；他们身上这台引擎的运作方式更加清晰……

—J AMES H ILLMAN

—詹姆斯·希尔曼

II

二

SUBMIT TO
接受
REALITY: THE IDEAL
现实：理想
APPRENTICESHIP
学徒制

After your formal education, you enter the most critical phase in your life—a second, practical education known as The Apprenticeship. Every time you change careers or acquire new skills, you reenter this phase of life. The dangers are many. If you are not careful, you will succumb to insecurities, become embroiled in emotional issues and conflicts that will dominate your thoughts; you will develop fears and learning disabilities that you will carry with you throughout your life. Before it is too late you must learn the lessons and follow the path established by the greatest Masters, past and present—a kind of Ideal Apprenticeship that transcends all fields. In the process you will master the necessary skills, discipline your mind, and transform yourself into an independent thinker, prepared for the creative challenges on the way to mastery.

完成正规教育后，你将进入人生中最关键的阶段——第二个实践性教育阶段，即学徒期。每当你转行或获得新技能，你都会重新进入这个人生阶段。其中危机重重。一不小心，你就会陷入不安全感，被情绪问题和冲突所困扰，这些情绪问题和冲突将主导你的思想；你还会滋生恐惧和学习障碍，并伴随你一生。趁现在还来得及，你必须汲取教训，追随古今最伟大的大师们所开辟的道路——这是一种超越所有领域的理想学徒期。在这个过程中，你将掌握必要的技能，训练你的思维，并将自己转变为一个独立的思考者，为通往大师之路上的创造性挑战做好准备。

# ↩

THE FIRST TRANSFORMATION

第一次转型

From early in his life, Charles Darwin (1809–82) felt the presence of his father bearing down on him. The father was a successful and wealthy country doctor who had high hopes for his two sons. But Charles, the youngest, seemed to be the one who was less likely to meet his expectations. He was not good at Greek and Latin, or algebra, or really anything in school. It wasn’t that he lacked ambition. It was just that learning about the world through books did not interest him. He loved the outdoors—hunting, scouring the countryside for rare breeds of beetles, collecting flower and mineral specimens. He could spend hours observing the behavior of birds and taking elaborate notes on their various differences. He had an eye for such things. But these hobbies did not add up to a career, and as he got older he could sense his father’s growing impatience. One day, his father rebuked him with words Charles would never forget: “You care for nothing but shooting, dogs, and rat-catching, and you will be a disgrace to yourself and all your family.”

查尔斯·达尔文（1809-1882）从小就感受到父亲的影响力。他的父亲是一位事业有成、富有的乡村医生，对两个儿子寄予厚望。但最小的儿子查尔斯似乎不太可能达到父亲的期望。他不擅长希腊语和拉丁语，也不擅长代数，在学校里什么都学不好。这并不是说他缺乏志向，只是他对通过书本了解世界不感兴趣。他热爱户外活动——打猎、在乡间搜寻珍稀甲虫品种、收集花卉和矿物标本。他可以一连几个小时观察鸟类的行为，并仔细记录它们的各种差异。他对这些东西很有眼光。但这些爱好并不能成为他的职业，随着年龄的增长，他能感觉到父亲越来越不耐烦。有一天，他的父亲用查尔斯永远不会忘记的话斥责他：“你除了射击、狗和捉老鼠之外什么也不关心，你会给自己和你的家人丢脸。”

When Charles turned fifteen, his father decided to become more actively involved in his life. He sent him off to medical school in Edinburgh, but Charles could not stand the sight of blood and so had to drop out. Determined to find some career for him, the father then secured for his son a future position in the church as a country parson. For this Charles would be well paid, and he would have plenty of spare time to pursue his mania for collecting specimens. The only requirement for such a position was a degree from an eminent university, and so Charles was enrolled at Cambridge. Once again, he had to confront his disinterest in formal schooling. He tried his best. He developed an interest in botany and became good friends with his instructor, Professor Henslow.
