He worked as hard as he could, and to his father’s relief he managed, barely, to earn his Bachelor of Arts in May 1831.

查尔斯十五岁时，父亲决定更加积极地参与他的生活。他送他去爱丁堡医学院学习，但查尔斯无法忍受血腥，不得不退学。父亲决心为他寻找一份职业，于是为儿子争取到了一份未来在教堂担任乡村牧师的职位。这份工作薪水优厚，查尔斯也有足够的空闲时间去追求他收集标本的狂热。这份工作的唯一要求是拥有一所著名大学的学位，于是查尔斯进入了剑桥大学。他再次面对自己对正规教育的不感兴趣。他尽了最大努力。他对植物学产生了兴趣，并与他的导师亨斯洛教授成为了好朋友。他竭尽全力学习，最终，令父亲欣慰的是，查尔斯在1831年5月勉强获得了文学学士学位。

Hoping that his schooling was forever over, Charles left on a tour of the English countryside where he could indulge in all of his passions for the outdoors and forget about the future, for the time being.

查尔斯希望他的学校生活永远结束，于是他开始了英国乡村之旅，在那里他可以尽情享受他对户外活动的所有热情，暂时忘记未来。

When he returned home in late August, he was surprised to see a letter waiting for him from Professor Henslow. The professor was recommending Charles for a position as an unpaid naturalist on the HMS Beagle , which was to leave in a few months on a several-year journey around the globe, surveying various coastlines. As part of his job, Charles would be in charge of collecting life and mineral specimens along the way and sending them back to England for examination. Evidently, Henslow had been impressed by the young man’s remarkable skill in collecting and identifying plant specimens.

八月底回家时，他惊讶地发现亨斯洛教授正在等他。教授推荐查尔斯担任贝格尔号上的无薪博物学家，这艘船将在几个月后启航，开启为期数年的环球航行，勘测不同的海岸线。查尔斯的工作职责之一，是负责沿途收集生物和矿物标本，并将它们送回英国进行鉴定。显然，亨斯洛对这位年轻人在收集和鉴定植物标本方面的卓越技艺印象深刻。

This offer confused Charles. He had never thought of traveling that far, let alone pursuing a career as a naturalist. Before he really had time to consider it, his father weighed in—he was dead set against his accepting the offer. Charles had never been to sea and would not take to it well. He was not a trained scientist, and lacked the discipline. Moreover, taking several years on this voyage would jeopardize the position his father had secured for him in the church.

这个提议让查尔斯感到困惑。他从未想过要去那么远的地方旅行，更别提成为一名博物学家了。还没等他认真考虑，他的父亲就插嘴了——他坚决反对他接受这个提议。查尔斯从未出过海，也不会适应。他并非受过专业训练的科学家，也缺乏自律性。此外，耗费数年时间进行这次航行，会危及他父亲为他争取到的教会职位。

His father was so forceful and persuasive that Charles could not help but agree, and he decided to turn the offer down. But over the next few days he thought about this voyage and what it could be like. And the more he imagined it, the more it appealed to him. Perhaps it was the lure of adventure after leading such a sheltered childhood, or the chance to explore a possible career as a naturalist, seeing along the way almost every possible life form the planet could offer. Or maybe he needed to get away from his overbearing father and find his own way. Whatever the reason, he soon decided that he had changed his mind and wanted to accept the offer. Recruiting an uncle to his cause, he managed to get his father to give his very reluctant consent. On the eve of the ship’s departure, Charles wrote to the captain of the Beagle , Robert FitzRoy: “My second life will then commence, and it shall be as a birthday for the rest of my life.”

父亲强势且极具说服力，查尔斯不得不答应，于是决定拒绝。但在接下来的几天里，他反复思考着这次航行，以及它将会是怎样一番景象。他越是想象，就越是被它吸引。或许是经历了如此被庇护的童年后，冒险的诱惑，或许是探索博物学家职业的可能性，一路上几乎可以观察到地球上所有可能的生命形态。又或许，他需要摆脱专横的父亲，找到自己的路。无论原因是什么，他很快就改变了主意，决定接受这个提议。他拉拢了一位叔叔，最终说服了父亲勉强答应。在船启航前夕，查尔斯写信给贝格尔号船长罗伯特·菲茨罗伊：“我的第二人生即将开启，它将是我余生的生日。”

The ship set sail in December of that year and almost instantly young Darwin regretted his decision. The boat was rather small and strongly buffeted by the waves. He was continually seasick and could not hold his food. His heart ached at the thought that he would not see his family for so long, and that he would have to spend so many years cooped up with all of these strangers. He developed heart palpitations and felt like he was dangerously ill. The sailors sensed his lack of seaworthiness and eyed him strangely. Captain FitzRoy proved to be a man of wildly swinging moods, suddenly turning furious over the most seemingly trivial events. He was also a religious fanatic who believed in the literal truth of the Bible; it was Darwin’s duty, FitzRoy told him, to find in South America evidence of the Flood and the creation of life as described in Genesis. Darwin felt like a fool for going against his father, and his sense of loneliness was crushing. How could he endure this cramped existence for months on end, living in close quarters with a captain who seemed half-insane?

那年十二月，船启航了，年轻的达尔文几乎立刻就后悔了自己的决定。船很小，而且海浪冲击得很厉害。他总是晕船，肚子也撑不住。想到这么长时间见不到家人，还要和这些陌生人一起度过这么多年，他的心就隐隐作痛。他开始心悸，感觉自己病得很重。水手们察觉到他不适应航海，用异样的眼光看着他。菲茨罗伊船长脾气暴躁，会因为一些看似微不足道的小事突然勃然大怒。他还是个宗教狂热分子，坚信圣经的字面意义；菲茨罗伊告诉他，达尔文的责任是在南美洲找到《创世纪》中所描述的大洪水和生命起源的证据。达尔文觉得自己违背了父亲的意愿，简直像个傻瓜，孤独感让他难以承受。他怎么能忍受连续数月这种拥挤的生活，与一位看上去半疯的船长住在狭小的空间里呢？

A few weeks into the journey, feeling somewhat desperate, he decided upon a strategy. Whenever he experienced such inner turmoil at home, what always calmed him down was to head outdoors and observe the life around him. In that way he could forget himself. This now was his world. He would observe life on board this ship, the characters of the various sailors and the captain himself, as if he were taking note of the markings of butterflies. For instance, he noticed that no one grumbled about the food or the weather or the tasks at hand. They valued stoicism. He would try to adopt such an attitude. It seemed that FitzRoy was slightly insecure and needed constant validation about his authority and high position within the navy. Darwin would supply that to no end. Slowly, he began to fit into the daily scheme of life. He even picked up some of the mannerisms of the sailors. All of this distracted him from his loneliness.

旅程开始几周后，他感到有些绝望，于是决定采取一个策略。每当他在家中感到内心翻江倒海时，总能让他平静下来的办法就是走到户外，观察周围的生活。这样他就能忘却自我。现在，这里就是他的世界。他会观察船上的生活，观察各种水手的性格，以及船长本人，就像观察蝴蝶的斑纹一样。例如，他注意到没有人抱怨食物、天气或手头的工作。他们重视坚忍不拔的精神。他会努力效仿这种态度。菲茨罗伊似乎有点缺乏安全感，需要不断确认他在海军中的权威和高位。达尔文会无休止地满足他的需求。慢慢地，他开始融入日常生活。他甚至学会了水手们的一些举止。所有这些都让他从孤独中解脱出来。

Several months later the Beagle arrived in Brazil, and now Darwin understood why he had wanted so badly to go on this voyage. He was completely mesmerized by the intense variety of the vegetation and wildlife—this was a naturalist’s paradise. It was not like anything he had observed or collected in England. One day on a walk through a forest, he stood to the side and witnessed the most bizarre and cruel spectacle he had ever seen: a march of tiny black ants, their columns over a hundred yards long, devouring every living thing in their path. Everywhere he turned he saw some example of the fierce struggle for survival in forests with overabundant life. In attending to his work, he quickly realized that he also faced a problem: All of the birds, the butterflies, the crabs, and the spiders he caught were so unusual. Part of his job was to choose judiciously what to send back, but how could he possibly distinguish what was worth collecting?

几个月后，贝格尔号抵达巴西，达尔文这才明白自己当初为何如此渴望踏上这趟旅程。他完全被这里丰富的植被和野生动物迷住了——这里简直就是博物学家的天堂。这与他在英国观察或收集到的任何东西都截然不同。一天，他在森林中漫步时，站在路边目睹了他一生中最为怪诞残酷的景象：一群小小的黑蚂蚁排成队伍，它们的队伍长达一百码，吞噬着沿途遇到的所有生物。他所到之处，都能看到在生命过剩的森林中激烈的生存斗争。在工作中，他很快意识到自己也面临着一个问题：他捕获的所有鸟类、蝴蝶、螃蟹和蜘蛛都如此奇特。他的工作之一就是明智地选择哪些东西可以送回，但他又该如何区分哪些东西值得收藏呢？

He would have to expand his knowledge. Not only would he have to spend endless hours studying everything in his sight on his walks, and take copious notes, but he would have to find a way to organize all of this information, catalog all of these specimens, bring some order to his observations. It would be a herculean task, but unlike schoolwork, it excited him. These were living creatures, not vague notions in books.

他必须拓展自己的知识面。他不仅要花无数时间研究散步时看到的一切，做大量的笔记，还要找到一种方法来整理所有这些信息，给所有这些标本分类，使他的观察结果井然有序。这将是一项艰巨的任务，但与学校作业不同，这让他兴奋不已。这些都是活生生的生物，而不是书本上模糊的概念。

As the ship headed south along the coast, Darwin realized that there were interior parts of South America that no naturalist had yet explored. Determined to see every form of life that he could possibly find, he began a series of treks into the Pampas of Argentina, accompanied only by gauchos, collecting all kinds of unusual animal and insect specimens. Adopting the same strategy as on the ship, he observed the gauchos and their ways, fitting into their culture as if one of them. On these and other jaunts, he would brave marauding Indians, poisonous insects, and jaguars lurking in the forests. Without thinking of it, he had developed a taste for adventure that would have shocked his family and friends.

当船沿着海岸向南航行时，达尔文意识到南美洲内陆还有许多博物学家尚未探索过的地区。他决心探索所有可能发现的生命形式，于是开始在阿根廷潘帕斯草原进行一系列徒步探险，只与高乔人同行，收集各种奇特的动物和昆虫标本。他采取了与在船上相同的策略，观察高乔人及其生活方式，融入他们的文化，仿佛他们中的一员。在这些以及其他的旅程中，他勇敢地面对劫掠的印第安人、有毒的昆虫以及潜伏在森林中的美洲虎。不知不觉中，他培养出了冒险的爱好，这或许会让他家人和朋友大吃一惊。

A year into the voyage, on a beach some 400 miles south of Buenos Aires, Darwin discovered something that would set his mind to thinking for many years to come. He came upon a cliff with streaks of white amid the rock. Seeing that they were enormous bones of some sort, he began to chip away at the rock, extracting as many of these remains as possible. They were of a size and kind he had never seen before—the horns and armor of what seemed to be a giant armadillo, the huge teeth of a mastodon, and then, most surprisingly, the tooth of a horse. When the Spaniards and Portuguese had first arrived in South America there were no horses to be found, and yet this tooth was quite old and predated their arrival. He began to wonder—if such species had died off long ago, the idea of all of life being created at once and for good seemed illogical. More important, how could so many species become extinct? Could life on the planet be in a state of constant flux and development?

航行一年后，在布宜诺斯艾利斯以南约400英里的一处海滩上，达尔文发现了一件让他多年后仍深思的事情。他来到一处悬崖，岩石之间有几道白色的条纹。他发现那是某种巨大的骨头，便开始凿开岩石，尽可能多地取出这些残骸。这些残骸的大小和种类他从未见过——像是巨型犰狳的犄角和盔甲，乳齿象的巨大牙齿，以及最令人惊讶的，一颗马的牙齿。西班牙人和葡萄牙人初到南美洲时，那里还没有马，但这颗牙齿却相当古老，甚至早于他们的到来。他开始思考——如果这些物种很久以前就灭绝了，那么所有生命都是一次性创造并永远存在的想法似乎就不合逻辑了。更重要的是，这么多物种怎么会灭绝？地球上的生命会处于不断变化和发展的状态吗？

Months later he was trekking through the high Andes, looking for rare geological specimens to send back. At an elevation of about 12,000 feet he discovered some fossilized seashells and deposits of marine rocks—a rather surprising find at such an altitude. As he examined them and the surrounding flora, he speculated that these mountains had once stood in the Atlantic Ocean. A series of volcanoes, thousands of years ago, must have raised them higher and higher. Instead of relics to support the stories in the Bible, he was finding evidence for something shockingly different.

几个月后，他徒步穿越安第斯山脉，寻找稀有的地质标本带回故乡。在海拔约12000英尺的地方，他发现了一些贝壳化石和海洋岩石沉积物——在如此高的海拔高度，这可谓令人震惊的发现。他仔细观察了这些化石和周围的植物群，推测这些山脉曾经矗立在大西洋中。几千年前，一系列火山喷发肯定将它们抬升得越来越高。然而，他发现的并非支持圣经故事的遗迹，而是某种令人震惊的截然不同的证据。

As the journey progressed, Darwin noted some obvious changes in himself. He used to find almost any kind of work boring, but now he could labor all hours of the day; in fact, with so much to explore and learn, he hated wasting a single minute of the voyage. He had cultivated an incredible eye for the flora and fauna of South America. He could identify local birds by their songs, the markings on their eggs, their manner of taking flight. All of this information he could catalog and organize in an efficient manner. More important, his whole way of thinking had changed. He would observe something, read and write about it, then develop a theory after even more observation, the theories and observations feeding off one another. Full of details about so many facets of the world he was exploring, ideas were sprouting up out of nowhere.

随着旅程的推进，达尔文注意到自己发生了一些明显的变化。过去，他几乎觉得任何工作都枯燥乏味，但现在他可以全天工作；事实上，有这么多东西要探索和学习，他恨不得在旅途中浪费哪怕一分钟。他培养了对南美洲动植物的敏锐观察力。他能通过鸣叫、蛋上的斑纹和飞行方式来识别当地鸟类。所有这些信息，他都能高效地进行分类和整理。更重要的是，他的整个思维方式都发生了改变。他会观察某个事物，阅读并记录它，然后在进一步观察的基础上发展出一个理论，这些理论和观察相互交织。他正在探索的世界方方面面，充满了各种细节，各种想法从天而降。

In September 1835, the Beagle left the Pacific Coast of South America and headed west for the journey home. Their first stop along the way was a series of virtually unoccupied islands known as the Galápagos. The islands were famous for their wildlife, but nothing could prepare Darwin for what he would find there. Captain FitzRoy gave him one week to explore one of the islands, and then they would be on their way. From the moment he stepped on the island, Darwin realized something was different: this small speck of land was crammed with life that was not like anywhere else—thousands of black marine iguanas swarming around him, on the beach and in the shallow water; 500-pound tortoises lumbering about the shore; seals, penguins, and flightless cormorants, all cold-water creatures, inhabiting a tropical island.

1835年9月，贝格尔号离开南美洲太平洋海岸，向西启程返航。他们沿途的第一站是一系列几乎无人居住的岛屿，被称为加拉帕戈斯群岛。这些岛屿以其丰富的野生动物而闻名，但达尔文对即将发现的一切毫无准备。菲茨罗伊船长给了他一周时间探索其中一个岛屿，然后他们就可以启程了。从踏上岛屿的那一刻起，达尔文就意识到这里有些不同寻常：这片小小的土地上充满了独一无二的生命——成千上万只黑色海鬣蜥在他周围、沙滩上和浅水中成群结队地游动；500磅重的陆龟在岸边笨拙地行走；海豹、企鹅和不会飞的鸬鹚，所有这些冷水生物都栖息在这个热带岛屿上。

By the end of the week, he had counted twenty-six unique species of land birds on this one island alone. His jars began to fill up with the most bizarre plants, snakes, lizards, fish, and insects. Back on board the Beagle , he began to catalog and categorize the remarkable number of specimens he had collected. He was struck by the fact that almost all of them represented completely new species. He then made an even more remarkable discovery: the species differed from island to island, even though they were only some fifty miles apart. The tortoise shells had different markings, and the finches had developed different types of beaks, each designed for a specific kind of food on their particular island.

到周末，仅在这座岛上，他就数出了26种独特的陆鸟。他的罐子里开始装满各种奇异的植物、蛇、蜥蜴、鱼类和昆虫。回到贝格尔号后，他开始对收集到的大量标本进行分类和编目。令他震惊的是，几乎所有标本都代表着全新的物种。随后，他又发现了一个更惊人的事实：尽管岛屿之间只有50英里的距离，但物种却因岛屿而异。龟壳上有不同的斑纹，雀类也进化出了不同类型的喙，每种喙都是为了各自岛上的特定食物而设计的。

Suddenly, as if the four years of this voyage and all of his observations had distilled in him a deeper way of thinking, a radical theory took shape in his mind: These islands, he speculated, had first been pushed up out of the water by volcanic eruptions, much like the Andes. In the beginning, there was no life to be found on them. Slowly, birds visited and deposited seeds. Various animals arrived by sea—lizards or insects floating on logs; tortoises, originally of a marine variety, swam over. Over thousands of years, each creature adapted to the food and predators that were found there, changing their shape and appearance in the process. Animals that failed to adapt died out, like the fossils of those giant creatures Darwin had unearthed in Argentina. It was a ruthless struggle for survival. Life was not created on these islands at one time and for good by some divine being. The creatures here had ever so slowly evolved to their present form. And these islands represented a microcosm of the planet itself.

突然间，仿佛四年的航行和所有的观察都让他有了更深刻的思考，一个激进的理论在他脑海中成形：他推测，这些岛屿最初是由火山喷发冲出水面的，就像安第斯山脉一样。起初，这些岛屿上没有任何生命。慢慢地，鸟类造访并播撒种子。各种各样的动物从海里来到这里——蜥蜴和昆虫漂浮在木头上；原本属于海洋的陆龟则游了过来。数千年来，每种生物都适应了那里的食物和捕食者，并在此过程中改变了自身的形态和外貌。未能适应的动物最终灭绝，就像达尔文在阿根廷发现的那些巨型生物的化石一样。这是一场残酷的生存斗争。这些岛屿上的生命并非由某种神灵一次性永久地创造出来的。这里的生物缓慢地进化到如今的形态。而这些岛屿正是地球本身的一个缩影。

On the journey home Darwin began to develop this theory further, so revolutionary in its implications. To prove his theory would now be his life’s work.

在回家的路上，达尔文开始进一步发展这一理论，其意义具有革命性。证明这一理论将成为他毕生的事业。

Finally, in October 1836, the Beagle returned to England after nearly five years at sea. Darwin hurried home, and when his father first saw him he was astonished. Physically, he had changed. His head seemed larger. His whole manner was different—a seriousness of purpose and sharpness could be read in his eyes, almost the opposite look of the lost young man who had gone to sea years before. Clearly, the voyage had transformed his son in body and spirit.

1836年10月，在海上航行近五年后，小猎犬号终于返回英国。达尔文匆匆赶回家，父亲第一眼见到他时，大吃一惊。他的体格发生了变化。他的头似乎更大了。他的举止举止也截然不同——从他的眼神中，我们可以看到一种严肃、坚定和敏锐的目光，几乎与多年前出海时那个迷途的年轻人截然相反。显然，这次航行彻底改变了他儿子的身心。

KEYS TO MASTERY

掌握诀窍

One can have no smaller or greater mastery than mastery of oneself.

一个人所能掌握的，不可以小于或大于对自己的掌握。

—L EONARDO DA V INCI

—列奥纳多·达·芬奇

In the stories of the greatest Masters, past and present, we can inevitably detect a phase in their lives in which all of their future powers were in development, like the chrysalis of a butterfly. This part of their lives—a largely self-directed apprenticeship that lasts some five to ten years—receives little attention because it does not contain stories of great achievement or discovery. Often in their Apprenticeship Phase, these types are not yet much different from anyone else. Under the surface, however, their minds are transforming in ways we cannot see but contain all of the seeds of their future success.

在古今最伟大的大师们的故事中，我们不可避免地能发现他们人生中某个阶段，即他们所有未来力量的孕育阶段，如同蝴蝶的蛹期。他们人生的这个阶段——一个主要由自己主导的、持续五到十年的学徒期——很少受到关注，因为它没有包含伟大的成就或发现的故事。通常，在学徒期，这些人与其他人并无太大区别。然而，在表面之下，他们的心智正在以我们无法察觉的方式转变，却蕴藏着他们未来成功的种子。

Much of how such Masters navigate this phase comes from an intuitive grasp of what is most important and essential for their development, but in studying what they did right we can learn some invaluable lessons for ourselves. In fact, a close examination of their lives reveals a pattern that transcends their various fields, indicating a kind of Ideal Apprenticeship for mastery. And to grasp this pattern, to follow it in our own ways, we must understand something about the very idea and necessity for passing through an apprenticeship.

这些大师们如何度过这一阶段，很大程度上源于他们对自身发展中最重要的、最关键因素的直觉把握。但通过研究他们做对的地方，我们也能学到一些宝贵的经验。事实上，仔细审视他们的生活，就能发现一种超越各自领域的模式，预示着一种通往大师之路的理想学徒期。为了掌握这种模式，并以我们自己的方式遵循它，我们必须理解学徒期的本质及其必要性。

In childhood we are inculcated in culture through a long period of dependency—far longer than any other animal. During this period we learn language, writing, math, and reasoning skills, along with a few others. Much of this happens under the watchful and loving guidance of parents and teachers. As we get older, greater emphasis is placed on book learning—absorbing as much information as possible about various subjects. Such knowledge of history, science, or literature is abstract, and the process of learning largely involves passive absorption. At the end of this process (usually somewhere between the ages of eighteen and twenty-five) we are then thrust into the cold, harsh work world to fend for ourselves.

在童年时期，我们通过长期的依赖——比其他任何动物都要长得多——来灌输文化。在此期间，我们学习语言、写作、数学、推理以及其他一些技能。这些技能大多是在父母和老师的悉心照料和关爱指导下进行的。随着年龄的增长，我们更加重视书本知识——尽可能多地吸收各种学科的知识。这类历史、科学或文学知识是抽象的，学习过程很大程度上是被动吸收。在这个过程的末尾（通常在18到25岁之间），我们就会被推入冰冷、严酷的工作世界，自谋生计。

When we emerge from the youthful state of dependency, we are not really ready to handle the transition to an entirely independent phase. We carry with us the habit of learning from books or teachers, which is largely unsuited for the practical, self-directed phase of life that comes next. We tend to be somewhat socially naïve and unprepared for the political games people play. Still uncertain as to our identity, we think that what matters in the work world is gaining attention and making friends. And these misconceptions and naïveté are brutally exposed in the light of the real world.

当我们摆脱年轻时的依赖状态时，我们还没有真正准备好过渡到完全独立的阶段。我们保留着从书本或老师那里学习的习惯，而这在很大程度上不适合接下来务实、自主的生活阶段。我们往往在社交方面有些幼稚，对人们玩弄的政治游戏毫无准备。由于对自己的身份仍不确定，我们认为在职场上重要的是获得关注和结交朋友。而这些误解和幼稚在现实世界中被残酷地暴露无遗。

If we adjust over time, we might eventually find our way; but if we make too many mistakes, we create endless problems for ourselves. We spend too much time entangled in emotional issues, and we never quite have enough detachment to reflect and learn from our experiences. The apprenticeship, by its very nature, must be conducted by each individual in his or her own way. To follow precisely the lead of others or advice from a book is self-defeating. This is the phase in life in which we finally declare our independence and establish who we are. But for this second education in our lives, so critical to our future success, there are some powerful and essential lessons that we all can benefit from, that can guide us away from common mistakes and save us valuable time.

如果我们随着时间的推移不断调整，或许最终能找到自己的方向；但如果我们犯了太多错误，就会给自己带来无穷无尽的问题。我们花费太多时间纠缠于情感问题，却从未真正抽离出来反思和学习经验。学徒期，就其本质而言，必须由每个人以自己的方式进行。完全照搬他人的指导或书本上的建议只会适得其反。在这个人生阶段，我们最终宣告独立，确立自我。但对于我们人生中这第二次教育，它对我们未来的成功至关重要，有一些重要而重要的经验教训，我们每个人都可以从中受益，它们可以引导我们避免常见的错误，并节省我们宝贵的时间。

These lessons transcend all fields and historical periods because they are connected to something essential about human psychology and how the brain itself functions. They can be distilled into one overarching principle for the Apprenticeship Phase, and a process that loosely follows three steps.

这些经验教训超越了所有领域和历史时期，因为它们与人类心理学以及大脑本身运作方式的本质息息相关。它们可以提炼为学徒阶段的一个总体原则，以及大致遵循三个步骤的流程。

The principle is simple and must be engraved deeply in your mind: the goal of an apprenticeship is not money, a good position, a title, or a diploma, but rather the transformation of your mind and character—the first transformation on the way to mastery. You enter a career as an outsider. You are naïve and full of misconceptions about this new world. Your head is full of dreams and fantasies about the future. Your knowledge of the world is subjective, based on emotions, insecurities, and limited experience. Slowly, you will ground yourself in reality, in the objective world represented by the knowledge and skills that make people successful in it. You will learn how to work with others and handle criticism. In the process you will transform yourself from someone who is impatient and scattered into someone who is disciplined and focused, with a mind that can handle complexity. In the end, you will master yourself and all of your weaknesses.

道理很简单，必须牢牢铭记于心：学徒期的目标并非金钱、职位、头衔或文凭，而是心智和性格的转变——这是迈向精通的第一步。你以局外人的姿态踏入职场。你天真烂漫，对这个新世界充满误解。你的脑海里充满了对未来的憧憬和幻想。你对世界的认知是主观的，基于情绪、不安全感和有限的经验。慢慢地，你会扎根于现实，扎根于客观世界，这个客观世界由那些使人们在其中取得成功的知识和技能所代表。你将学会如何与他人合作，以及如何应对批评。在这个过程中，你将从一个急躁、散漫的人转变为一个自律、专注的人，拥有一颗能够应对复杂事物的头脑。最终，你将掌控自己，克服所有的弱点。

This has a simple consequence: you must choose places of work and positions that offer the greatest possibilities for learning. Practical knowledge is the ultimate commodity, and is what will pay you dividends for decades to come—far more than the paltry increase in pay you might receive at some seemingly lucrative position that offers fewer learning opportunities. This means that you move toward challenges that will toughen and improve you, where you will get the most objective feedback on your performance and progress. You do not choose apprenticeships that seem easy and comfortable.

这有一个简单的结论：你必须选择能够提供最大学习机会的工作地点和职位。实践知识才是最终的财富，它将在未来几十年为你带来丰厚的回报——远胜于你在看似收入丰厚但学习机会却很少的职位上获得的微薄薪资增长。这意味着你将面临挑战，这些挑战将磨练你、提升你，你将获得关于你的表现和进步的最客观的反馈。你不会选择那些看似轻松舒适的学徒期。

In this sense you must see yourself as following in the footsteps of Charles Darwin. You are finally on your own, on a voyage in which you will craft your own future. It is the time of youth and adventure—of exploring the world with an open mind and spirit. In fact, whenever you must learn a new skill or alter your career path later in life, you reconnect with that youthful, adventurous part of yourself. Darwin could have played it safe, collecting what was necessary, and spending more time on board studying instead of actively exploring. In that case, he would not have become an illustrious scientist, but just another collector. He constantly looked for challenges, pushing himself past his comfort zone. He used danger and difficulties as a way to measure his progress. You must adopt such a spirit and see your apprenticeship as a kind of journey in which you will transform yourself, rather than as a drab indoctrination into the work world.

从这个意义上说，你必须把自己看作是追随查尔斯·达尔文的脚步。你终于可以独立自主，踏上一段将创造自己未来的航程。这是青春与冒险的时期——用开放的心态和精神探索世界。事实上，每当你在以后的生活中必须学习一项新技能或改变职业道路时，你都会重新与自己年轻时勇于冒险的一面建立联系。达尔文本可以谨慎行事，收集必需品，花更多时间在船上学习，而不是积极探索。那样的话，他就不会成为一位杰出的科学家，而只是一个普通的收藏家。他不断寻找挑战，突破自己的舒适区。他用危险和困难来衡量自己的进步。你必须秉持这样的精神，将你的学徒期视为一段自我蜕变的旅程，而不是被当作进入职场的枯燥灌输。

# ↩

The Apprenticeship Phase—The Three Steps or Modes

学徒阶段——三个步骤或模式

With the principle outlined above guiding you in your choices, you must think of three essential steps in your apprenticeship, each one overlapping the other. These steps are: Deep Observation (The Passive Mode) , Skills Acquisition (The Practice Mode) , and Experimentation (The Active Mode) . Keep in mind that an apprenticeship can come in many different forms. It can happen at one place over several years, or it can consist of several different positions in different places, a kind of compound apprenticeship involving many different skills. It can include a mix of graduate school and practical experience. In all of these cases, it will help you to think in terms of these steps, although you may need to give added weight to a particular one depending on the nature of your field.

在上述原则的指导下，你必须在学徒期中构思三个相互交织的关键步骤。这些步骤分别是：深度观察（被动模式）、技能习得（实践模式）和实验（主动模式）。请记住，学徒期可以有多种不同的形式。它可以在一个地方持续数年，也可以由在不同地方的多个职位组成，这是一种涉及多种不同技能的复合学徒期。它可以结合研究生学习和实践经验。在所有这些情况下，思考这些步骤都会有所帮助，尽管你可能需要根据你所在领域的性质，更加重视某个步骤。

# ↩

Step One: Deep Observation—The Passive Mode

第一步：深度观察——被动模式

When you enter a career or new environment, you move into a world with its own rules, procedures, and social dynamic. For decades or even centuries, people have compiled knowledge of how to get things done in a particular field, each generation improving on the past. In addition, every workplace has its own conventions, rules of behavior, and work standards. There are also all kinds of power relationships that exist between individuals. All of this represents a reality that transcends your individual needs and desires. And so your task upon entering this world is to observe and absorb its reality as deeply as possible.

当你踏入一份职业或新环境时，你就进入了一个拥有其自身规则、流程和社会动态的世界。几十年甚至几个世纪以来，人们积累了关于如何在特定领域完成工作的知识，每一代人都在不断改进。此外，每个工作场所都有其自身的惯例、行为准则和工作标准。个人之间也存在着各种各样的权力关系。所有这些都代表着一种超越你个人需求和愿望的现实。因此，你踏入这个世界后的任务就是尽可能深入地观察和吸收它的现实。

The greatest mistake you can make in the initial months of your apprenticeship is to imagine that you have to get attention, impress people, and prove yourself. These thoughts will dominate your mind and close it off from the reality around you. Any positive attention you receive is deceptive; it is not based on your skills or anything real, and it will turn against you. Instead, you will want to acknowledge the reality and submit to it, muting your colors and keeping in the background as much as possible, remaining passive and giving yourself the space to observe. You will also want to drop any preconceptions you might have about this world you are entering. If you impress people in these first months, it should be because of the seriousness of your desire to learn, not because you are trying to rise to the top before you are ready.

在学徒期的最初几个月里，你可能犯的最大错误就是想象自己必须吸引注意力、给人留下深刻印象并证明自己。这些想法会占据你的大脑，使你与周围的现实隔绝。你收到的任何积极关注都具有欺骗性；它并非基于你的技能或任何真实的东西，而且会反过来对你不利。相反，你会想要承认现实并屈服于它，淡化你的色彩，尽可能地保持低调，保持被动，给自己观察的空间。你也需要摒弃对这个即将进入的世界的任何先入之见。如果你在最初的几个月里给人留下了深刻的印象，那应该是因为你渴望学习的认真态度，而不是因为你在做好准备之前就试图爬到顶峰。

You will be observing two essential realities in this new world. First, you will observe the rules and procedures that govern success in this environment—in other words, “this is how we do things here.” Some of these rules will be communicated to you directly—generally the ones that are superficial and largely a matter of common sense. You must pay attention to these and observe them, but what is of more interest are the rules that are unstated and are part of the underlying work culture. These concern style and values that are considered important. They are often a reflection of the character of the man or woman on top.

在这个新世界里，你将观察到两个至关重要的现实。首先，你将观察到在这种环境下决定成功的规则和程序——换句话说，“这就是我们在这里做事的方式”。其中一些规则会直接传达给你——通常是那些肤浅的、在很大程度上是常识性的规则。你必须关注并遵守这些规则，但更令人感兴趣的是那些不言而喻的规则，它们是潜在工作文化的一部分。这些规则关乎被认为重要的风格和价值观。它们往往反映了高层领导的性格。

You can observe such rules by looking at those who are on their way up in the hierarchy, who have a golden touch. More tellingly, you can observe those who are more awkward, who have been chastised for particular mistakes or even been fired. Such examples serve as negative trip wires: do things this way and you will suffer.

你可以通过观察那些在层级中步步高升、拥有点石成金本领的人来观察这些规则。更能说明问题的是，你还可以观察那些比较笨拙、因为某些错误而受到严厉批评甚至被解雇的人。这些例子就像是负面的绊脚石：这样做事，你会吃亏。

The second reality you will observe is the power relationships that exist within the group: who has real control; through whom do all communications flow; who is on the rise and who is on the decline. (For more on this element of social intelligence, please see chapter 4 .) These procedural and political rules may be dysfunctional or counterproductive, but your job is not to moralize about this or complain, but merely to understand them, to get a complete lay of the land. You are like an anthropologist studying an alien culture, attuned to all of its nuances and conventions. You are not there to change that culture; you will only end up being killed, or in the case of work, fired. Later, when you have attained power and mastery, you will be the one to rewrite or destroy these same rules.

你将观察到的第二个现实是群体内部的权力关系：谁拥有真正的控制权；所有沟通都通过谁进行；谁正在崛起，谁正在衰落。（更多关于社交智力的这一要素，请参阅第四章。）这些程序性和政治性规则可能功能失调或适得其反，但你的工作不是对此进行道德说教或抱怨，而只是去理解它们，全面了解情况。你就像一位研究外星文化的人类学家，对其所有细微差别和习俗都了如指掌。你并非要改变这种文化；你最终只会被杀，或者在工作中被解雇。之后，当你获得权力和掌控力时，你将是改写或摧毁这些规则的人。

Every task you are given, no matter how menial, offers opportunities to observe this world at work. No detail about the people within it is too trivial. Everything you see or hear is a sign for you to decode. Over time, you will begin to see and understand more of the reality that eluded you at first. For instance, a person whom you initially thought had great power ended up being someone with more bark than bite. Slowly, you begin to see behind the appearances. As you amass more information about the rules and power dynamics of your new environment, you can begin to analyze why they exist, and how they relate to larger trends in the field. You move from observation to analysis, honing your reasoning skills, but only after months of careful attention.

你接到的每一项任务，无论多么琐碎，都为你提供了观察这个世界运作方式的机会。关于身处其中的人，任何细节都不容忽视。你所看到或听到的一切都是你解读的信号。随着时间的推移，你会开始看清并理解更多最初被你忽略的现实。例如，一个你最初认为权势显赫的人，最终却变成了一个只会咆哮却不会攻击的人。慢慢地，你开始看透表象背后的真相。随着你积累了更多关于新环境规则和权力动态的信息，你就能开始分析它们存在的原因，以及它们与该领域更大趋势的关系。你从观察走向分析，磨练你的推理能力，但这需要数月的悉心关注。

We can see how Charles Darwin followed this step quite clearly. By spending the first few months studying life on board the ship and perceiving the unwritten rules, he made his time for science much more productive. By enabling himself to fit in, he was able to avoid needless battles that would have later disrupted his scientific work, not to mention the emotional turmoil these would have presented to him. He later practiced the same technique with gauchos and other local communities he came in contact with. This allowed him to extend the regions he could explore and the specimens he could collect. On another level, he slowly transformed himself into perhaps the most astute observer of nature the world has ever known. Emptying himself of any preconceptions about life and its origins, Darwin trained himself to see things as they are. He did not theorize or generalize about what he was seeing until he had amassed enough information. Submitting to and absorbing the reality of all aspects of this voyage , he ended up piercing one of the most fundamental realities of all—the evolution of all living forms.

我们可以清楚地看到查尔斯·达尔文是如何遵循这一步骤的。通过在最初的几个月里研究船上的生活，并理解那些不成文的规则，他让自己的科研时间更加富有成效。通过让自己融入其中，他避免了不必要的争斗，这些争斗可能会在日后扰乱他的科研工作，更不用说这些争斗可能给他带来的情感波动了。后来，他与高乔人和其他他接触过的当地社群也运用了同样的技巧。这让他能够探索的区域和收集的标本数量得以扩大。在另一个层面上，他逐渐将自己打造成了或许是世界上最敏锐的自然观察者。达尔文摒弃了对生命及其起源的任何先入之见，训练自己如实地观察事物。在积累了足够的信息之前，他不会对所见所闻进行理论化或概括化。他坦然接受并吸收了这次航行中方方面面的现实，最终洞悉了所有生命形式中最根本的真理之一——所有生命形式的进化。

Understand: there are several critical reasons why you must follow this step. First, knowing your environment inside and out will help you in navigating it and avoiding costly mistakes. You are like a hunter: your knowledge of every detail of the forest and of the ecosystem as a whole will give you many more options for survival and success. Second, the ability to observe any unfamiliar environment will become a critical lifelong skill. You will develop the habit of stilling your ego and looking outward instead of inward. You will see in any encounter what most people miss because they are thinking of themselves. You will cultivate a keen eye for human psychology, and strengthen your ability to focus. Finally, you will become accustomed to observing first, basing your ideas and theories on what you have seen with your eyes, and then analyzing what you find. This will be a very important skill for the next, creative phase in life.

理解：有几个关键原因促使你必须遵循这一步。首先，彻底了解你所处的环境将有助于你更好地应对，避免代价高昂的错误。你就像一个猎人：你对森林和整个生态系统的每一个细节的了解，将为你提供更多生存和成功的选择。其次，观察任何陌生环境的能力将成为一项至关重要的终身技能。你将养成放下自我、向外看而不是向内看的习惯。你将在任何遭遇中发现大多数人因为只考虑自己而忽略的东西。你将培养出敏锐的洞察力，洞察人类心理，并增强你的专注力。最后，你将习惯于先观察，将你的想法和理论建立在你亲眼所见的基础上，然后再分析你的发现。这将是人生下一个创造性阶段中一项非常重要的技能。

# ↩

Step Two: Skills Acquisition—The Practice Mode

第二步：技能习得——练习模式

At some point, as you progress through these initial months of observation, you will enter the most critical part of the apprenticeship: practice toward the acquisition of skills . Every human activity, endeavor, or career path involves the mastering of skills. In some fields, it is direct and obvious, like operating a tool or machine or creating something physical. In others, it is more of a mix of the physical and mental, such as the observing and collecting of specimens for Charles Darwin. In still others, the skills are more nebulous, such as handling people or researching and organizing information. As much as possible, you want to reduce these skills to something simple and essential—the core of what you need to get good at, skills that can be practiced.

随着最初几个月的观察逐渐深入，你将进入学徒期最关键的阶段：通过练习掌握技能。每一项人类活动、努力或职业道路都离不开技能的掌握。在某些领域，技能的掌握是直接而明显的，例如操作工具或机器，或者创造实物。在其他领域，技能的掌握则更多地是体力和脑力的结合，例如为查尔斯·达尔文观察和收集标本。还有一些领域，技能的掌握则更加模糊，例如与人打交道或研究和组织信息。你应该尽可能地将这些技能简化为简单而必要的技能——你需要精通的核心技能，这些技能是可以练习的。

In acquiring any kind of skill, there exists a natural learning process that coincides with the functioning of our brains. This learning process leads to what we shall call tacit knowledg e—a feeling for what you are doing that is hard to put into words but easy to demonstrate in action. And to understand how this learning process operates, it is useful to look at the greatest system ever invented for the training of skills and the achievement of tacit knowledge—the apprenticeship system of the Middle Ages.

在习得任何技能的过程中，都存在一个与大脑运作相呼应的自然学习过程。这个学习过程会形成我们称之为“隐性知识”的东西——一种对所做之事的感受，这种感受难以言表，却易于在行动中展现。为了理解这一学习过程的运作方式，不妨看看有史以来最伟大的技能训练和隐性知识获取体系——中世纪的学徒制。

This system arose as a solution to a problem: As business expanded in the Middle Ages, Masters of various crafts could no longer depend on family members to work in the shop. They needed more hands. But it was not worth it for them to bring in people who would come and go—they needed stability and time to build up skills in their workers. And so they developed the apprenticeship system, in which young people from approximately the ages of twelve to seventeen would enter work in a shop, signing a contract that would commit them for the term of seven years. At the end of this term, apprentices would have to pass a master test , or produce a master work , to prove their level of skill. Once passed, they were now elevated to the rank of journeymen and could travel wherever there was work, practicing the craft.

这一制度的出现是为了解决一个问题：随着中世纪商业的扩张，各种手艺的师傅们再也无法依靠家人在店里工作。他们需要更多的人手。但对于他们来说，引进来来往往的人并不值得——他们需要稳定和时间来培养工人的技能。因此，他们发展了学徒制，让大约十二到十七岁的年轻人进入一家店里工作，签订一份为期七年的合同。期满后，学徒们必须通过师傅测试，或者制作出一件大师级的作品，以证明他们的技能水平。一旦通过测试，他们就被提升为熟练工，可以前往任何有工作机会的地方练习手艺。

Because few books or drawings existed at the time, apprentices would learn the trade by watching Masters and imitating them as closely as possible. They learned through endless repetition and hands-on work, with very little verbal instruction (the word “apprentice” itself comes from the Latin prehendere , meaning to grasp with the hand). Because resources such as textiles, wood, and metals were expensive and could not be wasted on practice runs, apprentices would spend most of their time working directly on materials that would be used for the final product. They had to learn how to focus deeply on their work and not make mistakes.

由于当时书籍和图纸稀缺，学徒们只能通过观察师傅并尽可能地模仿来学习这门手艺。他们通过不断的重复和亲自动手的工作来学习，几乎没有口头指导（“学徒”一词源于拉丁语“prehendere”，意为用手抓握）。由于纺织品、木材和金属等资源价格昂贵，不能浪费在练习上，学徒们大部分时间都会直接在最终产品所需的材料上进行操作。他们必须学会如何全身心投入工作，避免犯错。

If one added up the time that apprentices ended up working directly on materials in those years, it would amount to more than 10,000 hours, enough to establish exceptional skill level at a craft. The power of this form of tacit knowledge is embodied in the great Gothic cathedrals of Europe—masterpieces of beauty, craftsmanship, and stability, all erected without blueprints or books. These cathedrals represented the accumulated skills of numerous craftsmen and engineers.

如果把学徒们当年直接在材料上工作的时间加起来，总计超过10000小时，足以培养出一门技艺非凡的技艺。这种隐性知识的力量体现在欧洲那些伟大的哥特式教堂中——它们集美感、工艺和稳定性于一身，无需蓝图或书籍即可建成。这些教堂凝聚了无数工匠和工程师的精湛技艺。

What this means is simple: language, oral and written, is a relatively recent invention. Well before that time, our ancestors had to learn various skills—toolmaking, hunting, and so forth. The natural model for learning, largely based on the power of mirror neurons, came from watching and imitating others, then repeating the action over and over. Our brains are highly suited for this form of learning.

这意味着很简单：语言，无论是口头的还是书面的，都是相对较新的发明。早在那之前，我们的祖先就必须学习各种技能——制造工具、狩猎等等。自然的学习模式主要基于镜像神经元的力量，即观察和模仿他人，然后一遍又一遍地重复这些动作。我们的大脑非常适合这种学习方式。

In an activity such as riding a bicycle, we all know that it is easier to watch someone and follow their lead than to listen to or read instructions. The more we do it, the easier it becomes. Even with skills that are primarily mental, such as computer programming or speaking a foreign language, it remains the case that we learn best through practice and repetition—the natural learning process. We learn a foreign language by actually speaking it as much as possible, not by reading books and absorbing theories. The more we speak and practice, the more fluent we become.

在骑自行车这样的活动中，我们都知道，观察别人并效仿他们比听取或阅读说明更容易。我们练习得越多，就越容易。即使是一些主要依赖心智的技能，例如计算机编程或说外语，我们仍然认为练习和重复是学习的最佳方式——这是自然的学习过程。我们学习外语的方式是尽可能多地实际说出来，而不是通过阅读书籍和吸收理论。我们说得越多、练习得越多，我们的语言就越流利。

Once you take this far enough, you enter a cycle of accelerated returns in which the practice becomes easier and more interesting, leading to the ability to practice for longer hours, which increases your skill level, which in turn makes practice even more interesting. Reaching this cycle is the goal you must set for yourself, and to get there you must understand some basic principles about skills themselves.

一旦你达到这个程度，你就会进入一个加速回报的循环，练习会变得更容易、更有趣，从而能够练习更长时间，从而提高你的技能水平，这反过来又会让练习变得更有趣。达到这个循环是你必须为自己设定的目标，而要实现它，你必须了解一些关于技能本身的基本原则。

First, it is essential that you begin with one skill that you can master, and that serves as a foundation for acquiring others. You must avoid at all cost the idea that you can manage learning several skills at a time. You need to develop your powers of concentration, and understand that trying to multitask will be the death of the process.

首先，你必须从一项你能掌握的技能开始，并以此为基础学习其他技能。你必须不惜一切代价，避免认为自己可以同时学习多项技能。你需要培养专注力，并明白试图同时处理多项任务只会毁掉学习过程。

Second, the initial stages of learning a skill invariably involve tedium. Yet rather than avoiding this inevitable tedium, you must accept and embrace it. The pain and boredom we experience in the initial stage of learning a skill toughens our minds, much like physical exercise. Too many people believe that everything must be pleasurable in life, which makes them constantly search for distractions and short-circuits the learning process. The pain is a kind of challenge your mind presents—will you learn how to focus and move past the boredom, or like a child will you succumb to the need for immediate pleasure and distraction? Much as with physical exercise, you can even get a kind of perverse pleasure out of this pain, knowing the benefits it will bring you. In any event, you must meet any boredom head-on and not try to avoid or repress it. Throughout your life you will encounter tedious situations, and you must cultivate the ability to handle them with discipline.

其次，学习一项技能的初始阶段难免会感到乏味。然而，与其逃避这种不可避免的乏味，不如接受并拥抱它。我们在学习一项技能的初始阶段所经历的痛苦和无聊，就像体育锻炼一样，会磨练我们的心智。太多人认为生活中的一切都必须是快乐的，这让他们不断寻找分心的事情，从而缩短了学习过程。这种痛苦是对你的思维的一种挑战——你会学会集中注意力，摆脱无聊，还是会像孩子一样，屈服于对即时快乐和消遣的渴望？就像体育锻炼一样，你甚至可以从这种痛苦中获得一种反常的快乐，因为你知道它会给你带来好处。无论如何，你必须直面任何无聊，而不是试图逃避或压抑它。在你的一生中，你会遇到各种乏味的情况，你必须培养自律地应对它们的能力。

In practicing a skill in the initial stages, something happens neurologically to the brain that is important for you to understand. When you start something new, a large number of neurons in the frontal cortex (the higher, more conscious command area of the brain) are recruited and become active, helping you in the learning process. The brain has to deal with a large amount of new information, and this would be stressful and overwhelming if only a limited part of the brain were used to handle it. The frontal cortex even expands in size in this initial phase, as we focus hard on the task. But once something is repeated often enough, it becomes hardwired and automatic, and the neural pathways for this skill are delegated to other parts of the brain, farther down the cortex. Those neurons in the frontal cortex that we needed in the initial stages are now freed up to help in learning something else, and the area goes back to its normal size.

在练习一项技能的初始阶段，大脑会发生一些神经学上的变化，这对你理解这一点至关重要。当你开始学习新事物时，额叶皮层（大脑中更高级、更负责意识的指挥区域）中的大量神经元会被激活，从而帮助你学习。大脑需要处理大量的新信息，如果只使用有限的大脑区域来处理，就会让人感到压力重重，难以承受。在初始阶段，当我们全身心投入这项任务时，额叶皮层的大小甚至会扩大。但一旦某件事重复得足够多，它就会变得根深蒂固、自动化，负责这项技能的神经通路就会被委托到大脑的其他区域，也就是皮层更深处。那些在初始阶段我们需要的额叶皮层神经元现在被释放出来，用来帮助我们学习其他内容，额叶皮层也会恢复到正常大小。

In the end, an entire network of neurons is developed to remember this single task, which accounts for the fact that we can still ride a bicycle years after we first learned how to do so. If we were to take a look at the frontal cortex of those who have mastered something through repetition, it would be remarkably still and inactive as they performed the skill. All of their brain activity is occurring in areas that are lower down and require much less conscious control.

最终，一个完整的神经元网络会发展起来，用来记住这一项简单的任务，这解释了为什么我们学会骑自行车多年后还能继续骑。如果我们观察那些通过重复掌握技能的人的额叶皮层，会发现他们在执行这项技能时，额叶皮层会异常地静止和不活跃。他们所有的大脑活动都发生在脑下部，需要更少的意识控制的区域。

This process of hardwiring cannot occur if you are constantly distracted, moving from one task to another. In such a case, the neural pathways dedicated to this skill never get established; what you learn is too tenuous to remain rooted in the brain. It is better to dedicate two or three hours of intense focus to a skill than to spend eight hours of diffused concentration on it. You want to be as immediately present to what you are doing as possible.

如果你经常分心，从一个任务转到另一个任务，这种硬连接过程就无法发生。在这种情况下，负责这项技能的神经通路就无法建立；你学到的知识太过脆弱，无法在大脑中扎根。与其花八个小时分散注意力，不如花两三个小时专注于一项技能。你应该尽可能地专注于你正在做的事情。

Once an action becomes automatic, you now have the mental space to observe yourself as you practice. You must use this distance to take note of your weaknesses or flaws that need correction—to analyze yourself. It helps also to gain as much feedback as possible from others, to have standards against which you can measure your progress so that you are aware of how far you have to go. People who do not practice and learn new skills never gain a proper sense of proportion or self-criticism. They think they can achieve anything without effort and have little contact with reality. Trying something over and over again grounds you in reality, making you deeply aware of your inadequacies and of what you can accomplish with more work and effort.

一旦某个动作变成自动化，你就有了精神空间来观察自己练习的过程。你必须利用这段距离来留意自己需要改正的弱点或缺陷——分析自己。这也有助于尽可能多地从他人那里获得反馈，建立衡量进步的标准，从而了解自己还有多远的路要走。不练习和不学习新技能的人永远无法获得正确的分寸感或自我批评。他们认为自己可以不费吹灰之力就取得任何成就，很少接触现实。反复尝试某件事会让你脚踏实地，深刻认识到自己的不足，以及只要付出更多努力就能取得什么样的成就。

If you take this far enough, you will naturally enter the cycle of accelerated returns: As you learn and gain skills you can begin to vary what you do, finding nuances that you can develop in the work, so that it becomes more interesting. As elements become more automatic your mind is not exhausted by the effort and you can practice harder, which in turn brings greater skill and more pleasure. You can look for challenges, new areas to conquer, keeping your interest at a high level. As the cycle accelerates, you can reach a point where your mind is totally absorbed in the practice, entering a kind of flow in which everything else is blocked out. You become one with the tool or instrument or thing you are studying. Your skill is not something that can be put into words; it is embedded in your body and nervous system—it becomes tacit knowledge. Learning any kind of skill deeply prepares you for mastery. The sensation of flow and of being a part of the instrument is a precursor to the great pleasures that mastery can bring.

如果你足够深入地理解这一点，你自然会进入加速回报的循环：随着学习和技能的积累，你可以开始改变你的工作方式，找到可以在工作中发展的细节，从而使工作变得更有趣。随着元素变得更加自动化，你的大脑不会因努力而疲惫不堪，你可以更加努力地练习，这反过来会带来更高的技能和更多的乐趣。你可以寻找挑战，探索新的领域，保持高水平的兴趣。随着循环的加速，你会达到一个点，你的思想完全沉浸在练习中，进入一种心流状态，其他一切都被屏蔽。你会与你正在学习的工具、仪器或事物融为一体。你的技能无法用语言表达；它根植于你的身体和神经系统——成为隐性知识。学习任何一种技能都能为你精通做好充分的准备。心流的感觉以及成为工具一部分的感觉，是精通带来的巨大乐趣的先兆。

In essence, when you practice and develop any skill you transform yourself in the process. You reveal to yourself new capabilities that were previously latent, that are exposed as you progress. You develop emotionally. Your sense of pleasure becomes redefined. What offers immediate pleasure comes to seem like a distraction, an empty entertainment to help pass the time. Real pleasure comes from overcoming challenges, feeling confidence in your abilities, gaining fluency in skills, and experiencing the power this brings. You develop patience. Boredom no longer signals the need for distraction, but rather the need for new challenges to conquer.

本质上，当你练习和发展任何技能时，你都会在这个过程中改变自己。你会发现自己潜藏的全新能力，这些能力会随着你的进步而逐渐显露出来。你的情感也会得到发展。你的愉悦感会被重新定义。那些能带来即时愉悦的东西，最终会变成一种消遣，一种用来打发时间的空洞娱乐。真正的快乐来自于克服挑战，对自己的能力充满信心，技能的精进，以及由此带来的力量。你会培养耐心。无聊不再意味着需要分心，而是意味着需要征服新的挑战。

Although it might seem that the time necessary to master the requisite skills and attain a level of expertise would depend on the field and your own talent level, those who have researched the subject repeatedly come up with the number of 10,000 hours. This seems to be the amount of quality practice time that is needed for someone to reach a high level of skill and it applies to composers, chess players, writers, and athletes, among others. This number has an almost magical or mystical resonance to it. It means that so much practice time—no matter the person or the field—leads to a qualitative change in the human brain. The mind has learned to organize and structure large amounts of information. With all of this tacit knowledge, it can now become creative and playful with it. Although the number of hours might seem high, it generally adds up to seven to ten years of sustained, solid practice—roughly the period of a traditional apprenticeship. In other words, concentrated practice over time cannot fail but produce results.

虽然掌握必备技能并达到一定专业水平所需的时间似乎取决于领域和个人天赋，但那些反复研究该主题的人最终得出了10,000小时这个数字。这似乎是一个人达到高水平技能所需的高质量练习时间，适用于作曲家、棋手、作家和运动员等等。这个数字几乎具有一种神奇或神秘的共鸣。这意味着，如此多的练习时间——无论个人或领域——都会导致人脑发生质的变化。大脑已经学会了组织和构建大量信息。凭借所有这些隐性知识，它现在可以发挥创造力，并灵活运用这些信息。虽然这个小时数看起来很长，但通常需要七到十年持续扎实的练习——大致相当于传统学徒期的期限。换句话说，长期的专注练习必然会产生效果。

# ↩

Step Three: Experimentation—The Active Mode

第三步：实验——主动模式

This is the shortest part of the process, but a critical component nonetheless. As you gain in skill and confidence, you must make the move to a more active mode of experimentation . This could mean taking on more responsibility, initiating a project of some sort, doing work that exposes you to the criticisms of peers or even the public. The point of this is to gauge your progress and whether there are still gaps in your knowledge. You are observing yourself in action and seeing how you respond to the judgments of others. Can you take criticism and use it constructively?

这是整个过程中最短的环节，但却至关重要。随着技能和信心的提升，你必须转向更积极的实验模式。这可能意味着承担更多责任，启动某种项目，从事一些可能让你面临同行甚至公众批评的工作。这样做的目的是评估你的进步，以及你的知识是否仍然存在差距。你正在观察自己的行为，并观察自己如何回应他人的评判。你能接受批评并建设性地运用它吗？

With Charles Darwin, as the voyage progressed and he began to entertain the notions that would lead to his theory of evolution, he decided to expose his ideas to others. First, on the Beagle , he discussed them with the captain and patiently absorbed his vehement criticisms of the idea. This, Darwin told himself, would be more or less the reaction of the public, and he would have to prepare himself for that. He also began to write letters to various scientists and scientific societies back in England. The responses he received indicated he was on to something, but that he would need some more research. For Leonardo da Vinci, as he progressed in his studio work for Verrocchio, he began to experiment and to assert his own style. He found to his surprise that the Master was impressed with his inventiveness. For Leonardo, this indicated that he was near the end of his apprenticeship.

查尔斯·达尔文随着航程的推进，开始萌生一些可能促成其进化论的想法，并决定将自己的想法公之于众。首先，在贝格尔号上，他与船长进行了讨论，并耐心地听取船长对他的强烈批评。达尔文告诉自己，这或多或少会是公众的反应，他必须做好准备。他还开始给英国的各位科学家和科学协会写信。他收到的回信表明他有所发现，但还需要进一步研究。列奥纳多·达·芬奇在为韦罗基奥工作期间，随着工作室工作的进展，他开始进行实验并确立自己的风格。他惊讶地发现，大师对他的创造力印象深刻。对列奥纳多来说，这表明他的学徒生涯即将结束。

Most people wait too long to take this step, generally out of fear. It is always easier to learn the rules and stay within your comfort zone. Often you must force yourself to initiate such actions or experiments before you think you are ready . You are testing your character, moving past your fears, and developing a sense of detachment to your work—looking at it through the eyes of others. You are getting a taste for the next phase in which what you produce will be under constant scrutiny.

大多数人拖延了太久才迈出这一步，通常是出于恐惧。学习规则并待在舒适区总是更容易。通常情况下，在你认为自己准备好之前，你必须强迫自己开始这样的行动或实验。这是在考验你的性格，克服恐惧，并培养一种对工作的超脱感——用别人的眼光来看待它。你正在体验下一个阶段，你的作品将受到持续的审视。

You will know when your apprenticeship is over by the feeling that you have nothing left to learn in this environment. It is time to declare your independence or move to another place to continue your apprenticeship and expand your skill base. Later in life, when you are confronted with a career change or the need to learn new skills, having gone through this process before, it will become second nature. You have learned how to learn.

当你感觉在这个环境中已经没有什么可学的时候，你就会知道你的学徒期已经结束了。是时候宣布你的独立，或者换个地方继续你的学徒生涯，拓展你的技能基础了。以后，当你面临职业转变或需要学习新技能时，既然你已经经历过这个过程，它就会成为你的第二天性。你已经学会了如何学习。

Many people might find the notion of an apprenticeship and skill acquisition as quaint relics of bygone eras when work meant making things. After all, we have entered the information and computer age, in which technology makes it so we can do without the kinds of menial tasks that require practice and repetition; so many things have become virtual in our lives, making the craftsman model obsolete. Or so the argument goes.

很多人或许会觉得，学徒制和技能习得的概念，不过是过去那种“工作就是制造东西”的年代的遗物。毕竟，我们已经进入了信息和计算机时代，科技让我们不再需要那些需要练习和重复的琐碎工作；我们生活中的很多事情都变得虚拟了，工匠模式已经过时了。或者说，人们的观点是这样的。

In truth, however, this idea of the nature of the times we are living in is completely incorrect, even dangerous. The era we have entered is not one in which technology will make everything easier, but rather a time of increased complexity that affects every field. In business, competition has become globalized and more intense. A businessperson must have a command of a much larger picture than in the past, which means more knowledge and skills. The future in science does not lie in increased specialization, but rather in the combining and cross-fertilization of knowledge in various fields. In the arts, tastes and styles are changing at an accelerated rate. An artist must be on top of this and be capable of creating new forms, always remaining ahead of the curve. This often requires having more than just a specialized knowledge of that particular art form—it requires knowing other arts, even the sciences, and what is happening in the world.

然而，事实上，这种对我们身处时代本质的理解是完全错误的，甚至是危险的。我们进入的时代并非科技让一切变得更容易的时代，而是一个影响到各个领域的日益复杂的时代。在商业领域，竞争已经全球化，也更加激烈。商人必须比过去拥有更广阔的视野，这意味着拥有更多的知识和技能。科学的未来并非在于专业化的提升，而在于各个领域知识的融合和相互影响。在艺术领域，品味和风格正在加速变化。艺术家必须掌控这一切，并能够创造新的形式，始终保持领先地位。这通常需要的不仅仅是特定艺术形式的专业知识——它还需要了解其他艺术形式，甚至是科学，以及世界上正在发生的事情。

In all of these areas, the human brain is asked to do and handle more than ever before. We are dealing with several fields of knowledge constantly intersecting with our own, and all of this chaos is exponentially increased by the information available through technology. What this means is that all of us must possess different forms of knowledge and an array of skills in different fields, and have minds that are capable of organizing large amounts of information. The future belongs to those who learn more skills and combine them in creative ways. And the process of learning skills, no matter how virtual, remains the same.

在所有这些领域，人类大脑需要处理的任务比以往任何时候都多。我们正应对着多个知识领域，它们与我们自身的知识不断交叉，而所有这些混乱局面又因科技带来的信息量而呈指数级增长。这意味着我们每个人都必须掌握不同形式的知识和不同领域的一系列技能，并拥有能够组织海量信息的头脑。未来属于那些学习更多技能并以创造性方式将这些技能结合起来的人。而学习技能的过程，无论多么虚拟，都始终如一。

In the future, the great division will be between those who have trained themselves to handle these complexities and those who are overwhelmed by them—those who can acquire skills and discipline their minds and those who are irrevocably distracted by all the media around them and can never focus enough to learn. The Apprenticeship Phase is more relevant and important than ever, and those who discount this notion will almost certainly be left behind.

未来，巨大的分歧将出现在那些训练有素、能够应对这些复杂情况的人和那些被这些复杂情况压垮的人之间——那些能够掌握技能、训练有素的人，以及那些被周围各种媒体无情地分散注意力、永远无法集中精力学习的人。学徒阶段比以往任何时候都更加重要，那些忽视这一概念的人几乎肯定会被淘汰。

Finally, we live in a culture that generally values intellect and reasoning with words. We tend to think of working with the hands, of building something physical, as degraded skills for those who are less intelligent. This is an extremely counterproductive cultural value. The human brain evolved in intimate conjunction with the hand. Many of our earliest survival skills depended on elaborate hand-eye coordination. To this day, a large portion of our brain is devoted to this relationship. When we work with our hands and build something, we learn how to sequence our actions and how to organize our thoughts. In taking anything apart in order to fix it, we learn problem-solving skills that have wider applications. Even if it is only as a side activity, you should find a way to work with your hands, or to learn more about the inner workings of the machines and pieces of technology around you.

最后，我们生活在一个普遍重视智力和语言推理的文化中。我们倾向于认为动手工作、建造实体物品，是智力低下者的低级技能。这是一种极其适得其反的文化价值观。人类大脑的进化与手的紧密联系息息相关。我们许多早期的生存技能都依赖于精细的手眼协调能力。时至今日，我们大脑的很大一部分仍然致力于这种关系。当我们动手建造物品时，我们学会了如何安排动作顺序、如何组织思维。在拆卸和修理任何东西的过程中，我们学习了应用范围更广的解决问题的技能。即使只是作为一项业余活动，你也应该找到一种动手工作的方法，或者更多地了解你周围机器和科技产品的内部工作原理。

Many Masters in history intuited this connection. Thomas Jefferson, who himself was an avid tinkerer and inventor, believed that craftspeople made better citizens because they understood how things functioned and had practical common sense—all of which would serve them well in handling civic needs. Albert Einstein was an avid violinist. He believed that working with his hands in this way and playing music helped his thinking process as well.

历史上许多大师都敏锐地察觉了这种联系。托马斯·杰斐逊本人就是一位热衷于修补匠和发明家，他认为工匠能够成为更优秀的公民，因为他们了解事物的运作方式，并拥有实用的常识——所有这些都有助于他们更好地处理公民事务。阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦是一位狂热的小提琴手。他相信，用双手工作和演奏音乐也有助于他的思维过程。

In general, no matter your field, you must think of yourself as a builder, using actual materials and ideas. You are producing something tangible in your work, something that affects people in some direct, concrete way. To build anything well—a house, a political organization, a business, or a film—you must understand the building process and possess the necessary skills. You are a craftsman learning to adhere to the highest standards. For all of this, you must go through a careful apprenticeship. You cannot make anything worthwhile in this world unless you have first developed and transformed yourself.

总的来说，无论你从事哪个领域，你都必须把自己想象成一位建造者，运用真实的材料和理念。你的工作是在创造一些有形的东西，一些能够以直接、具体的方式影响他人的东西。要想建造好任何东西——一栋房子、一个政治组织、一家企业或一部电影——你都必须了解建造过程并掌握必要的技能。你是一位工匠，正在学习遵守最高标准。为了实现这一切，你必须经历一段刻苦钻研的学徒期。除非你首先发展和改变自己，否则你无法在这个世界上创造出任何有价值的东西。

STRATEGIES FOR COMPLETING
完成
THE IDEAL APPRENTICESHIP
理想学徒期的策略

Do not think that what is hard for you to master is humanly impossible; and if it is humanly possible, consider it to be within your reach.

不要认为你难以掌握的事情是人力不可能做到的；如果它是人力可以做到的，那就认为它是你力所能及的。

—M ARCUS A URELIUS

—马可·奥勒留

Throughout history, Masters in all fields have devised for themselves various strategies to help them pursue and complete an Ideal Apprenticeship. The following are eight classic strategies, distilled from the stories of their lives and illustrated with examples. Although some might seem more relevant than others to your circumstances, each of them relates fundamental truths about the learning process itself that you would be wise to internalize.

纵观历史，各行各业的大师们都为自己设计了各种各样的策略，以帮助他们追求并完成理想的学徒期。以下是从他们的人生故事中提炼出的八种经典策略，并附以实例。虽然有些策略可能看起来比其他策略更贴近你的处境，但每一种策略都与学习过程本身的基本真理息息相关，你应该明智地将其内化。

# ↩

1. Value learning over money

1. 学习比金钱更重要

In 1718, Josiah Franklin decided to bring his twelve-year-old son Benjamin into his lucrative, family-run candle-making business in Boston as an apprentice. His idea was that after a seven-year apprenticeship and a little experience, Benjamin would take over the business. But Benjamin had other ideas. He threatened to run away to sea if his father did not give him the choice of where he could apprentice. The father had already lost another son who had run away, and so he relented. To the father’s surprise, his son chose to work in an older brother’s recently opened printing business. Such a business would mean harder work and the apprenticeship would last nine instead of seven years. Also, the printing business was notoriously fickle, and it was quite a risk to bank one’s future on it. But that was his choice, his father decided. Let him learn the hard way.

1718年，约西亚·富兰克林决定让十二岁的儿子本杰明去波士顿他那家利润丰厚的家族蜡烛厂当学徒。他原本打算等到本杰明完成七年学徒期并积累一些经验后，再接手生意。但本杰明另有打算。他威胁说，如果父亲不让他选择学徒地点，他就逃亡当海员。父亲之前已经失去了另一个离家出走的儿子，所以他妥协了。令父亲惊讶的是，儿子选择在哥哥新开的印刷厂工作。这样的工作意味着更辛苦，学徒期也从七年延长到九年。此外，印刷业以变化无常而闻名，把未来押在上面风险很大。但这是他的选择，父亲决定让他吃点苦头。

What young Benjamin had not told his father was that he was determined to become a writer. Most of the work in the shop would involve manual labor and operating machines, but every now and then he would be asked to proofread and copyedit a pamphlet or text. And there would always be new books around. Several years into the process, he discovered that some of his favorite writing came from the English newspapers the shop would reprint. He asked to be the one to oversee the printing of such articles, giving him the chance to study these texts in detail and teach himself how to imitate their style in his own work. Over the years he managed to turn this into a most efficient apprenticeship for writing, with the added benefit of having learned the printing business well.

年轻的本杰明没有告诉父亲的是，他立志成为一名作家。店里的工作大多是体力劳动和操作机器，但他偶尔也会被要求校对和编辑小册子或文本。而且店里总是有新书出版。几年下来，他发现自己最喜欢的一些作品来自店里转载的英文报纸。他主动要求监督这些文章的印刷，这让他有机会仔细研究这些文本，并自学如何在自己的作品中模仿它们的风格。多年来，他成功地把这段经历变成了一次高效的写作学徒生涯，同时还对印刷业务有了深入的了解。

After graduating from the Zurich Polytechnic in 1900, the twenty-one-year-old Albert Einstein found his job prospects extremely meager. He had graduated near the bottom of the class, almost certainly nullifying any chance to obtain a teaching position. Happy to be away from the university, he now planned to investigate, on his own, certain problems in physics that had haunted him for several years. It would be a self-apprenticeship in theorizing and thought experiments. But in the meantime, he would have to make a living. He had been offered a job in his father’s dynamo business in Milan as an engineer, but such work would not leave him any free time. A friend could land him a well-paid position in an insurance company, but that would stultify his brain and sap his energy for thinking.

1900年从苏黎世理工学院毕业后，21岁的阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦发现自己的就业前景极其渺茫。他的成绩几乎垫底，几乎断送了他获得教职的任何机会。离开大学后，他欣喜若狂，现在计划独自研究困扰他多年的一些物理学难题。这将是一次理论构建和思想实验的自我学徒之旅。但与此同时，他还得谋生。他父亲在米兰的发电机公司曾给他提供了一份工程师的工作，但这份工作让他没有空闲时间。朋友可以帮他在保险公司找到一份薪水丰厚的职位，但这会让他大脑迟钝，消耗他思考的精力。

Then, a year later, another friend mentioned a job opening up in the Swiss Patent Office in Bern. The pay was not great, the position was at the bottom, the hours were long, and the work consisted of the rather mundane task of looking over patent applications, but Einstein leaped at the chance. It was everything he wanted. His task would be to analyze the validity of patent applications, many of which involved aspects of science that interested him. The applications would be like little puzzles or thought experiments; he could try to visualize how the ideas would actually translate into inventions. Working on them would sharpen his reasoning powers. After several months on the job, he became so good at this mental game that he could finish his work in two or three hours, leaving him the rest of the day to engage in his own thought experiments. In 1905 he published his first theory of relativity, much of the work having been done while he was at his desk in the Patent Office.

一年后，另一位朋友提到伯尔尼瑞士专利局有空缺职位。薪水不高，职位低微，工作时间长，而且工作内容只是审查专利申请这种相当平凡的工作，但爱因斯坦欣然接受了这个机会。这份工作满足了他的所有愿望。他的工作是分析专利申请的有效性，其中许多申请涉及他感兴趣的科学领域。这些申请就像小谜题或思维实验；他可以尝试想象这些想法如何转化为发明。研究这些申请可以提升他的推理能力。几个月后，他变得非常擅长这种智力游戏，可以在两三个小时内完成工作，剩下的时间可以用来进行自己的思维实验。1905年，他发表了他的第一个相对论，其中大部分工作都是在他坐在专利局的办公桌前完成的。

Martha Graham (see here for more on her early years) first trained as a dancer at the Denishawn School in Los Angeles, but after several years she determined she had learned enough and needed to go elsewhere to sharpen her skills. She ended up in New York, and in 1924 was offered a two-year stint as a dancer in a follies’ show; it was well paid, and so she accepted. Dancing is dancing, she thought, and she could always work on her own ideas in her free time. But near the end of the term, she decided she would never again accept commercial work. It drained her of all of her creative energy and destroyed her desire to work on her own time. It also made her feel dependent on a paycheck.

玛莎·格雷厄姆（点击此处了解更多关于她早年经历的信息）最初在洛杉矶的丹尼肖恩学校接受舞蹈训练，但几年后，她认为自己学得足够多了，需要去其他地方磨练技艺。她最终来到了纽约，并于1924年获得了一个为期两年的歌舞表演舞蹈演员的工作机会；这份工作报酬丰厚，于是她接受了。她想，跳舞就是跳舞，而且她总是可以在空闲时间里发挥自己的想法。但学期快结束时，她决定再也不接商业工作了。这耗尽了她所有的创造力，摧毁了她利用自己时间工作的愿望。这也让她觉得自己依赖于薪水。

What is important when you are young, she decided, is to train yourself to get by with little money and make the most of your youthful energy. For the next few years she would work as a dance teacher, keeping her hours to the minimum for survival. The rest of the time she would train herself in the new style of dancing she wanted to create. Knowing the alternative was slavery to some commercial job, she made the most of every free minute, creating in these few years the groundwork for the most radical revolution in modern dance.

她决定，年轻时最重要的是训练自己如何在有限的资金下生存，并充分利用青春的活力。接下来的几年里，她将成为一名舞蹈老师，尽量减少工作时间以维持生计。其余时间，她将学习自己想要创造的新舞蹈风格。她知道，不这样做就等于沦为商业工作的奴隶，因此她充分利用了每一分钟的空闲时间，并在这几年里为现代舞史上最彻底的革命奠定了基础。

As previously narrated in chapter 1 (see here ), when Freddie Roach’s career as a boxer came to an end in 1986, he took a job as a telemarketer in Las Vegas. One day, he entered the gym where he himself had trained under the legendary coach Eddie Futch. He found many boxers there who were not receiving any personalized attention from Futch. Even though he was not asked, he began to hang around the gym every afternoon and help out. It turned into a job for which he was not paid, so he held on to his telemarketing position. Working the two jobs left just enough time to sleep. It was almost unbearable, but he could withstand it because he was learning the trade for which he knew was destined. Within a few years he had impressed enough young boxers with his knowledge to set up his own business, and was soon to become the most successful boxing trainer of his generation.

正如第一章（见此处）所述，弗雷迪·罗奇的拳击生涯在1986年结束，之后在拉斯维加斯找到了一份电话营销员的工作。有一天，他走进了他曾经在传奇教练埃迪·富奇（Eddie Futch）手下训练的拳击馆。他发现那里有很多拳击手没有得到富奇的任何个性化关注。尽管富奇并没有邀请他，他还是开始每天下午在拳击馆里闲逛，帮忙。这份工作最终变成了一份没有报酬的工作，所以他继续做着电话营销。同时打两份工只剩下刚好够睡觉的时间。这几乎让他难以忍受，但他还是忍了下来，因为他正在学习这门他知道自己命中注定要从事的职业。几年之内，他的知识就打动了不少年轻拳击手，他们纷纷开始创办自己的拳击事业，并很快成为他那一代最成功的拳击教练。

It is a simple law of human psychology that your thoughts will tend to revolve around what you value most. If it is money, you will choose a place for your apprenticeship that offers the biggest paycheck. Inevitably, in such a place you will feel greater pressures to prove yourself worthy of such pay, often before you are really ready. You will be focused on yourself, your insecurities, the need to please and impress the right people, and not on acquiring skills. It will be too costly for you to make mistakes and learn from them, so you will develop a cautious, conservative approach. As you progress in life, you will become addicted to the fat paycheck and it will determine where you go, how you think, and what you do. Eventually, the time that was not spent on learning skills will catch up with you, and the fall will be painful.

人类心理学有一条简单的规律：你的思想往往会围绕你最看重的事物。如果是金钱，你就会选择薪水最高的学徒机构。不可避免的是，在这样的机构里，你会感受到更大的压力，需要证明自己配得上这份薪水，而这往往发生在你真正做好准备之前。你会专注于自己，你的不安全感，以及取悦和打动合适的人的需求，而不是学习技能。对你来说，犯错并从中吸取教训的代价太高，所以你会养成谨慎保守的作风。随着人生的进步，你会对丰厚的薪水上瘾，它会决定你的方向、你的思维方式以及你的行为。最终，那些没有花在学习技能上的时间会追上你，而这种损失将是痛苦的。

Instead, you must value learning above everything else. This will lead you to all of the right choices. You will opt for the situation that will give you the most opportunities to learn, particularly with hands-on work. You will choose a place that has people and mentors who can inspire and teach you. A job with mediocre pay has the added benefit of training you to get by with less—a valuable life skill. If your apprenticeship is to be mostly on your own time, you will choose a place that pays the bills—perhaps one that keeps your mind sharp, but that also leaves you the time and mental space to do valuable work on your own. You must never disdain an apprenticeship with no pay. In fact, it is often the height of wisdom to find the perfect mentor and offer your services as an assistant for free. Happy to exploit your cheap and eager spirit, such mentors will often divulge more than the usual trade secrets. In the end, by valuing learning above all else, you will set the stage for your creative expansion, and the money will soon come to you.

相反，你必须把学习放在首位。这将引导你做出所有正确的选择。你会选择能给你最多学习机会的环境，尤其是在实践工作方面。你会选择一个拥有能够激励和教导你的人和导师的地方。一份薪水平平的工作还能让你学会如何用更少的钱过活——这是一项宝贵的人生技能。如果你的学徒期大部分时间都在你自己的时间里，你会选择一个能养家糊口的地方——或许一个既能让你保持思维敏锐，又能给你时间和精神空间去独立完成有价值的工作的地方。你绝不能轻视没有报酬的学徒期。事实上，找到一位完美的导师并免费提供你的助手服务往往是明智之举。这样的导师乐于利用你廉价而热切的个性，他们往往会透露比通常的商业机密更多的信息。最终，通过把学习放在首位，你将为你的创造力拓展奠定基础，而金钱很快就会来到你身边。

# ↩

2. Keep expanding your horizons

2. 不断拓展你的视野

For the writer Zora Neale Hurston (1891–1960), her childhood represented a kind of Golden Age. She grew up in Eatonville, Florida, a town that was something of an anomaly in the South. It had been founded as an all-black township in the 1880s, governed and managed by its citizens. Its only struggles and sufferings came at the hands of its own inhabitants. For Zora, racism had no meaning. A spirited and strong-willed girl, she spent a lot of her time alone, wandering through the town.

对于作家佐拉·尼尔·赫斯顿（Zora Neale Hurston，1891-1960）来说，她的童年堪称黄金时代。她在佛罗里达州伊顿维尔长大，这座小镇在南方颇为另类。它于19世纪80年代建立，最初是一个全黑人居住的城镇，由镇上的居民管理和治理。这里唯一的挣扎和苦难都源于当地居民。对佐拉来说，种族主义毫无意义。她是一个充满活力、意志坚强的女孩，很多时间都独自在镇上闲逛。

She had two great passions in those years. First, she loved books and reading. She read everything she could get her hands on, but she was particularly drawn to books on mythology—Greek, Roman, and Norse. She identified with the strongest characters—Hercules, Odysseus, Odin. Second, she would spend much of her time listening to the stories of locals as they gathered on porches and gossiped or related folk tales, many of them dating back to the years of slavery. She loved their manner of telling stories—the rich metaphors, the simple lessons. In her mind, the Greek myths and the stories of Eatonville citizens all blended into one reality—human nature revealed in its most naked form. Walking alone, her imagination would take flight, and she would begin telling her own strange tales to herself. Someday she would write all of this down and become the Homer of Eatonville.

那些年，她有两大爱好。首先，她热爱书籍和阅读。她读遍所有能找到的书，尤其钟爱神话书籍——希腊、罗马和北欧神话。她对那些最强大的人物——赫拉克勒斯、奥德修斯、奥丁——感同身受。其次，她会花很多时间聆听当地人聚集在门廊上，闲聊或讲述民间故事，其中许多故事可以追溯到奴隶制时代。她喜欢他们讲故事的方式——丰富的隐喻，浅显易懂的道理。在她心中，希腊神话和伊顿维尔市民的故事融为一体，共同构成了一个现实——人性最赤裸裸的展现。独自行走时，她的想象力会飞扬，她会开始自言自语地讲述那些奇异的故事。总有一天，她会把这些故事都写下来，成为伊顿维尔的荷马。

Then in 1904 her mother died, and the Golden Age came to an abrupt end. It was her mother who had always protected and sheltered Zora from her father, who thought her strange and unlikeable. Eager to have her out of the house, he shipped her off to a school in Jacksonville. A few years later, he stopped paying her tuition and essentially abandoned her to the world. For five years she wandered from one relative’s house to another. She took up all kinds of jobs to support herself, mostly housekeeping.

1904年，母亲去世，黄金时代戛然而止。一直以来，母亲都守护着佐拉，让她免受父亲的伤害。父亲觉得她古怪又不讨人喜欢。父亲急于让她离开家，便把她送到了杰克逊维尔的一所学校。几年后，父亲不再支付她的学费，几乎把她抛弃在尘世。五年来，她辗转于各个亲戚家。为了养活自己，她做过各种各样的工作，大部分是家务。

Thinking back to her childhood, she could remember a sense of expansion—learning about other cultures and their history, learning about her own culture. There seemed to be no limits to what she could explore. Now, it was the opposite. Worn down by work and depression, everything was tightening around her until all she could think about was her own tiny world and how sorry it had become. Soon it would be hard to imagine anything besides cleaning houses. But the paradox is that the mind is essentially free. It can travel anywhere, across time and space. If she kept it confined to her narrow circumstances, it would be her own fault. No matter how impossible it seemed, she could not let go of her dream to become a writer. To realize this dream, she would have to educate herself and keep her mental horizons expanding by whatever means necessary. A writer needs knowledge of the world. And so, thinking in this way, Zora Neale Hurston proceeded to create for herself one of the most remarkable self-directed apprenticeships in history.

回想童年，她能记起一种拓展的感觉——学习其他文化及其历史，学习自己的文化。她曾经的探索似乎没有止境。如今，情况却截然相反。工作和抑郁让她疲惫不堪，周围的一切都让她感到无比压抑，她满脑子想的都是自己狭小的世界，以及这个世界如今变得多么可怜。很快，她就很难想象除了打扫房子之外的其他事情了。但矛盾的是，心灵本质上是自由的。它可以穿越时空，去任何地方。如果她将心灵禁锢在狭小的环境中，那将是她自己的错。无论这看起来多么遥不可及，她都无法放弃成为一名作家的梦想。为了实现这个梦想，她必须不断学习，并通过一切必要的方式不断拓展自己的思维视野。作家需要了解世界。于是，佐拉·尼尔·赫斯顿带着这种想法，开始为自己创造历史上最杰出的自主学徒制之一。

Since the only jobs she could get at that moment were housecleaning, she managed to land work in the homes of the wealthiest white people in town—there she would find plenty of books. Snatching a few moments here and there, she would read portions of these books on the sly, quickly memorizing passages so she could have something to go over in her head in her free time. One day, she discovered a discarded copy of Milton’s Paradise Lost in a garbage can. It was as good as gold for her. She took it wherever she went, and read it over and over. In this way, her mind did not stagnate; she had created for herself a strange sort of literary education.

由于当时她唯一能找到的工作就是家政，她设法在镇上最富有的白人家庭找到工作——在那里她能找到很多书。她会抽出一些时间，偷偷地读读这些书，快速地记住一些段落，这样空闲的时候就能有一些内容可以复习。有一天，她在垃圾桶里发现了一本被丢弃的弥尔顿的《失乐园》。这本书对她来说简直是金子。她走到哪里都带着它，一遍又一遍地读。就这样，她的思维从未停滞；她为自己创造了一种奇特的文学教育。

In 1915, she landed a job as a lady’s maid to the lead singer of an all-white traveling troupe of performers. For most, this would mean yet another subservient position, but for Hurston it was a godsend. Many of the members of the troupe were well educated. There were books everywhere to read and interesting conversations to overhear. By observing closely, she could see what passed for sophistication in the white world, and how she could make herself charming to them with her stories of Eatonville and her knowledge of literature. As part of the job, they had her trained as a manicurist. She would later use this skill to find jobs in the barbershops in Washington D.C., near the Capitol. The clientele included the most powerful politicians of the time, and they would often gossip as if she weren’t even there. For her, this was almost as good as reading any book—it taught her more about human nature, power, and the inner workings of the white world.

1915年，她找到了一份工作，为一个全白人巡回剧团的主唱做女仆。对大多数人来说，这不过是又一个卑微的职位，但对赫斯顿来说，这简直是天赐之物。剧团的许多成员都受过良好的教育。到处都有书籍可读，还有各种有趣的对话可供聆听。通过仔细观察，她洞悉了白人世界里所谓的世故，并知道如何利用自己在伊顿维尔的故事和文学知识来博取他们的青睐。作为工作的一部分，剧团还让她接受了美甲师的培训。后来，她凭借这项技能在华盛顿特区国会大厦附近的理发店找到了工作。理发店的顾客包括当时最有权势的政客，他们经常闲聊八卦，仿佛她根本不在场一样。对她来说，这份工作几乎和读书一样好——它让她更多地了解人性、权力以及白人世界的内部运作。

Her world was slowly expanding, but still there were severe limitations on where she could work, on the books she could find, on the people she could meet and associate with. She was learning, but her mind was unstructured and her thoughts unorganized. What she needed, she decided, was formal education and the discipline this would bring her. She could try to patch a degree together in various night schools, but what she really wanted was to regain what had been taken away from her by her father. At twenty-five she looked young for her age, and so chopping off ten years in her application, she gained admittance to a free public high school in Maryland as a freshman.

她的世界正在慢慢扩大，但她的工作地点、书籍种类、以及结识和交往的人仍然受到严重限制。她正在学习，但思维散漫，思路混乱。她决定，她需要的是正规教育以及由此带来的自律。她可以尝试在不同的夜校拼凑学位，但她真正想要的是重新找回被父亲夺走的东西。25岁的她看起来比实际年龄年轻，于是在申请时减少了10岁，最终以新生的身份被马里兰州一所免费公立高中录取。

She would have to make the most of this schooling—her future depended on it. She would read many more books than were required, and work particularly hard on any writing assignments. She would befriend teachers and professors with the charm she had established over the years, making the kinds of connections that had eluded her in the past. In this way, a few years later, she gained admittance to Howard University, the leading institution of black higher learning, and made the acquaintance of key figures in the black literary world. With the discipline she had gained in school, she began to write short stories. Now, with the help of one of her connections, she got a short story published in a prestigious Harlem literary journal. Seizing opportunities whenever they appeared, she decided to leave Howard and move to Harlem, where all of the leading black writers and artists were living. This would add another dimension to the world she was finally able to explore.

她必须充分利用这段求学时光——她的未来全靠它。她会读比要求多得多的书，并格外努力地完成写作作业。她会凭借多年来培养的魅力与老师和教授们交朋友，建立过去一直未能建立起来的人脉。就这样，几年后，她考入了黑人高等教育的领军学府霍华德大学，并结识了黑人文坛的关键人物。凭借在学校习得的自律，她开始创作短篇小说。现在，在一位熟人的帮助下，她的一篇短篇小说在一家享有盛誉的哈莱姆文学杂志上发表。她抓住一切机会，决定离开霍华德大学，搬到哈莱姆区，那里汇聚了所有顶尖的黑人作家和艺术家。这将为她终于能够探索的世界增添新的维度。

Over the years, Hurston had made a study of powerful, important people—black and white—and how to impress them. Now in New York, she used this skill to great effect, charming several wealthy white patrons of the arts. Through one of these patrons she was offered the opportunity to enroll in Barnard College, where she could finish her college education. She would be the first and only black student there. It had been her strategy to keep moving, keep expanding—the world could quickly close in on you if you stayed put or stagnated. And so she accepted the offer. The white students at Barnard were intimidated in her presence—her knowledge of so many fields far exceeded their own. Several professors in the anthropology department fell under her spell, and sent her on a tour through the South to gather folk tales and stories. She used the trip to immerse herself in hoodoo, the southern black version of voodoo, and in other ritual practices. She wanted to deepen her knowledge of black culture in all of its richness and variety.

多年来，赫斯顿一直在研究权贵人物——无论黑人还是白人——以及如何取悦他们。如今，她身处纽约，运用这项技能卓有成效，成功迷住了几位富有的白人艺术赞助人。其中一位赞助人向她提供了就读巴纳德学院的机会，让她在那里完成学业。她将成为那里第一个也是唯一一个黑人学生。她的策略是不断前进，不断拓展——如果你停滞不前或停滞不前，世界很快就会将你包围。于是，她接受了这份邀请。巴纳德学院的白人学生在她面前感到畏惧——她在众多领域的知识远超他们。人类学系的几位教授被她深深吸引，派她前往南方收集民间传说和故事。她利用这次旅行，沉浸在巫毒教（南方黑人版本的巫毒教）和其他仪式中。她希望加深对黑人文化丰富多彩的理解。

In 1932, with the Depression raging in New York and her employment opportunities drying up, she decided to return to Eatonville. There she could live cheaply, and the atmosphere would be inspiring. Borrowing money from friends, she proceeded to work on her first novel. From somewhere deep inside, all of her past experiences, her lengthy and multifaceted apprenticeship, rose to the surface—the stories from her childhood, the books she had read here and there over the years, the various insights into the dark side of human nature, the anthropological studies, every encounter that she had paid attention to with so much intensity. This novel, Jonah’s Gourd Vine , would recount the relationship of her parents, but it was really the distillation of all of her life’s work. It spilled out of her in a few intense months.

1932年，大萧条席卷纽约，她的就业机会骤减，她决定返回伊顿维尔。在那里，她生活成本低廉，而且那里的氛围也令人振奋。她向朋友借钱，开始创作她的第一部小说。在内心深处，她过去的所有经历，她漫长而多面的学徒生涯，都浮现在她的脑海中——童年的故事，多年来她四处阅读的书籍，对人性阴暗面的各种洞见，人类学研究，以及她曾如此专注地关注的每一次邂逅。这部名为《约拿的葫芦藤》的小说讲述了她父母的关系，但它实际上是她毕生创作的结晶。在几个月的紧张创作中，这一切都倾泻而出。

The novel was published the following year and became a great success. Over the next few years she wrote more novels at a furious pace. She soon became the most famous black writer of her time, and the first black female writer ever to make a living from her work.

这部小说于次年出版，并获得了巨大的成功。在接下来的几年里，她以惊人的速度创作了更多小说。她很快成为当时最著名的黑人作家，也是第一位靠作品谋生的黑人女作家。

Zora Neale Hurston’s story reveals in its barest form the reality of the Apprenticeship Phase—no one is really going to help you or give you direction. In fact, the odds are against you. If you desire an apprenticeship, if you want to learn and set yourself up for mastery, you have to do it yourself, and with great energy. When you enter this phase, you generally begin at the lowest position. Your access to knowledge and people is limited by your status. If you are not careful, you will accept this status and become defined by it, particularly if you come from a disadvantaged background. Instead, like Hurston, you must struggle against any limitations and continually work to expand your horizons. (In each learning situation you will submit to reality, but that reality does not mean you must stay in one place.) Reading books and materials that go beyond what is required is always a good starting point. Being exposed to ideas in the wide world, you will tend to develop a hunger for more and more knowledge; you will find it harder to remain satisfied in any narrow corner, which is precisely the point.

佐拉·尼尔·赫斯顿的故事最直白地揭示了学徒阶段的现实——没有人会真正帮助你或指引你。事实上，你的机会渺茫。如果你想成为学徒，如果你想学习并最终成为大师，你必须自己动手，并且投入巨大的精力。进入这个阶段，你通常从最底层开始。你获取知识和人脉的渠道受限于你的身份地位。如果你不小心，你就会接受这种身份地位，并被它所定义，尤其是在你出身贫寒的情况下。相反，你必须像赫斯顿一样，努力克服任何限制，不断拓展你的视野。（在每一个学习阶段，你都会屈服于现实，但现实并不意味着你必须固步自封。）阅读那些超越需求的书籍和资料始终是一个好的起点。接触广阔世界的思想，你会渴望获得越来越多的知识；你会发现在任何狭小的角落里都很难感到满足，而这正是关键所在。

The people in your field, in your immediate circle, are like worlds unto themselves—their stories and viewpoints will naturally expand your horizons and build up your social skills. Mingle with as many different types of people as possible. Those circles will slowly widen. Any kind of outside schooling will add to the dynamic. Be relentless in your pursuit for expansion. Whenever you feel like you are settling into some circle, force yourself to shake things up and look for new challenges, as Hurston did when she left Howard for Harlem. With your mind expanding, you will redefine the limits of your apparent world. Soon, ideas and opportunities will come to you and your apprenticeship will naturally complete itself.
