你所从事领域的人和你身边的人就像一个个独立的世界——他们的故事和观点自然会拓展你的视野，提升你的社交技能。尽可能多地与不同类型的人交往。这些圈子会慢慢扩大。任何形式的外部教育都会增强你的活力。坚持不懈地追求拓展。每当你觉得自己已经融入某个圈子时，就强迫自己打破常规，寻找新的挑战，就像赫斯顿离开霍华德大学前往哈莱姆区时那样。随着你思维的拓展，你将重新定义你表面上的世界。很快，你就会获得灵感和机遇，你的学徒生涯也将水到渠成。

# ↩

3. Revert to a feeling of inferiority

3. 重拾自卑感

Attending high school in the late 1960s, Daniel Everett was a bit of a lost soul. He felt trapped in the California border town of Holtville, where he grew up, and totally disconnected to the local cowboy way of life. As narrated in chapter 1 (see here ), Everett had always been drawn to the Mexican culture that existed among the migrant workers on the margins of the town. He loved their rituals and way of life, the sound of their language, and their songs. He seemed to have a knack for learning a foreign language and picked up Spanish rather quickly, gaining a bit of entrée into their world. To him, their culture represented a glimpse of a more interesting world beyond Holtville, but sometimes he despaired of ever really getting away from his hometown. He began to take drugs—for the time being, at least, they offered an escape.

20世纪60年代末，丹尼尔·埃弗里特（Daniel Everett）就读高中时，内心有些失落。他感觉自己被困在加州边境小镇霍尔特维尔（Holtville）——他从小长大的地方——与当地牛仔的生活方式完全脱节。正如第一章（见此处）所述，埃弗里特一直被小镇边缘移民工人的墨西哥文化所吸引。他热爱他们的仪式和生活方式，他们的语言和歌曲。他似乎很擅长学习外语，很快就学会了西班牙语，并逐渐融入了他们的世界。对他来说，他们的文化代表着霍尔特维尔之外更精彩世界的一瞥，但有时，他甚至对真正离开家乡感到绝望。他开始吸毒——至少在当时，毒品提供了一种逃避的途径。

Then, when he was seventeen, he met Keren Graham, a fellow student at his high school, and everything seemed to change. Keren had spent much of her childhood in northeastern Brazil, where her parents had served as Christian missionaries. He loved to hang out with her and listen to her stories of life in Brazil. He met her family and became a regular guest at their dinners. He admired their sense of purpose and dedication to their missionary work. A few months after meeting Keren he became a born-again Christian, and a year later they were married. Their goal was to start a family and become missionaries themselves.

十七岁时，他遇到了高中同学凯伦·格雷厄姆，一切似乎都改变了。凯伦童年的大部分时间都在巴西东北部度过，她的父母在那里担任基督教传教士。他喜欢和她一起出去玩，听她讲述在巴西的生活故事。他认识了她的家人，并成为他们晚餐的常客。他钦佩他们对传教工作的使命感和奉献精神。认识凯伦几个月后，他成为了一名重生的基督徒，一年后他们结婚了。他们的目标是组建家庭，并成为传教士。

Everett graduated from the Moody Bible Institute of Chicago with a degree in Foreign Missions, and in 1976 he and his wife enrolled in the Summer Institute of Linguistics (SIL)—a Christian organization that instructs future missionaries in the necessary linguistic skills to translate the Bible into indigenous languages and spread the Gospel. After going through the course work, he and his family (which now included two children) were sent to SIL’s jungle camp in the region of Chiapas, in southern Mexico, to prepare them for the rigors of missionary life. For a month the family had to live in a village and learn as best they could the indigenous language, a Mayan dialect. Everett passed all of the tests with flying colors. Based on his success in the program, the faculty at SIL decided to offer him and his family the greatest challenge of them all—to live in a Pirahã village, deep in the heart of the Amazon.

埃弗里特毕业于芝加哥慕迪圣经学院，获得外国传教学位。1976 年，他和妻子进入夏季语言学院 (SIL) 学习。这是一个基督教组织，旨在培训未来的传教士掌握将圣经翻译成当地语言并传播福音所需的语言技能。完成课程后，他和家人（现在有两个孩子）被派往 SIL 位于墨西哥南部恰帕斯州的丛林营地，为艰苦的传教生活做准备。全家必须在村子里住一个月，尽力学习当地语言，即玛雅方言。埃弗里特以优异的成绩通过了所有考试。鉴于他在项目中的出色表现，SIL 的老师决定给他和他的家人提供最大的挑战——住在亚马逊腹地的皮拉罕村落。

The Pirahã are among the oldest inhabitants of the Amazon. When the Portuguese arrived in the area in the early eighteenth century, most of the tribes learned their language and adopted many of their ways, but the Pirahã resisted and retreated further into the jungle. They lived in deep isolation, with little contact with outsiders. By the time missionaries arrived in their villages in the 1950s, there were only some 350 Pirahã still alive, scattered in the area. The missionaries who tried to learn their language found it impossible. The Pirahã spoke no Portuguese, had no written language, and their words, to Westerners, all sounded alike. SIL had sent a couple in 1967 to learn the language and finally translate part of the Bible into Pirahã, but they could make little progress. After more than ten years of struggling with the language, they were driven half-mad by the task and wanted to leave. Hearing all of this, Everett was more than happy to accept the challenge. He and his wife were determined to be the first ones to crack the code of Pirahã.

皮拉罕人是亚马逊地区最古老的居民之一。十八世纪初，葡萄牙人抵达此地时，大多数部落学习了他们的语言，并采纳了许多习俗，但皮拉罕人奋起反抗，退居丛林深处。他们过着与世隔绝的生活，很少与外界接触。到20世纪50年代，传教士来到他们的村庄时，皮拉罕人只剩下大约350人，分散在当地。那些试图学习皮拉罕人语言的传教士发现，这根本行不通。皮拉罕人不会说葡萄牙语，也没有书面语，而且在西方人听来，他们的语言听起来都一样。SIL于1967年派了一对夫妇去学习皮拉罕语，并最终将部分《圣经》翻译成皮拉罕语，但进展甚微。经过十多年的苦苦挣扎，他们几乎被这项任务逼疯了，想要离开。听到这些，埃弗里特欣然接受了挑战。他和他的妻子决心成为第一个破解皮拉罕语密码的人。

He and his family arrived at a Pirahã village in December 1977. In his first few days there, Everett used all of the strategies he had been taught—for instance, holding up a stick and asking for their word for it, then dropping the stick and asking for the phrase to describe the action. In the months to come, he made good progress learning basic vocabulary. The method he had learned at SIL worked well, and he worked assiduously. Every time he heard a new word, he wrote it down on three-by-five note cards. He punched holes in the corners of the cards, carried dozens of them on the loop of his pants, and repeatedly practiced them with villagers. He tried to apply these words and phrases in different contexts, sometimes making the Pirahã laugh. Whenever he felt frustrated, he would look at the Pirahã children who picked up the language with ease. If they could learn it, so could he, he kept telling himself. But every time he felt like he was learning more phrases, he had the equal sensation that he was really getting nowhere. He began to understand the frustration of the couple that had preceded him.

1977年12月，埃弗里特和家人抵达了一个皮拉罕人村庄。在那里的最初几天里，埃弗里特运用了他学到的所有策略——比如，举起一根棍子，请村民用这个词来形容它；然后扔下棍子，再请村民用一个短语来描述这个动作。在接下来的几个月里，他学习基本词汇的进度很快。他在SIL学到的方法很有效，而且他学习刻苦。每当听到一个新词，他就把它写在3x5英寸的卡片上。他在卡片的角上打孔，把几十张卡片挂在裤腰上，反复和村民练习。他尝试在不同的语境中运用这些单词和短语，有时还会逗得皮拉罕人哈哈大笑。每当他感到沮丧时，他就会看着那些轻松掌握语言的皮拉罕儿童。“如果他们能学会，他也能，”他不断地告诉自己。但每当他感觉自己学到了更多短语时，他又会感到自己一事无成。他开始理解在他之前那对夫妇的沮丧。

For instance, he kept hearing a word over and over again that seemed to translate as “just now,” as in “the man had just now left.” But later, hearing it in a different context, he realized that it in fact referred to the precise moment when something appears or disappears—a person, a sound, anything. The phrase was really about the experience of such transitory moments, he decided, which seemed to resonate a lot with the Pirahã. “Just now” did not begin to cover the rich meanings of it. This started to happen with all kinds of words he thought he had understood. He also began to discover things that were missing in their language that went against all of the linguistic theories he had been taught. They had no words for numbers, no concept of right and left, no simple words that designated colors. What could this mean?

比如，他反复听到一个词，似乎可以翻译成“刚才”，比如“那个人刚才离开了”。但后来，在不同的语境中听到这个词，他意识到它实际上指的是某物出现或消失的那一刻——一个人，一个声音，任何东西。他认定，这个短语实际上指的是这种转瞬即逝的体验，这似乎与皮拉罕人很能产生共鸣。“刚才”一词的含义远不足以概括其丰富的内涵。他自认为理解的各种词汇都出现了这种情况。他还开始发现皮拉罕语中缺失了一些与他所学语言理论相悖的东西。他们没有表示数字的词，没有左右的概念，也没有表示颜色的简单词汇。这究竟意味着什么？

One day, after more than a year living there, he decided to accompany some Pirahã men deep into the jungle, and to his surprise he discovered a whole other side to their existence and language. They acted and spoke differently; they employed a different form of communication, talking to one another in elaborate whistles that clearly replaced spoken language, making them stealthier in their hunting forays. Their ability to navigate this dangerous environment was impressive.

在那里生活了一年多之后，有一天，他决定陪同一些皮拉罕人深入丛林，令他惊讶的是，他发现了他们生存和语言的另一面。他们的行为和言语截然不同；他们使用一种不同的交流方式，用复杂的口哨声互相交谈，这显然取代了口头语言，使他们在狩猎时更加隐秘。他们在这种危险环境中的探索能力令人印象深刻。

Suddenly something became clear to Everett: his decision to confine himself to village life and simply to learn their language was the source of his problem. Their language could not be separated from their method of hunting, their culture, their daily habits. He had unconsciously internalized a sense of superiority to these people and their way of life—living among them like a scientist studying ants. His inability to pierce the secret of their language, however, revealed the inadequacies of his method. If he wanted to learn Pirahã as the children did, he would have to become like a child—dependent on these people for survival, participating in their daily activities, entering their social circles, feeling in fact inferior and in need of their support. (Losing any sense of superiority would later lead to a personal crisis, in which he would lose faith in his role as a missionary and leave the church for good.)

埃弗里特突然明白了一点：他决定把自己局限于村落生活，仅仅学习他们的语言，这正是他问题的根源。他们的语言与他们的狩猎方式、文化和日常生活密不可分。他潜意识里内化了一种对这些人及其生活方式的优越感——就像一位研究蚂蚁的科学家一样与他们生活在一起。然而，他无法洞悉他们语言的秘密，这暴露了他方法的不足。如果他想像孩子们一样学习皮拉罕语，他就必须变得像孩子一样——依赖这些人生存，参与他们的日常活动，融入他们的社交圈，感到自卑，需要他们的支持。（失去任何优越感后来都会导致他个人危机，最终他会对自己作为传教士的角色失去信心，并永远离开教会。）

He began to enact this strategy on all levels, entering a realm of their lives that had been hidden to him. Soon all kinds of ideas about their strange language came to him. The linguistic oddities of Pirahã reflected the unique culture that they had evolved from living in isolation for so long. Participating in their lives as if he was one of their children, the language came alive from within, and he began to make the kind of progress in Pirahã that had eluded everyone else before him.

他开始在各个层面运用这一策略，深入他们生活中一个他一直未曾涉足的领域。很快，关于他们奇特语言的各种想法涌入他的脑海。皮拉罕人的语言怪异之处反映了他们长期与世隔绝的生活所发展出的独特文化。他像他们的孩子一样融入他们的生活，语言从内心深处焕发出活力，他开始在皮拉罕语方面取得前所未有的进步，而这在之前都是其他人无法企及的。

In his apprenticeship in the jungles of the Amazon that would later lead to his career as a groundbreaking linguist, Daniel Everett came upon a truth that has application far beyond his field of study. What prevents people from learning, even something as difficult as Pirahã, is not the subject itself—the human mind has limitless capabilities—but rather certain learning disabilities that tend to fester and grow in our minds as we get older. These include a sense of smugness and superiority whenever we encounter something alien to our ways, as well as rigid ideas about what is real or true, often indoctrinated in us by schooling or family. If we feel like we know something, our minds close off to other possibilities. We see reflections of the truth we have already assumed. Such feelings of superiority are often unconscious and stem from a fear of what is different or unknown. We are rarely aware of this, and often imagine ourselves to be paragons of impartiality.

丹尼尔·埃弗里特在亚马逊丛林的学徒生涯，最终成就了他开创性的语言学家生涯。他发现了一个真理，其应用范围远远超出了他的研究领域。阻碍人们学习，即使是像皮拉罕语这样难学的语言，并非源于学习本身——人类的思维能力是无限的——而是某些学习障碍，这些障碍往往会随着年龄的增长而在我们的大脑中滋生和发展。这些障碍包括：每当我们遇到与我们习以为常的事物时，我们就会产生的沾沾自喜和优越感；以及对真实与否的刻板观念，这些观念通常由学校或家庭灌输给我们。如果我们觉得自己知道某件事，我们的大脑就会拒绝其他可能性。我们会看到那些我们早已认定的真理的影子。这种优越感通常是无意识的，源于对不同或未知事物的恐惧。我们很少意识到这一点，常常将自己想象成公正无私的典范。

Children are generally free of these handicaps. They are dependent upon adults for their survival and naturally feel inferior . This sense of inferiority gives them a hunger to learn. Through learning, they can bridge the gap and not feel so helpless. Their minds are completely open; they pay greater attention. This is why children can learn so quickly and so deeply. Unlike other animals, we humans retain what is known as neoteny—mental and physical traits of immaturity—well into our adult years. We have the remarkable capability of returning to a childlike spirit, especially in moments in which we must learn something. Well into our fifties and beyond, we can return to that sense of wonder and curiosity, reviving our youth and apprenticeships.

儿童通常没有这些障碍。他们依赖成人生存，自然而然地感到自卑。这种自卑感让他们渴望学习。通过学习，他们可以弥合差距，不再感到无助。他们的心胸完全开放，注意力更加集中。这就是为什么儿童学得如此迅速和深入。与其他动物不同，我们人类在成年后仍保留着所谓的幼态持续——未成熟的心理和生理特征。我们拥有回归童心的非凡能力，尤其是在我们必须学习的时刻。即使到了五十多岁甚至更久，我们仍然可以重拾那种好奇心和求知欲，重拾青春和学徒期。

Understand: when you enter a new environment, your task is to learn and absorb as much as possible. For that purpose you must try to revert to a childlike feeling of inferiority—the feeling that others know much more than you and that you are dependent upon them to learn and safely navigate your apprenticeship. You drop all of your preconceptions about an environment or field, any lingering feelings of smugness. You have no fears. You interact with people and participate in the culture as deeply as possible. You are full of curiosity. Assuming this sensation of inferiority, your mind will open up and you will have a hunger to learn. This position is of course only temporary. You are reverting to a feeling of dependence, so that within five to ten years you can learn enough to finally declare your independence and enter full adulthood.

要明白：当你进入一个新环境时，你的任务是尽可能多地学习和吸收。为此，你必须努力恢复童真的自卑感——那种感觉别人比你知道得多，你依赖他们学习，才能安全地度过你的学徒期。你要放下所有对某个环境或领域的先入之见，放下任何挥之不去的沾沾自喜。你无所畏惧。你与人互动，并尽可能深入地融入当地文化。你充满好奇心。承担起这种自卑感，你的心胸会开阔，你会渴望学习。当然，这种状态只是暂时的。你正在恢复一种依赖感，以便在五到十年内，你能够学到足够的知识，最终宣布独立，步入成年。

# ↩

4. Trust the process

4. 相信过程

Cesar Rodriguez’s father was a lifelong officer in the U.S. Army, but when Cesar (b. 1959) chose to attend the Citadel, the Military College of South Carolina, it was not because he was determined to follow in his father’s footsteps. He was probably heading toward a career in business. He decided, however, that he needed some discipline in life, and there was no more rigorous environment than the Citadel.

塞萨尔·罗德里格斯的父亲曾是美国陆军的终身军官，但塞萨尔（生于1959年）选择就读南卡罗来纳军事学院（Citadel），并非因为他决心追随父亲的脚步。他很可能是想从事商业事业。然而，他认为自己需要一些自律，而没有比Citadel更严格的环境了。

One morning in 1978, during his sophomore year, Rodriguez’s roommate told him that he was going to take the exams that the army, navy, and air force were offering for entrance into the aviation branches of their forces. Rodriguez decided to come along and take the exams just for the hell of it. To his surprise, a few days later he was notified that he had been accepted by the air force for their pilot training program. The initial training, to take place while he was still at the Citadel, meant taking flying lessons in a Cessna. Figuring that would be fun, he entered the program, not entirely sure how far he would take it. He passed the training exams rather easily. He enjoyed the mental challenge, the complete focus that flying required. Perhaps it would be interesting to take the next step. And so, after graduating from the Citadel in 1981, he was sent to the ten-month pilot instruction school at Vance Air Force Base in Oklahoma.

1978年的一个早晨，罗德里格斯还在读大二，他的室友告诉他，他要参加陆军、海军和空军的航空兵入学考试。罗德里格斯决定去参加，纯粹是为了好玩。令他惊讶的是，几天后，他收到通知，他已被空军录取，参加他们的飞行员训练项目。最初的训练将在他还在城堡军事学院的时候进行，内容是驾驶塞斯纳飞机飞行。他觉得这应该很有趣，于是报名参加了这个项目，但并不完全确定自己能坚持到什么时候。他相当轻松地通过了训练考试。他喜欢飞行带来的精神挑战，以及飞行所需的全神贯注。或许，迈出下一步会很有意思。于是，1981年从城堡军事学院毕业后，他被派往俄克拉荷马州万斯空军基地，参加为期十个月的飞行员指导学校。

At Vance, however, he discovered that he was suddenly in over his head. Now they were training on a subsonic jet, the T-37. He had to wear a ten-pound helmet and a forty-pound parachute on his back. The cockpit was unbearably small and hot. The instructor sat uncomfortably close in the seat beside him, observing his every move. The stress of performing, the heat, the physical pressures of flying at such speeds would make him sweat profusely and shake. He felt as though the jet itself was pounding and beating him as he flew. And then there were so many more variables to be aware of in flying a jet.

然而，在万斯，他突然发现自己陷入了困境。现在他们正在训练一架亚音速喷气式飞机——T-37。他必须戴着十磅重的头盔，背上四十磅重的降落伞。驾驶舱狭小闷热，令人难以忍受。教练坐在他身旁，离他很近，令人感到不适，密切观察着他的一举一动。训练的压力、酷热，以及高速飞行带来的身体压力，让他汗流浃背，浑身颤抖。他感觉就像喷气式飞机在飞行时撞击着他。而且，驾驶喷气式飞机时，还有太多的变数需要注意。

Working on the simulator, he could fly with relative confidence and feel as if he were in control. But once he was strapped into the jet itself he could not suppress a feeling of panic and uncertainty—his mind could not keep up with all of the information he had to process, and it was difficult to prioritize his tasks. Much to his dismay, several months into training he received failing marks on two consecutive flights, and was benched from flying for an entire week.

在模拟器上操作时，他飞行起来相对自信，感觉一切尽在掌握。但一旦系好安全带，他便无法抑制恐慌和不确定感——他的大脑无法处理所有需要处理的信息，也难以确定任务的轻重缓急。令他沮丧的是，训练几个月后，他连续两次飞行都获得了不及格的成绩，被禁止飞行整整一周。

He had never failed at anything before; it was a matter of pride that he had conquered everything that had been presented to him so far in life. Now he faced a possibility that would devastate him. Seventy students had started out in the course, but almost every week one of them was cut from the program. It was a ruthless, whittling-down process. It looked as if he would be the next one to be cut, and such cuts were final. Once he was allowed back into the plane, he would only have a few chances to prove himself. He had already been trying his hardest. Where had he gone wrong? Perhaps unconsciously, he had become intimidated and afraid of the flying process itself. Now he was more afraid of failing.

他以前从未失败过；人生中迄今为止遇到的所有挑战，他都值得骄傲。现在，他面临着一个可能让他崩溃的结局。这门课程最初有七十名学生，但几乎每周都会有一人被淘汰。这是一个残酷的淘汰过程。看起来，下一个被淘汰的就是他，而且是最终的淘汰。一旦他被允许重返飞机，他证明自己的机会就不多了。他已经尽了最大的努力。他到底错在哪里？或许在潜意识里，他已经对飞行过程本身感到畏惧和恐惧。现在，他更害怕失败。

He thought back to his days in high school. Despite his relatively short height, he had managed to become the quarterback of his high school football team. Back then he had also experienced moments of doubt and even panic. He had discovered, however, that through rigorous training—mental and physical—he could overcome his fear and almost any deficiency in his skill level. In football practice, placing himself in circumstances that had made him feel uncertain had helped him to become familiar with the situation and not so afraid. What was necessary was to trust the process and the results that would come from more practice. This would have to be the way forward in his current situation.

他回想起高中时光。尽管身高相对较矮，他还是成功成为高中橄榄球队的四分卫。那时，他也曾经历过怀疑甚至恐慌的时刻。然而，他发现，通过严格的训练——精神和体能——他能够克服恐惧，以及几乎所有技能上的不足。在橄榄球训练中，置身于那些让他感到不确定的环境中，帮助他熟悉了情况，不再那么害怕。重要的是要相信过程，以及通过更多练习获得的结果。在他目前的处境下，这必将是他前进的方向。

He tripled his time with the simulator, habituating his mind to the sensation of so many stimuli. He spent his off-hours visualizing himself in the cockpit, repeating the maneuvers he was weakest at. Once he was allowed back in the plane, he focused much harder, knowing he would have to make the most of each precious session. Whenever there was a chance to have more air time, for instance when another student was sick, he grabbed it. Slowly, day by day, he found a way to calm himself in the pilot seat and get a better handle on all of the complex operations. In the two weeks after being allowed back into the plane, he had managed to rescue his position for the time being; he was now ranked somewhere in the middle of the group.

他把使用模拟器的时间增加了两倍，让自己的大脑适应如此多刺激的感觉。他利用业余时间想象自己坐在驾驶舱里，重复练习他最不擅长的操作。一旦被允许重返飞机，他便更加专注，因为他知道必须充分利用每一次宝贵的飞行时间。只要有机会获得更多的飞行时间，比如有其他学生生病了，他就会抓住机会。慢慢地，一天天地，他找到了让自己在驾驶座上平静下来的方法，并更好地掌握了所有复杂的操作。在被允许重返飞机后的两周里，他设法暂时保住了自己的位置；现在他的排名在小组中游。

With ten weeks remaining in the program, Rodriguez took stock of the situation. He had come too far not to succeed. He enjoyed the challenge, he loved flying, and now what he wanted more than anything in life was to become a fighter pilot. That would mean graduating from the program near the very top. Among his group were several “golden boys”—young men who had a natural flair for flying. They not only handled the intense pressures, they fed off of them. He was the opposite of a golden boy, but that had been the story of his life. He had succeeded through his determination before, and now it would have to be the same. In these final weeks he was to train on the supersonic T-38, and he asked his new instructor, Wheels Wheeler, to work him to death—he had to move up in the rankings and he was prepared to do whatever it took.

训练还剩十周，罗德里格斯评估了形势。他已经走了很远，不可能不成功。他享受挑战，热爱飞行，现在他人生最大的愿望就是成为一名战斗机飞行员。这意味着他能以接近顶尖的成绩毕业。他的小组里有几位“金童”——天生具有飞行天赋的年轻人。他们不仅能应对巨大的压力，还能从中汲取力量。他与“金童”截然相反，但这恰恰是他人生的写照。他以前凭借自己的决心取得了成功，现在也必须如此。在最后几周，他将驾驶超音速T-38飞机进行训练，他要求他的新教练惠尔斯·惠勒让他拼尽全力——他必须在排名中不断提升，他已经准备好不惜一切代价。

Wheeler obliged him. He made Rodriguez repeat the same maneuver ten times more than the golden boys, until he was physically sick. He homed in on all of Rodriguez’s flying weaknesses and made him practice on the things he hated the most. His criticisms were brutal. One day, however, as he was flying the T-38, Rodriguez had a strange and wonderful sensation—it seemed like he could feel the plane itself at the edge of his fingertips. This is how it must be for the golden boys, he thought, only for him it had taken nearly ten months of intense training. His mind no longer felt mired in all of the details. It was vague, but he could sense the possibility of a higher way of thinking—seeing the larger picture of flying in formation, while also commanding the complex operations in the cockpit. This sensation would come and go, but the feeling made all of the work worthwhile.

惠勒答应了。他让罗德里格斯比“金童”们多做十次同样的动作，直到他身体不适。他抓住了罗德里格斯所有的飞行弱点，让他练习他最讨厌的动作。他的批评非常严厉。然而，有一天，当他驾驶T-38时，罗德里格斯突然有一种奇特而奇妙的感觉——他似乎能感觉到飞机就在指尖边缘。他心想，“金童”们肯定也经历过这种感觉，只是对他来说，这需要近十个月的高强度训练。他的思绪不再纠结于细节。虽然这种感觉很模糊，但他能感受到一种更高层次的思维方式的可能性——既能看到编队飞行的全局，又能指挥驾驶舱内的复杂操作。这种感觉时有时无，但这种感觉让所有的努力都值得。

In the end Rodriguez graduated third in his class, and was promoted to fighter-pilot lead-in training. The same process would now repeat itself in an even more competitive environment. He would have to outdo the golden boys through practice and sheer determination. In this manner, he slowly rose through the ranks to become a colonel in the U.S. Air Force. During the 1990s, his three air-to-air kills in active duty brought him closer to the designation of ace than any American pilot since the Vietnam War, and earned him the nickname the Last American Ace.

罗德里格斯最终以全班第三名的成绩毕业，并晋升为战斗机飞行员预备训练生。如今，同样的过程将在竞争更加激烈的环境中重演。他必须通过练习和坚定的决心超越那些“金童”们。就这样，他一步步晋升，最终成为美国空军上校。20世纪90年代，他在现役期间的三次空对空击落战绩使他比越南战争以来的任何美国飞行员都更接近王牌飞行员的称号，并赢得了“美国最后的王牌飞行员”的绰号。

What separates Masters from others is often something surprisingly simple. Whenever we learn a skill, we frequently reach a point of frustration—what we are learning seems beyond our capabilities. Giving in to these feelings, we unconsciously quit on ourselves before we actually give up. Among the dozens of pilots in Rodriguez’s class who never made the cut, almost all of them had the same talent level as he did. The difference is not simply a matter of determination, but more of trust and faith. Many of those who succeed in life have had the experience in their youth of having mastered some skill—a sport or game, a musical instrument, a foreign language, and so on. Buried in their minds is the sensation of overcoming their frustrations and entering the cycle of accelerated returns. In moments of doubt in the present, the memory of the past experience rises to the surface. Filled with trust in the process, they trudge on well past the point at which others slow down or mentally quit.

大师与普通人的区别往往出奇地简单。每当我们学习一项技能时，我们常常会感到沮丧——我们所学的东西似乎超出了我们的能力范围。屈服于这种情绪，我们会在真正放弃之前无意识地放弃。在罗德里格斯的班上，数十名未能晋级的飞行员中，几乎所有人都拥有与他相同的天赋。这种区别不仅仅在于决心，更在于信任和信念。许多人生成功的人，在年轻时都曾掌握过某种技能——一项运动或游戏、一种乐器、一门外语等等。他们心中埋藏着克服挫折、进入加速回报周期的那种感觉。在当下充满疑虑的时刻，过去经验的记忆浮现出来。他们对这个过程充满信心，能够艰难地坚持下去，远远超过其他人放慢脚步或放弃的阶段。

When it comes to mastering a skill, time is the magic ingredient. Assuming your practice proceeds at a steady level, over days and weeks certain elements of the skill become hardwired. Slowly, the entire skill becomes internalized, part of your nervous system. The mind is no longer mired in the details, but can see the larger picture. It is a miraculous sensation and practice will lead you to that point, no matter the talent level you are born with. The only real impediment to this is yourself and your emotions—boredom, panic, frustration, insecurity. You cannot suppress such emotions—they are normal to the process and are experienced by everyone, including Masters. What you can do is have faith in the process. The boredom will go away once you enter the cycle. The panic disappears after repeated exposure. The frustration is a sign of progress—a signal that your mind is processing complexity and requires more practice. The insecurities will transform into their opposites when you gain mastery. Trusting this will all happen, you will allow the natural learning process to move forward, and everything else will fall into place.

时间是掌握一项技能的神奇因素。假设你的练习进展平稳，经过数日数周，技能的某些要素就会逐渐成型。慢慢地，整项技能就会被内化，成为你神经系统的一部分。你的思维不再沉溺于细节，而是能够看到更广阔的图景。这是一种神奇的感觉，无论你与生俱来的天赋水平如何，练习都会引导你达到那种境界。唯一真正的障碍是你自己和你的情绪——无聊、恐慌、沮丧、不安全感。你无法压抑这些情绪——它们是学习过程中的正常现象，每个人都会经历，包括大师。你能做的就是对这个过程充满信心。一旦你进入这个循环，无聊感就会消失。恐慌也会在反复练习后消失。沮丧是进步的标志——它表明你的大脑正在处理复杂的问题，需要更多的练习。当你精通时，不安全感就会转化为它的对立面。相信这一切都会发生，你就能让学习过程自然而然地向前发展，其他一切都会水到渠成。

# ↩

5. Move toward resistance and pain

5. 走向阻力和痛苦

A. Bill Bradley (b. 1943) fell in love with the sport of basketball somewhere around the age of ten. He had one advantage over his peers—he was tall for his age. But beyond that, he had no real natural gift for the game. He was slow and gawky, and could not jump very high. None of the aspects of the game came easily to him. He would have to compensate for all of his inadequacies through sheer practice. And so he proceeded to devise one of the most rigorous and efficient training routines in the history of sports.

A. 比尔·布拉德利（生于1943年）大约在十岁左右爱上了篮球这项运动。他比同龄人有一个优势——身高体型比同龄人高。但除此之外，他并没有真正的篮球天赋。他动作缓慢、笨拙，跳得也不太高。篮球运动的任何方面对他来说都并非易事。他必须通过纯粹的练习来弥补自己的不足。于是，他着手设计出体育史上最严格、最高效的训练方案之一。

Managing to get his hands on the keys to the high school gym, he created for himself a schedule—three and a half hours of practice after school and on Sundays, eight hours every Saturday, and three hours a day during the summer. Over the years, he would keep rigidly to this schedule. In the gym, he would put ten-pound weights in his shoes to strengthen his legs and give him more spring to his jump. His greatest weaknesses, he decided, were his dribbling and his overall slowness. He would have to work on these and also transform himself into a superior passer to make up for his lack of speed.

他设法弄到了高中体育馆的钥匙，并为自己制定了一个训练计划——放学后和周日练习三个半小时，每周六练习八小时，暑假每天练习三个小时。多年来，他一直严格遵守这个计划。在体育馆里，他会在鞋子里放十磅重的哑铃来增强腿部力量，让跳跃更有弹性。他认为自己最大的弱点是运球和整体速度慢。他必须改进这些方面，同时还要把自己打造成一个更优秀的传球手，以弥补速度上的不足。

For this purpose, he devised various exercises. He wore eyeglass frames with pieces of cardboard taped to the bottom, so he could not see the basketball while he practiced dribbling. This would train him to always look around him rather than at the ball—a key skill in passing. He set up chairs on the court to act as opponents. He would dribble around them, back and forth, for hours, until he could glide past them, quickly changing direction. He spent hours at both of these exercises, well past any feelings of boredom or pain.

为了这个目的，他设计了各种各样的练习。他戴上眼镜框，框底用胶带粘着几块硬纸板，这样练习运球时就看不到篮球了。这能训练他始终环顾四周，而不是盯着球——这是传球的关键技能。他在球场上摆放椅子，充当对手。他会绕着他们来回运球，一连几个小时，直到他能快速变向，滑过他们。他花了几个小时做这两项练习，完全没有感到无聊或疼痛。

Walking down the main street of his hometown in Missouri, he would keep his eyes focused straight ahead and try to notice the goods in the store windows, on either side, without turning his head. He worked on this endlessly, developing his peripheral vision so he could see more of the court. In his room at home, he practiced pivot moves and fakes well into the night—such skills that would also help him compensate for his lack of speed.

走在密苏里州家乡的大街上，他总是目不转睛地注视前方，努力不回头地留意两旁商店橱窗里的商品。他不断练习，提升周边视觉，以便能够看到更多球场。在家的房间里，他练习着枢轴移动和假动作，直到深夜——这些技巧也帮助他弥补了速度上的不足。

Bradley put all of his creative energy into coming up with novel and effective ways of practicing. One time his family traveled to Europe via transatlantic ship. Finally, they thought, he would give his training regimen a break—there was really no place to practice on board. But below deck and running the length of the ship were two corridors, 900 feet long and quite narrow—just enough room for two passengers. This was the perfect location to practice dribbling at top speed while maintaining perfect ball control. To make it even harder, he decided to wear special eyeglasses that narrowed his vision. For hours every day he dribbled up one side and down the other, until the voyage was done.

布拉德利倾尽所有创造力，致力于寻找新颖有效的练习方法。有一次，他和家人乘坐横跨大西洋的轮船前往欧洲。他们终于想让他暂停训练了——船上实在没有地方练习。然而，甲板下方，沿着船身延伸着两条900英尺长的走廊，非常狭窄——仅够两名乘客通过。这简直是练习高速带球并保持完美控球的绝佳场所。为了增加难度，他决定戴上一副能缩小视野的特殊眼镜。每天，他都要花上几个小时，在船的两边来回练习，直到航程结束。

Working this way over the years, Bradley slowly transformed himself into one of the biggest stars in basketball—first as an All-American at Princeton University and then as a professional with the New York Knicks. Fans were in awe of his ability to make the most astounding passes, as if he had eyes on the back and sides of his head—not to mention his dribbling prowess, his incredible arsenal of fakes and pivots, and his complete gracefulness on the court. Little did they know that such apparent ease was the result of so many hours of intense practice over so many years.

多年来，布拉德利就这样努力训练，慢慢地将自己打造成了篮球界最耀眼的明星之一——先是普林斯顿大学的全美最佳球员，后来成为纽约尼克斯队的职业球员。球迷们惊叹于他那令人惊叹的传球能力，仿佛他的后脑勺和两侧长着眼睛——更不用说他精湛的运球技术、令人难以置信的假动作和转身技巧，以及他在球场上优雅的姿态。他们几乎不知道，如此看似轻松的球技，背后是多年高强度训练的成果。

B. When John Keats (1795–1821) was eight years old, his father died in a riding accident. His mother never quite got over the loss and died seven years later—essentially leaving John, his two brothers, and one sister orphaned and homeless in London. John, the eldest of the children, was taken out of school by the appointed trustee and guardian of the estate, and enrolled as an apprentice to a surgeon and apothecary—he would have to earn a living as quickly as possible, and this seemed the best career for that.

B. 约翰·济慈（1795-1821）八岁时，父亲在一次骑马事故中丧生。他的母亲从未完全从丧父的悲痛中走出来，七年后也去世了——留下约翰、他的两个兄弟和一个妹妹在伦敦沦为孤儿，无家可归。作为家中长子，约翰被指定的遗产托管人和监护人带离学校，去给一位外科医生和药剂师当学徒——他必须尽快谋生，而这似乎是最好的职业。

In his last few terms at school, Keats had developed a love for literature and reading. To continue his education, he would return to his school in his off-hours and read as many books as he could in the library. Sometime later, he had the desire to try his hand at writing poetry, but lacking any kind of instructor or literary circle he could frequent, the only way he knew to teach himself to write was to read the works of all of the greatest poets of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. He then wrote his own poems, using the poetic form and style of the particular writer he was trying to model himself after. He had a knack for imitation, and soon he was creating verses in dozens of different styles, always tweaking them a little with his own voice.

在学校的最后几个学期里，济慈对文学和阅读产生了浓厚的兴趣。为了继续深造，他经常在课余时间回到学校，在图书馆里尽可能多地读书。一段时间后，他萌生了尝试写诗的念头，但由于缺乏导师或文学圈子，他知道的唯一自学方法就是阅读十七、十八世纪所有伟大诗人的作品。之后，他开始创作自己的诗歌，并借鉴他所效仿的作家的诗歌形式和风格。他擅长模仿，很快便能创作出几十种不同风格的诗歌，并总是略加调整，融入自己的风格。

Several years into this process, Keats came to a fateful decision—he would devote his life to writing poetry. That was his calling in life and he would find a way to make a living at it. To complete the rigorous apprenticeship he had already put himself through, he decided that what he needed was to write a very long poem, precisely 4,000 lines. The poem would revolve around the ancient Greek myth of Endymion. “ Endymion ,” he wrote a friend, “will be a test, a trial of my Powers of Imagination and chiefly of my invention…—by which I must make 4000 lines of some circumstances and fill them with Poetry.” He gave himself a rather impossible deadline—seven months—and a task of writing fifty lines a day, until he had a rough draft.

经过数年的努力，济慈最终做出了一个决定命运的决定——他要将一生奉献给诗歌创作。这是他人生的使命，他要以此谋生。为了完成他已经完成的严苛学徒期，他决定写一首非常长的诗，恰好4000行。这首诗将围绕古希腊神话人物恩迪米翁展开。他写信给一位朋友说：“恩迪米翁将是一场考验，一场对我想象力，尤其是创造力的考验……——我必须用4000行诗来描述某些场景，并用诗歌来充实它们。” 他给自己设定了一个几乎不可能完成的期限——七个月——并要求每天写五十行，直到完成草稿。

Three-quarters of the way through, he came to thoroughly hate the poem he was writing. He would not quit, however, willing his way to the end, meeting the deadline he had set. What he did not like about Endymion was the flowery language, the overwriting. But it was only by means of this exercise that he could discover what worked for him. “In Endymion ,” he later wrote, “I leaped headlong into the Sea and thereby became better acquainted with the Soundings, the quicksands and the rocks, than if I had stayed upon the green shore and…took tea and comfortable advice.”

写到四分之三的时候，他开始彻底讨厌自己正在写的这首诗。然而，他不愿放弃，坚持写到最后，按时完成了自己设定的期限。他不喜欢《恩底弥翁》的华丽辞藻和过度的写作风格。但只有通过这种练习，他才能找到适合自己的写作方法。“在《恩底弥翁》中，”他后来写道，“我一头扎进大海，从而比待在碧绿的海岸上……品茶和寻求安慰更能理解水深、流沙和岩石。”

In the aftermath of writing what he considered to be a mediocre poem, Keats took stock of all of the invaluable lessons he had learned. Never again would he suffer from writer’s block—he had trained himself to write past any obstacle. He had acquired now the habit of writing quickly, with intensity and focus—concentrating his work in a few hours. He could revise with equal speed. He had learned how to criticize himself and his overly romantic tendencies. He could look at his own work with a cold eye. He had learned that it was in the actual writing of the poem that the best ideas would often come to him, and that he had to boldly keep writing or he would miss such discoveries. Most important of all, as a counterexample to Endymion, he had hit upon a style that suited him—language as compact and dense with imagery as possible, with not a single wasted line.

在写完那首自认为平庸的诗后，济慈总结了所有宝贵的经验教训。他再也没有遇到过写作瓶颈——他训练自己能够克服任何障碍。他现在已经养成了快速、专注、高强度写作的习惯——几个小时就能完成作品。他也能以同样的速度修改。他学会了如何批判自己以及自己过于浪漫的倾向。他能用冷静的眼光审视自己的作品。他明白，最好的灵感往往是在实际创作过程中涌现的，他必须大胆地继续写作，否则就会错失这样的发现。最重要的是，与《恩迪米翁》截然相反，他找到了一种适合自己的风格——语言尽可能紧凑、富有意象，没有一行多余的文字。

With these lessons in hand, in the years 1818 to 1819, before he became gravely ill, Keats would produce some of the most memorable poems in the English language, including all of his greatest odes. This added up to perhaps the most productive two years of writing in the history of Western literature—all of it set up by the rigorous self-apprenticeship he had put himself through.

凭借这些经验，在1818年至1819年病重之前，济慈创作了一些英语中最令人难忘的诗歌，包括他所有最伟大的颂歌。这或许是西方文学史上写作成果最丰硕的两年——这一切都源于他严谨的自我学徒训练。

By nature, we humans shrink from anything that seems possibly painful or overtly difficult. We bring this natural tendency to our practice of any skill. Once we grow adept at some aspect of this skill, generally one that comes more easily to us, we prefer to practice this element over and over. Our skill becomes lopsided as we avoid our weaknesses. Knowing that in our practice we can let down our guard, since we are not being watched or under pressure to perform, we bring to this a kind of dispersed attention. We tend to also be quite conventional in our practice routines. We generally follow what others have done, performing the accepted exercises for these skills.

人类天生会回避任何看似痛苦或过于困难的事情。我们将这种自然倾向带入任何技能的练习中。一旦我们熟练掌握了某项技能的某个方面（通常是那些对我们来说比较容易掌握的方面），我们就会喜欢反复练习。当我们回避自己的弱点时，技能就会变得不平衡。我们知道在练习中我们可以放松警惕，因为我们没有人监督，也没有压力要求我们表现，所以我们会将注意力分散到练习上。我们的练习方式也往往非常循规蹈矩。我们通常会效仿他人的做法，进行这些技能中公认的练习。

This is the path of amateurs. To attain mastery, you must adopt what we shall call Resistance Practice. The principle is simple—you go in the opposite direction of all of your natural tendencies when it comes to practice. First, you resist the temptation to be nice to yourself. You become your own worst critic; you see your work as if through the eyes of others. You recognize your weaknesses, precisely the elements you are not good at. Those are the aspects you give precedence to in your practice. You find a kind of perverse pleasure in moving past the pain this might bring. Second, you resist the lure of easing up on your focus. You train yourself to concentrate in practice with double the intensity, as if it were the real thing times two. In devising your own routines, you become as creative as possible. You invent exercises that work upon your weaknesses. You give yourself arbitrary deadlines to meet certain standards, constantly pushing yourself past perceived limits. In this way you develop your own standards for excellence, generally higher than those of others.

这是业余爱好者的路。要想精通，你必须采用我们称之为“抵抗练习”的方法。原理很简单——在练习时，你要与所有自然倾向背道而驰。首先，你要抵制对自己好一点的诱惑。你会成为自己最严厉的批评家；你会透过他人的眼光看待自己的工作。你会认识到自己的弱点，正是你不擅长的方面。这些正是你在练习中优先考虑的方面。你会在克服可能带来的痛苦中找到一种反常的快感。其次，你要抵制放松注意力的诱惑。你训练自己在练习中以双倍的强度集中注意力，仿佛这是真正的练习，强度是真正的练习的两倍。在设计自己的练习方案时，你会变得尽可能地富有创造力。你会发明针对自身弱点的练习。你会给自己设定任意的期限来达到某些标准，不断地挑战自己超越自己的极限。通过这种方式，你会发展出自己的卓越标准，这些标准通常高于他人的标准。

In the end, your five hours of intense, focused work are the equivalent of ten for most people. Soon enough you will see the results of such practice, and others will marvel at the apparent ease in which you accomplish your deeds.

最终，你五个小时的紧张专注工作，相当于大多数人十个小时的工作量。很快你就会看到这种练习的成果，其他人也会惊叹于你完成任务的轻松程度。

# ↩

6. Apprentice yourself in failure

6. 从失败中学习

One day in 1885, the twenty-three-year old Henry Ford got his first look at the gas-powered engine, and it was instant love. Ford had apprenticed as a machinist and had worked on every conceivable device, but nothing could compare to his fascination with this new type of engine, one that created its own power. He envisioned a whole new kind of horseless carriage that would revolutionize transportation. He made it his Life’s Task to be the pioneer in developing such an automobile.

1885年的一天，23岁的亨利·福特第一次看到汽油发动机，便立刻爱上了它。福特曾做过机械师学徒，也尝试过所有能想到的设备，但没有什么能比得上他对这种新型发动机的迷恋——它能够自行产生动力。他设想了一种全新的无马马车，它将彻底改变交通运输。他立志成为开发这种汽车的先驱，以此作为自己毕生的追求。

Working the night shift at the Edison Illuminating Company as an engineer, during the day he would tinker with the new internal-combustion engine he was developing. He built a workshop in a shed behind his home and started constructing the engine from pieces of scrap metal he salvaged from anywhere he could find them. By 1896, working with friends who helped him build a carriage, he completed his first prototype, which he called the Quadricycle, and debuted it on the streets of Detroit.

他在爱迪生照明公司担任工程师，上夜班，白天则摆弄自己正在研发的新型内燃机。他在自家后方的棚子里搭建了一个工作室，开始用从各处捡来的废金属碎片组装发动机。1896年，在朋友的帮助下，他制造了一辆四轮马车，完成了他的第一个原型车——四轮车，并在底特律街头首次亮相。

At the time there were many others working on automobiles with gas-powered engines. It was a ruthlessly competitive environment in which new companies died by the day. Ford’s Quadricycle looked nice and ran well, but it was too small and incomplete for large-scale production. And so he began work on a second automobile, thinking ahead to the production end of the process. A year later he completed it, and it was a marvel of design. Everything was geared toward simplicity and compactness. It was easy to drive and maintain. All that he needed was financial backing and sufficient capital to mass-produce it.

当时，还有很多人在研发燃气发动机汽车。竞争异常激烈，新公司层出不穷。福特的四轮车外观漂亮，性能出色，但体积太小，功能不完善，无法大规模生产。于是，他开始研发第二辆汽车，并提前考虑了生产环节。一年后，他完成了这辆汽车，堪称设计奇迹。一切都以简洁紧凑为目标，易于驾驶和维护。他所需要的只是资金支持和足够的资金来量产。

To manufacture automobiles in the late 1890s was a daunting venture. It required a tremendous amount of capital and a complex business structure, considering all of the parts that went into production. Ford quickly found the perfect backer: William H. Murphy, one of the most prominent businessmen in Detroit. The new company was dubbed the Detroit Automobile Company, and all who were involved had high hopes. But problems soon arose. The car Ford had designed as a prototype needed to be reworked—the parts came from different places; some of them were deficient and far too heavy for his liking. He kept trying to refine the design to come closer to his ideal. But it was taking far too long, and Murphy and the stockholders were getting restless. In 1901, a year and a half after it had started operation, the board of directors dissolved the company. They had lost faith in Henry Ford.

在19世纪90年代末，制造汽车是一项艰巨的任务。考虑到投入生产的所有零部件，它需要巨额资金和复杂的商业结构。福特很快找到了理想的支持者：威廉·H·墨菲，底特律最杰出的商人之一。新公司被命名为底特律汽车公司，所有参与者都寄予厚望。但问题很快就出现了。福特设计的原型车需要重新设计——零件来自不同的地方；其中一些零件存在缺陷，而且重量过重，他不喜欢。他不断尝试改进设计，使其更接近理想状态。但这耗时太长，墨菲和股东们开始焦躁不安。1901年，在公司投入运营一年半后，董事会解散了公司。他们对亨利·福特失去了信心。

In analyzing this failure, Ford came to the conclusion that he had been trying to make his automobile serve too many consumer needs. He would try a second time, starting out with a lightweight and smaller vehicle. He convinced Murphy to give him another chance, something rare in the fledgling automobile business. Still believing in Ford’s genius, he agreed, and together they formed the Henry Ford Company. Right from the start, however, Ford felt the pressure from Murphy to get the automobile ready for production so as to avoid the problems he’d had with the first company. Ford resented the interference from people who knew nothing about design or the high standards he was trying to establish for the industry.

在分析这次失败后，福特得出结论，他试图让自己的汽车满足太多消费者的需求。他决定再次尝试，从轻量化、小型化车型开始。他说服墨菲再给他一次机会，这在当时刚刚起步的汽车行业实属罕见。福特仍然相信福特的天才，于是同意了，两人共同创立了亨利·福特公司。然而，从一开始，福特就感受到了墨菲的压力，他要尽快为汽车投产做好准备，以避免重蹈第一家公司覆辙。福特对那些对设计一无所知的人的干涉感到愤怒，这些人也并不了解福特试图为行业树立的高标准。

Murphy and his men brought in an outsider to supervise the process. This was the breaking point—less than a year after its establishment, Ford left the company. The break with Murphy this time was final. In the car business, everyone wrote Henry Ford off. He had blown his two chances and nobody was ever given a third, not with the amount of money at stake. But to friends and family, Ford himself seemed blithely unconcerned. He told everyone that these were all invaluable lessons to him—he had paid attention to every glitch along the way, and like a watch or an engine, he had taken apart these failures in his mind and had identified the root cause: no one was giving him enough time to work out the bugs. The people with money were meddling in mechanical and design affairs. They were injecting their mediocre ideas into the process and polluting it. He resented the idea that having money gave them certain rights, when all that mattered was a perfect design.

墨菲和他的团队引入了一位外来者来监督整个流程。这成了转折点——公司成立不到一年，福特就离开了公司。这次与墨菲的决裂是彻底的。在汽车行业，每个人都对亨利·福特不屑一顾。他已经浪费了两次机会，而且考虑到涉及的金钱数额，再也没有人给他第三次机会。但在朋友和家人看来，福特本人似乎对此漠不关心。他告诉所有人，这些都是他宝贵的教训——他关注了一路走来的每一个小故障，就像手表或发动机一样，他在脑海中将这些故障拆解开来，并找到了根本原因：没有人给他足够的时间去解决问题。有钱人插手机械和设计事务。他们把平庸的想法注入到流程中，污染了流程。他憎恨金钱赋予他们某些权利的想法，而事实上，完美的设计才是最重要的。

The answer was to find a way to maintain complete independence from the financiers. This was not the usual way of doing business in America, which was becoming increasingly bureaucratic. He would have to invent his own form of organization, his own business model, one that suited his temperament and needs—including an efficient team he could trust, and the right to the final word on every decision.

答案是找到一种方法，保持完全独立于金融家。这并非美国常见的经商方式，因为美国正日益官僚化。他必须发明自己的组织形式和商业模式，一种适合自己性格和需求的模式——包括一支值得信赖的高效团队，以及对所有决策的最终决定权。

Considering his reputation, it would be almost impossible to find backing, but several months into the search he found an ideal partner—Alexander Malcomson, an émigré from Scotland who had made his fortune in the coal business. Like Ford, he had an unconventional streak and was a risk taker. He agreed to finance this latest venture and to not meddle in the manufacturing process. Ford worked at creating a new kind of assembly plant that would give him more control over the car he wanted to design, now known as the Model A. The Model A would be the lightest car ever made, simple and durable. It was the culmination of all of his tinkering and designing. It would be assembled along a line that would ensure speed of production.

鉴于他的名声，几乎不可能找到支持，但几个月后，他找到了一位理想的合作伙伴——亚历山大·马尔科姆森，一位来自苏格兰的移民，靠煤炭生意发家致富。和福特一样，他不落俗套，敢于冒险。他同意资助这项最新的冒险，并且不干预生产过程。福特致力于创建一种新型装配厂，以便更好地控制他想要设计的汽车——现在被称为A型车。A型车将是有史以来最轻的汽车，简洁耐用。这是他所有改进和设计的巅峰之作。它将在一条确保快速生产的生产线上进行组装。

With the assembly plant ready, Ford worked hard at getting the team of workers to churn out fifteen cars a day—a rather high number back then. He oversaw every aspect of the production—it was his car from the inside out. He even worked on the assembly line, endearing himself to the workers. Orders started pouring in for the well made yet inexpensive Model A, and by 1904 the Ford Motor Company had to expand its operations. Soon it would be one of the few survivors from the early era of the automobile business, and a giant in the making.

装配厂准备就绪后，福特努力让工人们每天生产15辆汽车——这在当时是一个相当高的数字。他监督生产的每一个环节——从内到外，这都是他的车。他甚至亲自在装配线上工作，赢得了工人们的喜爱。做工精良却价格低廉的A型车订单纷至沓来，到1904年，福特汽车公司不得不扩大业务。很快，它就成为汽车行业早期为数不多的幸存者之一，并逐渐成为一家巨头。

Henry Ford had one of those minds that was naturally attuned to the mechanical. He had the power of most great inventors—the ability to visualize the parts and how they functioned together. If he had to describe how something worked, Ford would inevitably take a napkin and sketch out a diagram rather than use words. With this type of intelligence, his apprenticeships on machines were easy and fast. But when it came to mass-producing his inventions, he had to confront the fact that he did not have the requisite knowledge. He needed an additional apprenticeship in becoming a businessman and entrepreneur. Fortunately, working on machines had developed in him a kind of practical intelligence, patience, and way of solving problems that could be applied to anything.

亨利·福特拥有与生俱来对机械的敏锐洞察力。他拥有大多数伟大发明家的非凡能力——能够将零件及其协同运作方式形象化。如果要描述某个东西的工作原理，福特总是会拿张餐巾纸画出一张示意图，而不是用文字。凭借这种智慧，他在机器上的学徒生涯轻松快捷。但当需要大规模生产他的发明时，他不得不面对一个现实：他缺乏必要的知识。要想成为一名商人和企业家，他还需要一段额外的学徒期。幸运的是，与机器打交道的经历培养了他实践智慧、耐心以及解决问题的技巧，这些都适用于任何领域。

When a machine malfunctions you do not take it personally or grow despondent. It is in fact a blessing in disguise. Such malfunctions generally show you inherent flaws and means of improvement. You simply keep tinkering until you get it right. The same should apply to an entrepreneurial venture. Mistakes and failures are precisely your means of education. They tell you about your own inadequacies. It is hard to find out such things from people, as they are often political with their praise and criticisms. Your failures also permit you to see the flaws of your ideas, which are only revealed in the execution of them. You learn what your audience really wants, the discrepancy between your ideas and how they affect the public. Pay close attention to the structure of your group—how your team is organized, the degree of independence you have from the source of capital. These are design elements as well, and such management issues are often hidden sources of problems.

当机器发生故障时，你不会介意，也不会灰心丧气。事实上，这反而是因祸得福。这类故障通常会显示出机器本身的缺陷和改进的途径。你只需不断修修补补，直到问题解决。创业也应如此。错误和失败正是你的教育方式。它们会告诉你自身的不足。从别人身上很难发现这些，因为他们的赞扬和批评往往带有政治色彩。你的失败也让你看到了你想法的缺陷，而这些缺陷只有在执行过程中才会显露出来。你会了解到你的受众真正想要什么，你的想法与它们对公众的影响之间的差异。密切关注你的团队结构——你的团队是如何组织的，你对资金来源的独立程度。这些也是设计要素，而这类管理问题往往是问题的隐藏根源。

Think of it this way: There are two kinds of failure. The first comes from never trying out your ideas because you are afraid, or because you are waiting for the perfect time. This kind of failure you can never learn from, and such timidity will destroy you. The second kind comes from a bold and venturesome spirit. If you fail in this way, the hit that you take to your reputation is greatly outweighed by what you learn. Repeated failure will toughen your spirit and show you with absolute clarity how things must be done. In fact, it is a curse to have everything go right on your first attempt. You will fail to question the element of luck, making you think that you have the golden touch. When you do inevitably fail, it will confuse and demoralize you past the point of learning. In any case, to apprentice as an entrepreneur you must act on your ideas as early as possible, exposing them to the public, a part of you even hoping that you’ll fail. You have everything to gain.

不妨这样想：失败有两种。第一种是源于你因为害怕或等待完美时机而从未尝试自己的想法。这种失败你永远无法从中吸取教训，而这种胆怯会摧毁你。第二种是源于你大胆冒险的精神。如果你以这种方式失败，你所获得的教训将远远抵消你声誉所遭受的打击。反复的失败会磨练你的精神，让你清晰地看到事情应该如何做。事实上，第一次尝试就一切顺利是一种诅咒。你不会质疑运气的成分，反而会以为自己点石成金。当你不可避免地失败时，它会让你感到困惑和沮丧，无法再学习新的知识。无论如何，作为一名创业学徒，你必须尽早将你的想法付诸实践，将它们公之于众，你内心深处甚至希望自己会失败。这样你就能获得一切。

# ↩

7. Combine the “how” and the “what”

7. 结合“如何”和“什么”

At a very early age, Santiago Calatrava (b. 1951) developed a love for drawing. He carried his pencils wherever he went. A certain paradox in drawing began to obsess him. In Valencia, Spain, where he grew up, the harsh Mediterranean sunlight would place in sharp relief the things he liked to draw—rocks, trees, buildings, people. Their outlines would slowly soften as the day progressed. Nothing he drew was ever really static; everything is in a state of change and motion—that is the essence of life. How could he capture this movement on paper, in an image that was perfectly still?

圣地亚哥·卡拉特拉瓦（生于1951年）自幼便热爱绘画。他无论走到哪里都带着铅笔。绘画中某种矛盾的特质开始让他着迷。在他成长的西班牙瓦伦西亚，地中海刺眼的阳光将他喜欢描绘的事物——岩石、树木、建筑、人物——映衬得格外醒目。随着时间的推移，它们的轮廓逐渐变得柔和。他画作中的一切从来都不是静止的；一切都处于变化和运动之中——这正是生命的本质。他如何才能在纸上，以一幅完美静止的画面，捕捉到这种运动？

He took classes and learned techniques for creating the various illusions of something caught in the moment of movement, but it was never quite enough. As part of this impossible quest he taught himself aspects of mathematics, such as descriptive geometry, that could help him understand how to represent his objects in two dimensions. His skill improved and his interest in the subject deepened. It seemed he was destined for a career as an artist, and so in 1969 he enrolled in art school in Valencia.

他参加各种课程，学习捕捉运动瞬间的各种幻觉技巧，但这远远不够。为了完成这项看似不可能的探索，他自学了数学，例如画法几何，这有助于他理解如何在二维空间中表现物体。他的技艺不断提升，对这门学科的兴趣也日益深厚。他似乎注定要成为一名艺术家，于是在1969年，他进入了瓦伦西亚的艺术学校学习。

A few months into his studies, he had a seemingly minor experience that would change the course of his life: browsing for supplies in a stationery store, his eye was drawn to a beautifully designed booklet describing the work of the great architect Le Corbusier. Somehow this architect had managed to create completely distinctive shapes. He turned even something as simple as a stairway into a dynamic piece of sculpture. The buildings he designed seemed to defy gravity, creating a feeling of movement in their still forms. Studying this booklet, Calatrava now developed a new obsession—to learn the secret of how such buildings came about. As soon as he could, he transferred to the one architecture school in Valencia.

学习几个月后，他经历了一段看似微不足道的经历，却改变了他的人生轨迹：在一家文具店选购文具时，他被一本设计精美的小册子吸引，小册子介绍了伟大建筑师勒·柯布西耶的作品。这位建筑师巧妙地创造出了截然不同的造型。他甚至能将像楼梯这样简单的建筑变成一件动态的雕塑。他设计的建筑似乎能够克服地心引力，在静止的形态中营造出一种动感。研究这本小册子后，卡拉特拉瓦对建筑产生了新的执念——探究这些建筑诞生的秘密。他一有机会，就转学到了瓦伦西亚的一所建筑学院。

Graduating from the school in 1973, Calatrava had gained a solid education in the subject. He had learned all of the most important design rules and principles. He was more than capable of taking his place in some architecture firm and working his way up. But he felt something elemental was missing in his knowledge. In looking at all of the great works of architecture that he most admired—the Pantheon in Rome, the buildings of Gaudí in Barcelona, the bridges designed by Robert Maillart in Switzerland—he had no solid idea about their actual construction. He knew more than enough about their form, their aesthetics, and how they functioned as public buildings, but he knew nothing about how they stood up, how the pieces fit together, how the buildings of Le Corbusier managed to create that impression of movement and dynamism.

卡拉特拉瓦于1973年从学校毕业，在建筑设计领域获得了扎实的教育。他掌握了所有最重要的设计规则和原则。他完全有能力在某个建筑公司找到一份工作，并逐步晋升。但他感觉自己的知识中缺少了某种基本的东西。纵观他最欣赏的所有伟大建筑作品——罗马的万神殿、巴塞罗那的高迪建筑、瑞士罗伯特·马亚尔设计的桥梁——他对它们的实际建造方式却一无所知。他对这些建筑的形式、美学以及它们作为公共建筑的功能了如指掌，但却对它们如何矗立、各个部分如何组合、以及勒·柯布西耶的建筑如何营造出动感和活力的印象一无所知。

It was like knowing how to draw a beautiful bird but not understanding how it could fly. As with drawing, he wanted to go beyond the surface, the design element, and touch upon the reality. He felt that the world was changing; something was in the air. With advances in technology and new materials, revolutionary possibilities had emerged for a new kind of architecture, but to truly exploit that he would have to learn something about engineering. Thinking in this direction, Calatrava made a fateful decision—he would virtually start over and enroll at the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich, Switzerland, to gain a degree in civil engineering. It would be an arduous process, but he would train himself to think and draw like an engineer. Knowing how buildings were constructed would liberate him and give him ideas about how to slowly expand the boundaries of what could be made.

这就像知道如何画一只美丽的鸟，却不明白它如何飞翔。如同绘画一样，他想要超越表面和设计元素，触及现实。他感觉到世界正在改变；某种东西正在酝酿。随着科技和新材料的进步，一种新型建筑的革命性可能性已经出现，但要真正利用这些可能性，他必须学习一些工程学知识。考虑到这一点，卡拉特拉瓦做出了一个决定命运的决定——他几乎要从头开始，去瑞士苏黎世联邦理工学院攻读土木工程学位。这将是一个艰苦的过程，但他将训练自己像工程师一样思考和绘画。了解建筑的建造方式将解放他，并让他有灵感逐渐拓展建筑的边界。

In the first few years he grounded himself in the rigors of engineering—all of the mathematics and physics required for the field. But as he progressed, he found himself returning to that paradox that he had been obsessed with in childhood—how to express movement and change. In architecture, the golden rule was that buildings had to be stable and stationary. Calatrava felt the desire to break up this rigid convention. For his PhD dissertation, he decided to explore the possibilities of bringing actual movement into architecture. Inspired by NASA and its designs for space travel, as well as the folding bird wings designed by Leonardo da Vinci, Calatrava chose as his topic the foldability of structures—how through advanced engineering structures could move and transform themselves.

在最初的几年里，他扎根于工程学的严谨性——该领域所需的所有数学和物理学。但随着学习的深入，他发现自己又回到了童年时痴迷的那个悖论——如何表达运动和变化。建筑的黄金法则是建筑必须稳定且静止。卡拉特拉瓦渴望打破这一僵硬的传统。在他的博士论文中，他决定探索将真实的运动引入建筑的可能性。受到美国国家航空航天局及其太空旅行设计以及列奥纳多·达·芬奇设计的折叠鸟翼的启发，卡拉特拉瓦选择结构的可折叠性作为他的研究主题——如何通过先进的工程技术使结构实现移动和自我变形。

Completing his dissertation in 1981, he finally entered the work world—after fourteen years of a university apprenticeship in art, architecture, and engineering. In the coming years he would experiment in designing new kinds of collapsible doors, windows, and roofs that would move and open up in new ways, altering the shape of the building. He designed a drawbridge in Buenos Aires that moved outward instead of up. In 1996 he took all of this a step further with his design and construction of an extension to the Milwaukee Art Museum. It consisted of a long glass-and-steel reception hall with an eighty-foot ceiling, all shaded by an enormous moveable sunscreen on the roof. The screen had two ribbed panels that opened and closed like the wings of a giant seagull, putting the entire edifice into motion, and giving the sense of a building that could take flight.

1981年，他完成了毕业论文，最终步入职场——此前，他在大学里完成了十四年的艺术、建筑和工程学徒生涯。在接下来的几年里，他尝试设计新型的可折叠门窗和屋顶，它们可以以新的方式移动和打开，从而改变建筑的形状。他在布宜诺斯艾利斯设计了一座向外移动而非向上移动的吊桥。1996年，他又迈进了一步，设计并建造了密尔沃基艺术博物馆的扩建部分。扩建部分由一个长长的玻璃钢结构的接待大厅组成，天花板高达八十英尺，屋顶上一个巨大的可移动遮阳板为整个大厅遮阳。遮阳板由两块肋状面板组成，它们像巨型海鸥的翅膀一样开合，使整座建筑动起来，给人一种可以展翅翱翔的感觉。

We humans live in two worlds. First, there is the outer world of appearances—all of the forms of things that captivate our eye. But hidden from our view is another world—how these things actually function, their anatomy or composition, the parts working together and forming the whole. This second world is not so immediately captivating. It is harder to understand. It is not something visible to the eye, but only to the mind that glimpses the reality. But this “how” of things is just as poetic once we understand it—it contains the secret of life, of how things move and change.

我们人类生活在两个世界中。首先是表象的外在世界——所有吸引我们眼球的事物形态。但隐藏在我们视野之外的，是另一个世界——这些事物如何运作，它们的解剖或构成，以及各个部分如何协同运作并构成整体。这第二个世界并非如此引人入胜，也更难理解。它并非肉眼可见，而只有心灵才能瞥见现实。但一旦我们理解了事物的“如何”，它同样充满诗意——它蕴含着生命的秘密，以及事物如何运动和变化的奥秘。

This division between the “how” and the “what” can be applied to almost everything around us—we see the machine, not how it works; we see a group of people producing something as a business, not how the group is structured or how the products are manufactured and distributed. (In a similar fashion, we tend to be mesmerized by people’s appearances, not the psychology behind what they do or say.) As Calatrava discovered, in overcoming this division, in combining the “how” and the “what” of architecture, he gained a much deeper, or rather more rounded knowledge of the field. He grasped a larger portion of the reality that goes into making buildings. This allowed him to create something infinitely more poetic, to stretch the boundaries, to break the conventions of architecture itself.

这种“如何”与“是什么”之间的区分几乎适用于我们周围的一切——我们看到的是机器，而不是它如何运作；我们看到的是一群人生产某种东西的生意，而不是这个群体的组织结构或产品是如何生产和分销的。（同样，我们往往会被人们的外表所吸引，而不是他们言行背后的心理。）正如卡拉特拉瓦所发现的，在克服这种区分，将建筑的“如何”与“是什么”结合起来的过程中，他获得了对该领域更深入、更全面的理解。他掌握了建筑建造的更多现实情况。这使得他能够创造出无限诗意的作品，拓展建筑的界限，打破建筑本身的常规。

Understand: we live in the world of a sad separation that began some five hundred years ago when art and science split apart. Scientists and technicians live in their own world, focusing mostly on the “how” of things. Others live in the world of appearances, using these things but not really understanding how they function. Just before this split occurred, it was the ideal of the Renaissance to combine these two forms of knowledge. This is why the work of Leonardo da Vinci continues to fascinate us, and why the Renaissance remains an ideal. This more rounded knowledge is in fact the way of the future, especially now that so much more information is available to all of us. As Calatrava intuited, this should be a part of our apprenticeship. We must make ourselves study as deeply as possible the technology we use, the functioning of the group we work in, the economics of our field, its lifeblood. We must constantly ask the questions—how do things work, how do decisions get made, how does the group interact? Rounding our knowledge in this way will give us a deeper feel for reality and the heightened power to alter it.

要知道：我们生活在一个令人悲伤的分离世界，这种分离始于大约五百年前，当时艺术与科学的分裂。科学家和技术人员活在自己的世界中，主要关注事物的“如何”。其他人则活在表象的世界里，使用这些东西，却并不真正理解它们是如何运作的。就在这种分裂发生之前，文艺复兴的理想是将这两种知识形式结合起来。这就是为什么列奥纳多·达·芬奇的作品至今仍让我们着迷，以及为什么文艺复兴至今仍是一个理想。这种更全面的知识实际上是未来的方向，尤其是在我们所有人都能获得更多信息的今天。正如卡拉特拉瓦所直觉的那样，这应该成为我们学徒期的一部分。我们必须尽可能深入地研究我们使用的技术、我们所在团队的运作方式、我们所在领域的经济学以及它的命脉。我们必须不断地提出问题——事物是如何运作的，决策是如何做出的，团队是如何互动的？以这种方式完善我们的知识将使我们更深刻地感受现实并增强改变现实的力量。

# ↩

8. Advance through trial and error

8.通过反复尝试取得进步

Growing up in a suburb of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in the early 1970s, Paul Graham (b. 1964) became fascinated with the depiction of computers in television and film. They were like electronic brains with limitless powers. In the near future, or so it seemed, you would be able to talk to your computer, and it would do everything you wanted.

保罗·格雷厄姆（Paul Graham，生于1964年）于20世纪70年代初在宾夕法尼亚州匹兹堡郊区长大，他对电视和电影中对计算机的描述着迷。它们就像拥有无限能力的电子大脑。在不久的将来，或者说，在当时看来，你将能够与你的计算机对话，它就能完成你想做的一切。

In junior high school he had been admitted into a program for gifted students that provided them with the chance to work on a creative project of their choosing. Graham decided to focus his project on the school’s computer, an IBM mainframe that was used for printing out grade reports and class schedules. This was the first time he had gotten his hands on a computer, and although it was primitive and had to be programmed with punch cards, it seemed like something magical—a portal to the future.

初中时，他被一个天才学生项目录取，该项目为学生提供自主选择的创意项目。格雷厄姆决定将他的项目重点放在学校的电脑上，那是一台IBM大型机，用来打印成绩报告和课程表。这是他第一次接触电脑，虽然它很原始，需要用穿孔卡片编程，但它却仿佛拥有某种魔力——一扇通往未来的大门。

Over the next few years, he taught himself how to program by consulting the few books then written on the subject, but mostly he learned by trial and error. Like painting on a canvas, he could see the results immediately of what he had done—and if the programming worked, it had a certain aesthetic rightness to it. The process of learning through trial and error was immensely satisfying. He could discover things on his own, without having to follow a rigid path set up by others. (This is the essence of being a “hacker.”) And the better he got at programming, the more he could make it do.

在接下来的几年里，他通过查阅当时为数不多的几本编程书籍自学编程，但大部分学习都是通过不断尝试和犯错。就像在画布上作画一样，他可以立即看到自己所做工作的结果——如果编程成功，还会有一种美感。不断尝试和犯错的过程让他感到无比满足。他可以自己探索新事物，而不必遵循别人设定的固定路径。（这就是“黑客”的精髓。）而且，他的编程水平越高，他就能做得越多。

Deciding to pursue his studies further, he chose to attend Cornell University, which at the time had one of the best computer science departments in the country. Here he finally received instruction in the basic principles of programming, cleaning up many of the bad hacking habits he had developed on his own. He became intrigued by the recently developed field of artificial intelligence—the key to designing the kinds of computers he had dreamed about as a child. To be on the frontier of this new field, he applied and was accepted to the graduate school in computer science at Harvard University.

为了继续深造，他选择了康奈尔大学，该校当时拥有全美最好的计算机科学系之一。在这里，他终于学习了编程的基本原理，改掉了许多自学成才的黑客坏习惯。他对新兴的人工智能领域产生了浓厚的兴趣——这正是设计他儿时梦想的计算机的关键。为了站在这个新领域的前沿，他申请并被哈佛大学计算机科学研究生院录取。

At Harvard Graham finally had to confront something about himself—he was not cut out for academia. He hated writing research papers. The university way of programming took all the fun and excitement out of it—the process of discovering through trial and error. He was a hacker at heart, one who liked to figure things out for himself. He found a fellow hacker at Harvard, Robert Morris, and together they began to explore the intricacies of the programming language Lisp. It seemed like the most potentially powerful and fluid language of them all. Understanding Lisp made you understand something essential about programming itself. It was a language suited for high-level hackers, a language specifically made for investigation and discovery.

在哈佛，格雷厄姆最终不得不正视自己的一个问题——他并不适合学术。他讨厌写研究论文。大学里的编程方式剥夺了它所有的乐趣和激情——一个通过反复试验来探索的过程。他骨子里是个黑客，喜欢自己解决问题。他在哈佛找到了一位黑客同伴罗伯特·莫里斯，他们一起开始探索Lisp编程语言的复杂性。它似乎是所有语言中最具潜力、最强大、最流畅的语言。理解Lisp让你理解编程本身的一些本质。它是一种适合高级黑客的语言，一种专为调查和发现而设计的语言。

Disillusioned with the computer science department at Harvard, Graham decided to design his own graduate school program: he would take a wide range of classes and discover what interested him the most. To his surprise, he found himself attracted to art—to painting, and to the subject of art history itself. What this meant to him was that he should follow this interest and see where it would lead. After completing his PhD at Harvard in computer science, he enrolled in the Rhode Island School of Design, then attended a painting program at the Accademia in Florence, Italy. He returned to the States broke but determined to try his hand at painting. He would pay for his lifestyle with intermittent consulting work in programming.

格雷厄姆对哈佛大学计算机科学系感到失望，于是决定设计自己的研究生课程：他将广泛选修各种课程，探索自己最感兴趣的领域。令他惊讶的是，他发现自己对艺术——绘画，以及艺术史本身——产生了浓厚的兴趣。这对他来说意味着，他应该追寻这份兴趣，看看它会引领他走向何方。在哈佛大学获得计算机科学博士学位后，他进入罗德岛设计学院学习，之后又在意大利佛罗伦萨学院学习绘画课程。他回到美国时身无分文，但决心尝试绘画。他断断续续地从事编程咨询工作，以此维持生活。

As the years went by, he would occasionally reflect on the course of his life. Artists in the Renaissance would go through clear-cut apprenticeships, but what could he say about his own apprenticeship? There seemed to be no real design or direction to his life. It was like the “cheesy hacks” he did in high school, patching things together, figuring things out through constant trial and error, finding out what worked by doing it. Shaping his life in this haphazard way, he learned what to avoid—academia; working for large companies; any political environment. He liked the process of making things. What really mattered to him in the end was having possibilities—being able to go in this or that direction, depending on what life presented to him. If over the years he had undergone an apprenticeship, it was almost by default.

随着岁月流逝，他偶尔会反思自己的人生轨迹。文艺复兴时期的艺术家都会经历清晰明确的学徒期，但他对自己的学徒期又有何感想？他的人生似乎没有真正的规划或方向。就像高中时那些“低俗的黑客”一样，东拼西凑，通过不断的尝试和错误来摸索，最终找到行之有效的方法。在这种随意的人生中，他学会了应该回避什么——学术界；在大公司工作；任何政治环境。他喜欢创造的过程。最终对他来说真正重要的是拥有各种可能性——能够根据生活给他的安排，选择不同的方向。如果说这些年来他经历过学徒期，那几乎是理所当然的。

One afternoon in 1995, he heard on the radio a story about Netscape—the company itself was touting its future and discussing how someday most businesses would be selling their products on the Internet itself, with Netscape leading the way. With his bank account getting desperately low again, yet dreading the idea of returning to another consulting job, he recruited his old hacker friend Robert Morris to help him create software for running an online business. Graham’s idea was to design a program that would run directly on the web server instead of having to be downloaded. No one had thought of this before. They would write the program in Lisp, taking advantage of the speed with which they could make changes to it. They called their business Viaweb, and it would be the first of its kind, the pioneer of online commerce. Just three years later they sold it to Yahoo! for $45 million.

1995年的一个下午，他在收音机里听到一则关于网景公司（Netscape）的消息——这家公司正在宣传自己的未来，并讨论未来某一天大多数企业都会在互联网上销售产品，而网景公司将引领这一潮流。他的银行账户再次陷入困境，但他又害怕再次从事咨询工作，于是他聘请了老黑客朋友罗伯特·莫里斯（Robert Morris）来帮助他开发运营在线业务的软件。格雷厄姆的想法是设计一个可以直接在网络服务器上运行的程序，而无需下载。此前从未有人想到过这一点。他们用Lisp编写程序，充分利用Lisp的速度优势，方便修改。他们将公司命名为Viaweb，这将成为同类公司中的首例，在线商务的先驱。仅仅三年后，他们就以4500万美元的价格将公司出售给了雅虎（Yahoo!）。

In the years to come Graham would continue on the path set in his twenties, moving to where his interests and skills converged, to wherever he could see possibilities. In 2005 he gave a talk at Harvard about his experiences with Viaweb. The students, excited by his advice, pleaded with him to start up some kind of consulting firm. Intrigued by the idea, he created Y Combinator, an apprenticeship system for young entrepreneurs in technology, with his company taking a stake in each successful startup. Over the years he would refine the system, learning as he went along. In the end, Y Combinator represented his ultimate hack—something he came upon by accident and improved through his own process of trial and error. The company is now valued at close to $500 million.

在接下来的岁月里，格雷厄姆继续沿着他二十多岁时设定的道路前进，去往他兴趣和技能交汇的地方，去往任何他认为有潜力的地方。2005年，他在哈佛大学做了一次演讲，讲述了他在Viaweb的经历。学生们对他的建议感到兴奋，恳求他创办一家咨询公司。这个想法让他着迷，于是他创建了Y Combinator，一个面向年轻科技创业者的学徒体系，他的公司会从每家成功的创业公司中持有股份。多年来，他不断完善这个体系，边学边做。最终，Y Combinator代表了他的终极方案——一个他偶然发现，并通过自己的反复试验不断改进的方案。该公司目前的估值接近5亿美元。

Each age tends to create a model of apprenticeship that is suited to the system of production that prevails at the time. In the Middle Ages, during the birth of modern capitalism and the need for quality control, the first apprenticeship system appeared, with its rigidly defined terms. With the advent of the Industrial Revolution, this model of apprenticeship became largely outmoded, but the idea behind it lived on in the form of self-apprenticeship—developing yourself from within a particular field, as Darwin did in biology. This suited the growing individualistic spirit of the time. We are now in the computer age, with computers dominating nearly all aspects of commercial life. Although there are many ways in which this could influence the concept of apprenticeship, it is the hacker approach to programming that may offer the most promising model for this new age.

每个时代都会创造出一种与当时盛行的生产体系相适应的学徒制模式。在中世纪，正值现代资本主义诞生和质量控制的需要，出现了第一个学徒制，其条款定义严格。随着工业革命的到来，这种学徒制模式在很大程度上变得过时，但其背后的理念却以自我学徒制的形式延续了下来——从特定领域内部发展自己，就像达尔文在生物学中所做的那样。这符合当时日益高涨的个人主义精神。我们现在正处于计算机时代，计算机几乎主宰着商业生活的方方面面。虽然这可能会以多种方式影响学徒制的概念，但黑客式的编程方式或许是这个新时代最有前途的模式。

The model goes like this: You want to learn as many skills as possible, following the direction that circumstances lead you to, but only if they are related to your deepest interests. Like a hacker, you value the process of self-discovery and making things that are of the highest quality. You avoid the trap of following one set career path. You are not sure where this will all lead, but you are taking full advantage of the openness of information, all of the knowledge about skills now at our disposal. You see what kind of work suits you and what you want to avoid at all cost. You move by trial and error. This is how you pass your twenties. You are the programmer of this wide-ranging apprenticeship, within the loose constraints of your personal interests.

这个模型是这样的：你想学习尽可能多的技能，顺应环境指引的方向，但前提是这些技能与你最深层的兴趣相关。就像黑客一样，你重视自我发现的过程，并致力于创造最高质量的产品。你会避免落入循规蹈矩的职业道路。你不确定这一切最终会引领你走向何方，但你充分利用了信息的开放性，以及我们目前掌握的所有技能知识。你会了解什么样的工作适合你，以及哪些工作是你想要不惜一切代价避免的。你不断尝试，不断求变。这就是你度过二十多岁的方式。你是这个广泛学徒期的程序员，但你的个人兴趣并不受任何限制。

You are not wandering about because you are afraid of commitment, but because you are expanding your skill base and your possibilities. At a certain point, when you are ready to settle on something, ideas and opportunities will inevitably present themselves to you. When that happens, all of the skills you have accumulated will prove invaluable. You will be the Master at combining them in ways that are unique and suited to your individuality. You may settle on this one place or idea for several years, accumulating in the process even more skills, then move in a slightly different direction when the time is appropriate. In this new age, those who follow a rigid, singular path in their youth often find themselves in a career dead end in their forties, or overwhelmed with boredom. The wide-ranging apprenticeship of your twenties will yield the opposite—expanding possibilities as you get older.

你徘徊不定并非因为害怕承诺，而是因为你在拓展自己的技能基础和可能性。到了某个时刻，当你准备好确定某件事时，各种想法和机遇自然会涌现。届时，你积累的所有技能都将变得无价。你将精通将这些技能以独特且符合你个性的方式巧妙地结合起来。你可能会在同一个领域或想法上停留数年，在这个过程中积累更多技能，然后在适当的时候转向略微不同的方向。在这个新时代，那些年轻时走僵化、单一道路的人，往往会在四十多岁时发现自己走进了职业生涯的死胡同，或者感到厌倦。而二十多岁时广泛的学徒生涯将带来相反的结果——随着年龄的增长，你将拥有更多的可能性。

REVERSAL

逆转

It might be imagined that certain people in history—the naturally gifted, the geniuses—have either somehow bypassed the Apprenticeship Phase or have greatly shortened it because of their inherent brilliance. To support such an argument, people will bring up the classic examples of Mozart and Einstein, who seemed to have emerged as creative geniuses out of nowhere.

人们或许会想象，历史上某些天赋异禀的人，比如那些天才，要么以某种方式跳过了学徒期，要么凭借其与生俱来的才华大大缩短了学徒期。为了支持这种观点，人们会举出莫扎特和爱因斯坦的经典例子，他们似乎是凭空出现的创意天才。

With the case of Mozart, however, it is generally agreed among classical music critics that he did not write an original and substantial piece of music until well after ten years of composing. In fact, a study of some seventy great classical composers determined that with only three exceptions, all of the composers had needed at least ten years to produce their first great work, and the exceptions had somehow managed to create theirs in nine years.

然而，就莫扎特而言，古典音乐评论家普遍认为，他作曲十年之后才创作出一部原创且具有实质意义的音乐作品。事实上，一项对大约七十位伟大古典作曲家的研究表明，除三位例外，所有作曲家都至少需要十年时间才能创作出他们的第一部伟大作品，而其他例外则以某种方式在九年内创作出他们的第一部作品。

Einstein began his serious thought experiments at the age of sixteen. Ten years later he came up with his first revolutionary theory of relativity. It is impossible to quantify the time he spent honing his theoretical skills in those ten years, but is not hard to imagine him working three hours a day on this particular problem, which would yield more than 10,000 hours after a decade. What in fact separates Mozart and Einstein from others is the extreme youth with which they began their apprenticeships and the intensity with which they practiced, stemming from their total immersion in the subject. It is often the case that in our younger years we learn faster, absorb more deeply, and yet retain a kind of creative verve that tends to fade as we get older.

爱因斯坦十六岁就开始进行严肃的思想实验。十年后，他提出了他的第一个革命性理论——相对论。在这十年里，他磨练理论技能的时间难以量化，但不难想象他每天要花三个小时来解决这个问题，十年后，他的投入将超过一万小时。莫扎特和爱因斯坦与其他人的不同之处在于，他们开始学徒生涯时极其年轻，并且练习的强度源于他们对学科的全身心投入。通常情况下，我们在年轻时学得更快，吸收得更深，却仍然保留着一种随着年龄增长而逐渐消退的创造热情。

There are no shortcuts or ways to bypass the Apprenticeship Phase. It is the nature of the human brain to require such lengthy exposure to a field, which allows for complex skills to become deeply embedded and frees the mind up for real creative activity. The very desire to find shortcuts makes you eminently unsuited for any kind of mastery. There is no possible reversal to this process.

没有捷径，也没有办法绕过学徒阶段。人脑的本质是需要长时间地接触某个领域，这样才能让复杂的技能根深蒂固，并解放思维，进行真正的创造性活动。渴望寻找捷径的人，极不适合任何形式的精通。这个过程不可能逆转。

It’s like chopping down a huge tree of immense girth. You won’t accomplish it with one swing of your axe. If you keep chopping away at it, though, and do not let up, eventually, whether it wants to or not, it will suddenly topple down. When that time comes, you could round up everyone you could find and pay them to hold the tree up, but they wouldn’t be able to do it. It would still come crashing to the ground…. But if the woodcutter stopped after one or two strokes of his axe to ask the third son of Mr. Chang, “Why doesn’t this tree fall?” And after three or four more strokes stopped again to ask the fourth son of Mr. Li, “Why doesn’t this tree fall?” he would never succeed in felling the tree. It is no different for someone who is practicing the Way.

就好比要砍倒一棵粗壮的大树，你不是一挥斧子就能砍倒的，但如果你不停地砍，不肯停下来，最终，不管它愿不愿意，都会突然倒下。到那时，你就是召集所有能找到的人，付钱让他们扶住这棵树，但他们也扶不动，它还是会轰然倒地……但如果樵夫挥动斧头砍了一两下，就停下来问张先生的三儿子：“这棵树为什么倒不下来？”又砍了三四下，又停下来问李先生的第四个儿子：“这棵树为什么倒不下来？”他永远也砍不倒这棵树。对于修行的人来说也是一样的。

—Z EN M ASTER H AKUIN

—白隐禅师

# ↩

III

三

ABSORB THE MASTER’S POWER: THE MENTOR DYNAMIC

汲取大师的力量：导师动力

Life is short, and your time for learning and creativity is limited. Without any guidance, you can waste valuable years trying to gain knowledge and practice from various sources. Instead, you must follow the example set by Masters throughout the ages and find the proper mentor. The mentor-protégé relationship is the most efficient and productive form of learning. The right mentors know where to focus your attention and how to challenge you. Their knowledge and experience become yours. They provide immediate and realistic feedback on your work, so you can improve more rapidly. Through an intense person-to-person interaction, you absorb a way of thinking that contains great power and can be adapted to your individual spirit. Choose the mentor who best fits your needs and connects to your Life’s Task. Once you have internalized their knowledge, you must move on and never remain in their shadow. Your goal is always to surpass your mentors in mastery and brilliance.

人生苦短，学习和创造的时间有限。若无任何指导，你或许会浪费宝贵的岁月，试图从各种渠道获取知识和实践。相反，你必须效仿历代大师的榜样，找到合适的导师。师徒关系是最高效、最富有成效的学习方式。合适的导师知道你应该关注什么，以及如何挑战你。他们的知识和经验将成为你的知识和经验。他们会为你的工作提供即时且切合实际的反馈，帮助你更快地进步。通过密切的人际关系，你将吸收一种蕴含强大力量、并能适应你个人精神的思维方式。选择最符合你需求、并与你的人生目标相契合的导师。一旦你内化了他们的知识，你就必须继续前进，永远不要活在他们的阴影下。你的目标始终是在精通和才华上超越你的导师。

# ↩

THE ALCHEMY OF KNOWLEDGE

知识的炼金术

Growing up amid poverty in London, it seemed that the fate of Michael Faraday (1791–1867) was pretty much sealed for him at birth—he would either follow in his father’s footsteps and become a blacksmith, or he would pursue some other manual trade. His options were severely limited by his circumstances. His parents had ten children to feed and support. The father worked sporadically because of illness, and the family needed additional income. The parents waited anxiously for the day when young Faraday would turn twelve and could get a job, or begin some kind of apprenticeship.

迈克尔·法拉第（1791-1867）在伦敦贫困的环境中长大，他的命运似乎从出生起就已注定——要么追随父亲的脚步成为一名铁匠，要么从事其他手工艺行业。他的选择受到了自身境遇的严重限制。他的父母要养活十个孩子。父亲因病只能断断续续地工作，而家里需要额外的收入。父母焦急地等待着法拉第十二岁那一天，盼望着有一天能找到工作，或者开始某种学徒生涯。

There was one trait, however, that marked him as different and was potentially troubling—he had an extremely active mind, one that was perhaps unsuited for a career that would entail mostly physical labor. Some of his mental restlessness was inspired by the peculiar religion his family belonged to—they were Sandemanians, a sect of Christianity. Its adherents believed that God’s presence was manifested in every living thing and every natural phenomenon. By communing with God on a daily basis and getting as inwardly close to him as possible, they could see and feel his presence everywhere in the world.

然而，他有一个特点却显得与众不同，甚至可能令人不安——他思维极其活跃，或许并不适合从事以体力劳动为主的职业。他的这种精神上的躁动，部分源于他家族的特殊宗教信仰——桑德曼派，基督教的一个分支。该派信徒相信上帝的存在体现在每一个生物和每一个自然现象中。通过每天与上帝交流，并尽可能地在内心深处接近上帝，他们能够在世界的每个角落看到并感受到上帝的存在。

Young Faraday was steeped in this philosophy. When he was not doing errands and chores for his mother, he would wander the streets of central London, observing the world around him with utmost intensity. Nature, it seemed to him, was full of secrets that he wanted to ponder and unravel. Because he was taught that the divine presence was everywhere, everything interested him, and his curiosity was limitless. He would ask endless questions of his parents, or anyone he could find, about plants or minerals or any seemingly inexplicable occurrence in nature. He seemed hungry for knowledge and frustrated by his lack of means to get it.

年轻的法拉第深受这种哲学的影响。当他不用为母亲跑腿做家务时，他会漫步在伦敦市中心的街道上，全神贯注地观察着周围的世界。在他看来，大自然充满了他想要思考和解开的秘密。因为他从小就被教导说神的存在无处不在，所以他对一切都感兴趣，他的好奇心也无止境。他会向父母或任何他能找到的人问无数的问题，关于植物、矿物，或者任何自然界中看似无法解释的现象。他似乎渴望知识，却又因缺乏获取知识的途径而感到沮丧。

One day he wandered into a nearby shop that bound and sold books. The sight of so many shiny books on the shelves astounded him. His own schooling had been minimal, and he had really only known one book in his life, the Bible. The Sandemanians believed that the Scripture was the living embodiment of the Lord’s will, and contained something of his presence. To Faraday this meant that the printed words of the Bible had a kind of magical power. He imagined that each of the books in this shop opened up different worlds of knowledge, a form of magic in its own right.

一天，他漫步走进附近一家装订售书的商店。书架上摆满了闪闪发光的书籍，令他惊叹不已。他本人的学识有限，一生中真正了解的只有一本书——《圣经》。桑德曼派信徒相信，圣经是上帝旨意的鲜活体现，蕴含着上帝存在的某种特质。对法拉第来说，这意味着印刷出来的《圣经》文字拥有一种神奇的力量。他想象着这家商店里的每一本书都开启了不同的知识世界，这本身就是一种魔法。

The owner of the shop, George Riebau, was instantly charmed by the young man’s reverence for his books. He had never met someone quite so intense at such a young age. He encouraged him to return, and soon Faraday began to frequent the shop. To help Faraday’s family, Riebau gave him a job as a delivery boy. Impressed with his work ethic, he invited him to join the shop itself as an apprentice bookbinder. Faraday happily accepted, and in 1805 he began his seven-year apprenticeship.

书店老板乔治·里博（George Riebau）立刻被这位年轻人对书籍的崇敬所吸引。他从未见过如此年轻就如此热情的人。里博鼓励法拉第再次光顾，很快，法拉第就开始频繁光顾他的书店。为了帮助法拉第的家人，里博给他提供了一份送货员的工作。里博对他的敬业精神印象深刻，于是邀请他加入书店，成为一名装订学徒。法拉第欣然接受，并于1805年开始了为期七年的学徒生涯。

In the initial months of the job, surrounded by all these books, the young man could hardly believe his good fortune—new books were rare commodities in those days, luxury items for the well-to-do. Not even a public library contained what could be found in Riebau’s shop. The owner encouraged him to read whatever he liked in his off-hours, and Faraday obliged by devouring almost every single book that passed through his hands. One evening he read an encyclopedia passage on the most recent discoveries in electricity, and he suddenly felt as if he had found his calling in life. Here was a phenomenon that was invisible to the eye, but that could be revealed and measured through experiments. This process of uncovering nature’s secrets through experiment enthralled him. Science, it seemed to him, was a great quest to unravel the mysteries of Creation itself. Somehow, he would transform himself into a scientist.

工作最初几个月，周围都是书籍，这个年轻人简直不敢相信自己竟然有如此好运——在那个年代，新书可是稀罕物，是富人的奢侈品。就连公共图书馆也找不到里博书店里能找到的书籍。店主鼓励他在业余时间阅读任何他喜欢的书籍，法拉第也欣然接受了，几乎把经他手的每一本书都读了个遍。一天晚上，他读到百科全书中关于电学最新发现的段落，突然觉得自己找到了人生的使命。这是一种肉眼看不见的现象，却可以通过实验揭示和测量。这种通过实验揭示自然奥秘的过程让他着迷。在他看来，科学就是解开宇宙奥秘的伟大探索。他要以某种方式成为一名科学家。

This was not a realistic goal on his part and he knew it. In England at the time, access to laboratories and to science as a career was only open to those with a university education, which meant those from the upper classes. How could a bookbinder’s apprentice even dream of overcoming such odds? Even if he had the energy and desire to attempt it, he had no teachers, no guidance, no structure or method to his studies. Then in 1809 a book came into the shop that finally gave him some hope. It was called Improvement of the Mind —a self-help guide written by Reverend Isaac Watts, first published in 1741. The book revealed a system of learning and improving your lot in life, no matter your social class. It prescribed courses of action that anyone could follow, and it promised results.
