Faraday read it over and over, carrying it with him wherever he went.

他知道这不是一个现实的目标。在当时的英国，只有受过大学教育的人，也就是来自上层社会的人，才能进入实验室从事科学事业。一个装订学徒怎么能梦想克服这样的困难呢？即使他有精力和愿望去尝试，他也没有老师、没有指导，也没有学习的结构或方法。后来，1809 年，一本书来到了书店，终于给了他一些希望。这本书叫做《心灵的改善》——一本由艾萨克·瓦茨牧师撰写的自助指南，首次出版于 1741 年。这本书揭示了一种学习和改善人生的系统，无论你的社会阶层如何。它规定了任何人都可以遵循的行动方针，并承诺会有效果。法拉第一遍又一遍地阅读这本书，无论走到哪里都随身携带。

He followed the book’s advice to the letter. For Watts, learning had to be an active process. He recommended not just reading about scientific discoveries, but actually re-creating the experiments that led to them. And so, with Riebau’s blessing, Faraday began a series of basic experiments in electricity and chemistry in the back room of the shop. Watts advocated the importance of having teachers and not just learning from books. Faraday dutifully began to attend the numerous lectures on science that were popular in London at the time. Watts advocated not just listening to lectures but taking detailed notes, then reworking the notes themselves—all of this imprinting the knowledge deeper in the brain. Faraday would take this even further.

他一字不差地遵循了书中的建议。对瓦茨来说，学习必须是一个主动的过程。他建议不仅要阅读科学发现，还要实际地重现导致这些发现的实验。于是，在里鲍的同意下，法拉第开始在商店的后屋里进行一系列电学和化学的基础实验。瓦茨强调师生情谊的重要性，而不仅仅是从书本上学习。法拉第开始认真听取当时在伦敦流行的众多科学讲座。瓦茨提倡不仅要听讲座，还要做详细的笔记，然后自己反复修改笔记——所有这些都能将知识深深地印在大脑中。法拉第将这一理念发扬光大。

Attending the lectures of the popular scientist John Tatum, each week on a different subject, he would note down the most important words and concepts, quickly sketch out the various instruments Tatum used, and diagram the experiments. Over the next few days he would expand the notes into sentences, and then into an entire chapter on the subject, elaborately sketched and narrated. In the course of a year this added up to a thick scientific encyclopedia he had created on his own. His knowledge of science had grown by leaps and bounds, and had assumed a kind of organizational shape modeled on his notes.

他每周都会去听著名科学家约翰·塔图姆的讲座，主题各不相同。他会记下最重要的词汇和概念，快速勾勒出塔图姆使用的各种仪器，并绘制实验图表。接下来的几天里，他会把笔记扩展成句子，然后写成关于这个主题的整整一章，并精心勾勒和叙述。一年下来，这些笔记积累起来，构成了他自己创作的一部厚厚的科学百科全书。他的科学知识突飞猛进，并形成了某种以笔记为蓝本的条理结构。

One day, Monsieur Riebau showed this rather impressive collection of notes to a customer named William Dance, a member of the prestigious Royal Institution, an organization that sought to promote the latest advances in science. Thumbing through Faraday’s chapters, Dance was astounded at how clearly and concisely he had summarized complicated topics. He decided to invite the young man to attend a series of lectures by the renowned and recently knighted chemist Humphry Davy, to be given at the Royal Institution where Davy was director of the chemistry laboratory.

一天，里博先生把这本令人印象深刻的笔记展示给一位名叫威廉·丹斯的顾客。丹斯是声名显赫的皇家学会（一个致力于推广最新科学进展的组织）的成员。丹斯翻阅着法拉第的章节，惊讶地发现法拉第对复杂主题的概括如此清晰简洁。于是，丹斯决定邀请这位年轻人去听著名化学家汉弗莱·戴维在皇家学会举办的一系列讲座，戴维当时担任皇家学会化学实验室主任。

The lectures had been sold out well in advance and this was a rare privilege for a young man of Faraday’s background, but for him it was much more fateful than that. Davy was the preeminent chemist of his time; he had made numerous discoveries and was advancing the new field of electrochemistry. His experiments with various gases and chemicals were highly dangerous and had led to numerous accidents. This only added to his reputation as a fearless warrior for science. His lectures were events—he had a flair for the dramatic, performing clever experiments before a dazzled audience. He came from a modest background and had raised himself to the heights of science, having gained the attention of some valuable mentors. To Faraday, Davy was the only living scientist he could model himself after, considering Davy’s lack of any solid formal education.

讲座门票早已提前售罄，对于像法拉第这样出身的年轻人来说，这实属难得，但对他来说，这远比这更具有决定性的意义。戴维是他那个时代杰出的化学家，他做出了无数发现，并推动了电化学这一新兴领域的发展。他用各种气体和化学物质进行的实验极其危险，并引发了多起事故。但这反而让他赢得了“无畏科学斗士”的美誉。他的讲座堪称盛事——他擅长营造戏剧效果，在目眩神迷的听众面前进行着巧妙的实验。他出身卑微，在获得几位宝贵导师的关注后，凭借自身努力登上了科学的顶峰。对法拉第来说，考虑到戴维缺乏扎实的正规教育，他是唯一一位在世的科学家可以效仿的榜样。

Arriving early each time and gaining the closest seat he could find, he soaked up every aspect of Davy’s lectures, taking the most detailed notes he had ever attempted. These lectures had a different effect upon Faraday than others he had attended. He was inspired and yet he also could not help but feel somewhat dejected. After all of these years of studying on his own, he had managed to expand his knowledge of science and of the natural world. But science does not consist of the accumulation of information. It is a way of thinking, of approaching problems. The scientific spirit is creative—Faraday could feel it in Davy’s presence. As an amateur scientist looking at the field from the outside, his knowledge was one-dimensional and would lead nowhere. He needed to move to the inside, where he could gain practical, hands-on experience, become part of the community and learn how to think like a scientist. And to move closer to this scientific spirit and absorb its essence, he would need a mentor.

每次他都早早到场，找到最近的座位，全神贯注地聆听戴维讲座，并做了前所未有的详细笔记。这些讲座对法拉第的影响与他以往听过的其他讲座不同。他深受启发，却又不禁感到些许沮丧。经过多年的自学，他已经拓展了对科学和自然界的认知。但科学并非信息的积累，而是一种思维方式，一种解决问题的方法。科学精神是富有创造力的——法拉第在戴维的陪伴下感受到了这一点。作为一名从外部观察这个领域的业余科学家，他的知识是单向的，毫无用处。他需要深入研究，获得实践经验，融入这个群体，学习如何像科学家一样思考。而为了更接近这种科学精神并汲取其精髓，他需要一位导师。

This seemed like an impossible quest, but with his apprenticeship coming to an end, and facing the prospect of being a bookbinder for life, Faraday went into desperation mode. He wrote letters to the president of the Royal Society and applied for the most menial jobs in any kind of laboratory. He was relentless, and yet months went by with no results. Then one day, out of the blue, he received a message from Humphry Davy’s office. The chemist had been blinded by yet another explosion in his laboratory at the Royal Institution, and the condition would last for several days. During this time he needed a personal assistant to take notes and organize his materials. Mr. Dance, a good friend of Davy’s, had recommended young Faraday for the job.

这看似不可能完成的任务，但随着学徒期即将结束，面对终生从事装订工作的前景，法拉第陷入了绝望。他给皇家学会主席写信，申请各种实验室里最琐碎的工作。他坚持不懈，然而几个月过去了，却毫无进展。有一天，他突然收到了汉弗莱·戴维办公室的消息。这位化学家在皇家学会实验室又一次发生爆炸，导致失明，这种情况将持续数天。在此期间，他需要一位私人助理来记录笔记并整理资料。戴维的好友丹斯先生推荐了年轻的法拉第担任这份工作。

There seemed something fateful, even magical, in this occurrence. Faraday would have to make the most of it, do whatever he could to impress the great chemist. Awestruck to be in Davy’s presence, Faraday listened with utmost intensity to every one of his instructions and did more than was asked for. When Davy, however, had recovered his sight, he thanked Faraday for his work but made it clear that the Royal Institution already had a laboratory assistant and there were simply no openings for him on any level.

这件事仿佛命中注定，甚至有些神奇。法拉第必须充分利用它，竭尽所能给这位伟大的化学家留下深刻印象。法拉第对戴维的到来感到敬畏，他全神贯注地听从戴维的每一条指示，并付出了超出要求的努力。然而，戴维恢复视力后，他感谢了法拉第的工作，但也明确表示，皇家研究所已经有一名实验助理，任何级别的职位都不适合他。

Faraday felt despondent, but he was not ready to give up; he would not let this be the end. Only a few days in Davy’s presence had revealed so many learning possibilities. Davy liked to talk about his ideas as they occurred to him and gain feedback from anyone around him. Discussing with Faraday one experiment he was planning afforded the young man a glimpse into how his mind worked, and it was fascinating. Davy would be the ultimate mentor, and Faraday determined that he would have to make this happen. He went back to the notes he had taken on Davy’s lectures. He worked them into a beautifully organized booklet, carefully handwritten, and full of sketches and diagrams. He sent this off to Davy as a gift. He then wrote to him a few weeks later, reminding Davy about the experiment he had mentioned but had probably forgotten about—Davy was notoriously absentminded. Faraday heard nothing. But then one day, in February 1813, he was suddenly summoned to the Royal Institution.

法拉第感到沮丧，但他不愿放弃；他不会就此结束。仅仅在戴维的陪伴下，短短几天就让他发现了如此多的学习机会。戴维喜欢畅所欲言，并与周围的人交流。与法拉第讨论他正在计划的一项实验，让这位年轻人得以一窥自己的思维方式，这令人着迷。戴维将成为他最终的导师，法拉第决心要做到这一点。他回顾了在戴维讲座上所做的笔记，并将它们整理成一本组织精美的小册子，字迹工整，充满了草图和图表。他把这本小册子作为礼物送给了戴维。几周后，他又写信给戴维，提醒他提到过但可能已经忘记的那个实验——戴维出了名的心不在焉。法拉第什么也没听到。然而，1813年2月的一天，他突然被召回皇家研究院。

That same morning the Institution’s laboratory assistant had been fired for insubordination. They needed to replace him immediately, and Davy had recommended young Faraday. The job mostly involved cleaning bottles and equipment, sweeping, and lighting fireplaces. The pay was low, considerably lower than what he could gain as a bookbinder, but Faraday, hardly believing his good fortune, accepted on the spot.

当天早上，研究所的实验室助理因不服从命令被解雇。他们需要立即找到替代者，戴维推荐了年轻的法拉第。这份工作主要包括清洗瓶子和设备、清扫以及点燃壁炉。工资很低，比他做装订工的工资低得多，但法拉第几乎不敢相信自己竟然有这么好运，当场就接受了这份工作。

His education was so rapid it shocked him; it was nothing like the progress he had made on his own. Under his mentor’s supervision, he learned how to prepare Davy’s chemical mixtures, including some of the more explosive varieties. He was taught the rudiments of chemical analysis from perhaps the greatest living practitioner of the art. His responsibilities began to grow, and he was given access to the lab for his own experiments. He worked night and day to bring a much-needed order to the laboratory and its shelves. And slowly, their relationship deepened—clearly Davy saw him as a younger version of himself.

他学习的速度之快令他震惊；这与他独自取得的进步截然不同。在导师的指导下，他学会了如何配制戴维的化学混合物，包括一些更具爆炸性的品种。他从或许是当今最伟大的化学分析实践者那里学习了化学分析的基础知识。他的责任开始加重，他被允许进入实验室进行自己的实验。他夜以继日地工作，为实验室及其架子带来了急需的秩序。慢慢地，他们的关系加深了——显然，戴维把他视为年轻时的自己。

That summer Davy prepared to go on an extended tour of Europe, and invited Faraday to come along as his laboratory assistant and valet. Although Faraday did not relish the thought of acting as a personal servant, the chance to meet some of Europe’s most preeminent scientists and work so closely with Davy on his experiments (he traveled with a kind of portable laboratory) was too much to pass up. It was best to be around him as much as possible and soak up his knowledge, his whole way of thinking.

那年夏天，戴维准备去欧洲进行一次长途旅行，并邀请法拉第一同前往，担任他的实验室助理和贴身男仆。尽管法拉第并不喜欢充当他的贴身男仆，但能与欧洲几位最杰出的科学家见面，并与戴维近距离合作进行实验（戴维出行时会携带一种便携式实验室），这样的机会实在令人难以抗拒。最好能尽可能多地与他相处，汲取他的知识和思维方式。

During the trip, Faraday assisted Davy on a particular experiment that would leave a lasting impression on him. The exact chemical composition of diamonds had long been in dispute. They appeared to be composed of carbon. But how could something so beautiful be made of exactly the same substance as charcoal? There had to be more to its chemical composition, but there was no known way to divide a diamond into its constituent elements. It was a problem that had baffled many scientists. Davy had long entertained the radical idea that it was not the elements themselves that determined the properties of things. Perhaps charcoal and diamonds had precisely the same chemical composition, but it was changes in their underlying molecular structure that determined their form. This was a much more dynamic view of nature, but Davy had no way to prove this until suddenly, traveling through France, an idea for the perfect experiment came to him.

旅途中，法拉第协助戴维进行了一项令他终生难忘的实验。钻石的确切化学成分长期以来一直存在争议。它们似乎由碳组成。但如此美丽的东西怎么可能由与木炭完全相同的物质构成呢？它的化学成分肯定不止这些，但当时还没有已知的方法将钻石分解成其组成元素。这个问题困扰了许多科学家。戴维长期以来一直持有一个激进的观点，认为元素本身并非决定事物性质的因素。或许木炭和钻石的化学成分完全相同，但它们底层分子结构的变化决定了它们的形态。这是一种更具动态性的自然观，但戴维一直无法证明这一点，直到在法国旅行时，他突然想到了一个完美的实验方法。

After being reminded that one of the most powerful lenses of the time resided at the Accademia del Cimento in Florence, Davy made a detour there. Gaining permission to use the lens, he placed a diamond in a tiny glass globe containing pure oxygen and used the lens to focus intense sunlight on the globe until the diamond completely evaporated. Inside the globe, all that remained of the diamond was carbon dioxide gas, proving that it was indeed composed of pure carbon. Therefore, what turned carbon into either charcoal or a diamond must involve a change in the underlying molecular structure. Nothing else could explain the results of his experiment. What impressed Faraday was the thought process that went into this. From a simple speculation, Davy found his way to the one experiment that would physically demonstrate his idea by excluding all other possible explanations. This was a highly creative way of thinking, and it was the source of Davy’s power as a chemist.

戴维得知当时最强大的透镜之一藏于佛罗伦萨的化学学院后，便绕道前往那里。获得使用透镜的许可后，他将一颗钻石放入一个装有纯氧的微型玻璃球中，并用透镜将强烈的阳光聚焦在玻璃球上，直到钻石完全蒸发。在玻璃球内部，钻石只剩下二氧化碳气体，证明它确实由纯碳组成。因此，碳变成木炭或钻石的原因必定涉及到底层分子结构的变化。其他任何解释都无法解释他的实验结果。令法拉第印象深刻的是他为此所进行的思考过程。戴维从一个简单的推测出发，排除了所有其他可能的解释，最终找到了一个能够从物理上验证他想法的实验。这是一种极具创造性的思维方式，也是戴维作为化学家力量的源泉。

On his return to the Royal Institution, Faraday was given a pay increase and a new title—Assistant and Superintendent of the Apparatus and Mineralogical Collection. And soon a pattern developed. Davy liked to spend most of his time on the road. Trusting Faraday’s growing skills, he would send back to him all kinds of mineral samples to analyze. Davy had slowly grown dependent on his assistant; in letters to Faraday he praised him as one of the best analytic chemists he knew—he had trained him well. But by the year 1821, Faraday had to confront an unpleasant reality: Davy was keeping him under his thumb. After eight years of an intense apprenticeship, he was now an accomplished chemist in his own right, with expanding knowledge of other sciences. He was doing independent research, but Davy was still treating him as an assistant, making him send packets of dead flies for his fishing lures and assigning him other menial tasks.

回到皇家研究院后，法拉第的薪水增加了，并获得了一个新头衔——仪器和矿物学收藏助理兼主管。很快，一种模式就形成了。戴维喜欢把大部分时间花在路上。他相信法拉第日益精湛的技艺，会把各种各样的矿物样品寄回给他分析。戴维逐渐对这位助手产生了依赖；在写给法拉第的信中，他称赞法拉第是他认识的最好的分析化学家之一——他把法拉第训练得井井有条。但到了1821年，法拉第不得不面对一个令人不快的现实：戴维把他控制在自己的手下。经过八年紧张的学徒期，他如今已是一位技艺精湛的化学家，并且在其他科学领域的知识也不断扩展。他开始独立进行研究，但戴维仍然把他当作助手，让他寄送一包包死蝇作为鱼饵，并给他分配其他琐碎的任务。

It was Davy who had rescued him from the drudgery of the bookbinding business. He owed him everything. But Faraday was now thirty years old, and if he were not allowed soon enough to declare his independence, his most creative years would be wasted as a laboratory assistant. To leave on bad terms, however, would ruin his name in the scientific community, especially considering his own lack of reputation. Then, finally, Faraday found a chance to separate himself from his overbearing mentor, and he exploited this opportunity to the maximum.

是戴维把他从繁重的装订工作中解救出来。他欠他一切。但法拉第如今已年逾三十，如果不让他尽快宣布独立，他最富有创造力的年华就只能浪费在实验室助理身上了。然而，如果不欢而散，又会毁掉他在科学界的声誉，尤其是在他自身名声不佳的情况下。后来，法拉第终于找到了一个机会，摆脱这位专横跋扈的导师，并充分利用了这个机会。

Scientists throughout Europe were making discoveries about the relationship between electricity and magnetism, but the effect they had on each other was strange—creating a movement that was not linear and direct, but apparently more circular. Nothing in nature was quite like this. How to reveal the exact shape of this effect or movement in an experiment became the rage, and soon Davy got involved. Working with a fellow scientist named William Hyde Wollaston, they proposed the idea that the movement created by electromagnetism was more like a spiral. Involving Faraday in their experiments, they devised a way to break up the movement into small increments that could be measured. Once this was all added up, it would show the spiral motion.

欧洲各地的科学家们正在探索电磁之间的关系，但它们之间的相互作用却十分奇特——产生的运动并非直线或直接，而是明显更接近圆形。自然界中没有任何东西能与之相比。如何在实验中揭示这种效应或运动的确切形状成为热门话题，戴维很快就参与其中。他们与一位名叫威廉·海德·沃勒斯顿的科学家合作，提出了电磁运动更像螺旋线的观点。他们邀请法拉第参与实验，设计出一种方法，将运动分解成可测量的小增量。一旦将这些小增量加起来，就能显示出螺旋运动。

At about the same time, Faraday was asked by a close friend to write a review of all that was known about electromagnetism for an established journal, and so he began a rigorous study of the field. Thinking like his mentor, he speculated that there must be a way to physically demonstrate the motion created by electromagnetism in a continual fashion, so that no one could dispute the results. One night in September 1821 he had a vision of just such an experiment, and he put it into practice. With a bar magnet secured upright in a cup of liquid mercury (a metal that conducts electricity), Faraday placed a suspended wire, buoyed by a cork, in the mercury. When the wire was charged with electricity, the cork moved around the magnet in a precise conical path. The reverse experiment (with the wire secured in the water) revealed the same pattern.

大约在同一时间，法拉第的一位密友请他为一家知名期刊撰写一篇关于电磁学已知知识的评论，于是他开始对该领域进行深入研究。他像导师一样思考，推测一定有一种方法可以连续地物理演示电磁学产生的运动，这样就不会有人对结果提出异议。1821 年 9 月的一个晚上，他突发奇想，想到了一个实验，并将其付诸实践。法拉第将一块条形磁铁竖直固定在一杯液态水银（一种导电的金属）中，然后将一根用软木塞浮起的悬浮金属丝放入水银中。当金属丝通电后，软木塞会沿着精确的圆锥形路径绕磁铁移动。相反的实验（将金属丝固定在水中）也揭示了同样的模式。

This was the first time in history that electricity had been used to generate continual motion, the precursor to all electric motors. The experiment was so simple and yet only Faraday had seen it so clearly. It revealed a way of thinking that was very much the product of Davy’s tutelage. Feeling the weight of years of poverty, crushed expectations, and servitude lifting off of him, he danced around the laboratory. This would be the discovery that would free him at last. Excited about what he had done, he rushed to have his results published.

这是历史上首次利用电产生持续运动，这是所有电动机的前身。这个实验非常简单，却只有法拉第看得如此透彻。它揭示了一种思维方式，而这种思维方式很大程度上是戴维悉心指导的结果。他感到多年贫困、渺茫的期望和奴役的重压从他身上卸下，在实验室里兴奋不已。这一发现最终将使他获得自由。他对自己的研究成果感到兴奋不已，急于发表自己的成果。

In his haste to get his report out, however, Faraday had forgotten to mention the research done by Wollaston and Davy. Soon enough, the rumor spread that Faraday had actually plagiarized their work. Realizing his mistake, Faraday met with Wollaston and showed him how he had reached his results independent of anyone else’s work. Wollaston agreed and let the matter drop. But the rumors continued, and soon it became clear that the source of them was Davy himself. He refused to accept Faraday’s explanation and no one knew quite why. When Faraday was nominated to the Royal Society because of his discovery, it was Davy, as president, who tried to block it. A year later, when Faraday made yet another important discovery, Davy claimed partial credit for it. He seemed to believe that he had created Faraday from nothing and so was responsible for everything he did.

然而，法拉第急于发表报告，却忘了提及沃拉斯顿和戴维的研究成果。很快，谣言四起，说法拉第剽窃了他们的成果。意识到自己的错误后，法拉第与沃拉斯顿见面，向他展示了自己如何独立于他人成果而获得成果。沃拉斯顿同意了，便将此事搁置。但谣言仍在继续，很快真相大白，传言的根源竟然是戴维本人。他拒绝接受法拉第的解释，而没有人知道确切原因。当法拉第因其发现被提名为皇家学会会员时，身为学会主席的戴维却极力阻挠。一年后，法拉第又有了一项重要发现，戴维却将部分功劳归于自己。他似乎认为是自己凭空创造了法拉第，因此应对法拉第的一切行为负责。

Faraday had seen enough—their relationship was essentially over. He would never correspond with or see him again. Now having authority within the scientific community, Faraday could do as he pleased. His coming experiments would soon pave the way for all of the most important advances in electrical energy, and for the field theories that would revolutionize science in the twentieth century. He would go on to become one of history’s greatest practitioners of experimental science, far outshining the fame of his one-time mentor.

法拉第看够了——他们的关系基本上结束了。他再也不会和他通信，也不会再见面。如今，法拉第在科学界拥有权威，可以随心所欲地行事了。他即将进行的实验，将为电能领域所有最重要的进步，以及那些将在20世纪彻底改变科学的场论铺平道路。他后来成为历史上最伟大的实验科学实践者之一，其声望远超他曾经的导师。

KEYS TO MASTERY

掌握诀窍

At table, the ladies praised a portrait by a young painter. “What is most surprising,” they added, “he has learned everything by himself.” This could be seen particularly in the hands, which were not correctly and artistically drawn. “We see,” said Goethe, “that the young man has talent; however, you should not praise, but rather blame him, for learning everything by himself. A man of talent is not born to be left to himself, but to devote himself to art and good masters who will make something of him.”

席间，女士们对一位年轻画家的肖像画赞不绝口。“最令人惊讶的是，”她们补充道，“他什么都是自学成才的。”这一点尤其体现在画中，画手的画法不够准确，也不够艺术性。歌德说：“我们看得出来，这位年轻人很有天赋；然而，你不应该称赞他，而应该责怪他什么都是自学成才。一个有天赋的人并非生来就自给自足，而是要全身心投入艺术，拜师学艺，才能有所成就。”

—J OHANN P ETER E CKERMANN , C ONVERSATIONS WITH G OETHE

—约翰·彼得·埃克曼，《与歌德的对话》

In the past, people of power had an aura of authority that was very real. Some of this aura emanated from their accomplishments, and some of it from the position they occupied—being a member of the aristocracy or a religious elite. This aura had a definite effect and could be felt; it caused people to respect and worship those who possessed it. Over the centuries, however, the slow process of democratization has worn away this aura of authority in all of its guises, to the point today of almost nonexistence.

过去，掌权者身上都弥漫着一种实实在在的权威光环。这种光环部分源于他们的成就，部分源于他们所处的地位——贵族或宗教精英阶层。这种光环具有显著的影响力，且易于感知；它使人们尊敬和崇拜拥有它的人。然而，几个世纪以来，缓慢的民主化进程逐渐消磨了这种权威光环的各种形式，如今几乎荡然无存。

We feel, rightly so, that no one should be admired or worshipped merely for the position they occupy, particularly if it comes from connections or a privileged background. But this attitude carries over to people who have reached their position mostly through their own accomplishments. We live in a culture that likes to criticize and debunk any form of authority, to point out the weaknesses of those in power. If we feel any aura, it is in the presence of celebrities and their seductive personalities. Some of this skeptical spirit toward authority is healthy, particularly in relation to politics, but when it comes to learning and the Apprenticeship Phase, it presents a problem.

我们理所当然地认为，任何人都不应仅仅因其所处的地位而受到钦佩或崇拜，尤其当这种地位源于人脉或特权背景时。但这种态度也适用于那些主要凭借自身成就获得地位的人。我们生活在一个热衷于批评和揭穿任何形式权威、指出当权者弱点的文化中。如果我们能感受到某种氛围，那就是名人和他们魅力四射的个性。这种对权威的怀疑精神在某种程度上是健康的，尤其是在政治领域，但在学习和学徒阶段，它就成了问题。

To learn requires a sense of humility. We must admit that there are people out there who know our field much more deeply than we do. Their superiority is not a function of natural talent or privilege, but rather of time and experience. Their authority in the field is not based on politics or trickery. It is very real. But if we are not comfortable with this fact, if we feel in general mistrustful of any kind of authority, we will succumb to the belief that we can just as easily learn something on our own, that being self-taught is more authentic. We might justify this attitude as a sign of our independence, but in fact it stems from basic insecurity. We feel, perhaps unconsciously, that learning from Masters and submitting to their authority is somehow an indictment of our own natural ability. Even if we have teachers in our lives, we tend not to pay full attention to their advice, often preferring to do things our own way. In fact, we come to believe that being critical of Masters or teachers is somehow a sign of our intelligence, and that being a submissive pupil is a sign of weakness.

学习需要谦逊。我们必须承认，有些人比我们更深入地了解我们的领域。他们的优越性并非源于天赋或特权，而是源于时间和经验。他们在该领域的权威并非基于政治或权术。这是千真万确的。但如果我们无法接受这一事实，如果我们普遍不信任任何权威，我们就会屈服于这样的信念：我们可以轻松地自学，自学更真实。我们或许会将这种态度视为我们独立的标志，但实际上它源于我们内心深处的不安全感。我们或许会无意识地觉得，向大师学习并屈从于他们的权威，在某种程度上是对我们自身能力的控诉。即使我们生活中有老师，我们也往往不会充分听取他们的建议，而常常更喜欢按照自己的方式行事。事实上，我们开始相信，批评大师或老师是我们智慧的标志，而顺从的学生则是软弱的表现。

Understand: all that should concern you in the early stages of your career is acquiring practical knowledge in the most efficient manner possible. For this purpose, during the Apprenticeship Phase you will need mentors whose authority you recognize and to whom you submit. Your admission of need does not say anything essential about you, but only about your temporary condition of weakness, which your mentor will help you overcome.

要知道：在职业生涯的早期阶段，你唯一应该关注的是如何以最高效的方式获取实践知识。为此，在学徒阶段，你需要一位你认可其权威并顺从其指导的导师。你承认需要指导并不代表你的任何本质问题，而只是表明你暂时处于弱势，你的导师会帮助你克服这一弱点。

The reason you require a mentor is simple: Life is short; you have only so much time and so much energy to expend. Your most creative years are generally in your late twenties and on into your forties. You can learn what you need through books, your own practice, and occasional advice from others, but the process is hit-and-miss. The information in books is not tailored to your circumstances and individuality; it tends to be somewhat abstract. When you are young and have less experience of the world, this abstract knowledge is hard to put into practice. You can learn from your experiences, but it can often take years to fully understand the meaning of what has happened. It is always possible to practice on your own, but you will not receive enough focused feedback. You can often gain a self-directed apprenticeship in many fields, but this could take ten years, maybe more.

你需要导师的原因很简单：人生苦短，你只有那么多时间和精力可以支配。你最有创造力的时期通常是在二十多岁后期到四十多岁之间。你可以通过书籍、自己的实践以及偶尔听取他人的建议来学习你需要的东西，但这个过程是碰运气的。书中的信息并不适合你的环境和个性，往往有些抽象。当你年轻，阅历较少时，这些抽象的知识很难付诸实践。你可以从经验中学习，但通常需要数年时间才能完全理解所发生的事情的意义。你总是可以自己练习，但你不会得到足够有针对性的反馈。你通常可以在许多领域获得自主的学徒机会，但这可能需要十年甚至更长时间。

Mentors do not give you a shortcut, but they streamline the process. They invariably had their own great mentors, giving them a richer and deeper knowledge of their field. Their ensuing years of experience taught them invaluable lessons and strategies for learning. Their knowledge and experience become yours; they can direct you away from unnecessary side paths or errors. They observe you at work and provide real-time feedback, making your practice more time efficient. Their advice is tailored to your circumstances and your needs. Working closely with them, you absorb the essence of their creative spirit, which you can now adapt in your own way. What took you ten years on your own could have been done in five with proper direction.

导师不会为你提供捷径，但他们会简化流程。他们通常都有自己的优秀导师，这让他们对各自领域有了更丰富、更深入的了解。他们随后多年的经验教会了他们宝贵的经验和学习策略。他们的知识和经验将成为你的；他们可以引导你避免不必要的岔路或错误。他们会观察你的工作并提供实时反馈，使你的实践更加高效。他们的建议会根据你的实际情况和需求量身定制。与他们紧密合作，你会吸收他们创新精神的精髓，现在你可以将其融入到自己的方式中。你独自一人花了十年时间完成的事情，如果得到正确的指导，五年就能完成。

There is more to this than just time saved. When we learn something in a concentrated manner it has added value. We experience fewer distractions. What we learn is internalized more deeply because of the intensity of our focus and practice. Our own ideas and development flourish more naturally in this shortened time frame. Having an efficient apprenticeship, we can make the most of our youthful energy and our creative potential.

这不仅仅是节省时间。当我们专心致志地学习时，它会带来额外的价值。我们会减少分心。由于我们专注和练习的强度，我们所学到的知识能够被更深入地内化。在这种缩短的时间内，我们的想法和发展会更加自然地蓬勃发展。拥有高效的学徒期，我们可以最大限度地发挥青春活力和创造潜力。

What makes the mentor-protégé dynamic so intense and so productive is the emotional quality of the relationship. By nature, mentors feel emotionally invested in your education. This can be for several reasons: perhaps they like you, or see in you a younger version of themselves, and can relive their own youth through you; perhaps they recognize in you a special talent that will give them pleasure to cultivate; perhaps you have something important to offer them, mostly your youthful energy and willingness to work hard. Being useful to them can build a powerful emotional connection to you over time. On your part, you also feel emotionally drawn to them—admiration for their achievements, a desire to model yourself after them, and so on. Mentors find this immensely flattering.

师徒关系之所以如此紧密有效，是因为这种关系中蕴含着情感。导师们天生就对你的教育充满情感。这可能出于多种原因：也许他们喜欢你，或者在你身上看到了自己年轻时的影子，并能通过你重温自己的青春岁月；也许他们认可你身上的特殊才能，乐于培养；也许你身上有一些重要的东西可以提供给他们，主要是你的青春活力和努力工作的意愿。随着时间的推移，对他们有用可以与你建立起强大的情感联系。而你也会在情感上被他们吸引——钦佩他们的成就，渴望以他们为榜样，等等。导师们对此感到非常荣幸。

With this two-way emotional connection you both open up to each other in a way that goes beyond the usual teacher-student dynamic. When you admire people, you become more susceptible to absorbing and imitating everything they do. You pay deeper attention. Your mirror neurons are more engaged, allowing for learning that involves more than the superficial transmission of knowledge, but also includes a style and way of thinking that is often powerful. On the other side, because of the emotional bond, mentors will tend to divulge more of their secrets than they would to others. You must not be afraid of this emotional component to the relationship. It is precisely what makes you learn more deeply and efficiently.

有了这种双向的情感联系，你们彼此敞开心扉，超越了通常的师生关系。当你钦佩他人时，你会更容易吸收和模仿他们的一举一动。你会更加专注。你的镜像神经元更加活跃，这使得学习不仅仅局限于肤浅的知识传递，还包含一种通常非常强大的风格和思维方式。另一方面，由于这种情感纽带，导师往往会比其他人更愿意透露自己的秘密。你不必害怕这种关系中的情感成分。它恰恰能让你学得更深入、更有效。

Think of it this way: the process of learning resembles the medieval practice of alchemy. In alchemy, the goal was to find a way to transform base metals or stones into gold. To effect this, alchemists searched for what was known as the philosopher’s stone—a substance that would make dead stones or metals come alive and organically change their chemical composition into gold. Although the philosopher’s stone was never discovered, it has profound relevance as a metaphor. The knowledge that you need to become a Master exists out there in the world—it is like a base metal or dead stone. This knowledge needs to be heated up and come alive within you, transforming itself into something active and relevant to your circumstances. The mentor is like the philosopher’s stone—through direct interaction with someone of experience, you are able to quickly and efficiently heat up and animate this knowledge, turning it into something like gold.

可以这样想：学习的过程类似于中世纪的炼金术。炼金术的目标是找到一种方法，将贱金属或石头变成黄金。为了实现这一目标，炼金术士们寻找一种被称为点金石的东西——这种物质能让死石头或金属活起来，并有机地将其化学成分转化为黄金。虽然点金石从未被发现，但它作为一个比喻却有着深远的意义。成为大师所需的知识存在于世间——它就像贱金属或死石头。这些知识需要在你的内心被加热、激活，转化为与你处境相关的、活跃的东西。导师就像点金石——通过与经验丰富的导师直接互动，你能够快速有效地加热和激活这些知识，将其转化为类似黄金的东西。

The story of Michael Faraday is the ultimate illustration of this alchemical process. His life seemed to progress almost through magic—falling into the one job where he could read books, learn about science, and impress exactly the right person with his notes, leading to a connection to the ultimate mentor, Humphry Davy. But there was a logic behind all of this apparent magic and good fortune. As a young man he possessed an intense energy and hunger for knowledge. A kind of inner radar directed him to the one bookshop in the area. Although it was pure luck that the book Improvement of the Mind fell into his hands, it took someone with such focus to recognize immediately its worth and exploit it fully. Under Watt’s guidance, his knowledge became more practical. But that same radar that directed him to the shop and to this book now pointed him somewhere else. The knowledge he had gained was still too diffused and disconnected. He intuited that the only way to transform it into something useful was to find a living mentor.

迈克尔·法拉第的故事是对这种炼金术般过程的终极诠释。他的人生仿佛魔法般进展——他找到了一份工作，可以读书、学习科学，还能用笔记打动合适的人，最终结识了终极导师汉弗莱·戴维。然而，所有这些看似神奇和幸运的背后却隐藏着某种逻辑。年轻时，他精力充沛，渴望知识。一种内在的雷达指引他找到了附近的一家书店。虽然《心智的提升》落入他的手中纯属运气，但只有如此专注的人才能立即意识到它的价值并充分利用它。在瓦特的指导下，他的知识变得更加实用。但指引他找到这家书店和这本书的雷达，如今却将他指向了别处。他所获得的知识仍然过于分散和脱节。他直觉地认为，将其转化为有用知识的唯一途径是找到一位在世的导师。

Once he secured Davy as his man, he threw himself into the relationship with the same focus that he had brought to everything else. Serving under Davy, Faraday learned all of the secrets of chemistry and electricity that the Master had gleaned throughout his life. He practiced with these ideas in the laboratory—mixing chemicals for Davy and doing his own experiments. In the process, he absorbed Davy’s patterns of thinking, of approaching chemical analysis and experimentation. His knowledge became increasingly active.

法拉第一旦得到戴维的信任，便全身心投入到这段关系中，如同他对待其他一切事物一样专注。在戴维手下，法拉第学习了这位大师毕生积累的化学和电学秘诀。他在实验室里实践这些理念——为戴维混合化学物质，并自己进行实验。在这个过程中，他吸收了戴维的思维模式，以及他处理化学分析和实验的方法。他的知识日益活跃。

After eight years, this interactive dynamic yielded one of the great discoveries of science—the uncovering of the secret of electromagnetism. Faraday’s own studies and what he had learned from Davy became transformed into creative energy, a form of gold. If he had stayed on the path of self-apprenticeship out of fear or insecurity, he would have remained a bookbinder—miserable and unfulfilled. Through the alchemy of intense mentorship he transformed himself into one of the most creative scientists in history.

八年后，这种互动催生了科学史上的伟大发现之一——电磁学的秘密被揭开。法拉第自身的研究以及他从戴维那里学到的知识，最终转化为创造力，如同黄金一般。如果他因为恐惧或不安全感而继续走自学之路，他或许只会是一个装订工——痛苦不堪，毫无成就感。在导师的悉心指导下，他最终蜕变为历史上最具创造力的科学家之一。

Certainly religion played an important role in Faraday’s education. Because he believed that everything in the universe was alive with God’s presence, he tended to animate whatever he encountered, including the books he read and the phenomenon of electricity itself. Since he saw these things as alive, he engaged with them on a deeper level, which intensified the learning process. This way of looking at the world, however, transcends religion and contains great power for all of us in our apprenticeships. We too can see the subjects that we study as possessing a kind of vital spirit with which we must interact, and which we must understand from the inside out. As with Faraday, this attitude will intensify our level of engagement with what we are learning.

宗教无疑在法拉第的教育中扮演着重要的角色。因为他相信宇宙万物因上帝的存在而生机勃勃，他倾向于赋予所见之物生命力，包括他所读的书籍以及电现象本身。正因为他将这些事物视为鲜活的生命，他才能在更深的层面上与它们互动，从而强化学习过程。然而，这种看待世界的方式超越了宗教，对我们所有学徒而言都蕴含着巨大的力量。我们也可以将所学的学科视为拥有某种生命力的精神，我们必须与之互动，并由内而外地理解它。正如法拉第一样，这种态度将增强我们对所学内容的投入程度。

To initially entice the right Master to serve as your mentor, you will want to mix in a strong element of self-interest. You have something tangible and practical to offer them, in addition to your youth and energy. Before he had ever met him, Davy was aware of Faraday’s work ethic and organizational skills. That alone made him a desirable assistant. Considering this, you may not want to go in search of mentors until you have acquired some elementary skills and discipline that you can rely upon to interest them.

为了最初吸引合适的大师担任你的导师，你需要融入强烈的个人利益元素。除了你的青春活力之外，你还可以提供一些切实可行的东西。在与法拉第见面之前，戴维就注意到了他的敬业精神和组织能力。仅凭这一点，他就成为了一位理想的助手。考虑到这一点，在你掌握了一些能够吸引导师的基本技能和纪律之前，你最好不要去寻找导师。

Almost all Masters and people of power suffer from too many demands on their time and too much information to absorb. If you can demonstrate the ability to help them organize themselves on these fronts to a degree that others cannot, it will be much easier to get their attention and interest them in the relationship. Do not shy away from anything menial or secretarial. You want person-to-person access, however you can get it. Once you establish a relationship, you will find other ways to continually hook them through their self-interest. Try to see the world through their eyes and ask the simple question of what it is they need most. Keeping their self-interest involved will only enhance any emotional connection they feel toward you.

几乎所有大师级人物和权势人物都饱受时间过长、信息量过大之苦。如果你能展现出帮助他们在这些方面自我组织的能力，达到别人无法企及的程度，就能更容易地吸引他们的注意力，并激发他们对这段关系的兴趣。不要回避任何琐碎或文秘般的事务。无论你如何努力，你都需要人际交往。一旦建立了关系，你就会找到其他方法，不断利用他们的个人利益来吸引他们。试着用他们的眼睛看世界，问问他们最需要什么。让他们关注自身利益，只会增进他们对你的情感联系。

If you work on yourself first, as Faraday did, developing a solid work ethic and organizational skills, eventually the right teacher will appear in your life. Word will spread through the proper channels of your efficiency and your hunger to learn, and opportunities will come your way. In any event, you should not feel timid in approaching Masters, no matter how elevated their position. You will be frequently surprised at how open they can be to serving as a mentor, if the fit is right and you have something to offer. The ability to transfer their experience and knowledge to someone younger often provides them with a great pleasure, akin to parenting.

如果你像法拉第一样，先提升自我，培养扎实的职业道德和组织能力，最终你的人生中就会出现一位合适的老师。你的高效和求知欲会通过合适的渠道传播开来，机会自然会降临到你身上。无论如何，无论大师的地位多么崇高，你都不应该羞于接近他们。你会常常惊讶地发现，如果合适，并且你也能有所贡献，他们往往乐于成为你的导师。能够将他们的经验和知识传授给后辈，往往会给他们带来莫大的快乐，如同为人父母一般。

The best mentors are often those who have wide knowledge and experience, and are not overly specialized in their field—they can train you to think on a higher level, and to make connections between different forms of knowledge. The paradigm for this is the Aristotle–Alexander the Great relationship. Philip II, Alexander’s father and king of Macedonia, chose Aristotle to mentor his thirteen-year-old son because the philosopher had learned and mastered so many different fields. He could thus impart to Alexander an overall love of learning, and teach him how to think and reason in any kind of situation—the greatest skill of all. This ended up working to perfection. Alexander was able to effectively apply the reasoning skills he had gained from Aristotle to politics and warfare. To the end of his life he maintained an intense curiosity for any field of knowledge, and would always gather about him experts he could learn from. Aristotle had imparted a form of wisdom that played a key role in Alexander’s success.

最好的导师往往知识渊博、经验丰富，且并非在其领域过于专业化——他们可以培养你更深入的思考，并帮助你在不同的知识形式之间建立联系。亚里士多德与亚历山大大帝的关系便是这种关系的典范。亚历山大的父亲、马其顿国王腓力二世选择亚里士多德作为他十三岁儿子的导师，因为这位哲学家学识渊博，精通众多领域。因此，他能够培养亚历山大对学习的热爱，并教会他如何在任何情况下思考和推理——这是最伟大的技能。最终，这种做法取得了完美的效果。亚历山大能够将从亚里士多德那里学到的推理技巧有效地运用到政治和战争中。直到生命的尽头，他都对任何知识领域都保持着强烈的好奇心，并且总是聚集在他身边，向他们学习。亚里士多德传授的智慧在亚历山大的成功中发挥了关键作用。

You will want as much personal interaction with the mentor as possible. A virtual relationship is never enough. There are cues and subtle aspects you can only pick up through a person-to-person interaction—such as a way of doing things that has evolved through much experience. These patterns of action are hard to put into words, and can only be absorbed through much personal exposure. In crafts or in sports this is more obvious. Tennis instructors, for example, can only reveal many secrets of their skills by demonstrating things before their pupils’ eyes. Instructors may not in fact be completely conscious of what makes their backhand so effective, but in watching them in action pupils can pick up the pattern and motion, exploiting the power of mirror neurons. But this process of absorption is also relevant to nonmanual skills. It was only through constant exposure to Davy’s thought process that Faraday understood the power of finding the crucial experiment to demonstrate an idea, something he would adapt later on with great success.

你需要尽可能多地与导师进行个人互动。虚拟的关系永远不够。有些线索和微妙之处只有通过人际互动才能掌握——比如，通过丰富的经验发展而形成的做事方式。这些行为模式难以用语言表达，只有通过大量的个人接触才能吸收。在手工艺或体育运动中，这一点更为明显。例如，网球教练只有通过在学生眼前演示才能揭示许多技巧的秘密。教练实际上可能并不完全意识到是什么让他们的反手如此有效，但通过观察他们的动作，学生可以利用镜像神经元的力量，掌握其中的模式和动作。但这种吸收过程也适用于非体力技能。正是通过不断接触戴维的思维过程，法拉第才理解了找到关键实验来验证一个想法的力量，后来他运用这个实验并取得了巨大的成功。

As the relationship progresses you can make this absorption process more conscious and direct, questioning them about the principles underlying their way of doing things. If you are clever, you can be a kind of midwife, getting them to analyze their own creativity for you, and mining all kinds of rich ideas in the process. They are often grateful for the opportunity to reveal the inner workings of their power, particularly to someone they do not perceive as a threat.

随着关系的进展，你可以让这种吸收过程更加自觉和直接，向他们询问做事背后的原则。如果你足够聪明，你可以扮演助产士的角色，让他们为你分析自己的创造力，并在此过程中挖掘各种丰富的想法。他们通常会感激有机会展现自己力量的内在运作，尤其是向那些他们并不认为是威胁的人。

Although one mentor at a time is best, it is not always possible to find the perfect one. In such a case, an alternate strategy is to find several mentors in your immediate environment, each one filling strategic gaps in your knowledge and experience. Having more than one mentor has side benefits, giving you several connections and important allies to rely upon later on. Similarly, if your circumstances limit your contacts, books can serve as temporary mentors, as The Improvement of the Mind did for Faraday. In such a case you will want to convert such books and writers into living mentors as much as possible. You personalize their voice, interact with the material, taking notes or writing in the margins. You analyze what they write and try to make it come alive—the spirit and not just the letter of their work.

虽然一次只有一位导师是最好的，但并非总能找到一位完美的导师。在这种情况下，另一种策略是在你的周围环境中寻找几位导师，每位导师都能填补你知识和经验方面的战略空白。拥有多位导师还有额外的好处，可以为你提供日后可以信赖的人脉和重要盟友。同样，如果你的处境限制了你的人脉，书籍可以充当你的临时导师，就像《心智的提升》之于法拉第一样。在这种情况下，你应该尽可能地将这些书籍和作家转化为活生生的导师。你可以个性化他们的声音，与作品互动，做笔记或在页边空白处书写。你可以分析他们的作品，并努力使其鲜活起来——不仅是作品的字面意思，更是精神的体现。

In a looser sense, a figure from the past or present can serve as an ideal, someone to model yourself after. Through much research and some imagination on your part, you turn them into a living presence. You ask yourself—what would they do in this situation or that? Countless generals have used Napoleon Bonaparte for just such a purpose.

更宽泛地说，过去或现在的人物可以作为理想，成为你的榜样。通过大量的研究和一些想象，你可以将他们塑造成一个鲜活的存在。你会问自己——在这种情况下，他们会怎么做？无数将军都曾将拿破仑·波拿巴作为榜样。

Mentors have their own strengths and weaknesses. The good ones allow you to develop your own style and then to leave them when the time is right. Such types can remain lifelong friends and allies. But often the opposite will occur. They grow dependent on your services and want to keep you indentured. They envy your youth and unconsciously hinder you, or become overcritical. You must be aware of this as it develops. Your goal is to get as much out of them as possible, but at a certain point you may pay a price if you stay too long and let them subvert your confidence. Your submitting to their authority is by no means unconditional, and in fact your goal all along is eventually to find your way to independence, having internalized and adapted their wisdom.

导师各有优缺点。好的导师会允许你发展自己的风格，并在适当的时候离开他们。这样的人可以成为你一生的朋友和盟友。但通常情况下，情况会相反。他们会逐渐依赖你的服务，并想让你成为他们的奴隶。他们会嫉妒你的年轻，不知不觉地阻碍你，或者变得过于挑剔。你必须意识到这种情况的发展。你的目标是尽可能多地从他们身上获取知识，但到了一定程度，如果你待得太久，让他们摧毁你的自信，你可能会付出代价。你对他们权威的服从绝非无条件，事实上，你一直以来的目标都是在内化和吸收他们的智慧之后，最终找到通往独立的道路。

In this respect, the mentor relationship often replays elements from our childhood. Although a mentor can be a man or a woman, he or she often assumes the form of a father figure—there to guide and help us, but sometimes trying to control too much and plot our life for us. He may take any attempt at independence, even later in the relationship, as a personal assault on his authority. You must not allow yourself to feel any guilt when the time comes to assert yourself. Instead, as Faraday did, you should feel resentful and even angry about his desire to hold you back, using such emotions to help you leave him. It is often best to set up this move earlier on so that you are emotionally prepared to make it. As the relationship progresses, you can begin to slightly distance yourself from the mentor, perhaps taking note of some of his weaknesses or character flaws, or even finding fault with his most cherished beliefs. Establishing your differences with the mentor is an important part of your self-development, whether he is of the good or bad parent type.

从这个角度来看，导师关系常常会重现我们童年时期的一些元素。虽然导师可以是男性或女性，但他或她通常扮演着父亲的角色——引导和帮助我们，但有时也会试图控制太多，为我们规划人生。即使在关系后期，他也可能将任何试图独立的尝试视为对其权威的人身攻击。当你需要展现自我时，你绝不能让自己感到内疚。相反，你应该像法拉第一样，对他试图阻碍你的欲望感到怨恨甚至愤怒，并利用这种情绪来帮助你离开他。通常最好尽早做好准备，以便你在情感上做好准备。随着关系的发展，你可以开始与导师稍微保持距离，或许可以注意到他的一些弱点或性格缺陷，甚至挑剔他最珍视的信念。无论导师是好父母还是坏父母，明确你与导师之间的差异都是你自我发展的重要组成部分。

In Spanish they say al maestro cuchillada —to the Master goes the knife. It is a fencing expression, referring to the moment when the young and agile pupil becomes skillful enough to cut his Master. But this also refers to the fate of most mentors who inevitably experience the rebellion of their protégés, like the cut from a sword. In our culture, we tend to venerate those who seem rebellious or at least strike the pose. But rebellion has no meaning or power if it occurs without something solid and real to rebel against. The mentor, or father figure, gives you just such a standard from which you can deviate and establish your own identity. You internalize the important and relevant parts of their knowledge, and you apply the knife to what has no bearing on your life. It is the dynamic of changing generations, and sometimes the father figure has to be killed in order for the sons and daughters to have space to discover themselves.

西班牙语里有“al maestro cuchillada”（刀向师父）。这是一个剑术术语，指的是年轻敏捷的学生技艺精湛，足以斩断师父的那一刻。但这也指大多数导师的命运，他们不可避免地会经历弟子的反抗，就像被剑砍了一刀一样。在我们的文化中，我们倾向于崇敬那些看似叛逆，或至少摆出一副叛逆姿态的人。但如果反抗缺乏坚实而真实的支撑，它就毫无意义，也毫无力量。导师，或者说父亲，正是为你设定了这样一个标准，让你可以偏离它，建立自己的身份认同。你内化他们知识中重要且相关的部分，然后将刀砍向与你的生活无关的部分。这是世代更迭的动力，有时，为了让儿女们有空间去发现自我，必须先斩后奏。

In any event, you will probably have several mentors in your life, like stepping-stones along the way to mastery. At each phase of life you must find the appropriate teachers, getting what you want out of them, moving on, and feeling no shame for this. It is the path your own mentor probably took and it is the way of the world.

无论如何，你的人生中或许会遇到几位导师，就像通往精通之路上的垫脚石。在人生的每个阶段，你都必须找到合适的老师，从他们身上汲取你想要的，继续前进，并且不为此感到羞耻。你的导师或许也曾走过这样的路，这也是世界的常态。

STRATEGIES FOR DEEPENING
深化导师互动的策略
THE MENTOR DYNAMIC

One repays a teacher badly if one remains only a pupil.

如果一个人只是个学生，那么他对老师的回报就太差了。

—F RIEDRICH N IETZSCHE

—弗里德里希·尼采

Although you must submit to the authority of mentors in order to learn from and absorb their power to the highest degree, this does not mean you remain passive in the process. At certain critical points, you can set and determine the dynamic, personalize it to suit your purposes. The following four strategies are designed to help you exploit the relationship to the fullest and transform the knowledge you gain into creative energy.

虽然你必须服从导师的权威，才能最大限度地学习和吸收他们的力量，但这并不意味着你在这个过程中会处于被动地位。在某些关键时刻，你可以设定和决定这种动态，并根据你的目标进行个性化调整。以下四个策略旨在帮助你最大限度地利用这种关系，并将你获得的知识转化为创造力。

# ↩

1. Choose the mentor according to your needs and inclinations

1. 根据你的需求和倾向选择导师

In 1888 the twenty-year-old Frank Lloyd Wright was an apprentice draftsman at the prestigious Chicago firm of Joseph Lyman Silsbee. He had been there a year and was learning much about the business, but he was getting restless. In his mind he could already envision a totally new style of architecture that would revolutionize the field, but he lacked the experience to set up his own practice. Silsbee was a shrewd businessman who saw that his fortune was tied to staying true to the Victorian style of design that was popular with his clients. Wright cringed at what he was being asked to draw; he was learning antiquated design principles that offended him.

1888年，二十岁的弗兰克·劳埃德·赖特在芝加哥著名的约瑟夫·莱曼·西尔斯比公司担任绘图员学徒。他在那里待了一年，学习了很多业务知识，但却越来越焦躁不安。他心中已经可以构想出一种全新的建筑风格，足以彻底改变整个建筑行业，但他缺乏创办自己事务所的经验。西尔斯比是一位精明的商人，他明白自己的命运取决于是否忠于客户喜爱的维多利亚式设计风格。赖特对被要求绘制的图纸感到畏缩；他正在学习那些让他感到不适的过时的设计原则。

Then, out of the blue, he heard that the great Chicago architect Louis Sullivan was looking for a draftsman to help finish the drawings for a particular building. It would be dangerous to leave Silsbee after such a short time and burn his bridge there, but working for Sullivan would be infinitely more stimulating for his personal development as an architect. Sullivan’s firm was at the forefront of designing skyscrapers, utilizing the latest advances in materials and technology.

后来，他意外听说芝加哥伟大的建筑师路易斯·沙利文正在寻找一位绘图员来帮助完成一座特定建筑的图纸。在西尔斯比工作这么短的时间就离开，断送前程，这很危险，但为沙利文工作对他作为建筑师的个人发展来说，无疑更有激励意义。沙利文的公司在摩天大楼设计方面处于领先地位，运用最新的材料和技术。

Wright went on a charm offensive to secure the position. He managed to get a personal interview and showed Sullivan some of the more interesting drawings he had done on his own; he engaged him in a conversation about art and philosophy, knowing Sullivan’s own aesthetic predilections. Sullivan hired him for the job, and a few months later made him an apprentice draftsman in his firm. Wright cultivated a personal relationship with him, eagerly playing the role of the son that Sullivan had never had. With his talent and Sullivan’s blessing, he quickly rose to the position of head draftsman in the firm. Wright became, as he put it, “the pencil in Sullivan’s hand.” In 1893 Sullivan fired him for moonlighting, but by then Wright had learned everything he could and was more than prepared to step out on his own. Sullivan had given him in those five years an education in modern architecture that no one else could have provided.

为了获得这个职位，赖特不惜展现个人魅力。他设法争取到一次面谈机会，向沙利文展示了一些他独立创作的有趣图纸；他了解沙利文的审美偏好，并与沙利文探讨了艺术和哲学。沙利文聘用了他，几个月后，又让他在公司担任绘图员学徒。赖特与沙利文建立了私人关系，热切地扮演着沙利文从未有过的儿子的角色。凭借自己的天赋和沙利文的认可，赖特迅速晋升为公司首席绘图员。用赖特的话来说，他成了“沙利文手中的铅笔”。1893年，沙利文以兼职为由解雇了他，但那时赖特已经学尽了一切，完全准备好独立自主。在那五年里，沙利文给予了他无人能及的现代建筑教育。

In 1906 Carl Jung was a promising thirty-one-year-old psychiatrist, renowned for his work in experimental psychology and holding an important position at the famous Burghölzli Psychiatric Hospital in Zurich. But despite the apparent success in his life, he felt insecure. He believed that his interest in the occult and strange psychic phenomena was a weakness he needed to work through. He was frustrated that his treatment of patients was often not effective. He worried that his work had no legitimacy and that he lacked a certain rigor. He began to correspond with the founder of the psychoanalytic field, Sigmund Freud, fifty-one years old at the time. Jung was ambivalent about Freud—he admired, even worshipped him as a pioneer in the field, but he did not like his emphasis on sex as the determining factor in neurosis. Perhaps his aversion to this aspect of Freudian psychology stemmed from his own prejudices or ignorance, and needed to be overcome by talking it out. In their correspondence they quickly developed a good rapport, and Jung was able to question the Master about matters of psychology he did not fully understand.

1906年，卡尔·荣格是一位前途无量的精神科医生，年仅31岁，以其实验心理学的工作而闻名，并在苏黎世著名的伯格霍兹利精神病院担任要职。然而，尽管他表面上事业有成，却依然感到不安全。他认为自己对神秘学和奇异精神现象的兴趣是他需要克服的弱点。他对患者的治疗常常收效甚微感到沮丧。他担心自己的工作缺乏权威性，也缺乏一定的严谨性。他开始与精神分析领域的创始人西格蒙德·弗洛伊德通信，当时弗洛伊德51岁。荣格对弗洛伊德的态度很矛盾——他钦佩甚至崇拜他作为该领域的先驱，但他不喜欢弗洛伊德强调性别是神经症的决定性因素。或许，他对弗洛伊德心理学这一方面的厌恶源于他自身的偏见或无知，需要通过倾诉来克服。在通信中，他们很快建立了良好的关系，荣格能够向大师询问他不完全理解的心理学问题。

A year later they finally met in Vienna, and talked nonstop for thirteen hours. The younger man charmed Freud—he was so much more creative than his other acolytes. He could serve as his successor in the psychoanalytic movement. For Jung, Freud could be the father figure and mentor he so desperately needed—a grounding influence. They traveled together to the United States, saw each other on frequent visits, and corresponded incessantly. But some five years into the relationship, Jung’s initial ambivalence returned. He began to find Freud rather dictatorial. He chafed at the idea of having to follow Freudian dogma. He now clearly understood why he had initially disagreed with the emphasis on sexuality as the root of all neuroses.

一年后，他们终于在维也纳见面，一聊就是十三个小时。这个年轻人深深地吸引了弗洛伊德——他比其他追随者更有创造力。他可以成为弗洛伊德在精神分析运动中的继任者。对荣格来说，弗洛伊德可以成为他迫切需要的父亲形象和导师——一种根基般的影响力。他们一起前往美国，频繁见面，并保持着不间断的通信。但交往五年后，荣格最初的矛盾心理又回来了。他开始觉得弗洛伊德有些独断专行。他一想到要遵循弗洛伊德的教条就恼火。现在，他清楚地明白了为什么自己最初不同意将性作为所有神经症的根源。

By 1913 they had a definitive break, Jung forever banished from Freud’s inner circle. But through this relationship, Jung had worked out all of his doubts and sharpened certain core ideas about human psychology. In the end, the struggle had strengthened his sense of identity. Without this mentorship, he would have never come to such a clear resolution and been capable of starting his own rival school of psychoanalysis.

1913年，他们彻底决裂，荣格永远被逐出弗洛伊德的核心圈子。但通过这段关系，荣格解决了他所有的疑虑，并强化了关于人类心理学的一些核心理念。最终，这场斗争增强了他的自我认同感。如果没有这段导师关系，他永远不可能得出如此清晰的结论，也无法创立一个与他自身竞争的精神分析学派。

Sometime in the late 1960s, V. S. Ramachandran, a medical student at a college in Madras, came upon a book called Eye and Brain, written by an eminent professor of neuropsychology, Richard Gregory. (For more on Ramachandran’s early years, see here .) The book excited him—the style of writing, the anecdotes, the provocative experiments he recounted. Inspired by the book, Ramachandran did his own experiments on optics, and soon realized that he was better suited for the field than medicine. In 1974 he was admitted into the PhD Program at Cambridge University, in visual perception.

20世纪60年代末，马德拉斯一所大学的医学院学生V. S. Ramachandran偶然读到了一本名为《眼睛与大脑》的书，作者是著名神经心理学教授理查德·格雷戈里。（更多关于Ramachandran早年经历的信息，请参见此处。）这本书让他兴奋不已——无论是文笔、趣闻轶事，还是他讲述的那些引人深思的实验。受此书启发，Ramachandran自己进行了光学实验，并很快意识到自己更适合这个领域，而不是医学。1974年，他被剑桥大学视觉感知博士学位项目录取。

Ramachandran had been raised on stories of the great English scientists of the nineteenth century, and the almost romantic quest for truth that science seemed to represent. He loved the part that speculation played in the great theories and discoveries of men such as Faraday and Darwin. He imagined it would be somewhat similar at Cambridge, but to his surprise the students and professors tended to treat science as a kind of nine-to-five job; it was a competitive, cutthroat, almost corporate environment. He began to feel gloomy and alone in a strange country.

拉马钱德兰从小就听着十九世纪英国伟大科学家的故事长大，也听着科学似乎代表着一种近乎浪漫的对真理的追求。他热爱思辨在法拉第和达尔文等人的伟大理论和发现中所扮演的角色。他想象着剑桥的情况会有些类似，但令他惊讶的是，学生和教授们往往把科学视为一种朝九晚五的工作；那是一个竞争激烈、残酷无情、近乎公司化的环境。在这个陌生的国家，他开始感到沮丧和孤独。

Then one day Richard Gregory himself, a professor at Bristol University, came to Cambridge to give a lecture. Ramachandran was mesmerized—it was like something right out of the pages of Humphry Davy. Gregory performed thought-provoking demonstrations of his ideas on stage; he had a flair for drama and a great sense of humor. This is what science should be like, Ramachandran thought. He went up after the talk and introduced himself. They had an instant rapport. He mentioned to Gregory an optical experiment he had been pondering, and the professor was intrigued. He invited Ramachandran to visit Bristol and to stay in his home, where they could try out his idea together. Ramachandran took up the offer, and from the moment he saw Gregory’s house he knew he had found his mentor—it was like something out of Sherlock Holmes, full of Victorian instruments, fossils, and skeletons. Gregory was precisely the kind of eccentric Ramachandran could identify with. Soon he was commuting to Bristol regularly experiments. He had found a lifelong mentor to inspire and guide him, and over the years he would come to adapt much of Gregory’s style of speculation and experiment.

后来有一天，布里斯托大学教授理查德·格雷戈里亲自到剑桥做报告。拉马钱德兰听得入迷——他的报告简直就像汉弗莱·戴维笔下的场景。格雷戈里在台上用引人深思的演讲阐述了自己的观点；他既有戏剧天赋，又极富幽默感。拉马钱德兰心想，科学就该如此。报告结束后，他走上前去，做了自我介绍。两人一拍即合。他向格雷戈里提到了自己一直在思考的一个光学实验，教授听后大为光火。他邀请拉马钱德兰到布里斯托尔做客，住在他家，一起验证他的想法。拉马钱德兰接受了邀请，从看到格雷戈里家的那一刻起，他就知道自己找到了导师——就像福尔摩斯笔下的场景一样，到处都是维多利亚时代的仪器、化石和骷髅。格雷戈里正是拉马钱德兰能够感同身受的那种古怪之人。很快，他就开始定期往返布里斯托尔进行实验。他找到了一位终身导师来激励和指导他，多年来，他逐渐适应了格雷戈里的很多思考和实验风格。

Growing up in Japan in the late 1970s, Yoky Matsuoka felt like an outsider. As discussed in chapter 1 ( here ), she liked to do things her own way in a country that esteemed social cohesion and conformity above everything else. When she decided to take up tennis seriously at the age of eleven, she used the players John McEnroe and Andre Agassi as her role models, consummate rebels in what had been a very genteel sport. Later, when she moved to the United States and began attending university, she brought with her the same need to go her own way in whatever she did. If there was a field no one was studying, it excited her. Following this instinct she got into the then-esoteric field of robotics, and was admitted to the PhD program at MIT.

20世纪70年代末，松冈洋基（Yoky Matsuoka）在日本长大，她觉得自己像个局外人。正如第一章（此处）所述，在这个将社会凝聚力和一致性置于一切之上的国家，她喜欢按照自己的方式做事。11岁那年，她决定认真学习网球，并以约翰·麦肯罗和安德烈·阿加西为榜样，他们都是这项曾经非常文雅的运动中彻头彻尾的叛逆者。后来，她移居美国，开始上大学，她也带着同样的渴望，无论做什么都要坚持自己的道路。如果某个领域没人研究，她就会感到兴奋。凭借这种直觉，她进入了当时还很冷门的机器人领域，并被麻省理工学院的博士项目录取。

There, for the first time in her life, she met someone of her own temperament—Rodney Brooks, professor of robotics at MIT, and the bad boy of the department. He was bold, taking on the higher-ups in the department and arguing against some of the most entrenched ideas in the field of artificial intelligence. He had developed a completely novel approach to robotics. It excited her that a professor could get away with such an unconventional attitude. She began to spend as much time around him as possible, soaking up his style of thinking, and turning him into her de facto mentor. He was not a teacher who told you what to do; he let you find your own way, including your own mistakes, but would lend you support when you needed it. This style suited her need for independence. It was only later that she realized how much his ideas had gotten under her skin. Unconsciously following his lead, she would eventually create her own approach to robotics and pioneer a totally new field, known as neurobotics.

在那里，她生平第一次遇到了和她性情相投的人——罗德尼·布鲁克斯，麻省理工学院机器人学教授，系里的“坏小子”。他胆识过人，敢于挑战系里的高层，并批判人工智能领域一些根深蒂固的观念。他发展了一种全新的机器人学方法。一位教授竟然能如此标新立异，这让她兴奋不已。她开始尽可能多地和他相处，吸收他的思维方式，把他变成了自己事实上的导师。他不是那种只会告诉你该做什么的老师；他让你自己去探索道路，包括你自己的错误，但会在你需要的时候给予支持。这种风格很符合她对独立性的渴望。直到后来，她才意识到他的想法深深地触动了她。在不知不觉中，她追随他的脚步，最终创造了自己的机器人学方法，并开创了一个全新的领域——神经机器人学。

The choice of the right mentor is more important than you might imagine. Because so much of her future influence upon you can be deeper than you are consciously aware of, the wrong choice can have a net negative effect upon your journey to mastery. You could end up absorbing conventions and styles that don’t fit you and that will confuse you later on. If she is too domineering, you could end up becoming a lifelong imitation of the mentor, instead of a Master in your own right. People often err in this process when they choose someone who seems the most knowledgeable, has a charming personality, or has the most stature in the field—all superficial reasons. Do not simply choose the first possible mentor who crosses your path. Be prepared to put as much thought into it as possible.

选择合适的导师比你想象的更重要。由于导师对你未来的影响可能远超你的认知，错误的选择可能会对你的成就之路产生负面影响。你可能会吸收一些不适合你的传统和风格，并在日后感到困惑。如果导师过于专横，你可能会终生模仿导师，而不是成为一名真正的大师。人们常常在这个过程中犯错，选择那些看起来知识渊博、个性迷人或在领域内声望最高的人——所有这些都是肤浅的原因。不要轻易选择你遇到的第一个可能的导师。做好充分的准备，尽可能多地思考。

In selecting a mentor, you will want to keep in mind your inclinations and Life’s Task, the future position you envision for yourself. The mentor you choose should be strategically aligned with this. If your path is in a more revolutionary direction, you will want a mentor who is open, progressive, and not domineering. If your ideal aligns more with a style that is somewhat idiosyncratic, you will want a mentor who will make you feel comfortable with this and help you transform your peculiarities into mastery, instead of trying to squelch them. If, like Jung, you are somewhat confused and ambivalent about your direction, it can be useful to choose someone who can help you gain some clarity about what you want, someone important in the field who might not fit perfectly with your tastes. Sometimes part of what a mentor shows us is something we will want to avoid or actively rebel against. In this latter case, you might initially want to maintain a little more emotional distance than normally recommended, particularly if she is the domineering type. Over time you will see what to absorb and what to reject.

在选择导师时，你需要牢记自己的志向和人生目标，也就是你为自己设想的未来位置。你选择的导师应该与你的目标在战略上保持一致。如果你的道路更具革命性，你需要一位开放、进步、而非专横跋扈的导师。如果你的理想更倾向于某种略带个性的风格，你需要一位能让你感到舒适自在，并帮助你将特质转化为精湛技艺，而不是试图压制它们的导师。如果你像荣格一样，对自己的方向感到困惑和矛盾，那么选择一个能够帮助你明确目标的人会很有帮助，这个人在该领域很重要，但可能与你的品味并不完全契合。有时，导师向我们展示的某些东西是我们想要避免或积极反抗的。在后一种情况下，你可能最初需要保持比通常建议更远的情感距离，尤其是当她是专横跋扈的类型时。随着时间的推移，你会明白哪些应该吸收，哪些应该拒绝。

Remember: the Mentor Dynamic replays something of the parental or father-figure dynamic. It is a cliché that you do not get to choose the family you are born into, but you are happily free to choose your mentors. In this case, the right choice can perhaps provide what your parents didn’t give you—support, confidence, direction, space to discover things on your own. Look for mentors who can do that, and beware of falling into the opposite trap—opting for a mentor who resembles one of your parents, including all of his negative traits. You will merely repeat what hampered you in the first place.

记住：导师动态在某种程度上类似于父母或父亲的动态。俗话说，你无法选择自己的出生家庭，但你可以自由地选择你的导师。在这种情况下，正确的选择或许能提供你父母未曾给予的东西——支持、信心、方向以及独立探索的空间。寻找能够做到这一点的导师，并谨防落入相反的陷阱——选择一个与你父母相似（包括其所有负面特质）的导师。你只会重复最初阻碍你前进的那些因素。

# ↩

2. Gaze deep into the mentor’s mirror

2. 凝视导师的镜子

Hakuin Zenji (1685–1769) was born in a village near the town of Hara in Japan, his family on his father’s side coming from an illustrious line of samurai warriors. As a child, Hakuin had the kind of relentless energy that would seem to mark him for a life dedicated to the martial arts. But at around the age of eleven, he heard a priest deliver a sermon about the torments of hell for those who were not careful, and this talk filled the young boy with an intense anguish that nothing could extinguish. All of his tenacious energy was now directed toward doubts about his own worth, and by the age of fourteen he decided that the only way to quell his anxiety was to pursue the religious path and become a priest. He was particularly attracted to Zen Buddhism, having read stories of great Masters in China and Japan overcoming endless obstacles and suffering to reach enlightenment. The idea of passing through a phase of suffering accorded well with his innermost doubts about himself.

白隐禅师（1685-1769）出生于日本原町附近的一个村庄，他父亲的家族出身于一个显赫的武士世家。白隐自幼便拥有一种永不放弃的精力，这似乎预示着他终生致力于武术。然而，大约在十一岁时，他听到一位僧侣布道，讲述那些不谨慎之人将遭受地狱般的折磨，这番话让这个小男孩心中充满了无法平息的强烈痛苦。他所有顽强的精力都转向了对自身价值的怀疑。十四岁时，他决定，平息焦虑的唯一途径就是走上宗教之路，成为一名僧侣。他尤其对禅宗佛教着迷，因为他读过中国和日本的伟大大师们克服重重障碍和苦难，最终获得觉悟的故事。经历苦难的阶段与他内心深处对自我的怀疑不谋而合。

At the age of eighteen he was sent to a training center to prepare him for his life as a priest. The method of teaching, however, disappointed him. He had imagined twenty-four-hour sessions of meditation and other ordeals. Instead, he was made to study all kinds of Chinese and Japanese texts. What he read and heard from his instructors did not change him at all. It was merely intellectual knowledge that had little connection to his daily life. His anxieties only increased. He left this temple and began to wander, looking for the mentor who could guide him.

十八岁时，他被送往一个训练中心，为成为一名僧侣做准备。然而，那里的教学方式令他失望。他原本想象着二十四小时的冥想和其他严酷的考验。结果，他被要求学习各种各样的中文和日文经文。他从导师那里读到的和听到的，丝毫没有改变他。这些仅仅是些与他的日常生活毫无关联的知识。他的焦虑只增不减。他离开了寺庙，开始四处漂泊，寻找能够指引他的导师。

He entered one Zen school after another, in every corner of Japan, and he began to get a clear idea of the state of Zen instruction at that time. It revolved around simple sessions of seated meditation, with little instruction, until finally a giant bell would sound and the monks would hurry to eat or sleep. In their spare time, they would chant for happiness and peace. Zen had turned into one large soporific, designed to lull students into a state of rest and lethargy. It was deemed too invasive and too overbearing to give students any direction; they were supposed to find their own way to enlightenment. Naturally, when given such free rein, they would opt for the easiest path—doing nothing. This trend had spread throughout Japan; monks everywhere had convinced themselves that Zen was easy and simple, and that whatever felt right was right.

他走进日本各地的一所又一所禅宗学校，开始对当时禅宗的教学状态有了清晰的认识。当时的禅宗教学以简单的坐禅为主，几乎没有任何指导，直到最后响起一口大钟，僧侣们便匆匆进食或入睡。闲暇时，他们会诵经祈福，寻求幸福与安宁。禅宗已然沦为一剂催眠剂，旨在使学生进入休息和慵懒的状态。禅宗被认为过于咄咄逼人，无法为学生提供任何指导；他们应该自己寻找通往开悟的道路。自然而然，当学生拥有如此自由的自由时，他们会选择最轻松的路径——无所事事。这种趋势席卷了整个日本；各地的僧侣都坚信禅宗简单易行，只要感觉正确，就是正确的。

Occasionally Hakuin would hear of some school or priest that was creating a stir somewhere, and he would travel to see for himself. In 1708, he spent weeks traveling to reach a temple at a coastal town where just such a provocative priest was making an appearance, but after hearing a few sentences from his lips, Hakuin felt the same profound boredom and disappointment—quotes from texts, clever stories, all to cover up the deadness of the words. He began to wonder if it was time to give up, if true enlightenment no longer existed. At the temple he met another young monk who was equally disappointed with the talk of the priest. They became friends, and one day the monk mentioned that he had studied for a few days under a strange and completely reclusive Master named Shoju Rojin, who was not like any other teacher he had encountered. He lived in a hard-to-reach village, accepted only a handful of students, and was very demanding. This was all Hakuin needed to hear. He asked the young monk to guide him right away to Shoju.

白隐偶尔会听说某个学校或僧侣在某个地方引起了轰动，于是便会亲自前往一探究竟。1708年，他花了数周时间，来到一座沿海小镇的寺庙，那里恰巧出现了一位颇具挑衅意味的僧侣。然而，听到僧侣几句话后，白隐却感到了同样深深的厌倦和失望——那些引经据典、妙趣横生的故事，都是为了掩盖那些枯燥乏味的言辞。他开始怀疑，是否该放弃，真正的开悟是否已不复存在。在寺庙里，他遇到了另一位同样对僧侣的言辞感到失望的年轻僧侣。他们成为了朋友。有一天，僧侣提到，他曾在一位陌生而隐居的大师——昭寿老神——的指导下学习了几天。这位大师与他遇到的其他老师都不一样。他住在一个偏僻的村庄，只收少数学生，而且要求非常严格。这正是白隐想要听到的。他请求这位年轻僧侣立即带他去昭寿。

When he met the Master, he could see something in his eyes that was different from any other priest or teacher. He radiated power and self-mastery; you could read in his expression the pain he had endured to reach his current state. This man had lived and suffered. Hakuin was delighted when Shoju said he would accept him as a pupil, but his excitement soon turned to fear. During their first personal interview, Shoju asked him, “How do you understand the koan (a Zen anecdote designed for instruction) about the Dog and the Buddha-Nature?” “No way to lay a hand or foot on that,” Hakuin replied, imagining that was a clever response, at which point Shoju reached out and grabbed his nose, pushing it with a harsh twist and yelling in his face, “Got a pretty good hand on it there!” He held on tightly for several minutes, giving Hakuin a feeling of utter paralysis.

当他见到师父时，他能从师父的眼神中看出一种不同于其他僧侣或老师的特质。他浑身散发着力量和自制力；从他的表情中，你能读出他为了达到如今的境界所承受的痛苦。这个人经历过苦难，也饱经沧桑。当昭树表示愿意收他为徒时，白隐欣喜若狂，但很快他的兴奋就变成了恐惧。在他们第一次单独会面时，昭树问他：“你如何理解公案（一个旨在教导的禅宗轶事）中关于狗和佛性的部分？”“根本无法触及，”白隐回答道，他自以为这是一个巧妙的回答。就在这时，昭树伸手抓住他的鼻子，用力一拧，对着他的脸大喊：“你抓得真牢！”他紧紧地抓住了好几分钟，让白隐感觉自己完全瘫痪了。

Over the course of the next few days he endured more and more abuse. Shoju made him feel that all of his studies and traveling had taught him nothing. He could not say or do one right thing. Out of nowhere he would receive a blow or a gob of spit in his face. He began to doubt every element of his previous knowledge, and he lived in complete terror of what Shoju would do next.

接下来的几天里，他遭受的辱骂越来越多。翔寿让他觉得，他所有的学习和旅行都没教给他什么。他一句话也说不出来，什么也做不出来。不知怎么的，他会挨一拳，或者被人吐口水。他开始怀疑自己之前所学的一切，并且完全生活在对翔寿接下来会做什么的恐惧之中。

Shoju gave him a series of the most difficult koans Hakuin had ever heard to ponder and discuss. He could not make heads or tails of them. His feelings of dejection and demoralization were reaching a breaking point, but knowing that persistence was important, he kept at it night and day. Soon he had doubts about Shoju himself, and entertained thoughts of leaving him in the near future.

翔树给了他一系列白隐听过的最难的公案，让他思考和讨论。他完全无法理解。他沮丧和失落的情绪已经到了崩溃的边缘，但他知道坚持的重要性，于是夜以继日地坚持着。很快，他就对翔树产生了怀疑，并萌生了不久后离开翔树的想法。

One day, feeling particularly agitated, he wandered into a nearby village, and without knowing why or how, he began to contemplate one of the thorniest koans Shoju had given him. Deep in thought, he strayed into the garden of a private house. The woman who lived there yelled at him to leave, but Hakuin seemed oblivious. Thinking he was a madman or a bandit she attacked him with a stick, knocking him hard to the ground. When he came to, minutes later, he suddenly felt different—he had finally penetrated to the core of Shoju’s koan! He understood it from the inside out! It was alive within him! Everything fell into place and he was certain that he had finally reached enlightenment, the world appearing to him in a totally new guise. He began clapping his hands and screaming with delight. For the first time he felt the weight of all of his anxieties lifted from him.

一天，他心情格外烦躁，便漫步到附近的一个村庄。不知何故，不知何故，他开始思考翔鹤传授给他的最棘手的公案之一。他陷入沉思，误入一户人家的花园。住在那里的女人大声呵斥他离开，但白隐似乎浑然不觉。她以为他是疯子或强盗，便挥起一根棍子袭击他，将他重重地打倒在地。几分钟后，他苏醒过来，突然感觉不同了——他终于洞悉了翔鹤公案的核心！他彻底理解了它！它活生生地存在于他的内心深处！一切都豁然开朗，他确信自己终于开悟了，世界以全新的面貌展现在他面前。他开始拍手，欢呼雀跃。他第一次感到所有的焦虑都消失了。

He ran all the way back to Shoju, who recognized right away what had happened to his pupil. This time the Master was gentle with him, stroking Hakuin’s back with his fan. He finally revealed to his pupil his thoughts—from the first time they had met, he had recognized in Hakuin the necessary ingredients for true learning. He was fierce, determined, and hungry for enlightenment. The problem with all students, he said, is that they inevitably stop somewhere. They hear an idea and they hold on to it until it becomes dead; they want to flatter themselves that they know the truth. But true Zen never stops, never congeals into such truths. That is why everyone must constantly be pushed to the abyss, starting over and feeling their utter worthlessness as a student. Without suffering and doubts, the mind will come to rest on clichés and stay there, until the spirit dies as well. Not even enlightenment is enough. You must continually start over and challenge yourself.

他一路跑回昭树身边，昭树一眼就看出了学生发生了什么事。这次，师父对他很温柔，用扇子轻抚着白隐的背。他终于向学生吐露了自己的想法——从他们第一次见面开始，他就在白隐身上看到了真正学习的必备要素。白隐勇猛、坚定，渴望顿悟。他说，所有学生的问题在于，他们不可避免地会在某个地方止步不前。他们听到一个想法，就紧紧抓住它不放，直到它消亡；他们自以为掌握了真理。但真正的禅宗永不止息，永远不会凝结成这样的真理。这就是为什么每个人都必须不断地被推向深渊，重新开始，感受自己作为学生的无力。没有痛苦和怀疑，思想就会停留在陈词滥调上，直到灵魂也消亡。即使是顿悟也不够。你必须不断地重新开始，挑战自己。

Shoju had faith that Hakuin would continue in this process because he was tenacious. Zen was dying throughout Japan. He wanted Hakuin to stay with him and serve as his successor. He believed the young man would someday be responsible for reviving the religion. In the end, however, Hakuin could not tame his restlessness. After eight months he left Shoju, certain he would return as soon as he could. But the years went by, and once again he fell into new doubts and anxieties. He wandered from temple to temple, experiencing continual highs and lows.

昭树坚信白隐会坚持下去，因为他意志坚定。禅宗在日本各地日渐式微。昭树希望白隐能留下来，成为他的继承者。他相信这位年轻人终有一天会复兴禅宗。然而，白隐最终还是无法抑制自己的躁动。八个月后，他离开了昭树，确信自己会尽快回来。然而，岁月流逝，他再次陷入新的疑虑和焦虑。他辗转于各个寺庙之间，经历着不断的起起伏伏。

At the age of forty-one, he finally had his ultimate and deepest moment of enlightenment, bringing with it a mind-set that would not leave him for the rest of his life. At this point, all of the ideas and teachings of Shoju came back to him as if he had heard them yesterday, and he realized that Shoju was the only true Master he had ever known. He wanted to return to thank him, but the Master had died some five years earlier. His way to repay him was to become a teacher himself, keeping alive his Master’s teachings. In the end, it was indeed Hakuin who rescued Zen practice from the decay it had fallen into, just as Shoju had predicted.

四十一岁时，他终于获得了终极、最深刻的顿悟，并由此获得了终生难忘的境界。此时，昭树的所有理念和教诲仿佛昨日重现，他意识到昭树才是他所认识的唯一真正的大师。他想回去感谢大师，但大师五年前就去世了。他报答大师的方式就是成为一名教师，传承大师的教诲。最终，正如昭树所预言的那样，正是白隐将禅宗从衰败的泥沼中拯救了出来。

To reach mastery requires some toughness and a constant connection to reality. As an apprentice, it can be hard for us to challenge ourselves on our own in the proper way, and to get a clear sense of our own weaknesses. The times that we live in make this even harder. Developing discipline through challenging situations and perhaps suffering along the way are no longer values that are promoted in our culture. People are increasingly reluctant to tell each other the truth about themselves—their weaknesses, their inadequacies, flaws in their work. Even the self-help books designed to set us straight tend to be soft and flattering, telling us what we want to hear—that we are basically good and can get what we want by following a few simple steps. It seems abusive or damaging to people’s self-esteem to offer them stern, realistic criticism, to set them tasks that will make them aware of how far they have to go. In fact, this indulgence and fear of hurting people’s feelings is far more abusive in the long run. It makes it hard for people to gauge where they are or to develop self-discipline. It makes them unsuited for the rigors of the journey to mastery. It weakens people’s will.

要想达到精通，需要一定的韧性和持续的与现实的联系。作为学徒，我们很难以正确的方式挑战自己，也很难清楚地认识到自身的弱点。我们所处的时代让这一切变得更加困难。通过挑战性的处境，甚至一路承受苦难来培养自律，这已不再是我们文化所推崇的价值观。人们越来越不愿意告诉彼此关于自己的真相——他们的弱点、不足之处、工作中的缺陷。即使是那些旨在纠正我们错误的自助书籍，也往往言辞轻描淡写、奉承奉承，只说我们想听到的话——我们本质上是好的，只需遵循几个简单的步骤就能得到我们想要的东西。给予人们严厉而现实的批评，给他们布置任务，让他们意识到自己还有很长的路要走，这似乎是一种虐待，甚至会损害他们的自尊。事实上，这种纵容和害怕伤害他人感情的态度，从长远来看，才是更有害的。它使人们难以判断自身水平，也难以培养自律。它使他们无法适应通往精通的艰辛历程。它削弱了人们的意志。

Masters are those who by nature have suffered to get to where they are. They have experienced endless criticisms of their work, doubts about their progress, setbacks along the way. They know deep in their bones what is required to get to the creative phase and beyond. As mentors, they alone can gauge the extent of our progress, the weaknesses in our character, the ordeals we must go through to advance. In this day and age, you must get the sharpest dose of reality that is possible from your mentor. You must go in search of it and welcome it. If possible, choose a mentor who is known for supplying this form of tough love. If they shy away from giving it, force them to hold up the mirror that will reflect you as you are. Get them to give you the proper challenges that will reveal your strengths and weaknesses and allow you to gain as much feedback as possible, no matter how hard it might be to take. Accustom yourself to criticism. Confidence is important, but if it is not based on a realistic appraisal of who you are, it is mere grandiosity and smugness. Through the realistic feedback of your mentor you will eventually develop a confidence that is much more substantial and worth possessing.

大师们天生就饱经磨难，才走到今天。他们经历过无数次对工作的批评、对进步的质疑，以及一路上的挫折。他们深知如何才能进入创作阶段，甚至更远。作为导师，只有他们才能衡量我们进步的程度、性格中的弱点，以及我们前进道路上必须经历的磨难。在这个时代，你必须从导师那里获得尽可能深刻的现实感。你必须去寻找它，并欣然接受它。如果可能，选择一位以提供这种“严厉的爱”而闻名的导师。如果他们不愿给予，那就让他们像一面镜子，照出真实的你。让他们给你适当的挑战，让你展现自己的优势和劣势，并让你尽可能多地获得反馈，无论这有多么难以接受。让自己习惯于接受批评。自信固然重要，但如果它不建立在对自身现状的现实评估之上，就只是自大和自鸣得意。通过导师的务实反馈，你最终会培养出一种更加充实、更值得拥有的自信。

# ↩

3. Transfigure their ideas

3. 改变他们的想法

In 1943 the eminent pianist and teacher Alberto Guerrero accepted a new pupil, a precocious eleven-year-old named Glenn Gould who was unlike any other student he had ever encountered. Glenn had been playing since he was four years old, having been taught by his mother, who was an accomplished piano player in her own right. After a few years under her tutelage, Glenn had surpassed his mother in skill on many levels; he began to argue and correct her; he wanted more challenging work. Guerrero was well known in Toronto, Canada, where the Goulds lived; he was reputed to be very patient, yet also demanding—traits that could serve him well as a teacher for the young Gould, which is why the parents chose him. From the very first session, Guerrero could sense an unusual seriousness and intensity in someone so young. Gould listened with complete attention and could absorb Guerrero’s style of playing in a way he had never seen in a pupil. He was a consummate mimic.

1943年，著名钢琴家兼教师阿尔贝托·格雷罗（Alberto Guerrero）收了一位新学生，这位早熟的十一岁少年名叫格伦·古尔德（Glenn Gould），与他以往遇到的任何其他学生都截然不同。格伦从四岁起就开始弹奏钢琴，师从他的母亲，她本身就是一位技艺精湛的钢琴演奏家。在她几年的悉心指导下，格伦的技艺在很多方面都超越了母亲；他开始与母亲争论，纠正她；他渴望更具挑战性的工作。格雷罗在古尔德一家居住的加拿大多伦多颇有名气；他以耐心和严谨著称——这些特质非常适合他成为年幼古尔德的老师，因此父母选择了他。从第一节课开始，格雷罗就能感受到如此年轻的古尔德身上散发出一种不同寻常的严肃和专注。古尔德全神贯注地聆听，并以一种他从未在学生身上见过的方式吸收了格雷罗的演奏风格。他是一位完美的模仿者。

Soon, however, Guerrero began to notice some strange traits in his pupil. On one occasion he decided to expand Gould’s repertoire, introducing him to the music of Arnold Schoenberg—the great composer of atonal music whose work Guerrero liked to champion. Expecting his pupil to be excited by the newness of the sound, he was surprised instead to see an expression of complete disgust. Gould took the sheet music home with him, but apparently he never practiced the pieces, and Guerrero let the matter drop. Then, a few weeks later, he shared with his teacher some of his own recent compositions—interesting work that was clearly inspired by Schoenberg. Soon after that, he brought in sheet music that he wanted to practice with Guerrero—all atonal music from various composers, including Schoenberg, but not the pieces Guerrero had originally given him. He had obviously been studying the music on his own and had decided he liked it.

然而，格雷罗很快就注意到他的学生身上出现了一些怪异的特质。有一次，他决定拓展古尔德的曲目，向他推荐阿诺德·勋伯格的音乐——这位伟大的无调性音乐作曲家，格雷罗一直推崇他的作品。他本以为学生会对这种新奇的声音感到兴奋，却意外地看到他脸上露出了极度厌恶的表情。古尔德把乐谱带回家，但显然他从未练习过这些曲子，格雷罗也就此作罢。几周后，他与古尔德分享了他最近创作的一些作品——这些有趣的作品显然受到了勋伯格的启发。不久之后，他又带来了想与格雷罗练习的乐谱——这些乐谱都是来自不同作曲家的无调性音乐，包括勋伯格，但不包括格雷罗最初给他的作品。显然，古尔德一直在自学这些音乐，并且已经认定自己喜欢它们。

It became almost impossible for Guerrero to gauge how Gould would respond to his ideas. For instance, he recommended to his pupils that they learn and memorize a piece by studying it on paper, before ever trying to play it. In this way, it would come alive first in their minds and they would be able to envision it as a whole, instead of merely playing the notes. Gould dutifully followed this advice with a particular composition of Bach’s, but when they discussed the structure and concept behind the piece, the young man had his own notions that were rather strange and quite contrary to Guerrero’s, which Gould found romantic and quaint. On another occasion Guerrero revealed his idea that it was often best to imagine you were playing a piano piece by Bach as if it were on a harpsichord. Gould warmed to this idea, then a few months later said that he preferred imagining a different instrument with Bach.

格雷罗几乎无法预知古尔德会如何回应他的想法。例如，他建议学生们在尝试演奏之前，先在纸上研读并记住一首曲子。这样，乐曲会首先在他们的脑海中活跃起来，他们能够将其作为一个整体来想象，而不仅仅是弹奏音符。古尔德在演奏巴赫的一首作品时忠实地遵循了这一建议，但当他们讨论乐曲背后的结构和概念时，这位年轻人却提出了自己的想法，这些想法相当奇特，与格雷罗的想法截然相反，古尔德觉得这既浪漫又古怪。还有一次，格雷罗透露了他的想法：通常情况下，最好将演奏巴赫的钢琴曲想象成在羽管键琴上演奏。古尔德对这个想法很感兴趣，但几个月后又表示，他更喜欢想象用另一种乐器演奏巴赫。

Guerrero’s most important ideas revolved around the physical aspects of playing the piano. He had spent years studying human physiology, particularly anything related to the hands and fingers. His goal was to impart in his pupils a relaxed yet powerful style, in which they would gain complete command of the keyboard with fingers that had a lightning touch. He spent hours indoctrinating Gould in his approach, working on the peculiar posture he advocated—a kind of slump or hunch over the keyboard, with all of the action coming from the lower back and hands, the shoulders and arms completely still. He demonstrated this technique endlessly to his pupil. He gave Gould all kinds of unusual exercises he had developed to strengthen the fingers. Gould seemed interested enough, but as with everything, Guerrero had the impression he would soon forget it all and go his own way.

格雷罗最重要的理念都围绕着钢琴演奏的生理层面。他多年来一直致力于研究人体生理学，尤其是与手和手指相关的任何领域。他的目标是将一种轻松而有力的演奏风格传授给学生，让他们能够用闪电般的手指完全掌控键盘。他花费大量时间向古尔德灌输他的演奏方法，并练习他所提倡的那种奇特姿势——一种弓着背或俯身演奏键盘的姿势，所有动作都集中在下背部和双手上，肩膀和手臂则保持静止。他不断地向学生演示这种技巧。他还给古尔德练习各种他自己开发的特殊练习，以增强手指的力量。古尔德似乎很感兴趣，但正如对待其他一切一样，格雷罗觉得古尔德很快就会忘记这一切，走自己的路。

As the years went by, Gould began to argue with his teacher more and more. He found Guerrero’s ideas and approach to music too Latin, too mired in another era. Finally, at the age of nineteen, Gould announced that he was going to proceed on his own. He had no more need for a mentor, a fact that Guerrero graciously accepted. It was clear that by now the young man needed to work through his own ideas about music and performing.

随着岁月流逝，古尔德与格雷罗的争论愈演愈烈。他觉得格雷罗的音乐理念和方法过于拉丁化，过于落入另一个时代的泥沼。最终，在十九岁那年，古尔德宣布他要独立发展。他不再需要导师，格雷罗欣然接受了这个事实。显然，现在的年轻人需要探索自己对音乐和表演的理解。

Over the years, however, as Gould slowly established himself as one of the greatest pianists who has ever lived, Guerrero began to realize how deeply his former pupil had absorbed all of his ideas. He would read reviews of Gould’s performances in which the critic would note how he seemed to play Bach as if it were on the harpsichord, something soon echoed by others. His posture, his way of crouching and leaning over the instrument made him look like an uncanny double of the younger Guerrero; his finger work was so unusually powerful, it was clear he had spent years using the exercises Guerrero had taught him. In interviews, Gould would talk about the importance of learning a piece of music on paper before performing it, but he would say it all as if it were his own idea. Strangest of all, Gould played particular pieces of music as Guerrero had always imagined them in his mind, but with a verve and style that he could never have matched. It was as if his former protégé had internalized the essence of his style and transfigured it into something greater.

然而，随着古尔德逐渐成为有史以来最伟大的钢琴家之一，格雷罗开始意识到，这位昔日的学生对他的所有理念都吸收得多么深刻。他读到古尔德演出的评论，评论家们会指出，古尔德演奏巴赫的作品时，仿佛就像在演奏羽管键琴，其他人很快也纷纷效仿。他的演奏姿势，他蹲伏在乐器前，俯身的姿势，让他看起来与年轻时的格雷罗如出一辙；他的指法异常有力，显然他多年来一直致力于格雷罗教给他的练习。在采访中，古尔德会谈到在演奏前在纸上学习乐曲的重要性，但他总是把这些说得像是自己的想法。最奇怪的是，古尔德演奏的某些乐曲，与格雷罗一直以来在脑海中的想象完全一致，但其热情和风格却是他永远无法比拟的。就好像他以前的门生已经内化了他的风格精髓并将其转化为更伟大的东西。

As a child, Glenn Gould intuited his great dilemma.
