He had an uncanny ear for music; he was so responsive that he could pick up the nuances of another piano player and reproduce them after a single hearing. At the same time, he knew that he was a peculiar young man with very distinct tastes. He had the ambition to become a master performer. If he listened too closely to teachers and other performers and picked up their ideas or styles, he would lose his sense of identity in the process. But he also needed knowledge and mentorship. This dilemma became particularly acute with Alberto Guerrero, who was a charismatic teacher. It is often a curse to learn under someone so brilliant and accomplished—your own confidence becomes crushed as you struggle to follow all of their great ideas. Many pianists become lost in the shadow of their illustrious mentors and never amount to anything.

格伦·古尔德孩童时期就意识到自己面临的巨大困境。他拥有一副不可思议的音乐耳朵；他反应灵敏，能够捕捉到其他钢琴演奏家的细微差别，并在一次聆听后将其再现。同时，他也知道自己是个品味独特的年轻人。他渴望成为演奏大师。如果他过于专注于聆听老师和其他演奏家的演奏，并盲目地模仿他们的想法或风格，他就会在这个过程中迷失自我。但他也需要知识和指导。这种困境在魅力非凡的阿尔贝托·格雷罗的指导下尤为突出。在如此才华横溢、成就卓著的老师手下学习往往是一种诅咒——当你努力追随他们所有的伟大理念时，你的自信心就会被摧毁。许多钢琴家最终迷失在他们杰出导师的阴影下，最终一事无成。

Because of his ambition, Gould found his way to the only real solution to this dilemma. He would listen to all of Guerrero’s ideas about music and try them out. In the course of playing, he would subtly alter these ideas to suit his inclinations. This would make him feel that he had his own voice. As the years went by, he made this differentiation between himself and his instructor more pronounced. Because he was so impressionable, over the course of the apprenticeship he had unconsciously internalized all of the important ideas of his mentor, but through his own active engagement he had managed to adapt them to his individuality. In this way, he could learn and yet incubate a creative spirit that would help set him apart from everyone else once he left Guerrero.

古尔德雄心勃勃，最终找到了解决这一困境的唯一途径。他会聆听格雷罗所有关于音乐的想法，并加以实践。在演奏过程中，他会根据自己的喜好巧妙地调整这些想法。这让他感觉自己拥有了属于自己的声音。随着岁月的流逝，他与导师之间的这种差异愈发明显。由于他非常敏感，在学徒期间，他无意识地内化了导师的所有重要思想，但通过自身的积极参与，他成功地将这些思想融入到自己的个性中。通过这种方式，他既能学习，又能培养出一种创造性的精神，这种精神将帮助他在离开格雷罗之后脱颖而出。

As apprentices, we all share in this dilemma. To learn from mentors, we must be open and completely receptive to their ideas. We must fall under their spell. But if we take this too far, we become so marked by their influence that we have no internal space to incubate and develop our own voice, and we spend our lives tied to ideas that are not our own. The solution, as Gould discovered, is subtle: Even as we listen and incorporate the ideas of our mentors, we must slowly cultivate some distance from them. We begin by gently adapting their ideas to our circumstances, altering them to fit our style and inclinations. As we progress we can become bolder, even focusing on faults or weaknesses in some of their ideas. We slowly mold their knowledge into our own shape. As we grow in confidence and contemplate our independence, we can even grow competitive with the mentor we once worshipped. As Leonardo da Vinci said, “Poor is the apprentice who does not surpass his Master.”

作为学徒，我们都面临着同样的困境。要向导师学习，我们必须敞开心扉，完全接受他们的想法。我们必须被他们的魅力所吸引。但如果我们过度沉迷，就会被他们的影响所深深烙印，以至于没有内在空间去孕育和发展自己的声音，最终将一生束缚于非自身的想法。正如古尔德所发现的，解决办法很微妙：即使我们倾听并吸收导师的想法，也必须慢慢与他们保持距离。我们首先要根据自身情况，逐渐调整他们的想法，使其适应我们的风格和倾向。随着我们不断进步，我们可以变得更加大胆，甚至关注他们某些想法中的缺陷或弱点。我们慢慢地将他们的知识融入我们自己的风格。随着我们信心的增长，并开始思考自己的独立性，我们甚至会与曾经崇拜的导师竞争。正如列奥纳多·达·芬奇所说：“不能超越师父的学徒是可怜的。”

# ↩

4. Create a back-and-forth dynamic

4. 创造一种来回的动态

In 1978, a promising lightweight boxer named Freddie Roach traveled to Las Vegas with his father in search of a trainer that could elevate him to the next level. And as previously narrated in chapter 1 (see here ), Freddie and his father quickly settled on Eddie Futch, one of the most legendary boxing coaches in the field.

1978年，一位名叫弗雷迪·罗奇（Freddie Roach）的轻量级拳击手，与父亲一同前往拉斯维加斯，寻找一位能够帮助他更上一层楼的教练。正如第一章（见此处）所述，弗雷迪和父亲很快就选中了埃迪·富奇（Eddie Futch），这位拳击界最具传奇色彩的教练之一。

Futch had a magnificent résumé. As a young man he had sparred with Joe Louis. Barred from turning professional because of a heart murmur, he became a trainer, working later with some of the most illustrious heavyweights, including Joe Frazier. He was a quiet, patient man who knew how to give precise instructions; he was a master at improving a fighter’s technique. Under his guidance, Roach advanced quickly, winning his first ten bouts.

富奇拥有辉煌的履历。年轻时，他曾与乔·路易斯对练。由于心脏杂音，他未能成为职业拳手，于是成为了一名教练，后来与包括乔·弗雷泽在内的多位重量级拳王合作。他为人沉稳，耐心十足，善于精准指导；他是提升拳手技术的大师。在他的指导下，罗奇进步神速，赢得了职业生涯的前十场比赛。

Soon, however, Roach began to notice a problem: in training he listened intently to what Futch had to say, and put it into practice with relative ease. But in actual bouts, the moment he exchanged blows with his opponent, he would suddenly throw out all the technique he had learned and fight on pure emotion. Sometimes this worked, but he took a lot of blows, and his career started to sputter. What surprised him several years into the process was that Futch did not really seem to notice this problem of his. With so many fighters in his stable, he tended to keep his distance; he did not give much personalized attention.

然而，罗奇很快就发现了一个问题：训练时，他专心听福奇的讲解，并相对轻松地将其付诸实践。但在实际比赛中，一旦与对手交手，他就会突然抛开所有习得的技巧，纯粹凭情绪进行搏斗。有时这种方法有效，但他也因此遭受了太多打击，职业生涯也开始走下坡路。令他惊讶的是，几年过去了，福奇似乎并没有真正注意到自己的这个问题。由于他的拳房里有这么多拳手，他倾向于与对手保持距离；他很少给予对手个性化的关注。

Finally, in 1986, Roach retired. Living in Vegas and moving from one bad job to another, in his off-hours he began to frequent the gym where he had trained. Soon he was giving advice to fighters and helping out. Without getting paid, he became a de facto assistant to Futch, even directly training a few of the fighters himself. He knew Futch’s system well and had internalized many of the techniques he taught. He added his own wrinkle to the training sessions. He took the mitt work—the large padded gloves that a trainer uses in the ring to practice various punches and combinations with his fighter—to a higher level, creating a longer and more fluid practice session. It also gave Roach a chance to be more involved in the action, something he missed. After several years he realized he was good at this and so left Futch to begin his own career as a trainer.

最终，在1986年，罗奇退役了。他住在拉斯维加斯，换了一份又一份糟糕的工作，闲暇时开始频繁光顾他曾经训练过的拳馆。很快，他就开始为拳手提供建议并提供帮助。他不拿报酬，实际上成了富奇的助手，甚至亲自训练了几位拳手。他熟知富奇的体系，并将富奇传授的许多技巧内化于心。他为训练课程增添了自己的特色。他将拳击手套（教练在擂台上戴着的大号带衬垫手套，与拳手练习各种拳法和组合拳）提升到了更高的水平，使训练时间更长、更流畅。这也让罗奇有机会更多地参与到比赛中，而这正是他所缺乏的。几年后，他意识到自己在这方面很擅长，于是离开富奇，开始了自己的教练生涯。

To Roach, the sport was changing. Fighters had become faster, but trainers such as Futch still promoted a rather static style of boxing that did not exploit these changes. Slowly, Roach began to experiment with the whole training dynamic. He expanded the mitt work into something larger, a simulation of a fight that could go on for several rounds. This allowed him to get closer to his fighters, to literally feel their full arsenal of punches over time, to see how they moved in the ring. He began to study tapes of opponents, looking for any kind of pattern or weakness in their style. He would devise a strategy around this weakness and go over it with his boxers in the mitt work. Interacting so closely with his fighters, he would develop a different kind of rapport than what he had with Futch—more visceral and connected. But no matter the boxer, these moments of connection would inevitably fade in and out. As they improved, the fighters would begin to tune him out, feeling like they already knew enough. Their egos would get in the way and they would stop learning.

对罗奇来说，这项运动正在发生变化。拳手的速度变得更快，但像富奇这样的教练仍然推崇一种相当静态的拳击风格，无法利用这些变化。慢慢地，罗奇开始尝试整体训练动态。他将拳击手套训练扩展为更大的训练内容，模拟一场可以持续数轮的比赛。这让他能够更接近他的拳手，随着时间的推移，真实地感受他们所有的出拳方式，观察他们在擂台上的移动。他开始研究对手的录像，寻找他们风格中的任何规律或弱点。他会针对这些弱点制定策略，并在拳击手套训练中与他的拳手们一起进行练习。与拳手如此密切的互动，让他与拳手们建立了一种与富奇时期不同的默契——更本能、更紧密的联系。但无论是哪位拳手，这种联系的瞬间都会不可避免地时有时无。随着他们的进步，拳手们开始对他失去兴趣，觉得自己已经掌握了足够多的知识。他们的自尊心会成为阻碍，从而导致他们停止学习。

Then, in 2001, an entirely different kind of fighter came through the doors of Roach’s gym in Hollywood, California. His name was Manny Pacquiao, a 122-pound left-handed featherweight fighter, who had had some success in his native Philippines but was looking for a trainer in the States, someone who could elevate his game to another level. Many trainers had already passed on Pacquiao—they watched him work out and spar, and he was impressive, but there was no money to be made from someone in such a lightweight division.

2001年，一位截然不同的拳手走进了罗奇位于加州好莱坞的拳馆。他的名字叫曼尼·帕奎奥，一位体重122磅的左手羽量级拳手。帕奎奥在自己的祖国菲律宾取得了一些成功，但当时正在美国寻找一位能够将他的水平提升到更高水平的教练。许多教练已经放弃了帕奎奥——他们观察了他的训练和实战，帕奎奥的确令人印象深刻，但在轻量级这样的级别，他根本赚不到钱。

Roach, however, was a different breed of trainer—he immediately went to mitt work with Pacquiao, and from the first punch he knew something was different about this fighter. It had an explosive, intense quality, a snap unlike any another fighter’s. The other trainers had only watched and could not feel what he now felt. After one round Roach was certain he had found the boxer he had always been looking to train, one who could help initiate the new style of boxing he wanted to introduce. Pacquiao was equally impressed.

然而，罗奇是一位与众不同的教练——他立即开始与帕奎奥进行拳击练习，从第一拳开始，他就察觉到这位拳手的与众不同。他的拳法充满爆发力，充满力量，如同其他任何拳手都无法比拟的迅猛。其他教练只是旁观，无法体会他此刻的感受。一回合之后，罗奇确信自己找到了自己一直渴望训练的拳手，一位能够帮助他开创全新拳击风格的拳手。帕奎奥也同样对他印象深刻。

To Roach, Pacquiao had the material to be an unbeatable fighter, but he was somewhat one-dimensional: he had a great left hand and not much else. He was constantly looking for the knockout blow, to the exclusion of everything else. Roach’s goal was to transform Pacquiao into a multi-dimensional beast in the ring. He began with heavy mitt practice, trying to develop a powerful right hand and more fluid footwork. What immediately struck him was the intensity with which Pacquiao focused on his instructions and how quickly he caught on. He was eminently teachable, and so the progress was more rapid than it had ever been with any other fighter. Pacquiao seemed to never tire of training or to worry about overdoing it. Roach kept waiting for the inevitable dynamic in which the fighter would begin to tune him out, but this never came. This was a boxer he could work harder and harder. Soon, Pacquiao had developed a devastating right hand, and his footwork could match the speed of his hands. He began to win fight after fight, in impressive fashion.

在罗奇看来，帕奎奥拥有成为无敌拳手的潜质，但他的拳法略显单一：左手力量强大，其他方面则一无是处。他总是追求致命一击，而忽略了其他一切。罗奇的目标是将帕奎奥打造成拳台上的多面野兽。他从高强度的带拳套训练开始，努力练就一副强有力的右手和更流畅的步法。帕奎奥对他的指示专注投入，并且能够迅速掌握，这让他印象深刻。帕奎奥极易接受训练，因此他的进步速度比任何其他拳手都要快。帕奎奥似乎永远不会厌倦训练，也从不担心训练过度。罗奇一直在等待对手开始对他失去兴趣的必然时机，但这始终没有到来。帕奎奥是一位值得他不断努力训练的拳手。很快，帕奎奥就练就了一副毁灭性的右手，他的步法也与出拳的速度相匹配。他开始以令人印象深刻的方式赢得一场又一场的胜利。

As the years went by, the relationship began to evolve. In their mitt work, Pacquiao would adjust or improve upon the maneuvers Roach had been developing for the next bout. He gave input on Roach’s strategy, altering it on occasion. Pacquiao had gained a sixth sense for what Roach was getting at and could take his thinking further. On one occasion Roach watched Pacquiao improvise a maneuver on the ropes in which he ducked out and attacked a fighter from an angle instead of head-on. To Roach, this was a move that made instant sense. He wanted to develop this further into a whole new possible style of fighting. He was now learning almost as much from Pacquiao. The previous trainer-fighter relationship had now morphed into something interactive and alive. To Roach, this meant that they could move past the seemingly inevitable plateau for fighters in which it all became stale and opponents would catch on to their weaknesses.

随着岁月的流逝，两人的关系开始演变。在拳台练习中，帕奎奥会调整或改进罗奇为下一场比赛所制定的招式。他会为罗奇的策略提供意见，并偶尔进行修改。帕奎奥对罗奇的意图有了第六感，并能进一步思考。有一次，罗奇看到帕奎奥在围绳上即兴表演一个招式：他躲开对手，从某个角度而不是正面攻击对手。对罗奇来说，这个招式一看就懂。他想进一步发展成一种全新的格斗风格。现在，他从帕奎奥身上学到的东西几乎一样多。之前的教练与拳手关系如今已演变成一种互动且充满活力的关系。对罗奇来说，这意味着他们可以跨越拳手之间看似不可避免的瓶颈期，在这个阶段，一切都会变得乏味，对手也会抓住他们的弱点。

Working together in this way, Roach was able to transform this one-dimensional, relatively unknown fighter into perhaps the greatest boxer of his generation.

通过这样的合作，罗奇将这位实力单一、相对不为人知的拳击手打造成了或许是他那一代最伟大的拳击手。

In theory, there should be no limit to what we can learn from mentors who have wide experience. But in practice, this is rarely the case. The reasons are several: at some point the relationship can become flat; it is difficult for us to maintain the same level of attention that we had in the beginning. We might come to resent their authority a little, especially as we gain in skill and the difference between us becomes somewhat less. Also, they come from a different generation, with a different worldview. At a certain point, some of their cherished principles might seem a bit out of touch or irrelevant, and we unconsciously tune them out. The only solution is to evolve a more interactive dynamic with the mentor. If they can adapt to some of your ideas, the relationship becomes more animated. Feeling a growing openness on their part to your input, you are less resentful. You are revealing to them your own experiences and ideas, perhaps loosening them up so their principles don’t harden into dogma.

理论上，我们可以从经验丰富的导师那里学到的东西应该是无限的。但实际上，情况并非如此。原因有很多：在某种程度上，这种关系可能会变得平淡；我们很难像最初那样保持同样的关注度。我们可能会对他们的权威产生一些怨恨，尤其是随着我们技能的提升，我们之间的差异逐渐缩小。此外，他们来自不同的时代，拥有不同的世界观。到了一定时候，他们所珍视的一些原则可能会显得有些脱节或无关紧要，我们会不自觉地忽略它们。唯一的解决办法是与导师建立更互动的动态。如果他们能够适应你的一些想法，你们的关系就会变得更加活跃。当你感受到他们对你的意见越来越开放时，你的怨恨感就会减少。你正在向他们分享你自己的经历和想法，或许可以让他们放松下来，这样他们的原则就不会僵化成教条。

Such a style of interaction is more in tune with our democratic times and can serve as something of an ideal. But it should not go along with a rebellious attitude or a lessening in respect. The dynamic sketched out earlier in this chapter remains the same. Like Pacquiao, you bring to the relationship the utmost in admiration and your total attention. You are completely open to their instruction. Gaining their respect for how teachable you are, they will fall a bit under your spell, as Roach did with Pacquiao. With your intense focus, you improve in your skill levels, giving you the power to introduce more of yourself and your needs. You give them feedback to their instruction, perhaps adjust some of their ideas. This must begin with you, as you set the tone with your hunger to learn. Once a back-and-forth dynamic is sparked, the relationship has almost limitless potential for learning and absorbing power.

这种互动方式更符合我们这个民主时代的潮流，堪称理想之选。但它不应伴随叛逆或尊重的减少。本章前面概述的互动机制保持不变。像帕奎奥一样，你对这段关系倾注了最大的敬佩和全部的关注。你对他们的指导完全敞开心扉。他们会因为你的可教性而对你产生敬意，并逐渐被你迷住，就像罗奇对待帕奎奥一样。你高度集中的注意力会让你的技能水平提升，从而有能力更多地展现自我和需求。你会对他们的指导给出反馈，或许还会调整他们的一些想法。这必须从你开始，因为你渴望学习，以此奠定基调。一旦这种互动机制被激发，这段关系就拥有几乎无限的学习和吸收潜力。

REVERSAL

逆转

It is never wise to purposefully do without the benefits of having a mentor in your life. You will waste valuable time in finding and shaping what you need to know. But sometimes you have no choice. There is simply no one around who can fill the role, and you are left to your own devices. In such a case, you must make a virtue of necessity. That was the path taken by perhaps the greatest historical figure to ever attain mastery alone—Thomas Alva Edison (1847–1931).

故意放弃人生导师的帮助永远是不明智的。你会浪费宝贵的时间来寻找和塑造你需要的知识。但有时你别无选择。周围根本没有人能胜任这个角色，你只能靠自己。在这种情况下，你必须将需要变成一种美德。这或许是历史上最伟大的独自成就大师的人物——托马斯·阿尔瓦·爱迪生（1847-1931）所走的道路。

From a very early age Edison became used to doing things for himself, by necessity. His family was poor, and by the age of twelve he had to earn money to help his parents. He sold newspapers on trains, and traveling around his native Michigan for his job, he developed an ardent curiosity about everything he saw. He wanted to know how things worked—machines, gadgets, anything with moving parts. With no schools or teachers in his life, he turned to books, particularly anything he could find on science. He began to conduct his own experiments in the basement of his family home, and he taught himself how to take apart and fix any kind of watch. At the age of fifteen he apprenticed as a telegraph operator, then spent years traveling across the country plying his trade. He had no chance for a formal education, and nobody crossed his path who could serve as a teacher or mentor. And so in lieu of that, in every city he spent time in, he frequented the public library.

爱迪生从小就习惯于自己动手做事，因为他家境贫寒，十二岁时就不得不自己挣钱补贴家用。他曾在火车上卖报纸，也曾在家乡密歇根州四处奔波，这份工作让他对所见所闻充满了好奇。他想知道事物的运作方式——机器、小工具，任何带有活动部件的东西。由于没有学校或老师，他便开始求助于书籍，尤其是任何他能找到的科学书籍。他开始在自家地下室进行实验，并自学了如何拆卸和修理各种手表。十五岁时，他成为一名电报员学徒，之后花了数年时间在全国各地奔波，从事他的职业。他没有机会接受正规教育，也没有人能成为他的老师或导师。因此，在他所到之处，他都会经常光顾公共图书馆。

One book that crossed his path played a decisive role in his life: Michael Faraday’s two-volume Experimental Researches in Electricity . This book became for Edison what The Improvement of the Mind had been for Faraday. It gave him a systematic approach to science and a program for how to educate himself in the field that now obsessed him—electricity. He could follow the experiments laid out by the great Master of the field and absorb as well his philosophical approach to science. For the rest of his life, Faraday would remain his role model.

一本在他人生中擦肩而过的书对他的人生起到了决定性的作用：迈克尔·法拉第的两卷本《电学实验研究》。这本书之于爱迪生，如同《心智的提升》之于法拉第。它为爱迪生提供了系统的科学方法，并指导他如何在如今令他痴迷的领域——电学——自学成才。他可以跟随这位伟大的电学大师所做的实验，并吸收他哲学式的科学方法。在爱迪生的余生中，法拉第一直是他的榜样。

Through books, experiments, and practical experience at various jobs, Edison gave himself a rigorous education that lasted about ten years, up until the time he became an inventor. What made this successful was his relentless desire to learn through whatever crossed his path, as well as his self-discipline. He had developed the habit of overcoming his lack of an organized education by sheer determination and persistence. He worked harder than anyone else. Because he was a consummate outsider and his mind had not been indoctrinated in any school of thought, he brought a fresh perspective to every problem he tackled. He turned his lack of formal direction into an advantage.

爱迪生通过书籍、实验以及各种工作实践，在成为发明家之前，用大约十年的时间完成了严谨的自我教育。成功的关键在于他那永不放弃的学习欲望，以及他严于律己的自律。他养成了依靠坚定的决心和毅力克服缺乏系统性教育的习惯。他比任何人都更加努力。由于他是一位彻头彻尾的局外人，他的思想从未被任何学派灌输，因此他能够以全新的视角看待每一个问题。他将缺乏正式指导转化为优势。

If you are forced onto this path, you must follow Edison’s example by developing extreme self-reliance. Under these circumstances, you become your own teacher and mentor. You push yourself to learn from every possible source. You read more books than those who have a formal education, developing this into a lifelong habit. As much as possible, you try to apply your knowledge in some form of experiment or practice. You find for yourself second-degree mentors in the form of public figures who can serve as role models. Reading and reflecting on their experiences, you can gain some guidance. You try to make their ideas come to life, internalizing their voice. As someone self-taught, you will maintain a pristine vision, completely distilled through your own experiences—giving you a distinctive power and path to mastery.

如果你被迫走上这条路，你必须效仿爱迪生，培养极度自立的精神。在这种情况下，你会成为自己的老师和导师。你会强迫自己从一切可能的资源中学习。你会比那些受过正规教育的人读更多的书，并将其培养成终身习惯。你会尽可能地将你的知识应用于某种实验或实践。你会为自己找到公众人物作为你的二级导师，他们可以成为你的榜样。阅读并反思他们的经验，你可以获得一些指导。你会努力将他们的想法付诸实践，将他们的声音内化。作为一个自学成才的人，你将保持一种纯粹的视野，这种视野完全源于你自己的经历——这赋予你独特的力量和通往精通的道路。

To learn by example is to submit to authority. You follow your master because you trust his manner of doing things even when you cannot analyze and account in detail for its effectiveness. By watching the master and emulating his efforts…the apprentice unconsciously picks up the rules of the art, including those which are not explicitly known to the master himself.

以身作则就是服从权威。你追随师傅，是因为你信任他的做事方式，即使你无法详细分析和解释其有效性。通过观察师傅并效仿他的努力……学徒会无意识地掌握技艺的规则，包括那些师傅本人并不明确知道的规则。

—M ICHAEL P OLANYI

—迈克尔·波兰尼

# ↩

IV

四

SEE PEOPLE AS THEY ARE: SOCIAL INTELLIGENCE

看清人的本质：社交智力

Often the greatest obstacle to our pursuit of mastery comes from the emotional drain we experience in dealing with the resistance and manipulations of the people around us. If we are not careful, our minds become absorbed in endless political intrigues and battles. The principal problem we face in the social arena is our naïve tendency to project onto people our emotional needs and desires of the moment. We misread their intentions and react in ways that cause confusion or conflict. Social intelligence is the ability to see people in the most realistic light possible. By moving past our usual self-absorption, we can learn to focus deeply on others, reading their behavior in the moment, seeing what motivates them, and discerning any possible manipulative tendencies. Navigating smoothly the social environment, we have more time and energy to focus on learning and acquiring skills. Success attained without this intelligence is not true mastery, and will not last.

我们追求精通的最大障碍往往来自于应对周围人的抵制和操纵时所经历的情感耗竭。一不小心，我们的思绪就会被无休止的政治阴谋和争斗所吞噬。我们在社交领域面临的主要问题是，我们天真地倾向于将自己当下的情感需求和欲望投射到他人身上。我们误读了他们的意图，并做出了导致混乱或冲突的反应。社交智力是一种以最现实的眼光看待他人的能力。通过摆脱惯常的自我中心，我们可以学会深入关注他人，解读他们当下的行为，了解他们的动机，并辨别任何可能的操纵倾向。在社交环境中游刃有余，我们就能拥有更多时间和精力专注于学习和掌握技能。缺乏这种智慧的成功并非真正的精通，也不会持久。

# ↩

THINKING INSIDE

内心思考

In 1718, Benjamin Franklin (1706–90) went to work as an apprentice in his brother James’s printing shop in Boston. His dream was to transform himself into a great writer. At the printing shop he would not only be taught how to handle the machines, but also how to edit manuscripts. Surrounded by books and newspapers, he would have plenty of examples of good writing to study and learn from. It would be the perfect position for him.

1718年，本杰明·富兰克林（1706-1790）到波士顿他哥哥詹姆斯的印刷厂当学徒。他的梦想是成为一名伟大的作家。在印刷厂，他不仅学会了操作机器，还学会了编辑手稿。周围都是书籍和报纸，他可以学习和借鉴许多优秀的作品。这对他来说是一个完美的职位。

As the apprenticeship progressed, the literary education he had imagined for himself came to pass, and his writing skills improved immensely. Then, in 1722, it seemed that he would finally have the perfect opportunity to prove himself as a writer—his brother was about to launch his own large-scale newspaper called The New-England Courant . Benjamin approached James with several interesting ideas for stories he could write, but to his great disappointment, his brother was not interested in his contributing to the new paper. This was a serious venture, and Benjamin’s work was too immature for The Courant.

随着学徒生涯的推进，他梦想中的文学教育逐渐实现，写作技巧也得到了极大的提升。1722年，他似乎终于迎来了证明自己作家身份的绝佳机会——他的哥哥即将创办自己的大型报纸《新英格兰报》。本杰明向詹姆斯提出了几个有趣的故事构思，但令他大失所望的是，哥哥对他为新报投稿并不感兴趣。这是一次严肃的冒险，而本杰明的作品对于《新英格兰报》来说还太过稚嫩。

Benjamin knew it was pointless to argue with James; he was a very stubborn young man. But as he thought about the situation, an idea suddenly came to him: what if he were to create a fictional character who would write letters to The Courant ? If he wrote them well enough, James would never suspect they were from Benjamin, and he would print them. In this way, he would have the last laugh. After much thinking, he decided upon the perfect character to create: a young female widow named Silence Dogood who had lots of strong opinions about life in Boston, many of them rather absurd. To make this believable, Benjamin spent long hours imagining a detailed past for her. He thought so deeply into the character that she began to come alive within him. He could hear her way of thinking, and soon there emerged a very realistic writing voice all her own.

本杰明知道和詹姆斯争论毫无意义；他是个非常固执的年轻人。但当他思考这个问题时，一个想法突然闪过：如果他创造一个虚构的人物，专门给《康涅狄格报》写信，会怎么样？如果他的信写得足够好，詹姆斯就不会怀疑是本杰明写的，他就可以把信发表出来。这样，他就能笑到最后了。经过深思熟虑，他选定了一个完美的人物：一位名叫西伦斯·多古德的年轻寡妇，她对波士顿的生活有很多强烈的看法，其中很多都相当荒谬。为了让这个人物可信，本杰明花了很长时间为她构思一个详细的过去。他对这个人物进行了深入的思考，以至于她开始在他心中鲜活起来。他能听到她的思考方式，很快，她独特的、非常真实的写作风格便浮现出来了。

He sent the first, rather lengthy letter to The Courant and watched with amusement as his brother published it and added a note in the newspaper asking for more letters from her. James probably suspected it was the work of some established writer in town using a pseudonym—the letter was so witty and satirical—but he clearly had no idea it was from Benjamin. James continued publishing the subsequent letters, and they quickly became the most popular part of The Courant .

他给《康涅狄格新闻报》寄出了第一封相当长的信，饶有兴致地看着哥哥刊登了这封信，并在报纸上附上说明，请求她继续写信。詹姆斯可能怀疑这是镇上某位知名作家用笔名写的——这封信妙趣横生、讽刺意味十足——但他显然不知道这是本杰明写的。詹姆斯继续发表后续信件，这些信件很快就成为《康涅狄格新闻报》最受欢迎的部分。

Benjamin’s responsibilities at the shop began to grow, and he proved to be quite an adept editor for the newspaper as well. Feeling proud of all his precocious achievements, one day he could not help himself—he confessed to James that he was the author of the Dogood letters. Expecting some praise for this, he was surprised by James’s vitriolic response—his brother did not like being lied to. To make matters worse, over the next few months he turned increasingly cold and even abusive to Benjamin. It soon became impossible to work for him, and by the fall of 1723, feeling somewhat desperate, Benjamin decided to flee Boston, turning his back on brother and family.

本杰明在书店的责任开始加重，他也证明了自己是一位相当称职的报社编辑。他为自己早熟的成就感到自豪，有一天，他忍不住向詹姆斯坦白，自己就是杜古德信件的作者。他本以为会因此得到一些赞扬，却意外地被詹姆斯尖刻的回应所震惊——他的哥哥不喜欢被欺骗。更糟糕的是，在接下来的几个月里，詹姆斯对本杰明的态度越来越冷淡，甚至辱骂。很快，他便无法再为他工作了。到了1723年秋天，绝望的本杰明决定逃离波士顿，背弃了哥哥和家人。

After several weeks of wandering he ended up in Philadelphia, determined to settle there. He was only seventeen, with virtually no money and no contacts, but for some reason he felt full of hope. In the five years working for his brother he had learned more about the business than men twice his age. He was fiercely disciplined and ambitious. And he was a talented and successful writer to boot. With no more limitations on his freedom, Philadelphia would be his to conquer. Surveying the scene in his first few days there, his confidence only increased. The two printing shops in town at the time were well below the level of anything in Boston, and the writing in the local papers was abysmal. This meant endless opportunities to fill a void and make his way.

经过几周的漂泊，他最终来到了费城，决心在那里定居。他只有十七岁，几乎身无分文，也没有任何人脉，但不知为何，他却充满希望。在为哥哥工作的五年里，他学到的生意比年龄两倍的男人还要多。他严守纪律，雄心勃勃。此外，他还是一位才华横溢、事业有成的作家。自由不再受限制，费城将成为他的天下。在最初几天的考察中，他的信心倍增。当时城里只有两家印刷厂，远不及波士顿，当地报纸的稿件质量更是糟糕透顶。这意味着他有无限的机会填补空缺，闯出一片天地。

Sure enough, within a few weeks he managed to secure a position at one of the two printing shops in town, owned by a man named Samuel Keimer. Philadelphia was still relatively small and provincial at the time—word spread quickly of the newcomer and his literary skills.

果然，几周之内，他就在镇上两家印刷店之一谋得了一份工作。这家店的老板名叫塞缪尔·凯默。当时的费城还比较小，而且偏僻——这位新来者和他的文学才能很快就传开了。

The governor of the colony of Pennsylvania, William Keith, had ambitions of transforming Philadelphia into a cultural center, and was not happy with the two established printing businesses. Hearing of Benjamin Franklin and of his writing talent, he sought him out. Clearly impressed with the young man’s intelligence, he urged him to start his own printing shop, promising to lend him the initial amount that was needed to get the business going. The machines and materials would have to come from London, and Keith advised him to go there personally to supervise the acquisition. He had contacts there and would bankroll it all.

宾夕法尼亚殖民地总督威廉·基思雄心勃勃，想把费城打造成文化中心，他对当时已有的两家印刷厂并不满意。他听说了本杰明·富兰克林及其写作天赋，便主动联系了他。基思显然对这位年轻人的才智印象深刻，鼓励他开办自己的印刷厂，并承诺提供启动资金。机器和材料必须从伦敦运来，基思建议他亲自前往伦敦监督采购事宜。他在那里有关系，可以资助一切。

Franklin could hardly believe his good fortune. Only a few months earlier he was a menial apprentice to his brother. Now, thanks to the generous and enterprising governor, he would soon have his own printing business, and through it he could start a newspaper and become a leading voice in the city, all before he turned twenty. As he made his plans for London, the money Keith had promised as a loan was not forthcoming, but after writing to him a few times, word finally came from the governor’s office not to worry—letters of credit would be waiting for him once he disembarked in England. And so, without explaining to Keimer what he was up to, he quit his job and bought his passage for the transatlantic journey.

富兰克林简直不敢相信自己竟然有如此好运。几个月前，他还只是哥哥的卑微学徒。如今，多亏了这位慷慨大方、富有进取心的州长，他很快就能拥有自己的印刷厂，并借此创办一家报纸，成为这座城市的领军人物，而这一切都发生在他二十岁之前。就在他规划伦敦之行时，基思承诺的贷款迟迟未到，但在给他写了几封信之后，州长办公室终于传来消息，让他不用担心——一旦他抵达英国，信用证就会等着他。于是，他没有向凯默解释自己的计划，就辞去了工作，买了横跨大西洋的船票。

When he got to England there were no letters waiting. Feeling there must have been some kind of miscommunication, he frantically looked in London for a representative of the governor to whom he could explain their agreement. In his search he came upon a wealthy merchant from Philadelphia who, hearing his story, revealed to him the truth—Governor Keith was a notorious talker. He was always promising everything to everyone, trying to impress people with his power. His enthusiasm for a scheme would rarely last more than a week. He had no money to lend, and his character was worth about as much as his promises.

当他抵达英国时，却没有收到任何信件。他觉得肯定是沟通出了问题，于是在伦敦疯狂地寻找总督的代表，以便向他解释他们的协议。在寻找的过程中，他遇到了一位来自费城的富商，富商听了他的故事后，向他吐露了真相——基思总督是个出了名的能说会道的人。他总是对每个人都承诺一切，试图用自己的权力来博取人们的欢心。他对一个计划的热情很少能持续超过一周。他没有钱可以借贷，他的信誉也几乎和他的承诺一样不值钱。

As Franklin took this all in and considered his current predicament, what disturbed him was not that he now found himself in a precarious position—alone and without money, far from home. There was no place more exciting for a young man than London, and he would somehow make his way there. What bothered him was how badly he had misread Keith and how naïve he had been.

富兰克林消化了这一切，思考着自己目前的困境，让他不安的并非他如今的处境岌岌可危——孤身一人，身无分文，远离家乡。对一个年轻人来说，没有比伦敦更令人兴奋的地方了，他总得想办法去那里。真正让他不安的是，他当初对基思的误解有多么严重，以及他当时有多么天真。

Fortunately, London was teeming with large-scale printing shops, and within a few weeks of his arrival he found a position within one of them. To forget about the Keith fiasco he threw himself into the work, quickly impressing his employer with his dexterity with the various machines and with his editing skills. He got along well enough with his colleagues, but soon he encountered a strange British custom: five times a day his fellow printers would take a break to drink a pint of beer. It fortified them for the work, or so they said. Every week Franklin was expected to contribute to the beer fund for those in the room, including himself, but he refused to pay up—he did not like to drink during working hours, and the idea that he should give up a part of his hard-earned wages for others to ruin their health made him angry. He spoke honestly about his principles, and they politely accepted his decision.

幸运的是，伦敦大型印刷厂林立，他抵达伦敦几周后就在其中一家找到了一份工作。为了忘掉基思的惨败，他全身心投入工作，很快便以其熟练的操作和高超的编辑技巧给雇主留下了深刻的印象。他与同事们相处融洽，但很快便遇到了一个奇怪的英国习俗：他的印刷同事们每天五次会休息，喝上一品脱啤酒。他们说，这能让他们更有精神地投入工作。富兰克林每周都要为在场的同事（包括他自己）捐献啤酒基金，但他拒绝了——他不喜欢在工作时间喝酒，想到要放弃自己辛苦挣来的一部分工资去损害他人的健康，他感到愤怒。他坦诚地表达了自己的原则，同事们也礼貌地接受了他的决定。

Over the ensuing weeks, however, strange things began to happen: mistakes kept popping up in texts he had already proofread, and almost every day he noticed some new error for which he was blamed. He started to feel like he was losing his mind. If this continued any longer he would be fired. Clearly, somebody was sabotaging his work, and when he complained to his fellow printers, they attributed it all to a mischievous ghost who was known to haunt the room. Finally figuring out what this meant, he let go of his principles and contributed to the beer fund; the mistakes suddenly disappearing along with the ghost.

然而，接下来的几周里，怪事接踵而至：他已经校对过的文本里不断出现错误，几乎每天都会发现新的错误，并被指责。他开始觉得自己快要疯了。如果这种情况继续下去，他会被解雇的。显然，有人在破坏他的工作。当他向印刷工同事抱怨时，他们却把这一切都归咎于一个以经常出没于此而闻名的恶作剧鬼魂。最终，他明白了这意味着什么，于是放弃了自己的原则，为啤酒基金捐款；那些错误突然和鬼魂一起消失了。

After this incident and several other indiscretions in London, Franklin began to seriously wonder about himself. He seemed hopelessly naïve, constantly misreading the intentions of the people around him. Thinking about this problem, he was struck by an apparent paradox: when it came to his work, he was supremely rational and realistic, always looking to improve himself. With his writing, for instance, he could see his weaknesses clearly and practiced hard to overcome them. But with people it was virtually the opposite: he would inevitably become swept up in his emotions and lose all contact with reality. With his brother, he wanted to impress him by revealing his authorship of the letters, totally unaware of the envy and malevolence he would unleash; with Keith, he was so wrapped up in his dreams that he paid no attention to obvious signs that the governor was all talk; with the printers, his anger blinded him to the fact that they would obviously resent his attempts at reform. What was worse, he seemed incapable of changing this self-absorbed dynamic.

经历了这件事以及在伦敦发生的几起其他失当行为后，富兰克林开始认真审视自己。他似乎无可救药地天真，总是误读周围人的意图。思考这个问题时，他被一个看似矛盾的现象所震撼：在工作方面，他极其理性和现实，总是寻求提升自己。比如在写作方面，他能清楚地认识到自己的弱点，并努力练习以克服它们。但与人相处却几乎截然相反：他不可避免地会陷入情绪的漩涡，完全脱离现实。对他的兄弟，他想通过透露信件的作者身份来给他留下深刻印象，却完全没有意识到自己会引发的嫉妒和怨恨；对基思，他沉浸在自己的幻想中，对州长只是空谈的明显迹象视而不见；对印刷工人，他的愤怒蒙蔽了他，让他看不到他们显然会憎恨他试图改革的事实。更糟糕的是，他似乎无力改变这种以自我为中心的状态。

Determined to break this pattern and change his ways, he decided there was only one solution: in all of his future interactions with people, he would force himself to take an initial step backward and not get emotional. From this more detached position, he would focus completely on the people he was dealing with, cutting off his own insecurities and desires from the equation. Exercising his mind this way every time, it would turn into a habit. In imagining how this would work, he had a strange sensation. It reminded him of the process he went through in creating the Dogood letters—thinking inside the character he had created, entering her world, and making her come alive in his mind. In essence, he would be applying this literary skill to everyday life. Gaining position inside people’s minds, he could see how to melt their resistance or thwart their malevolent plans.

他决心打破这种模式，改变自己的行事方式，并认定只有一个解决方案：在未来所有与人交往中，他要强迫自己先退一步，不要情绪化。从这种更加超然的立场出发，他将完全专注于与他打交道的人，将自身的不安全感和欲望从中剔除。每次都这样锻炼他的思维，它就会成为一种习惯。想象着这将如何运作，他心中涌起一种奇特的感觉。这让他想起创作杜古德信件的过程——在自己创造的角色内部思考，进入她的世界，让她在他的脑海中鲜活地出现。本质上，他将把这种文学技巧运用到日常生活中。深入人们的内心，他就能找到如何化解他们的抵抗，或挫败他们险恶计划的方法。

To make this process foolproof, he decided he would also have to adopt a new philosophy: complete and radical acceptance of human nature. People possess ingrained qualities and characters. Some are frivolous like Keith, or vindictive like his brother, or rigid like the printers. There are people like this everywhere; it has been that way since the dawn of civilization. To get upset or try to alter them is futile—it will only make them bitter and resentful. Better to accept such people as one accepts the thorns on a rose. Better to observe and accumulate knowledge on human nature, as one accumulates knowledge in the sciences. If he could follow this new path in life, he would rid himself of his terrible naïveté and bring some rationality to his social relations.

为了确保这一过程万无一失，他决定也必须采用一种新的理念：彻底彻底地接受人性。人具有根深蒂固的品质和性格。有些人像基思一样轻浮，有些人像他哥哥一样记仇，有些人像印刷工一样刻板。这样的人到处都有；自文明诞生以来就一直如此。生气或试图改变他们是徒劳的——只会让他们充满怨恨和怨恨。最好像接受玫瑰上的刺一样接受这样的人。最好像积累科学知识一样观察和积累人性知识。如果他能走上这条新的人生道路，他就能摆脱可怕的天真，为他的社会关系带来一些理性。

After more than a year and a half of work in London, Franklin finally saved enough money for his return journey to the colonies, and in 1727 he found himself back in Philadelphia, looking once more for work. In the midst of his search, his former employer, Samuel Keimer, surprised him by offering Franklin a nice position in the printing shop—he would be in charge of the staff and training the others Keimer had recently hired as part of his expanding business. For this he would receive a nice yearly salary. Franklin accepted, but almost from the beginning he could sense something was not right. And so, as he had promised himself, he took a step back and calmly reviewed the facts.

在伦敦工作了一年半多之后，富兰克林终于攒够了返回殖民地的旅费。1727年，他回到费城，再次寻找工作。在寻找工作的过程中，他的前雇主塞缪尔·凯默给了富兰克林一个惊喜，他给富兰克林提供了一个印刷厂的好职位——他将负责管理员工，并培训凯默最近为扩张业务而招聘的其他员工。这份工作将为他带来丰厚的年薪。富兰克林接受了这份工作，但几乎从一开始就感觉到有些不对劲。于是，他像自己承诺的那样，退一步冷静地审视现实。

He had five men to train, but once he accomplished this task there would be little work left over for him. Keimer himself had been acting strangely—much friendlier than usual. He was an insecure and prickly gentleman, and this friendly front did not fit him. Imagining the situation from Keimer’s perspective, he could sense that he must have greatly resented Franklin’s sudden departure for London, leaving him in the lurch. He must have seen Franklin as a young whippersnapper who needed his comeuppance. He was not the type to discuss this with anyone, but would seethe from within and scheme on his own. Thinking in this way, Keimer’s intentions became clear to him: he was planning to get Franklin to impart his extensive knowledge of the business to the new employees, then fire him. This would be his revenge.

他有五个人要培训，但一旦完成这项任务，剩下的工作就不多了。凯默本人最近表现得很奇怪——比平时友好得多。他是个缺乏安全感、脾气暴躁的绅士，这种友好的姿态与他格格不入。站在凯默的角度想象一下当时的情形，他能感觉到，凯默一定对富兰克林突然离开伦敦、让自己陷入困境感到非常不满。他肯定把富兰克林看作一个需要得到应有惩罚的毛头小子。富兰克林不是那种会和任何人讨论这件事的人，他会内心愤怒，独自谋划。这样想着，凯默的意图就清晰起来：他打算让富兰克林把自己丰富的业务知识传授给新员工，然后解雇他。这将是他的报复。

Certain he had read this correctly, he decided to quietly turn the tables. He used his new managerial position to build relationships with customers and to connect with successful merchants in the area. He experimented with some new manufacturing methods he had learned in England. When Keimer was away from the shop, he taught himself new skills such as engraving and ink-making. He paid close attention to his pupils, and carefully cultivated one of them to be a first-rate assistant. And just when he suspected that Keimer was about to fire him, he left and set up his own shop—with financial backing, greater knowledge of the business, a solid base of customers who would follow him everywhere, and a first-rate assistant whom he had trained. In executing this strategy, Franklin noticed how free he was from any feelings of bitterness or anger toward Keimer. It was all maneuvers on a chessboard, and by thinking inside Keimer he was able to play the game to perfection, with a clear and level head.

他确信自己理解得没错，于是决定悄悄扭转局面。他利用新的管理职位与客户建立关系，并与当地一些成功的商人建立联系。他尝试了一些在英国学到的新制造方法。凯默不在店里的时候，他自学了雕刻和制墨等新技能。他密切关注学生，并精心培养其中一名成为一流的助手。就在他怀疑凯默即将解雇他时，他离开并开设了自己的店铺——有了资金支持、更深入的业务知识、坚实的客户基础（这些客户会追随他到任何地方），以及一位他亲自培养的一流助手。在执行这一策略的过程中，富兰克林注意到自己对凯默没有任何怨恨或愤怒的情绪。一切都像棋盘上的棋步，通过与凯默的内心沟通，他能够以清晰而冷静的头脑将棋局进行得完美无缺。

Over the ensuing years, Franklin’s printing business prospered. He became a highly successful newspaper publisher, a best-selling writer, a scientist renowned for his experiments with electricity, and an inventor of such things as the Franklin stove (and later in his life that of the lightning rod, bifocal glasses, and so on). As an increasingly prominent member of the Philadelphia community, in 1736 he decided it was time to take his career further and enter politics, becoming a delegate to Pennsylvania’s colonial legislature. Within a few months he was chosen unanimously by fellow members to serve as the clerk to the legislature, a position of some influence. But when it was time to renew the appointment, a new member of the legislature, Isaac Norris, suddenly voiced his vehement opposition, supporting another candidate. After much heated debate Franklin won the vote, but in contemplating the situation, he saw danger on the horizon.

在接下来的几年里，富兰克林的印刷业蒸蒸日上。他成为了一位非常成功的报纸出版商、一位畅销书作家、一位以电学实验闻名的科学家，以及富兰克林炉（后来又发明了避雷针、双光眼镜等等）等物品的发明者。随着他在费城社区日益显赫的地位，1736年，他决定进一步发展事业，投身政界，成为宾夕法尼亚州殖民地立法机构的代表。几个月后，他被其他成员一致推选为立法机构书记员，这是一个颇具影响力的职位。然而，就在续任之际，一位新当选的立法机构成员艾萨克·诺里斯突然强烈反对，支持另一位候选人。经过一番激烈的辩论，富兰克林最终赢得了选举，但深思熟虑后，他意识到危机即将来临。

Norris was a wealthy, well-educated, and charismatic businessman. He was also ambitious and certain to rise within the ranks. If Franklin became antagonistic toward him, as would be expected after what had happened with the battle over the clerk position, he would confirm any unpleasant notions Norris had entertained of him and convert him into an implacable foe. On the other hand, if he ignored him, Norris might read this as an example of Franklin’s haughtiness and hate him all the more. To some it might seem to be the strong and manly thing to go on the attack and fight back, proving he was not someone to mess with. But would it not be infinitely more powerful to work against Norris’s expectations and subtly convert him into an implacable ally?

诺里斯是一位富有、受过良好教育且魅力十足的商人。他雄心勃勃，势必会步步高升。如果富兰克林像在争夺职员职位之后预料的那样对他表现出敌意，他就会印证诺里斯对他的任何负面看法，并将他变成一个不共戴天的敌人。另一方面，如果他置之不理，诺里斯可能会认为这是富兰克林傲慢自大的表现，从而更加憎恨他。对某些人来说，主动出击并反击，证明自己不是好惹的，似乎是强势且有男子气概的做法。但反过来说，如果能与诺里斯的期望背道而驰，巧妙地将他转变为一个不共戴天的盟友，岂不是更有力？

And so Franklin went to work. He observed the man closely in the legislature, gathered information from insiders, and thought himself deeply into Norris’s mind. He came to the conclusion that Norris was a proud and somewhat emotional young man who harbored a few insecurities as well. He seemed impatient for attention, for being liked and admired by others; perhaps he envied Franklin’s popularity and achievements. Through his insiders, he learned that Norris had one rather odd obsession—an extensive personal library containing many rare books, including one that was particularly rare and that he prized above all others. These books seemed to represent to him his own feelings of distinction and nobility.

于是富兰克林开始行动。他在立法机构密切观察诺里斯，从内部人士那里收集信息，并深入地了解他的内心世界。他得出结论：诺里斯是一个骄傲且略带情绪化的年轻人，同时也有一些不安全感。他似乎渴望得到关注，渴望被他人喜欢和钦佩；或许他嫉妒富兰克林的声望和成就。通过内部人士，他了解到诺里斯有一个相当奇怪的癖好——一个庞大的私人图书馆，里面藏有许多珍本书籍，其中一本尤为稀有，是他最珍爱的。这些书似乎代表着他自身的尊贵和高贵。

Knowing all of this, Franklin decided upon the following course of action: he wrote to Norris a very polite note, expressing admiration for his collection. He was an avid book lover himself, and hearing so much about that one rare book in Norris’s collection, he would be excited beyond belief if he could somehow peruse it at his leisure. If Norris would lend it to him for a few days, he would take great care of it and return it promptly.

了解了这一切后，富兰克林决定采取以下行动：他给诺里斯写了一封非常礼貌的信，表达了对诺里斯藏书的钦佩。他本人也是一位狂热的书籍爱好者，听说诺里斯藏书中那本稀有书籍的传闻甚多，如果能在闲暇时翻阅一番，他会兴奋不已。如果诺里斯愿意把书借给他几天，他会好好保管，并尽快归还。

Clearly pleased by this attention, Norris sent the book over right away and Franklin returned it as promised, with another note expressing his gratitude for the favor. At the next meeting of the legislature, Norris came up to Franklin and engaged him in friendly conversation, something he had never done before. As he had predicted, he had created doubt in Norris’s mind. Instead of his suspicions being confirmed about Franklin, he was confronted with the fact that the man behaved as a true gentleman, shared his interest in rare books, and kept to his word. How could he continue to harbor bad feelings without wondering about himself and why he had sent the book? Playing on Norris’s emotional nature, Franklin shifted his feelings from antagonism to warmth. They became close friends and then staunch political allies to the end of their careers. (Franklin would go on to practice similar magic on many of his future political foes.)

诺里斯显然对这份关怀感到欣慰，立即将书送了过去。富兰克林也如约归还了书，并附上另一张纸条表达谢意。在下一次立法会议上，诺里斯来到富兰克林面前，友好地交谈，这是他以前从未做过的事。正如他所料，他让诺里斯心生疑虑。然而，诺里斯对富兰克林的怀疑非但没有得到证实，反而被摆到一旁：富兰克林举止得体，和他一样对珍本书籍感兴趣，而且信守承诺。他怎么能继续心怀怨恨，而不去反思自己，也不去想自己为什么要送书呢？富兰克林利用诺里斯情绪化的天性，将诺里斯的敌意转化为温暖。他们成为了亲密的朋友，并成为坚定的政治盟友，直至他们职业生涯的尽头。（富兰克林后来也对他未来的许多政敌施展了类似的魔法。）

In Philadelphia, Benjamin Franklin was thought of as the quintessence of the trustworthy merchant and citizen. Like his fellow townsfolk, he dressed plainly; he worked harder than anyone they knew; he never frequented bars or gambling houses; and he had a folksy and even humble manner. His popularity was almost universal. But in the last public chapter of his life, he acted in a way that seemed to indicate that he had changed and lost his common touch.

在费城，本杰明·富兰克林被认为是值得信赖的商人和公民的典范。和他的同乡一样，他衣着朴素；他比他们认识的任何人都努力工作；他从不经常光顾酒吧或赌场；他举止平易近人，甚至可以说是谦逊。他几乎人人都爱戴。然而，在他人生的最后公开篇章中，他的行为举止似乎表明他已经改变了，失去了他那份平易近人的气质。

In 1776, a year after the outbreak of the War of Independence, Benjamin Franklin—now a distinguished political figure—was dispatched to France as a special commissioner to obtain arms, financing and an alliance. Soon stories spread throughout the colonies of his various intrigues with French women and courtesans, and of his attendance at lavish parties and dinners—much of which was true. Prominent politicians such as John Adams accused him of becoming corrupted by the Parisians. His popularity among Americans plummeted. But what the critics and public did not realize was that wherever he went he assumed the look, the outward morals, and the behavior of the culture at hand, so that he could better make his way. Desperate to win the French over to the American cause and understanding their nature quite well, he had transformed himself into what they had wanted to see in him—the American version of the French spirit and way of life. He was appealing to their notorious narcissism.

1776年，独立战争爆发一年后，本杰明·富兰克林——如今已是杰出的政治人物——被派往法国担任特别专员，以获取武器、资金和联盟。很快，他与法国女性和交际花的各种勾结，以及他出席奢华派对和晚宴的传闻便传遍了整个殖民地——其中很多都是真的。约翰·亚当斯等著名政治家指责他被巴黎人腐蚀。他在美国人心目中的声望一落千丈。但批评家和公众没有意识到的是，无论走到哪里，他都会伪装成当地文化的外貌、外在道德和行为举止，以便更好地为自己谋利。他渴望赢得法国人的支持，并且深谙他们的本性，于是将自己打造成他们希望看到的那种人——美国版的法国精神和生活方式。他正在迎合法国人臭名昭著的自恋心理。

All of this worked to perfection—Franklin became a beloved figure to the French, and a man of influence with their government. In the end, he brokered an important military alliance and gained the kind of financing nobody else could have wrested from the stingy French king. This final public act in his life was not an aberration, but the ultimate application of his social rationality.

这一切完美地实现了——富兰克林成为法国人敬爱的人物，并在法国政府中拥有影响力。最终，他促成了一场重要的军事联盟，并获得了其他人无法从吝啬的法国国王手中夺取的资金。他人生中最后的公开举动并非偶然，而是他社会理性的终极体现。

KEYS TO MASTERY

掌握诀窍

You must allow everyone the right to exist in accordance with the character he has, whatever it turns out to be: and all you should strive to do is to make use of this character in such a way as its kind of nature permits, rather than to hope for any alteration in it, or to condemn it offhand for what it is. This is the true sense of the maxim—Live and let live…. To become indignant at [people’s] conduct is as foolish as to be angry with a stone because it rolls into your path. And with many people the wisest thing you can do, is to resolve to make use of those whom you cannot alter.

你必须赋予每个人根据其性格生存的权利，无论其性格如何：你唯一应该努力做的，就是以其本性所允许的方式去利用这种性格，而不是指望它有任何改变，或随意地谴责它的本质。这才是“自己活，也让别人活”这句格言的真谛……对他人的行为感到愤慨，就像因为一块石头滚到你面前而生气一样愚蠢。对许多人来说，你能做的最明智的事情，就是下定决心去利用那些你无法改变的人。

—A RTHUR S CHOPENHAUER

—亚瑟·叔本华

We humans are the preeminent social animal. Hundreds of thousands of years ago, our primitive ancestors developed complex social groupings. To adapt to this, they evolved mirror neurons (see introduction, here ), which were more refined and sensitive than those of other primates. This meant that they could use these mirror neurons not only to imitate those around them, but also to imagine what others might be thinking and feeling, all on a preverbal level. Such empathy allowed for a higher degree of cooperation.

我们人类是卓越的社会动物。数十万年前，我们的原始祖先发展出了复杂的社会群体。为了适应这种变化，他们进化出了镜像神经元（参见此处的引言），这种神经元比其他灵长类动物的神经元更加精细和敏感。这意味着他们不仅可以利用这些镜像神经元来模仿周围的人，还可以想象他人的想法和感受，所有这些都是在语言能力之前的层面上进行的。这种同理心使得更高程度的合作成为可能。

With the invention of language and the reasoning powers it brought them, our ancestors could take this empathic ability further—seeing patterns in people’s behavior and deducing their motivations. Over the years, these reasoning skills have become infinitely more powerful and refined. In theory, all of us today possess the natural tools—empathy, rational thinking—to have a supreme understanding of our fellow humans. In practice, however, these tools remain mostly undeveloped, and the explanation for this can be found in the peculiar nature of our childhood, and our extended period of dependency.

随着语言的发明及其赋予我们的推理能力，我们的祖先得以进一步发展这种共情能力——洞察他人行为模式并推断其动机。多年来，这些推理能力已变得无比强大和精妙。理论上，如今我们所有人都拥有与生俱来的工具——共情、理性思考——来对人类同胞进行至高无上的理解。然而，在实践中，这些工具大多仍未得到充分开发，其原因可以归咎于我们童年时期的特殊性以及我们长期的依赖性。

Compared to other animals, we humans enter the world remarkably weak and helpless. We remain relatively weak for many years before we can truly operate on our own. This extended period of immaturity, lasting some twelve to eighteen years, serves a valuable function: it gives us a chance to focus on developing our brain—by far the most important weapon in the human arsenal. But this prolonged childhood comes with a price. During this time of weakness and dependency, we experience the need to idealize our parents. Our survival depends on their strength and reliability. To think of them as having their own frailties would fill us with unbearable anxiety. And so we inevitably see them as stronger, more capable, and more selfless than they are in reality. We come to view their actions through the lens of our needs, and so they become extensions of ourselves.

与其他动物相比，我们人类来到这个世界时显得格外虚弱无助。在真正能够独立自主之前，我们会在很多年里保持相对虚弱的状态。这段长达十二到十八年的不成熟期，有着宝贵的功能：它让我们有机会专注于开发大脑——迄今为止人类武器库中最重要的武器。但这段延长的童年是有代价的。在这段虚弱和依赖的时期，我们体验到将父母理想化的需要。我们的生存依赖于他们的力量和可靠性。认为他们也有自己的弱点，会让我们充满难以忍受的焦虑。因此，我们不可避免地会把他们看得比现实中更强大、更有能力、更无私。我们开始用自身需求的视角来看待他们的行为，于是他们就成了我们自身的延伸。

During this long period of immaturity, we often transfer these idealizations and distortions to teachers and friends, projecting onto them what we want and need to see. Our view of people becomes saturated with various emotions—worship, admiration, love, need, anger. Then inevitably, often in adolescence, we start to glimpse a less-than-noble side to many people, including our parents, and we cannot help but feel upset at the disparity between what we had imagined and the reality. In our disappointment, we tend to exaggerate their negative qualities, much as we once had exaggerated the positive ones. If we had been forced earlier on in life to make it on our own, practical needs would have come to dominate our thinking, and we would have become more detached and realistic. But as it is, the many years of viewing people through the lens of our emotional needs turns into a habit that we can hardly control.

在漫长的不成熟时期，我们常常将这些理想化和扭曲的自我形象转移到老师和朋友身上，将我们想要和需要看到的投射到他们身上。我们对人的看法充斥着各种情绪——崇拜、钦佩、爱、需要、愤怒。然后，不可避免地，通常是在青春期，我们开始瞥见许多人，包括父母身上不那么高尚的一面，我们禁不住为想象与现实之间的差距而感到沮丧。失望之余，我们往往会夸大他们的负面品质，就像我们曾经夸大他们的优点一样。如果我们早年被迫独立生活，实际需求就会主导我们的思维，我们也会变得更加超然和现实。但事实上，多年来用情感需求的眼光看待他人，已经变成了一种我们难以控制的习惯。

Let us call this the Naïve Perspective . Although it is natural to have such a perspective because of the unique character of our childhood, it is also dangerous because it envelops us in childish illusions about people, distorting our view of them. We carry this perspective with us into the adult world, into the Apprenticeship Phase. In the work environment the stakes are suddenly raised. People are no longer struggling for good grades or social approval, but for survival. Under such pressure, they reveal qualities of their characters that they normally try to conceal. They manipulate, compete, and think of themselves first. We are blindsided by this behavior and our emotions are churned up even more than before, locking us into the Naïve Perspective.

我们姑且称之为“幼稚视角”。虽然由于童年时期的独特性，拥有这种视角很自然，但它也很危险，因为它会让我们陷入对他人幼稚的幻想，扭曲我们对他人的看法。我们会带着这种视角进入成人世界，进入学徒阶段。在职场中，风险突然升高。人们不再为好成绩或社会认可而奋斗，而是为生存而奋斗。在这样的压力下，他们会暴露出平时试图隐藏的性格特质。他们会操纵他人、竞争，并且首先考虑自己。我们被这种行为蒙蔽了双眼，情绪比以往更加激动，最终被困在了“幼稚视角”中。

The Naïve Perspective makes us feel sensitive and vulnerable. Looking inward as to how the words and actions of others implicate us in some way, we continually misread their intentions. We project our own feelings onto them. We have no real sense of what they are thinking or what motivates them. With colleagues in the work environment, we fail to see the source of their envy or the reason for their manipulations; our attempts at influencing them are based on the assumptions that they want the same things as ourselves. With mentors and bosses, we project onto them our childhood fantasies, becoming unnecessarily adoring or fearful of authority figures and creating stormy and brittle relationships in the process. We think we understand people, but we are viewing them through a distorted lens. In this state, all of our empathic powers are rendered useless.

朴素视角让我们感到敏感脆弱。我们总是内省地看待他人的言行举止，试图从中窥探自身，却总是误读他们的意图。我们将自己的感受投射到他们身上，无法真正理解他们的想法和动机。在工作中与同事相处时，我们无法理解他们嫉妒的根源，也无法理解他们操控他人的动机；我们试图影响他们，只是基于这样的假设：他们和我们想要的是一样的。在与导师和老板相处时，我们把自己童年的幻想投射到他们身上，对权威人物产生不必要的崇拜或恐惧，并在此过程中制造出紧张而脆弱的关系。我们自以为理解他人，但却带着扭曲的眼光看待他们。在这种状态下，我们所有的共情能力都变得毫无用处。

With the inevitable mistakes we make, we become entangled in battles and dramas that consume our minds and distract us from learning. Our sense of priorities becomes warped—we end up giving far too much importance to social and political issues because we are not handling them well. If we are not careful, we carry these patterns over to the next phase in life, the Creative-Active Phase, in which we are in a more public position. At this level, being socially inept can prove particularly embarrassing, even fatal to our careers. People who retain their childish attitudes will rarely be able to hold on to the success they may achieve through their talent.

我们难免会犯错，陷入纷争和闹剧，这些纷争和闹剧吞噬着我们的思绪，分散了我们学习的注意力。我们的轻重缓急变得扭曲——最终，我们过于重视社会和政治问题，因为我们没有妥善处理这些问题。如果我们不小心，这些模式就会延续到人生的下一个阶段，即创造性活跃阶段，届时我们将处于更加公众的视野中。在这个阶段，社交能力的匮乏会让我们格外尴尬，甚至会对我们的职业生涯造成致命打击。那些仍然保持幼稚心态的人，很少能够保持他们凭借天赋可能获得的成功。

Social intelligence is nothing more than the process of discarding the Naïve Perspective and approaching something more realistic. It involves focusing our attention outward instead of inward, honing the observational and empathic skills that we naturally possess. It means moving past our tendency to idealize and demonize people, and seeing and accepting them as they are. It is a way of thinking that must be cultivated as early as possible, during the Apprenticeship Phase. But before we can begin to acquire this intelligence we must first come to grips with the Naïve Perspective itself.

社交智力无非就是摒弃朴素视角，趋向更现实的事物的过程。它要求我们将注意力转向外部而非内部，磨练我们与生俱来的观察力和共情能力。这意味着我们要克服理想化和妖魔化他人的倾向，以真实的视角看待和接受他们。这种思维方式必须在学徒阶段尽早培养。但在我们开始获得这种智慧之前，我们必须首先认真对待朴素视角本身。

Look at the case of Benjamin Franklin, the icon of social intelligence and the clearest example of the role it plays in mastery. As the second youngest of a large extended family, he learned to get his way through charm. As he got older he came to believe, as many young people do, that getting along with others is a function of behaving charmingly and winning them over with a friendly manner. But as he engaged with the real world, he began to see his charm as the actual source of his problem. Being charming was a strategy he had developed out of childish need; it was a reflection of his narcissism, of the love he had of his own words and wit. It had no relation to other people and their needs. It did not prevent them from exploiting or attacking him. To be truly charming and socially effective you have to understand people, and to understand them you have to get outside yourself and immerse your mind in their world.

以本杰明·富兰克林为例，他是社交智力的典范，也是社交智力在成就卓越中所起作用的最清晰例证。作为大家族中的老二，他学会了如何通过魅力来获得成功。随着年龄的增长，他和许多年轻人一样，开始相信与人相处的关键在于展现魅力，用友好的方式赢得他人的支持。但随着他逐渐融入现实世界，他开始将魅力视为问题的真正根源。展现魅力是他出于幼稚需求而发展起来的一种策略；它反映了他的自恋，反映了他对自身言语和智慧的热爱。这与他人及其需求无关。它并不能阻止他人利用或攻击他。要想真正拥有魅力并在社交上取得成功，你必须理解他人；而要理解他人，你必须跳出自我，将你的思想融入他们的世界。

Only when he realized how deeply naïve he had been could he take the necessary steps to move past this naïveté. His focus on gaining social intelligence was the turning point of his career—it transformed him into the preeminent observer of human nature, a man with a magical ability to see into people. It also made him the perfect social companion—men and women everywhere fell under his spell because of his ability to attune himself to their energies. With tranquil and productive social relations, he could focus more of his time and attention to writing, to questions of science, to his endless inventions—to mastery.

只有当他意识到自己曾经多么天真时，他才得以采取必要的措施摆脱这种天真。他对社交智力的专注成就了他职业生涯的转折点——这使他成为杰出的人性观察者，拥有洞察人性的神奇能力。这也使他成为完美的社交伴侣——世界各地的男男女女都为他倾倒，因为他能够与他人的能量和谐共处。凭借宁静而富有成效的社交关系，他可以将更多的时间和精力投入到写作、科学研究以及他无尽的发明创造中——最终成就一番事业。

It might be deduced from Benjamin Franklin’s story that social intelligence requires a detached, emotionless approach to people, making life rather dull in the process, but this is hardly the case. Franklin himself was by nature a very emotional man. He did not repress this nature, but rather turned his emotions in the opposite direction. Instead of obsessing over himself and what other people were not giving him, he thought deeply of how they were experiencing the world, what they were feeling and missing. Emotions seen inside other people create empathy and bring a deep understanding of what makes them tick. For Franklin, this outward focus gave him a pleasant feeling of lightness and ease; his life was hardly dull, but simply free of unnecessary battles.

从本杰明·富兰克林的故事中，我们或许可以推断，社交智力要求以超然、冷漠的态度对待他人，这会让生活变得相当乏味，但事实并非如此。富兰克林天生就是一个非常情绪化的人。他没有压抑这种天性，而是将情绪转向了相反的方向。他没有沉迷于自己和别人没有给予他的东西，而是深入思考他们是如何体验这个世界的，他们有何感受和缺失。看到他人内心的情绪会产生同理心，并能深刻理解他们的动力。对富兰克林来说，这种外在的关注让他感到轻松自在；他的生活并非乏味，只是没有了不必要的争吵。

Understand: you will continue to have problems in attaining social intelligence until you come to the realization that your view of people is dominated by the Naïve Perspective. Following Franklin’s example, you can reach this awareness by reviewing your past, paying particular attention to any battles, mistakes, tensions, or disappointments on the social front. If you look at these events through the lens of the Naïve Perspective, you will focus only on what other people have done to you—the mistreatments you endured from them, the slights or injuries you felt. Instead, you must turn this around and begin with yourself—how you saw in others qualities they did not possess, or how you ignored signs of a dark side to their nature. In doing this, you will be able to clearly see the discrepancy between your illusions about who they are and the reality, and the role you played in creating this discrepancy. If you look closely enough, you can often perceive in your relationships with bosses or superiors reenactments of the childhood family dynamic—the idealizing or demonizing that has become habitual.

要知道：除非你意识到自己对人的看法被“天真视角”所主导，否则你在提升社交智力方面会一直遇到困难。效仿富兰克林的例子，你可以通过回顾过去，特别关注社交方面发生的任何争执、错误、紧张或失望来获得这种认识。如果你用“天真视角”的眼光看待这些事件，你只会关注别人对你做了什么——你遭受的虐待，你感受到的轻视或伤害。相反，你必须扭转局面，从自身入手——你是如何看待别人身上他们所不具备的品质，或者你是如何忽视他们性格中阴暗面的迹象。这样做，你就能清楚地看到你对他们的幻想与现实之间的差异，以及你在造成这种差异中所扮演的角色。如果你仔细观察，你常常会在与老板或上司的关系中发现童年家庭关系的重演——理想化或妖魔化已经成为习惯。

By making yourself aware of the distorting process of the Naïve Perspective, you will naturally grow less comfortable with it. You will realize that you are operating in the dark, blind to people’s motivations and intentions, vulnerable to the same mistakes and patterns that occurred in the past. You will feel your lack of real connection to other people. The desire will naturally arise from within to change this dynamic—to start looking outward instead of focusing only on your own feelings, to observe before you react.

通过意识到“天真视角”的扭曲过程，你自然会感到越来越不舒服。你会意识到自己在黑暗中行动，对他人动机和意图视而不见，容易犯下过去同样的错误和模式。你会感到自己与他人缺乏真正的联系。改变这种状态的渴望会自然而然地从内心升起——开始向外看，而不是只关注自己的感受，先观察再做出反应。

This new clarity about your perspective should be accompanied by an adjustment of your attitude. You must avoid the temptation to become cynical in your approach as an overreaction to your prior naïveté. The most effective attitude to adopt is one of supreme acceptance. The world is full of people with different characters and temperaments. We all have a dark side, a tendency to manipulate, and aggressive desires. The most dangerous types are those who repress their desires or deny the existence of them, often acting them out in the most underhanded ways. Some people have dark qualities that are especially pronounced. You cannot change such people at their core, but must merely avoid becoming their victim. You are an observer of the human comedy, and by being as tolerant as possible, you gain a much greater ability to understand people and to influence their behavior when necessary.

这种对视角的全新清晰应该伴随着态度的调整。你必须避免因为之前的天真而反应过度而变得愤世嫉俗。最有效的态度是完全接受。这个世界充满了性格和性情各异的人。我们都有阴暗面、操纵倾向和侵略性欲望。最危险的是那些压抑或否认自身欲望存在的人，他们常常以最卑鄙的方式将其付诸行动。有些人的阴暗特质尤为明显。你无法从根本上改变这些人，而只能避免成为他们的受害者。你是人间喜剧的观察者，通过尽可能地宽容，你将更有能力理解他人，并在必要时影响他们的行为。

With this new awareness and attitude in place, you can begin to advance in your apprenticeship in social intelligence. This intelligence consists of two components, both equally important to master. First, there is what we shall call specific knowledge of human natur e—namely the ability to read people, to get a feel for how they see the world, and to understand their individuality. Second, there is the general knowledge of human nature , which means accumulating an understanding of the overall patterns of human behavior that transcend us as individuals, including some of the darker qualities we often disregard. Because we are all a mix of unique qualities and traits common to our species, only the possession of both forms of knowledge can give you a complete picture of the people around you. Practice both forms of knowledge and they will yield invaluable skills that are essential in the quest for mastery.

有了这种新的意识和态度，你就可以开始提升社交智力了。社交智力包含两个要素，掌握它们同等重要。首先，我们称之为关于人性的专项知识——即读懂他人、感受他人的世界观以及理解他人个性的能力。其次，是关于人性的常识，这意味着积累对超越个体的人类行为整体模式的理解，包括一些我们常常忽视的阴暗特质。由于我们每个人都是物种共同特质和特征的混合体，因此只有同时掌握这两种知识，才能让你全面地了解周围的人。实践这两种知识，你将获得在追求精通的过程中必不可少的宝贵技能。

# ↩

Specific Knowledge—Reading People

专业知识——读懂人心

Most of us have had the sensation at some point in our lives of experiencing an uncanny connection with another person. In such moments we have an understanding that is hard to put into words; we even feel that we can anticipate the thoughts of the other person. Such communication generally occurs with close friends and partners, people whom we trust and feel attuned to on many levels. Because we trust them, we open up to their influence and vice versa. In our normal state we are often nervous, defensive, and self-absorbed, and our minds are turned inward. But in these moments of connection, the internal monologue is shut off, and we pick up more cues and signals from the other person than usual.

我们大多数人在人生的某个时刻都曾体验过与他人之间不可思议的联结。在这样的时刻，我们会产生一种难以言喻的默契；我们甚至感觉能够预知对方的想法。这种交流通常发生在亲密的朋友和伴侣之间，我们信任他们，并在很多层面上与他们产生共鸣。正因为我们信任他们，我们才会敞开心扉，接受他们的影响，反之亦然。在正常情况下，我们常常感到紧张、防御、自我陶醉，思绪也随之转向内心。但在这些联结的时刻，内心独白被关闭，我们会比平时从对方那里接收到更多暗示和信号。

What this means is that when we are not inward-directed but attending more deeply to another person, we gain access to forms of communication that are largely nonverbal in nature, and quite effective in their own way. We can imagine that our primitive ancestors, needing to cooperate on a high level yet not experiencing the kind of interior monologue that comes with words, possessed an incredibly powerful sensitivity to the moods and feelings of others within the group, bordering on telepathy. This would be similar to what other social animals possess, but in this case this sensitivity would have been heightened by our ancestor’s ability to place themselves in the minds of others.

这意味着，当我们不再内向，而是更深入地关注他人时，我们就能接触到本质上主要为非语言的沟通形式，而这些沟通形式本身就非常有效。我们可以想象，我们的原始祖先需要高层次的合作，却无法体验到语言带来的那种内心独白，他们对群体中其他人的情绪和感受有着极其敏锐的感知力，近乎心灵感应。这与其他社会动物拥有的相似之处，但在这种情况下，这种感知力会因为我们祖先能够设身处地为他人着想的能力而增强。

The intense nonverbal connection we experience with those we are close to is clearly not appropriate in a work environment, but to the degree we open ourselves up and direct our attention outward to other people, we can access a part of the sensitivity that our ancestors had, and become much more effective at reading people.

我们与亲近的人之间所经历的强烈的非语言联系显然不适合工作环境，但只要我们敞开心扉，将注意力转向其他人，我们就能获得祖先所具有的部分敏感性，并更有效地了解他人。

To begin this process, you need to train yourself to pay less attention to the words that people say and greater attention to their tone of voice, the look in their eye, their body language—all signals that might reveal a nervousness or excitement that is not expressed verbally. If you can get people to become emotional, they will reveal a lot more. Cutting off your interior monologue and paying deep attention, you will pick up cues from them that will register with you as feelings or sensations. Trust these sensations—they are telling you something that you will often tend to ignore because it is not easy to verbalize. Later you can try to find a pattern to these signals and attempt to analyze what they mean.

要开始这个过程，你需要训练自己少关注别人说的话，多关注他们的语气、眼神和肢体语言——所有这些信号都可能揭示出你未曾用言语表达的紧张或兴奋。如果你能让人们动情，他们就会流露出更多情感。停止内心独白，深入倾听，你就能从中获得一些线索，这些线索最终会被你识别为感受或感觉。相信这些感觉——它们正在告诉你一些你常常会忽略的东西，因为它们难以用语言表达。之后，你可以尝试找出这些信号的规律，并尝试分析它们的含义。

On this nonverbal level, it is interesting to observe how people behave around those in positions of power and authority. They will tend to reveal an anxiety, a resentment, or a sycophantic falseness that betrays something essential about their psychological makeup, something that goes back to their childhoods and that can be read in their body language.

从非语言层面观察人们在权贵面前的行为举止颇有趣味。他们往往会流露出焦虑、怨恨或阿谀奉承的虚伪，这暴露了他们心理构成中的一些本质特征，这些特征可以追溯到他们的童年，并且可以通过他们的肢体语言解读出来。

When you drop your defense mechanisms and pay deep attention to others, you will need to lower your guard and open yourself up to their influence as well. But as long as your emotions and empathy are directed outward, you will be able to detach yourself when necessary and analyze what you have gleaned. Resist the temptation to interpret what they say or do as somehow implicitly involving you—this will cause you to turn your thoughts inward and close off the immediacy of the connection.

当你放下防御机制，全身心关注他人时，你也需要放下戒备，敞开心扉，接受他们的影响。但只要你的情绪和同理心向外释放，你就能适时抽离，分析你所收集到的信息。要抵制将他人言行解读为某种程度上暗示你参与其中的诱惑——这会导致你转而思考内心，并切断与他人的直接联系。

As an exercise, after you have known people for a while, try to imagine that you are experiencing the world from their point of view, placing yourself in their circumstances and feeling what they feel. Look for any common emotional experiences—a trauma or difficulty you’ve had, for instance, that resembles in some way what they are going through. Reliving a part of that emotion can help you begin the identifying process. The goal is not to literally inhabit their mind, which is impossible, but to practice your empathic powers and gain a more realistic appraisal of their worldview. Being able to place yourself to any degree in the mind-set of others is a brilliant means of loosening up your own thought process, which will tend to get locked into certain ways of seeing things. Your ability to empathize with others is related to the creative process of feeling your way into the subject you are studying.

作为练习，在你认识一些人一段时间后，试着想象你正从他们的角度体验世界，设身处地地感受他们的感受。寻找任何共同的情感体验——例如，你经历过的创伤或困境，是否在某种程度上与他们正在经历的相似。重温那种情感的一部分可以帮助你开始认同的过程。目标并非完全融入他们的思维，这是不可能的，而是练习你的共情能力，并对他们的世界观进行更现实的评估。能够在某种程度上设身处地地为他人着想，是放松自身思维的绝佳方式，因为你的思维往往会被某些特定的视角所束缚。你对他人的共情能力与你探索所研究主题的创造性过程息息相关。

This intuitive form of reading people becomes more effective and accurate the more you use it, but it is best to combine it with other, more conscious forms of observation. For instance, you should take particular note of people’s actions and decisions. Your goal is to figure out the hidden motives behind them, which will often revolve around power. People will say all kinds of things about their motives and intentions; they are used to dressing things up with words. Their actions, however, say much more about their character, about what is going on underneath the surface. If they present a harmless front but have acted aggressively on several occasions, give the knowledge of that aggression much greater weight than the surface they present. In a similar vein, you should take special note of how people respond to stressful situations—often the mask they wear in public falls off in the heat of the moment.

这种直觉式的解读方式用得越多，就越有效、越准确，但最好将其与其他更有意识的观察方式结合起来。例如，你应该特别注意人们的行为和决定。你的目标是找出他们背后隐藏的动机，而这些动机通常与权力有关。人们会用各种各样的方式来描述自己的动机和意图；他们习惯于用言语来粉饰事情。然而，他们的行为更多地反映了他们的性格，以及他们内心深处的想法。如果他们表面上看似无害，但实际上却多次表现出攻击性，那么，比起他们表面上的表现，更应该重视他们内心的攻击性。同样，你应该特别注意人们如何应对压力——他们在公共场合戴的面具往往会在情绪激动时脱落。

When looking for cues to observe, you should be sensitive to any kind of extreme behavior on their part—for instance, a blustery front, an overly friendly manner, a constant penchant for jokes. You will often notice that they wear this like a mask to hide the opposite, to distract others from the truth. They are blustery because they are inwardly very insecure; they are overly friendly because they are secretly ambitious and aggressive; or they joke to hide a mean-spiritedness.

在寻找观察线索时，你应该对他们的任何极端行为保持敏感——例如，咄咄逼人的外表、过分友好的举止、以及爱开玩笑的习惯。你会经常注意到，他们戴着这些面具，就像戴着面具一样，掩盖着相反的一面，转移别人对真相的注意力。他们咄咄逼人，是因为他们内心非常缺乏安全感；他们过分友好，是因为他们内心雄心勃勃、咄咄逼人；或者，他们开玩笑是为了掩饰内心的刻薄。

In general, you are reading and decoding every possible sign—including the clothes they wear and the organized or disorganized nature of their workspace. The choice of mate or partner can be quite eloquent too, particularly if it seems slightly inconsistent with the character they try to project. In this choice they can reveal unmet needs from childhood, a desire for power and control, a low self-image, and other qualities they normally seek to disguise. What might seem like small issues—chronically being late, insufficient attention to detail, not returning any favors on your part—are signs of something deeper about their character. These are patterns you must pay attention to. Nothing is too small to notice.

总的来说，你会解读并解读所有可能的迹象——包括他们穿的衣服，以及他们工作空间的整洁程度。伴侣的选择也可能颇具说服力，尤其是在他们试图展现的性格略有不符的情况下。这种选择可能会暴露出他们童年时期未得到满足的需求、对权力和控制的渴望、低落的自我形象，以及其他他们通常试图掩饰的特质。一些看似微不足道的小问题——比如经常迟到、对细节不够关注、对你不予理睬——其实都揭示了他们性格中更深层次的东西。这些是你必须关注的规律。没有什么是微不足道而无法察觉的。

You must avoid the common mistake of making judgments based on your initial impressions of people. Such impressions can sometimes tell you something, but more often they are misleading. There are several reasons for this. In your initial encounter you tend to be nervous, less open, and more inward. You are not really paying attention. Furthermore, people have trained themselves to appear a certain way; they have a persona they use in public that acts like a second skin to protect them. Unless you are incredibly perceptive, you will tend to mistake the mask for the reality. For instance, the man you judged to be so powerful and assertive may be merely masking his fears and may have far less power than you first imagined. Often it is the quiet ones, those who give out less at first glance, who hide greater depths, and who secretly wield greater power.

你必须避免一个常见的错误，那就是根据对人的初印象来下判断。这种印象有时能说明一些问题，但更多的时候，它们会误导你。造成这种情况的原因有很多。初次见面时，你往往会紧张，不太坦诚，也更内向。你并没有真正注意。此外，人们已经训练自己表现出某种特定的形象；他们在公众场合会使用一种人格面具，就像第二层皮肤一样保护着自己。除非你洞察力极强，否则你很容易把面具误认为是真实的。例如，你原本认为非常强大和自信的人，可能只是在掩饰他的恐惧，他的权力可能远没有你最初想象的那么大。通常，那些安静的人，那些乍一看不太显眼的人，隐藏的更深，暗中掌握着更大的权力。

What you want is a picture of a person’s character over time, which will give you a far more accurate sense of their true character than any first impression could. So restrain yourself from the natural tendency to judge right away, and let the passing months reveal more and more about who people are, as you get better at reading them.

你想要的是随着时间的推移，了解一个人的性格，这比任何第一印象都能更准确地展现他们的真实性格。所以，要克制自己立即下结论的本能，让时间的流逝，随着你对一个人的了解越来越深入，逐渐揭示出他的真实性格。

In the end, your goal is to identify and pierce through to what makes people unique, to understand the character and values that lie at their cores. The more you can fathom about people’s pasts and their way of thinking about things, the more deeply you can enter into their spirit. In this way you will be able to understand their motivations, foresee their actions, and recognize how best to win them to your side. You will no longer be operating in the dark.

最终，你的目标是识别并洞察人们的独特之处，理解他们内心深处的性格和价值观。你越了解人们的过去和思维方式，就越能深入他们的内心。这样，你就能理解他们的动机，预见他们的行为，并知道如何最好地赢得他们的支持。你将不再在黑暗中摸索。

You will encounter thousands of various individuals in your life, and the ability to see them as they are will prove invaluable. Keep in mind, however, that people are in a state of continual flux. You must not let your ideas about them harden into a set impression. You are continually observing them and bringing your readings of them up to date.

你的一生中会遇到成千上万个形形色色的人，能够洞察他们的真面目将无比宝贵。然而，请记住，人们总是处于不断变化的状态。你绝不能让你对他们的印象固化成一种固定的印象。你正在不断地观察他们，并不断更新你对他们的解读。

# ↩

General Knowledge—The Seven Deadly Realities

常识——七大致命现实

Throughout recorded history we can detect patterns of human behavior that transcend culture and time, indicating certain universal features that belong to us as a species. Some of these traits are quite positive—for instance, our ability to cooperate with one another in a group—while some of them are negative and can prove destructive. Most of us have these negative qualities— Envy, Conformism, Rigidity, Self-obsessiveness, Laziness, Flightiness, and Passive Aggression —in relatively mild doses. But in a group setting, there will inevitably be people who have one or more of these qualities to a high enough degree that they can become very destructive. We shall call these negative qualities the Seven Deadly Realities.

纵观人类有记载的历史，我们能够发现超越文化和时间的人类行为模式，这些模式表明我们作为一个物种拥有某些普遍的特征。其中一些特质非常积极——例如，我们在群体中相互合作的能力——而另一些则是消极的，甚至可能具有破坏性。我们大多数人都具有这些消极特质——嫉妒、墨守成规、刻板、自我痴迷、懒惰、轻浮和被动攻击——但程度相对较轻。但在群体环境中，不可避免地会有人拥有一种或多种这些特质，并且达到一定程度，以至于变得极具破坏性。我们将这些消极特质称为“七大致命现实”。

The problem for us is that people do not like to display these traits publicly because they are seen as ugly and undesirable. They tend to disguise them from view, finally revealing their reality through some action that blindsides and harms us. In our surprise, we tend to react emotionally, increasing the damage, the effects of which we can carry with us the rest of our lives. Through study and observation, we must understand the nature of these Seven Deadly Realities so that we can detect their presence and avoid triggering them in the first place. Consider the following as essential knowledge in acquiring social intelligence.

我们面临的问题在于，人们不愿公开展现这些特质，因为它们被视为丑陋和不受欢迎的。他们倾向于掩饰这些特质，最终通过一些出其不意、伤害我们的行为，暴露出它们的真面目。在惊愕之余，我们往往会情绪化地做出反应，从而加剧伤害，而这种伤害可能会伴随我们一生。通过学习和观察，我们必须理解这七大致命现实的本质，这样才能察觉它们的存在，并从一开始就避免触发它们。以下是获取社交智力的必备知识。

Envy: It is our nature to constantly compare ourselves to others—in terms of money, looks, coolness, intelligence, popularity, or any number of categories. If we are upset that someone we know is more successful than we are, we will naturally experience some envy, but often we will find a way to minimize it because it is an unpleasant emotion. We tell ourselves that the success of another person is a matter of luck or came through their connections, or that it won’t last. But for some people it goes much deeper than this, usually because of the level of their insecurities. Seething with envy, the only way to discharge it is to find a way to obstruct or sabotage the person who elicited the emotion. If they take such action they will never say it is because of envy, but will find some other, more socially acceptable excuse. They often won’t even admit their envy to themselves. This makes it a quality very hard to recognize in people. There are, however, a few indications you can look for. People who praise you too much or who become overly friendly in the first stages of knowing you are often envious and are getting closer in order to hurt you. You should be wary of such behavior. Also, if you detect unusual levels of insecurity in a person, he or she will certainly be more prone to envy.

嫉妒：我们天性如此，总是会拿自己和别人比较——无论是金钱、外貌、酷劲、智力、人气，还是其他任何方面。如果我们因为认识的人比自己成功而感到沮丧，自然会感到嫉妒，但通常会想方设法淡化这种情绪，因为这是一种令人不快的情绪。我们会告诉自己，别人的成功是运气使然，或是来自他们的人脉关系，又或是这种成功不会长久。但对某些人来说，嫉妒的根源远流长，通常是因为他们内心的不安全感。嫉妒之火熊熊燃烧，唯一的发泄方式就是想方设法阻挠或破坏引发这种情绪的人。即使他们真的这么做了，他们也绝不会说是因为嫉妒，而是会找一些其他更能被社会接受的借口。他们通常甚至不会主动承认自己的嫉妒。这使得嫉妒这种特质在人们身上很难被发现。不过，还是有一些迹象可以让你留意。那些过度赞美你，或者在认识你初期就对你表现得过于友好的人，往往是出于嫉妒，他们试图拉近关系，目的是伤害你。你应该警惕这种行为。此外，如果你察觉到一个人异常缺乏安全感，他或她肯定更容易嫉妒。

In general, however, envy is very difficult to discern, and the most prudent course of action is to make sure your own behavior does not inadvertently trigger it. If you have a gift for a certain skill, you should make a point of occasionally displaying some weakness in another area, avoiding the great danger of appearing too perfect, too talented. If you are dealing with insecure types, you can display great interest in their work and even turn to them for advice. You must be careful not to boast of any success, and if necessary, to ascribe it to just good luck on your part. It is always wise to occasionally reveal your own insecurities, which will humanize you in other people’s eyes. Self-deprecating humor will work wonders as well. You must be particularly careful to never make people feel stupid in your presence. Intelligence is the most sensitive trigger point for envy. In general, it is by standing out too much that you will spark this ugly emotion, and so it is best to maintain a nonthreatening exterior and to blend in well with the group, at least until you are so successful it no longer matters.

然而，一般来说，嫉妒很难辨别，最谨慎的做法是确保自己的行为不会无意中触发嫉妒。如果你在某项技能上很有天赋，你应该偶尔展现一下自己在其他领域的弱点，避免显得过于完美、才华横溢所带来的巨大风险。如果你面对的是缺乏安全感的人，你可以对他们的工作表现出极大的兴趣，甚至向他们寻求建议。你必须注意不要吹嘘任何成就，必要时，可以将其归因于你的好运。偶尔展现自己的不安全感总是明智的，这会让你在别人眼中显得更有人情味。自嘲式的幽默也会产生奇效。你必须特别注意，不要让别人在你面前觉得自己很愚蠢。智力是嫉妒最敏感的触发点。一般来说，太过引人注目会激发这种丑陋的情绪，所以最好保持不具威胁性的外表，并与群体很好地融合，至少在你成功之前，这一点不再重要。

Conformism: When people form groups of any type, a kind of organizational mind-set inevitably sets in. Although members of the group might trumpet their tolerance and celebration of people’s differences, the reality is that those who are markedly different make them feel uncomfortable and insecure, calling the values of the dominant culture into question. This culture will have unwritten standards of correctness that shift with the times we live in. In some environments, physical appearance is important. But generally, the spirit of correctness runs deeper than that. Often unconsciously conforming to the spirit of the man or woman on top, members will share the same values about morals or politics. You can become aware of this group spirit by observing how much people feel the need to display certain opinions or ideas that conform to the standards. There will always be a few within the group who are the overseers of correctness and who can be quite dangerous.

墨守成规：当人们组成任何类型的群体时，一种组织心态不可避免地会形成。尽管群体成员可能会宣称自己宽容并鼓励人们的差异，但现实是，那些明显不同的人会让他们感到不舒服和不安全，从而对主流文化的价值观产生质疑。这种文化会有一些不成文的正确性标准，这些标准会随着我们生活的时代而变化。在某些环境中，外表很重要。但通常情况下，正确的精神比这更深。成员们通常会无意识地顺从上层男性或女性的精神，在道德或政治方面拥有相同的价值观。你可以通过观察人们在多大程度上感到有必要表达符合标准的某些观点或想法来了解这种群体精神。群体中总会有一些人是正确性的监督者，这些人可能非常危险。

If you have a rebellious or naturally eccentric streak, as is often the case with those who are aiming for mastery, you must be careful in displaying your difference too overtly, particularly in the Apprenticeship Phase. Let your work subtly demonstrate your individual spirit, but when it comes to matters of politics, morals, and values, make a show of adhering to the accepted standards of your environment. Think of the workplace as a kind of theater in which you are always wearing a mask. (Reserve your most interesting and colorful thoughts for your friends, and for those whom you can trust outside work.) Be careful in what you say—it is not worth the bother of freely expressing your opinions. If you sin against this Deadly Reality, people will not acknowledge the cause of their disaffection, because they do not want to think of themselves as conformists. They will find some other reason to ostracize or sabotage you. Do not give them material for this kind of attack. Later, as you gain mastery, you will have ample opportunity to let your individuality shine through and to reveal your contempt for people’s correctness.

如果你有叛逆或天生古怪的性格——那些渴望成就大师的人通常如此——你必须小心，不要过于公开地展现你的与众不同，尤其是在学徒阶段。让你的工作巧妙地展现你的个人精神，但在涉及政治、道德和价值观等问题时，要表现出对你所在环境的公认标准的遵守。把职场想象成一个剧场，你永远戴着面具。（把你最有趣、最精彩的想法留给你的朋友，以及那些你在工作之外可以信任的人。）说话要谨慎——自由表达你的观点不值得费心。如果你违背了这一致命的现实，人们不会承认他们不满的原因，因为他们不想把自己视为墨守成规的人。他们会找其他理由来排斥或破坏你。不要给他们提供这种攻击的素材。之后，当你掌握了技巧，你将有充足的机会展现你的个性，并表现出你对人们正确性的蔑视。

Rigidity: The world has become increasingly complex in many ways, and whenever we humans face a situation that seems complicated our response is to resort to a kind of artificial simplicity, to create habits and routines that give us a sense of control.
