情报的策略

We must, however, acknowledge…that man with all his noble qualities, with sympathy which feels for the most debased, with benevolence which extends not only to other men but to the humblest living creature, with his god-like intellect which has penetrated into the movements and constitution of the solar system—with all these exalted powers—Man still bears in his bodily frame the indelible stamp of his lowly origin.

然而，我们必须承认……尽管人类拥有高尚的品质，对最卑微的人也抱有同情心，对其他人和最卑微的生物也怀有仁慈，拥有洞察太阳系运动和构造的神一般的智慧——尽管拥有所有这些崇高的力量——但人类的身体结构中仍然带有其卑微出身的不可磨灭的印记。

—C HARLES D ARWIN

—查尔斯·达尔文

In dealing with people, you will often encounter particular problems that will tend to make you emotional and lock you into the Naïve Perspective. Such problems include unexpected political battles, superficial judgments of your character based on appearances, or petty-minded criticisms of your work. The following four essential strategies, developed by Masters past and present, will help you to meet these inevitable challenges and maintain the rational mind-set necessary for social intelligence.

在与人交往中，你常常会遇到一些容易让你情绪化、陷入“天真视角”的问题。这些问题包括意想不到的政治斗争、基于外表对你性格的肤浅判断，以及对你工作的狭隘批评。以下由历代大师们总结的四大基本策略，将帮助你应对这些不可避免的挑战，并保持社交智慧所必需的理性思维。

# ↩

1. Speak through your work

1. 通过你的作品说话

A. In 1846, a twenty-eight-year-old Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis began work as an assistant in the obstetrics department of the University of Vienna, and almost from the beginning he was a man obsessed. The great disease that plagued the maternity wards in Europe at the time was that of childbed fever. At the hospital where young Semmelweis worked, one in six mothers died of the disease shortly after giving birth. When their bodies were dissected, doctors would discover the same whitish pus that smelled horrifically, and an unusual amount of putrid flesh. Seeing the effects of the disease on almost a daily basis, Semmelweis could think of nothing else. He would devote his time to solving the riddle of its origins.

答：1846年，一位名叫伊格纳兹·塞麦尔维斯的28岁匈牙利医生开始在维也纳大学产科担任助理医生。几乎从一开始，他就对产褥热就痴迷不已。当时，欧洲产科病房里最严重的疾病莫过于产褥热。在年轻的塞麦尔维斯工作的医院里，六分之一的母亲在产后不久就会死于这种疾病。解剖她们的尸体时，医生们会发现同样散发着可怕气味的白色脓液，以及大量腐烂的血肉。塞麦尔维斯几乎每天都能看到这种疾病的肆虐，他一心只想着这件事。他全身心投入到解开病根之谜中。

At the time, the most common explanation for the cause of the disease revolved around the idea that airborne particles, ingested through the lungs, brought on the fever. But to Semmelweis, this made no sense. The epidemics of childbed fever did not seem to depend on weather, atmospheric conditions, or anything in the air. He noted, as did a few others, that the incidence was much higher among women who had had their babies delivered by a doctor as opposed to a midwife. Nobody could explain the reason for such a difference, and few seemed perturbed by this.

当时，最常见的病因解释是，通过肺部吸入的空气颗粒物引发了发烧。但塞麦尔维斯认为这说不通。产褥热的流行似乎与天气、大气条件或空气中的任何物质无关。他和其他一些人指出，由医生接生的妇女比由助产士接生的妇女发病率要高得多。没有人能解释这种差异的原因，而且似乎很少有人对此感到不安。

After much thinking and studying of the literature on the subject, Semmelweis came to the startling conclusion that it was the direct, hand-to-hand contact between doctor and patient that caused the disease—a revolutionary concept at the time. As he was formulating this theory, an event occurred that seemed to prove it conclusively: A leading doctor in the department had been accidently pricked in the finger by a knife while conducting an autopsy on a woman who had had childbed fever, and the doctor died within a few days of a massive infection. When they dissected his body, he had the same white pus and putrid flesh as the woman.

经过大量思考和研究相关文献，塞麦尔维斯得出了一个惊人的结论：正是医生与患者之间直接的手与手的接触导致了这种疾病——这在当时是一个革命性的概念。就在他构思这一理论之际，发生了一件似乎最终证实了这一理论的事情：科室一位主任医生在对一位患产褥热的妇女进行尸检时，手指不慎被刀刺伤，随后在几天内因大规模感染而死亡。解剖他的尸体时，发现他和那位妇女一样，身上有白色的脓液和腐烂的肉。

It now seemed clear to Semmelweis that in the autopsy room the physicians’ hands became infected, and in examining the women and delivering the babies, they passed the disease into the women’s blood through various open wounds. The physicians were literally poisoning their patients with childbed fever. If this was the cause, it would be simple to solve—doctors would have to wash and disinfect their hands before handling any patients, a practice no one followed in any hospital at the time. He instituted this practice in his ward, and the number of mortalities was instantly halved.

塞麦尔维斯现在似乎明白了，在尸检室里，医生的手被感染了，在检查产妇和接生婴儿的过程中，他们通过各种开放性伤口将病菌传染给了产妇的血液。医生们实际上是在用产褥热毒害他们的病人。如果这是原因，那么解决起来也很简单——医生在处理任何病人之前都必须洗手消毒，而当时任何医院都没有这样做。他把这种做法推广到自己的病房，死亡人数立刻减少了一半。

On the brink of perhaps a major discovery in science—the connection between germs and contagious disease—Semmelweis seemed to be on his way to an illustrious career. But there was one problem. The head of the department, Johann Klein, was a most conservative gentleman who wanted his doctors to adhere to strict medical orthodoxies established by previous practice. He believed that Semmelweis was an inexperienced doctor turned radical, who wanted to overturn the establishment and make a name for himself in the process.

塞麦尔维斯即将在科学上取得一项重大发现——细菌与传染病之间的联系——他似乎即将走向辉煌的职业生涯。但有一个问题。科室主任约翰·克莱因是一位极其保守的绅士，他希望他的医生们严格遵守以往实践中确立的医学正统观念。他认为塞麦尔维斯是一位缺乏经验却变得激进的医生，他想要颠覆既定的体制，并借此扬名立万。

Semmelweis argued with him incessantly over the subject of childbed fever, and when the young man finally promulgated his theory, Klein became furious. The implication was that doctors, including Klein himself, had been murdering their patients, and this was too much to take. (Klein himself ascribed the lower number of mortalities in Semmelweis’s ward to a new ventilation system he had installed.) When in 1849 Semmelweis’s assistantship was nearing its end, Klein refused to renew it, essentially leaving the young man without a job.

塞麦尔维斯就产褥热问题与克莱因争论不休，当这位年轻人最终公开自己的理论时，克莱因勃然大怒。他暗示医生，包括克莱因本人，一直在谋杀病人，这实在令人难以接受。（克莱因本人将塞麦尔维斯病房的死亡率较低归因于他安装的新通风系统。）1849年，塞麦尔维斯的助理职位即将到期，克莱因拒绝续约，这实际上让这位年轻人失业了。

By now, however, Semmelweis had gained several key allies within the medical department, particularly among the younger set. They urged him to conduct some controlled experiments to strengthen his case, and then to write up his findings in a book that would spread his theory throughout Europe. Semmelweis, however, could not turn his attention away from the battle with Klein. Day by day his anger rose. Klein’s adherence to a ridiculous and disproven theory about the fever was criminal. Such blindness to the truth made his blood boil. How could one man have such power in his field? Why should Semmelweis have to take so much of his time to do experiments and write books, when the truth was already so apparent? He decided instead to give a series of lectures on the subject, in which he could also express his scorn toward the closed-mindedness of so many in the profession.

然而，此时塞麦尔维斯已在医学界，尤其是年轻一代，获得了几位关键盟友。他们敦促他进行一些对照实验来强化自己的观点，然后将他的发现写成一本书，将他的理论传播到整个欧洲。然而，塞麦尔维斯无法将注意力从与克莱因的争论中转移开。他的怒火与日俱增。克莱因坚持一个荒谬且已被证伪的发热理论，简直是犯罪。这种对真相的盲目让他怒火中烧。一个人怎么可能在他的领域拥有如此大的影响力？既然真相已经如此明显，塞麦尔维斯为什么还要花费如此多的时间去做实验和写书呢？他决定就此主题举办一系列讲座，同时也表达他对业内众多思想狭隘者的蔑视。

Doctors from all over Europe attended Semmelweis’s lectures. Although some remained skeptical, he won over more converts to his cause. His allies at the university pressed him to continue the momentum by doing more research and by writing a book on his theory. But within a few months of the lectures, and for reasons no one could understand, Semmelweis suddenly left town and returned to his native Budapest, where he found the university and medical position that had eluded him in Vienna. It seemed he could not endure another moment in the same city as Klein, and required complete freedom to operate on his own—even though Budapest was somewhat of a medical backwater at the time. His friends felt completely betrayed. They had staked their reputations on supporting him, and now he had left them in the lurch.

来自欧洲各地的医生聆听了塞麦尔维斯的讲座。尽管仍有一些人持怀疑态度，但他还是赢得了更多支持者。他在大学里的盟友敦促他继续推进这一势头，进行更多研究，并撰写一本关于其理论的著作。然而，讲座结束后几个月，不知何故，塞麦尔维斯突然离开家乡布达佩斯，回到了他在维也纳一直未能获得的大学和医学职位。他似乎无法再忍受和克莱因待在同一座城市，需要完全的自主行动自由——尽管当时布达佩斯在医学界可以说是一个死胡同。他的朋友们感到彻底被背叛了。他们曾用自己的名誉来支持他，而现在他却抛弃了他们。

In the Budapest hospitals where he now worked, Semmelweis instituted his disinfection policies with such a rigor and tyrannical intensity that he cut the mortality rates but alienated almost all of the doctors and nurses he worked with. More and more people were turning against him. He had forced upon everyone his novel ideas on disinfection, but without books or the proper experiments to back them up it seemed that he was merely promoting himself, or obsessed with some fanciful idea of his own creation. The vehemence with which he insisted on its truth only called more attention to the lack of scholarly rigor to back it up. Doctors speculated about other possible causes for his success in cutting the incidence of childbed fever.

在塞麦尔维斯如今工作的布达佩斯医院里，他制定的消毒政策极其严格，专制至极。他降低了死亡率，却疏远了几乎所有与他共事的医生和护士。越来越多的人开始反对他。他曾强迫每个人都接受自己关于消毒的新想法，但由于缺乏书籍或合适的实验来佐证，他似乎只是在自我推销，或者沉迷于自己发明的某些奇思妙想。他如此强烈地坚持其真实性，反而更加凸显了其缺乏严谨的学术论证。医生们推测，他之所以能够成功降低产褥热的发病率，还有其他可能的原因。

Finally in 1860, under pressure from colleagues yet again, he decided to write the book that would explain his theory in full. When he was finished with it, what should have been a relatively small volume had ballooned into a 600-page diatribe that was nearly impossible to read. It was hopelessly repetitive and convoluted. His arguments would turn into polemics as he enumerated the doctors who had opposed him and who were therefore murderers. During such passages his writing became almost apocalyptic.

最终，在1860年，在同事们再次施压之下，他决定写一本书来完整地解释他的理论。当他写完这本书时，原本应该篇幅不大的一本书却膨胀成了一篇长达600页的长篇大论，几乎无法阅读。它的内容重复且令人费解。当他列举那些反对他的医生，并因此被认为是凶手时，他的论点变成了一场论战。在这样的段落里，他的文笔几乎变成了末日论调。

Now his opponents came out of the woodwork. He had committed himself to writing but had done such a bad job that they could poke holes through his arguments, or merely call attention to his violent tone, which was self-damning enough. His former allies did not rally to his cause. They had come to hate him. His behavior became increasingly grandiose and erratic, until his employers at the hospital had to dismiss him. Virtually penniless and abandoned by almost everyone, he fell ill and died in 1865 at the age of forty-seven.

如今，他的对手们纷纷现身。他曾致力于写作，但成果惨淡，以至于他们要么挑剔他的论点，要么仅仅指出他那足以自取灭亡的暴力语气。他昔日的盟友不再支持他，反而开始憎恨他。他的行为变得越来越浮夸和反复无常，直到医院的雇主不得不将他解雇。他几乎身无分文，几乎被所有人抛弃，最终于1865年病逝，享年47岁。

B. As a medical student at the University of Padua in Italy in 1602, the Englishman William Harvey (1578–1657) began to entertain doubts about the whole conception of the heart and its function as an organ. What he had been taught in school was based on the theories of the second-century Greek physician Galen, which stated that some blood was manufactured in the liver and some in the heart, and was transported by veins and absorbed by the body, supplying it with nutrition. According to the theory, this blood flowed ever so slowly from the liver and heart to the various parts of the body that needed it, but did not flow back—it was merely consumed. What troubled Harvey was how much blood the body contained. How could it possibly produce and consume so much liquid?

B. 1602年，英国人威廉·哈维（William Harvey，1578-1657）还是意大利帕多瓦大学的一名医学院学生时，就开始对心脏的概念及其器官功能产生怀疑。他在学校学到的知识基于公元二世纪希腊医生盖伦的理论，该理论认为，一部分血液由肝脏制造，一部分由心脏制造，并通过静脉输送到身体吸收，为身体提供营养。根据该理论，这些血液从肝脏和心脏缓慢地流向身体需要的各个部位，但不会回流——只是被身体消耗掉了。令哈维感到困惑的是，身体到底有多少血液？身体怎么可能产生并消耗这么多液体呢？

Over the ensuing years his career prospered, culminating in his appointment as Royal Physician to King James I. During these years, he continued to ponder the same questions about blood and the role of the heart. And by the year 1618 he had come up with a theory: blood flows through the body not slowly but rapidly, the heart acting as a pump. Blood is not produced and consumed; instead it circulates continually.

随后几年，他的事业蒸蒸日上，最终被任命为詹姆斯一世国王的御医。这些年里，他不断思考关于血液和心脏作用的相同问题。到1618年，他提出了一个理论：血液在体内流动并非缓慢，而是快速，心脏就像一个泵。血液并非产生和消耗，而是持续循环。

The problem with this theory was that he had no direct means of verifying it. At the time, to open the heart of a human to study it would spell instant death. The only means available for research was vivisection of animals and the dissection of human corpses. Once the heart was opened in animals, however, it would behave erratically and pump far too rapidly. The mechanics of the heart were complex, and for Harvey they could only be deduced through controlled experiments—such as using elaborate tourniquets on human veins—and could never be observed directly with the eyes.

这个理论的问题在于，他没有直接的验证手段。当时，切开人类心脏进行研究意味着立即死亡。唯一可用的研究手段是动物活体解剖和人体尸体解剖。然而，一旦动物心脏被切开，它就会出现异常，泵血速度过快。心脏的运作机制非常复杂，哈维只能通过受控实验来推断——例如在人体静脉上使用精密的止血带——而且无法直接用肉眼观察。

After many such controlled experiments Harvey felt certain he was correct, but he knew he would have to carefully strategize his next step. His theory was radical. It would overturn many concepts about anatomy that had been accepted as fact for centuries. He knew that to publish his results so far would only stir up enmity and create many enemies for himself. And so, thinking deeply about people’s natural reluctance to accept new ideas, he decided to do the following: he delayed publishing the results of his findings, waiting until he had firmed up his theory and amassed more evidence. In the meantime, he involved his colleagues in further experiments and dissections, always eliciting their opinions. Increasing numbers of them were impressed and supported his new theory. Slowly winning most of them to his side, in 1627 he was appointed to the highest position within the College of Physicians, virtually ensuring him of employment for the rest of his life and freeing him from the worry that his theory would jeopardize his livelihood.

经过多次这样的对照实验后，哈维确信自己是正确的，但他知道下一步必须谨慎规划。他的理论是彻底的，它将颠覆许多几个世纪以来被奉为真理的解剖学概念。他知道，公开发表迄今为止的研究成果只会激起敌意，给自己树敌。因此，考虑到人们天生不愿接受新观点，他决定：推迟公开研究结果，等到他的理论更加稳固，并积累了更多证据之后再发表。与此同时，他邀请同事们参与进一步的实验和解剖，并不断征求他们的意见。越来越多的同事对他的新理论印象深刻，并开始支持他。他慢慢地赢得了大多数同事的支持，并于1627年被任命为内科医师学院的最高职位，这几乎确保了他终身的职位，也让他不再担心他的理论会危及他的生计。

As the court physician, first to James I and then to Charles I who ascended the throne in 1625, Harvey worked diligently to gain royal favor. He played the court diplomat, and avoided aligning himself with any faction or becoming involved in any intrigues. He behaved humbly and with self-deprecation. He confided his discoveries to the king early on to gain his trust and support. In the country, there was a young man who had severely broken ribs on the left side of his chest, leaving a cavity through which one could see and touch the heart. He brought the young man to the king’s court and used him to demonstrate to Charles the nature of the heart’s contractions and expansions, and how the heart worked as a pump for the blood.

哈维先是詹姆斯一世的宫廷御医，后又于1625年加冕为查理一世，他勤勉工作，力求赢得皇室的青睐。他扮演着宫廷外交官的角色，避免与任何派系结盟或卷入任何阴谋。他举止谦逊，不轻易发怒。他很早就向国王吐露了自己的发现，以赢得国王的信任和支持。在当时的乡下，有一位年轻人左胸肋骨严重骨折，留下一个空腔，透过这个空腔可以看到并触摸到心脏。他把这位年轻人带到国王的宫廷，让他向查理一世演示心脏收缩和扩张的本质，以及心脏如何泵送血液。

Finally, in 1628 he published the results of his years of work, opening the book with a very clever dedication to Charles I: “Most serene King! The animal’s heart is the basis of its life, its chief member, the sun of its microcosm; on the heart all its activity depends, from the heart all its liveliness and strength arise. Equally is the King the basis of his kingdom, the sun of his microcosm, the heart of the state; from him all power arises and all grace stems.”

最终，他于1628年出版了多年心血的成果，并以一段非常巧妙的献词开篇，献给查理一世：“至尊的君王！动物的心脏是其生命之基，其主要器官，其微观世界的太阳；其一切活动都依赖于心脏，其一切活力和力量都源于心脏。同样，国王也是其王国之基，其微观世界的太阳，其国家之心脏；一切权力和一切恩典都源于他。”

The book naturally created a stir, particularly on the Continent, where Harvey was less known. Opposition primarily came from older physicians who could not reconcile themselves with a theory that so completely overturned their idea of anatomy. To the numerous publications that came out to discredit his ideas, Harvey remained mostly silent. An occasional attack from eminent physicians would cause him to write personal letters in which he very politely and yet thoroughly refuted their ideas.

这本书自然引起了轰动，尤其是在哈维名气尚不大在欧洲大陆。反对者主要来自一些老一辈的医生，他们无法接受这个彻底颠覆了他们解剖学观念的理论。面对层出不穷的质疑其观点的出版物，哈维大多保持沉默。偶尔，一些著名医生会对他进行攻击，于是他便写信给他们，非常礼貌地、却又彻底地驳斥他们的观点。

As he had foreseen, with the strength of his position within the medical profession and the court, and with the great amount of evidence he had accumulated over the years, which was clearly outlined in his book, his theory slowly gained acceptance. By the time of Harvey’s death in 1657, his work had become an accepted part of medical doctrine and practice. As his friend Thomas Hobbes would write: “[Harvey was] the only man I know, who, conquering envy, hath established a new doctrine in his life-time.”

正如他所预见的那样，凭借他在医学界和宫廷的强大地位，以及他多年来积累的大量证据（这些证据在他的书中清晰地阐述），他的理论逐渐获得认可。到1657年哈维去世时，他的著作已成为医学理论和实践中公认的组成部分。正如他的朋友托马斯·霍布斯所写：“哈维是我认识的唯一一个在有生之年克服嫉妒，创立新学说的人。”

The common historical accounts of Semmelweis and Harvey reveal our tendency to ignore the critical role of social intelligence in all fields, including the sciences. For instance, most versions of the Semmelweis story emphasize the tragic shortsightedness of men like Klein who pushed the noble-minded young Hungarian over the edge. With Harvey, they emphasize his theoretical brilliance as the singular cause of his success. But in both cases, social intelligence played a key role. Semmelweis completely ignored its necessity; such considerations annoyed him; all that mattered was the truth. But in his zeal, he unnecessarily alienated Klein, who had faced other disagreements with students before but never to such a degree. Through constant arguing, Semmelweis had pushed Klein to the point of having to fire him, and thus lost an important position within the university from which he could spread his ideas. Consumed with his battle with Klein, he failed to express his theory in a clear and reasonable form, displaying a monumental disregard for the importance of persuading others. If he had merely devoted his time to making his case in writing, he would have saved far more lives in the long run.

关于塞麦尔维斯和哈维的常见历史记载，揭示了我们倾向于忽视社交智力在所有领域（包括科学领域）的关键作用。例如，塞麦尔维斯故事的大多数版本都强调了像克莱因这样的人的悲剧性短视，他们把这位高尚的匈牙利青年逼到了绝境。而关于哈维，人们则强调他的理论才华是他成功的唯一原因。但在这两个例子中，社交智力都发挥了关键作用。塞麦尔维斯完全忽视了社交智力的必要性；这些顾虑让他恼火；他只在乎真相。但他一时冲动，不必要地疏远了克莱因。克莱因以前也曾与学生发生过分歧，但从未达到如此程度。通过不断的争论，塞麦尔维斯把克莱因逼到了不得不解雇他的地步，并因此失去了在大学里传播自己思想的重要职位。他沉迷于与克莱因的争斗，未能以清晰合理的形式表达自己的理论，完全无视说服他人的重要性。如果他只是花时间以书面形式阐述自己的观点，从长远来看，他本可以拯救更多的生命。

Harvey’s success, on the other hand, was greatly due to his social agility. He understood that even a scientist must play the courtier. He involved others in his work, making them emotionally attached to his theory. He published his results in a thoughtful, well-reasoned, and easy-to-read book. And then he quietly allowed his book to speak for itself, knowing that by asserting himself after its publication, he would merely call attention to the person and not the work. He did not give fuel to the foolishness of others by engaging in petty battles, and any opposition to his theories withered away on its own.

另一方面，哈维的成功很大程度上归功于他的社交敏捷。他深知，即使是科学家也必须扮演好自己的谄媚者的角色。他让其他人参与到自己的工作中，让他们对他的理论产生情感上的依恋。他将自己的研究成果发表在一本深思熟虑、论证充分、通俗易懂的著作中。然后，他默默地让书自己说话，因为他知道，在书出版后再宣称自己的观点，只会让人们关注他本人，而不是他的研究成果。他不会通过参与琐碎的争论来助长他人的愚蠢，任何对他理论的反对都会自然消散。

Understand: your work is the single greatest means at your disposal for expressing your social intelligence. By being efficient and detail oriented in what you do, you demonstrate that you are thinking of the group at large and advancing its cause. By making what you write or present clear and easy to follow, you show your care for the audience or public at large. By involving other people in your projects and gracefully accepting their feedback, you reveal your comfort with the group dynamic. Work that is solid also protects you from the political conniving and malevolence of others—it is hard to argue with the results you produce. If you are experiencing the pressures of political maneuvering within the group, do not lose your head and become consumed with all of the pettiness. By remaining focused and speaking socially through your work, you will both continue to raise your skill level and stand out among all the others who make a lot of noise but produce nothing.

要明白：你的工作是你展现社交智慧的唯一最佳途径。高效且注重细节地完成工作，表明你正在为整个群体着想，并致力于推进其事业。清晰易懂地撰写或呈现内容，则展现了你对受众或公众的关怀。让其他人参与你的项目并欣然接受他们的反馈，则展现了你对团队活力的适应。扎实的工作还能保护你免受他人政治阴谋和恶意的影响——你取得的成果很难被质疑。如果你正承受着群体内部政治角力的压力，不要失去理智，被各种琐碎琐事所困扰。通过保持专注，并在工作中保持社交性，你既能不断提升自己的技能水平，又能在那些喧嚣却无所作为的人中脱颖而出。

# ↩

2. Craft the appropriate persona

2. 塑造合适的角色

From early on in life, Teresita Fernández (b. 1968) had the feeling that she was watching the world around her from a distance, like a voyeur. As a young girl growing up in Miami, Florida, she would observe the adults around her, eavesdropping on their conversations, trying to decode the secrets of their strange world. As she got older, she applied her observational skills to her classmates. In high school, people were expected to fit into one of the various cliques. She could see clearly the rules and conventions that went into being a part of these groups, and the kinds of behavior that were considered correct. She felt alienated from all of these different cliques, and so she remained on the outside.

特雷西塔·费尔南德斯（生于1968年）从小就有一种感觉，她像个偷窥狂一样，从远处观察着周围的世界。在佛罗里达州迈阿密长大的她，总是观察周围的成年人，偷听他们的谈话，试图解读他们奇异世界中的秘密。随着年龄的增长，她将自己的观察能力运用到同学身上。高中时，人们被期望融入各种小圈子。她清楚地了解加入这些团体需要遵守的规则和惯例，以及哪些行为被认为是正确的。她对所有这些不同的小圈子感到疏远，因此一直保持着局外状态。

She had a similar experience in relation to Miami itself. Although she had an affinity with the Cuban culture that was part of her own background as a first generation Cuban-American, she could not identify with the happy beach lifestyle that prevailed there. There was something more somber and edgier to her spirit. All of this accentuated her sense of being an outsider, a floater that did not fit in anywhere. There were other floaters in school, and they tended to drift into theater or the art scene—places where it was safer to be unconventional. Teresita had always liked making things with her hands, and so she began to take art classes. But the art she produced in high school did not seem to connect to that grittier side of her character. It came too easily; her work was too glib and superficial; something was lacking.

她在迈阿密也有类似的经历。虽然作为第一代古巴裔美国人，她对古巴文化情有独钟，这源于她的背景，但她无法认同那里盛行的快乐海滩生活方式。她的内心深处弥漫着一种更加阴郁和尖锐的气息。所有这些都加深了她作为局外人、一个在任何地方都格格不入的漂泊者的感觉。学校里也有其他的漂泊者，他们往往会游走于戏剧或艺术圈——在这些地方，打破常规会更安全。特雷西塔一直喜欢亲自动手做东西，所以她开始上艺术课。但她在高中创作的艺术作品似乎与她性格中更坚韧的一面格格不入。一切都来得太容易了；她的作品过于浮夸和肤浅；总觉得缺少了点什么。

In 1986, still uncertain of her direction in life, she entered Florida International University, in Miami. Following her high school inclinations, she took a sculpture class. But working in clay, with its softness and ease of manipulation, gave her the same feeling she’d had in high school of making things that were merely artificial and pretty. Then one day, spending time in the sculpture building, she noticed some artists working in metal, crafting large-scale pieces. These sheets of steel had a visceral effect upon her unlike any other artwork she had seen, and she felt in some way that this was the material that had been meant for her all along. It was gray and heavy and resistant, requiring great effort to shape it. The properties of steel corresponded to the sense of resiliency and power that she had always felt inside herself, despite her petite size, and that she had always wanted to express.

1986年，尚不确定人生方向的她进入了迈阿密的佛罗里达国际大学。她追随高中时代的爱好，选修了雕塑课。然而，用黏土创作，因其柔软易操作的特性，让她重拾高中时那种纯粹做作、美轮美奂的感觉。后来有一天，在雕塑楼里闲逛时，她注意到一些艺术家正在用金属创作大型作品。这些钢板对她产生了一种前所未有的震撼，让她觉得这才是她一直以来的专属材料。它灰色、沉重、坚韧，需要付出巨大的努力才能塑造。钢铁的特性与她内心深处的韧性和力量相呼应，尽管她身材娇小，但这种力量她一直渴望表达。

And so she began to apply herself feverishly to her newfound medium. To work in metal required firing up the foundry and using acetylene torches. The tropical heat of Miami could make such labor intensely uncomfortable during the daytime hours, so she began to work on her sculptures exclusively at night. This led to an unusual schedule—starting at nine, working until two or three in the morning, then sleeping through a good part of the next day. Besides the cooler air, working at night had other advantages—with few people around, the studio was quite peaceful and conducive to serious work. She could focus deeply. She could experiment with her pieces, make mistakes that no one would see. She could be fearless and take chances.

于是，她开始全身心投入到这门新艺术媒介中。金属创作需要点燃铸造炉并使用乙炔喷灯。迈阿密的热带高温会让白天的劳动极其不适，于是她开始只在晚上创作雕塑。这让她养成了一个不同寻常的作息时间——早上九点开始，一直工作到凌晨两三点，然后第二天大部分时间都在睡觉。除了凉爽的空气外，晚上工作还有其他好处——工作室人少，非常安静，有利于认真创作。她可以全神贯注，在作品中不断尝试，犯一些别人看不到的错误。她可以无所畏惧，勇于冒险。

Slowly Fernández began to take command of the medium, and in making her sculptures, she felt like she was forging and transforming herself. She was interested in creating pieces that were large and impressive, but to make such work she had to devise her own method. She would design the pieces on paper, but would work on them in smaller sections that she could manage by herself. Then, in the quiet of her studio, she would assemble the sculptures. Soon her pieces began to be displayed within the department and on campus.

费尔南德斯逐渐掌握了这种媒介，在创作雕塑的过程中，她感觉自己在不断磨练和蜕变。她对创作大型且令人印象深刻的作品很感兴趣，但要创作这样的作品，她必须找到自己的创作方法。她会在纸上设计作品，但会将它们分成几个小部分，以便自己独立完成。然后，在安静的工作室里，她会组装这些雕塑。很快，她的作品就开始在系里和校园里展出。

Almost everyone was quite impressed by her work. Standing in the bright Miami sunshine, her enormous steel sculptures conveyed that sense of power she had always felt within her. But there was another response to her pieces that surprised her. Because few people had seen her at work, it appeared that these sculptures flowed out of her effortlessly—as if she had some unusual gift. This drew attention to her personality. Sculpture was a largely male domain that tended to attract the most macho male artists. As she was one of the few female artists working in heavy steel, people naturally projected onto her all kinds of preconceptions and fantasies. The discrepancy between her slight, feminine appearance and her large-scale, imposing works was quite glaring, and people would wonder how she managed to make such work, and who she really was. Intrigued by her character, and also by the way her beautifully crafted sculptures seemed to appear out of nowhere, they saw her as alluringly mysterious, a mix of hard and soft qualities, an anomaly, a magician with metal.

几乎每个人都对她的作品印象深刻。在迈阿密明媚的阳光下，她巨大的钢铁雕塑传达着她内心深处一直感受到的力量。但她的作品还引发了另一种反响，这让她感到惊讶。由于很少有人见过她创作，这些雕塑仿佛是她毫不费力地创作出来的——仿佛她拥有某种非凡的天赋。这让人们注意到了她的人格魅力。雕塑领域主要由男性主导，往往吸引着最具男子气概的男性艺术家。由于她是少数使用重型钢铁进行创作的女性艺术家之一，人们自然而然地将各种先入之见和幻想投射到她身上。她纤细柔美的外表与她气势恢宏的作品之间，反差十分明显，人们不禁好奇她是如何创作出如此作品的，以及她究竟是谁。她的性格，以及她那些仿佛凭空而来的精美雕塑，都令人着迷，人们觉得她神秘而迷人，刚柔并济，如同一个异类，如同一位金属魔术师。

With all of this scrutiny, Fernández suddenly became aware that she was no longer a voyeur, watching others from a distance, but was at the center of attention. The art world felt right to her. For the first time in her life she had the sensation of fitting in, and she wanted to hold on to this interest that others had in her work. Now that she was thrust into a more public position, it would be natural for her to want to talk about herself and her experiences, but she intuited that it would be a mistake to deflate the powerful effect her work had on others by suddenly revealing to everyone how many hours she had applied herself to these sculptures, and how they were really the product of intense labor and discipline. Sometimes, she reasoned, what you do not reveal to people is all the more eloquent and powerful. She decided to go along with the image that others had of her and her work. She would create an air of mystery around her, making sure not to talk about her process, keeping details of her life hidden, and allowing people to project onto her their own fantasies.

在所有这些审视之下，费尔南德斯突然意识到，她不再是一个远远地注视着他人的偷窥者，而是成为了众人关注的焦点。艺术世界对她来说恰到好处。她生平第一次感受到融入其中的快感，并渴望保持住别人对她作品的这份兴趣。如今，她被推到了一个更加公开的立场上，自然而然地想要谈论自己和自己的经历，但她直觉地意识到，如果突然向所有人透露她为这些雕塑倾注了多少心血，以及它们是如何凝聚了辛勤的劳动和严谨的纪律，那么她的作品对他人产生的强大影响力将是一个错误。她认为，有时候，你不向人们透露的东西反而更有说服力，更有力量。她决定顺应别人对她和她作品的印象。她会在自己周围营造一种神秘的氛围，确保不谈论她的创作过程，隐藏她的生活细节，让人们将自己的幻想投射到她身上。

As she progressed in her career, however, something about the persona she had created in her university years no longer felt appropriate. She noted an element in her public personality that could play against her—if she were not careful, people would judge her based on her physical appearance as an attractive young woman. They would not see her as a serious artist. Her elusiveness might seem like a cover for a lack of intelligence, as if she were merely feeling her way through things, and not on a par with the heavy-hitting intellectuals in the field. It was a prejudice female artists had to deal with. Any hint of being wishy-washy or inarticulate when it came to talking about her work carried the danger of feeding the preconception that she was frivolous, merely dabbling in the arts. And so she slowly developed a new style that suited her well—she would be assertive and speak with authority about the content of her work, while still enveloping her work process in mystery. She was not weak or vulnerable, but in clear command of the subject. If male artists needed to seem serious and articulate, as a woman she would have to appear even more so. Her assertive tone was always dignified and respectful, but she made it clear she was no lightweight.

然而，随着职业生涯的推进，她在大学时期塑造的形象似乎有些不合时宜。她注意到自己公众形象中存在一个可能对她不利的因素——如果她不小心，人们会根据她年轻貌美的外表来评判她。他们不会把她视为一位严肃的艺术家。她那难以捉摸的性格或许会让人觉得她只是在摸索，与业内那些重量级的知识分子格格不入。这是女性艺术家必须面对的偏见。在谈论她的作品时，任何含糊其辞或表达不清的暗示，都可能加深人们对她轻浮、仅仅是艺术爱好者的先入之见。于是，她逐渐形成了自己独特的风格——她会自信满满地、权威地谈论作品内容，同时又将创作过程笼罩在神秘之中。她并非软弱或脆弱，而是对主题有着清晰的掌控。如果说男艺术家需要显得严肃、善于表达，那么作为女性，她就更需要如此。她自信的语气始终带着一丝庄重和尊重，但她也明确地表明，自己绝非等闲之辈。

Over the years, as Teresita Fernández became a world-renowned conceptual artist working in all types of materials, she continued to play with her appearance and make it fit her changing circumstances. The stereotype for artists is that they are disorganized and only interested in what is happening in the art world. She would play against these expectations. She transformed herself into an eloquent lecturer, exposing her work and ideas to the public at large. Audiences would ponder and be intrigued by the discrepancy between her pleasant, composed surface and the complex, challenging content of her discourse. She became versed in many fields outside art, combining these interests in her work, and in the process exposed herself to a wide range of people outside the art world. She taught herself to mingle equally well with the workers mining the graphite for her pieces as with gallery dealers—a kind of courtier flexibility that made her life as an artist much easier and made it impossible for her to be typecast. In essence, her public persona became another form of art—a material she could cast and transform according to her needs and desires.

多年来，特雷西塔·费尔南德斯逐渐成为一位享誉全球的概念艺术家，运用各种材料进行创作。她不断调整自己的形象，使其与不断变化的环境相契合。人们对艺术家的刻板印象是，他们缺乏条理，只对艺术界的动态感兴趣。但她却打破了这种刻板印象。她化身为一位雄辩的演讲者，向公众展现自己的作品和理念。观众会思考，并被她愉悦沉稳的外表与复杂而富有挑战性的话语内容之间的反差所吸引。她精通艺术之外的诸多领域，并将这些兴趣融入到自己的作品中，并在此过程中接触到艺术界以外的各类人士。她自学成才，既能与为她的作品采石的工人打成一片，也能与画廊经纪人打成一片——这种如同侍臣般的灵活变通，让她的艺术家生涯更加轻松，也让她避免被定型。本质上，她的公众形象成为了另一种艺术形式——一种她可以根据自己的需要和愿望铸造和改造的材料。

It is not generally acknowledged or discussed, but the personality we project to the world plays a substantial role in our success and in our ascension to mastery. Look at the case of Teresita Fernández. If she had merely kept to herself and focused exclusively on her work, she would have found herself defined by others in a way that would have hindered her progress. If, after her initial success, she had boasted about all the hours of practice that went into training herself in metalwork, people would have seen her as a mere laborer and craftsman. They would have inevitably pegged her as the female artist who was using metal as a gimmick to promote herself and get attention. They would have found weaknesses in her character to exploit. The public arena, in art or any endeavor, can be ruthless that way. Able to look at herself and at the art world with a level of detachment, Fernández intuited the power she could possess by being conscious of her persona and taking control of the appearance dynamic.

鲜为人知或讨论，但我们展现给世界的个性在我们的成功和提升至大师的过程中扮演着至关重要的角色。以特雷西塔·费尔南德斯为例。如果她只是独来独往，专注于自己的作品，她就会发现自己被他人以一种阻碍其进步的方式定义。如果在最初的成功之后，她炫耀自己在金属工艺方面的大量练习，人们就会将她视为一个普通的工人和工匠。他们必然会将她视为一个利用金属作为噱头来推销自己、博取关注的女艺术家。他们会找出她性格中的弱点加以利用。无论是在艺术领域还是其他任何领域，公众视野都可能如此残酷。费尔南德斯能够以一种超然的视角审视自己和艺术界，她敏锐地意识到，通过关注自身形象并掌控外在动态，她能够拥有强大的力量。

Understand: people will tend to judge you based on your outward appearance. If you are not careful and simply assume that it is best to be yourself, they will begin to ascribe to you all kinds of qualities that have little to do with who you are but correspond to what they want to see. All of this can confuse you, make you feel insecure, and consume your attention. Internalizing their judgments, you will find it hard to focus on your work. Your only protection is to turn this dynamic around by consciously molding these appearances, creating the image that suits you, and controlling people’s judgments. At times you will find it appropriate to stand back and create some mystery around you, heightening your presence. At other times you will want to be more direct and impose a more specific appearance. In general, you never settle on one image or give people the power to completely figure you out. You are always one step ahead of the public.

要知道：人们往往会根据你的外表来评判你。如果你不小心，只是简单地认为做自己就好，他们就会开始赋予你各种各样的特质，这些特质与你本人无关，但却符合他们想要看到的形象。所有这些都会让你感到困惑，让你感到不安全，并消耗你的注意力。内化他们的评判，你会很难专注于工作。你唯一的保护措施就是有意识地塑造这些外表，打造适合你的形象，并控制人们的评判，从而扭转这种局面。有时，你会发现退一步，在周围营造一些神秘感，提升你的存在感是合适的。有时，你会想要更直接，展现更独特的形象。一般来说，你永远不会固守于某种形象，也不会让别人完全了解你。你总是比公众领先一步。

You must see the creation of a persona as a key element in social intelligence, not something evil or demonic. We all wear masks in the social arena, playing different roles to suit the different environments we pass through. You are simply becoming more conscious of the process. Think of it as theater. By creating a persona that is mysterious, intriguing, and masterful, you are playing to the public, giving them something compelling and pleasurable to witness. You are allowing them to project their fantasies onto you, or directing their attention to other theatrical qualities. In your private life, you can let the mask fall. In this diverse, multicultural world, it is best that you learn how to mingle and blend into all types of environments, giving yourself maximum flexibility. You must take pleasure in creating these personas—it will make you a better performer on the public stage.

你必须将人格面具的塑造视为社交智慧的关键要素，而非某种邪恶或魔鬼般的存在。在社交舞台上，我们每个人都戴着面具，扮演着不同的角色以适应不同的环境。你只是越来越意识到这个过程。不妨把它想象成一场戏剧。通过塑造一个神秘、迷人、精湛的人格面具，你就是在向公众表演，为他们提供引人入胜、赏心悦目的表演。你允许他们将自己的幻想投射到你身上，或将他们的注意力引向其他戏剧特质。在私人生活中，你可以摘下面具。在这个多元文化的世界中，你最好学会如何融入各种环境，赋予自己最大的灵活性。你必须乐于塑造这些人格面具——这将使你在公众舞台上表现得更出色。

# ↩

3. See yourself as others see you

3. 像别人看待你一样看待自己

Growing up with autism, Temple Grandin (see chapter 1 , here , for more on this) had much to overcome in life, but by the end of high school she had managed to transform herself—through keen desire and discipline—into a gifted student with a promising future in the sciences. She understood that her greatest weakness was in the social arena. With animals, she had almost telepathic powers to read their moods and desires, but with humans it was the opposite. People were too tricky for her; they often seemed to communicate with one another through subtle, nonverbal cues—for instance, falling into patterns of laughter in a group, according to some interpersonal rhythm she could not fathom. She felt as if she were an alien, watching these strange creatures interact.

坦普·格兰丁（Temple Grandin，详见此处第一章）从小就患有自闭症，在生活中克服了许多困难。但到了高中毕业时，她凭借着强烈的求知欲和严谨的纪律，成功地将自己打造成了一名天才学生，未来在科学领域大有可为。她深知自己最大的弱点在于社交。与动物相处时，她几乎拥有心灵感应的能力，能够读懂它们的情绪和欲望，但与人类相处时却恰恰相反。人对她来说太难对付了；他们似乎常常通过微妙的非语言暗示来沟通——例如，在群体中，他们会根据某种她无法理解的人际节奏，形成一种笑声的模式。看着这些奇异的生物互动，她感觉自己仿佛置身于外星人之中。

It seemed to her that there was nothing she could do about her awkwardness with people. What she could control, however, was her own work. She decided she would make herself so efficient in whatever job she had that her social handicap would not matter. But after graduating college with a degree in animal behavior and entering the work world as a consultant in the design of feedlots and cattle handling facilities, she realized, through a series of mistakes on her part, that this was completely unrealistic.

在她看来，自己与人相处的尴尬似乎无能为力。然而，她能掌控的只有自己的工作。她决定，无论从事什么工作，都要让自己高效，这样社交障碍就不成问题了。然而，大学毕业并获得动物行为学学位后，她以饲养场和牲畜处理设施设计顾问的身份进入职场，经历了一系列错误后，她意识到，这完全不现实。

On one occasion, Grandin had been hired by the manager of a plant to improve its overall design. She did an excellent job, but soon she began to notice that the machinery was constantly breaking down, as if it were the fault of her design. She knew that the malfunctioning could not be because of any flaws in her work, and with further investigation she discovered that the machinery had problems only when a certain man was working in the room. The only possible conclusion was that he was sabotaging the equipment to make her look bad. This made no sense to her—why would he deliberately work against the interests of the company that employed him? This was not a design problem she could solve intellectually. She simply had to give up and leave the job.

有一次，格兰丁受雇于一家工厂的经理，负责改进工厂的整体设计。她工作出色，但很快她就发现机器经常出故障，仿佛是她设计的错。她知道故障不可能是她工作上的瑕疵，经过进一步调查，她发现只有当某个男人在房间里工作时，机器才会出问题。唯一可能的解释是，他故意破坏设备，让她难堪。这让她百思不得其解——他为什么要故意损害公司利益？这不是她能够用理智解决的设计问题。她只能放弃，辞去这份工作。

On another occasion, a plant engineer had hired her to fix a particular problem, but after a few weeks on the job she noticed that there were other parts of the factory that were very poorly designed and clearly dangerous. She wrote to the president of the company to point this out. Her tone in the letter was a bit brusque, but she was annoyed that people could be so blind to such design issues. A few days later she was fired. Although no explanation was given, it was clear that her letter to the president must have been the cause.

还有一次，一位工厂工程师雇她来解决一个问题，但工作几周后，她发现工厂里其他一些部分设计得很差，显然存在危险。她写信给公司总裁指出了这一点。信中她的语气略显生硬，但她对人们竟然对这些设计问题如此视而不见感到恼火。几天后，她被解雇了。虽然没有给出任何解释，但很明显，她写给总裁的信一定是导致这一事件的原因。

As she mulled over these incidents, and other similar ones that had marred her career, she felt that the source of the problem had to be herself. She had known for years that she often did things that rubbed people the wrong way, and that they avoided her for that reason. In the past she had tried to go about her life ignoring this painful reality, but now her social deficiencies were threatening her ability to make a living.

当她仔细思考这些事件以及其他类似的损害她职业生涯的事件时，她觉得问题的根源肯定在她自己身上。多年来，她一直知道自己经常做一些惹恼别人的事情，而人们也因此而疏远她。过去，她曾试图无视这个痛苦的现实，继续生活，但现在，她的社交缺陷正威胁着她的谋生能力。

Ever since she was a child, Grandin had the peculiar ability to see herself from the outside, as if she were looking at another person. It was more of a sensation that would come and go, but as an adult she realized she could use this gift for practical effect, by looking at her past mistakes as if watching another person in action.

格兰丁从小就拥有一种奇特的能力，能从外部审视自己，仿佛在观察另一个人。这种感觉时有时无，但成年后，她意识到自己可以运用这种天赋，就像观察另一个人的行为一样，审视自己过去的错误。

For instance, in the case of the man who had sabotaged the machinery, she could clearly recall how she had barely interacted with him and the other engineers, and how she had made a point of doing everything herself. She could see in her mind the meetings in which she had presented her design ideas with rigorous logic and not opened them up for discussion. In the case of the letter to the president, she could recall how she had bluntly criticized people in front of their peers and had made no attempt to interact with the man who had hired her. Visualizing these moments with such clarity, she could finally understand the problem—she was making her coworkers feel insecure, useless, and inferior. She had injured their male egos and had paid a price.

例如，在那个破坏机器的男人的案例中，她清晰地记得自己几乎与他和其他工程师没有任何交流，而且她总是事必躬亲。她还能在脑海中浮现出那些会议，在会上她用严谨的逻辑阐述了自己的设计理念，却没有公开讨论。在写给总裁的信的案例中，她还记得自己如何在同事面前直言不讳地批评别人，却从未尝试与雇佣她的那位男士沟通。清晰地回想起这些瞬间，她终于明白了问题所在——她让同事们感到不安全、无用和自卑。她伤害了他们的男性自尊，并为此付出了代价。

Her realization of what had gone wrong did not stem from empathy as it might have for other people—it was an intellectual exercise, like solving a puzzle or a design problem. But because her emotions were not so deeply involved, it was easier to go through the process and make the necessary corrections. In the future, she would discuss her ideas with engineers, involve them as much as possible in her work, and never directly criticize people for anything. She would practice this in every subsequent job until it became second nature.

她意识到问题所在，并非源于对其他人可能产生的同理心——这是一种智力活动，就像解决一个谜题或一个设计问题一样。但由于她的情绪没有被深深地牵扯进去，所以更容易理解整个过程并做出必要的修正。以后，她会和工程师们讨论自己的想法，尽可能让他们参与到工作中来，并且永远不要直接批评别人。她会在之后的每一份工作中都练习这一点，直到它成为她的第二天性。

Slowly, developing social intelligence in her own way, Temple ironed out much of her awkwardness and her career prospered. In the 1990s, as she grew famous, she was increasingly invited to give talks—initially about her experiences as a professional who had overcome autism, and later as an expert on animal behavior.

坦普尔以自己的方式慢慢提升社交智力，克服了大部分尴尬，事业也蒸蒸日上。20世纪90年代，随着她名声渐长，邀请她做讲座的次数也越来越多——最初是讲述她作为一名战胜自闭症的专业人士的经历，后来则讲述她作为动物行为专家的经历。

In giving these talks, she had imagined that they had gone quite well. They were full of information and appropriate slides to illustrate her ideas. But after a few such lectures she was handed the evaluations from the audience, and what she read was shocking. People complained that she made no eye contact, read her talk mechanically from her notes, and did not engage with the audience, to the point of rudeness. The audience had the impression that she was simply repeating the same talk over and over, with the same slides, as if she were a machine.

在做这些演讲时，她原以为效果会很好。演讲内容丰富，幻灯片也恰如其分地阐述了她的观点。但几次这样的演讲之后，她收到了听众的评价，而她所读的内容却令人震惊。人们抱怨她没有眼神交流，机械地照着笔记念讲稿，不与听众互动，甚至到了粗鲁的地步。听众觉得她只是在一遍又一遍地重复同样的演讲，用同样的幻灯片，就像一台机器。

Strangely enough, none of this bothered Temple. In fact, the idea of these evaluations excited her. They gave her a clear and realistic picture of herself as others saw her, and that is all she ever needed for self-correction. She pursued this process with great zeal, determined to transform herself into a skilled lecturer. As enough evaluations came in, she pored over them, looking for patterns and criticisms that made sense. Working from this feedback, she taught herself to mix in anecdotes and even jokes, and to make her slides not so logical and tight. She shortened the length of her talks, trained herself to speak without notes, and made sure to take as many questions as the audience wanted to ask at the end.

奇怪的是，这些评估并没有让她感到困扰。事实上，这些评估让她兴奋不已。它们让她清晰而真实地了解了别人眼中的自己，而这正是她自我修正所需要的一切。她满怀热情地坚持这个过程，决心将自己打造成一名技艺精湛的讲师。收到足够多的评估后，她便会仔细研读，寻找其中合理的模式和批评。根据这些反馈，她学会了在演讲中穿插一些趣闻轶事，甚至笑话，并让自己的幻灯片不那么逻辑严谨、条理分明。她缩短了演讲时长，训练自己不看笔记演讲，并确保在演讲结束时尽可能多地回答观众的提问。

For those who had seen her initial efforts and then attended her lectures years later, it was hard to believe she was the same person. She was now an entertaining and engaging speaker, one who could hold the attention of an audience better than most. They could not imagine how this had come about, which made her transformation seem all the more miraculous.

对于那些见证了她最初的努力，并在多年后再次聆听她讲座的人来说，很难相信她已经是同一个人了。如今的她是一位风趣幽默、引人入胜的演讲者，比大多数人都能更好地吸引听众的注意力。他们无法想象这一切是如何发生的，这让她的转变显得更加神奇。

Almost all of us have social flaws of some sort, ranging from the relatively harmless to those that can get us in trouble. Perhaps it could be that we talk too much, or are too honest in our criticisms of people, or take offense too easily when others do not respond positively to our ideas. If we repeat instances of such behavior often enough, we tend to offend people without ever really knowing why. The reason for this is twofold: first, we are quick to discern the mistakes and defects of others, but when it comes to ourselves we are generally too emotional and insecure to look squarely at our own. Second, people rarely tell us the truth about what it is that we do wrong. They are afraid to cause conflict or to be viewed as mean-spirited. And so it becomes very difficult for us to perceive our flaws, let alone correct them.

我们几乎所有人都或多或少地存在一些社交缺陷，有些相对无害，有些则会给我们带来麻烦。我们或许话太多，或许批评别人过于坦诚，又或许当别人对我们的想法没有积极回应时，我们很容易生气。如果我们经常重复这样的行为，我们往往会冒犯别人，却始终不知道原因。原因有两个：首先，我们能很快地发现别人的错误和缺点，但当涉及到我们自己时，我们通常过于情绪化和缺乏安全感，无法直面自己的错误。其次，人们很少告诉我们真相，告诉我们我们做错了什么。他们害怕引发冲突，或者被视为心胸狭窄。因此，我们很难察觉自己的缺点，更不用说改正它们了。

We sometimes have the experience of doing work that we consider to be quite brilliant, and then are rather shocked when we receive feedback from others who do not see it the same way at all. In such moments we are made aware of the discrepancy between our emotional and subjective relationship to our own work, and the response of others who view it with complete detachment, capable of pointing out flaws we could never see. The same discrepancy, however, exists on the social level. People see our behavior from the outside, and their view of us is never what we imagine it to be. To have the power to see ourselves through the eyes of others would be of immense benefit to our social intelligence. We could begin to correct the flaws that offend, to see the role that we play in creating any kind of negative dynamic, and to have a more realistic assessment of who we are.

我们有时会有这样的经历：我们自认为做得非常出色，但当收到来自他人截然不同的反馈时，我们却感到震惊。在这样的时刻，我们意识到，我们对自身工作的情感和主观感受与他人的反馈之间存在着巨大的差异，后者以完全客观的视角看待我们的工作，能够指出我们从未发现的缺陷。然而，同样的差异也存在于社会层面。人们从外部看待我们的行为，他们对我们的看法从来都不是我们所想象的那样。能够通过他人的视角看待自己，将极大地提升我们的社交智力。我们可以开始改正那些令人不快的缺陷，认识到我们在造成任何负面动态中所扮演的角色，并更现实地评估自己。

To see ourselves objectively, we must follow the example of Temple Grandin. We can begin this process by looking at negative events in our past—people sabotaging our work, bosses firing us for no logical reason, nasty personal battles with colleagues. It is best to start with events that are at least several months old, and thus not so emotionally charged. In dissecting these occurrences, we must focus on what we did that either triggered or worsened the dynamic. In looking at several such incidents, we might begin to see a pattern that indicates a particular flaw in our character. Seeing these events from the perspective of the other people involved will loosen the lock our emotions have on our self-image, and help us understand the role we play in our own mistakes. We can also elicit opinions from those we trust about our behavior, making certain to first reassure them that we want their criticisms. Slowly, in this way, we can develop increasing self-detachment, which will yield us the other half of social intelligence—the ability to see ourselves as we really are.

要客观地看待自己，我们必须效仿坦普·格兰丁。我们可以从回顾过去的负面事件开始——有人破坏我们的工作，老板无缘无故地解雇我们，以及与同事之间激烈的个人争吵。最好从至少几个月前发生的事件开始，这样就不会那么情绪化。在剖析这些事件时，我们必须关注我们做了什么，是触发了这种情绪，还是加剧了这种情绪。回顾几起这样的事件，我们或许能发现一些规律，表明我们性格中存在着某种缺陷。从其他人的角度来看待这些事件，能够打破情绪对自我形象的束缚，帮助我们理解自己在自身错误中所扮演的角色。我们也可以向信任的人征求对我们行为的意见，务必首先让他们明白，我们渴望得到他们的批评。慢慢地，我们就能逐渐培养出对自我的超脱，这将赋予我们社会智力的另一半——看清真实的自我的能力。

# ↩

4. Suffer fools gladly

4. 乐意忍受愚人

In 1775, the twenty-six-year-old German poet and novelist Johann Wolfgang Goethe (later von Goethe) was invited to spend some time at the court of Weimar by its eighteen-year-old Duke Karl August. The duke’s family had been trying to transform the isolated and less renowned duchy of Weimar into a literary center, and the addition of Goethe to their court would be a great coup. Shortly after his arrival, the duke offered him a prominent position in his cabinet and the role of personal adviser, and so Goethe decided to stay. The poet saw this as a way to broaden his experience in the world and perhaps apply some enlightened ideas to the government of Weimar.

1775年，二十六岁的德国诗人兼小说家约翰·沃尔夫冈·歌德（后改名为冯·歌德）受十八岁的魏玛公爵卡尔·奥古斯特邀请，前往魏玛宫廷居住一段时间。公爵家族一直致力于将与世隔绝、名声不佳的魏玛公国打造成文学中心，而歌德的加入无疑将带来巨大的成功。歌德抵达后不久，公爵便在内阁中提拔他为重要职位，并任命他为私人顾问，于是歌德决定留下来。这位诗人认为，这是拓展人生阅历，或许还能将一些开明思想应用于魏玛政府的良机。

Goethe came from a solid middle-class background, and had never really spent much time around nobility. Now, as a prized member of the duke’s court, he was to have his apprenticeship in aristocratic manners. After only a few short months, however, he found court life quite unbearable. The lives of the courtiers revolved around rituals of card games, shooting parties, and the exchanging of endless bits of gossip. A passing remark by Herr X, or the failure of Frau Y to show up at a soirée, would be blown up into something of great importance, and courtiers would strain to interpret the meaning of it. After attending the theater they would chat endlessly about who had shown up accompanied by whom, or dissect the look of the new actress on the scene, but they would never discuss the play itself.

歌德出身于稳固的中产阶级家庭，从未真正与贵族相处过。如今，作为公爵宫廷中备受珍视的成员，他即将开始学习贵族礼仪。然而，短短几个月后，他就发现宫廷生活令人难以忍受。廷臣们的生活充斥着纸牌游戏、狩猎聚会以及无休止的闲聊。某先生的一句随口之语，或是某女士未能出席晚会，都会被夸大成一件大事，廷臣们会竭力解读其中的含义。看完戏后，他们会没完没了地谈论谁和谁一起来的，或是分析新上场女演员的造型，但从不讨论戏剧本身。

In conversation, if Goethe dared to discuss some reform he was considering, suddenly a courtier would get all up in arms about what this might mean for a particular minister, and how it could jeopardize his position within the court, and Goethe’s idea would get lost in the ensuing heated dialog. Even though he was the author of the most famous novel of the day, The Sorrows of Young Werther , nobody seemed particularly interested in his opinions. They found it more interesting to tell the celebrated novelist their own ideas and to see his reaction. In the end, their interests seemed constricted to the claustrophobic court and its intrigues.

在谈话中，如果歌德胆敢谈论他正在考虑的某项改革，就会突然有朝臣勃然大怒，质疑这可能对某位大臣意味着什么，以及这会如何危及他在宫廷中的地位。歌德的想法往往会在随后的激烈争论中被淹没。尽管他是当时最著名的小说《少年维特的烦恼》的作者，但似乎没有人对他的观点特别感兴趣。他们觉得更有趣的是向这位著名小说家讲述自己的想法，并观察他的反应。最终，他们的兴趣似乎局限于令人窒息的宫廷及其阴谋诡计。

Goethe felt trapped—he had accepted a position with the duke and took it most seriously, but he found it hard to tolerate the social life to which he was now condemned. As a confirmed realist in life, however, he found it useless to complain about what he could not change. And so, accepting his fellow courtiers as his companions for the next few years, Goethe devised a strategy, making a virtue out of necessity: He would talk very little, rarely venturing an opinion on anything. He would get his interlocutors to go on and on and about this or that subject. He would wear a pleasant mask as he listened, but inwardly he would observe them as if they were figures in a stage play. They would reveal to him their secrets, their petty dramas, and their inane ideas, and all the while he would smile and always take their side.

歌德感到自己陷入了困境——他接受了公爵的职位，并认真对待，但他发现难以忍受如今注定要经历的社交生活。然而，作为一个坚定的现实主义者，他发现抱怨那些无法改变的事情毫无意义。于是，在接下来的几年里，歌德接受了他的廷臣同伴作为自己的同伴，并制定了一个策略，将需要变成了美德：他很少说话，很少对任何事情发表意见。他会让对话者滔滔不绝地谈论这个或那个话题。他戴着一副和蔼的面具倾听，但内心却像观察舞台剧中的人物一样观察着他们。他们会向他吐露他们的秘密、他们的琐碎戏剧和他们愚蠢的想法，而他则始终微笑着，始终站在他们一边。

What the courtiers did not realize was that they were supplying him with endless material—for characters, bits of dialogue, and stories of folly that would fill the plays and novels he was to write in the future. In this way he transformed his social frustrations into a most productive and pleasant game.

朝臣们没有意识到，他们为他提供了无尽的素材——人物、对话片段和荒诞故事，这些都充斥着他未来创作的戏剧和小说。就这样，他将自己在社交方面的挫败感转化为一场极其富有成效、令人愉悦的游戏。

The great Austrian-American film director Josef von Sternberg (1894–1969) had risen from studio errand boy to become one of the most successful directors in Hollywood during the 1920s and ’30s. He developed along the way a particular philosophy that would serve him well throughout his directorial career, which would last into the 1950s: all that mattered was the final product. His role was to get everyone on the same page and guide the production according to the vision he had, employing whatever means necessary to get the results he wanted. And the greatest impediment to realizing his vision came inevitably from the actors. They thought first and foremost of their careers. The film as a whole mattered less than the attention they received for their part. This would make them try to steal the limelight, and in the process they would alter the quality of the film. With such actors, von Sternberg would have to find a way to trick or beguile them into doing his bidding.

伟大的奥地利裔美国电影导演约瑟夫·冯·斯登堡（1894-1969）从制片厂的跑腿小弟一跃成为20世纪二三十年代好莱坞最成功的导演之一。他在此过程中形成了一套独特的理念，并贯穿了他的整个导演生涯，直至20世纪50年代：最终成品才是最重要的。他的职责是让每个人都达成共识，并根据自己的设想指导制作，不惜一切代价来达到他想要的效果。而实现他愿景的最大障碍不可避免地来自演员。他们首先考虑的是自己的职业生涯。整部电影的重要性远不及他们因角色而获得的关注。这会促使他们试图抢风头，并在此过程中影响影片的质量。面对这样的演员，冯·斯登堡必须想方设法地欺骗或诱骗他们为他效力。

In 1930, von Sternberg was invited to Berlin to direct what would be his most famous film, The Blue Angel , which would feature the world-renowned actor Emil Jannings. In looking for the female lead for the film, von Sternberg discovered a relatively unknown German actress named Marlene Dietrich, whom he would go on to direct in seven feature films, singlehandedly transforming her into a star. Von Sternberg had worked with Jannings before and knew that the actor was an impossibly foolish person. Jannings did everything he could to disrupt the flow of the production. He took as a personal affront any attempt by the director to direct him. His whole method was to goad the director into useless battles and wear him down until he relented and let Jannings do as he wished.

1930年，冯·斯登堡受邀前往柏林执导他最著名的影片《蓝天使》，该片由世界著名演员埃米尔·强宁斯主演。在寻找女主角的过程中，冯·斯登堡发现了一位名不见经传的德国女演员玛琳·黛德丽。之后，他又执导了她七部故事片，并凭借一己之力将她打造成了明星。冯·斯登堡之前曾与强宁斯合作过，他知道这位演员愚蠢至极。强宁斯竭尽所能地扰乱影片的制作流程。导演任何试图指挥他的举动，他都视为对他个人的侮辱。他的伎俩就是激怒导演，让他与导演进行无谓的争吵，直到导演屈服，让强宁斯为所欲为。

Von Sternberg was prepared for all of this and went to war in his own way. He steeled himself against Jannings’s childish games. Jannings demanded that the director show up every morning in his dressing room to reassure the actor of his undying love and admiration for his work—von Sternberg did this without complaint. He asked that the director take him to lunch every day and listen to his ideas about the film—von Sternberg indulged him in this, listening patiently to Jannings’s horrible suggestions. If von Sternberg showed attention to any other actor, Jannings would throw a jealous fit, and von Sternberg would have to act the role of the contrite spouse. Letting him have his way on these petty matters, he took much of the bite out of Jannings’s strategy. On the set, he would not become entangled in any battles. But since time was of the essence, he would inevitably have to trick the actor into doing what he wanted.

冯·斯登堡对这一切早有准备，并以自己的方式迎战。他坚决抵制詹宁斯幼稚的把戏。詹宁斯要求导演每天早上到他的化妆间，向这位演员保证他对他作品永恒的爱与钦佩——冯·斯登堡对此毫无怨言。他要求导演每天带他去吃午饭，听取他对电影的想法——冯·斯登堡对此百依百顺，耐心倾听詹宁斯那些糟糕的建议。如果冯·斯登堡对其他演员表现出兴趣，詹宁斯就会妒火中烧，而冯·斯登堡则不得不扮演后悔莫及的丈夫的角色。冯·斯登堡在这些琐事上任其所为，大大削弱了詹宁斯的策略。在片场，他不会卷入任何争执。但由于时间紧迫，他不可避免地要哄骗这位演员，让他按自己的意愿行事。

When for some unknown reason Jannings refused to pass through a doorway and make his entrance into a scene, von Sternberg set up the hottest light available to boil the back of his neck every time Jannings stood there, forcing him to pass through. When Jannings declaimed his first scene in the most ridiculously elevated German, von Sternberg congratulated him for his fine tone and said he would be the only person in the film to talk like that, which would make him stand out and look bad, but so be it. Jannings quickly dropped the haughty accent. Whenever he went into a pout and remained in his room, von Sternberg would get the word passed to him that the director was lavishing attention on Marlene Dietrich, which would promptly make the jealous actor hurry to the set to compete for attention. Scene by scene, von Sternberg maneuvered him into the position he desired, managing to extract out of Jannings perhaps the greatest performance of his career.

当詹宁斯不知何故拒绝穿过门口进入场景时，冯·斯登堡每次都会打开最热的灯，让詹宁斯站在那里时后颈都被灼伤，迫使他穿过。当詹宁斯用极其夸张的德语朗诵他的第一场戏时，冯·斯登堡称赞他的音调优美，并说他是电影中唯一一个这样说话的人，这会让他显得格格不入，看起来很糟糕，但就这样吧。詹宁斯很快就放弃了傲慢的口音。每当他撅着嘴留在房间里时，冯·斯登堡就会传话给他，说导演把大量注意力放在了玛琳·黛德丽身上，这就会立刻让这位妒火中烧的演员冲进片场争夺注意力。一幕又一幕，冯·斯登堡把詹宁斯安排到他想要的位置，成功地从詹宁斯身上榨取了也许是他职业生涯中最精彩的表演。

As previously discussed in chapter 2 ( here ), Daniel Everett and his family moved to the heart of the Amazon in 1977, to live among people known as the Pirahã. Everett and his wife were missionaries, and their task was to learn the Pirahã language—which was then considered the hardest in the world to decipher—and to translate the Bible into their indigenous tongue. Slowly, Everett made progress, using the various devices he had been taught in his training in linguistics.

正如之前在第二章（此处）所讨论的，丹尼尔·埃弗里特和他的家人于1977年迁至亚马逊腹地，与皮拉罕人（Pirahã）一起生活。埃弗里特和他的妻子是传教士，他们的任务是学习皮拉罕语——这种语言当时被认为是世界上最难解读的语言——并将《圣经》翻译成他们的母语。埃弗里特运用他在语言学训练中学到的各种技巧，慢慢地取得了进步。

He had studied in depth the works of the great MIT linguist Noam Chomsky, who advocated the idea that all languages are essentially related because grammar itself is hardwired into the human brain, and is part of our genetic code. This would mean that by their nature all languages share the same features. Convinced that Chomsky was correct, Everett worked hard to find these universal features in Pirahã. Over the years of studying it, however, he began to find many exceptions to Chomsky’s theory, and this troubled him.

他深入研究了麻省理工学院伟大的语言学家诺姆·乔姆斯基的著作。乔姆斯基主张所有语言本质上都是相关的，因为语法本身根植于人类大脑，是人类遗传密码的一部分。这意味着所有语言本质上都具有相同的特征。埃弗里特坚信乔姆斯基是正确的，并努力在皮拉罕语中寻找这些普遍特征。然而，在多年的研究中，他开始发现许多与乔姆斯基理论相悖的地方，这让他感到困惑。

After much thought, Everett came to the conclusion that the Pirahã language reflected many peculiarities of their life in the jungle. He determined, for instance, that their culture placed a supreme value on “immediacy of experience”—what was not before their eyes did not exist, and therefore there were almost no words or concepts for things outside immediate experience. In elaborating this concept, he theorized that the basic features of all languages are not simply genetic in origin and universal, but that each language has elements that reflect the uniqueness of its culture. Culture plays a larger role than we might imagine in how we think and communicate.

经过深思熟虑，埃弗里特得出结论：皮拉罕人的语言反映了他们丛林生活的诸多特质。例如，他断定，他们的文化极其重视“体验的直接性”——他们眼中不存在的事物就不存在，因此几乎没有词汇或概念来描述直接经验之外的事物。在阐述这一概念时，他提出理论，认为所有语言的基本特征并非仅仅源于遗传和普遍性，每种语言都包含反映其文化独特性的元素。文化在我们的思维和交流方式中扮演着比我们想象中更大的角色。

In 2005 he finally felt ready to make all of this public, and had an article published in an anthropology journal that expressed these revolutionary ideas. He expected that his findings might stir up some animated discussion, but he was not prepared at all for what would ensue.

2005年，他终于准备好将这一切公之于众，并在一份人类学期刊上发表了一篇文章，表达了这些革命性的观点。他期待着自己的发现能引发一些热烈的讨论，但他对接下来发生的事情毫无准备。

People at MIT (linguists and graduate students) associated with Chomsky began to hound Everett. When he gave a talk at an important symposium at the University of Cambridge about his findings, some of these linguists flew over to attend it. They peppered him with questions meant to poke holes in his ideas and publicly embarrass him. Not ready for this, Everett fumbled and did not handle it well. This continue with subsequent lectures. They zeroed in on any kind of inconsistency in his talk or his writings, and used these inconsistencies to discredit his overall idea. Some of their attacks on him became personal—they publicly called him a charlatan, and questioned his motives. Even Chomsky himself implied that Everett was out for fame and money.

麻省理工学院里与乔姆斯基关系密切的人（语言学家和研究生）开始纠缠埃弗雷特。当他在剑桥大学一个重要的研讨会上就自己的研究成果发表演讲时，一些语言学家特地飞过来旁听。他们接二连三地向他提出问题，试图戳穿他的观点，并让他当众出丑。埃弗雷特对此毫无准备，笨手笨脚地应对，没有妥善处理。这种情况在之后的讲座中依然存在。他们抓住埃弗雷特演讲或著作中任何前后矛盾之处，并利用这些矛盾来诋毁他的整体观点。有些攻击甚至演变成人身攻击——他们公开称他为骗子，并质疑他的动机。就连乔姆斯基本人也暗示埃弗雷特一心追求名利。

When Everett published his first book, Don’t Sleep, There are Snakes , some of these linguists wrote letters to critics who were going to review it, trying to dissuade them from even discussing his material—it was too far below academic standards, they claimed. They went so far as to put pressure on National Public Radio, which was about to do a large segment on Everett. The show was canceled.

埃弗里特出版他的处女作《别睡觉，蛇在那儿》（Don’t Sleep, There are Snakes）时，一些语言学家写信给那些打算评论这本书的评论家，试图劝阻他们甚至不要讨论他的内容——他们声称，这本书远远不符合学术标准。他们甚至向美国国家公共广播电台（National Public Radio）施压，当时该电台正准备制作一个关于埃弗里特的大型节目。结果节目被取消了。

At first Everett could not help but become emotional. What his detractors were bringing up in their arguments did not discredit his theory, but merely revealed some possible weak points. They seemed less interested in the truth and more concerned with making him look bad. Quickly, however, he moved past this emotional stage and began to use these attacks for his own purpose—they forced him to make sure everything he wrote was airtight; they made him rethink and strengthen his arguments. He could hear their possible criticisms in his head, and he addressed them one by one in his subsequent writings. This made him a better writer and thinker, and the controversy they stirred up only increased the sales of Don’t Sleep, There are Snakes , winning many converts to his argument in the process. In the end, he came to welcome the attacks of his enemies for how much they had improved his work and toughened him up.

起初，埃弗里特忍不住情绪激动。批评者们提出的论点并没有让他的理论失去可信度，只是暴露了一些可能的弱点。他们似乎对真相不太感兴趣，更关心的是让他丢脸。然而，他很快就过了情绪化的阶段，开始利用这些攻击来达到自己的目的——它们迫使他确保自己所写的一切都无懈可击；它们迫使他重新思考并强化自己的论点。他能清晰地听到他们可能提出的批评，并在随后的写作中逐一回应。这让他成为了一名更优秀的作家和思想家，而他们引发的争议也增加了《别睡觉，有蛇》的销量，并在此过程中赢得了许多人的支持。最终，他开始欢迎敌人的攻击，因为他们极大地改进了他的作品，让他变得更加坚强。

In the course of your life you will be continually encountering fools. There are simply too many to avoid. We can classify people as fools by the following rubric: when it comes to practical life, what should matter is getting long-term results, and getting the work done in as efficient and creative a manner as possible. That should be the supreme value that guides people’s actions. But fools carry with them a different scale of values. They place more importance on short-term matters—grabbing immediate money, getting attention from the public or media, and looking good. They are ruled by their ego and insecurities. They tend to enjoy drama and political intrigue for their own sake. When they criticize, they always emphasize matters that are irrelevant to the overall picture or argument. They are more interested in their career and position than in the truth. You can distinguish them by how little they get done, or by how hard they make it for others to get results. They lack a certain common sense, getting worked up about things that are not really important while ignoring problems that will spell doom in the long term.

在你的一生中，你会不断遇到傻瓜。他们实在太多了，难以避免。我们可以按照以下标准来划分傻瓜：在实际生活中，真正重要的是取得长远成果，并尽可能高效、有创意地完成工作。这应该是指导人们行动的最高价值观。但傻瓜的价值观却截然不同。他们更看重短期利益——攫取眼前的利益，吸引公众或媒体的关注，以及展现良好的形象。他们被自我和不安全感所支配。他们往往为了自己的利益而沉迷于戏剧性和政治阴谋。当他们提出批评时，他们总是强调与全局或论点无关的事情。他们对自己的事业和地位比对真相更感兴趣。你可以通过他们完成的事情有多少，或者他们给他人带来多大的困难来区分他们。他们缺乏一定的常识，对一些并不真正重要的事情感到烦恼，而忽视那些从长远来看会带来灾难的问题。

The natural tendency with fools is to lower yourself to their level. They annoy you, get under your skin, and draw you into a battle. In the process, you feel petty and confused. You lose a sense of what is really important. You can’t win an argument or get them to see your side or change their behavior, because rationality and results don’t matter to them. You simply waste valuable time and emotional energy.

愚人天生就会把自己降低到他们的水平。他们会惹你生气，让你心烦意乱，把你卷入争吵。在这个过程中，你会感到自己渺小而困惑。你会失去判断力，不知道什么才是真正重要的。你赢不了争论，也拿他们没办法，让他们站在你这边，或者改变他们的行为，因为他们不在乎理性和结果。你只会浪费宝贵的时间和情感。

In dealing with fools you must adopt the following philosophy: they are simply a part of life, like rocks or furniture. All of us have foolish sides, moments in which we lose our heads and think more of our ego or short-term goals. It is human nature. Seeing this foolishness within you, you can then accept it in others. This will allow you to smile at their antics, to tolerate their presence as you would a silly child, and to avoid the madness of trying to change them. It is all part of the human comedy, and it is nothing to get upset about or lose sleep over. This attitude—“Suffer Fools Gladly”—should be forged in your Apprenticeship Phase, during which you are almost certainly going to encounter this type. If they are causing you trouble, you must neutralize the harm they do by keeping a steady eye on your goals and what is important, and ignoring them if you can. The height of wisdom, however, is to take this even further and to actually exploit their foolishness—using them for material for your work, as examples of things to avoid, or by looking for ways to turn their actions to your advantage. In this way, their foolishness plays into your hands, helping you achieve the kind of practical results they seem to disdain.

对待傻瓜，你必须秉持以下理念：他们只是生活的一部分，就像石头或家具一样。我们每个人都有愚蠢的一面，有时会失去理智，更多地考虑自我或短期目标。这是人之常情。看到自己身上的这种愚蠢，你就能接受别人身上的这种愚蠢。这会让你对他们的滑稽行为报以微笑，像对待一个傻乎乎的孩子一样容忍他们的存在，并避免试图改变他们的疯狂行为。这都是人类喜剧的一部分，没什么好生气或失眠的。这种“欣然接受傻瓜”的态度应该在你的学徒阶段培养，在此期间，你几乎肯定会遇到这种类型的人。如果他们给你带来麻烦，你必须通过专注于你的目标和重要的事情来抵消他们造成的伤害，并尽可能地忽略他们。然而，智慧的顶峰在于更进一步，真正利用他们的愚蠢——利用他们作为你工作的素材，作为应该避免的事情的范例，或者寻找方法将他们的行为转化为你的优势。这样，他们的愚蠢就被你利用了，帮助你取得了他们似乎不屑一顾的实际成果。

REVERSAL

逆转

While studying for his PhD at Harvard University in Computer Science, Paul Graham (b. 1964) discovered something about himself: he had a profound distaste for any kind of politicking or social maneuvering. (For more on Graham, see here .) He was not good at it, and it irritated him to no end to be dragged into situations in which others behaved manipulatively. His brief encounter with politics within the department convinced him he was not cut out for a life in academia. This lesson became strengthened a few years later when he went to work for a software company. Almost everything they did was irrational—firing the original tech people, making a salesperson the head of the company, creating too long a time between releases of new products. All of these bad choices came about because in a group, politics and ego often trump sound decision making.

在哈佛大学攻读计算机科学博士学位期间，保罗·格雷厄姆（生于 1964 年）发现了自己的一些特点：他非常厌恶任何形式的政治活动或社交手腕。（有关格雷厄姆的更多信息，请参见此处。）他不擅长这些，而且被卷入其他人玩弄手腕的境地让他非常恼火。他在系里与政治斗争的短暂接触让他确信自己不适合从事学术工作。几年后，当他进入一家软件公司工作时，这一认识得到了进一步的强化。他们做的几乎所有事情都是不合理的——解雇原来的技术人员，让销售人员担任公司负责人，在新产品发布之间设置过长的时间间隔。所有这些糟糕的选择都是因为在一个团队中，政治和自负往往会压倒合理的决策。

Unable to tolerate this, he came up with his own solution: as much as possible, he would avoid any environment that involved politicking. This meant sticking to doing startups on the smallest scale—a constraint that made him disciplined and creative. Later, when he founded Y Combinator , a kind of apprenticeship system for tech startups, he could not prevent the company from growing in size—it was too successful. His solution was twofold: One, he had his wife and partner in the company, Jessica Livingston, handle all of the tricky social situations, since she possessed a high level of social intelligence. Two, he maintained a very loose, non-bureaucratic structure to the company.

他无法忍受这种情况，于是想出了自己的解决办法：尽可能避免任何涉及政治活动的环境。这意味着他坚持以最小的规模创业——这种限制让他更加自律，也更加富有创造力。后来，他创立了Y Combinator，一个面向科技初创企业的学徒制系统，却无法阻止公司规模的扩大——它太成功了。他的解决方案有两个方面：第一，他让妻子兼公司合伙人杰西卡·利文斯顿（Jessica Livingston）处理所有棘手的社交场合，因为她拥有很高的社交智商。第二，他保持了公司非常松散、非官僚的架构。

If, like Graham, you simply do not have the patience that is required for managing and mastering the more subtle and manipulative sides of human nature, then your best answer is to keep yourself away from those situations as best as possible. This will rule out working in groups larger than a handful of people—above a certain number, political considerations inevitably rise to the surface. This means working for yourself or on very small startups.

如果你像格雷厄姆一样，缺乏管理和掌控人性中更微妙、更易操控的一面所需的耐心，那么最好的办法就是尽可能远离这些情况。这样就避免了在人数超过一小撮人的团队中工作——人数超过一定数量，政治考量就不可避免地会浮现出来。这意味着你不适合为自己工作，或者在规模很小的初创公司工作。

Even still, it is generally wise to try to gain the rudiments of social intelligence—to be able to read and recognize the sharks, and to charm and disarm difficult people. The reason is that no matter how hard you might try to avoid situations that call for such knowledge, the world is one large teeming court of intrigue, and it will inevitably pull you in. Your conscious attempt to opt out of the system will retard your apprenticeship in social intelligence and can make you vulnerable to the worst forms of naïveté, with all of the disasters that are likely to ensue.

即便如此，尝试掌握社交智力的基础知识——能够解读和识别“鲨鱼”，并迷惑和化解难缠之人的敌意——通常仍是明智之举。原因在于，无论你多么努力地回避需要这些知识的场合，这个世界仍然是一个充满阴谋诡计的大舞台，它最终会把你卷入其中。你刻意选择脱离这个体系，会阻碍你学习社交智力，并可能使你容易受到最恶劣的天真行为的影响，最终酿成各种灾难。

It is a great folly to hope that other men will harmonize with us; I have never hoped this. I have always regarded each man as an independent individual, whom I endeavored to understand with all his peculiarities, but from whom I desired no further sympathy. In this way have I been enabled to converse with every man, and thus alone is produced the knowledge of various characters and the dexterity necessary for the conduct of life.

指望别人能与我们和睦相处是极其愚蠢的；我从未如此奢望过。我一直视每个人为独立的个体，我努力去理解他的一切特质，但我并不奢望从他身上获得更多的同情。正是通过这种方式，我才得以与每个人交谈，也正是如此，我才得以了解不同的性格，并拥有处世处世所需的智慧。

—J OHANN W OLFGANG VON G OETHE

-约翰·沃尔夫冈·冯·歌德

V

五

AWAKEN THE
唤醒
DIMENSIONAL MIND:
维度思维：
THE CREATIVE-ACTIVE
创造与活跃

As you accumulate more skills and internalize the rules that govern your field, your mind will want to become more active, seeking to use this knowledge in ways that are more suited to your inclinations. What will impede this natural creative dynamic from flourishing is not a lack of talent, but your attitude. Feeling anxious and insecure, you will tend to turn conservative with your knowledge, preferring to fit into the group and sticking to the procedures you have learned. Instead, you must force yourself in the opposite direction. As you emerge from your apprenticeship, you must become increasingly bold. Instead of feeling complacent about what you know, you must expand your knowledge to related fields, giving your mind fuel to make new associations between different ideas. You must experiment and look at problems from all possible angles. As your thinking grows more fluid your mind will become increasingly dimensional, seeing more and more aspects of reality. In the end, you will turn against the very rules you have internalized, shaping and reforming them to suit your spirit. Such originality will bring you to the heights of power.

随着你积累更多技能，并将领域规则内化，你的思维会变得更加活跃，寻求以更符合你偏好的方式运用这些知识。阻碍这种与生俱来的创造力蓬勃发展的，并非缺乏天赋，而是你的态度。焦虑和不安全感会让你倾向于保守地运用你的知识，更倾向于融入群体，固守你已学的规矩。相反，你必须强迫自己反其道而行之。当你走出学徒期，你必须变得更加大胆。你不应该满足于你所掌握的知识，而应该将你的知识扩展到相关领域，为你的思维注入新的活力，在不同的想法之间建立新的联系。你必须不断尝试，从所有可能的角度看待问题。随着你的思维变得更加流畅，你的思维将变得更加立体，能够洞察现实的更多面向。最终，你将打破你内化的规则，并根据你的精神世界来塑造和改造它们。这种独创性将引领你走向权力的巅峰。

THE SECOND TRANSFORMATION

第二次转变

From the moment he was born, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–91) was surrounded by music. His father, Leopold, was a violinist and composer in the court of Salzburg, Austria, as well as a music instructor. All during the day, Wolfgang would hear Leopold and his students practicing in the house. In 1759, his seven-year-old sister Maria Anna began taking piano lessons from their father. She showed great promise and practiced at all hours. Wolfgang, enchanted by the simple melodies that she played, began to hum along to the music; he would sometimes sit at the family’s harpsichord and try to imitate what his sister had played. Leopold could soon detect something unusual in his son. For a three-year-old, the child had a remarkable memory for melody and an impeccable sense of rhythm, all without having had any instruction.

沃尔夫冈·阿马德乌斯·莫扎特（1756-1791）从出生起就被音乐包围着。他的父亲利奥波德是奥地利萨尔茨堡宫廷的小提琴手兼作曲家，同时也是一位音乐教师。沃尔夫冈整天都能听到利奥波德和他的学生们在家里练习。1759年，他七岁的妹妹玛丽亚·安娜开始跟父亲学习钢琴。她表现出了极高的天赋，整天练习。沃尔夫冈被她弹奏的简单旋律迷住了，开始跟着哼唱；他有时会坐在家里的大键琴前，试着模仿姐姐的弹奏。利奥波德很快就发现了儿子身上一些不同寻常的东西。对于一个三岁的孩子来说，这个孩子拥有惊人的旋律记忆力和无可挑剔的节奏感，而这一切都是无需任何指导就能做到的。

Although he had never attempted to teach someone so young, Leopold decided to begin teaching piano to Wolfgang when he turned four, and after only a few sessions he realized the boy had other interesting qualities. Wolfgang listened more deeply than other students, his mind and body completely absorbed in the music. With such intensity of focus, he learned more quickly than other children. Once when he was five years old, he stole a rather complicated exercise meant for Maria Anna, and within thirty minutes he could play it with ease. He had heard Maria Anna practice the piece, and remembering it vividly, the moment he saw the notes on the page he could rapidly reproduce the music.

尽管利奥波德从未尝试教过这么小的孩子，但他还是决定在沃尔夫冈四岁时开始教他钢琴。仅仅几节课之后，他就发现这个男孩还有其他有趣的特质。沃尔夫冈比其他学生听得更认真，他的身心完全沉浸在音乐中。如此专注的专注力，让他学得比其他孩子更快。五岁时，他偷了一首原本要给玛丽亚·安娜弹的相当复杂的练习曲，不到三十分钟就能轻松弹奏。他听过玛丽亚·安娜练习这首曲子，并且记忆犹新，一看到乐谱上的音符，就能快速地弹奏出来。

This remarkable focus had its roots in something that Leopold saw almost from the beginning—the boy had an intense love of music itself. His eyes would light up with excitement the moment Leopold laid out a new challenging piece for him to conquer. If the piece was new and hard to figure out, he would attack it day and night with such tenacity that it would soon become part of his repertoire. At night, his parents would have to force him to stop practicing and send him to bed. This love of practice only seemed to increase with the years. When it came time to play with other children, he would find a way to transform a simple game into something that involved music. His favorite game, however, was to take some piece he had been playing and improvise on it, giving it a personal flair that was quite charming and inventive.

这种非凡的专注力源于利奥波德几乎从一开始就发现的一点——这个男孩对音乐本身有着强烈的热爱。每当利奥波德摆出一首新的、颇具挑战性的乐曲让他征服时，他的眼睛里总会闪烁着兴奋的光芒。如果乐曲新颖难懂，他会日夜坚持不懈地练习，很快这首乐曲就成了他的必备曲目。晚上，父母不得不强迫他停止练习，让他上床睡觉。这种对练习的热爱似乎与日俱增。等到和其他孩子一起玩的时候，他总能想办法把简单的游戏变成与音乐相关的活动。然而，他最喜欢的游戏，却是拿出他正在演奏的乐曲，进行即兴创作，赋予它一种充满魅力和创意的个人风格。

From his earliest years, Wolfgang was exceptionally emotional and sensitive. His moods would swing wildly—he would be petulant one moment, highly affectionate the next. He had a perpetually anxious look on his face that would only disappear when he sat down at the piano; then he was in his element, losing himself in the music.

沃尔夫冈从小就异常情绪化和敏感。他的情绪起伏不定——一会儿任性，一会儿又热情似火。他脸上总是挂着焦虑的表情，只有当他坐在钢琴前时，这种表情才会消散；那时，他便进入状态，沉浸在音乐之中。

One day in 1762, as Leopold Mozart heard his two children playing a piece for two pianos, an idea came to him. His daughter Maria Anna was a very talented piano player in her own right, and Wolfgang was a veritable marvel. Together, they were like precious toys. They had a natural charisma, and Wolfgang had a showman’s flair. As a mere court musician, Leopold’s income was rather limited, but he could see the potential for making a fortune through his children. And so, thinking this through, he decided to take his family on a grand tour of the capitals of Europe, playing before royal courts and the public and charging money for the entertainment. To add to the spectacle, he dressed the children up—Maria Anna as a princess, and Wolfgang as a court minister, complete with wig, elaborate waistcoat, and a sword dangling from his belt.

1762年的一天，利奥波德·莫扎特听到他的两个孩子在演奏一首双钢琴曲，一个念头油然而生。他的女儿玛丽亚·安娜本身就是一位才华横溢的钢琴家，而沃尔夫冈则是一位真正的天才。他们就像珍贵的玩具。他们拥有与生俱来的魅力，而沃尔夫冈则拥有表演天赋。作为一名宫廷乐师，利奥波德的收入相当有限，但他看到了通过孩子们发财的潜力。于是，经过深思熟虑，他决定带着家人在欧洲各国首都进行一次盛大的巡演，在宫廷和公众面前演奏，并收取演出费用。为了增添视觉效果，他把孩子们打扮得漂漂亮亮——玛丽亚·安娜扮成公主，沃尔夫冈则扮成宫廷大臣，戴着假发，穿着精致的马甲，腰带上还挂着一把宝剑。

They began in Vienna, where the children charmed the Austrian emperor and empress. They then spent months in Paris, where they played for the royal court and Wolfgang bounced on the knee of the delighted King Louis XV. They continued to London where they ended up staying for over a year, playing before all kinds of large crowds. And while the sight of the two children in their costumes charmed audiences enough, Wolfgang’s playing astounded them. He had developed numerous parlor tricks, stage-managed by his father. He would play a minuet on a keyboard that was hidden from his view by a cloth, using only one finger. He would deftly sight-read the latest composition by a famous composer. He would play his own compositions—it was impressive to hear a sonata composed by a seven-year-old, no matter how simple it was. Most marvelous of all, Wolfgang could play at an incredible speed, his tiny fingers flying over the keyboard.

他们从维也纳出发，在那里，这两个孩子迷住了奥地利皇帝和皇后。随后，他们在巴黎待了几个月，为宫廷演奏，沃尔夫冈在欣喜若狂的路易十五国王的膝盖上蹦蹦跳跳。他们继续前往伦敦，在那里一待就是一年多，为各种各样的大批观众表演。虽然两个孩子穿着戏服的样子已经足够吸引观众，但沃尔夫冈的演奏更让他们惊叹不已。在父亲的指导下，他发明了许多客厅魔术。他会用一根手指在用布遮住视线的键盘上弹奏小步舞曲。他会熟练地视奏著名作曲家的最新作品。他会演奏自己的作品——听到一个七岁孩子创作的奏鸣曲，无论它有多简单，都令人印象深刻。最令人惊奇的是，沃尔夫冈的演奏速度惊人，他的小手指在键盘上飞快地移动。

As the tour continued, an amusing pattern began to develop. The family would be invited to do some sightseeing, tour the countryside, or attend a soirée, while Wolfgang would find some excuse to stay behind—a feigned illness or complaints of exhaustion—and would devote his time instead to music. His favorite ploy in this vein was to attach himself to the most illustrious composers in the particular court they were visiting. In London, for instance, he managed to charm the great composer Johann Christian Bach, son of Johann Sebastian Bach. When the family was invited out on a jaunt, he declined to join them with the perfect excuse—he had already engaged Bach to give him lessons in composition.

随着巡游的继续，一种有趣的模式开始形成。这家人会被邀请去观光、游览乡村或参加晚会，而沃尔夫冈则会找个借口留下——比如装病或抱怨疲惫——然后把时间花在音乐上。他最喜欢的伎俩就是与他们所拜访的宫廷里最杰出的作曲家攀附。例如，在伦敦，他成功地迷住了伟大的作曲家约翰·塞巴斯蒂安·巴赫的儿子约翰·克里斯蒂安·巴赫。当这家人被邀请出去郊游时，他以一个完美的借口拒绝了——他已经聘请了巴赫来教他作曲。

The education he received in this fashion, from all of the composers he met, went far beyond anything any child could hope to receive. Although some argued that it was a waste of childhood for someone so young to be so single-minded, Wolfgang felt such an ardent love for music and the constant challenges it presented that in the end he derived much greater pleasure from his obsession than any amusement or game could provide.

他以这种方式从所有他所结识的作曲家那里获得的教育，远远超出了任何孩子所能期望的范围。尽管有人认为，如此年轻就如此专心致志是在浪费童年，但沃尔夫冈对音乐以及音乐带来的持续挑战怀有如此炽热的热爱，最终让他从这种痴迷中获得的乐趣远胜于任何娱乐或游戏所能提供的。

The tour was a great financial success, but it nearly ended in tragedy. In Holland in 1766, as the family was beginning its return journey, Wolfgang fell ill with a powerful fever. Losing weight rapidly, he drifted in and out of consciousness, and at one point appeared near death. But miraculously, the fever passed, and over the course of several months he slowly recovered. The experience, however, altered him. From that moment on, he had a constant feeling of melancholy and a foreboding that he would die young.

这次巡演获得了巨大的经济成功，但却险些以悲剧收场。1766年，在荷兰，当全家踏上返程时，沃尔夫冈突然发高烧。他体重迅速下降，时而清醒时而昏迷，一度濒临死亡。但奇迹般地，高烧退了，几个月后，他慢慢康复。然而，这段经历却改变了他。从那一刻起，他一直感到忧郁，并预感到自己会英年早逝。

The Mozart family had come now to depend on the money that the children had generated through the tour, but as the years went by the invitations began to dry up. The novelty had worn off, and the children no longer seemed so young and precious. Desperate to generate money, Leopold came up with a different scheme. His son was turning into a serious composer, with the ability to compose in different genres. What was needed was to secure for him a stable position as a court composer, and attract commissions for concertos and symphonies. With this goal in mind, in 1770 father and son embarked on series of tours of Italy, then the center of all things musical in Europe.

莫扎特家族如今开始依赖孩子们巡演赚来的钱，但随着时间的推移，邀请函开始减少。新鲜感消退，孩子们也不再显得那么年轻和珍贵。为了赚钱，利奥波德想出了一个不同的方案。他的儿子正逐渐成为一名严肃的作曲家，能够创作不同类型的音乐。当务之急是为他争取一个稳定的宫廷作曲家职位，并吸引协奏曲和交响曲的委托。怀揣着这个目标，父子俩于1770年开始了一系列意大利巡演，当时意大利是欧洲音乐的中心。

The trip went well. Wolfgang performed his magic on the piano before all of the major courts in Italy. He gained acclaim for his symphonies and concert pieces—they were quite impressive for a teenager. He mingled yet again with the most celebrated composers of his time, intensifying the musical knowledge he had gained on his previous tours.
