动物世界可以分为两种类型——专精型和机会型。专精型，例如鹰，拥有一项赖以生存的主导技能。当它们不捕猎时，可以进入完全放松的状态。另一方面，机会型动物没有特别的专长。它们依靠技能嗅探环境中的任何机会并抓住它。它们处于持续紧张的状态，需要持续的刺激。我们人类是动物世界中终极的机会主义者，是所有生物中最不专精的。我们的整个大脑和神经系统都致力于寻找任何机会。我们最原始的祖先最初并没有想过要创造一种工具来帮助他们觅食和捕杀。相反，他们偶然发现了一块岩石，也许是一块异常锋利或细长的岩石（这是一种异常现象），并从中看到了可能性。在捡起和处理它的过程中，他们萌生了将其用作工具的想法。人类思维的这种机会主义倾向是我们创造力的源泉和基础，正是通过顺应大脑的这种倾向，我们才能最大限度地发挥这些力量。

And yet when it comes to creative endeavors, so often we find people going at them from the wrong end. This generally afflicts those who are young and inexperienced—they begin with an ambitious goal, a business, or an invention or a problem they want to solve. This seems to promise money and attention. They then search for ways to reach that goal. Such a search could go in thousands of directions, each of which could pan out in its own way, but in which they could also easily end up exhausting themselves and never find the key to reaching their overarching goal. There are too many variables that go into success. The more experienced, wiser types, such as Ramachandran, are opportunists. Instead of beginning with some broad goal, they go in search of the fact of great yield—a bit of empirical evidence that is strange and does not fit the paradigm, and yet is intriguing. This bit of evidence sticks out and grabs their attention, like the elongated rock. They are not sure of their goal and they do not yet have in mind an application for the fact they have uncovered, but they are open to where it will lead them. Once they dig deeply, they discover something that challenges prevailing conventions and offers endless opportunities for knowledge and application.

然而，在创造性努力方面，我们常常发现人们的出发点是错误的。这通常困扰着那些年轻且缺乏经验的人——他们一开始就设定了一个雄心勃勃的目标，一门生意，一项发明，或者一个他们想要解决的问题。这似乎能带来金钱和关注。然后，他们会四处寻找实现目标的方法。这样的探索可能涉及千万个方向，每个方向都有各自的发展方向，但他们也可能最终精疲力竭，永远找不到实现最终目标的钥匙。成功的变数太多了。而像拉马钱德兰这样经验更丰富、更睿智的人，则是机会主义者。他们不会从某个宏大的目标入手，而是去寻找丰厚回报的事实——一些奇特的、不符合范式却又引人入胜的经验证据。这些证据就像一块细长的岩石一样，引人注目，吸引了他们的注意力。他们尚不确定自己的目标，也尚未构思如何应用所发现的事实，但他们对未来发展持开放态度。一旦深入挖掘，他们就会发现一些挑战既有传统观念的东西，并为知识和应用提供无限可能。

In looking for facts of great yield, you must follow certain guidelines. Although you are beginning within a particular field that you understand deeply, you must not allow your mind to become tethered to this discipline. Instead you must read journals and books from all different fields. Sometimes you will find an interesting anomaly in an unrelated discipline that may have implications for your own. You must keep your mind completely open—no item is too small or unimportant to escape your attention. If an apparent anomaly calls into question your own beliefs or assumptions, so much the better. You must speculate on what it could mean, this speculation guiding your subsequent research but not determining your conclusions. If what you have discovered seems to have profound ramifications, you must pursue it with the utmost intensity. Better to look into ten such facts, with only one yielding a great discovery, than to look into twenty ideas that bring success but have trivial implications. You are the supreme hunter, ever alert, eyes scanning the landscape for the fact that will expose a once-hidden reality, with profound consequences.

在寻找意义重大的事实时，你必须遵循某些准则。即使你刚开始研究某个你深谙的领域，也不能让你的思维局限于该领域。相反，你必须阅读各个领域的期刊和书籍。有时，你会在不相关的学科中发现有趣的异常现象，它可能对你的研究方向产生影响。你必须保持开放的心态——任何细节，无论大小或无关紧要，都应引起你的注意。如果一个明显的异常现象让你对自己的信念或假设产生质疑，那就更好了。你必须推测它可能意味着什么，这种推测将指导你后续的研究，但不会决定你的结论。如果你的发现似乎具有深远的影响，你必须全力以赴地去探究。与其研究二十个看似成功但影响微不足道的想法，不如研究十个这样的事实，最终只有一个能带来重大发现。你是顶尖的猎手，时刻保持警惕，目光扫视着周围，寻找那些能够揭示曾经被隐藏的真相并带来深远影响的事实。

# ↩

3. Mechanical Intelligence

3.机械智能

From their earliest years the brothers Wilbur Wright (1867–1912) and Orville Wright (1871–1948) displayed a rather unusual interest in the working parts of any kind of device, particularly the elaborate toys their father often brought home to them from his travels as a bishop in the United Brethren Church. They would take these toys apart in a state of extreme excitement, avid to figure out what made them tick. Then they would reassemble them, always with some modification.

威尔伯·莱特（Wilbur Wright，1867-1912）和奥维尔·莱特（Orville Wright，1871-1948）兄弟俩从小就对各种设备的部件表现出异乎寻常的兴趣，尤其是他们的父亲在担任联合弟兄会主教期间经常带回家的那些精致玩具。他们会兴奋地拆开这些玩具，渴望弄清楚它们的工作原理。然后，他们会重新组装，每次都会进行一些修改。

Although the boys were reasonably good at schoolwork, neither of them received a high school diploma. They wanted to live in a world of machines, and the only knowledge that really interested them was that which related to the design and construction of some new device. They were extremely practical.

虽然这两个男孩的学习成绩还算不错，但他们都没有高中毕业。他们渴望生活在一个充满机械的世界里，唯一真正让他们感兴趣的知识是与某种新设备的设计和制造相关的知识。他们非常注重实践。

In 1888 their father needed to quickly print out a pamphlet for his work. To help him, the brothers cobbled together their own small job press, using the hinge from a folding buggy top in the backyard, rusty springs, and other pieces of scrap. The press worked brilliantly. Inspired by their success, they improved the design, using better parts, and opened their own printing shop. Those who knew the business marveled at the peculiar press the brothers had concocted, which managed to spit out 1,000 pages per hour, double the usual rate.

1888年，他们的父亲需要快速印制一本小册子。为了帮助父亲，兄弟俩用后院折叠马车顶篷上的铰链、生锈的弹簧和其他废料，拼凑了一台小型印刷机。这台印刷机运转良好。受此启发，他们改进了设计，使用了更好的零件，并开设了自己的印刷店。了解这家印刷店的人都对兄弟俩发明的这台奇特的印刷机赞叹不已，它每小时可以印制1000页，是普通印刷机的两倍。

The brothers, however, had a restless spirit. They needed constant challenges, and in 1892 Orville discovered the perfect new outlet for them. With the invention of the safety bicycle (the first bicycle featuring two wheels of the same size), America had become seized with a biking craze. The brothers purchased their own bicycles, entered races, and became fanatics in the sport. Soon they were taking their bicycles apart and making minor adjustments. Seeing them at work in the backyard, friends and acquaintances would bring them their own bicycles for repairs. Within months they knew bicycle technology from the inside out, and decided to open their own shop in their native Dayton, Ohio, where they sold, repaired and even modified the latest models.

然而，兄弟俩却有着永不满足的精神。他们需要不断的挑战。1892年，奥维尔找到了一个绝佳的机会，让他们找到了新的出路。随着安全自行车（第一辆拥有相同尺寸两个轮子的自行车）的发明，美国掀起了一股自行车热潮。兄弟俩购买了自己的自行车，参加比赛，并成为了这项运动的狂热爱好者。很快，他们就开始拆卸自行车，并进行细微的调整。朋友和熟人看到他们在后院工作，便会把自行车拿来修理。几个月后，他们对自行车技术了如指掌，并决定在家乡俄亥俄州代顿市开设自己的商店，销售、维修甚至改装最新款自行车。

This seemed to be the perfect match for their skills. They could make various changes on a bicycle, take it out for a test ride, feel what worked and didn’t work, and then make further improvements. They were constantly striving to make the bicycles more maneuverable and aerodynamic, changes that would qualitatively alter the experience of riding and give the rider a feeling of being in complete control. Dissatisfied with the latest designs, they decided that the next logical step was to build their own aluminum frames and design their own custom-built bicycle. This represented a steep challenge—it would require months of on-the-job learning to be able to properly build frames. The slightest flaw could cause all kinds of horrifying accidents. In the process of learning this skill, they purchased a slew of the latest tools, built their own one-cylinder engine to power them, and steadily became master bicycle craftsmen. Those who rode the Wright brothers’ bicycles could feel right away the superiority of their version, which included technological improvements that would soon become industry standards.

这似乎与他们的技能完美契合。他们可以对自行车进行各种改造，试骑，感受哪些地方有效，哪些地方无效，然后进一步改进。他们不断努力，使自行车更加灵活，更符合空气动力学，这些改变将彻底改变骑行体验，让骑行者感觉完全掌控。由于对最新的设计不满意，他们决定下一步是自己打造铝制车架，设计一辆专属定制的自行车。这代表着一项艰巨的挑战——需要数月的在职学习才能熟练地打造车架。哪怕是最轻微的瑕疵都可能导致各种可怕的事故。在学习这项技能的过程中，他们购买了大量最新的工具，打造了自己的单缸发动机，并逐渐成为自行车工匠大师。那些骑过莱特兄弟自行车的人，可以立即感受到他们自行车的优越性，其中包括一些即将成为行业标准的技术改进。

In 1896, while convalescing from an injury, Wilbur read an article that would haunt him for years. It concerned the death of Otto Lilienthal, the leading designer of gliders and an expert in the growing field of aviation. He had died in a crash with his latest glider design. The photographs of the various gliders he had built, all in flight, astounded Wilbur—they looked like the wings of a giant prehistoric bird. As someone with a powerful sense of visualization, Wilbur could imagine the sensation of flying itself, and it thrilled him. But what surprised him in the article was that over many years of test flights, perhaps numbering in the hundreds, Lilienthal had never been able to maintain the flight long enough to get a feel for the necessary improvements, and had probably died because of this.

1896年，威尔伯在养伤期间读到了一篇萦绕他多年的文章。这篇文章讲述了滑翔机领域的领军设计师、新兴航空领域的专家奥托·李林塔尔的逝世。他驾驶自己最新的滑翔机设计坠毁身亡。他所制造的各种滑翔机的飞行照片令威尔伯惊叹不已——它们看起来就像史前巨鸟的翅膀。威尔伯拥有强大的视觉感知能力，他能够想象飞翔的感觉，这让他兴奋不已。但文章中让他感到惊讶的是，在多年的试飞中，李林塔尔可能进行了数百次试飞，却从未能够维持足够长的飞行时间来感受必要的改进，他很可能因此丧生。

Several years later, newspapers were filled with stories about the latest pioneers in aviation, many of whom appeared to be getting closer to the goal of creating a motored flying machine. It was now turning into a race to be the first to succeed. His curiosity on the subject getting deeper, Wilbur decided to write to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., requesting all of their available information on aeronautics and flying machines. For the next few months he pored over the materials, reading about the physics and mathematics behind flight, the designs of Leonardo da Vinci, and the gliders of the nineteenth century. He added to his reading list books about birds, which he now began to observe and study. And the more he read, the more he had the strange sensation that he and his brother could actually be the ones to win such a race.

几年后，报纸上充斥着关于航空领域最新先驱的报道，其中许多人似乎离发明动力飞行器的目标越来越近。现在，这变成了一场谁先成功的竞赛。威尔伯对这个问题越来越感兴趣，于是决定写信给华盛顿特区的史密森学会，索取他们所有关于航空和飞行器的资料。在接下来的几个月里，他仔细研读了这些资料，阅读了飞行背后的物理和数学原理、列奥纳多·达·芬奇的设计以及十九世纪的滑翔机。他还在阅读书单上添加了关于鸟类的书籍，现在他开始观察和研究鸟类。他读得越多，就越有一种奇怪的感觉：他和他的兄弟实际上可能就是这场竞赛的赢家。

At first glance this would seem an absurd idea. The men in the field were all experts with incredible technical knowledge, some with impressive college degrees. They had an enormous head start over the Wright brothers. Designing and building a flying machine was an expensive venture that could total thousands of dollars and lead to yet another crash. The favorite to win the race was Samuel Langley, the secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, who had an enormous government grant to pursue his work and had already successfully flown a steam-powered, unmanned model. The brothers came from a modest background, and the only money they had was the slender profits from their bicycle shop. But what all of these men lacked, in Wilbur’s mind, was some basic common sense when it came to any kind of machine.

乍一看，这个想法似乎荒唐可笑。参赛选手都是技术精湛的专家，其中一些人甚至拥有令人艳羡的大学学位。他们比莱特兄弟领先了一大截。设计和制造飞行器是一项耗资巨大的冒险，可能耗资数千美元，而且很容易再次坠毁。最有希望获胜的是史密森学会秘书长塞缪尔·兰利，他获得了巨额政府资助来继续他的研究，并且已经成功试飞了一架蒸汽动力的无人驾驶飞机。兄弟俩出身贫寒，唯一的收入来源就是他们自行车店微薄的利润。但在威尔伯看来，这些人都缺乏一些关于任何机器的基本常识。

These aviators had begun with the premise that what mattered was to get the machine in the air using a powerful engine of some sort, figuring the rest out once flight had been achieved. Getting in the air would impress the public, gain attention, and attract financial backing. This led to many crashes, constant redesigns, the search for the perfect engine, new materials, and more crashes. They were getting nowhere, and the reason was simple. As Wilbur knew, the key to building anything right is repetition. It was only by getting their hands on bicycles, fiddling and tinkering with them, then riding them and gaining a feel for what worked, that the brothers had been able to design a superior variety of bicycle. Because the designers of the flying machines could not fly for more than a minute, they were locked into a vicious cycle—they were never airborne long enough to learn how to fly and properly test out their designs, or get a feel for what might work. They were doomed to failure.

这些飞行员最初的设想是，重要的是用某种强大的引擎让机器飞上天空，等到飞行成功后再考虑剩下的事情。飞上天空能给公众留下深刻印象，引起关注，并获得资金支持。这导致了无数次坠机事故、不断的重新设计、对完美引擎和新材料的探索，以及更多的坠机事故。他们一事无成，原因很简单。正如威尔伯所知，做好任何事的关键在于重复。正是通过亲手操作自行车，摆弄、改装，然后骑上去，感受一下哪种方法有效，兄弟俩才得以设计出更优秀的自行车。由于飞行器的设计者每次飞行时间都不能超过一分钟，他们陷入了一个恶性循环——他们从来没有足够长的飞行时间来学习如何飞行，如何正确地测试他们的设计，或者感受一下哪种方法可能有效。他们注定要失败。

Wilbur discovered another great flaw in their thinking that shocked him: they all overvalued the importance of stability. They thought in terms of a ship floating through the air. A ship is designed to maintain balance, and to move in as stable and straight a manner as possible; tipping from side to side is far too dangerous. Based on this analogy, they decided to design the wings of their flying machines in a slight V shape, to compensate for any sudden gusts of wind and to keep the cruising aircraft in a straight line. But Wilbur felt that thinking in terms of ships was the wrong analogy. Instead, it was far wiser to think in terms of a bicycle. A bicycle is inherently unstable. It is the rider who learns quickly enough how to keep the bike in a secure position, and to steer it properly by leaning to the side. A pilot of a flying machine, as he imagined it, should be able to safely bank and turn, or tilt up or down, and not be locked into a rigid horizontal line, like a ship. Trying to free the machine from the effects of the wind was actually quite dangerous, because it would remove the ability of the pilot to adjust.

威尔伯发现了他们思维中另一个令他震惊的重大缺陷：他们都高估了稳定性的重要性。他们把飞行器比作漂浮在空中的船。船的设计目的是保持平衡，尽可能稳定、笔直地行驶；左右倾覆太危险了。基于这个类比，他们决定将飞行器的机翼设计成略呈V形，以抵消突如其来的阵风，并保持巡航飞机的直线飞行。但威尔伯认为，用船来类比是错误的。相反，用自行车来思考更为明智。自行车天生就不稳定。骑车人很快就能学会如何将自行车保持在安全的位置，并通过侧倾来正确操控。在他看来，飞行器的驾驶员应该能够安全地进行倾斜、转弯或上下倾斜，而不是像船一样被锁定在一条僵硬的水平线上。试图让飞机摆脱风的影响实际上非常危险，因为这会使飞行员失去调整的能力。

Armed with this knowledge, it was easy enough for Wilbur to convince his brother that a flying machine should be their next and ultimate challenge. They would have to use their limited profits from the bicycle shop to fund the project. This would force them to be creative, using scrap parts and never trying anything beyond their means. Instead of beginning with a grandiose device to test out their ideas, they would have to slowly evolve the perfect design, just as they had done with the printing press and the bicycle.

有了这些知识，威尔伯轻而易举地说服弟弟，飞行器应该是他们下一个也是终极的挑战。他们必须用自行车店有限的利润来资助这个项目。这将迫使他们发挥创造力，利用废弃的零件，绝不尝试超出自身能力范围的事情。他们不必一开始就用一个宏大的装置来测试他们的想法，而是必须慢慢地完善设计，就像他们发明印刷机和自行车一样。

They decided to begin as modestly as possible. They designed various kites to help them determine the perfect overall shape for a test glider. Then, based on what they had learned, they fashioned the glider itself. They wanted to teach themselves how to fly. The usual method of launching a glider off the crest of a hill was too dangerous. Instead, they decided to move operations to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, the site of the strongest winds in the United States. There, on the sand dunes of the beaches at Kitty Hawk, they could get airborne from small elevations, fly close to the ground, and land in a soft bed of sand. In the year 1900 alone they were able to perform more test flights than Lilienthal had attempted over many years. They slowly perfected the design, and improved the materials and configuration—for instance, they learned to make the wings longer and thinner to improve the lift. By 1903 they had a glider they could fly for considerable distances, with remarkable control over turning and banking. It was indeed like a flying bicycle.

他们决定尽可能从简。他们设计了各种风筝，以确定测试滑翔机的完美整体形状。然后，根据他们所学到的知识，他们制作了滑翔机本身。他们想自学飞行。通常从山顶发射滑翔机的方法太危险了。于是，他们决定将飞行基地转移到北卡罗来纳州的基蒂霍克，那里是美国风力最强的地方。在那里，在基蒂霍克海滩的沙丘上，他们可以在低海拔地区起飞，贴近地面飞行，最后降落在柔软的沙床上。仅在1900年，他们进行的试飞就比李林塔尔多年来尝试的还要多。他们慢慢完善设计，改进材料和结构——例如，他们学会了把机翼做得更长更薄，以提高升力。到1903年，他们制造出了一架可以飞行相当远距离的滑翔机，并且能够出色地控制转弯和倾斜。它真的就像一辆会飞的自行车。

Now it was time to take the final step—adding the engine and propellers to their design. As before, they looked at the designs of their rivals and noticed another weakness: they had modeled their propellers on those of boats, once again opting for stability. Based on their own research, the brothers decided that the blades should be cambered, like the wings of a bird—that would give the plane more thrust. Looking to purchase the lightest engine to power the machine, they found it was far beyond their budget. So with the help of a mechanic in their shop, they built their own engine. In total, the cost of their flying apparatus would come in under $1,000—considerably less than any of the designs of their competitors.

现在到了最后一步——在他们的设计中添加发动机和螺旋桨。和以前一样，他们参考了竞争对手的设计，发现了另一个弱点：他们的螺旋桨模仿了船用螺旋桨，同样是为了提高稳定性。根据自己的研究，兄弟俩决定，叶片应该像鸟翼一样呈弧形，这样可以增加飞机的推力。他们想购买最轻的发动机来驱动这架飞机，但发现这远远超出了他们的预算。于是，在店里一位机械师的帮助下，他们自己制造了发动机。最终，他们的飞行器成本不到1000美元——远低于任何竞争对手的设计。

On December 17, 1903, Wilbur piloted their flying machine at Kitty Hawk for an impressive fifty-nine seconds—the first manned, controlled, and powered flight in history. Over the years they would improve the design, and the flight times would increase. For the other competitors in the race it was a complete mystery how two men without any engineering or aeronautic experience or financial backing had managed to get there first.

1903年12月17日，威尔伯驾驶他们的飞行器在小鹰号上飞行了令人印象深刻的59秒——这是历史上首次载人、可控、动力飞行。多年来，他们不断改进设计，飞行时间也不断延长。对于比赛中的其他竞争对手来说，这两个没有任何工程或航空经验，也没有任何资金支持的人是如何率先到达那里的，这完全是个谜。

The development of the airplane represents one of the greatest technological achievements in our history, with profound ramifications for the future. There simply was no real precedent or model to base the flying machine on. It was a genuine puzzle, and it required the highest degree of ingenuity to solve it. In the history of its invention, we can observe two radically different approaches. On the one side was a large group of engineers and designers with backgrounds in the sciences who saw the problem in abstract terms: how to get the plane launched and propelled, how to overcome wind resistance, and so on. They focused largely on the technology and worked to create the most efficient parts—the most powerful engines, the best-designed wings, all of this based on elaborate lab research. Money was no object. This process depended on specialization—individuals who focused on different parts and who specialized in different materials. In many cases, the designer would not end up being the pilot; someone else would do the test flights.

飞机的研发代表了人类历史上最伟大的技术成就之一，对未来有着深远的影响。当时根本没有真正的先例或模型可以作为飞行器的基础。这简直是一个难题，需要极高的创造力才能解决。在其发明史上，我们可以看到两种截然不同的方法。一方面，一大批拥有科学背景的工程师和设计师，他们以抽象的视角看待问题：如何让飞机升空和推进，如何克服风阻等等。他们主要专注于技术，致力于打造最高效的部件——最强大的发动机、设计最佳的机翼，所有这些都基于精心的实验室研究。资金并非问题。这个过程依赖于专业化——专注于不同部件和不同材料的个人。在很多情况下，设计师最终并不会成为飞行员；而是其他人进行试飞。

On the other side were two men from a completely different background. For them, the pleasure and excitement of design was in doing everything themselves. They designed the machine, built it, and flew it. Their model depended not on superior technology, but on the highest number of test runs, creating an optimal learning curve. This revealed flaws to be worked on and gave them a feel for the product that could never be had in the abstract. The emphasis was not on the parts, but on the overall flying experience; not on power, but on control. Since money was a factor, supreme importance was placed on ingenuity in getting the most out of the least. The differences between the two approaches can be seen in the analogies they chose to base their designs on. The abstract thinkers opted for the ship analogy, working on the similarity of navigating an alien medium (water or air), which made them place importance on stability. The Wright brothers chose the bicycle, which emphasized the rider or pilot, the user-friendliness of the machine, and its overall functionality. Focusing on the pilot instead of the medium ended up being the right answer to the puzzle, because it led to the design of something that could be maneuvered. From that starting point, a more complex airplane could be easily evolved.

另一边是两位背景截然不同的男士。对他们来说，设计的乐趣和激情在于亲力亲为。他们设计、制造、飞行，最终实现飞行。他们的模型并非依赖于先进的技术，而是依靠大量的测试，从而创造出最佳的学习曲线。这揭示了有待改进的缺陷，并让他们对产品有了抽象概念无法企及的感受。设计重点并非部件，而是整体的飞行体验；并非动力，而是操控。由于资金是一个因素，因此至关重要的是运用独创性，以最少的投入获得最大的收益。两种设计方法的差异可以从他们为设计所选择的类比中看出。抽象思维者选择以船舶为类比，认为船舶与在外星介质（水或空气）中航行存在相似性，因此他们非常重视稳定性。莱特兄弟则选择了自行车，这更注重骑行者或飞行员、机器的用户友好性以及其整体功能性。专注于飞行员而非媒介最终成为了解决这一难题的正确答案，因为它引领我们设计出一种可操控的飞行器。从这个出发点出发，更复杂的飞机可以轻松演化出来。

Understand: mechanical intelligence is not a degraded form of thinking, as compared to abstract reasoning. It is in fact the source of many of our reasoning skills and creative powers. Our brain developed to its present size because of the complex operations of our hands. In working with resistant materials to create tools, our ancestors developed a pattern of thinking that transcends manual labor itself. The principles behind mechanical intelligence can be summarized as follows: whatever you are creating or designing, you must test and use it yourself. Separating out the work will make you lose touch with its functionality. Through intense labor on your part, you gain a feel for what you are creating. In doing this work, you see and feel the flaws in the design. You do not look at the parts separately but at how they interact, experiencing what you produce as a whole. What you are trying to create will not magically take off after a few creative bursts of inspiration, but must be slowly evolved through a step-by-step process as you correct the flaws. In the end, you win through superior craftsmanship, not marketing. This craftsmanship involves creating something with an elegant, simple structure, getting the most out of your materials—a high form of creativity. These principles work with the natural bent of your brain, and are to be violated at your own peril.

要明白：与抽象推理相比，机械智能并非一种低级的思维形式。事实上，它是我们许多推理技能和创造力的源泉。我们的大脑之所以发展到如今的大小，得益于双手的复杂操作。在使用坚固耐用的材料制造工具的过程中，我们的祖先发展出了一种超越体力劳动本身的思维模式。机械智能背后的原理可以概括如下：无论你正在创造或设计什么，你都必须亲自测试和使用。将工作分离开来会让你失去对其功能的理解。通过你自身的高强度劳动，你会对你所创造的东西产生感觉。在工作中，你会看到并感受到设计中的缺陷。你不是孤立地看待各个部分，而是观察它们如何相互作用，将你的作品作为一个整体来体验。你试图创造的东西不会在几次灵感迸发后就奇迹般地飞速发展，而必须通过一步步的改进和修正缺陷的过程慢慢地发展。最终，你凭借精湛的工艺而非市场营销赢得胜利。这种工艺意味着创造出结构优雅简洁的作品，最大限度地利用你的材料——这是一种高级的创造力。这些原则与你大脑的本能相符，违反这些原则后果自负。

# ↩

4. Natural Powers

4.自然力量

After graduating from architecture school in Spain in 1973, Santiago Calatrava experienced some anxiety at the thought of rushing into an architecture practice. (For more on Calatrava, see here .) He had ambitions early in life of becoming an artist, but gravitated toward architecture as a more expansive form of expression—something functional yet sculptural, something that could be realized on a large public scale. Architecture is a strange profession. It involves so many constraints when it comes to actually realizing a structure—the desires of the client, the budget, the materials available, the landscape, and even political issues. In the works of great architects in history, such as Le Corbusier, we can see a lot of their personal style in the finished product, but with many others their work becomes overwhelmed by the various constraints and interferences. Calatrava felt that he had not developed a sufficiently large vocabulary or mastered enough elements to be able to assert himself. If he went to work at a firm, his creative energies would be buried beneath all of the commercial pressures, and he would never recover.

1973年从西班牙建筑学院毕业后，圣地亚哥·卡拉特拉瓦（Santiago Calatrava）对于匆忙进入建筑行业的想法感到有些焦虑。（更多关于卡拉特拉瓦的信息，请参见此处。）他早年曾立志成为一名艺术家，但后来更倾向于将建筑视为一种更具拓展性的表达形式——兼具功能性和雕塑感，能够应用于大型公共建筑。建筑是一个奇怪的职业。在实际建造建筑时，它面临着诸多限制——客户的需求、预算、可用的材料、景观，甚至政治因素。在勒·柯布西耶等历史上伟大建筑师的作品中，我们可以在最终作品中看到许多他们的个人风格，但其他许多建筑师的作品则因各种限制和干扰而显得力不从心。卡拉特拉瓦觉得自己还未积累足够丰富的词汇，也未掌握足够多的元素来展现自己的风格。如果他去公司工作，他的创造力就会被商业压力所埋没，而且永远无法恢复。

And so he made an unusual decision: he would attend the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich to gain a degree in civil engineering. He wanted to become an engineer so that he could understand the limits of what was possible in designing buildings and structures. He had the idea of someday attempting the construction of buildings that could move, transgressing some of the most fundamental principles of architecture. For such a purpose, he studied designs by NASA in which various devices had been made that could fold up and expand, making them practical for space missions. Such designs required mastering new engineering principles that Calatrava immersed himself in at the Institute.

于是，他做出了一个非同寻常的决定：前往苏黎世联邦理工学院攻读土木工程学位。他立志成为一名工程师，从而探索建筑和结构设计所能达到的极限。他梦想着有朝一日能够尝试建造可以移动的建筑，突破一些最基本的建筑原则。为此，他研究了美国国家航空航天局（NASA）的各种可折叠和展开的装置设计，使其能够应用于太空任务。这类设计需要掌握新的工程原理，而卡拉特拉瓦在苏黎世联邦理工学院期间全身心投入其中。

After graduating in 1981 with an engineering degree, he finally began his practice as an architect and engineer. He was now well versed in the technical aspects of his job and in the basic requirements for completing a work, but no one had instructed him in the creative process itself. He would have to learn and invent such a process for himself.

1981年获得工程学位后，他终于开始了建筑师和工程师的实践。他现在已经精通工作中的技术层面以及完成作品的基本要求，但从未有人指导过他的创作过程。他必须自己学习和发明这样的流程。

His first big project came in 1983, when he was asked to design the façade of an already existing structure—an enormous warehouse for Ernsting, a well-known clothing manufacturer in Germany. He decided to cover the structure with untreated aluminum. This would tie the entire building together, but on each side the sunlight would create different, sometimes dazzling effects. To Calatrava the key part of the design was that of the three loading bay doors, each on different sides of the warehouse. Here he could experiment with his ideas of movement and foldability. And so, not certain where or how to begin the actual process, he started to sketch out various possibilities for these doors. As a child he had loved to draw, and he was constantly sketching. He had become so proficient with a pencil or brush that he could draw almost anything with great speed and accuracy. He could sketch as fast as he could think, his innermost visions translated with ease onto paper.

他的第一个大项目是在1983年，当时他被要求为一个现有建筑——德国知名服装制造商恩斯廷（Ernsting）的巨型仓库——设计立面。他决定用未经处理的铝材覆盖整个结构。这样可以将整座建筑连接在一起，但阳光会在每一侧产生不同的、有时甚至令人眼花缭乱的效果。对卡拉特拉瓦来说，设计的关键部分是三个装卸区的门，分别位于仓库的不同侧面。在这里，他可以尝试他对移动和折叠的构想。因此，尽管不确定从哪里或如何开始实际设计，他还是开始勾勒出这些门的各种可能性。卡拉特拉瓦从小就喜欢画画，并且经常进行素描。他已经非常熟练地使用铅笔和画笔，几乎可以快速准确地绘制任何东西。他的素描速度和他思考的速度一样快，他内心深处的构想可以轻松地在纸上呈现。

Without any sense of where he was headed, he began to draw in watercolors, putting everything that came to him on paper, almost in a free-associative manner. For some reason, the image of a beached whale occurred to him and so he drew it. He took it further and metamorphosed the whale into the warehouse, the teeth and mouth of the whale opening into the bay door. Now he understood the image. It was as if the warehouse had become Jonah’s whale, disgorging trucks and materials from its mouth. On the margin of the drawing he wrote, “the building as a living organism.” As he stared at the sketch, his attention was drawn to the rather large whale eye he had painted to the side of the mouth/bay door. It seemed like an interesting metaphor all by itself, and indicated a new direction to take.

他毫无头绪地开始用水彩作画，几乎是以一种自由联想的方式，将脑海中浮现的一切描绘在纸上。不知何故，他突然想到了搁浅鲸鱼的形象，于是便画了下来。他进一步将鲸鱼转化为仓库，鲸鱼的牙齿和嘴巴张开，直通舱门。现在他理解了这个意象。仿佛仓库变成了约拿的鲸鱼，从嘴里吐出卡车和物资。他在画的空白处写道：“建筑如同一个活的有机体。” 当他凝视着草图时，他的注意力被他画在鲸鱼嘴/舱门侧面的一只相当大的鲸鱼眼睛所吸引。这本身就仿佛是一个有趣的比喻，并指明了一个新的方向。

He began to do different drawings of eyes on the sides of the warehouse, with the eyes turning into the doors. Now his drawings took on more detail and became more architectural as he began to sketch out the actual sides of the building and the doors in a more realistic rendering, but still based on the opening and closing of an enormous eye. In the end, this would turn into the actual design of the folding doors that would raise themselves up in the curved shape of an eyelid.

他开始在仓库的两侧画不同的眼睛，这些眼睛最终变成了门。随着他开始以更写实的方式勾勒出建筑的实际侧面和门，他的画作变得更加细致，更具建筑感，但仍然以一只巨大眼睛的开合为基础。最终，这变成了折叠门的实际设计，折叠门会以眼睑般的弧形向上翘起。

By the end of the design process Calatrava had generated a large number of sketches, and as he thumbed through them in sequential order, he could see a most interesting progression—from the loose imaginings of his unconscious to more and more precise renderings. Even in the most accurate sketches of the façade, however, there was still apparent some kind of artistic and playful element. To look at the drawings was almost to see the gradual development of a photograph in a chemical tray. Taking this form of attack was immensely satisfying. It gave him the feeling of creating something that was alive. Working in this way, his emotions were deeply engaged as he played upon all kinds of metaphors, both mythical and Freudian.

设计过程结束时，卡拉特拉瓦绘制了大量草图。当他按顺序翻阅这些草图时，他看到了一个非常有趣的进程——从他潜意识中模糊的想象，到越来越精准的效果图。然而，即使在最精准的立面草图中，仍然隐约可见某种艺术性和趣味性。观看这些图纸，就像看到照片在化学托盘中逐渐显影。这种形式的创作让他感到无比满足，仿佛在创造某种鲜活的东西。在这种创作方式下，他的情感被深深地投入其中，他运用了各种隐喻，既有神话的，也有弗洛伊德式的。

In the end, his design had a strange and powerful effect. Working with only the façade of the building, he had created the look of a Greek temple, the aluminum undulating like silver columns. The bay doors added a surreal touch, and when folded up, looked even more like the entranceway to a temple. All of this blended perfectly with the functionality of the structure. It was a great success, and garnered him immediate attention.

最终，他的设计产生了一种奇特而强大的效果。他仅凭建筑的立面，就创造出了希腊神庙的造型，铝材如同银柱般起伏。凸门增添了一丝超现实主义的气息，折叠起来时，更像神庙的入口。所有这些与建筑结构的功能性完美融合。这件作品获得了巨大的成功，并立即引起了他的注意。

As the years went by, one important commission followed another. Working on increasingly larger projects, Calatrava could see clearly the dangers ahead of him. Completing a design could often take ten years or more, from the initial sketch to the actual construction. In that time, all kinds of problems and conflicts could arise, which could end up spoiling the initial vision. With larger budgets would come more constraints, and the need to please many different people. If he were not careful, his desire to transgress the rules and to express a personal vision would get lost in the process. And so, as his career progressed, something inside him made him return to the method he had developed for the Ernsting warehouse, and to elaborate it even further.

随着岁月流逝，重要的委托一个接一个。卡拉特拉瓦接手的项目规模越来越大，他清楚地意识到前方的风险。完成一项设计通常需要十年甚至更长时间，从最初的草图到实际建造。在此期间，各种各样的问题和冲突可能会出现，最终可能会破坏最初的设想。预算的增加会带来更多的限制，以及取悦不同客户的需求。如果他不小心，打破常规、表达个人愿景的渴望就会在这个过程中迷失。因此，随着职业生涯的进展，他内心深处的某种力量促使他回归为恩斯廷仓库设计时所开发的方法，并将其进一步完善。

He would always begin with the drawings. Drawing by hand had become increasingly unusual in the era of computer graphics that had come to dominate so many aspects of architectural design in the 1980s. As a trained engineer, Calatrava knew the tremendous advantages the computer provided for running models and testing the soundness of a structure. But working exclusively on a computer, he could not create in the same way as he could with pencil or brush and paper. The intervention of the computer screen cut off the dreamlike process of sketching, the direct contact it gave him with his unconscious. His hand and his mind seemed to work together in a way that was primal and real, and that could not be duplicated through a computer.

他总是从图纸开始。在20世纪80年代计算机图形学时代，手绘变得越来越不寻常，计算机图形学在建筑设计的诸多方面占据了主导地位。作为一名训练有素的工程师，卡拉特拉瓦深知计算机在运行模型和测试结构稳固性方面的巨大优势。但仅仅在电脑上工作，他无法像用铅笔、画笔和纸张那样进行创作。电脑屏幕的介入切断了如梦似幻的素描过程，切断了他与潜意识的直接联系。他的手和他的思维似乎以一种原始而真实的方式协同工作，而这种方式是电脑无法复制的。

Now his drawings for a single project would number in the hundreds. He would start out in the same loose manner, building up all kinds of associations. He would begin with a feeling or an emotion that the idea of the design sparked in him. This would lead to an image, however vague. For instance, when asked to design an elaborate addition to the Milwaukee Art Museum, what first came to mind and then to paper was the image of a bird about to take flight. This image would go through the mill of his sketching process, but in the end the roof of the building he designed featured two enormous, ribbed panels that would open and close according to the sunlight, giving the impression of an enormous prehistoric bird about to fly over Lake Michigan.

现在，他为一个项目绘制的图纸多达数百张。他总是以同样随意的方式开始，建立各种联想。他会从设计理念在他心中激起的一种感觉或情感入手。这会催生出一幅图像，无论它多么模糊。例如，当他被要求为密尔沃基艺术博物馆设计一个精致的附加建筑时，他首先想到并最终落到纸上的是一只即将展翅高飞的鸟的形象。这幅形象会在他的草图过程中反复出现，但最终他设计的建筑屋顶由两块巨大的肋状面板组成，可以根据阳光的照射开合，给人一种史前巨鸟即将飞过密歇根湖的印象。

Most of these early, free associations would revolve around nature—plants, trees, human figures in various poses, skeletal ribbing—and would be intimately tied to the landscape. Slowly, the shape of the overall structure would come into focus through this process, as he would make the idea increasingly rational and architectural. As an adjunct to this process he would build models, sometimes beginning with a completely abstract sculptural shape that in subsequent versions would become the design for the structure itself. All of these drawings and sculptures were like exteriorizations of his unconscious and nonverbal thought processes.

这些早期的自由联想大多围绕着自然——植物、树木、姿态各异的人物、骨架结构——并与景观紧密相连。随着他逐渐将想法理性化、更具建筑感，整体结构的形态也逐渐清晰。作为这一过程的辅助，他会构建模型，有时从一个完全抽象的雕塑形状开始，在后续版本中逐渐成为结构本身的设计。所有这些绘画和雕塑都像是他无意识和非语言思维过程的外化。

Inevitably, as he moved closer to the construction phase, he would come up against constraints, such as the materials to be used and budgetary considerations. But working from this initial strategy, he experienced these factors merely as creative challenges: for instance, how could he incorporate certain materials into the vision he had sketched out and make it all work? If it were a train or subway station, how could he make the platforms and the movement of the trains fit into the overall vision, even enhancing their functionality? Such challenges excited him.

随着施工阶段的临近，他不可避免地会遇到一些限制因素，例如所需材料和预算方面的考量。但从最初的策略出发，他将这些因素视为纯粹的创意挑战：例如，如何将某些材料融入他勾勒出的愿景中，并使其完美运作？如果是火车站或地铁站，他该如何使站台和列车的运行与整体愿景相契合，甚至提升其功能性？这些挑战让他兴奋不已。

The greatest danger he faced was that his energy would go flat over time as the design dragged on into years, and he would lose touch with his original vision. To combat this, Calatrava would maintain an attitude of constant dissatisfaction. The drawings were never quite right. They had to be continually improved and perfected. By pushing for perfection and holding on to this constant feeling of uncertainty, the project never froze into something rigid and lifeless. It had to feel alive in the moment, as his brush touched the paper. If what he was designing began to feel dead in any way, it was time to start over. This not only required tremendous patience on his part, but a good deal of courage, as he wiped out the work of several months. Maintaining the edge and feeling of aliveness, however, was more important.

他面临的最大危险是，随着设计拖延数年，他的精力会逐渐枯竭，最终与最初的设想失去联系。为了应对这种情况，卡拉特拉瓦始终保持着一种不满足的态度。图纸永远不可能完全准确，必须不断改进和完善。通过追求完美，并保持这种持续的不确定性，项目才不会僵化、毫无生气。它必须在画笔触纸的那一刻，给人以鲜活的感觉。如果他的设计开始有任何死气沉沉的感觉，那就该重新开始了。这不仅需要他极大的耐心，更需要极大的勇气，因为他要将几个月的成果付诸东流。然而，保持活力和活力感更为重要。

As the years went by and Calatrava was able to look back on all of his projects, he had a strange sensation. The process he had evolved felt as if it had come from outside of him. It was not something he had created through his own imagination, but rather it was nature itself that had led him to this perfectly organic and beautifully effective process. The projects would take root in his mind with some emotion or idea, and slowly grow through the drawings, always alive and as fluid as life itself, like the stages of a plant leading to a flower. Feeling such vitality during the work, he would translate this sensation into the structures themselves, evoking awe and wonder in the public that saw and used them.

随着岁月流逝，卡拉特拉瓦回顾他所有的项目，心中涌起一种奇特的感觉。他所演绎的那些过程仿佛源于自身之外。这并非他凭空想象所造，而是自然本身引领他走向这完美有机、优美高效的创作过程。这些项目会带着某种情感或想法在他的脑海中扎根，并通过图纸缓缓生长，如同生命本身般鲜活流畅，如同植物绽放花朵的阶段。在创作过程中，他感受到这种活力，并将这种感觉转化为建筑结构本身，在参观和使用它们的公众中激起敬畏与惊叹。

Because the creative process is an elusive subject and one for which we receive no training, in our first creative endeavors we are most often left to our own devices, to sink or swim. And in these circumstances we have to evolve something that suits our individual spirit and our profession. Often, however, we can go quite wrong in evolving this process, particularly with the pressure to produce results and the fear this instills in us. In the process Calatrava developed for his work, we can discern an elemental pattern and principles that have wide application, built as they are on the natural inclinations and strengths of the human brain.

由于创作过程是一个难以捉摸的主题，而且我们从未接受过任何相关的训练，因此在最初的创作尝试中，我们常常只能依靠自己的力量，要么沉浮，要么自生自灭。在这种情况下，我们必须发展出一些符合我们个人精神和职业的东西。然而，在发展这一过程的过程中，我们常常会犯下很大错误，尤其是在追求成果的压力和由此产生的恐惧感之下。在卡拉特拉瓦为其作品所发展的过程中，我们可以辨别出一种具有广泛应用的基本模式和原则，它们建立在人类大脑的自然倾向和优势之上。

First, it is essential to build into the creative process an initial period that is open-ended. You give yourself time to dream and wander, to start out in a loose and unfocused manner. In this period, you allow the project to associate itself with certain powerful emotions, ones that naturally come out of you as you focus on your ideas. It is always easy to tighten up your ideas later on, and to make your project increasingly realistic and rational. But if you begin with a feeling of tightness and pressure, focusing on the funding, the competition, or people’s opinions, you will stifle the associative powers of the brain and quickly turn the work into something without joy or life. Second, it is best to have wide knowledge of your field and other fields, giving your brain more possible associations and connections. Third, to keep this process alive, you must never settle into complacency, as if your initial vision represents the endpoint. You must cultivate profound dissatisfaction with your work and the need to constantly improve your ideas, along with a sense of uncertainty—you are not exactly sure where to go next, and this uncertainty drives the creative urge and keeps it fresh. Any kind of resistance or obstacle that crosses your path should be seen as yet another chance to improve your work.

首先，在创作过程中，必须有一个开放的初始阶段。给自己时间去梦想和徘徊，以一种轻松随意、漫无目的的方式开始。在这个阶段，你让项目与某些强烈的情感联系起来，这些情感在你专注于自己的想法时自然而然地涌现。之后，你总是很容易收紧你的想法，让你的项目变得更加现实和理性。但是，如果你一开始就感到紧张和压力，关注资金、竞争或人们的意见，你就会抑制大脑的联想能力，很快就会把工作变成一件毫无乐趣或活力的事情。其次，最好对你所在领域和其他领域都有广泛的了解，让你的大脑有更多可能的联想和联系。第三，为了保持这个过程的活力，你绝不能自满，仿佛你最初的愿景就代表了终点。你必须培养对工作的强烈不满，不断改进想法的渴望，以及一种不确定性——你不确定下一步该去哪里，而这种不确定性驱动着你的创作冲动，并使其保持新鲜感。任何阻碍你前进的阻力或障碍都应该被视为改进作品的又一次机会。

Finally, you must come to embrace slowness as a virtue in itself. When it comes to creative endeavors, time is always relative. Whether your project takes months or years to complete, you will always experience a sense of impatience and a desire to get to the end. The single greatest action you can take for acquiring creative power is to reverse this natural impatience. You take pleasure in the laborious research process; you enjoy the slow cooking of the idea, the organic growth that naturally takes shape over time. You do not unnaturally draw out the process, which will create its own problems (we all need deadlines), but the longer you can allow the project to absorb your mental energies, the richer it will become. Imagine yourself years in the future looking back at the work you have done. From that future vantage point, the extra months and years you devoted to the process will not seem painful or laborious at all. It is an illusion of the present that will vanish. Time is your greatest ally.

最后，你必须接受缓慢本身就是一种美德。对于创造性工作而言，时间总是相对的。无论你的项目需要几个月还是几年才能完成，你总会感到一种迫不及待，渴望完成。而获得创造力的最好方法就是扭转这种与生俱来的急躁。你乐于享受艰苦的研究过程；你享受想法慢慢酝酿的过程，享受随着时间的推移自然成形的有机增长。你不会不自然地拖延这个过程，这本身也会带来问题（我们都需要截止日期），但你让项目吸收你的精神能量的时间越长，它就会变得越丰富。想象一下多年后的你回顾你所做的工作。从未来的视角来看，你为这个过程投入的额外几个月和几年，一点也不痛苦或费力。这只是对当下的一种幻觉，终将消失。时间是你最强大的盟友。

# ↩

5. The Open Field

5. 旷野

Martha Graham’s father, Dr. George Graham, was one of the few pioneering doctors in the 1890s to specialize in the treatment of mental illness. (For more on Martha Graham, see here and here .) Around the family he did not talk much about his work, but one subject he would discuss openly with Martha completely fascinated her. In working with his patients, Dr. Graham had developed the ability to judge much about their states of mind from their body language. He could read their level of anxiety in how they walked or moved their arms or fixed their eyes on something. “The body does not lie,” he would often tell her.

玛莎·格雷厄姆的父亲乔治·格雷厄姆医生是19世纪90年代少数几位专门治疗精神疾病的先驱医生之一。（更多关于玛莎·格雷厄姆的信息，请参见此处和此处。）在家人面前，他很少谈论自己的工作，但他会和玛莎开诚布公地讨论的一个话题却让她完全着迷。在与病人相处的过程中，格雷厄姆医生培养出了一种能力，可以通过肢体语言来判断他们的心理状态。他能从病人走路的方式、手臂的摆动方式，以及目光注视的方式，读出他们的焦虑程度。“身体不会说谎，”他经常这样告诉她。

In high school in Santa Barbara, California, Martha developed an interest in theater. But one evening in 1911, Dr. Graham took his seventeen-year-old daughter to Los Angeles to see a performance of the famous dancer Ruth St. Denis, and from then on all she could think about was becoming a dancer. Influenced by her father, she was intrigued by the ability to express emotions without any words, strictly through the movement of the body. As soon as St. Denis opened up her own dance school (along with her partner, Ted Shawn) in 1916, Martha enrolled as one of its first pupils. Much of the choreography was a kind of free-form ballet, with an emphasis on making everything seem easy and natural. There was a lot of posing and moving about with scarves, similar to the work of Isadora Duncan.

在加州圣巴巴拉读高中时，玛莎对戏剧产生了兴趣。1911年的一个晚上，格雷厄姆博士带着他17岁的女儿去洛杉矶观看著名舞蹈家露丝·圣丹尼斯的演出。从那时起，玛莎就一心想着成为一名舞蹈家。受父亲的影响，她对无需言语，仅通过肢体动作就能表达情感的能力十分着迷。1916年，圣丹尼斯（与她的舞伴泰德·肖恩一起）开办了自己的舞蹈学校，玛莎立即报名成为首批学生之一。学校的舞蹈编排大多属于自由形式的芭蕾，强调让一切看起来轻松自然。舞蹈中有很多摆姿势和用围巾四处走动的场景，类似于伊莎多拉·邓肯的作品。

At first, Graham was not considered a promising dancer. She was shy, always staying toward the back of the class. She was not particularly built for the art (she did not have a lithe ballerina’s body), and she was slow to pick up the choreography. But when she was given her first solo, St. Denis and Shawn saw something that surprised them: she exploded with an energy they had not suspected in her. She had charisma. St. Denis compared her to “a young tornado” when she took the stage. Everything they taught her she had a way of transforming into something sharper and more aggressive.

起初，格雷厄姆被认为并非一位有前途的舞者。她很害羞，总是坐在教室后排。她并非天生就适合这门艺术（她没有芭蕾舞演员那样轻盈的身材），而且学习舞蹈也很慢。但当她第一次独舞时，圣丹尼斯和肖恩看到了让他们惊讶的东西：她爆发出一种他们从未料到的能量。她魅力十足。圣丹尼斯把她登台时比作“年轻的龙卷风”。他们教给她的一切，她都能以某种方式转化为更敏锐、更具侵略性的东西。

After several years she became one of their leading students, a major performer in their troupe and a teacher of the Denishawn method, as it came to be known. But soon she began to tire of this form of dancing. It did not suit her temperament. To get some distance from the school she moved to New York, and to support herself she taught classes in the Denishawn method. Then one day in 1926, perhaps upset at her leaving the troupe, Ted Shawn surprised her with an ultimatum—she would have to pay $500 for the right to teach Denishawn exercises and dance material. If not, she was strictly forbidden, under penalty of a lawsuit, ever to use any of their methods in her classes or personal work.

几年后，她成为他们班里的佼佼者，成为舞团的主力演员，同时也是丹尼肖恩舞蹈教学法（后来被称为丹尼肖恩教学法）的老师。但她很快开始厌倦这种舞蹈形式，觉得它不适合她的性格。为了远离学校，她搬到了纽约，并开始教授丹尼肖恩教学法来维持生计。1926年的一天，或许是因为她离开舞团而感到不满，泰德·肖恩突然给她下了最后通牒——她必须支付500美元才能获得教授丹尼肖恩舞蹈练习和舞蹈教材的权利。否则，她将被严禁在课堂或个人作品中使用丹尼肖恩的任何教学法，否则将面临诉讼。

For Graham, this precipitated a crisis of sorts. She was now thirty-two years old, no longer young for a career in dance. She had barely $50 to her name, which meant that she could never pay Shawn even if she had wanted to. To earn extra money she had already tried working in popular dance shows on Broadway and had hated it, vowing never to go back. But as she weighed her options, one idea kept recurring to her. In her mind she had always been able to envision a kind of dance that did not exist in the world but that spoke to her innermost desires, both as a performer and a spectator. This dance was the polar opposite of the Denishawn method, which now seemed to her like empty, arty gesturing. It was more related to what she had seen of modern art—somewhat jagged and occasionally dissonant, full of power and rhythm. It was a visceral form of dance that she envisioned, and as she imagined it her thoughts kept returning to her father and their discussions about the body, about the language that all animals express through their movement.

对格雷厄姆来说，这引发了一场危机。她如今已32岁，对于舞蹈事业来说已不再年轻。她名下只有区区50美元，这意味着即使她想付钱给肖恩，也永远付不起。为了赚点外快，她曾尝试在百老汇的热门舞蹈剧目中工作，但她讨厌这份工作，并发誓再也不回去了。但当她权衡各种选择时，一个想法不断浮现在她的脑海中。在她心中，她一直能够想象一种世间并不存在，却能触动她内心深处渴望的舞蹈，无论是作为表演者还是观众。这种舞蹈与丹尼肖恩的舞蹈方法截然相反，后者现在在她看来只是空洞的、装腔作势的姿态。它更接近于她所见的现代艺术——略显参差不齐，偶尔不和谐，却充满力量和节奏。她想象中的是一种发自内心的舞蹈形式，当她想象时，她的思绪不断回到她的父亲身上，以及他们关于身体的讨论，关于所有动物通过运动表达的语言。

This dance she could visualize was rigorous, based on a new kind of discipline—not at all free-floating and spontaneous like the Denishawn style. It would have its own vocabulary. She could not shake the image of the beauty of this nonexistent dance. She would never have this chance again. With age comes conservatism and the need for comfort. To create what was not out there, she would have to start her own school and dance troupe, building up the technique and discipline on her own. To support herself, she would have to give classes, teaching the new dance movements she would be in the process of creating. It would entail a tremendous risk, and money would be a constant problem, but her desperation to create what she could imagine would fuel her past any obstacles.

她想象中的舞蹈是严谨的，基于一种全新的纪律——完全不同于丹尼肖恩风格的自由飘逸和即兴发挥。它将拥有自己的语言。她无法摆脱这种不存在的舞蹈之美的印象。她再也不会有这样的机会了。随着年龄的增长，她变得保守，也更注重舒适。为了创作出前所未有的舞蹈，她必须创办自己的学校和舞蹈团，独自积累技巧和纪律。为了养活自己，她必须开设课程，教授她正在创作的新舞蹈动作。这将带来巨大的风险，资金也将是一个持续的问题，但她对创造自己想象的事物的渴望，将驱使她克服任何障碍。

Within weeks of Ted Shawn’s ultimatum, she made her first move. She rented out a studio, and to show her pupils that this was a new kind of dance they were going to learn, she covered the walls in burlap. Unlike other dance studios, her studio would have no mirrors. The dancers would have to focus intensely on what she was teaching and learn how to correct themselves by feeling the movement in their bodies, not becoming fixated on their images. Everything she wanted in this new form of dance was outwardly directed at the audience, without self-consciousness.

在泰德·肖恩发出最后通牒后的几周内，她迈出了第一步。她租了一间舞蹈工作室，为了让学生们了解他们将要学习的是一种全新的舞蹈，她用粗麻布覆盖了墙壁。与其他舞蹈工作室不同，她的工作室没有镜子。舞者必须全神贯注于她所教的内容，并学习如何通过感受身体的动作来调整自己，而不是被自己的形象所束缚。她希望这种新舞蹈形式的一切都直接面向观众，无需刻意掩饰。

At first, it all seemed rather impossible. She had only a few students, just enough to cover rent. They would often have to wait for her as she slowly invented some new kind of movement or exercise, which they would then practice together and refine. A few early performances, although awkward, managed to attract more recruits, enough for Graham to think of creating a small troupe. From this group, she demanded the utmost discipline. They were creating a new language and would have to work hard. Week by week she built up a set of exercises that would bring the dancers more control, along with an entirely new mechanics of movement. She and her recruits would spend an entire year working on and perfecting one simple new technique, until it became second nature.

起初，这一切似乎遥不可及。她只有几个学生，仅够支付房租。学生们常常不得不等她慢慢发明新的动作或练习，然后一起练习、改进。早期的几次演出虽然略显尴尬，却吸引了更多新人，这足以让格雷厄姆萌生组建一个小舞团的想法。她要求这群舞者必须严格遵守纪律。他们正在创造一种新的舞蹈语言，必须努力学习。她每周都会建立一套练习，让舞者们更好地控制舞蹈，并掌握全新的动作技巧。她和她的新学员们会花上一整年的时间，练习和完善一个简单的新技巧，直到它成为他们的第二天性。

To distinguish her method from other forms of dance, she placed all of the emphasis on the torso. She called the torso “the house of the pelvic truth.” She had determined that the most expressive part of the human body came from the contractions of the diaphragm and the sharp movements of the torso. This would be the center of focus, not the face and arms that made dance too romantic. She created endless exercises to build up this area, and she encouraged her dancers to feel the deep well of emotions that came from using these muscles.

为了将自己的舞蹈方法与其他形式的舞蹈区分开来，她将所有的重点都放在了躯干上。她称躯干为“骨盆真相之屋”。她坚信，人体最富表现力的部位来自横膈膜的收缩和躯干的剧烈运动。躯干才是舞蹈的焦点，而不是让舞蹈显得过于浪漫的面部和手臂。她创造了无数的练习来锻炼躯干，并鼓励舞者们感受这些肌肉带来的深沉情感。

Much of what stimulated her in this early phase was the desire to create something that had never been seen before on the stage. In Western dance, for instance, it was taboo for a dancer to fall—that would be a sign of a mistake and loss of control. The ground was something to resist and never surrender to. She decided to turn this around by creating a new sequence of controlled falls in which the dancer would melt into the ground and reascend, ever so slowly. This required building up a whole new series of muscles. She took this concept further, using the ground itself as a space upon which the dancer could move like a coiled snake. In her new system, suddenly the knee became a different instrument of expression—a hinge upon which the dancer could balance and move, giving the effect of weightlessness.

在早期阶段，她最大的灵感源于渴望创造一些舞台上前所未有的东西。例如，在西方舞蹈中，舞者摔倒是禁忌——那将是失误和失控的标志。地面是需要抵抗、永不屈服的东西。她决定扭转这种局面，创造一套新的受控的摔倒序列，舞者在其中融入地面，然后缓慢地重新上升。这需要锻炼一系列全新的肌肉。她进一步拓展了这一概念，将地面本身作为舞者可以像盘绕的蛇一样移动的空间。在她的新体系中，膝盖突然变成了一种不同的表达工具——一个舞者可以借此保持平衡和移动的铰链，营造出一种失重的效果。

Slowly, as the work progressed, she could see coming to life the new form of dance that she had visualized. To add to the effect of newness, Graham decided to design and sew her own costumes. These costumes, often made out of stretch materials, would turn the dancers into almost abstract shapes, accentuating their sharp movements. Unlike the usual fairy-tale decor that was used for ballets, her sets would be minimal and stark. The dancers would wear little makeup. Everything would be designed to set them off from the stage and make their movements explode.

随着工作的进展，她逐渐看到自己设想的全新舞蹈形式逐渐鲜活地呈现在观众眼前。为了增添新意，格雷厄姆决定自己设计和缝制服装。这些服装通常采用弹力面料制成，将舞者塑造成近乎抽象的造型，从而突显他们灵动的动作。与芭蕾舞剧中常见的童话般的装饰不同，她的布景简洁朴素。舞者们几乎不化妆。一切都经过精心设计，力求让他们在舞台上脱颖而出，并展现出爆发力。

The response to her first series of performances was electrifying. The public had never seen anything remotely like it before. Many were disgusted and repulsed. Others found the work strangely emotional, giving dance an expressive quality they had never suspected it could possess. The work elicited extremes of reaction, a sign of its power. Over the years, what had seemed initially so harsh and ugly began to be accepted, as Martha Graham had indeed single-handedly created a new genre—modern dance as we know it today. To avoid this dance turning into yet another convention, she would constantly struggle to upset people’s expectations, never going over old ground, and constantly changing the subject matter of the dances, from Greek myths to Americana and depictions from literature. For close to sixty years after the formation of her troupe, she continued to drive herself to create that feeling of newness and immediacy she had always wanted.

她首批演出的反响令人振奋。观众此前从未见过如此类似的表演。许多人感到厌恶和反感。另一些人则觉得这件作品异常感人，赋予了舞蹈一种他们从未想过其拥有的表现力。作品引发了极端的反响，这体现了它的力量。多年来，最初看似刻板丑陋的表演开始被接受，因为玛莎·格雷厄姆确实一手创造了一种新的舞蹈流派——我们今天所知的现代舞。为了避免这种舞蹈沦为另一种传统，她不断努力打破人们的预期，从不重复老套，并不断变换舞蹈的主题，从希腊神话到美国风情，再到文学作品中的描写。在剧团成立后的近六十年里，她始终致力于创造她一直渴望的那种新鲜感和即时性。

Perhaps the greatest impediment to human creativity is the natural decay that sets in over time in any kind of medium or profession. In the sciences or in business, a certain way of thinking or acting that once had success quickly becomes a paradigm, an established procedure. As the years go by, people forget the initial reason for this paradigm and simply follow a lifeless set of techniques. In the arts, someone establishes a style that is new and vibrant, speaking to the particular spirit of the times. It has an edge because it is so different. Soon imitators pop up everywhere. It becomes a fashion, something to conform to, even if the conformity appears to be rebellious and edgy. This can drag on for ten, twenty years; it eventually becomes a cliché, pure style without any real emotion or need. Nothing in culture escapes this deadening dynamic.

人类创造力的最大障碍或许在于，任何媒介或职业都会随着时间的推移而自然衰退。无论是在科学领域还是商业领域，某种曾经成功的思维方式或行为方式很快就会成为一种范式，一种既定的程序。随着岁月的流逝，人们忘记了这种范式最初存在的意义，而只是沿用一套毫无生气的技巧。在艺术领域，有人创立了一种新颖而充满活力的风格，体现着特定的时代精神。它的独特之处就在于它与众不同。很快，模仿者便会蜂拥而至。它成为一种时尚，一种需要效仿的东西，即使这种效仿看起来叛逆而前卫。这种情况可能会持续十年、二十年；最终，它沦为一种陈词滥调，成为一种纯粹的风格，缺乏任何真正的情感或需求。文化中的任何事物都无法逃脱这种令人麻木的动态。

We may not be aware of it, but we suffer from the dead forms and conventions that clutter our culture. This problem, however, sets up a tremendous opportunity for creative types, one epitomized by the example of Martha Graham. The process goes as follows: You begin by looking inward. You have something you want to express that is unique to yourself and related to your inclinations. You must be sure it is not something that is sparked by some trend or fashion, but that it comes from you and is real. Perhaps it is a sound you are not hearing in music, a type of story not being told, a type of book that does not fit into the usual tidy categories. Perhaps it is even a new way of doing business. Let the idea, the sound, the image take root in you. Sensing the possibility of a new language or way of doing things, you must make the conscious decision to play against the very conventions that you find dead and want to get rid of. Martha Graham did not create her work out of a vacuum; her vision corresponded to what ballet and modern dance of the time were not giving her. She took their conventions and turned them upside down. Following this strategy will give your work a kind of reverse reference point and a way to shape it.

我们可能没有意识到，但我们正遭受着充斥着我们文化的僵化形式和习俗的困扰。然而，这个问题为富有创造力的人提供了巨大的机会，玛莎·格雷厄姆就是其中的典型代表。这个过程如下：你首先从内心开始。你想表达一些你独有的东西，并且与你的倾向有关。你必须确定它不是由某种潮流或时尚引发的，而是来自你并且是真实的。也许它是你在音乐中听不到的声音，一种没有被讲述的故事，一种无法归入通常整齐类别的书籍。也许它甚至是一种新的经营方式。让这个想法、声音和图像在你心中扎根。感觉到一种新语言或新做事方式的可能性，你必须有意识地决定对抗那些你认为已经过时并想要摆脱的习俗。玛莎·格雷厄姆的作品并非凭空创作；她的视野恰好契合了当时芭蕾舞和现代舞未能赋予她的东西。她汲取了这些舞蹈的传统，并将其彻底颠覆。遵循这一策略，你的作品将拥有一种反向的参照点，并找到塑造它的方式。

Like Graham, you must not mistake newness with wild spontaneity. There is nothing that becomes repetitive and boring more quickly than free expression that is not rooted in reality and discipline. You must bring to your new idea all of the knowledge you have acquired in your field, but for the purpose of reversing it, as Graham did with the Denishawn method. In essence, what you are doing is creating some space in a cluttered culture, claiming for yourself an open field in which you can finally plant something new. People are dying for the new, for what expresses the spirit of the time in an original way. By creating something new you will create your own audience, and attain the ultimate position of power in culture.

像格雷厄姆一样，你绝不能将“新意”与狂野的自发性混为一谈。没有什么比脱离现实和学科的自由表达更容易变得重复和乏味。你必须将你在领域内积累的所有知识融入到你的新想法中，但目的在于颠覆它，就像格雷厄姆运用丹尼肖恩的方法一样。本质上，你所做的是在杂乱的文化中开辟空间，为自己开辟一片开放的领域，最终在其中播撒新种子。人们渴望新事物，渴望以原创的方式表达时代精神。通过创造新事物，你将创造自己的受众，并在文化中获得最终的权力地位。

# ↩

6. The High End

6. 高端

Yoky Matsuoka (see chapter 1 , here ) always had the feeling that she was different from others. It wasn’t so much how she dressed or looked, but her interests that set her apart. As a teenager in Japan in the early 1980s, she was expected to focus on a particular subject that she would transform into a career. But as she got older, her interests only widened. She had a love for physics and mathematics, but was attracted to biology and physiology as well. She was also a talented athlete with a future as a professional tennis player, until an injury cut this short. On top of it all, she loved working with her hands and tinkering with machines.

松冈洋基（Yoky Matsuoka，见此处第一章）总觉得自己与众不同。让她与众不同的并非她的衣着或外貌，而是她的兴趣爱好。20世纪80年代初，日本的她还是个十几岁的少女，人们期望她专注于某一特定学科，并将其转化为职业。但随着年龄的增长，她的兴趣却越来越广泛。她热爱物理和数学，同时也对生物学和生理学充满兴趣。她也是一位才华横溢的运动员，未来有望成为一名职业网球运动员，但一场伤病让她不得不放弃这份职业。最重要的是，她热爱动手和摆弄机器。

Much to her relief, when she began her undergraduate studies at the University of California at Berkeley, she fell upon a subject that seemed to open up all sorts of larger questions that would satisfy her voracious, wide-ranging interests—the relatively new field of robotics. After completing her undergraduate studies, curious to explore this subject further, she entered the masters program in robotics at MIT. As part of her work in the department, she was to help in the design of the large-scale robot they were building, and soon she chose to work exclusively on the design of the robot’s hands. She had always been fascinated by the complexity and power of the human hand, and with the chance to combine so many of her interests (mathematics, physiology, and building things), it seemed she had finally found her niche.

令她如释重负的是，当她开始在加州大学伯克利分校攻读本科学位时，她偶然发现了一个似乎能引发各种更宏大问题、满足她广泛而广泛兴趣的领域——机器人技术。完成本科学习后，出于对进一步探索这一领域的好奇，她进入了麻省理工学院攻读机器人技术硕士课程。作为系里工作的一部分，她负责协助设计他们正在建造的大型机器人，很快，她就决定专注于机器人手部的设计。她一直对人类手部的复杂性和力量着迷，而这次有机会将自己众多的兴趣（数学、生理学和建筑）结合起来，她似乎终于找到了自己的方向。

As she began her work on the hands, however, she realized yet again how different she was in her way of thinking. The other students in the department were mostly men, and they tended to reduce everything to questions of engineering—how to pack the robot with as many mechanical options as possible so it could move and act in reasonably human ways. They thought of their robot as intrinsically a machine. To build it meant solving a series of technical issues and creating a kind of moving computer that could mimic some basic thought patterns.

然而，当她开始动手做实验时，她再次意识到自己的思维方式有多么不同。系里的其他学生大多是男生，他们倾向于把所有事情都归结为工程问题——如何给机器人配备尽可能多的机械选项，让它能够像人类一样移动和行动。他们认为他们的机器人本质上就是一台机器。制造它意味着要解决一系列技术问题，并创造一种能够模仿一些基本思维模式的移动计算机。

Matsuoka had a much different approach. She wanted to create something as lifelike and anatomically correct as possible. That was the real future of robotics, and to reach such a goal meant engaging in questions that were on a much higher level—what makes anything alive and organically complex? To her, it was as important to study evolution, human physiology, and neuroscience as it was to immerse oneself in engineering. Perhaps it would complicate her career path, but she would follow her own inclinations and see where they led.

松冈的方法截然不同。她想要创造出尽可能逼真、符合人体解剖学的东西。这才是机器人技术的真正未来，而要实现这一目标，就意味着要探究更高层次的问题——是什么让任何事物都具有生命力和有机复杂性？对她来说，研究进化论、人体生理学和神经科学与全身心投入工程学同样重要。或许这会让她的职业道路变得复杂，但她会追随自己的意愿，看看它会引领她走向何方。

In going about her design, Matsuoka made a key decision: she would begin by building a model of a robotic hand that would replicate the human hand as closely as possible. In attempting such an enormous task, she would be forced to truly understand how each part functioned. For instance, in trying to recreate all of the various bones of the hand, she came upon all kinds of seemingly irrelevant bumps and grooves. The bone at the knuckle of the index finger has a bump that makes it larger on one side. In studying this one detail, she discovered its function—giving us the ability to grasp objects in the center of the hand with more power. It seemed odd that such a bump would evolve expressly for that purpose. Probably it was some mutation that ended up becoming a part of our evolution, as the hand became increasingly important in our development.

在设计过程中，松冈做出了一个关键的决定：她首先要构建一个尽可能逼真地复制人手的机械手模型。在完成如此艰巨的任务时，她必须真正理解每个部件的功能。例如，在尝试重现手部所有骨骼的过程中，她发现了各种看似无关紧要的凸起和凹槽。食指关节处的骨骼有一个凸起，使一侧的骨骼更大。在研究这个细节时，她发现了它的功能——使我们能够用更大的力量抓住手掌中心的物体。这种凸起竟然专门为此目的而进化，这似乎有些奇怪。或许，这是某种突变，最终成为我们进化的一部分，因为手在人类进化过程中变得越来越重要。

Continuing in this line she worked on the palm of her robotic hand, which she had determined was in many ways the key to the design. For most engineers, robotic hands were designed for optimal power and maneuverability. They would build in all kinds of mechanical options, but to make it work they would have to pack all of the motors and cables in the most convenient place, the palm, rendering it completely rigid. After designing hands like this, they would then fob them off to software engineers to try to figure out to how bring back maneuverability. Because of the built-in rigidity, however, the thumb would never be able to touch the pinky, and engineers would inevitably end up with the same highly limited robotic hand.

她继续沿着这条思路，致力于机械手手掌的设计，她认为手掌在很多方面都是设计的关键。对于大多数工程师来说，机械手的设计都以最佳的力量和机动性为目标。他们会加入各种各样的机械选项，但要让它工作，就必须把所有的电机和线缆都塞进最方便的地方——手掌，让它完全僵硬。设计好这样的机械手后，他们会把设计成果交给软件工程师，让他们尝试如何恢复机动性。然而，由于机械手本身的刚性，拇指永远无法触碰到小指，最终工程师们最终还是会设计出同样功能受限的机械手。

Matsuoka started from the other end. Her goal was to discover what makes the hand dexterous, and it was clear that one critical requisite was to have a flexible, curved palm. Thinking on this higher level, it then became clear that the motors and cables had to be placed somewhere else. Instead of jamming the hand with motors everywhere so that everything could move, she determined that the most important maneuverable part of the hand was the thumb, the key to our grasping skills. That is where she would put more power.

松冈从另一个角度出发。她的目标是探索手部灵巧的奥秘，而显而易见的是，一个关键的先决条件是拥有灵活、弯曲的手掌。从更高的层面思考，她意识到电机和线缆必须放置在其他地方。她没有在手部到处塞满电机，让所有部件都能动起来，而是确定了手部最重要的可操控部位是拇指，这是我们抓握技能的关键。她会把更多力量放在拇指上。

She continued on this path, uncovering more and more of the details that went into the marvelous mechanics of the human hand. As she worked in this peculiar way, other engineers would scoff at her and her strange biological approach. What a waste of time, they would tell her. In the end, however, what she called her anatomically correct test-bed hand soon became the model for the industry, revealing whole new possibilities for prosthetic hands, vindicating her approach, and gaining her fame and recognition for her engineering skills.

她继续沿着这条路前行，不断探索人类手部奇妙力学的奥秘。当她以这种奇特的方式工作时，其他工程师会嘲笑她和她那奇特的生物学方法。他们会告诉她，这简直是浪费时间。然而，最终，她所谓的符合解剖学原理的试验手很快成为了行业的典范，揭示了假肢手的全新可能性，证明了她的方法的正确性，也为她的工程技术赢得了名声和认可。

This, however, was only the beginning of her quest to get at the organic nature of the hand and to literally recreate it. After graduating with a master’s degree in robotics, she returned to MIT to pursue a PhD in neuroscience. Currently, armed with deep knowledge about the neuro-signals that make the hand-brain connection so unique, she is pursuing the goal of creating a prosthetic hand that can actually connect to the brain, operating and feeling as if it were real. To reach such a goal, she continues to work on high-end concepts, such as the influence of the hand-brain connection on our thinking in general.

然而，这仅仅是她探索手的有机本质并真正重现它的开始。获得机器人学硕士学位后，她回到麻省理工学院攻读神经科学博士学位。目前，凭借对使手脑连接如此独特的神经信号的深入了解，她正在努力创造一只能够真正连接到大脑的假手，使其操作和感觉如同真手一样。为了实现这一目标，她继续研究高端概念，例如手脑连接对我们整体思维的影响。

In her lab she has done tests to see how people manipulate ambiguous objects with their eyes closed. She studies how they explore them with their hands, and records the elaborate neuro-signals that are generated in the process. She wonders if there could be a connection between such exploration and abstract thought processes (perhaps involving similar neuro-signals), such as when we are confronted with a problem that seems difficult to solve. She is interested in building such exploratory sensations into the prosthetic hand. In other experiments, in which subjects move a virtual-reality hand, she has discovered that the more people are made to feel that the hand is literally a part of their bodies, the greater the degree of control they have. Creating such sensations will be a part of the ultimate prosthetic hand she is working on. Although its realization is years away, the design of such a neurologically connected hand will have technological consequences far beyond robotics.

在她的实验室里，她做过一些测试，观察人们闭着眼睛如何操控模糊的物体。她研究人们如何用手探索这些物体，并记录在此过程中产生的复杂神经信号。她想知道这种探索与抽象思维过程（或许也涉及类似的神经信号）之间是否存在联系，例如当我们面对一个看似难以解决的问题时。她对在假肢中融入这种探索性感觉很感兴趣。在其他实验中，受试者移动虚拟现实手，她发现，人们越是感觉到手实际上是他们身体的一部分，他们的控制力就越强。创造这种感觉将成为她正在研发的终极假肢的一部分。尽管距离最终实现还需要数年时间，但设计出这种神经连接的手，其技术影响将远远超出机器人技术。

In many fields we can see and diagnose the same mental disease, which we shall call technical lock . What this means is the following: in order to learn a subject or skill, particularly one that is complex, we must immerse ourselves in many details, techniques, and procedures that are standard for solving problems. If we are not careful, however, we become locked into seeing every problem in the same way, using the same techniques and strategies that became so imprinted in us. It is always simpler to follow such a route. In the process we lose sight of the bigger picture, the purpose of what we are doing, how each problem we face is different and requires a different approach. We adopt a kind of tunnel vision.

在许多领域，我们都能看到并诊断出同一种心理疾病，我们称之为“技术锁”。其含义如下：为了学习一门学科或技能，尤其是复杂的学科或技能，我们必须沉浸在解决问题的众多细节、技术和标准程序中。然而，如果我们不小心，就会被困在用同一种方式看待每个问题，使用那些根深蒂固的技术和策略。遵循这样的路线总是更容易。在这个过程中，我们忽略了更广阔的视野，忽略了我们做事的目的，忽略了我们面临的每个问题是如何不同的，需要不同的方法。我们陷入了一种狭隘的视野。

This technical lock afflicts people in all fields as they lose a sense of the overall purpose of their work, of the larger question at hand, of what impels them to do their work in the first place. Yoky Matsuoka hit upon a solution to this that propelled her to the forefront of her field. It came as a reaction against the engineering approach that prevailed in robotics. Her mind naturally works better on a larger scale, continually pondering the connections between things on high levels—what makes the human hand so weirdly perfect, how the hand has influenced who we are and how we think. With these large questions governing her research, she avoids becoming narrowly focused on technical issues without understanding the bigger picture. Thinking on such a high level frees the mind up to investigate from all different angles: Why are the bones of the hand this way? What makes the palm so malleable? How does the sense of touch influence our thinking in general? It allows her to go deeply into the details without losing a sense of the why.

这种技术上的“锁”困扰着各行各业的人们，因为他们无法理解工作的总体目标，无法理解眼前的宏观问题，也无法理解最初驱使他们从事工作的动力。Yoky Matsuoka 找到了解决这个问题的方法，并因此跻身该领域的前列。这源于她对机器人领域盛行的工程学方法的反抗。她的思维天生更倾向于宏观层面，不断思考事物之间的高层次联系——是什么让人类的手如此完美，手如何影响了我们以及我们的思维方式。这些宏大的问题主导着她的研究，使她避免了狭隘地关注技术问题而忽略了全局。如此高层次的思考使她的思维得以解放，可以从各个角度进行探究：为什么手的骨骼是这样的？是什么让手掌如此具有可塑性？触觉如何影响我们的整体思维？这让她能够深入探究细节，同时又不失对“为什么”的理解。

You must make this a model for your own work as well. Your project or the problem you are solving should always be connected to something larger—a bigger question, an overarching idea, an inspiring goal. Whenever your work begins to feel stale, you must return to the larger purpose and goal that impelled you in the first place. This bigger idea governs your smaller paths of investigation, and opens up many more such paths for you to look into. By constantly reminding yourself of your purpose, you will prevent yourself from fetishizing certain techniques or from becoming overly obsessed with trivial details. In this way you will play into the natural strengths of the human brain, which wants to look for connections on higher and higher levels.

你也必须以此为范本，用于你自己的工作。你的项目或你正在解决的问题应该始终与更大的目标相联系——一个更大的问题、一个包罗万象的理念、一个鼓舞人心的目标。每当你的工作开始感到乏味时，你必须回归最初激励你的那个更大的目的和目标。这个更大的理念会引导你探索的细小路径，并为你开辟更多类似的路径。通过不断提醒自己你的目标，你就能避免迷恋某些技巧或过度沉迷于琐碎的细节。这样，你就能发挥人类大脑的天然优势，即渴望在越来越高的层次上寻找联系。

# ↩

7. The Evolutionary Hijack

7. 进化劫持

In the summer of 1995, Paul Graham (see chapter 2 , here ) heard a story on the radio promoting the endless possibilities of online commerce, which at the time hardly existed. The promotion came from Netscape, which was trying to drum up interest in its business on the eve of its IPO. The story sounded so promising, yet so vague. At the time, Graham was at a bit of a crossroads. After graduating from Harvard with a PhD in computer engineering, he had fallen into a pattern: he would find some part-time consulting job in the software business; then, with enough money saved, he would quit the job and devote his time to his real love—art and painting—until the money ran out, and then he would scramble for another job. Now thirty-one-years old, he was getting tired of the pattern, and he hated consulting. The prospect of making a lot of money quickly by developing something for the Internet suddenly seemed very appealing.

1995年夏天，保罗·格雷厄姆（Paul Graham，参见此处第二章）在广播里听到一个故事，宣传当时几乎不存在的在线商务的无限可能。这个宣传来自网景公司（Netscape），该公司正试图在IPO前夕吸引公众对其业务的兴趣。这个故事听起来前景光明，却又如此模糊。当时，格雷厄姆正处于人生的十字路口。从哈佛大学获得计算机工程博士学位后，他陷入了一种模式：在软件行业找一份兼职咨询工作；然后，攒够了钱，就辞掉这份工作，全身心投入到他真正热爱的艺术和绘画中，直到钱花光，再去找另一份工作。如今，31岁的格雷厄姆已经厌倦了这种模式，他讨厌咨询工作。通过开发互联网产品快速赚大钱的前景突然变得非常诱人。

He called up his old programming partner from Harvard, Robert Morris, and interested him in the idea of collaborating on their own startup, even though Graham had no clue where they would start or what they would develop. After a few days of discussing this, they decided they would try to write software that would enable a business to generate an online store. Once they were clear about the concept, they had to confront a very large obstacle in their way. In those days, for a program to be popular enough it would have to be written for Windows. As consummate hackers, they loathed everything about Windows and had never bothered to learn how to develop applications for it. They preferred to write in Lisp and have the program run on Unix, the open-source operating system.

他打电话给他在哈佛大学的老编程搭档罗伯特莫里斯，让他对合作创办自己的初创公司感兴趣，尽管格雷厄姆对他们从哪里开始或要开发什么都一无所知。经过几天的讨论，他们决定尝试编写一个软件，让企业能够开设一个网上商店。在明确了这个概念之后，他们不得不面对一个巨大的障碍。在那个年代，一个程序要想足够流行，就必须为 Windows 编写。作为十足的黑客，他们厌恶 Windows 的一切，也从未费心学习如何为它开发应用程序。他们更喜欢用 Lisp 编写程序，并让程序在开源操作系统 Unix 上运行。

They decided to postpone the inevitable and wrote the program for Unix anyway. To translate this later into Windows would be easy, but as they contemplated doing this, they realized the terrible consequences it would lead to—once the program was launched in Windows, they would have to deal with users and perfect the program based on their feedback. This would mean they would be forced to think and program in Windows for months, perhaps years. This was too awful a prospect, and they seriously considered giving up.

他们决定推迟不可避免的事情，无论如何都要为 Unix 编写程序。以后再把程序翻译成 Windows 版本很容易，但当他们考虑这样做时，他们意识到这将导致可怕的后果——一旦程序在 Windows 上发布，他们就必须与用户打交道，并根据用户的反馈来完善程序。这意味着他们将被迫在 Windows 上思考和编程数月，甚至数年。这是一个可怕的前景，他们认真考虑过放弃。

One morning Graham, who had been sleeping on a mattress on the floor in Morris’s Manhattan apartment, woke up repeating certain words that must have come to him from a dream: “You could control the program by clicking on links.” He suddenly sat bolt upright, as he realized what these words could mean—the possibility of creating a program to set up an online store that would run on the web server itself. People would download and use it through Netscape, clicking various links on the web page to set it up. This would mean he and Morris would bypass the usual route of writing a program that users would download to their desktop. It would cut out the need ever to have to dabble in Windows. There was nothing out there like this, and yet it seemed like such an obvious solution. In a state of excitement he explained his epiphany to Morris, and they agreed to give it a try. Within a few days they finished the first version, and it functioned beautifully. Clearly, the concept of a web application would work.

一天早上，格雷厄姆睡在莫里斯曼哈顿公寓的地板上，突然醒来，嘴里念叨着几句似曾相识的梦话：“你可以通过点击链接来控制程序。” 他猛地坐直，意识到这句话的含义——可以创建一个程序，建立一个在网络服务器上运行的在线商店。人们可以通过网景公司下载并使用该程序，点击网页上的各种链接即可完成设置。这意味着他和莫里斯可以绕过编写程序、用户下载到桌面的常规流程。这样一来，用户就无需再费心钻研 Windows 系统了。虽然市面上没有类似的方案，但这似乎是一个显而易见的解决方案。他兴奋地向莫里斯解释了自己的顿悟，两人同意尝试一下。几天之内，他们就完成了第一个版本，而且运行良好。显然，网络应用程序的概念是可行的。

Over the next few weeks they refined the software, and found their own angel investor who put up an initial $10,000 for a 10 percent share in the business. In the beginning, it was quite hard to interest merchants in the concept. Their application server provider was the very first Internet-run program for starting a business, at the very frontier of online commerce. Slowly, however, it began to take off.

在接下来的几周里，他们不断完善软件，并找到了自己的天使投资人，后者最初投资了1万美元，获得了10%的股份。起初，很难让商家对这个概念产生兴趣。他们的应用服务器提供商是第一个基于互联网的创业项目，处于在线商务的最前沿。然而，它慢慢地开始腾飞。

As it panned out, the novelty of their idea, which Graham and Morris had come upon largely because of their distaste for Windows, proved to have all kinds of unforeseen advantages. Working directly on the Internet, they could generate a continuous stream of new releases of the software and test them right away. They could interact directly with consumers, getting instant feedback on their program and improving it in days rather than the months it could take with desktop software. With no experience running a business, they did not think to hire salespeople to do the pitching; instead, they made the phone calls to potential clients themselves. But as they were the de facto salespeople, they were also the first to hear complaints or suggestions from consumers, and this gave them a real feel for the program’s weaknesses and how to improve it. Because it was so unique and came out of left field, they had no competitors to worry about; nobody could steal the idea because they were the only ones who were insane enough to attempt it.

格雷厄姆和莫里斯最初是因为厌恶Windows系统而萌生了这个想法，但最终，这个想法被证明拥有各种意想不到的优势。直接在互联网上工作，他们可以持续不断地发布新版本的软件，并立即进行测试。他们可以直接与消费者互动，即时获得程序反馈，并在几天内改进程序，而不像桌面软件那样需要几个月的时间。由于缺乏经营企业的经验，他们没有想到雇佣销售人员来推销，而是亲自给潜在客户打电话。但由于他们实际上是销售人员，所以他们也是第一批听到消费者抱怨或建议的人，这让他们真正了解了程序的弱点以及如何改进。由于程序如此独特且出乎意料，他们无需担心竞争对手；没有人能够窃取这个想法，因为他们是唯一一个疯狂到敢于尝试的人。

Naturally, they made several mistakes along the way, but the idea was too strong to fail; and in 1998 they sold their company, named Viaweb, to Yahoo! for $50 million.

当然，他们在这一过程中也犯过一些错误，但是这个想法太强大了，不可能失败；1998 年，他们以 5000 万美元的价格将自己的公司 Viaweb 卖给了雅虎。

As the years went by and Graham looked back at the experience, he was struck by the process he and Morris had gone through. It reminded him of so many other inventions in history, such as microcomputers. The microprocessors that made the microcomputer possible had originally been developed to run traffic lights and vending machines. They had never been intended to power computers. The first entrepreneurs to attempt this were laughed at; the computers they had created looked hardly worthy of the name—they were so small and could do so little. But they caught on with just enough people for whom they saved time, and slowly, the idea took off. The same story had occurred with transistors, which in the 1930s and ’40s were developed and used in electronics for the military. It was not until the early 1950s that several individuals had the idea of applying this technology to transistor radios for the public, soon hitting upon what would become the most popular electronic device in history.

随着岁月流逝，格雷厄姆回首往事，不禁被他和莫里斯经历的历程所震撼。这让他想起了历史上许多其他的发明，比如微型计算机。构成微型计算机的微处理器最初是为了控制交通信号灯和自动售货机而开发的，从未被设计用于驱动计算机。第一批尝试这种技术的企业家曾被嘲笑；他们创造的计算机看起来几乎名不副实——体积如此之小，功能如此之少。但他们的发明很快便获得了一定程度的认可，为人们节省了时间，于是这个想法逐渐流行起来。晶体管也经历了同样的发展历程，它在20世纪30年代和40年代被开发并应用于军用电子设备。直到20世纪50年代初，才有几个人萌生了将这项技术应用于面向大众的晶体管收音机的想法，并很快发明了后来成为历史上最受欢迎的电子设备。

What was interesting in all of these cases was the peculiar process that led to these inventions: generally, the inventors had a chance encounter with the available technology; then the idea would come to them that this technology could be used for other purposes; and finally they would try out different prototypes until the right one fell into place. What allows for this process is the willingness of the inventor to look at everyday things in a different light and to imagine new uses for them. For people who are stuck in rigid ways of seeing, the familiarity of an old application hypnotizes them into not seeing its other possibilities. What it all really comes down to is the possession of a flexible, adaptable mind—something that is often enough to separate a successful inventor or entrepreneur from the rest of the crowd.

所有这些案例中，有趣的是促成这些发明的奇特过程：通常，发明者偶然接触到现有技术；然后他们就会想到这项技术可以用于其他用途；最后他们会尝试不同的原型，直到找到合适的方案。这个过程之所以能够进行，是因为发明者愿意以不同的眼光看待日常事物，并设想它们的新用途。对于那些思维僵化的人来说，对旧应用的熟悉会让他们看不到它的其他可能性。归根结底，这一切都取决于是否拥有灵活、适应性强的头脑——这往往足以将一位成功的发明家或企业家从人群中脱颖而出。

After cashing in on Viaweb, Graham hit upon the idea of writing essays for the Internet—his rather peculiar form of blogging. These essays made him a celebrity among young hackers and programmers everywhere. In 2005 he was invited by undergraduates in the computer science department at Harvard to give a talk. Instead of boring them and himself by analyzing various programming languages, he decided to discuss the idea of technology startups themselves—why some work, why some fail. The talk was so successful, and Graham’s ideas so illuminating, that the students began to besiege him with questions about their own startup ideas. As he listened, he could sense that some of their concepts were not far off the mark, but that they badly needed shaping and guidance.

在利用 Viaweb 赚钱之后，格雷厄姆萌生了为互联网撰写文章的想法——这是一种颇为独特的博客形式。这些文章让他在世界各地的年轻黑客和程序员中名声大噪。2005 年，他受哈佛大学计算机系本科生邀请去做演讲。他没有选择枯燥地分析各种编程语言，而是决定探讨科技创业公司本身——为什么有些公司成功，有些公司失败。这次演讲非常成功，格雷厄姆的想法也极具启发性，学生们开始围着他问关于他们自己创业想法的问题。在聆听的过程中，他能感觉到学生们的一些想法并非遥不可及，但迫切需要一些引导和塑造。

Graham had always intended to try his hand at investing in other people’s ideas. He had been the beneficiary of an angel investor in his project, and it was only right to return the favor by helping others. The problem was where to begin. Most angel investors had some related experience before they began investing, and they tended to start out on a small scale to get their feet wet. Graham had no such business experience. Based on this weakness, he hit upon an idea that at first glance seemed ridiculous—he would synchronously invest $15,000 in ten startups all at once. He would find these ten prospects by advertising his offer and choosing the best among the applicants. Over the course of a few months he would shepherd these novices and help guide them to the point of launching their idea. For this he would take 10 percent from any successful startup. It would be like an apprenticeship system for tech founders, but it really had another purpose—it would serve as a crash course for him in the investing business. He would be a lousy first investor and his pupils would be lousy entrepreneurs, making them a perfect match.

格雷厄姆一直想尝试投资别人的想法。他的项目曾受益于一位天使投资人，因此帮助他人回报这份恩情理所当然。问题在于从何入手。大多数天使投资人在开始投资之前都有一些相关经验，而且他们倾向于从小规模开始尝试。格雷厄姆没有这样的商业经验。基于这个弱点，他突发奇想，想出了一个乍一看似乎荒谬的想法——他计划同时向10家初创公司投资1.5万美元。他会通过宣传自己的项目，并从申请者中选出最优秀的公司，从而找到这10家公司。在几个月的时间里，他会引导这些新手，帮助他们实现自己的创意。为此，他会从任何一家成功的初创公司中抽取10%的佣金。这就像科技创始人的学徒制，但实际上还有另一个目的——这将成为他投资行业的速成课程。他会是一个糟糕的初始投资者，而他的学生则会是一个糟糕的企业家，他们是完美的一对。

Yet again he recruited Robert Morris to join him in the business. A couple of weeks into the training, however, he and Morris realized that they were actually on to something powerful. Because of their experience with Viaweb they were able to give clear and effective advice. The startup ideas they were shepherding looked quite promising. Perhaps this system they had adopted as a way to learn quickly was an interesting model in itself. Most investors only handle a few startups a year; they are too overwhelmed with their own businesses to handle much more. But what if Graham and Morris were to devote their time exclusively to this apprenticeship system? They could mass-produce the service. They could fund hundreds instead of dozens of such startups. In the process they would learn in leaps and bounds, and this exponentially increasing knowledge would lead to increasing numbers of successful startups.

他再次招募罗伯特·莫里斯加入他的事业。然而，培训几周后，他和莫里斯意识到，他们实际上正在做一件大事。凭借在Viaweb的经验，他们能够提供清晰有效的建议。他们正在培育的创业想法看起来前景光明。或许，他们采用的这种快速学习的系统本身就是一种有趣的模式。大多数投资者每年只投资几家初创公司；他们自己的业务已经让他们应接不暇，无暇顾及更多。但如果格雷厄姆和莫里斯将时间全部投入到这个学徒制中呢？他们可以批量生产这项服务。他们可以资助数百家而不是数十家这样的初创公司。在这个过程中，他们将突飞猛进地学习，而这种指数级增长的知识将催生出越来越多的成功初创公司。

If it really took off, not only would they make a fortune, but they would also have a decided impact on the economy, unleashing into the system thousands of savvy entrepreneurs. They called their new company Y Combinator and considered it their ultimate hack to change the shape of the world’s economy.

如果真的成功了，他们不仅能赚大钱，还能对经济产生决定性的影响，为整个经济体系注入成千上万精明的创业者。他们将新公司命名为 Y Combinator，并视其为改变世界经济格局的终极方案。
