They coached their apprentices in all of the principles they had learned along the way—the benefit in looking for new applications of existing technology and needs that are not being met; the importance of maintaining the closest possible relationship with customers; the need to keep ideas as simple and realistic as possible; the value of creating a superior product and of winning through craftsmanship, as opposed to fixating on making money.

他们向学徒传授一路走来学到的所有原则——寻找现有技术的新应用和尚未满足的需求的好处；与客户保持最密切关系的重要性；让想法尽可能简单和现实的必要性；创造优质产品和通过工艺取胜的价值，而不是一心想着赚钱。

As their apprentices learned, they learned as well. Oddly enough, they discovered that what really makes successful entrepreneurs is not the nature of their idea, or the university they went to, but their actual character—their willingness to adapt their idea and take advantage of possibilities they had not first imagined. This is precisely the trait—fluidity of mind—that Graham had identified in himself and in other inventors. The other essential character trait was supreme tenacity.

他们的学徒们在学习的同时，他们也学习。奇怪的是，他们发现，真正成就成功企业家的并非他们创意的本质，也不是他们就读的大学，而是他们真实的性格——他们愿意调整自己的想法，并利用最初未曾想象到的可能性。这正是格雷厄姆在自己和其他发明家身上发现的特质——思维的流动性。另一个重要的性格特质是无比的坚韧。

Over the years, evolving in its own way, Y Combinator has continued to grow at an astounding rate. It is valued now at $500 million, with the clear potential for further growth.

多年来，Y Combinator 一直以独特的方式不断发展，并保持着惊人的增长速度。目前，它的估值已达 5 亿美元，并且拥有明显的增长潜力。

We generally have a misconception about the inventive and creative powers of the human mind. We imagine that creative people have an interesting idea, which they then proceed to elaborate and refine in a somewhat linear process. The truth, however, is much messier and more complex. Creativity actually resembles a process known in nature as evolutionary hijacking. In evolution, accidents and contingencies play an enormous role. For instance, feathers evolved from reptilian scales, their purpose being to keep birds warm. (Birds evolved from reptiles.) But eventually, those existing feathers became adapted for the purpose of flying, transforming into wing feathers. For our own primate ancestors living in trees, the form of the hand largely evolved out of the need to grasp branches with speed and agility. Our early hominid ancestors, walking on the ground, found this intricately developed hand quite useful for manipulating rocks, making tools, and gesturing in communication. Perhaps language itself developed as a strictly social tool and became hijacked as a means of reasoning, making human consciousness itself the product of an accident.

我们通常对人类思维的创造力存在误解。我们以为富有创造力的人会有一个有趣的想法，然后他们会以某种线性过程对其进行完善和提炼。然而，事实远比这更混乱、更复杂。创造力实际上类似于自然界中被称为“进化劫持”的过程。在进化过程中，意外和偶然事件扮演着重要的角色。例如，羽毛是由爬行动物的鳞片进化而来的，其目的是为鸟类保暖。（鸟类是由爬行动物进化而来的。）但最终，这些现有的羽毛适应了飞行，变成了翼羽。对于我们生活在树上的灵长类祖先来说，手的形状很大程度上是出于快速敏捷地抓住树枝的需要而进化而来的。我们早期在地面行走的类人猿祖先发现，这种进化精巧的手在操纵岩石、制造工具和用手势交流方面非常有用。也许语言本身是作为一种严格的社会工具而发展起来的，并被劫持为一种推理手段，使得人类意识本身成为意外的产物。

Human creativity generally follows a similar path, perhaps indicating a kind of organic fatality to the creation of anything. Ideas do not come to us out of nowhere. Instead, we come upon something by accident—in the case of Graham, a radio announcement that he hears, or questions from the audience after a lecture. If we are experienced enough and the moment is ripe, this accidental encounter will spark some interesting associations and ideas in us. In looking at the particular materials we can work with, we suddenly see another way to use them. All along the way, contingencies pop up that reveal different paths we can take, and if they are promising, we follow them, not sure of where they will lead. Instead of a straight-line development from idea to fruition, the creative process is more like the crooked branching of a tree.

人类的创造力通常遵循类似的路径，这或许表明任何创造都具有某种有机的宿命性。灵感并非凭空而来。相反，我们偶然遇到一些事情——以格雷厄姆为例，他听到的广播公告，或是讲座后听众的提问。如果我们经验丰富，时机成熟，这种偶然的相遇会激发我们一些有趣的联想和想法。在审视我们可以使用的特定材料时，我们突然发现了另一种使用方法。一路走来，各种偶然事件不断涌现，揭示出我们可以选择的不同路径。如果这些路径有希望，我们就会追随它们，而不确定它们最终会通向何方。创造过程并非从想法到成果的直线发展，而更像是树木弯曲的枝干。

The lesson is simple—what constitutes true creativity is the openness and adaptability of our spirit. When we see or experience something we must be able to look at it from several angles, to see other possibilities beyond the obvious ones. We imagine that the objects around us can be used and co-opted for different purposes. We do not hold on to our original idea out of sheer stubbornness, or because our ego is tied up with its rightness. Instead, we move with what presents itself to us in the moment, exploring and exploiting different branches and contingencies. We thus manage to turn feathers into flying material. The difference then is not in some initial creative power of the brain, but in how we look at the world and the fluidity with which we can reframe what we see. Creativity and adaptability are inseparable.

道理很简单——真正的创造力源于我们心灵的开放性和适应性。当我们看到或体验到某种事物时，我们必须能够从多个角度审视它，发现显而易见之外的其他可能性。我们想象周围的事物可以被用于不同的目的。我们并非出于纯粹的固执，或因为自我被其正确性所束缚而坚持最初的想法。相反，我们会顺应当下呈现在我们面前的事物，探索和利用不同的分支和偶然性。我们就这样将羽毛化为飞翔的素材。差异并非在于大脑最初的创造力，而在于我们如何看待世界，以及我们重构所见事物的流畅性。创造力和适应性密不可分。

# ↩

8. Dimensional Thinking

8. 维度思维

In 1798 Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Egypt in an attempt to transform it into a colony, but the invasion bogged down as the British, seeking to block the French, became involved. A year later, as the war dragged on, a soldier working on the reinforcement of a French fort near the town of Rosetta dug into the ground and hit a rock. In extracting the rock, he discovered that it was some kind of relic from ancient Egypt—a slab of basalt covered in writing. Napoleon had been motivated to invade Egypt partially by his intense curiosity for all things Egyptian, and had taken along with his troops French scientists and historians to help analyze the relics he hoped to find.

1798年，拿破仑·波拿巴入侵埃及，试图将其变为殖民地。但由于英国为阻止法国而介入，入侵计划陷入停滞。一年后，随着战争的拖延，一名士兵在罗塞塔镇附近加固法国堡垒时，挖掘出一块岩石。在挖出岩石的过程中，他发现这是某种古埃及文物——一块刻满文字的玄武岩板。拿破仑入侵埃及的部分动机是他对埃及所有事物的强烈好奇，并带上法国科学家和历史学家随军前往，帮助分析他希望找到的文物。

In looking at the slab of basalt, which came to be known as the Rosetta stone, the French savants grew excited. It contained text written out in three different scripts—on the top, Egyptian hieroglyphs; in the middle, what is known as demotic (the language and script of the common people of ancient Egypt), and on the bottom, ancient Greek. In translating the ancient Greek, they discovered that the text was a mundane proclamation celebrating the reign of Ptolemy V (203–181 B.C.). At the end of the text, however, it stated that the proclamation was to be written out in three versions, meaning that the content was the same in the demotic and the hieroglyphic. With the ancient Greek text as the key, it suddenly seemed possible to decipher the other two versions. Since the last known hieroglyphs had been written in A.D. 394, anyone who could read them had long died off, making it a completely dead and untranslatable language and leaving a seemingly unsolvable mystery as to the content of so many of the writings in temples and on papyri. Now, perhaps, these secrets could finally be revealed.

看着这块后来被称为罗塞塔石碑的玄武岩石板，法国学者们兴奋不已。石板上刻有三种不同文字——最上面是埃及象形文字，中间是俗语（古埃及平民的语言和文字），最下面是古希腊文。在翻译古希腊文时，他们发现这是一份庆祝托勒密五世（公元前203-181年）统治的世俗宣言。然而，文本的末尾却注明，宣言需要三个版本，这意味着世俗体和象形文字的内容相同。有了古希腊文本作为钥匙，解读其他两个版本似乎就变得可能了。自从已知的最后一批象形文字于公元394年写下以来，能够阅读这些文字的人早已消亡，使其成为一种完全消亡且无法翻译的语言，也留下了关于神庙和纸莎草纸上众多文字内容的疑云。如今，或许这些秘密终于可以揭晓了。

The stone was carted off to an institution in Cairo, but in 1801 the English defeated the French in Egypt and threw them out. Knowing of the extremely high value of the Rosetta stone, they hunted it down in Cairo and shipped it off to London, where it remains to this day in the British Museum. As drawings of the stone began to be passed around, intellectuals from all parts of Europe became involved in a competition to be the first to decipher the hieroglyphs and unlock the mysteries. As they began to tackle the puzzle, some progress was made. Certain hieroglyphs were outlined in a rectangle, known as cartouches. It was determined that these cartouches contained the names of various royal figures. One Swedish professor had been able to make out the name of Ptolemy in the demotic, and speculated on the sound values the characters might have. But the initial enthusiasm for deciphering the hieroglyphs eventually died out, and many worried that they would remain undecipherable. The further anyone got with the puzzle, the more questions that were raised about the kind of writing system represented by the symbols themselves.

这块石碑被运往开罗的一家机构，但1801年，英国人在埃及击败了法国人，将他们驱逐出境。由于知道罗塞塔石碑的极高价值，英国人在开罗找到了它，并将其运往伦敦，至今仍保存在大英博物馆。随着石碑上的图画开始流传，来自欧洲各地的知识分子开始参与一场比赛，看谁能率先破译象形文字，解开谜团。随着他们开始破解谜团，取得了一些进展。某些象形文字被框在一个矩形框内，称为涡卷图案。人们确定这些涡卷图案上刻有各种皇室人物的名字。一位瑞典教授辨认出了托勒密在世俗体文字中的名字，并推测这些字符可能具有的音值。但最初破译象形文字的热情最终消退，许多人担心这些文字将永远无法破译。随着人们对这个谜题的了解不断深入，人们对这些符号本身所代表的书写体系的疑问也越来越多。

In 1814 a new figure entered the fray—an Englishman named Dr. Thomas Young—who quickly became the leading candidate to be the first to decipher the Rosetta stone. Although a medical doctor, he was a man who had dabbled in all the sciences and was considered something of a genius. He had the blessing of the English establishment and full access to all of the various papyri and relics the English had confiscated, including the stone itself. Furthermore, he was independently wealthy and could devote all of his time to the study. And so, throwing himself into the work with great enthusiasm, Young began to make some progress.

1814年，一位新人加入战局——一位名叫托马斯·杨博士的英国人——他很快成为破译罗塞塔石碑的首要候选人。虽然他是一位医生，但他涉猎了所有科学领域，被认为是一位天才。他得到了英国权威机构的庇护，可以自由查阅英国没收的各种纸莎草纸和文物，包括罗塞塔石碑本身。此外，他经济条件优渥，可以全身心投入研究。于是，杨博士满怀热情地投入到研究中，并开始取得一些进展。

He had a computational approach to the problem. He counted the number of times a particular word, such as “god,” appeared in the Greek text, then found a word that appeared the same number of times in the demotic, assuming they were the same word. He did everything he could to make the letters in demotic fit his scheme—if the apparent equivalent word of “god” seemed too long, he would simply deduce that certain letters were meaningless. He assumed that the three texts went in the same order, and that he could match words by their location. Sometimes he guessed right; most often he got nowhere. He made some key discoveries—that demotic and hieroglyphs were related, the one being a kind of loose handwritten form of the other; and that demotic used a phonetic alphabet to spell out foreign names, but that it was mostly a system of pictograms. But he kept hitting dead ends, and he never got close to trying his hand at the hieroglyphs. After a few years, he essentially gave up.

他用计算的方法解决这个问题。他计算某个特定词（例如“god”）在希腊文本中出现的次数，然后在世俗体中找到一个出现次数相同的词，假设它们是同一个词。他竭尽所能使世俗体中的字母符合他的方案——如果“god”的对应词看起来太长，他就会推断某些字母毫无意义。他假设这三个文本的顺序相同，并且他可以根据单词的位置进行匹配。有时他猜对了；但大多数时候他一无所获。他有一些关键的发现——世俗体和象形文字是相关的，一个是另一个的一种松散的手写形式；世俗体使用语音字母拼写外国名字，但它主要是一种象形文字系统。但他总是遇到死胡同，从未尝试过象形文字。几年后，他基本上放弃了。

In the meantime, there appeared on the scene a young man who seemed to be an unlikely candidate to succeed in this race—Jean-Francois Champollion (1790–1832). He came from a small town near Grenoble. His family was relatively poor, and until the age of seven Champollion had no formal education. But he had one advantage over all the others: from his earliest years he had been drawn to the history of ancient civilizations. He wanted to discover new things about the origins of mankind, and for this purpose he took up the study of ancient languages—Greek, Latin, and Hebrew, as well as several other Semitic languages—all of which he mastered with remarkable speed by the age of twelve.

与此同时，一位看似不太可能在这场竞选中胜出的年轻人——让-弗朗索瓦·商博良（1790-1832）——出现在了舞台上。他来自格勒诺布尔附近的一个小镇。家境相对贫困，商博良直到七岁才接受过正规教育。但他比其他人有一个优势：他从小就对古代文明史充满热情。他渴望探索人类起源的新奥秘，为此，他开始学习古代语言——希腊语、拉丁语、希伯来语以及其他几种闪族语言——十二岁时，他便以惊人的速度掌握了所有这些语言。

Quickly his attention was drawn to ancient Egypt. In 1802 he heard about the Rosetta stone, and he told his older brother that he would be the one to decipher it. The moment he began to study the ancient Egyptians, he experienced a vivid identification with everything that had to do with the civilization. As a child, he had a powerful visual memory. He could draw with exceptional skill. He tended to see the writings in books (even books in French) as if they were drawings instead of an alphabet. When he first laid eyes on hieroglyphs they seemed almost familiar to him. Soon his relationship to hieroglyphs bordered on a fanatical obsession.

很快，他的注意力就被古埃及所吸引。1802年，他听说了罗塞塔石碑，便告诉哥哥，他要破译它。从他开始研究古埃及文明的那一刻起，他对与这个文明相关的一切都产生了一种鲜活的共鸣。孩提时代，他就拥有强大的视觉记忆，绘画技艺精湛。他常常把书中的文字（即使是法语书籍）看作图画，而不是字母。当他第一次看到象形文字时，它们对他来说几乎是熟悉的。很快，他与象形文字的联系就近乎狂热。

To really make progress, he decided he would have to learn the language known as Coptic. After Egypt became a Roman colony in 30 B.C., the old language, demotic, slowly died out, and was replaced by Coptic—a mix of Greek and Egyptian. After the Arabs conquered Egypt and converted it to Islam, making Arabic the official idiom, the remaining Christians in the land retained Coptic as their language. By Champollion’s time only a few Christians remained who still spoke the ancient language, mostly monks and priests. In 1805 just such a monk passed through Champollion’s small town, and he quickly befriended him. The monk taught him the rudiments of Coptic, and when he returned a few months later, he brought Champollion a grammar book. The boy worked at the language day and night, with a fervor that others saw as madness. He wrote his brother: “I do nothing else. I dream in Coptic…. I am so Coptic, that for fun, I translate into Coptic everything that comes into my head.” When he later went to Paris for schooling he found more monks, and he practiced to the point where he was told that he spoke the dying language as well as any native.

为了真正取得进步，他决定学习科普特语。公元前 30 年埃及沦为罗马殖民地后，古老的世俗语逐渐消亡，取而代之的是科普特语——一种混合了希腊语和埃及语的语言。阿拉伯人征服埃及并将其皈依伊斯兰教，阿拉伯语成为官方语言后，这片土地上幸存的基督徒仍将科普特语作为他们的语言。到了商博良的时代，只剩下少数基督徒仍然讲这种古老的语言，其中大部分是僧侣和牧师。1805 年，一位这样的僧侣路过商博良的小镇，他很快就与他成为了朋友。僧侣教给了他科普特语的基础知识，几个月后，僧侣回来时给商博良带来了一本语法书。这个男孩没日没夜地学习这门语言，他的热情在别人看来简直是疯狂。他写信给弟弟说：“我什么都不做。我用科普特语做梦……我太科普特了，为了好玩，我会把脑子里想到的一切都翻译成科普特语。”后来，他去巴黎求学，遇到了更多的僧侣，他不断修行，直到有人告诉他，他能说一口科普特语，和任何当地人一样流利。

With only a poor reproduction of the Rosetta stone at his disposal, he began to attack it with various hypotheses, all of which were later proven quite wrong. Unlike the others, however, Champollion’s enthusiasm never dampened. The problem for him was the political turmoil of his time. An avowed son of the French Revolution, he finally came to support the cause of Napoleon just as the emperor lost power. When King Louis XVIII came to the throne as the new French king, Champollion’s Napoleonic sympathies cost him his job as a professor. Years of grinding poverty and ill health forced him to abandon his interest in the Rosetta stone. But in 1821, finally rehabilitated by the government and living in Paris, Champollion returned to the quest with a renewed energy and determination.

由于手头只有一张质量很差的罗塞塔石碑复制品，他开始用各种假设来攻击它，但后来都被证明是完全错误的。然而，与其他人不同，商博良的热情从未减弱。他面临的问题是当时的政治动荡。作为法国大革命的公开支持者，他最终在拿破仑皇帝丧失权力时转而支持他。当路易十八登基成为法国新国王时，商博良对拿破仑的同情使他失去了教授的工作。多年的极度贫困和疾病迫使他放弃了对罗塞塔石碑的兴趣。但在 1821 年，政府最终恢复了他的名誉并居住在巴黎，商博良带着新的活力和决心重返探索之路。

Having been away from the study of hieroglyphics for some time, he came back with a fresh perspective. The problem, he decided, was that others were approaching decipherment as if it involved some kind of mathematical code. But Champollion, who spoke dozens of languages and could read many dead languages, understood that languages evolve in a haphazard manner, influenced by the influx of new groups into a society and shaped by the passage of time. They are not mathematical formulas, but living, evolving organisms. They are complex. He now approached the hieroglyphs in a more holistic fashion. His goal was to figure out exactly what kind of script it was—pictograms (literally the picture representing the thing), ideograms (the picture representing ideas), some kind of phonetic alphabet, or perhaps a mix of all three.

离开象形文字研究一段时间后，他带着全新的视角回归。他认为，问题在于其他人在解读象形文字时，仿佛这涉及某种数学密码。但商博良精通数十种语言，能够阅读许多已消亡语言，他明白语言的演变是随机的，受到新群体涌入社会的影响，并受到时间流逝的影响。它们不是数学公式，而是活生生的、不断进化的有机体。它们非常复杂。现在，他以一种更全面的方式研究象形文字。他的目标是弄清楚它究竟是一种什么样的文字——象形文字（字面意思是代表事物的图形）、表意文字（代表思想的图形）、某种语音字母，或者三者的混合。

With this in mind, he tried something that strangely enough no one had thought of—he made a comparison of the number of words in the Greek and hieroglyphic sections. He counted 486 words in the Greek text, and 1,419 hieroglyphic signs. Champollion had been operating under the assumption that hieroglyphs were ideograms, each symbol representing an idea or word. With such a discrepancy in number, this assumption was no longer possible. He then tried to identify groups of hieroglyphic symbols that would constitute words, but this numbered only 180. He could find no clear numerical relationship between the two, and so the only possible conclusion from all of this was that hieroglyphic writing is a mixed system of ideograms, pictograms, and a phonetic alphabet, making it more complex than anyone had imagined.

考虑到这一点，他尝试了一件奇怪的事情——他比较了希腊文和象形文字部分的词汇数量。他统计出希腊文文本中有486个词汇，而象形文字符号有1419个。商博良一直假设象形文字是表意文字，每个符号代表一个概念或词语。由于数量上的差异，这一假设不再成立。他随后尝试识别构成词语的象形文字符号组，但数量只有180个。他无法找到两者之间明确的数字关系，因此，由此得出的唯一可能结论是：象形文字是表意文字、象形文字和语音字母的混合系统，这使其比任何人想象的都要复杂。

He next decided to attempt something that anyone else would have thought insane and useless—to apply his visual powers to the demotic and hieroglyphic texts, looking exclusively at the shapes of the letters or signs. In doing so he began to see patterns and correspondences—for instance, a particular sign in the hieroglyph, such as the depiction of a bird, had a rough equivalent in demotic, the image of the bird becoming less realistic and more like an abstract shape. Because of his incredible photographic memory, he could identify hundreds of these equivalences between symbols, although he could not say what any one of them meant. They remained merely images.

接下来，他决定尝试一件在其他人看来疯狂而无用的事情——将他的视觉能力运用到世俗体和象形文字文本中，专注于字母或符号的形状。通过这样做，他开始发现其中的模式和对应关系——例如，象形文字中的某个符号，比如鸟的图案，在世俗体中有一个大致对应的符号，鸟的形象变得不那么逼真，更像是一个抽象的形状。凭借他惊人的过目不忘的能力，他能够识别出数百个符号之间的对应关系，尽管他无法说出其中任何一个符号的含义。它们仅仅停留在图像层面。

Armed with this knowledge, he went on the attack. On the Rosetta stone, he examined the royal cartouche in the demotic that had been previously identified as containing the name of Ptolemy. Knowing now many equivalent signs between hieroglyphs and demotic, he transposed the demotic symbols into what they should look like in the hieroglyphic version, to create what should be the word for Ptolemy. To his surprise and delight, he found such a word—making this the first successful decipherment of a hieroglyph. Knowing that this name was probably written out in phonetics (as would be all foreign names), he deduced the sound equivalences in both demotic and hieroglyph for Ptolemy. With the letters P T L now identified, he found another cartouche in a papyrus document that he was certain would have to be that of Cleopatra, now adding new letters to his knowledge. Ptolemy and Cleopatra had two different letters for T. For others this might prove baffling, but to Champollion he understood that it merely represented homophones—much as the f sound in “ ph one” and “ f old.” With growing knowledge of letters he proceeded to decipher the names of all of the royal cartouches he could find, giving him a treasure trove of alphabetic information.

有了这些知识，他便开始进攻。在罗塞塔石碑上，他检查了先前被确认为包含托勒密名字的世俗体皇家涡卷装饰。现在，他知道了象形文字和世俗体符号之间的许多对应符号，他将世俗体符号转换成象形文字版本中的样子，从而创造出了托勒密的单词。令他又惊又喜的是，他找到了这样一个词——这是第一次成功破译象形文字。他知道这个名字很可能是用语音书写的（所有外国名字都是如此），于是他推断出托勒密在世俗体和象形文字中的发音对应关系。现在，字母 P T L 已经确定，他在一份纸莎草文献中发现了另一个涡卷装饰，他确信那一定是克利奥帕特拉的，现在他的知识中又增加了新的字母。托勒密和克利奥帕特拉的T字母各有两个不同的含义。其他人或许会对此感到困惑，但商博良明白，T只是同音词——就像“phone”（电话）和“fold”（折叠）中f的发音一样。随着对字母的了解不断加深，他开始破译所有能找到的皇家涡卷纹饰的名称，从而获得了大量的字母信息。

Then in September 1822 it all became unlocked in the most surprising way, in the course of one day. A temple had been discovered in a desolate part of Egypt whose walls and statues were covered in hieroglyphs. Accurate drawings of the hieroglyphs fell into Champollion’s hands, and in looking at them he was struck by something curious—none of the cartouches corresponded to the names he had already identified. He decided to apply the phonetic alphabet he had developed to one of them, but could only see the letter S at the end. The first symbol reminded him of the image of the sun. In Coptic, which was a distant relative of ancient Egyptian, the word for sun is Re . In the middle of the cartouche was a trident symbol with three prongs that looked eerily like an M. With great excitement he realized this could be the name Ramses. Ramses was a pharaoh of the thirteenth century B.C., and this would mean that the Egyptians had a phonetic alphabet dating back who knows how far in time—an earth-shattering discovery. He needed more proof to assert this.

1822年9月，一切谜底在一天之内以最令人惊奇的方式揭开。在埃及一处荒凉之地，人们发现了一座神庙，其墙壁和雕像上刻满了象形文字。商博良得到了象形文字的精确图画，仔细查看后，他被一种奇怪的现象所震惊——所有符号都与他已经识别出的名字不符。他决定将自己开发的语音字母表应用到其中一个符号上，但只看到字母末尾的S。第一个符号让他想起了太阳的形象。在与古埃及语关系较远的科普特语中，“太阳”的单词是Re。在符号的中央是一个三叉戟符号，它有三个尖头，看起来怪异地像一个M。他兴奋地意识到，这可能就是拉美西斯这个名字。拉美西斯是公元前十三世纪的法老，这意味着埃及人拥有一套不知何时诞生的语音字母——这可是个惊天动地的发现。他需要更多证据来佐证这一点。

Another cartouche in the temple drawing had the same M-shaped symbol. The first symbol in the cartouche was that of an ibis. With his knowledge of ancient Egyptian history, he knew that the bird was the symbol of the god Thoth. This cartouche could now spell out Thot-mu-sis, or Thuthmose, yet another name of an ancient pharaoh. In another part of the temple he saw a hieroglyphic word that consisted entirely of the equivalent letters of M and S. Thinking in Coptic, he translated the word as mis, which means to “give birth.” Sure enough, in the Greek text of the Rosetta stone he found a phrase referring to a birthday, and identified the equivalent of it in the hieroglyph section.

神庙图画中的另一个漩涡图案也呈现出同样的M形符号。漩涡图案中的第一个符号是一只朱鹭。凭借他对古埃及历史的了解，他知道这只鸟是托特神的象征。现在，这个漩涡图案可以拼出“Thot-mu-sis”（托特穆西斯）或“Thuthmose”（图特摩斯），这是另一位古代法老的名字。在神庙的另一处，他看到了一个象形文字，完全由M和S两个字母组成。他用科普特语思考，将这个词翻译成“mis”，意思是“生育”。果然，他在罗塞塔石碑的希腊文本中找到了一个指生日的短语，并在象形文字部分找到了与之对应的词。

Overwhelmed by what he had found, he ran through the streets of Paris to find his brother. He shouted upon entering the room, “I’ve got it!” and then fainted, falling to the floor. After nearly twenty years of a continuous obsession, through endless problems and poverty and setbacks, Champollion had uncovered the key to the hieroglyphs in a few short months of intense labor.

他的发现让他激动不已，他跑遍巴黎街头寻找他的兄弟。他一进房间就大喊：“我找到它了！”然后就晕倒在地。经过近二十年的不懈努力，克服了无数的困难、贫困和挫折，商博良终于在短短几个月的紧张工作中找到了象形文字的钥匙。

In the aftermath of his discovery, he would continue to translate one word after another and figure out the exact nature of the hieroglyphs. In the process he would completely transform our knowledge and concept of ancient Egypt. His earliest translations revealed that hieroglyphs, as he suspected, were a sophisticated combination of all three forms of symbols, and had the equivalent of an alphabet far before anyone had imagined the invention of an alphabet. This was not a backward civilization of priests dominating a slave culture and keeping secrets through mysterious symbols, but a vibrant society with a complicated and beautiful written language, one that could be considered the equal of ancient Greek.

在他的发现之后，他继续翻译一个又一个词语，试图弄清楚象形文字的真正含义。在此过程中，他彻底改变了我们对古埃及的认知和概念。他最早的翻译揭示，正如他所猜测的那样，象形文字是三种符号的复杂组合，早在人们想象字母表发明之前，它就拥有了相当于字母表的符号。这并非一个由祭司统治奴隶文化、用神秘符号保守秘密的落后文明，而是一个充满活力的社会，拥有复杂而优美的书面语言，堪比古希腊语。

When his discovery was broadcast, Champollion became an instant hero in France. But Dr. Young, his main rival in the field, could not accept defeat. He spent the ensuing years accusing Champollion of fraud and plagiarism, unable to conceive of the idea that someone from such a modest background could pull off such an amazing intellectual feat.

商博良的发现被广播后，他立即成为法国的英雄。但他在该领域的主要竞争对手杨博士却无法接受失败。在接下来的几年里，他一直指责商博良欺诈和剽窃，无法想象一个出身如此卑微的人竟然能取得如此惊人的智力成就。

The story of Champollion versus Dr. Young contains an elemental lesson about the learning process, and illustrates two classic approaches to a problem. In the case of Young, he came to the hieroglyphic puzzle from the outside, fueled by the ambition to be the first to decipher the hieroglyphs and gain fame in the process. To expedite matters, he reduced the writing system of the ancient Egyptians into tidy mathematical formulas, assuming that they represented ideograms. In such a way, he could approach decipherment as if it were a computational feat. To do so, he had to simplify what ended up being revealed as an extremely complex and layered system of writing.

商博良与杨博士的故事蕴含着关于学习过程的基本教训，并阐释了两种经典的解题思路。杨博士最初是从外部接触象形文字之谜的，他渴望成为第一个破译象形文字的人，并因此声名鹊起。为了加快进程，他将古埃及文字系统简化为简洁的数学公式，假设它们代表表意文字。这样，他就能像处理计算难题一样处理破译问题。为此，他必须简化最终揭示的极其复杂且层层递进的文字系统。

For Champollion, it was the opposite. He was fueled by a genuine hunger to understand the origins of mankind, and by a deep love of ancient Egyptian culture. He wanted to get at the truth, not gain fame. Because he saw the translation of the Rosetta stone as his Life’s Task, he was willing to devote twenty or more years to the job, or whatever it took to solve the riddle. He did not attack the problem from the outside and with formulas, but rather went through a rigorous apprenticeship in ancient languages and Coptic. It ended up that his knowledge of Coptic proved the decisive key to unraveling the secret. His knowledge of languages made him understand how complex they can be, reflecting the complexity of any great society. When he finally returned to the Rosetta stone with undistracted attention in 1821, his mind shifted to the Creative-Active. He reframed the problem in holistic terms. His decision to first look at the two scripts—demotic and hieroglyph—as purely visual was a stroke of creative genius. In the end, he thought in greater dimensions and uncovered enough aspects of the language to unlock it.

而商博良则恰恰相反。他渴望了解人类的起源，并对古埃及文化怀有深厚的热爱。他追求真理，而非名利双收。他将翻译罗塞塔石碑视为毕生追求，因此愿意为此投入二十年甚至更长时间，甚至不惜一切代价来解开谜团。他没有从外部或公式入手，而是在古代语言和科普特语方面进行了严格的学习。最终，他对科普特语的了解成为解开谜团的关键。他对语言的了解使他理解语言的复杂性，这反映了任何伟大社会的复杂性。1821年，当他终于全神贯注地重温罗塞塔石碑时，他的思维转向了“创造-能动”的理念。他以整体的视角重新审视这个问题。他决定首先将世俗体和象形文字视为纯粹的视觉语言，这无疑是他独创的天才之举。最终，他从更大的维度进行思考，发现了该语言的足够多方面，从而解开了它的谜团。

Many people in various fields tend to follow the Young method. If they are studying economics, or the human body and health, or the workings of the brain, they tend to work with abstractions and simplifications, reducing highly complex and interactive problems into modules, formulas, tidy statistics, and isolated organs that can be dissected. This approach can yield a partial picture of reality, much in the way that dissecting a corpse can tell you some things about the human body. But with these simplifications the living, breathing element is missing. You want to follow instead the Champollion model. You are not in a hurry. You prefer the holistic approach. You look at the object of study from as many angles as possible, giving your thoughts added dimensions. You assume that the parts of any whole interact with one another and cannot be completely separated. In your mind, you get as close to the complicated truth and reality of your object of study as possible. In the process, great mysteries will unravel themselves before your eyes.

各行各业的许多人都倾向于遵循杨氏方法。如果他们研究经济学、人体与健康，或大脑的运作机制，他们往往会运用抽象和简化的方法，将高度复杂且互动性强的问题简化为模块、公式、简洁的统计数据以及可解剖的孤立器官。这种方法可以描绘出现实的片面图景，就像解剖尸体可以揭示人体的一些信息一样。但这种简化方法缺失了鲜活的、呼吸的元素。相反，你会遵循商博良模型。你不着急，更喜欢整体观。你会从尽可能多的角度审视研究对象，让你的思维更具维度。你认为任何整体的各个部分都相互作用，无法完全分离。在你的脑海中，你会尽可能地接近研究对象复杂的真相和现实。在这个过程中，巨大的谜团将在你的眼前逐渐解开。

9. Alchemical Creativity and the Unconscious

9.炼金术创造力与潜意识

The artist Teresita Fernández (b. 1968) has long been fascinated by alchemy—an early form of science whose goal was to transform base materials into gold. (For more on Fernández, see here .) Alchemists believed that nature itself operates through the constant interaction of opposites—earth and fire, sun and moon, male and female, dark and light. By somehow reconciling these opposites, the alchemist believed he could discover the deepest secrets of nature, gain the power to create something out of nothing, and turn dust into gold.

艺术家特雷西塔·费尔南德斯（生于1968年）长期以来一直对炼金术着迷——炼金术是一门早期的科学，其目标是将基础物质转化为黄金。（更多关于费尔南德斯的信息，请参见此处。）炼金术士认为，自然界本身就是通过对立面——土与火、日与月、男性与女性、黑暗与光明——的不断相互作用而运作的。炼金术士相信，通过某种方式调和这些对立面，他能够发现自然界最深层的秘密，获得无中生有的力量，将尘埃变成黄金。

To Fernández, the art of alchemy resembles in many ways the artistic and creative process itself. First, a thought or idea stirs in the mind of the artist. Slowly he or she transforms this idea into a material work of art, which creates a third element, a response in the viewer—an emotion of some sort that the artist wishes to provoke. This is a magical process, the equivalent of creating something out of nothing, a kind of transmutation of dirt into gold—in this case, the artist’s idea becoming realized, and leading to the stirring of powerful emotions in the spectator.

对费尔南德斯而言，炼金术在很多方面与艺术创作过程本身相似。首先，一个想法或理念在艺术家的脑海中萌生。他或她会慢慢地将这个想法转化为一件物质化的艺术作品，从而创造出第三个元素，即观者的回应——艺术家希望激发的某种情感。这是一个神奇的过程，如同无中生有，化泥土为金——在这种情况下，艺术家的想法得以实现，并在观者心中激起强烈的情感。

Alchemy depends on the reconciliation of various opposite qualities, and in thinking about herself, Fernández can identify many contrary impulses that are reconciled in her work. She is personally drawn to minimalism—a form of expression that communicates through the most minimal amount of material. She likes the discipline and rigor this paring down of materials imposes on her thinking process. At the same time she has a streak of romanticism, and an interest in work that produces strong emotional reactions in viewers. In her work, she likes to mix the sensual with the austere. She has noticed that expressing this and other tensions within herself gives her work a particularly disorienting and dreamlike effect upon viewers.

炼金术依赖于各种对立特质的调和。费尔南德斯在反思自身时，能够识别出许多相互对立的冲动，而这些冲动在她的作品中得到了调和。她个人偏爱极简主义——一种通过极简材料进行交流的表达形式。她喜欢这种对材料的精简赋予她思考过程的纪律性和严谨性。同时，她也拥有浪漫主义的特质，并热衷于创作能够引发观者强烈情感共鸣的作品。在她的作品中，她喜欢将感性与朴素融合。她注意到，表达这种以及自身其他方面的张力，会让她的作品给观者带来一种格外迷离和梦幻般的效果。

Since childhood, Fernández has always had a peculiar sense of scale. She would find it odd and disturbing that a relatively small space or room could evoke a much larger and even a vast space by its layout or the arrangement of windows. Children are generally obsessed with scale, playing with miniaturized versions of the adult world, yet feeling as if these miniatures represent real objects that are much larger. We generally lose this interest as we get older, but in Fernández’s piece Eruption (2005), she brings us back to an awareness of the potentially disturbing emotions that can be evoked by playing with our sense of scale. The piece is a relatively small floor sculpture in the shape of a blob that resembles an artist’s palette. It consists of thousands of clear glass beads layered on the surface. Below the beads lies an enlarged image of an abstract painting, which makes the beads reflect various colors, giving the piece the distinct look of the mouth of a bubbling volcano. We cannot see the underlying image, and we are not aware that the beads themselves are clear. Our eye is simply drawn into the effect, as we imagine much more than is actually there. In the smallest of spaces she has thus created a feeling of a deep and vast landscape. We know it is an illusion, but are moved by the sensations and tensions that the piece creates.

费尔南德斯自幼便对尺度有着独特的感知。她会觉得一个相对狭小的空间或房间，通过布局或窗户的排列，就能唤起一个更大甚至更广阔的空间，这让她感到既奇怪又不安。孩子们通常对尺度感着迷，他们会把玩成人世界的微缩模型，却又感觉这些微缩模型代表着比我们想象的要大得多的真实物体。随着年龄的增长，我们通常会失去这种兴趣，但在费尔南德斯的作品《喷发》（2005）中，她让我们重新意识到，玩弄尺度感可能会引发一些令人不安的情绪。这件作品是一个相对较小的地面雕塑，形状像一个斑点，形似艺术家的调色板。它由数千颗透明玻璃珠层叠而成，珠子下方是一幅放大的抽象画，珠子反射出各种色彩，赋予作品独特的火山口外观。我们无法看到底层的图像，也意识不到珠子本身是透明的。我们的目光被这种效果所吸引，因为我们想象的远比实际存在的要多。在最小的空间里，她营造出一种深邃广阔的景观感。我们知道这只是幻觉，但却被作品营造的感受和张力所触动。

In making work for an outdoor public space, artists generally go in one of two directions—creating something that blends into the landscape in an interesting way, or instead making something that stands out from the surroundings and calls attention to itself. In creating her piece Seattle Cloud Cover (2006)—at the Olympic Sculpture Park in Seattle, Washington—Fernández navigated a space between these two opposite approaches. Along the length of an outdoor pedestrian bridge spanning railroad tracks, she placed large colored glass panes, laminated with photographic images of clouds. The panes, which also extend overhead, are semitransparent and are marked with hundreds of clear polka dots at equal lengths that reveal bits of the sky above. As people walk along the bridge, they see above them realistic photographic images of clouds, often standing out against the usual grey skies of Seattle, or sometimes brightened by the sun, or turning kaleidoscopic at sunset. Moving over the bridge, the alternation between real and unreal makes it hard for us to distinguish between the two—a surreal effect that causes powerful feelings of disorientation in the viewer.

在为户外公共空间创作作品时，艺术家通常会选择两个方向——要么创作出以有趣的方式融入景观的作品，要么创作出从周围环境中脱颖而出、引人注目的作品。费尔南德斯在华盛顿州西雅图奥林匹克雕塑公园创作作品《西雅图云层》（2006 年）时，巧妙地在这两种截然相反的方法之间找到了平衡。她沿着一座横跨铁轨的户外人行天桥，放置了巨大的彩色玻璃板，上面贴满了云朵的摄影图像。这些玻璃板也延伸到头顶，呈半透明状，上面点缀着数百个等长的清晰圆点，可以透出上方天空的点点滴滴。当人们沿着天桥行走时，他们会看到上方逼真的云朵摄影图像，这些图像通常在西雅图通常灰蒙蒙的天空中格外醒目，有时被阳光照得明亮，或在日落时分变成万花筒般的色彩。越过桥梁，真实与虚幻的交替让我们难以区分两者——这种超现实的效果让观众产生强烈的迷失感。

Perhaps the ultimate expression of Fernández’s alchemy can be experienced in her piece Stacked Waters (2009) at the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas. For this commission, she was confronted with the challenge of creating a striking piece for the vast open space of the museum’s multi-layered atrium, an entryway to the rest of the museum. The atrium is generally bathed in bright light from the large skylights on the ceiling. Instead of struggling to create a sculpture for such a space, Fernández attempted to invert our whole experience of art. When people enter a museum or gallery space, it is most often with a sense of distance and coldness; they stand back and view something for a few moments, then move on. Aiming for a more visceral contact with the viewer than a traditional sculpture could provide, she decided to use the cold white walls of the atrium and its constant flow of patrons as the basis for her alchemical experiment.

或许，费尔南德斯炼金术的终极体现，可以在她位于德克萨斯州奥斯汀的布兰顿艺术博物馆的作品《叠水》（Stacked Waters，2009）中感受到。为了完成这项委托，她面临的挑战是为博物馆多层中庭的广阔开放空间创作一件引人注目的作品，该中庭是通往博物馆其他部分的入口。中庭通常沐浴在来自天花板上巨大天窗的明亮光线中。费尔南德斯并没有费力地为这样的空间创作雕塑，而是试图颠覆我们对艺术的整体体验。当人们进入博物馆或画廊空间时，通常会感到距离和冰冷；他们会退后一步，欣赏片刻，然后离开。为了与观众建立比传统雕塑更深刻的情感联系，她决定以中庭冰冷的白色墙壁和川流不息的观众作为她炼金术实验的基础。

She covered the walls with bands of thousands of highly reflective acrylic strips, saturated in swirls of color from shades of blue to white. The overall effect from standing in the atrium is that of being immersed in an enormous pool of blue water that shimmers from the sunlight above. As people ascend the stairs, they can see in the acrylic strips their own reflections, which are oddly distorted, similar to the effect of seeing things through water. Viewing the strips from up close, it is clear that it is all an illusion created by the most minimal amount of material, and yet the feel of water, the sense of being immersed, remains palpable and strange. The spectators thus become actual parts of the artwork itself, with their own reflections helping to create the illusion. The experience of moving through this dreamlike space makes us conscious once more of the tensions between art and nature, illusion and reality, coldness and warmth, wet and dry, and provokes a powerful intellectual and emotional response.

她在墙上覆盖了数千条高反光亚克力条，条带上点缀着从蓝色到白色的各种色彩漩涡。置身于中庭，整体效果如同置身于一个巨大的蓝色水池中，水面在阳光的照射下波光粼粼。拾级而上，人们可以在亚克力条上看到自己的倒影，这些倒影奇异地扭曲，如同透过水看世界。近距离观看这些条带，便会发现这一切都是由极简材料营造的幻觉，然而水的触感，那种沉浸其中的奇特感，依然清晰可见，令人感到奇特。观者由此成为艺术品本身的一部分，自身的倒影也共同营造出这种幻觉。穿梭于这如梦似幻的空间，让我们再次感受到艺术与自然、虚幻与现实、冷暖、干湿之间的张力，并激发出强烈的理性与情感共鸣。

Our culture depends in many ways on the creation of standards and conventions that we all must adhere to. These conventions are often expressed in terms of opposites—good and evil, beautiful and ugly, painful and pleasurable, rational and irrational, intellectual and sensual. Believing in these opposites gives our world a sense of cohesion and comfort. To imagine that something can be intellectual and sensual, pleasurable and painful, real and unreal, good and bad, masculine and feminine is too chaotic and disturbing for us. Life, however, is more fluid and complex; our desires and experiences do not fit neatly into these tidy categories.

我们的文化在很多方面依赖于我们所有人都必须遵守的标准和惯例的制定。这些惯例通常以对立的事物来表达——善与恶、美与丑、痛苦与快乐、理性与非理性、智性与感性。相信这些对立赋予了我们的世界一种凝聚力和舒适感。想象某种事物可以兼具智性与感性、快乐与痛苦、真实与虚幻、善与恶、阳刚与阴柔，对我们来说过于混乱和令人不安。然而，生活更加流动和复杂；我们的欲望和经历并不能被简单地归类到这些整齐的类别中。

As the work of Teresita Fernández demonstrates, the real and the unreal are concepts that exist for us as ideas and constructions, and thus can be played with, altered, commanded, and transformed at will. Those who think in dualities—believing that there is such a thing as “real” and such a thing as “unreal,” and that they are distinct entities that can never become blended into a third, alchemical element—are creatively limited, and their work can quickly become dead and predictable. To maintain a dualistic approach to life requires that we repress many observable truths, but in our unconscious and in our dreams we often let go of the need to create categories for everything, and are able to mix seemingly disparate and contradictory ideas and feelings together with ease.

正如特蕾西塔·费尔南德斯的作品所展现的，真实与虚幻，对我们来说，都是以观念和建构的形式存在的概念，因此可以被随意操控、改变、操控和转化。那些持有二元论思维的人——相信存在“真实”与“虚幻”之分，认为它们是截然不同的实体，永远无法融入第三种炼金术元素——创造力有限，他们的作品很快就会变得枯燥乏味、千篇一律。要保持二元论的人生观，我们就必须压抑许多可见的真理，但在潜意识和梦境中，我们常常会放下为万物划分类别的需要，从而能够轻松地将看似迥然不同、相互矛盾的想法和感受融合在一起。

Your task as a creative thinker is to actively explore the unconscious and contradictory parts of your personality, and to examine similar contradictions and tensions in the world at large. Expressing these tensions within your work in any medium will create a powerful effect on others, making them sense unconscious truths or feelings that have been obscured or repressed. You look at society at large and the various contradictions that are rampant—for instance, the way in which a culture that espouses the ideal of free expression is charged with an oppressive code of political correctness that tamps free expression down. In science, you look for ideas that go against the existing paradigm, or that seem inexplicable because they are so contradictory. All of these contradictions contain a rich mine of information about a reality that is deeper and more complex than the one immediately perceived. By delving into the chaotic and fluid zone below the level of consciousness where opposites meet, you will be surprised at the exciting and fertile ideas that will come bubbling up to the surface.

作为一名创造性思考者，你的任务是积极探索自身个性中潜意识中相互矛盾的部分，并审视整个世界中类似的矛盾和张力。在你的作品中，通过任何媒介表达这些张力，都会对他人产生强大的影响，使他们感受到那些被遮蔽或压抑的潜意识真相或感受。你审视整个社会，以及其中猖獗的各种矛盾——例如，一个拥护言论自由理想的文化，却充斥着压制性的政治正确准则，压制着言论自由。在科学领域，你寻找那些违背现有范式，或因矛盾重重而显得难以解释的思想。所有这些矛盾都蕴藏着丰富的信息宝库，揭示着一个比你直接感知到的现实更深层、更复杂的现实。通过深入探究意识层面之下对立面交汇的混乱流动区域，你会惊讶地发现，那些激动人心、富有创造力的想法会涌现出来。

REVERSAL

逆转

In Western culture, a particular myth has evolved that drugs or madness can somehow lead to creative bursts of the highest order. How else to explain the work that John Coltrane did while hooked on heroin, or the great works of the playwright August Strindberg, who seemed clinically insane? Their work is so spontaneous and free, so far beyond the powers of the rational, conscious mind.

在西方文化中，一种特殊的迷思逐渐形成：毒品或疯狂能够以某种方式激发出最高层次的创造力。否则，如何解释约翰·柯川（John Coltrane）在吸食海洛因后创作的作品，以及看似精神错乱的剧作家奥古斯特·斯特林堡（August Strindberg）的伟大作品呢？他们的作品如此自发、自由，远远超出了理性和意识思维的能力。

This is a cliché, however, that is easily debunked. Coltrane himself admitted that he did his worst work during the few years he was addicted to heroin. It was destroying him and his creative powers. He kicked the habit in 1957 and never looked back. Biographers who later examined the letters and journals of Strindberg discovered a man who was quite histrionic in public, but who in private life was extremely disciplined. The effect of madness created in his plays is very consciously crafted.

然而，这句老生常谈很容易被揭穿。科尔特兰本人也承认，他最糟糕的作品创作于他沉迷于海洛因的那几年。海洛因摧毁了他和他的创造力。他于1957年戒掉了毒瘾，从此再也没有回头。后来，传记作者们研究了斯特林堡的信件和日记，发现他在公众场合颇具戏剧性，但在私下生活中却极其自律。他剧作中营造的疯狂效果是经过精心设计的。

Understand: to create a meaningful work of art or to make a discovery or invention requires great discipline, self-control, and emotional stability. It requires mastering the forms of your field. Drugs and madness only destroy such powers. Do not fall for the romantic myths and clichés that abound in culture about creativity—offering us the excuse or panacea that such powers can come cheaply. When you look at the exceptionally creative work of Masters, you must not ignore the years of practice, the endless routines, the hours of doubt, and the tenacious overcoming of obstacles these people endured. Creative energy is the fruit of such efforts and nothing else.

要明白：创作一件有意义的艺术作品，或做出一项发现或发明，需要高度的自律、自控力和稳定的情绪。这需要精通你所在领域的形式。毒品和疯狂只会摧毁这种力量。不要被文化中充斥的关于创造力的浪漫神话和陈词滥调所迷惑——它们给我们提供了借口或灵丹妙药，认为这种力量可以轻易获得。当你欣赏大师们非凡的创造力作品时，你绝不能忽视他们多年的实践、无休止的例行公事、数小时的怀疑以及他们克服重重障碍的顽强精神。创造力正是这些努力的成果，仅此而已。

Our vanity, our passions, our spirit of imitation, our abstract intelligence, our habits have long been at work, and it is the task of art to undo this work of theirs, making us travel back in the direction from which we have come to the depths where what has really existed lies unknown within us.

我们的虚荣心、激情、模仿精神、抽象智慧和习惯早已在起作用，而艺术的任务就是消除它们的这种作用，让我们回到原来方向，来到内心深处，那里真正存在的东西却不为人知。

—M ARCEL P ROUST

—马塞尔·普鲁斯特

VI

六

FUSE THE INTUITIVE
融合直觉
WITH THE RATIONAL:
与理性：
MASTERY
精通

All of us have access to a higher form of intelligence, one that can allow us to see more of the world, to anticipate trends, to respond with speed and accuracy to any circumstance. This intelligence is cultivated by deeply immersing ourselves in a field of study and staying true to our inclinations, no matter how unconventional our approach might seem to others. Through such intense immersion over many years we come to internalize and gain an intuitive feel for the complicated components of our field. When we fuse this intuitive feel with rational processes, we expand our minds to the outer limits of our potential and are able to see into the secret core of life itself. We then come to have powers that approximate the instinctive force and speed of animals, but with the added reach that our human consciousness brings us. This power is what our brains were designed to attain, and we will be naturally led to this type of intelligence if we follow our inclinations to their ultimate ends.

我们每个人都拥有一种更高级的智慧，它能让我们看清世界，预测趋势，并快速准确地应对任何情况。这种智慧的培养源于我们深入钻研某个领域，并忠于自己的兴趣，无论我们的方法在他人眼中多么标新立异。通过多年的深入钻研，我们逐渐内化并获得对领域复杂组成部分的直觉。当我们将这种直觉与理性思维融合时，我们的思维便能拓展到潜能的极限，并洞察生命本身的奥秘核心。如此一来，我们将拥有接近动物本能的力量和速度，同时又拥有人类意识所能带来的额外延伸。这种力量正是我们大脑的本能，如果我们追随自己的兴趣，并最终将其发挥到极致，我们自然而然地就会获得这种智慧。

# ↩

THE THIRD TRANSFORMATION

第三次转型

For the writer Marcel Proust (1871–1922), his fate seemed set at birth. He was born incredibly small and frail; for two weeks he hovered near death, but finally pulled through. As a child, he had frequent bouts of illness that kept him at home for months at a time. When he was nine years old, he suffered his first asthma attack and nearly died. His mother, Jeanne, continuously worried about his health, doted on Marcel and accompanied him on his regular trips to the countryside to convalesce.

对于作家马塞尔·普鲁斯特（1871-1922）来说，他的命运似乎从出生起就注定了。他出生时体型瘦小，体弱多病；有两周时间，他濒临死亡，但最终还是挺了过来。童年时期，他经常生病，有时甚至需要在家休养数月。九岁时，他第一次哮喘发作，险些丧命。他的母亲珍妮一直担心他的健康，对马塞尔宠爱有加，经常陪他去乡下疗养。

And it was on such trips that the pattern of his life became set. Often alone, he developed a passion for reading books. He loved to read about history, and he devoured all forms of literature. His main physical outlet was taking long walks in the country, and here certain sights seemed to captivate him. He would stop and stare for hours at apple blossoms or hawthorn flowers, or at any kind of slightly exotic plant; he found the spectacle of marching ants or spiders working on their webs particularly compelling. He would soon add books on botany and entomology to his reading list. His closest companion in these early years was his mother, and his attachment to her soon went beyond all bounds. They looked alike and shared similar interests in the arts. He could not stand to be away from her for more than a day, and in the few hours in which they were separated he would write her endless letters.

正是在这样的旅行中，他的生活模式逐渐成型。他经常独自一人，对读书产生了浓厚的兴趣。他热爱阅读历史，并如饥似渴地阅读各种文学作品。他主要的休闲方式是在乡间长途散步，而这里的某些景色似乎总能让他着迷。他会驻足数小时，凝视着苹果花、山楂花，或是任何一种略带异域风情的植物；行军蚁或蜘蛛织网的景象尤其引人入胜。很快，他就把植物学和昆虫学的书籍也加进了自己的阅读清单。早年他最亲密的伙伴是母亲，他对母亲的依恋很快就超越了界限。他们长得一模一样，对艺术也抱有共同的兴趣。他无法忍受离开母亲超过一天，在他们分别的几个小时里，他会给她写无数封信。

In 1886 he read a book that would forever change the course of his life. It was an historical account of the Norman conquest of England written by Augustin Thierry. The narration of events was so vivid that Marcel felt himself transported back in time. The writer alluded to certain timeless laws of human nature that were revealed in this story, and the possibility of uncovering such laws made Marcel’s head spin with excitement. Entomologists could discover the hidden principles that governed the behavior of insects. Could a writer do the same with humans and their complicated nature? Captivated by Thierry’s ability to make history come to life, it came to Marcel in a flash that this would be his Life’s Task—to become a writer and illuminate the laws of human nature. Haunted by the sense that he would not live long, he would have to hurry this process and do all that he could to develop his writing powers.

1886年，他读了一本永远改变他人生轨迹的书。这本书由奥古斯丁·蒂埃里撰写，讲述了诺曼征服英格兰的历史。书中对事件的叙述如此生动，马塞尔感觉自己仿佛回到了过去。作者暗示了故事中揭示的某些永恒的人性法则，而揭示这些法则的可能性让马塞尔兴奋不已，头晕目眩。昆虫学家可以发现控制昆虫行为的隐秘原理。作家能否以同样的方式解读人类及其复杂的本性？蒂埃里赋予历史鲜活生命的能力深深吸引着马塞尔，他突然意识到，这将成为他毕生的使命——成为一名作家，阐明人性的法则。他深知自己命不久矣，因此必须加快这一进程，并竭尽所能提升自己的写作能力。

At school in Paris, where he lived, Marcel impressed his classmates with his strangeness. He had read so much that his head was teeming with ideas; he would talk about history, ancient Roman literature, and the social life of bees all in the same conversation. He would mix the past and the present, talking about a Roman writer as if he were alive, or describing a friend of theirs as if he were a character from history. His large eyes, which a friend later compared to that of a fly, would seem to bore right into the person he was talking to. In his letters to friends, he could dissect their emotions and problems with such exactitude that it was unnerving, but then he would direct his attention to himself as well, mercilessly exposing his own weaknesses. Despite his propensity for being alone, he was incredibly sociable and a real charmer. He knew how to flatter and ingratiate himself. No one could quite figure him out or gain any sense of what the future might hold for such an oddball.

在巴黎上学期间，马塞尔的古怪给同学们留下了深刻的印象。他博览群书，脑子里充满了各种奇思妙想；他能在同一次谈话中谈论历史、古罗马文学以及蜜蜂的社会生活。他会把过去和现在混在一起，谈论一位罗马作家仿佛他活在世上，或者描述一位朋友仿佛他是历史人物。他那双大眼睛，后来一位朋友把它比作苍蝇的眼睛，仿佛能直视与他交谈的人。在写给朋友的信中，他能精准地剖析他们的情绪和问题，甚至令人感到不安，但他也会将注意力转向自己，毫不留情地暴露自己的弱点。尽管他喜欢独处，但他却非常善于交际，魅力十足。他知道如何奉承和讨好自己。没有人能完全理解他，也不知道这样一个怪人的未来会怎样。

In 1888 Marcel met a thirty-seven-year-old courtesan named Laure Hayman, who was the mistress of his uncle, among many others, and for him it was instant infatuation. She was like a character out of a novel. Her clothes, her coquettish manner, her power over men fascinated him. Charming her with his witty conversation and polite manners, they quickly became close friends. In France there had long been the tradition of salons—gatherings where people of like mind discussed literary and philosophical ideas. In most cases women ran these various salons, and depending on the social status of the hostess, they could attract important artists, thinkers, and political figures. Laure had her own infamous salon, frequented by artists, bohemians, actors, and actresses. Soon Marcel became a regular.

1888年，马塞尔邂逅了一位名叫劳雷·海曼的三十七岁交际花，她是他叔叔的情妇，也曾是其他许多人的情妇。马塞尔一见倾心，对她一见倾心。她宛如小说中的人物。她的衣着、她那风骚的举止以及她对男人的掌控力，都深深地吸引了他。他风趣的谈吐和彬彬有礼的举止深深地吸引了她，两人很快便成为了挚友。在法国，沙龙的传统由来已久——志同道合的人聚集在一起，探讨文学和哲学思想。这些沙龙大多由女性经营，根据女主人的社会地位，她们可能会吸引到重要的艺术家、思想家和政治人物。劳雷拥有她自己那家声名显赫的沙龙，经常有艺术家、波西米亚人、男女演员光顾。马塞尔很快就成了那里的常客。

He found the social life in these upper echelons of French society endlessly fascinating. It was a world full of subtle signs—an invitation to a ball, or the particular seating position at a dinner table would indicate the status of an individual, whether they were on the rise or the decline. Clothes and gestures and certain phrases of conversation would lead to endless critiques and judgments about people. He wanted to explore this realm and learn all of its intricacies. The attention he used to direct toward history and literature he now directed toward the world of high society. He inveigled his way into other salons, and was soon mingling with upper aristocracy.

他发现法国上流社会的社交生活魅力无穷。那里充满了微妙的暗示——一张舞会邀请函，或是餐桌上的某个座位，都能体现一个人的地位，无论其地位是上升还是下降。衣着、举止以及某些特定的谈话用语，都会引发人们对他人无休止的批评和评判。他渴望探索这个领域，了解其中的奥秘。他过去专注于历史和文学，如今则转向了上流社会。他设法进入其他沙龙，并很快与上流贵族混迹于此。

Although he was determined to become a writer, Marcel had never been able to figure out what he wanted to write about, and this had troubled him to no end. Now, however, he had his answer: this social world would be the ant colony that he would analyze as ruthlessly as an entomologist. For this purpose he began to collect characters for novels. One such character was the Count Robert de Montesquiou, a poet, aesthete, and notorious decadent who had a pronounced weakness for handsome young men. Another was Charles Haas, the epitome of high-society chicness and an expert art collector who couldn’t help falling in love with lower-class women. He studied these characters, listened intently to their way of talking, followed their mannerisms, and in his notebooks he would try to bring them to life in small literary sketches. In his writing, Marcel was a master mimic.

马塞尔立志成为一名作家，却始终无法确定自己想写什么，这让他苦恼不已。然而，现在他找到了答案：这个社会世界就像一个蚁群，他将像昆虫学家一样对其进行无情的分析。为此，他开始为小说收集人物。其中一个人物是罗伯特·德·孟德斯基伯爵，他是一位诗人、唯美主义者，也是出了名的颓废派，对英俊的年轻男子有着明显的偏爱。另一个是查尔斯·哈斯，他是上流社会时尚的典范，也是一位精通艺术品收藏的收藏家，却总是情不自禁地爱上下流社会的女性。他研究这些人物，仔细聆听他们的谈话方式，观察他们的举止举止，并在笔记本中尝试用文学速写的方式，将他们栩栩如生地描绘出来。在写作方面，马塞尔是一位模仿大师。

Everything he wrote about had to be something real, something he had witnessed or experienced firsthand; otherwise, his writing came out lifeless. His own fear of intimate personal relationships, however, presented him with a problem. Attracted to both men and women, he tended to keep his distance when it came to any type of close physical and emotional relationship. This made it hard for him to write about romance and love from the inside. So he initiated a practice that served him well. If he were attracted to a particular woman, he would befriend her fiancé or boyfriend and, gaining his trust, would probe him for the most intimate details about their relationship. Since he was such an acute psychologist he could give excellent advice. Later, in his own mind, he would completely reconstruct the affair, feeling as deeply as possible the ups and downs, the bouts of jealousy, as if it were all happening to him. He would do this with either gender.

他所写的一切都必须是真实的，是他亲眼目睹或亲身经历的；否则，他的作品就会显得毫无生气。然而，他自身对亲密人际关系的恐惧，却给他带来了一个问题。他同时被男性和女性所吸引，因此在涉及任何亲密的肉体和情感关系时，他倾向于保持距离。这使得他很难从内心深处描写浪漫和爱情。于是，他开创了一种对他很有帮助的做法。如果他被某个女人吸引，他会与她的未婚夫或男朋友交朋友，在赢得他的信任后，会向他探寻他们关系中最私密的细节。由于他是一位敏锐的心理学家，他能给出绝妙的建议。之后，他会在自己的脑海中完整地重建这段恋情，尽可能深刻地感受其中的起伏，以及一阵阵的嫉妒，仿佛这一切都发生在他身上。无论面对哪个性别，他都会这样做。

Marcel’s father, a prominent doctor, began to despair for his son. Marcel would attend parties all night, return late in the morning, and sleep through the day. To fit in with high society, he was spending vast amounts of money. He seemed to have no discipline and no real career aspirations. With his health problems and his mother always spoiling him, his father feared Marcel would be a failure and a continuous burden. He tried to push him into a career. Marcel placated him as best he could—one day he told his father he would study law; the next day he talked of getting a job as a librarian. But in truth, he was banking everything on the publication of his first book, Pleasures and Days . It would be a collection of stories and sketches of the society he had infiltrated. Like Thierry with the Norman Conquest, he would make this world come to life. With the success of this book, he would win over his father and all the other doubters. To ensure its success and make it into more than a book, Pleasures and Days would feature the beautiful drawings of a high-society lady he had befriended, and it would be printed on the finest paper.

马塞尔的父亲是一位杰出的医生，他开始对儿子感到绝望。马塞尔经常彻夜参加派对，早上很晚才回来，然后整天睡觉。为了融入上流社会，他挥霍无度。他似乎缺乏自律，也没有真正的职业抱负。由于身体健康问题，加上母亲对他的溺爱，父亲担心马塞尔会成为一个失败者，并成为他日后的负担。他试图鼓励马塞尔发展事业。马塞尔竭尽所能地安抚他——有一天，他告诉父亲他要学习法律；第二天，他又说要找一份图书管理员的工作。但实际上，他把一切都寄托在他的第一本书《快乐与时光》的出版上。这本书将会是一本关于他所渗透的那个社会的故事和速写集。就像蒂埃里对诺曼征服的描写一样，他会让这个世界变得生动活泼。随着这本书的成功，他将赢得父亲和所有其他怀疑者的支持。为了确保成功并使其成为一本书，《快乐与日子》将采用他结识的一位上流社会女士的美丽画作，并使用最好的纸张印刷。

After numerous delays, the book was finally published in 1896. Although many of the reviews were positive, they kept referring to the writing as exquisite and delicate, implying a sort of superficiality to the work. More disturbing, the book hardly sold. Considering the printing costs it was an enormous financial fiasco, and the public image of Marcel Proust became permanently cemented—he was an elegant dandy, a snob who wrote of the only world he knew, a young man who had no practical sense, a social butterfly who dabbled in literature. It was an embarrassment and it demoralized him.

几经拖延，这本书终于在1896年出版。尽管许多评论都持正面评价，但他们始终认为这本书的文笔精美细腻，暗示着作品略显肤浅。更令人不安的是，这本书几乎销路不佳。考虑到印刷成本，这无疑是一场巨大的财务惨败，而马塞尔·普鲁斯特的公众形象也因此被永久地固化——他是一个优雅的花花公子，一个只写自己所了解世界的势利小人，一个缺乏实际意识的年轻人，一个涉猎文学的社交名媛。这让他感到尴尬，也让他士气低落。

The family pressures to finally choose a career now grew intense. Still confident in his skills, he decided the only answer was to write another novel, but one that would be the opposite of Pleasures and Days . It would be much longer and weightier than the first book. In it he would mix childhood memories and recent social experiences. It would depict the lives of all classes of people and an entire period in French history. It could not be seen as superficial. But as the novel became longer and longer, he could not figure out how to make it cohere into something logical, or even into something resembling a story. He found himself getting lost in the immensity of his ambition, and despite having written hundreds of pages, by the end of 1899 he gave up the project.

家庭的压力让他最终选择职业，如今压力越来越大。他对自己的能力依然充满信心，决定唯一的出路是再写一部小说，但要与《快乐与日子》截然相反。这部小说会比第一部更长、更有分量。他会在书中融合童年记忆和近期的社会经历，描绘各阶层人士的生活，以及法国历史上的一段时期。它绝不能显得肤浅。但随着小说越来越长，他却无法使其逻辑清晰，甚至无法形成一个像故事一样的框架。他发现自己迷失在宏大的志向中，尽管已经写了数百页，但到1899年底，他还是放弃了这个项目。

He began to grow increasingly depressed and despondent. He was tired of the salons and mingling with the rich. He had no career, no position to rely upon; nearing thirty years of age, he was still living at home, dependent on his parents for money. He felt constantly anxious about his health, certain he was doomed to die within a few years. He heard endless stories of his friends from school becoming prominent members of society, with growing families of their own. In comparison he felt like a total failure. All that he had accomplished was a few articles in newspapers about high society and a book that had made him the laughingstock of Paris. The only thing he could rely on was the continued devotion of his mother.

他开始变得越来越沮丧和失落。他厌倦了沙龙和与富人的交往。他没有事业，没有地位可以依靠；快三十岁了，他仍然住在家里，依靠父母的钱财。他总是担心自己的健康，确信自己注定几年内就会死去。他听到无数关于校友成为社会名流、成家立业的故事。相比之下，他觉得自己彻底失败了。他所取得的成就，不过是几篇关于上流社会的文章和一本让他成为巴黎笑柄的书。他唯一可以依靠的，就是母亲持续的关爱。

In the midst of his despair he had an idea. For several years he had been devouring the works of the English art critic and thinker John Ruskin. He would teach himself English and translate Ruskin’s work into French. This would require years of scholarly research into the various topics Ruskin specialized in, such as gothic architecture. It would consume much of his time, and he would have to put off any ideas of writing a novel. But it would show his parents that he was serious about making a living and that he had chosen a career. Clinging to this as his last hope, he poured himself into the task with all of his energy.

绝望之际，他突然有了个主意。多年来，他一直在如饥似渴地研读英国艺术评论家兼思想家约翰·罗斯金的作品。他决定自学英语，并将罗斯金的作品翻译成法语。这需要他多年时间对罗斯金所擅长的诸多领域进行学术研究，例如哥特式建筑。这会耗费他大量的时间，他不得不暂时搁置写小说的念头。但这能让他父母看到，他认真地谋生，并且选择了一项事业。他把这当作最后的希望，全身心地投入到这项工作中。

After several years of intense labor, a few of his translations of Ruskin were published to great acclaim. His introductions and the essays that accompanied the translations finally erased the reputation of the idle dilettante that had haunted him since Pleasures and Days . He was seen as a serious scholar. Through his work, he had managed to hone his own style of writing; internalizing the work of Ruskin, he could now write essays that were thoughtful and precise. He had finally gained some discipline, something to build on. But in the midst of this modest success, his network of emotional support suddenly teetered and then vanished. In 1903 his father died. Two years later his mother, unable to get over the loss, passed away as well. They had hardly ever been apart from each other, and he had dreaded the moment of her death since childhood. He felt completely alone, and he feared that he had nothing left to live for.

经过数年辛勤耕耘，他翻译的几部罗斯金作品得以出版，并获得了广泛赞誉。他为译作所写的序言和随笔，终于洗刷了自《快乐与日子》出版以来一直萦绕在他心头的“游手好闲的业余爱好者”的恶名。他被视为一位严肃的学者。通过译作，他磨练了自己的写作风格；将罗斯金的作品内化，他现在可以写出深刻而精准的文章。他终于获得了一些自律，并以此为基础继续前行。然而，就在这小小的成功中，他赖以生存的情感网络突然摇摇欲坠，最终消失殆尽。1903年，他的父亲去世。两年后，他的母亲因无法承受失去父亲的痛苦，也随之离世。他们几乎从未分开过，从童年起，他就一直害怕母亲去世的那一刻。他感到彻底的孤独，害怕自己活着已经没有任何意义。

In the months to come he slowly withdrew from society, and as he took stock of his life up to that point he discerned a pattern that actually gave him the faintest amount of hope. To compensate for his physical weakness he had taken to reading, and in the process had discovered his Life’s Task. Over the course of the last twenty years he had accumulated a vast amount of knowledge about French society—an incredibly wide variety of real-life characters of all types and classes lived inside of his head. He had written thousands of pages—including the failed novel, short sketches for newspapers, and various essays. Using Ruskin as a mentor, in translating his works he had developed discipline and some organizing skills. He had long thought of life as an apprenticeship in which we are all slowly instructed in the ways of the world. Some people learn to read the signs and heed the lessons from this apprenticeship, developing themselves in the process; others do not. He had served an elaborate twenty-year apprenticeship in writing and in human nature, and it had altered him deeply. Despite his ill health and his failures, he had never given up. This must mean something—perhaps a destiny of sorts. All of his failures had a purpose, he decided, if he knew how to exploit them. His time had not been wasted.

在接下来的几个月里，他慢慢地退出了社交圈，回顾此前的生活，他发现了一种模式，这实际上给了他一丝希望。为了弥补身体上的虚弱，他开始阅读，并在此过程中发现了自己人生的使命。在过去的二十年里，他积累了丰富的法国社会知识——各种类型、各种阶层的现实生活中形形色色的人物都生活在他的脑海中。他写了数千页书——包括那部失败的小说、为报纸撰写的短篇小说和各种散文。在罗斯金的指导下，他翻译了罗斯金的作品，培养了自律性和一些组织能力。他一直认为人生就像一场学徒期，我们每个人都在慢慢地学习世事。有些人学会了解读迹象，并从学徒期中汲取教训，并在这个过程中不断提升自己；而有些人则没有。他在写作和人性方面经历了长达二十年的艰苦学徒期，这段经历深刻地改变了他。尽管身体欠佳，屡屡失败，他却从未放弃。这一定意味着什么——或许是某种宿命。他心想，只要懂得如何利用，所有的失败都有其意义。他的时间没有被浪费。

What he needed to do was to put all of this knowledge to work. This meant returning to the novel that had continually eluded him. What it would be about—the plot, the narrator’s voice—he still had no idea. The material was all there in his head. If in his loneliness he could not bring back his mother or his childhood or his youth, he would somehow re-create these things in their entirety, here in the study of his apartment where he now holed himself up. What mattered was to get to work. Something would come of it.

他需要做的是把所有这些知识运用起来。这意味着要重新审视那本他一直无法触及的小说。小说的主题——情节，叙述者的声音——他仍然一无所知。素材都在他的脑海中。如果在孤独中他无法找回他的母亲、他的童年或青春，他会想办法把这些全部重现，就在他如今躲藏的公寓书房里。重要的是开始行动。一定会有所收获。

In the fall of 1908 he purchased dozens of notebooks, the kind he used to use in school, and began to fill them with notes. He wrote essays on aesthetics, sketches of characters, childhood memories that he strained to recall. And as he went deep into this process, he felt a change within himself. Something clicked. He did not know where it came from, but a voice emerged, his own voice, which would be that of the narrator himself. The story would revolve around a young man who becomes too neurotically attached to his mother and cannot forge his own identity. He discovers that he wants to be a writer, but he cannot figure out what he should write about. As he grows up, he starts to explore the two social realms of bohemia and landed aristocracy. He dissects the various people he meets, uncovering the essence of their characters that lies underneath their superficial social personalities. He has several failed love affairs in which he suffers the extremes of jealousy. After numerous adventures and a creeping sense of failure as he advances in life, at the very end of the novel he discovers what he wants to write—it will be the book that we have just been reading.

1908年秋天，他买了几十本笔记本，就是他上学时用的那种，开始在里面记笔记。他写美学论文、人物速写，以及努力回忆的童年记忆。随着他深入写作，他感到内心发生了变化。某种东西触动了他。他不知道这声音从何而来，但一个声音浮现出来，他自己的声音，那将是叙述者自己的声音。故事围绕着一个年轻人展开，他神经质地依恋母亲，无法塑造自己的身份。他发现自己想成为一名作家，但却不知道该写些什么。随着年龄的增长，他开始探索波西米亚和地主贵族这两个社会阶层。他剖析自己遇到的形形色色的人，揭示他们表面社会人格之下的性格本质。他经历了几段失败的恋情，并因此饱受极度的嫉妒之苦。在经历了无数次冒险以及人生中逐渐滋生的失败感之后，他在小说的最后发现了自己想要写的东西——那就是我们刚刚读过的那本书。

The novel would be called In Search of Lost Time , and in the end it would recount much of Proust’s own life, all of the various characters he knew disguised under different names. In the course of the narration he would cover the entire history of France from the moment he was born to the present, whatever the present was. It would be a portrait of society as a whole; he would be the entomologist uncovering the laws that governed the behavior of all the inhabitants of the anthill. His only concern now was his health. The task ahead of him was immense. Would he live long enough to complete it?

这部小说的名字是《追忆似水年华》，最终将讲述普鲁斯特的大部分人生经历，以及他所认识的形形色色的人物，他们都以不同的名义伪装着。在叙述的过程中，他将涵盖法国从他出生到现在的整个历史，无论现在是什么样。这将是一幅社会的画像；他将扮演一位昆虫学家，揭示蚁丘中所有居民行为的规律。他现在唯一关心的只是自己的健康。他面前的任务艰巨无比。他能活到完成它的那一天吗？

Over the course of several years, he finished the first part of the book, known as Swann’s Way . It was published in 1913, and the reviews were extremely positive. No one had ever read a novel quite like it. It seemed that Proust had created his own genre—part novel, part essay. But as he was making plans for the final half of the book, war broke out across Europe and the publishing business essentially ground to a halt. Proust continued working on the novel unremittingly, but as he did so, something strange happened—the book kept expanding in size and scope, one volume after the next. His method of working was partially responsible for this increase. He had collected over the years thousands of bits of stories, characters, lessons on life, laws of psychology that he slowly pieced together in the novel, like tiles of a mosaic. He could not foresee the end.

几年之后，他完成了小说的前半部分，即《在斯万家那边》的创作。该书于1913年出版，评论一片好评。从未有人读过如此优秀的小说。普鲁斯特似乎创造了自己的体裁——一半是小说，一半是散文。然而，就在他筹划小说后半部分时，欧洲爆发了战争，出版业几乎停滞。普鲁斯特坚持不懈地继续创作，但与此同时，奇怪的事情发生了——随着一卷又一卷的出版，小说的篇幅和内容不断扩大。他的创作方法在一定程度上促成了这种增长。多年来，他收集了成千上万个故事片段、人物、人生哲理和心理法则，并将它们像马赛克瓷砖一样慢慢拼凑成这部小说。他无法预知结局。

And as the book grew in size, it suddenly assumed a different form—real life and the novel became inextricably interwoven. When he needed a new character, a wealthy debutante for instance, he would hunt down her equivalent in society and get himself invited to balls and soirées where he could study her. Phrases she used would find their way into the book. One evening, he reserved several boxes at the theater for his friends. In these boxes he gathered the real-life people upon whom he had based his characters. Later they attended a dinner, and around the table he could observe, like a chemist, the various elements of his book, there before his eyes. None of them of course knew what was going on. Everything became material for him—not only the past, but present events and encounters would suddenly suggest a new idea or direction.

随着书的篇幅增长，它突然呈现出一种不同的形式——现实生活与小说密不可分。当他需要一个新角色，比如一个初入社交圈的富家女时，他会在社交圈里寻找与她相当的人，并受邀参加舞会和晚会，在那里他可以研究她。她使用的短语也会出现在书中。一天晚上，他为朋友们预订了剧院的几个包厢。他把现实生活中的人物聚集在这些包厢里，这些人物正是他笔下人物的原型。后来，他们参加了一场晚宴，在餐桌旁，他像化学家一样，观察着眼前呈现在他笔下的各种元素。当然，他们中没有人知道发生了什么。一切都成了他的素材——不仅是过去，就连现在的事件和遭遇，也会突然暗示出一个新的想法或方向。

When he wished to write about the particular plants and flowers that had obsessed him as a boy, he would drive to the country and spend hours lost in observation, trying to get at the essence of their uniqueness and at what had fascinated him, so he could recreate the original sensation for the reader. Fictionalizing the Count de Montesquiou as a character named Charlus, a notorious homosexual, he visited the most secretive male brothels in Paris that the count was known to frequent. His book had to be as real as possible, including graphic sex scenes. For things he could not personally witness, he would pay others to supply him gossip, information, even do some spying. As the book grew in length and intensity, he had the sensation that this social realm he was depicting had come alive within him, and feeling it from the inside, it would flow out of him with increasing ease. He had a metaphor to explain this sensation, which he included in the novel—he was like a spider sitting on its web, feeling the slightest vibration, knowing it so deeply as the world he had created and mastered.

当他想描写儿时令他痴迷的某些植物和花卉时，他会驱车前往乡间，花上数小时潜心观察，试图捕捉它们独特之处的精髓，以及是什么让他如此着迷，以便为读者重现最初的感受。他虚构了臭名昭著的同性恋者夏吕斯，将孟德斯鸠伯爵塑造成他常去的巴黎最隐秘的男妓院。他的书必须尽可能真实，包括生动的性爱场景。对于他无法亲眼目睹的事情，他会花钱请人提供八卦、信息，甚至进行一些侦察。随着书的篇幅和内容的丰富，他感觉自己所描绘的这个社会领域在他内心深处鲜活地涌现，而这种从内心深处感受到的感受，会越来越轻松地流淌出来。他在小说中用了一个比喻来解释这种感觉——他就像一只坐在网上的蜘蛛，感受到最轻微的震动，并深深地了解它，就像了解他所创造和掌握的世界一样。

After the war Proust’s book continued to be published, one volume after another. Critics were completely astounded at the depth and breadth of his work. He had created, or rather recreated, an entire world. But this was not simply a realistic novel, for much of the work included discourses on art, psychology, the secrets of memory, and the workings of the brain itself. Proust had delved so deeply into his own psychology that he had made discoveries about memory and the unconscious that seemed uncannily accurate. Going through volume after volume, readers would have the sensation that they were actually living and experiencing this world from within, the narrator’s thoughts becoming one’s own thoughts—the boundaries between narrator and reader disappearing. It was a magical effect; it felt like life itself.

战后，普鲁斯特的作品一卷接一卷地出版。评论家们对他作品的深度和广度感到无比震惊。他创造，或者更确切地说，重塑了一个完整的世界。但这并非仅仅是一部现实主义小说，因为作品的大部分内容都探讨了艺术、心理学、记忆的奥秘以及大脑本身的运作方式。普鲁斯特对自身心理的探索如此深入，以至于他对记忆和潜意识的发现似乎精准得令人难以置信。一卷一卷地阅读，读者会感觉自己仿佛置身于这个世界之中，并从内心体验着这个世界，叙述者的思想变成了自己的思想——叙述者和读者之间的界限消失了。这是一种神奇的效果；感觉就像生活本身一样。

Straining to finish the final volume, the point at which the narrator would be finally able to write the novel we have been reading, Proust was in a hurry. He could feel his energy waning and death approaching. All through the publishing process, he would make the publishers stop the printing, as some new incident he had personally witnessed had to be included in the book. Now, sensing himself near death, he made his female attendant take some final notes. He finally understood how it felt to be dying, and he had to rewrite a previous deathbed scene—it was not psychologically real enough. He died two days later, never to see the full seven volumes in print.

普鲁斯特竭尽全力完成最后一卷，等到叙述者终于能够写出我们一直在读的这部小说时，他却急匆匆地赶工。他能感觉到自己的精力正在消退，死亡正在逼近。在整个出版过程中，他总是让出版商停印，因为他亲眼目睹的一些新事件必须被收录进书里。现在，他感到自己即将死去，便让女侍做了最后的记录。他终于理解了死亡的滋味，不得不重写之前的一个临终场景——它在心理层面上不够真实。两天后他就去世了，没能亲眼看到七卷书全部付梓。

KEYS TO MASTERY

掌握诀窍

Cook Ting was cutting up an ox for Lord Wen-hui…. “Ah, this is marvelous!” said Lord Wen-hui. “Imagine skill reaching such heights!” Cook Ting laid down his knife and replied, “What I care about is the Way, which goes beyond skill. When I first began cutting up oxen, all I could see was the ox itself. After three years I no longer saw the whole ox. And now—now I go at it by spirit and don’t look with my eyes. Perception and understanding have come to a stop and spirit moves where it wants.”

庶丁正在为文惠君宰牛……“啊，这太神奇了！”文惠君说。“想象一下技术达到如此高度！”庶丁放下刀，回答道：“我在乎的是道，它超出了技术。当我刚开始宰牛时，我只能看到牛本身。三年后，我再也看不到整头牛了。而现在——现在我用精神去宰牛，而不是用眼睛去看。感觉和理解都停止了，精神随心所欲地移动。”

—C HUANG T ZU, ANCIENT C HINESE
WRITER, FOURTH CENTURY B.C.

—庄子，中国古代作家，公元前四世纪

Throughout history we read of Masters in every conceivable form of human endeavor describing a sensation of suddenly possessing heightened intellectual powers after years of immersion in their field. The great chess Master Bobby Fischer spoke of being able to think beyond the various moves of his pieces on the chessboard; after a while he could see “fields of forces” that allowed him to anticipate the entire direction of the match. For the pianist Glenn Gould, he no longer had to focus on notes or parts of the music he was playing, but instead saw the entire architecture of the piece and could express it. Albert Einstein suddenly was able to realize not just the answer to a problem, but a whole new way of looking at the universe, contained in a visual image he intuited. The inventor Thomas Edison spoke of a vision he had for illuminating an entire city with electric light, this complex system communicated to him through a single image.

纵观历史，我们读到过许多大师级人物，他们各自领域都曾描述过多年潜心钻研后，突然拥有了高度智力提升的感觉。伟大的国际象棋大师鲍比·菲舍尔曾说过，他能够超越棋盘上棋子的各种走法去思考；不久之后，他就能看到“力场”，从而预测比赛的整个走向。钢琴家格伦·古尔德不再需要专注于演奏的音符或乐曲的片段，而是看到了乐曲的整体架构并能够将其表达出来。阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦突然意识到，他不仅找到了问题的答案，还以一种全新的视角看待宇宙，这一切都包含在他直觉感知到的视觉图像中。发明家托马斯·爱迪生曾谈到他想要用电灯照亮整座城市的愿景，而这个复杂的系统通过一幅图像传达给了他。

In all of these instances, these practitioners of various skills described a sensation of seeing more . They were suddenly able to grasp an entire situation through an image or an idea, or a combination of images and ideas. They experienced this power as intuition , or a fingertip feel.

在所有这些例子中，这些不同技能的实践者都描述了一种“看得更远”的感觉。他们突然能够通过一个图像、一个想法，或者图像与想法的结合，掌握整个局面。他们体验到这种力量，就像直觉，或者指尖的触觉。

Considering the power such intelligence can bring us, and the tremendous contributions to culture made by Masters who possess it, it would seem logical that such high-level intuition would be the subject of countless books and discussions, and that the form of thinking that goes with it would be elevated into an ideal for all of us to aim at. But oddly enough, this is not at all the case. This form of intelligence is either ignored, relegated to the inexplicable realms of the mystical and occult, or ascribed to genius and genetics. Some even try to debunk this type of power in general, claiming that these Masters are exaggerating their experiences, and that their so-called intuitive powers are nothing more than extended forms of normal thinking, based on superior knowledge.

考虑到这种智慧所能赋予我们的力量，以及拥有这种智慧的大师们对文化做出的巨大贡献，如此高水平的直觉成为无数书籍和讨论的主题，并被提升为我们所有人追求的理想，这似乎是合乎逻辑的。但奇怪的是，事实并非如此。这种智慧要么被忽视，要么被贬低到神秘莫测的领域，要么被归因于天才和遗传。有些人甚至试图从整体上揭穿这种力量的真面目，声称这些大师们夸大了他们的经历，他们所谓的直觉能力不过是基于高级知识的正常思维的延伸。

The reason for this overall disregard is simple: we humans have come to recognize only one form of thinking and intelligence—rationality. Rational thinking is sequential by nature. We see a phenomenon A, and we deduce a cause B, and maybe anticipate a reaction C. In all cases of rational thinking, we can reconstruct the various steps that were taken to arrive at some kind of conclusion or answer. This form of thinking is extremely effective and has brought us great powers. We developed it to help make sense of our world and to gain some control over it. The process that people go through when they arrive at an answer through rational analysis can generally be examined and verified, which is why we esteem it so highly. We prefer things that can be reduced to a formula and described in precise words. But the types of intuitions discussed by various Masters cannot be reduced to a formula, and the steps they took to arrive at them cannot be reconstructed. We cannot go inside the mind of Albert Einstein and experience his sudden grasp of the nature of the relativity of time. And because we recognize rationality as the only legitimate form of intelligence, these experiences of “seeing more” must either be forms of rational thinking that just happen faster, or are simply miraculous by nature.

这种普遍忽视的原因很简单：我们人类只认识到一种思维和智慧的形式——理性。理性思维本质上是连续的。我们看到一个现象A，然后推断出原因B，并可能预测到反应C。在所有理性思维的情况下，我们都可以重建得出某种结论或答案的各个步骤。这种思维方式极其有效，并赋予我们强大的力量。我们发展它是为了帮助我们理解世界并对其进行某种程度的控制。人们通过理性分析得出答案的过程通常可以被检验和验证，这就是我们如此推崇它的原因。我们更喜欢那些可以简化成公式并用精确的语言描述的事物。但是，各种大师所讨论的直觉类型无法简化成公式，他们得出这些直觉的步骤也无法重建。我们无法进入阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦的内心世界，体验他对时间相对性本质的顿悟。因为我们承认理性是唯一合法的智慧形式，所以这些“看得更多”的体验要么是更快发生的理性思维形式，要么本质上就是奇迹。

The problem we are facing here is that high-level intuition, the ultimate sign of mastery, involves a process that is qualitatively different from rationality, but is even more accurate and perceptive. It accesses deeper parts of reality. It is a highly legitimate type of intelligence, but one that has to be understood in its own right. And in understanding it, we can begin to see that such power is not miraculous, but intrinsically human and accessible to us all.

我们面临的问题是，高层次直觉，即精通的终极标志，所涉及的过程在本质上与理性不同，但更加精准，也更具洞察力。它能够触及现实的更深层层面。这是一种高度合理的智慧，但必须理解其本身的意义。理解了它，我们就能开始明白，这种力量并非奇迹，而是人之常情，人人皆可拥有。

Let us try to make sense of this form of thinking by examining how it might operate in two very different forms of knowledge—the life sciences and warfare.

让我们尝试通过研究这种思维方式如何在两种截然不同的知识形式——生命科学和战争中发挥作用来理解这种思维方式。

If we were to study a particular animal in order to understand it, we would break up our analysis into several parts. We would study its various organs, brain, and anatomical structure in order to see how it has adapted differently from other animals to its environment. We would study its behavior patterns, how it gathers food, and its mating rituals. We would look at how it functions within an ecosystem. In this way, we would be able to piece together an accurate picture of this animal, covering it from all angles. With warfare, we would go through a similar process, breaking it up into parts—field maneuvers, weaponry, logistics, strategy. Having deep knowledge of these subjects, we could analyze the results of a battle and come to some interesting conclusions; or, with some field experience, we could lead an army into battle and do an effective job.

如果我们要研究某种动物以了解它，我们会将分析过程分解成几个部分。我们会研究它的各种器官、大脑和解剖结构，以了解它与其他动物相比如何适应不同的环境。我们会研究它的行为模式、觅食方式以及交配仪式。我们会观察它在生态系统中如何运作。通过这种方式，我们就能从各个角度拼凑出一幅关于这种动物的精确图景。对于战争，我们也会经历类似的过程，将其分解成几个部分——战地演习、武器装备、后勤、战略。凭借对这些主题的深入了解，我们可以分析战斗结果并得出一些有趣的结论；或者，凭借一些实战经验，我们可以率领一支军队投入战斗并取得卓有成效的成果。

In taking these analyses as far as possible, however, something is inevitably missing. An animal is not merely the sum of its parts that we can understand by adding them up. It has its own experience and emotions, which play an enormous role in its behavior, but which are elements we cannot see or measure. It has its own highly complex interactions with the environment that become distorted when we break them up into parts. The animal’s continuously fluid, dimensional interaction with its environment is also something that is not visible to our eyes. With warfare, once battle is engaged, we become susceptible to what is known as the fog of war—the highly unpredictable element that comes into play when two opposing forces square up and nothing can be precisely anticipated. The situation is continuously fluid, as one side reacts to the other and the unexpected intervenes. This battle in real time has an interactive, changing element that cannot be reduced to its parts or to simple analysis, and is not something we can see and measure.

然而，在尽可能深入地进行这些分析时，不可避免地会遗漏一些东西。动物并非仅仅是我们可以通过将其各部分相加来理解的总和。它拥有自身的经验和情感，这些经验和情感在其行为中发挥着巨大的作用，但这些因素是我们无法看到或衡量的。它与环境之间存在着高度复杂的互动，当我们将其分解成各个部分时，这些互动就会被扭曲。动物与环境之间持续流动、多维度的互动也是我们肉眼无法看到的。在战争中，一旦战斗打响，我们就会容易受到所谓的战争迷雾的影响——当两支敌对力量正面交锋，且无法准确预测任何情况时，就会出现这种高度不可预测的因素。局势瞬息万变，一方会对另一方做出反应，而意外情况也会介入。这场实时战斗具有互动性、变化性，它无法被简化为各个部分或进行简单的分析，也不是我们能够看到和衡量的。

This unseen element that constitutes the animal’s entire experience, and that makes battle a fluid, organic entity, can be called various things. To the ancient Chinese, who understood this very well, it was known as the Tao or Way, and this Way inhabits everything in the world and is embedded in the relationships between things. The Way is visible to the expert—in cooking, carpentry, warfare, or philosophy. We shall call it the dynamic , the living force that inevitably operates in anything we study or do. It is how the whole thing functions, and how the relationships evolve from within. It is not the moves of the pieces on the chessboard but the entire game, involving the psychologies of the players, their strategies in real time, their past experiences influencing the present, the comfort of the chairs they are sitting in, how their energies affect each other—in a word, everything that comes into play, all at once.

这种构成动物全部体验，并使战斗成为流动的有机整体的不可见元素，可以有多种名称。对于深谙此道的古代中国人来说，它被称为“道”，而“道”栖息于世间万物，并根植于事物之间的关系之中。“道”对于烹饪、木工、战争或哲学领域的专家而言，是可见的。我们将其称为“动力”，一种在我们研究或实践的任何事物中都不可避免地运作的生命力。它决定了整体的运作方式，以及各种关系如何从内部演变。它并非棋盘上棋子的移动，而是整个游戏，涉及棋手的心理状态、他们实时的策略、过去的经历对现在的影响、他们所坐椅子的舒适度，以及他们的能量如何相互影响——总之，所有同时发生作用的事物。

Through intense absorption in a particular field over a long period of time, Masters come to understand all of the parts involved in what they are studying. They reach a point where all of this has become internalized and they are no longer seeing the parts, but gain an intuitive feel for the whole . They literally see or sense the dynamic. In the living sciences, we have the example of Jane Goodall, who studied chimpanzees in the wilds of East Africa for years as she lived among them. Interacting with them constantly, she reached a point where she began to think like a chimpanzee, and could see elements of their social life that no other scientist had come close to fathoming. She gained an intuitive feel for not only how they functioned as individuals but as a group, which is an inseparable part of their lives. She made discoveries about the social life of chimpanzees that forever altered our conception of the animal, and that are no less scientific for depending on this deep level of intuition.

通过长期深入钻研特定领域，大师们逐渐理解了他们所研究内容的各个部分。他们达到了内化的境界，不再只看到局部，而是对整体有了直觉的感知。他们能够真实地看到或感受到整体的动态。在生命科学领域，我们有珍·古道尔的例子，她在东非荒野与黑猩猩生活在一起，对它们进行了多年的研究。通过与黑猩猩的不断互动，她开始像黑猩猩一样思考，并能够洞察黑猩猩社会生活中其他科学家难以企及的元素。她不仅对黑猩猩作为个体如何运作，而且对它们作为群体如何运作有着直觉，群体是它们生活中不可分割的一部分。她对黑猩猩社会生活的发现永远改变了我们对这种动物的认知，而这些发现的科学性丝毫不逊于基于这种深层直觉的发现。

In warfare, we can point to the great German general Erwin Rommel, who was said to possess the highest form of the fingertip feel ever chronicled in the history of battle. He could sense exactly where the enemy was thinking of striking and foil their plans; he could launch an offensive at precisely the weak point in their lines of defense. He seemed to have eyes in the back of his head, and oracular powers for reading the future. He did all of this in the deserts of North Africa where it was nearly impossible to get any clear sense of the terrain. Rommel’s power, however, was not occult in nature. He simply had a much deeper knowledge than other generals of all of the aspects of battle. He constantly flew over the desert in his own plane, gaining a bird’s-eye feel for the terrain.
